11344-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number 415, dated December 15, 1883, covers carbon in steel, heat in forging. alkaloid chemistry, starch extraction from potatoes, an apparatus for ellipses, a novel propeller engine, a Russian torpedo boat. hydraulic-reaction steamers, camera lenses and plates, charcoal kilns, the German national monument, artisans' dwellings at Hornsey. an ancient church found in Jerusalem, See's gas stove, mineral localities, London zoo gardens, the kauri pine, and congestive treatment.

The issue's breadth, from metals to medicine, served readers who followed applied science. Its articles are short, with pictures, and plain. For historians of technology, the number shows the state of photography, steam, and electricity just before the great electrical growth of the later 1880s.
13529-the-influence-of-sea-power-upon-hi:
A. T. Mahan's classic study, first published in 1890, argues that command of the sea shaped the history of nations between 1660 and 1783. Fleets, trade, colonies, and naval stations, not armies alone, decided the fate of empires in the age of sail. Mahan follows England, France, Spain, and the Netherlands through wars where sea power tipped the balance.

A simple, heroic Dutch admiral in the Four Days' Fight, even-tempered and giving victory to God, contrasts with the politics of Corsica, Minorca, and the Falkland dispute of 1770. Mahan's book became a textbook for navies and statesmen, and still frames how historians talk about trade, empire, and the sea.
13926-an-history-of-birmingham-1783:
William Hutton published An History of Birmingham in a second, enlarged edition in 1783. Hutton's preface jokes that speaking of himself is the worst subject, harder than history itself. In history, facts lie ready to hand and breed thought; in a preface, an author must forge from the brain, sometimes without fire. His candour sets a friendly tone.

Contents cover situation, soil, water, baths, and air, then trade, buildings, and people. Hutton, a Birmingham bookseller, knew the town's growth first-hand. His history mixes topography with civic pride. The volume suits local historians and students of industrial England. It remains a classic town history.
15417-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This June 9, 1883 number of the Scientific American Supplement, volume fifteen, number 388, gathers technical articles for engineers, makers, and curious readers. The parent journal dated from 1845, and the supplement cost five dollars a year alone, seven with the weekly. Figures and diagrams fill its pages.

Engineering pieces cover Farcot's improved Woolf compound engine, a new vehicle called the Swallow, boring an oil well, and a cement reservoir. Technology sections take up iron and steel, Bessemer progress, the Siemens-Martin process, and photo plates wet and dry. Medicine adds notes on hair care and on breathing against pneumonia and consumption. The issue shows American industry in mid-stride, eager for new machines and methods.
21434-letters-of-edward-fitzgerald-to-fa:
Edward FitzGerald wrote to the famed actress Fanny Kemble for over a decade, and the letters are gathered in this volume. William Aldis Wright edited the set, first issued in 1895 and again in 1902. The first letters came from the publisher George Bentley, who had printed some in a magazine.

Mrs Kemble gave the rest to Wright in 1883, the year the flow of letters ends. Notes explain the many names and hints that fill FitzGerald's chatty pages. Readers meet the poet of the Rubaiyat in private mood, witty and warm. The book adds much to what is known of his last years.
4290-the-dominion-in-1983:
Ralph Centennius, a pen name whose true author is unknown, first published this short Canadian forecast in 1883. It appeared as a thirty-page booklet. Looking a century ahead to 1983, it imagines the Dominion of Canada grown and changed. New arts of travel appear, such as the rocket-car.

A country shaped by a hundred years of growth fills the forecast. The present text was proofread word by word against a microfiche copy. It keeps the original spelling and mixed American and British forms. As early Canadian future fiction, it shows what one Victorian writer hoped, or feared, for Canada's second century.
8718-scientific-american-supplement-no-4:
Scientific American Supplement number 401, dated September 8, 1883, leads with chemistry. Articles cover different forms of silver bromide and silver chloride, analysis of New Zealand coal, determination of manganese in steel, cast iron. Ferro-manganese, manganese and its uses, and ozokerite, or earth-wax, in a paper by William L. Lay read before the New York Academy of Sciences. The Supplement cost five dollars a year, seven with the main journal.

Practical chemistry for industry dominates: how to test metals, what new materials can do, and where useful minerals are found. Silver chemistry mattered for photography, manganese for steelmaking, and earth-wax for candles and insulation. The issue gives a precise view of applied science in 1883, when laboratory results moved quickly into factories and mines. Readers interested in industrial history will find it a compact primary source.
8742-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
Scientific American Supplement number 392, dated July 7, 1883, leads with electricity and magnetism. An improved dynamo machine with eight figures, an improved manganese battery by George Leuchs, and Professor D. E. Hughes on why iron, steel, and other metals act as magnets fill the opening pages. Hughes writes of neutral states, layered magnetic force, and the thin medium around magnetic bits, with three figures.

The issue shows electrical science moving from curiosity to industry, as dynamos and batteries promised light and power for shops and cities. Practical readers got working drawings and explanations they could apply. Historians of technology will find a clear record of what electricians knew, and argued about, in 1883. General readers can enjoy the confidence of an age that believed magnetism's secrets were nearly in hand.
8862-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
Scientific American Supplement number 384, dated May 12, 1883, leads with engineering: a locomotive for the St Gothard Railway, the Mersey Railway Tunnel. A dam across the Ottawa River with a new canal at Carillon, Quebec, illustrated with figures and a map. Architecture follows, with William Hennan's hints on building dwelling houses, considerations for thoroughly sweet homes, and an experiment showing the need for damp courses. The Supplement cost five dollars a year, seven with the main journal.

Railways, tunnels, and waterways dominate an issue that shows Victorian engineering at full stretch, boring under rivers and over Alpine passes. Practical builders get details they can use, and general readers get a sense of the age's confidence in iron, steam, and masonry. Historians of technology will find a precise snapshot of 1883 projects, from Swiss mountains to Canadian rivers, in one weekly number.
8950-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
Scientific American Supplement number 385, dated May 19, 1883, leads with natural history: fishes of Cuban waters. Panax Victoriae with an illustration, a note on sap by Professor Attfield, the crow, the praying mantis and its allies. May flies with two illustrations. Technology follows, with a quick way to ascertain the focus of a lens with a diagram, and A. J. Hipkins's history of the pianoforte, describing its different parts and their uses. The Supplement cost five dollars a year, seven with the main journal.

Natural history and workshop practice sit side by side, as the Supplement's readers expected: specimens and instruments, music and optics in one number. The pianoforte history shows the journal's range, treating a domestic instrument with engineering seriousness. Historians of science and music alike will find a lively, illustrated snapshot of 1883 curiosity, from Cuban fish to the mechanics of the piano in the parlour.
9163-scientific-american-supplement-no-4:
Dated New York, December 29, 1883, this issue of the Scientific American Supplement reports new craft and science. The magazine, founded in 1845, cost five dollars a year alone. Its pages mix engravings with short, practical notes for engineers, makers, and curious readers. Readers of the day prized such clear, brief reports.

Contents include a machine for making electric light carbons, the earliest gas engine, and the moving of huge masses. China grass, gas burners, and printing presses also appear. The issue is a brisk snapshot of an age learning to light, print, and build with new power.
arxiv-2509-00083:
Laksh Patel and Neel Shanbhag present Generative Data Cartography in 2025, a data-led way to curb memorization in generative models. Such models can memorize rare training items, which foes can extract and which can inflate test scores. Each training sample here gets two scores: a difficulty score from early loss, and a memorization score from how often it is forgotten in training.

Samples split into four groups to guide pruning and reweighting. The team proves the memorization score bounds classic influence under smooth conditions, and that down-weighting hotspots shrinks the gap between training and new data. Pruning a tenth of the data cuts fake canary extraction by more than forty percent. Validation cost stays tiny, which makes the fix practical.
arxiv-2509-00383:
Dibyayan Chakraborty, Florent Foucaud, and Anni Hakanen study covering problems on graphs in 2025 where distances set the rules and the cycle count is bounded. The cyclomatic number of a graph counts how many edges must be cut to destroy all cycles. A covering problem asks for a small set that reaches every vertex or edge in a set sense.

Three families are treated. Metric dimension variants ask that distance vectors to a chosen set pick out each vertex in a unique way. Geodetic sets ask that each vertex lie on a shortest path between two chosen vertices. Path covers ask that chosen paths pass through all vertices or edges. The authors extend and improve prior bounds on the best set sizes when the cycle count stays bounded.
arxiv-2509-00983:
Sadia Zaman Mishu and S M Rafiuddin analyze supervised learning methods for text classification. Demand for this task grows in web searching and data mining. It also grows in ranking and recommendation systems. Documents can be sorted by various kinds of classifiers. Supervised methods use labeled documents to learn the categories.

The paper shows the process on different datasets. It applies standard supervised techniques to those sets. Accuracy of each classifier is measured for comparison. A neural network with back propagation is used with other models. Together they form a platform for labeled text sorting. A benchmark approach is used to analyze performance. Tests on real data reveal which model works well in accuracy.
arxiv-2509-01583:
Robots that navigate by camera need to know where an object is. They also need to know how unsure that reading is. Thomas Jantos, Stephan Weiss, and Jan Steinbrener extend deep learning pose predictors. These estimate an object's six-dimensional pose. The extension makes them report their own aleatoric uncertainty, the noise inherent in the data. Two small added networks handle the shift and rotation parts separately.

The add-ons sit apart from the original predictor. Training stays efficient, and the pre-trained model can remain frozen. The predicted pose and its uncertainty then feed an extended Kalman filter. They enter as a measurement with its matching noise matrix. The authors stress the low added computation. The approach suits object-relative navigation, where a robot steers by the objects it sees and weighs each reading by its trust.
arxiv-2509-01683:
Matej Steinbacher, Mitja Steinbacher, and Matjaz Steinbacher test how the coding of a fake stock market can skew its prices. Their market uses software agents that trade many assets under set budget rules. They compare clearing trades one book at a time with clearing all books at once. Clearing is the step that matches buys and sells and moves cash.

Handling books in order gives early assets first claim on each trader's cash within a step. That edge bends demand and price paths for each asset in a steady, clear way. Broad price levels still track big factors such as cash supply. The lesson is that market model builders must check clearing code with care, or risk fake results.
arxiv-2509-01783:
Abdelkrim Barbara, Ahmed Bousmaha, and Mohammed Shimi prove a new embedding result for fractional function spaces on unbounded domains. Embedding here means one function space sits inside another with control on size. Their spaces use variable exponents, where the power in the size measure changes from point to point. Unbounded domains stretch to infinity, which removes compactness tools that many proofs rely on.

As a use case, they study nonlocal elliptic problems driven by a fractional operator of the same variable type. Nonlocal means the value at a point depends on values far away. With variational methods, meaning methods that turn equations into energy problems, they prove nontrivial weak solutions exist. Growth and smoothness conditions on the nonlinear term complete the result.
arxiv-2509-01883:
Max T M Ng leads four co-authors on a transit feeder that mixes fixed stops with on-demand rides in self driving vans. Fixed routes are cheap but rigid, while demand services bend to riders at higher cost. Their hybrid starts with set stops near a terminus, then serves flexible pickups in a set zone. A learning controller assigns vans to subzones as demand shifts in real time.

Simulations on a real Munich bus route test the design with agent based models. After training, the hybrid serves more riders than fixed service at a modest cost rise. The learning control alone adds a small rider gain for a small cost rise. The study targets first and last mile gaps in wider transit networks.
arxiv-2509-01983:
D Jaffino Stargen and Vivishek Sudhir examine where thermal balance holds in the Unruh effect for an accelerated atom. That effect says an accelerated detector in empty space feels a heat bath tied to its acceleration. Ideal treatments fix the atom path in advance, so its center of mass cannot recoil. Real setups let the center move and couple to the bath through recoil kicks.

With recoil included, the fluctuation dissipation balance fails for the center of mass motion. The same balance still holds for the atom internal energy levels. So the internal state thermalizes while the motion does not share that equilibrium. The split matters for any lab attempt to observe the effect. It also sharpens theory on how quantum fields heat moving bodies.
arxiv-2509-02783:
Arnab Mazumder, Javier E. Santos, Noah Hobbs, Mohamed Mehana, and Daniel O'Malley present a 2025 geoscience AI paper introducing Transparent Earth, a foundation model for the planet's subsurface. Underground properties must be inferred from scattered observations of many types, each sparse in its own way.

The transformer model ingests eight observation types, from stress angles to mantle temperature and plate type. Each observation carries a position code plus a modality code derived from a text description of its type, so new data types can be added freely. The model can predict with no inputs or with any mix of extra observations, an in-context learning style. Validation showed stress angle errors dropping more than threefold. Performance grew with model size, supporting the authors' foundation model ambition.
arxiv-2509-03183:
Karl Lapo, Samuele Mosso, and J. Nathan Kutz introduced phasor notation for Dynamic Mode Decomposition in a 2025 paper. That decomposition, called DMD, fits data as a sum of spatial patterns, each pulsing or fading at its own rate. It is widely used to diagnose complex dynamics in fluids and other systems.

Modes usually come as complex numbers, and their spatial parts lack a clear physical reading. For paired modes, the authors rewrite the model in phasor form, yielding a strictly positive, real spatial pattern plus a readable waveform. A toy model demonstrates the clearer diagnosis this affords. They also adapt the notation to a multi-resolution variant that windows data in time. A multi-scale dataset shows the adjusted terms at work.
arxiv-2509-03383:
Yiyang Huang and 6 co-authors presented ANNIE in 2025, a systematic study of adversarial attacks on robots driven by vision-language-action models. These models let robots perform long, complex tasks around people. A compromised model can turn tampered sensory input directly into unsafe physical action, a risk classic software safety ideas do not cover.

The study grounds its safety definitions in ISO standards for human-robot interaction. It sorts violations into critical, dangerous, and risky tiers using separation distance, velocity, and collision limits. A benchmark of nine safety-critical scenarios holds thousands of video-action sequences. Their attack framework splits long goals into frame-level perturbations guided by a leader model. Attack success exceeded half across all categories in their evaluations. Physical robot experiments confirmed real-world impact.
arxiv-2509-03483: Viktor Panshin wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on recognising finite simple groups from their spectra. Two groups are called isospectral when the orders of their elements form exactly the same set. Some simple groups have a prime graph, a network built from those orders, that splits into separate pieces. Panshin completes the description of all finite groups that share a spectrum with such a simple group. The result finishes a classification problem in group theory, the branch of algebra that studies symmetry through sets with an operation.
arxiv-2509-03683:
A 2025 research paper by Chun-Tse Li and four co-authors carries a claim in its title: attention is all you need to solve chiral superconductivity. Attention is the core mechanism of modern neural networks, relating distant parts of an input. Neural quantum states use such networks as flexible guesses for a system's quantum wavefunction.

Their self-attention Fermi neural network minimises the energy of an attractive Fermi gas with no prior knowledge and no bias toward pairing. From the optimised wavefunction, measurements identify a chiral p-wave superconducting state, where pairs of particles orbit in a handed pattern. A symmetry projection method reveals the ground state's angular momentum and its breaking of time-reversal symmetry. The two-body density matrix spectrum confirms long-range order from the dominant chiral pairing channel. The authors present it as a route to AI-driven discovery of unconventional superconductors.
arxiv-2509-03783:
In a 2025 expository survey, Nathan Chen and one co-author examine measures of irrationality in algebraic geometry. A variety is an abstract shape defined by polynomial equations, and rationality asks whether it can be described by simple rational coordinates. Measures of irrationality turn that yes-or-no question into a number: how far a variety sits from being rational, or from related classes like rationally connected or uniruled varieties.

Interest in these invariants has revived over the last two decades, with steady new results. The survey organises what is known through the classic Kodaira-Enriques scheme for sorting surfaces by geometric type. That viewpoint lets the authors highlight recent progress family by family. Open problems and questions are discussed throughout, marking where the invariants are still poorly understood. The paper is a primer, written to give newcomers and specialists one shared map of the field.
arxiv-2509-04083:
Alexander Beiser and two co-authors show that word choice in a formal language can make or break machine reasoning in a 2025 research paper. A popular setup pairs a large language model with a logic solver. The model translates plain questions into a strict formal language, and the solver derives the answer. That pairing is called neurosymbolic reasoning, since it mixes neural software with symbols.

Four candidate formal languages were tested across three data sets and seven language models. Results shifted in both grammar handling and meaning, depending on the language picked. Effects also differed from model to model. Picking the in-between language deserves real care, the authors conclude, rather than being treated as a fixed detail.
arxiv-2509-04183:
Aishik Mandal and two co-authors generate pretend therapy conversations with a team of specialized language-model agents in a 2025 research paper. Real counseling records are scarce because privacy rules protect them, yet training and testing tools need examples. Their framework, MAGneT, splits writing a counselor's reply into sub-tasks. Separate agents each handle a distinct therapy technique, and their work is coordinated into full multi-turn sessions.

Judges rated the sessions on nine aspects of counseling quality, wider than earlier four-part checks. Experts preferred MAGneT sessions over the strongest rival in about three quarters of comparisons. A model fine-tuned on the synthetic sessions also scored better on a standard therapy rating scale. Code, data, and the tuned model are public.
arxiv-2509-04483:
Minghui Huang, writing alone, introduces ways to grade the breaking apart of claims for fact-checking in a 2025 research paper. Claim decomposition splits a complex claim into small atomic pieces so false parts can be spotted. Research has chased better decomposition generators while neglecting how to judge the pieces they produce. DecMetrics supplies three automatic scores: completeness, correctness, and semantic entropy, each probing a different failure mode of decomposed claims.

Those scores then become a reward function for training a lightweight decomposition model, which improves by chasing higher marks. Automatic evaluation supports the approach as a benchmark for the task. Fact-checking pipelines gain a quality gate between decomposition and verification, where weak atomic claims once slipped through unnoticed.
arxiv-2509-04683:
Flickering, the noisy jumping between two stable states, can warn that a system is losing resilience. Yazdan Babazadeh Maghsoodlo, lead author with two co-authors, show deep learning can detect it in a 2025 paper. Their models combine convolutional and long short-term memory networks, trained on synthetic time series with added noise.

Although training used simplified dynamics, the models generalise to varied stochastic systems. They detect flickering in real records, including dormouse body temperature and palaeoclimate proxies from the African Humid Period. The authors offer the approach as a flexible early warning tool for climate, ecological, and other complex systems.
arxiv-2509-04883:
Short intervals should still contain many arithmetic progressions made only of primes, past a known barrier. Le Duc Hieu proves that claim in a solo-authored 2025 number theory paper. For intervals whose length passes a stated exponent threshold, he counts progressions of every fixed length of at least three primes.

The proof combines a uniform short-interval prime number theorem, resting on recent zero-density estimates, with a transference principle in relative Szemerédi form. An appendix supplies a mean square bound used for variance estimates. The author also notes that the paper's proofs were assisted by GPT-5, a disclosure included in the record.
arxiv-2509-04983:
Support vector machines can be run end to end on quantum hardware by pairing quantum kernels with quantum annealing. Mario Bifulco and one co-author explore such a pipeline in a 2025 quantum machine learning paper. They build quantum kernels from varied feature maps and qubit configurations, judging them by kernel-target alignment.

The support vector machine dual problem is rewritten as a binary optimisation problem suited to quantum annealers. Experiments show strong alignment and a suitable regularisation parameter give competitive performance in their tests. The authors present the results as evidence for hybrid quantum architectures in high-performance computing settings.
arxiv-2509-05183:
Equations that run time backwards with rough driving signals are treated in a 2025 paper by Jian Song and two co-authors, the second part of a series. Such backward stochastic equations, used for pricing and control problems, here include a Young integral, a way to integrate against signals too rough for normal calculus.

The hard case is an unbounded driver, meaning the signal term can grow without a fixed cap. The team builds a localisation method that extends known solutions from the bounded case to this harder one. From it they derive a Feynman-Kac link to partial differential equations and error estimates comparing bounded regions with the whole space.
arxiv-2509-05383:
Thin liquid films that tear themselves apart are modelled for non-Newtonian fluids by Michael C Dallaston, Steven A Kedda, and Scott W McCue in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. Surface tension fights attractive forces between molecules, and for ordinary fluids the film ruptures in finite time in a self-similar pattern.

The authors extend the similarity calculations to power-law fluids, whose thickness response depends on a single exponent. The solution diagram over that exponent is tangled, with branches merging near the Newtonian case. In the extreme shear-thinning limit they find infinitely many solutions with a tiny inner region. Time-based simulations are drawn to the single main branch, giving the theory a clear physical anchor.
arxiv-2509-05483:
Knee implants moving under X-ray video form a large open dataset from Jinhao Wang and four co-authors in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Veriserum supports training deep learning systems that register, or align, two-plane fluoroscopic images, which are X-ray movies taken from two directions.

The set holds around a hundred thousand images from ten implant pair combinations, captured across many trials involving walking poses and ramp descent. Each image carries an automatically registered ground-truth pose, and a smaller subset has poses registered by hand for benchmarking. Calibration tools are included. The authors intend the data for registration, segmentation, distortion correction, and three-dimensional reconstruction research, with free public access.
arxiv-2509-05583: Finite rewriting systems for a family of algebras are computed by Karol Herrera, Sebastián Higuera, and Andrés Rubiano in a 2025 algebra paper. Their algebras are double extension regular algebras of one named type. The authors compute Gröbner-Shirshov bases for them. These bases are sets of rules that reduce any expression to a standard form. The work uses an algorithm the team implemented in Matlab. They also establish that these families admit a PBW basis. That is a structured basis modelled on polynomial rings.
arxiv-2509-05783:
Spherical infall of gas onto a black hole that sits in modified gravity is the subject of a 2025 study by Ayyesha K. Ahmed and one co-author. The black hole follows the Schwarzschild form, but gravity carries an extra strength parameter from the MOG theory, short for modified gravity. The authors ask how that change alters matter falling straight inward.

Working with steady fluids that hold one temperature, the authors track the flow at its sonic point, where infall speed matches the speed of sound. Stiff and highly relativistic fluids can move on either side of that speed, while radiation-like fluids stay more restricted. The mass inflow rate grows with distance and with the gravity parameter, so the modified theory feeds the hole faster.
arxiv-2509-05883:
Attacks that hide instructions inside text or images fed to a language model are tested in a 2025 paper by Andrew Yeo and Daeseon Choi. As companies build these models into consulting and search tools, prompt injection has become a leading security risk. An injected instruction can make a model leak data or ignore its owner's rules.

The authors attack eight commercial models with no added filtering, relying only on built-in safeguards. They sort attacks into four kinds: direct injection, indirect injection through external content, image-based injection, and prompt leakage. Every model showed exploitable weaknesses, though one system held up better than the rest. Their comparison argues that extra defenses, such as normalizing inputs before they reach the model, remain necessary for reliable protection.
arxiv-2509-05983:
Recognizing speech that flips between Vietnamese and English mid-sentence is the challenge taken up in a 2025 paper led by Tran Nguyen Anh with three co-authors. Code-switching strains general speech recognizers, and this language pair is especially tricky because the two phonologies differ sharply yet some sounds are easily confused. The authors answer with TSPC, a two-stage phoneme-centric architecture.

TSPC routes recognition through an extended Vietnamese phoneme set, an intermediate alphabet of sounds shared across both languages, while staying light on computing resources. In experiments it consistently beats existing baselines, including PhoWhisper-base, reaching a much lower word error rate with less training. The two-stage design also allows phoneme adaptation and language conversion to clean up hard mixed-language stretches.
arxiv-2509-06083:
Traffic on multi-lane roads gets two new second-order mathematical models in a 2025 paper by Matteo Piu and two co-authors. Most earlier multilane work stopped at first-order models, which track density alone. The authors instead derive macroscopic models rigorously from a microscopic follow-the-leader description, lane by lane, and the closure choice during that limit splits the result in two.

One model projects the velocity dynamics directly; the other conserves a generalized momentum across lanes. Numerical experiments reproduce congestion waves, capacity drops, and asymmetric lane use. Against real highway data, the momentum-based model fits critical densities and lane patterns better, and it relaxes to a known first-order model. The authors offer it as a robust tool for realistic traffic analysis.
arxiv-2509-06183:
Light traveling through tissue obeys a transport equation whose absorption can depend on the light itself, and Kui Ren and Yimin Zhong study that semilinear model in a 2025 paper. Their forward results give well-posedness for general boundary data, improving earlier theories that needed small data. The setting is motivated by photoacoustic imaging of multiphoton absorption in mixed media.

The inverse problem asks to rebuild the nonlinear absorption coefficient from internal measurements. The authors prove stability for the reconstruction and unify the theory across diffusion and transport regimes with a weighted norm that discounts the boundary region. Together the results firm up the mathematics behind imaging methods that infer tissue properties from light.
arxiv-2509-06783:
Whole solutions of an equation mixing derivatives and shifts are pinned to an exact form by Junfeng Xu and two co-authors in a 2025 complex analysis paper. The equation sets a derivative of an unknown entire function equal to a sum of its shifted values, with constant coefficients. Entire functions are defined across the whole complex plane.

The authors find the precise form of all finite-order entire solutions. They then study a differential-difference analogue of the Brück conjecture, a uniqueness question in value distribution theory. Their result concerns an entire function whose derivative and shifted sum share a small function, under a Borel exceptional condition. The theorems generalize and improve earlier work by Liu and Dong. Examples are included to show that the conditions in the main results cannot simply be dropped.
arxiv-2509-06883:
Pulling check-worthy claims out of social media posts is compared across prompting and fine-tuning by Joe Wilder and eight co-authors in a 2025 shared-task paper. The work is the University of New Hampshire entry to the CheckThat! 2025 task for English. Claim extraction is the first step in automated fact-checking pipelines.

Methods tried include few-shot prompting, in-context learning, and fine-tuning across several language model families. The best score on the METEOR metric came from a fine-tuned FLAN-T5 model. Scores did not tell the whole story, though: the authors observe that other methods sometimes produced higher-quality claims despite lower METEOR numbers. That gap between metric and judgment is a useful caution for fact-checking system builders, since a claim can be well worded yet miss what most needs checking.
arxiv-2509-06983:
Data spaces, the architectures for sharing data while keeping control of it, are surveyed by Bojana Marojevikj and one co-author in a 2025 paper. Data spaces aim at secure, efficient exchange between organizations that do not fully trust each other. Sovereignty, interoperability, and trust are their recurring design problems.

Foundational principles come first, then the core design principles and building blocks of data space systems. Real implementations across several industries show how the ideas address sovereignty and interoperability in practice. For the future, the authors propose leaning on semantic data models to improve interoperability and integration. They also suggest using the SPARQL query language as an authorization layer, for finer control over who may access what. The paper is a map of a fast-moving field, meant to guide its next steps.
arxiv-2509-07083:
Sanghyuk Moon and Eve C. Ostriker study simulated prestellar cores inside turbulent clouds in a 2025 paper. A prestellar core is a dense pocket of interstellar gas on its way to forming a star. Theory gives a typical density for star formation, but the exact critical density differs among cores, so any observed sample mixes cores at many stages.

By looking at how much life each core has left, the pair find a clear pattern. Cores collapsing in near balance take about twice their freefall time to finish, for most of their lives. They also show a practical shortcut for observers. The central column density, together with its full-width half maximum, estimates the central volume density, and so the freefall time, well enough. Observed lifetimes then seem to fall off faster than the apparent freefall time would suggest.
arxiv-2509-07283:
Saakaar Bhatnagar, writing alone in 2025, presents an AI agent workflow that automates the fitting of differential equation models. Ordinary differential equations describe how quantities change over time in fields from biology to engineering. Fitting their parameters to data is slow manual work: data are noisy and partial, models can be stiff, and coding a fast version demands special skill.

The user supplies a light XML description of the problem and fills in a code skeleton. The agent checks that the two agree, fixes flaws in the input, and converts the code into JAX functions, a form that compiles and runs in parallel. A two-stage search then scans broadly before refining with gradients. The open-source release aims to move users from a problem statement to an interpretable fitted model with far less effort, while experts keep control.
arxiv-2509-07583:
Ludovico Tesser, joined by 2 co-authors, bounds electrical noise in conductors driven by time-varying forces in a 2025 paper. Noise, the random fluctuation of current, limits sensors and quantum devices. Their setting is a multi-terminal, multi-channel conductor under arbitrary time-dependent driving, with possibly large steady voltage and temperature differences applied as well, far from equilibrium.

The full low-frequency noise obeys a fluctuation-dissipation bound, an upper limit written through weighted current components of the separate Floquet bands created by the driving. At large temperature bias, the bound reads intuitively as the sum of powers dissipated by the steady bias and by the driving. A second bound, based on the exact shape of the electron distribution under driving, is often tighter still. A two-terminal conductor with an alternating bias serves as the worked example. Such bounds tell engineers what noise floors no design can beat.
arxiv-2509-07783:
Zhiteng Zhou and 3 co-authors decompose aerodynamic force into its distributed sources in a 2025 paper. Total force on a body is not enough for flow control design. Engineers need to know which vortex structures produce force, and where along the surface. The traditional force element method credits vortex structures with the resultant force only. The distribution along the body stays unknown.

The distributed version projects the Navier-Stokes equations onto a divergence-free space. That gives a Poisson equation for pressure. A Green's function then expresses surface pressure stress as volume and surface integrals. The parts are split into acceleration, vorticity, and convection contributions. The method of fundamental solutions, with singular value decomposition, computes the needed functions with speed. Validation covers laminar flow around still and oscillating cylinders. It also covers three-dimensional flow around a sphere, laminar and turbulent.
arxiv-2509-07983:
Protein language models can be steered toward desired properties by editing their internal activations, report Long-Kai Huang and 3 co-authors in a 2025 computational biology paper. These models learn from vast evolutionary data and design new protein sequences, but precisely controlling what they generate is hard. Users may need a specific function or stability profile, not just any plausible protein.

Activation steering, borrowed from text models, nudges the model's hidden activity in a chosen direction during generation. The authors adapt that idea to protein models with a simple activation editing method. Controllable generation matters for engineering enzymes and therapeutics: a steering knob is far cheaper than retraining a giant model for every new design target.
arxiv-2509-08083:
Laurie Williams and 1 co-author set out to learn which supply-chain security tasks software organisations actually adopt, in a 2025 software engineering study. Attacks on software supply chains have grown sharply since 2020, arriving through components, build infrastructure, and people. Risk frameworks list more protective tasks than any team can adopt at once, forcing hard prioritisation.

A baseline of real adoption would guide that prioritisation: teams could see what comparable organisations already do and where common gaps remain. The study aims to supply exactly that evidence. Without a baseline, each organisation guesses alone, either overspending on rare risks or neglecting the tasks attackers most often exploit. Shared adoption data turns isolated judgement into a community-informed defence strategy.
arxiv-2509-08883:
Raghu Mahajan and 1 co-author write a brief note on complex black holes in anti-de Sitter space in a 2025 paper. At very low temperature, thermal anti-de Sitter space is usually taken as the only saddle point. Black hole solutions still exist there, but with complex values.

The real part of their action looks smaller than that of thermal space, which would naively make them dominant. That would clash with the dual gauge theory picture. With a small model space and a contour based argument, the authors show these saddles do not add to the path integral at all. The standard low temperature conclusion therefore stands. Related criteria and the small black hole case are also discussed.
arxiv-2509-09083:
Linpu Zhang and 1 co-author give a bosonic realization of SU(3) chiral Haldane phases in a 2025 paper. Haldane phases are topological phases of quantum spin chains, protected by symmetry. The SU(3) case generalizes the familiar SU(2) chain to three internal states.

An antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain in alternating conjugate representation is studied as interactions vary. A chiral reversed transition appears, with each phase linked to a predicted chiral Haldane phase. Near the Heisenberg point, a protected topological state appears at the first excited level. A variational wavefunction captures the move to a trivial phase. An optical lattice realization with spin one-half bosons is proposed.
arxiv-2509-09183:
Jiasheng Guo and 4 co-authors propose Dark-ISP for low light object detection from RAW images in a 2025 paper. Low light detection is hard due to degraded image quality. RAW sensor data hold more potential than processed RGB, but earlier uses lost information or were complex.

Conventional image signal processing is split into linear calibration and nonlinear tone mapping steps, recast as trainable parts. Each part adapts to content with physics informed priors, aligned to detection goals. A self-boost mechanism lets the cascade steps cooperate. Tests on three RAW datasets beat RGB and RAW based methods with minimal parameters. End to end training is seamless.
arxiv-2509-09583:
Brittany Harbison and 3 co-authors ask whether detecting personality can improve social matching for online students in a 2025 paper on SAMI. Feeling connected helps people learn, yet online courses rarely let groups form naturally. SAMI, an agent that introduces students to one another, works from an incomplete mental model of each person, and personality is one missing piece of that model.

The team tests whether a language model can infer Big Five traits with no training examples, reading only forum introduction posts. Scores looked promising on their data set but varied a lot by trait, with a lean toward optimistic readings. A proof-of-concept then feeds three socially relevant traits into SAMI's matchmaking.
arxiv-2509-09683:
Predicting tomorrow's advertising clicks from numbers alone misses the memos: keyword changes and campaign edits live in text logs. Briti Gangopadhyay, Zhao Wang, and Shingo Takamatsu build a forecaster that reads both in a 2025 research paper. Their framework combines click time series with textual logs from real campaigns. It outputs explanations a human can audit alongside the numeric forecast.

Reinforcement learning trains the model to comprehend the textual stream better and to fuse the two modalities well. Experiments ran on a large-scale industry dataset. The method beat baselines on forecast accuracy and on reasoning quality. Click volume drives revenue and strategy decisions, so a forecast whose reasoning can be inspected is worth more than a slightly sharper black box. The work treats interpretability as a feature of the prediction, not a report written afterward.
arxiv-2509-10883:
Michael Perryman is the sole author of this 2025 review of Gaia, the European Space Agency satellite that is measuring the Milky Way with unmatched precision. Gaia is cataloguing the positions, distances, and motions of about two billion stars, plus asteroids in our solar system and millions of distant quasars.

Perryman first sets out the history of measuring star positions from space and the principles behind Gaia's measurements. He then surveys what the data are revealing: the makeup and life cycles of stars, the structure and history of our galaxy, and details of the solar system. Repeated brightness and spectrum measurements also let astronomers estimate each star's mass, age, and chemistry, making the catalogue a foundation for a generation of astronomy.
arxiv-2509-10983:
Mai Pham and 2 co-authors plan cyber defense with auctions guided by reinforcement learning in this 2025 paper. Defenders must assign scarce actions across many hosts under uncertainty, thinking far ahead. The authors price bundles of defensive actions with values taken from a learning agent's long-term utility estimates, then let a transformer-based auction mechanism divide the bundles.

The learned auctions stay roughly honest even when participants misreport their values. Against oracle and rule-based allocations, the method earned competitive returns and resisted manipulation. Its choices also lined up with where attacks and defenses were actually active. The authors present the work as a proof that auction-based planning, fed by learned values, can organize strategic defense.
arxiv-2509-11083:
Daniel Strömbom and Catherine Futterman wrote this 2025 biology paper. It studies how groups of moving animals escape a predator as one unit. Fish schools and bird flocks both do this.

The standard account stresses alignment. Group members supposedly line up their directions with their neighbors. Yet some species do not seem to do this. The authors show that attraction and repulsion alone are enough. These simple forces produce a fast, group-wide escape. No alignment rule is needed. Animals that spot the predator directly also move at different speeds. That speed gap makes the escape faster. But the gap is not required for escape to happen. The results suggest tests that could settle how real groups pull off the maneuver.
arxiv-2509-11183:
Emmanouil Karystinaios, writing alone, presents WeaveMuse, an open multi-agent system for music, in this 2025 paper. The system handles three jobs that usually live apart: understanding music, composing in symbolic notation, and synthesizing audio. Specialist agents read each user request, work out what formats and constraints it implies, and check their own outputs.

A manager agent picks and orders the tools, talks with the user, and keeps state across turns. The whole setup runs locally on varied hardware or through a hosted API, keeping open models within community reach. Structured constraints, decoding rules, and small adapter modules let users steer results. The author aims to make music information tools easier to build, share, and reproduce.
arxiv-2509-11383:
Lin Franklin Feng, Yue Hu, and Xu Kuang study scheduling when customers come back. This 2025 operations research paper treats queues with reentrance. A finished job may later return for more work. Such loops upset the classic rules for who goes first.

The authors model two sides of return. One is the chance a job comes back. The other is how fast it returns. Their product is what counts, they show. They call it the effective return rate. A clean split in policy follows. If the smaller class has the lower rate, one fixed priority rule is best. If it has the higher rate, no fixed rule can be best. The best policy must react to the system's state.
arxiv-2509-11483:
Franziska Weber's 2025 paper in numerical analysis proves a workhorse fluid scheme converges. Projection methods enforce incompressibility in the Navier-Stokes equations step by step. Past proofs for rough solutions covered first-order schemes only.

Weber analyzes a second-order version. A two-step backward formula handles time. Conforming finite elements handle space. The domain is bounded with Lipschitz boundary. A discrete energy bound gives uniform control of the discrete speeds. A compactness argument does the rest. It rests on Simon's theorem and refined time estimates. Part of the approximations then tends to a Leray-Hopf weak solution. The starting data and forcing need only minimal assumptions. This is the first such proof for a higher-order method.
arxiv-2509-11583:
Pavel Chvykov and Jeremy England give evidence for a surprising conjecture in a 2025 paper linking thermodynamics with dynamical systems. They propose that Hamiltonian systems with mixed chaos, part orderly and part chaotic, find regular behavior on their own when lightly coupled to a cold enough thermal bath.

Numeric evidence across five varied dynamical systems supports the claim. The authors gauge how long order takes to form and how higher heat disrupts it. Balancing damping-driven contraction of phase space against thermal search predicts the transition points from relaxation times. That relation formally links the two viewpoints. The findings suggest cold settings could induce robust dynamical order in many real systems, rather than merely freezing motion.
arxiv-2509-11983:
Training giant neural networks is, underneath, a huge matrix optimization problem, and Chuan He with two co-authors exploit that fact in 2025. Their starting point is Muon, an optimizer whose strong results in foundation model training come partly from orthogonalizing gradient matrices.

Full orthogonalization is expensive, so the authors note that gradients during training are nearly low-rank and orthogonalize only that lean structure. Two algorithms follow: a low-rank signed gradient method and a low-rank Muon. Tests on GPT-2 and LLaMA pretraining match or beat the carefully tuned original, with the clearest gains on larger models. Theory backs the practice, giving iteration complexity bounds for both methods, including a version that tolerates heavy-tailed noise in the stochastic setting.
arxiv-2509-12283:
Ana Elisa Lopez-Miranda and 2 co-authors report how data science instructors view large language models in a 2025 qualitative study. Tools that once took students hours for coding, writing, and problem solving can now be done quickly by these models. Educators must rethink both teaching and assessment in response.

The team interviewed forty-two instructors from thirty-three institutions in ten countries during mid-2025. Many saw the models as inevitable classroom tools, comparable to calculators or Wikipedia, while others worried about de-skilling and misplaced confidence. Over half had already introduced demonstrations or guided activities, though a sizable minority had not used the models for teaching and did not plan to. The study highlights innovations such as AI-aware assessments.
arxiv-2509-12483:
Wave scattering problems can be solved in two very different ways. One is an old boundary method. The other is a neural network trained on the equation itself. Oscar Rincón-Cardeno and three co-authors race the two head-to-head in 2025. Their test problem is the two-dimensional Helmholtz equation.

At matched accuracy, the contrast is stark. The boundary element method assembles and solves in a hundredth of a second. Training the physics-informed network takes on the order of a hundred seconds. Once trained, though, the network is the fast one. It evaluates new points about a hundred times faster than the boundary method. The authors tuned the network carefully first. They also lay out a reusable comparison procedure.
arxiv-2509-13583:
Varsha Rao and Andrew A. Chien measure the carbon footprint of high-performance computing in a 2025 paper. Standard greenhouse gas accounting is hard for one supercomputer and nearly impossible across the whole field, so even the biggest sites do not report it. The pair focus on the Top 500 list of the world's fastest systems.

Their tool, EasyC, models emissions from only a few disclosed metrics. It covered operational carbon for most listed systems and embodied carbon, the emissions from building the hardware, for over half, and interpolation filled the rest. Their first full estimates put the Top 500 at well over a million tonnes of operational emissions per year, with projections rising through 2030.
arxiv-2509-13683:
Suyuchen Wang and eight co-authors address context fidelity in a 2025 language model paper, the tendency of models to contradict the very documents they are given. Earlier fixes either fine-tune models to cite evidence after answering, at real cost, or teach web search without improving how the provided context itself gets used.

Their framework, CARE, teaches a model to retrieve evidence from its own context and weave those passages directly into its chain of reasoning. The training needs only limited labeled evidence. Across real-world and deliberately counterfactual question answering benchmarks, CARE beat supervised fine-tuning, standard retrieval-augmented generation, and external retrieval systems on both retrieval accuracy and final answer quality.
arxiv-2509-13783:
Tianshuo Zhang and five co-authors build physics-structured neural networks for floating bodies in a 2025 paper. Buoys, boats, and offshore platforms move under added mass, drag, and background currents, and plain black-box networks that regress motion directly tend to be hard to interpret and unstable over long predictions.

Their Floating-Body Hydrodynamic Neural Networks predict interpretable physical parameters instead: directional added masses, drag coefficients, and a background flow described by a streamfunction. Analytic equations of motion then turn those parameters into trajectories, constraining the model's guesses. On synthetic vortex datasets the method cut error by up to about tenfold against neural ODE baselines, recovered consistent flow fields, and handled energy loss, which Hamiltonian-style networks cannot, more faithfully.
arxiv-2509-13883:
Zhen Xu and three co-authors present EvHand-FPV in a 2025 computer vision paper. It is a lightweight system that tracks a hand in three dimensions from a first-person view. It uses a single event camera. Event cameras report brightness changes with microsecond timing at milliwatt power. That suits extended reality headsets, where ordinary cameras are too slow or hungry.

To fix the shortage of egocentric benchmarks, they built a new dataset. It pairs synthetic training data with three-dimensional labels. It also pairs real event data with two-dimensional labels for evaluation. The tracker locates a wrist-based region of interest from geometric cues. It folds the region's offset into the network to save computation. An auxiliary geometry head improves the learning at no test-time cost. Accuracy rose while parameters and compute each fell by nearly ninety percent.
arxiv-2509-14183:
Le Coent and three co-authors fix a timing flaw in externally controlled trials in a 2025 biostatistics paper. Such trials compare a single treatment arm against controls borrowed from older studies or registries. Trouble starts when follow-up counts from different moments. In the trial it counts from treatment initiation; in control records, from diagnosis. Patients must survive to start treatment, so the mismatch breeds immortal time bias and distorts survival comparisons.

Their method, Index Date Imputation, estimates how treatment start times are distributed in the trial population. It corrects for the fact that starts are only observed in patients who lived long enough to begin. It then imputes matching index dates for controls. The alignment pairs with propensity weighting or matching. Simulations and an emulated oncology analysis moved results closer to the randomized benchmark.
arxiv-2509-14483:
Thanh-Long Bui, Hoa Khanh Dam and Rashina Hoda propose a multi agent language model framework in 2025 for agile effort estimation. Agile teams estimate user story effort together through discussion. Gut feel estimates are often inaccurate and inconsistent across teams.

Machine learning estimators can be accurate but cannot explain themselves or talk with the team. Their framework uses several language model agents that coordinate, discuss and justify estimates with human members. Estimation becomes a conversation rather than a single number from a black box. The authors argue explainable, interactive estimates fit how agile planning actually works. Teams can challenge an agent reasoning, surface hidden assumptions, and settle on estimates they collectively own.
arxiv-2509-14683:
Jing-Jing Zhang and Jin-Wu Jiang study nanotubes rolled from Janus monolayers in 2025, sheets with unlike faces that bend spontaneously. A Janus layer has a built in bending radius from its out of plane asymmetry. Rolling it into a tube imposes a second, extrinsic radius.

Atomistic simulations plus continuum mechanics show total energy is lowest when the tube radius equals the intrinsic bending radius. Away from that match, phonon behaviour, the vibrational modes of the tube, shows anomalies the authors trace to the radius mismatch. Transition metal dichalcogenide nanotubes are candidates for flexible electronics and sensors. Knowing the energetically natural radius guides synthesis toward tubes that want to exist.
arxiv-2509-14883:
Can Cui and five co-authors study secure computation offloading from ground users to drone-mounted edge servers in a 2025 wireless communications paper. Drones carrying servers can cut task delays, but a hostile drone may eavesdrop on the offloaded data. Uncertain task demands and flexible drone flight paths make the protection problem harder still.

The team models a network with ground users, service drones with edge servers, and malicious eavesdropping drones. They formulate an energy minimization problem covering user connections, drone trajectories, and offloading shares, with chance constraints handling the uncertainty. Distributionally robust optimization and a conditional value-at-risk step turn the hard nonlinear problem into a second-order cone program that standard tools can solve. The goal is offloading that stays dependable even when conditions differ from the plan.
arxiv-2509-14983:
P. Cox leads a team of twenty-seven authors reporting an Einstein cross that betrays an invisible mass, in a 2025 astronomy paper. HerS-3 is a dusty star-forming galaxy whose light is bent by foreground galaxies into four images arranged as a cross, plus a fifth image at the center. Such strong lensing magnifies the distant galaxy for detailed study.

Millimeter spectroscopy and imaging confirm all five images share one redshift, so they are copies of a single galaxy. Hubble imaging shows a lensing group of four galaxies, but models using only those four cannot reproduce the five images. Adding a fifth massive component with no visible galaxy fixes the reconstruction completely. The missing mass points to a hefty dark matter halo sitting where no galaxy shines.
arxiv-2509-15083:
Jisoo Lee and seven co-authors test public AI lung segmentation models on transplant candidates with severe lung disease, in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Segmenting lungs on CT scans supports surgical planning before transplantation, but heavy disease distorts anatomy. Models trained on healthier lungs may fail exactly where planning matters most.

The retrospective study covers thirty-two patients scanned at one university health system, totaling several thousand CT slices, each patient carrying at least two lung pathologies of varying severity. Three published deep learning models were compared with volume, overlap, and boundary metrics plus a clinical acceptability rating. One model consistently beat the others overall, yet performance varied by disease severity, pathology type, and lung side. The authors map where current tools can be trusted for transplant planning and where they cannot.
arxiv-2509-15183:
Cai-Chang Li and Gui-Jun Ding catalog every minimal lepton model built on a non-holomorphic modular flavor symmetry in a 2025 particle physics paper. Flavor symmetries try to explain the pattern of lepton masses and mixing with few parameters. Their framework uses the A5-prime modular group in its non-holomorphic form, where Yukawa couplings become special functions called polyharmonic Maaß forms.

Assuming Majorana neutrinos, the authors consider both the Weinberg operator route and the type-I seesaw route to neutrino mass. Every minimal model respects a generalized CP symmetry and depends on a handful of real parameters plus two scales. Numerical scans find dozens of viable models across both routes and both mass orderings. Predictions for mixing angles and mass observables are tabulated for each survivor.
arxiv-2509-16083:
District heating pipes serve whole blocks, but demand shifts and plant settings are often unknown in advance. Xinyi Yi and Ioannis Lestas design a learning controller that shares energy well across a district system while holding indoor heat steady. Their method updates its rules from live data, in step with the system's own flow.

They prove the controller settles at the best balance point for the system. It also settles on the best rule of a classic control type, which keeps short-term behavior smooth. Long runs in simulation back up the claims. The approach suits districts where exact models are hard to build.
arxiv-2509-16283:
Fast charged particles in a thick material emit a cone of light called Cherenkov radiation, a signal many detectors rely on. Dmytro Minchenko, Juan Pablo Yañez, and Aksel Hallin review how current simulation tools handle this light and where they fall short. Standard tools assume perfect coherence of the emitted waves, which thick media break.

The authors derive the light's spectrum and angular shape with interference counted, then add the effect of the particle's path. Their model plugs into a standard toolkit and is tuned on data from a real detector. The tuned model matches data far better and is shared for wider use.
arxiv-2509-16683:
Kaixing Cao builds a sorting tool for abstract geometric objects in a 2025 solo math paper. The objects, called rigid analytic motives, live over a local field. Past work defined a weight structure only for objects with good behavior. Cao extends that structure to the full class, using a descent method tied to symmetry groups.

As a payoff, a classic realization map is shown to pass through a weight-based path. That path yields a chain of groups that ends at a known cohomology for smooth spaces. In turn, the chain places a weight grading on that cohomology. The work links deep parts of modern geometry in a cleaner way.
arxiv-2509-16783:
Vladislav Trifonov, Ivan Oseledets, and Ekaterina Muravleva analyze a weighted loss for matrix work in a 2025 paper. Solvers for large linear systems use a helper matrix, called a preconditioner, to speed things up. Judging that helper by a plain norm can miss key errors. Their loss punishes errors tied to small eigenvalues more heavily.

The theory does not depend on how the helper is built. It covers factored, algebraic, and learned helpers alike. Tests confirm what the theory predicts. In one case, sparse factors were trained by direct updates with no neural model at all. Sharper losses could make big solvers faster and more reliable.
arxiv-2509-17083:
Zipeng Wang and Dan Xu render new views of a scene with far less memory in a 2025 paper. A popular method stores a scene as many soft 3D blobs, each with its own settings. That gives fast, sharp views but eats memory. Their hybrid radiance field keeps the speed while shrinking the model.

Experiments show top rendering quality at over twenty times smaller size than the blob method. Real-time performance is maintained. Smaller scene files matter for phones, headsets, and web viewers, where memory and download size are tight. The project page shares demos and details for others to test the trade-off themselves.
arxiv-2509-17383:
Nikita Ratanov, writing alone, studies a system pulled toward two stable states while a random switch keeps flipping its drift. His 2025 arXiv paper pairs a double-well potential with a telegraph process, a noise source that jumps between two velocities. When the switching speeds are small, the dynamics settle into a telling pattern.

The system holds one interval of metastable uncertainty and two invariant attractors. Ratanov finds the odds of leaving the interval through its upper boundary, along with traits of the first crossing times. He also derives the invariant measures of the motion. When the telegraph velocity lines up with the periodic change of the potential, the system can slip into a metastable state and gain a window for jumping wells. The results offer an alternative to classic stochastic resonance models.
arxiv-2509-17583:
Shinya Tomizawa, Jun-ichi Sakamoto, and Ryotaku Suzuki construct a family of rotating black holes with both kinds of charge. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton theory in four dimensions. The solution describes several black hole centers at once, each spinning and carrying electric and magnetic charge in unequal amounts, a dyonic mix.

The construction comes from reducing five-dimensional Einstein gravity by one dimension. It generalizes the classic Majumdar-Papapetrou solution to the spinning case and extends recent multi-center work by Teo and Wan to uneven charges. The team checks the spacetimes for the usual pathologies and finds none: no curvature singularities, conical defects, or closed timelike curves, on or outside the horizons. One condition is needed: the spins must all align or all anti-align. The result widens the shelf of exact black hole solutions.
arxiv-2509-17683:
Jonas Gruetter, Lorenzo Terenzi, Pascal Egli, and Marco Hutter teach a hydraulic excavator to dig out boulders. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts on real construction sites, where big rocks must go before grading can proceed. Human operators free them with the standard bucket, dodging slow tool changes, while dust, glare, and occlusion foul machine perception.

The team trains a reinforcement learning policy in simulation, with rigid-body dynamics and analytic soil models. The policy reads sparse LiDAR points from vision-based segmentation, just a handful per rock, plus the machine's own joint sensing. It must adapt to soil that ranges from hard-packed to soft, and coordinate several hydraulic joints to cage a rock with the shovel. Past autonomy handled soil and gravel, or grippers with full geometric plans. This work targets the messy middle: irregular rocks, standard tools.
arxiv-2509-17783:
Robots learn better when they can poke and probe the things they must move. Yibo Peng and 7 co-authors put that idea at the heart of RoboSeek, a 2025 robot learning frame. Long tasks are hard due to step-by-step choice, tight space, and blurry sight.

The team first rebuilds the real room in a sim, with true look and feel. Plans are trained there with search and reward, then moved to real robots. Across eight long tasks and more than one robot type, the method won about four times in five. That beat base methods, which won less than half the time.
arxiv-2509-18083:
Valentin Lacombe, Valentin Quesnel, and Damien Sileo build a gym where language models train on symbolic tasks. Their 2025 system, Reasoning Core, makes tasks on the fly across core formal fields. Those fields span planning, first-order logic, grammar parsing, cause thought, and equation solving.

Three design rules drive the gym: broad task spread, checks by outside tools, and a smooth difficulty dial. That mix gives a near endless supply of fresh tasks with sure right answers. First tests with top models, with no training in the gym, show the tasks are hard. The gym aims to grow base reasoning skill, not just test it.
arxiv-2509-18383:
Top AI models now shine at school and college math contests. Moran Feldman and Amin Karbasi ask a harder question: can a model prove fresh, simple conjectures in advanced math? Their 2025 paper sets up what they call the Gödel Test. They gave GPT-5 five unsolved conjectures from combinatorial optimization, along with the papers each one grew from.

The authors kept their own guesses hidden and read each proof attempt with care. On the three easier problems, GPT-5 came close to correct proofs. For one, it derived a different bound that actually refuted the authors' conjecture while solving the problem. It failed on a problem that needed results merged from two papers. On the hardest, it picked the right algorithm but stumbled in the proof. The small study shows real progress, flashes of originality, and clear limits.
arxiv-2509-18583:
Compilers that turn physics descriptions into quantum circuits rarely carry proof that the translation is right. Liyi Li and five co-authors present QBlue, a verified compiler for Hamiltonian simulation, in this 2025 paper. Hamiltonian simulation models how quantum systems evolve, a core use of quantum computers. Older compilers work at a low level with Pauli operators, which limits how users can write programs.

QBlue starts from second quantization, the standard language of particle creation and removal. A type system tracks particle types and enforces the symmetry the physics demands. The compiler targets both digital and analog quantum circuits. Every part, from language design to the correctness proof, is mechanized in the Rocq proof framework. The authors call it the first compiler for this class of simulation verified end to end. It aims to make quantum chemistry and materials programs safer to build.
arxiv-2509-18683:
Finding the standout object in a photo gets easier when depth data joins the color image. Lanhu Wu, Zilin Gao, Hao Fei, Mong-Li Lee, and Wynne Hsu present LEAF-Mamba for that task in this 2025 paper. Classic networks see only local patches, while transformers cost grows steeply with image size. A newer family, state space models, reads long ranges at linear cost.

Plain state space models, though, can miss local detail and fuse the two data streams weakly. LEAF-Mamba adds a local module that reads fine detail at several scales for both streams. An adaptive fusion module then mixes color and depth in a controlled way. Across benchmarks, the method beat sixteen top rivals on both accuracy and efficiency. It also transferred well to a thermal variant of the task. The authors present it as a balanced design for salient object detection.
arxiv-2509-19783:
Autonomous agents in low-code tools can loop forever, drift off task, or fail without warning. Jiexi Xu proposes a second agent that watches the first, a metacognitive layer in the mold of human self-awareness. It tracks triggers such as long latency and repeated actions. From those signs it predicts failure before the run collapses.

On a predicted failure, the watcher hands the task to a human with a summary of the agent's reasoning and the blocker it hit. A prototype study reports clear gains in user trust and task success. Low-code platforms invite non-programmers to automate work, so silent failure is a trust killer. A self-aware handoff pattern could make agent tools safer for everyday users. The report frames the design as reusable architecture, not a one-off fix.
arxiv-2509-19983:
Splitting a molecule's binding energy into meaningful parts explains why molecules stick. Hossein Tahmasbi and four co-authors teach a neural network to predict one such part, the electron delocalization energy, for water systems. The underlying analysis uses orbitals pinned to single molecules, so charge transfer between them can be isolated. Locality of electronic structure lets the model scale.

Trained on modest systems, the network predicts accurately for complexes far beyond quantum chemistry's reach. Hydration effects in large assemblies, including metal-organic structures, demonstrate the reach. Energy decomposition guides solvent and drug design by naming the forces at play. A learned surrogate keeps that insight while dropping the cost. The authors position the model as a tool for aqueous chemistry at scale.
arxiv-2509-20383:
Federated learning trains one model across many owners without pooling their data, but that openness invites backdoor attacks. Wei Wan and nine co-authors defend against them with MARS, presented in a 2025 arXiv paper. A recent attack family adapts once it senses rejection, and older defenses miss it. The authors trace those failures to loose statistical heuristics.

Their defense measures each neuron's backdoor energy, a signal of how strongly it serves the hidden trigger. The largest values across a model are pooled into a concentrated score that amplifies malignity. A clustering method based on Wasserstein distance then separates poisoned models from clean ones. Extensive experiments showed the defense holding against state-of-the-art attacks. It also beat existing defenses by clear margins in their tests.
arxiv-2509-20683:
Simulating turbulence in full detail costs too much, so engineers upscale coarse flow fields with machine learning. Julia Balla and six co-authors ask whether such models learn physical symmetry on their own in a 2025 paper. The symmetry at stake is rotational equivariance, the idea that a rotated flow should give a rotated answer.

Using three-dimensional channel-flow data, the team finds that ordinary convolutional networks pick up part of this symmetry without special designs. Turbulence itself acts like built-in rotation practice. Models trained on more even, mid-plane data made fewer symmetry errors than those trained near walls. More time or space samples helped further. The paper was accepted to a NeurIPS 2025 workshop on machine learning and the physical sciences.
arxiv-2509-21383:
Breast cancer screening works best when risk models use a woman full imaging history. Most deep learning models use one mammogram or just a few. Real screening data is messy, with uneven follow up and far more healthy cases than cancers. Manel Rakez and 6 co-authors built a model for that setting in 2025. It reads current and prior mammograms together.

LongiMam combines a convolutional network, which reads image patterns, with a recurrent network, which reads change over time. It uses up to four prior exams plus the current one. Training used a large population based screening data set. Adding prior visits improved prediction over single visit models in several scenarios. The design fits risk adapted screening in real clinics.
arxiv-2509-21483:
Spectral local systems can decorate Lagrangians in a spectral Fukaya category, changing their bordism classes. Noah Porcelli and Ivan Smith develop that theory in a 2025 paper, a companion to their bordism work. Rank one spectral local systems are incorporated into the spectral category. The open closed map then defines a bordism class for a decorated Lagrangian. That class differs from the undecorated one in a precise way.

The difference is a multiplicative two torsion element determined by the Hopf map action on the local system. Methods include a twisting construction that builds flow categories from spectral local systems. A model for the open closed map uses Schlichtkrull trace map construction. The results refine how bordism classes are computed in spectral symplectic topology.
arxiv-2509-21583:
Layered films of three oxides can gain optical properties none of them has alone. Martin Mičulka and 12 co-authors study amorphous ABC heterostructures at the atomic scale in a 2025 paper. The films were made by plasma enhanced atomic layer deposition of silica, titania, and alumina. Stacking breaks centrosymmetry at the nanoscale. That creates an artificial second order nonlinear response.

Nanoscale morphological changes markedly improved the artificial susceptibility. Nonlinearity depends on thickness variation of the three materials, from tens of nanometres down to the atomic scale. Interfaces carry the second order response. High layer density and superior interface quality correlate with stronger effects. Interface nonlinearity transitions toward bulk like second harmonic making in the best films. Thin films like these could serve in small light based tools where a weak input must yield a strong new tone.
arxiv-2509-21683:
Quantum Monte Carlo with operator loop updates samples thermal and ground states of local Hamiltonians efficiently in practice. Chaithanya Rayudu and Jun Takahashi prove why it mixes fast for one model class in a 2025 paper. Their setting is the stoquastic XY model, which has no sign problem. The method uses a path integral formulation of the partition function, built from Suzuki Trotter world lines.

Mixing time of the Markov chain is polynomial in system size and inverse temperature, they prove. Fast mixing lets users estimate partition functions in polynomial time. That is a significant theoretical gain for a widely used algorithm. Condensed matter systems with spin, bosonic, and fermionic degrees of freedom motivate the analysis.
arxiv-2509-21983:
Robots planning long tasks must decide both what to do and how to move, and doing only the second part well is not enough. Sigmund Hennum Høeg and four co-authors show in this 2025 paper that diffusion models, which generate smooth motion paths, stumble on long tasks with complex choices.

The team built a hybrid diffusion process that generates a high-level symbolic plan at the same time as the continuous motion path. That requires mixing two kinds of diffusion, one for discrete symbols and one for smooth values, in a single process. The hybrid beat the baselines by a wide margin. It also allows flexible synthesis. Generated actions can be steered by giving part or all of the symbolic plan in advance. A user or a higher-level system can pin down the intent while the model fills in the motion.
arxiv-2509-22283:
Michael Jungo and Andreas Fischer study whether reinforcement learning can teach vision-language models to classify document images better. Sorting scanned documents into types is a basic task in document analysis, yet reinforcement learning has rarely been applied there. Their 2025 paper uses the rule-based style of reinforcement learning made popular by reasoning models. The reward is a simple checkable rule, such as whether the predicted class is right, rather than a learned judge.

The authors find that reinforcement learning tends to generalize better to data unlike the training set. They test that claim in three scenarios: images from a different distribution, classes the model never saw in training, and documents arriving in a different modality. In each case the reinforcement-learned model held up better than the comparison. The work suggests that the reasoning gains associated with this training style transfer to document tasks.
arxiv-2509-22483:
Sadia Asif and Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri tackle machine unlearning for large language models. Deployed models must sometimes forget user data, copyrighted text, or stale facts without full retraining. The usual fix blends a forgetting loss and a retention loss into one sum. That blend often trains unstably, since the two gradients pull against each other.

Their framework, OFMU, puts forgetting first in a two-level setup. An inner step pushes forgetting up, with a penalty that separates the two gradient directions. An outer step then restores general skill. They prove convergence in convex and non-convex cases. Tests on vision and language benchmarks beat prior methods on both forgetting and retained skill.
arxiv-2509-22583:
Gaole Dai and 8 co-authors built one processor for many biomedical image jobs. Registration, fusion, restoration, and super-resolution all matter in life science work. Tools like ImageJ host plugins, but each plugin fits one task and data set, which burdens biologists. Their system, Orochi, pre-trains on patches drawn from over a hundred public studies, sampled at many scales.

A task-related pre-training scheme uses realistic degradations as self-supervision, which beat masked image modeling for these jobs. A multi-head Mamba design keeps compute linear and cheap. Three tiers of fine-tuning let users trade effort for accuracy. Even the light tier matched or beat specialist models on several tasks.
arxiv-2509-22883:
Kaleb Ben Naveed, Haejoon Lee, and Dimitra Panagou assign robot teams to map fields that change over space and time. Such fields include wind, heat, and gas levels. Their setting splits the space into regions, and each region shifts in its own way. Gaussian processes, a stats tool for smooth maps, guide the estimates.

A wrong length scale, which sets how far points stay linked, can make error bars far off. Their two-phase plan first learns a scale for each region from a variogram.
