Robots then move to where doubt is highest, while time scales get refined. The team proves bounds on how close the plan stays to an ideal one.
arxiv-2509-23183:
Adapting a model at test time by shrinking its own uncertainty can collapse into one lazy answer. Guohao Chen and 7 co-authors found that asymmetry blocks that collapse. Their ZeroSiam design is an asymmetric Siamese setup for test-time entropy work. A learnable predictor plus a stop-gradient step create the asymmetry cheaply. Constant one-hot outputs no longer trivially win.

Theory and tests both support the design. It also regularizes biased learning signals when no collapse threatens. Gains held on vision adaptation and language model reasoning tasks. Tiny, collapse-prone models benefited as well. Overhead stayed negligible next to prior methods.
arxiv-2509-23283:
Each isogeny class of elliptic curves hides one curve with the smallest Faltings height. Enrique González-Jiménez and Joan-C Lario find that curve after quadratic twisting. Vertices of a graph stand for the curves in the class. Edges stand for prime-degree rational isogenies between them. Twisting by a square-free integer gives a twin graph with the same shape.

The twist graph and the base graph match as abstract graphs, vertex by vertex through equal j-invariants. The question is which vertex becomes the Faltings curve after twisting. The pair answer that and give the chance a given vertex wins. The odds rest on p-adic valuations of modular function values.
arxiv-2509-23383:
Pretraining experiments are so costly that most data questions get asked one run at a time. Sebastian Bordt and Martin Pawelczyk run ten experiments inside a single training run instead. Their run covers two hundred ten billion tokens with models up to two point seven billion parameters. Past results on contamination, poisoning, and memorization were replicated from the one run. New probes cover knowledge gain, math reasoning, and watermarking.

One probe updates data live until the model learns a target fact. Cross-talk between experiments stayed minimal in their checks. A new dependence test, built for this setting, found interactions negligible. Rigorous large-model science may thus fit a modest compute budget.
arxiv-2509-23483:
A long-open case in design theory falls in work by Michael Kiermaier and 2 co-authors. They construct a Steiner system with parameters S(3,6,42), one of the smallest parameter sets that had stayed open for Steiner 3-designs. Such systems arrange points into blocks so that every small set of points lies in exactly one block. Their method grows Steiner 2-designs into stronger ones using chosen extension groups.

The same approach yields rotational Steiner quadruple systems on forty-six and ninety-two points. The article also looks at extensions to still higher strength. A table and discussion review the status of all workable parameter sets for Steiner 3-designs on up to fifty points.
arxiv-2509-23583:
Forecasting many linked series far ahead fails when a model sees each channel and each chunk in isolation. Zhangyao Song and 4 co-authors propose CTPNet, which learns from three angles at once. Attention across channels tracks how series move together. A transformer inside each downsampled chunk follows trend changes. Reusing the encoder across chunks then picks up global periodic patterns that link the chunks.

Downsample-based rivals mostly miss those cross-chunk and cross-channel ties, the authors argue. By joining all three views, CTPNet forms a fuller picture of the dynamics. Wide experiments show the method ahead of prior approaches on long-term forecasting tasks.
arxiv-2509-23683:
Clients in federated learning face new tasks over time, and a single global model can import knowledge that hurts more than helps. Danni Yang and 8 co-authors let clients form shifting coalitions instead, keeping models personalized. Each client allies only with partners that promise real gains, so coalitions stay separate and change at each stage. A coalitional affinity game models these ties.

Gradient coherence and model similarity score how much each partnership should pay off. Two algorithms, merge-blocking and cooperative evolution, steer the system toward a dynamic balance. Wide experiments show the framework ahead of many baselines for federated continual learning.
arxiv-2509-23783:
Judging whether a multimodal model's answer is harmful takes more than reading its words; the picture matters too. Qi Xue and 5 co-authors built Falcon, a safety data set of more than fifty-seven thousand visual question-answering pairs across thirteen harm categories. Each item carries explicit labels for harmful attributes in the image, the instruction, and the response, plus the harm category and an explanation of the judgment. That depth is meant to support full audits of multimodal dialogue.

They also fine-tuned FalconEye, an evaluator based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. It beat all baselines on their test set and two public benchmarks, and the authors offer it as a practical auditing tool.
arxiv-2509-23983:
Two particle lanes fed from shared, finite reservoirs can develop walls between dense and sparse regions that refuse to sit still. Sourav Pal and 2 co-authors analyze such a pair of antiparallel asymmetric exclusion processes, building on a model by Haldar and co-workers. The lanes couple to two reservoirs with no spatial extent. For some entry and exit rates, the steady state holds a pair of delocalized domain walls.

Unlike earlier variants, where wandering walls appear only along a line of settings, here they fill an extended region of parameter space. Particle numbers then fluctuate strongly even in the thermodynamic limit. The phase diagrams differ in shape from those of open or reservoir-linked exclusion models.
arxiv-2509-24083:
Bent wire can form light, strong frames, but shaping it by hand into three-dimensional forms is slow and error-prone. Faraz Faruqi and 9 co-authors present WireBend-kit, a desktop machine plus design software for custom wireframe structures. Users sketch a design in free software and check whether it can be built.

A planner then turns the design into feed, bend, and rotate steps for the machine. The planner accounts for the spring of the metal and for errors in the machine's motion. The machine itself costs under three hundred dollars in parts. Tests show it can hold accuracy despite errors that build up step by step, and sample builds show the range of forms it opens.
arxiv-2509-24283:
An Dao and 3 co-authors report on SCIDOCA 2025, a shared task on citations in scientific writing. Systems faced three tests: find fitting references for a given paragraph, pick the right citation for a masked slot, and name the correct reference for a cited sentence. The data came from a large open research corpus.

The released set holds over sixty thousand annotated paragraphs and a curated reference pool. The test set spans a thousand paragraphs from distinct papers, each with true citations and decoy candidates. Seven teams registered and three submitted results. The overview gives scores for all subtasks and weighs how well each system worked, setting a benchmark for citation modeling.
arxiv-2509-24383:
Single-photon detectors count light events well, but they throw away rich facts about each photon, such as wavelength and polarization. Karl C Linne and 7 co-authors built SQuaD, a smart detection system that pairs a programmable chip with a neural network. It aims to recognize photon features and to weed out dark counts, the false events detectors produce on their own.

The system counts photons on par with leading commercial gear and processes each event at high throughput. It spotted and removed dark counts well and identified wavelength and polarization with up to full accuracy. Deployed on an erbium-ion emitter, it enabled clean control and readout of a telecom-band spin qubit.
arxiv-2510-00283:
Huanshu Zhang and four colleagues at Pennsylvania State University wrote this 2025 review of AI-driven design in nanophotonics. Photonic metadevices steer light with patterned surfaces thinner than a wavelength. Designing them once meant slow electromagnetic simulations and much trial and error. The review surveys how deep learning has taken over large parts of that design work.

The authors organize the field by model type, from convolutional networks to generative models and transformers. Image-based and parameter-based methods both get systematic treatment. Attention goes to hard realities: mutual coupling between elements, fabrication limits, and devices serving several functions at once. Language model assistants for design also earn a section as an emerging direction. The review closes with open problems and opportunities for the next design generation. It serves as a map for researchers entering AI-enabled meta-optics.
arxiv-2510-00383:
Yu Cheng and Tianle Liu published this 2025 paper on using generative AI to model turbulence inside weather simulations. Large-eddy simulations resolve big swirls but must guess the effect of smaller, unresolved eddies. Classic recipes for that guess are deterministic, while real turbulence is stochastic at heart. The authors train a denoising diffusion model to reconstruct the missing subgrid stresses.

The model learned from direct simulations of the atmospheric boundary layer at high Reynolds numbers. It beat Smagorinsky-type models and earlier neural networks on spatial correlation and stress distributions. A small three-by-three-by-three patch of velocity proved enough for accurate stress estimates. Training on two extreme stability regimes generalized well to conditions in between. The authors present generative modeling as a new direction for subgrid turbulence closures in climate and weather codes.
arxiv-2510-00783:
Nguyen Canh, Zhang, HoangVan, and Chong survey semantic visual SLAM in this 2025 arXiv paper on robotics and computer vision. A robot running SLAM builds a map while locating itself, and semantic SLAM adds object-level meaning to that map. The field has grown for over two decades without a survey that covers recent advances and challenges. The authors supply one, starting from how visual SLAM evolved and where earlier surveys fell short.

They propose a problem formulation and split the pipeline into visual localization, semantic feature extraction, mapping, data association, and loop closure. Deep learning approaches and large language model methods get separate treatment, alongside the datasets. Two shifts stand out in their account: neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splatting are remaking map fidelity, and foundation models are opening closed vocabularies. Open problems include benchmarks for long-term dynamics and lifelong operation.
arxiv-2510-00983:
Cheng and five co-authors bring consistency models to curved spaces in this 2025 arXiv paper on generative modelling. Consistency models shortcut diffusion sampling, producing samples in only a few steps instead of hundreds. They were built for flat Euclidean data such as images, yet many real targets live on manifolds, from spheres to the rotation group behind protein and RNA design. Curved geometry breaks the standard training objectives.

Their Riemannian Consistency Model respects the manifold constraint through covariant derivatives and exponential-map parameterization. They derive closed-form objectives for both discrete and continuous time, then prove the distillation and training variants are mathematically equivalent. A simplified objective drops the hardest differential calculations while keeping performance. On tori, spheres, and the rotation group SO(3), the model beat vanilla flow matching and Euclidean consistency models in few-step generation quality.
arxiv-2510-01183:
Wang and co-authors at Johns Hopkins University build a world model that remembers the three-dimensional layout of scenes it invents. Video generators wander and drift, forgetting what stood behind the camera a moment earlier. Starting from one panoramic image, their system, EvoWorld, generates future views while rebuilding the scene in 3D.

The evolving reconstruction is projected back into each new viewpoint as spatial guidance. Video and memory update each other in a loop, curbing drift over long explorations. A new benchmark and dataset, covering synthetic, indoor, and real scenes, test that consistency. Gains in realism and coherence were substantial across all three domains. Feedforward reconstruction keeps the memory update fast enough for generation loops. Spatial360 is the dataset released alongside the model. Long-horizon exploration is where drift normally destroys believability. Geometry, once explicit, can correct the video instead of merely describing it.
arxiv-2510-01283:
Azime, Belay, and Tonja create a grading sheet for judging the long reports that deep-research AI tools now produce. These agents browse the web and write multi-page surveys unaided, but nobody had a standard for scoring them. Academic survey writing serves as the test case in this study.

Two flagship deep-research products each wrote a survey for evaluation. The comparison exposed a wide gap between search engines and dedicated research tools. Coverage of the target area fell short in ways the sheet made visible. The authors argue that carefully crafted evaluation standards must come before trust. Report quality dimensions like coverage and faithfulness need explicit rubric lines. A worked example with Kenyan language technology shows the sheet in action. Standalone research tools outclassed search-engine answers on the survey task. Representation gaps, not prose polish, were the failing grade.
arxiv-2510-01483:
Al Mdfaa and co-authors give navigating robots a persistent memory by converting video into a queryable knowledge graph that tracks objects through time. Vision-language models reason well about single frames but forget scenes and reason weakly about space. Their system processes video in chunks and stitches object identities across the stream.

The graph stores rich descriptors, so navigation goals can be answered with explainable spatial queries. A new benchmark of two hundred hand-annotated questions over eight trajectories enables fair comparison. On a real differential-drive robot, the structured approach matched a flagship model's accuracy. Success near seventy-seven percent matched the far larger general model. Language-model reasoning associates objects semantically across chunks. About one hundred minutes of video span the benchmark trajectories. Explainability comes free when answers are graph queries. Memory, not raw perception, was the missing faculty.
arxiv-2510-01683:
Shu and six co-authors study hidden failures in chest X-ray models in this 2025 medical imaging paper. Deep learning systems read chest radiographs with strong average scores. Yet their accuracy varies across patient subgroups, and some wrong answers come with high confidence. Standard checks based on confidence or outlier detection miss those quiet, risky errors.

The authors propose a risk score based on augmentation sensitivity, called ASRS. It rotates each X-ray by small, clinically plausible angles and watches the model's internal representation shift. Cases that shift a lot form a high-risk group under the score. Those cases showed much lower recall despite high confidence and strong headline metrics. ASRS needs no labels, so clinics could use it to route shaky cases to human review.
arxiv-2510-01883:
Dopico, Nicolai, and Stern revisit a strategy for defining truth without paradox in this 2025 logic paper. Supervaluation semantics handles self-referential truth elegantly, but its complexity blocks any axiomatization. Stern proposed a tamer variant in 2018 that kept the essential behavior at lower complexity. That variant promised categorical axiom systems that pin down the natural numbers.

The authors show that Stern's original construction did not fully deliver on that promise. They exhibit counterexamples to some of his key claims about the semantics. Rather than abandoning the project, they repair it with new semantic incarnations of the same idea. Those versions do support the categorical axiomatizations Stern wanted. All the operators they study preserve the penumbral truths of classical logic and arithmetic. The paper sharpens the map between full supervaluationism and its more tractable cousins.
arxiv-2510-01983:
Hayata, Seki, and Yunoki run a localization experiment on a real quantum processor in this 2025 paper. Many-body localization keeps disordered quantum systems from thermalizing, trapping memory of their start. Simulating that driven dynamics faithfully is a flagship task for noisy quantum hardware. The team chose a disordered, periodically kicked Ising model for the test.

They ran the simulation on sixty qubits of an IBM Heron processor with a heavy-hex layout. Out-of-time-ordered correlators served as their indicator of the crossover between chaos and localization. The late-time behavior of those correlators mapped the two regimes against disorder strength. Two independent error mitigation methods, operator renormalization and zero-noise extrapolation, produced consistent results. That agreement supports the validity of the hardware findings. The study shows present-day processors can already chart nonequilibrium phase behavior. Large Trotter steps, usually a liability, become part of the Floquet design here.
arxiv-2510-02083:
Pallis revisits grand-unified Higgs inflation in light of new telescope data in this 2025 paper. The model drives inflation with Higgs fields tied to breaking a grand unification symmetry at the MSSM scale. A continuous R symmetry fixes its potential uniquely. Two fractional shift-symmetric potentials add just two free parameters.

Fresh Atacama Cosmology Telescope results, from Data Release 6, sharpen the targets. The model's predictions match the new data across a wide parameter band. The inflaton stays below the Planck scale throughout, which keeps the theory controlled. For parameter values of order unity, early gravitational waves could reach detectable levels. Extensions of the potential also solve the MSSM mu problem within the same setup. Added terms can seed the cosmic matter imbalance as well. The update keeps GUT-scale pole inflation alive and testable after ACT.
arxiv-2510-02383:
Bhowmik proposes a transparent way to generate the elliptic curves behind modern encryption. His 2025 cryptography paper questions how standard curves were chosen. Curve parameters usually come from opaque seed processes. Users must trust that nothing was hidden in the choice. Bhowmik borrows tools from classical number theory instead. Descent methods produce quartic and cubic equations with known invariants. Those invariants fix the curve parameters by a clear recipe. Local solubility checks, modeled on Selmer tests, filter weak candidates early.

Surviving curves then face standard security screening. Group order, cofactor, twist, and embedding checks all apply. A proof of concept program runs the whole pipeline. It retries until a passing curve appears, Las Vegas style. Every step leaves a transcript that others can verify. Arithmetic structure replaces blind trust in seeds. Auditable curve design answers a long standing complaint.
arxiv-2510-02583:
Hambardzumyan, Lovett, and Shirley add fresh equivalent forms to a famous open conjecture. Their 2025 theoretical computer science paper studies the log-rank conjecture. The conjecture links two measures of a Boolean matrix. Rank counts its algebraic size in the usual sense. Partition number counts how many flat rectangles tile it. They should stay quasi-polynomially close, the conjecture claims. The authors define a new measure called signed rectangle rank. It counts all-one rectangles in a signed sum decomposition. That measure provably sits between rank and partition number. Their main result ties it to rank within a log factor.

The conjecture now becomes one clean question. Can every signed decomposition turn positive at modest cost? The team extends the result from matrices to tensors. An application links the conjecture to cross-intersecting set systems. Equivalent forms give attackers new angles on old problems.
arxiv-2510-02683:
Gao and co-authors argue that neural operators must become interpretable to reveal hidden physics. Their 2025 position paper surveys how these models learn dynamics. Neural operators map between function spaces directly. They now simulate complex systems from data alone. Success has outrun understanding of their inner logic. The authors sort operators into two families. Grid based models learn on spatial meshes. Basis based models learn with function expansions. Their analysis shows operators can absorb real physical patterns. One explanation method works, but only in narrow cases.

A simple dual-space model reached top performance in their tests. Mixing both families across scales looks promising for complex physics. General explanation tools remain the missing piece. Science needs models whose reasoning can be checked. A simulator that hides its rules limits discovery. Interpretable operators could turn data into laws. The paper maps where that research should go next.
arxiv-2510-02783:
Mark studies when a Banach space basis that behaves well at every Schreier level must behave well outright. His 2025 mathematics paper works in functional analysis. Schreier families grade the complexity of index sets by countable ordinals. A basis can be unconditional relative to one such family. Requiring that at every ordinal is far stronger. The author introduces Condition A, a set theoretic assumption. It is weaker than the Continuum Hypothesis. Under that assumption, the level by level property upgrades. Any basis unconditional for all Schreier orders is unconditional, period.

Greedy basis results travel alongside the main theorem. Interval arguments show long blocks escape every fixed family. The proof leans on bounding functions for the top family. Unconditionality is the backbone property of basis theory. Knowing when partial versions collapse into it matters. Set theory quietly steers the answer here. The paper marks exactly how much assumption the upgrade needs.
arxiv-2510-02883:
Matsuura, Hayashi, and Hsieh build private codes that work on any quantum channel. A classical-quantum channel takes letters in and gives quantum states out. Private coding must hide the message from an eavesdropper. Universal coding must work without knowing the channel in detail. Prior work made decoding universal, but encoding leaned on random codebooks. The team closes it with a graph property.

Each codebook defines a Schreier graph built from its structure. When that graph has a large spectral gap, a key effect follows. Random codewords then mimic the target output pattern closely. The match holds no matter which channel carries them. This yields the first fixed, channel-free resolvability codebooks. Paired with universal channel coding, the result is a full private protocol. It reaches the known best rate for such coding. The work ties secure communication to expander graph theory.
arxiv-2510-02983:
Dang and Liang speed up the fair sampling of points inside convex bodies. Picking points evenly from a high-dimensional shape is a classic task. Their method builds on the proximal sampler frame. That frame needs a helper called a restricted Gaussian oracle. The helper adds noise, then pulls points back toward the shape. No fast version of the helper existed for plain access models.

They build the helper with rejection sampling instead. It works given either a projection tool or a separation tool. Both tools are standard ways to describe a convex body. The team proves firm, non-asymptotic cost bounds for the sampler. Accuracy is graded by two divergence measures from information theory. The bounds hold for samples that are exactly unbiased. Earlier schemes often settled for near misses. The result makes a clean theory tool ready for practice.
arxiv-2510-03083:
Shirali and co-authors test whether symmetry helps or hurts adaptive quantum simulations. Adaptive solvers grow a circuit by picking useful operations from a pool. The test system is the lattice Schwinger model. It mimics electrodynamics in one space dimension. Each pool kept or broke three traits in a planned pattern. The traits were shift symmetry, charge conservation, and fermionic locality.

Circuit depth is the scarce resource on today's hardware. Pools that broke shift symmetry won on depth. Keeping charge conservation also helped the near-term runs. Their circuits stayed shallow while reaching the ground state. Tomorrow's error-corrected machines face a different scarcity. There, the count of measurement shots will pinch hardest. Pools that keep shift symmetry look better for that era. The study thus splits its advice by hardware age. Symmetry breaking is a tool, not a sin, the authors argue.
arxiv-2510-03483:
Saeed and colleagues at MBZUAI in Abu Dhabi present a 2025 arXiv paper on one model that can outline organs in many kinds of medical scans. Hospitals usually train a separate model for each scan type and body part, which multiplies upkeep. Their framework, DuPLUS, steers the analysis with text prompts at two levels, giving fine control over what to find. It also reads health record data to forecast how a patient's disease may progress.

Across ten data sets spanning three scan types and more than thirty organs and tumor kinds, DuPLUS beat leading specialist and universal models on eight sets in the study. On a head and neck cancer set, its prognosis score reached a solid level for ranking patient outcomes. Light fine tuning lets the model adapt to new centers and tasks quickly. One prompt driven tool for both mapping and forecasting could simplify clinical AI pipelines greatly.
arxiv-2510-03583:
Dos Santos, Vieira, and Vieira present a 2025 arXiv paper in algebra on when the multiplicities in an algebra's cocharacter sequence stay bounded. Cocharacters package the polynomial identities an algebra obeys, and their multiplicities measure how rich that identity structure is. The authors study algebras graded by a finite group, over a field of characteristic zero. They pin down which varieties of graded algebras have multiplicities capped by a constant. The answer is phrased through the graded identities the algebras satisfy.

A second part adds a graded involution, a symmetry operation on the algebra. For those structures, the authors list the polynomial identities that mark varieties whose multiplicities stay capped by one. Bounded multiplicity is a tameness condition, so an identity based test is valuable. The results extend the theory of polynomial identities into graded and involution settings. Algebraists who classify varieties gain tools for telling tame families from wild ones.
arxiv-2510-03783:
Kumar and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper sharpening an interferometer's phase estimates by feeding its output light back for another pass. The displacement assisted SU(1,1) interferometer beats classical precision limits using squeezed light. Photon recycling re-injects one output mode into the input with a phase shift, squeezing more information from the photons. The authors analyze the scheme under two readout styles, single intensity detection and homodyne detection, and compute the quantum Cramér-Rao bound, the precision limit.

Under conditions, the recycled device outperformed its counterpart in detection schemes. Its sensitivity approached the Cramér-Rao bound, meaning little precision is left. Enhancement factors are reported against the device and the shot noise limit. Phase sensing underlies gyroscopes, gravitational wave detectors, and quantum imaging systems. Recycling light is an upgrade because it adds passes, not sources. The analysis maps when the trick pays and when loss eats the gain.
arxiv-2510-04083:
Cao and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on the hidden cost function behind an optimal controller. A linear quadratic regulator balances state error against control effort through cost matrices chosen by its designer. Watching the controller's optimal behavior, can an observer recover those matrices? Earlier work recovered state costs only, assuming the control cost matrix was given and the system controllable.

The authors first tackle recovering the control cost matrix itself, using the full trajectory of the feedback gain. They give a condition for unique recovery, plus the solution when it holds. A second, cheaper method samples the feedback gain at time points instead. They then revisit state and cost recovery without assuming controllability, deriving solution spaces for both controllable and uncontrollable systems.
arxiv-2510-04183:
Pacheco and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on choosing millimeter-wave beams for moving vehicles without flooding the network. Millimeter-wave links need narrow beams from massive antenna arrays, and searching all sectors costs latency that fast vehicles cannot afford. Federated learning lets vehicles train a shared selection model without uploading sensitive sensor data. Full-model aggregation, however, is itself heavy and fragile.

Their algorithm, sigla, aggregates only the most important layers of the model, cutting overhead and failure risk. A clustering scheme groups similar vehicles, aggregating within clusters strongly and between clusters gently to fight overfitting on non-identical data. On a real-world multimodal dataset, accuracy improved by about seven percent over existing methods. Inference time fell by more than four-fifths, and model size shrank by up to about half. Faster sector selection keeps high-bandwidth links alive at highway speeds.
arxiv-2510-04583:
Carlo Kneissl and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on regression that reports a full distribution, not just one number. A point forecast hides how unsure the model is, and many decisions hinge on that doubt. Diffusion models generate rich distributions for images, yet regression work rarely grades their uncertainty. The team built a diffusion framework that learns the predictive distribution without a fixed shape. It models the spread of the diffusion noise itself.

Different ways to parameterize that noise carry different trade offs, which the paper maps in detail. The framework adapts to scalars, images, and paths as target types. Tests covered low and high dimensional tasks across that range. On several tasks, the method beat established baselines on accuracy. Its uncertainty estimates also stayed calibrated, matching how often the truth landed in each range. The authors frame diffusion as a general tool for prediction under doubt.
arxiv-2510-05483:
Turner reviews the state of modern cosmology and its standard model, called Lambda CDM. That model describes the universe from an early burst of inflation to today's faster expansion. It rests on three pillars, dark matter, dark energy, and inflation. The 2025 essay asks whether the model deserves praise or replacement.

Turner grants the model its big wins, above all its match with microwave background measurements. Critics still point to cracks, from oddly early giant galaxies seen by the Webb telescope to gaps in inflation theory. Supporters and critics agree on one point, since both expect a better theory someday. The essay traces how the model grew from the older hot big bang picture. Turner hopes the successor will rest more on first principles than the current patchwork. He also weighs the Hubble tension, a dispute over the expansion rate, as a possible clue.
arxiv-2510-05683:
Jena and colleagues explain quantum graph neural networks despite their randomness. Quantum models learn on graph data, but measurement makes their outputs stochastic. That noise, plus combinatorial graph structure, defeats classical explanation tools. Their 2025 QGraphLIME framework reports explanations as distributions, not single answers.

The method perturbs the graph while preserving its structure. Local surrogate models fit on those perturbations produce importance scores. Aggregating many surrogates, with their spread, yields uncertainty-aware rankings of nodes and edges. A Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz bound guarantees how many surrogates suffice for a target accuracy. Synthetic graphs with known ground truth confirm accurate, stable explanations. Ablations show nonlinear surrogates beat linear ones clearly. Perturbation design matters too, and the study probes that sensitivity. Trustworthy explanations matter most in regulated, high-stakes uses of quantum models. The code is publicly available for other researchers.
arxiv-2510-06183:
Iyer, Wu, Belzig, and Smith analyze quantum f-divergences through relative expansion coefficients. Any sensible distinguishability measure must obey data processing: it cannot grow under a quantum channel. The key question is how much information a channel loses or preserves, captured by contraction and expansion coefficients.

They merge the two into a single relative expansion coefficient. They study standard quantum f-divergences and their second-order local behavior, which induces a monotone Riemannian semi-norm tied to chi-squared divergence. They find new families of f where global and local coefficients coincide for every channel pair, and clarify how rare that is. An equivalence framework transfers traits like strict positivity across coefficients. Applied to approximate recoverability, the approach proves a reverse quantum Markov convergence theorem. Positive expansion coefficients become quantitative lower bounds on convergence rates for primitive channels.
arxiv-2510-06283:
Makanaboyina tackles catastrophic forgetting in brain tumor segmentation with diffusion-based replay in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Clinical datasets keep evolving, but retraining on all past data is costly, often impossible. Models updated only on new scans forget earlier tumor appearances.

SER-Diff is the first framework uniting diffusion-based refinement with incremental learning. A frozen teacher diffusion model generates synthetic error maps from past tasks. Those maps replay during new-task training, reminding the model where it used to err. A dual loss pairs Dice on new cases with distillation loss on replayed errors. On BraTS 2020, 2021, and 2023, SER-Diff beat prior incremental methods consistently. It posted the highest Dice scores, near ninety-six percent on BraTS2020, with boundary errors under five millimeters. Hospitals could keep segmentation models current without warehousing every old scan.
arxiv-2510-06383:
Lison and Anderson protect de-identified documents against search-based linkage attacks in a 2025 computational linguistics paper. Removing names hides who a document mentions, but not where it came from. An attacker can extract distinctive phrases and search the original collection, relinking text to source.

Their defense works in two steps. An inverted index finds every phrase rare enough to identify a document, occurring in fewer than a chosen threshold of texts. A language-model rewriter reformulates those spans, iterating until linkage becomes impossible. Experiments on court cases and Wikipedia biographies show the method blocks such linkages. Rewritten texts remain faithful to the original content. The authors are candid about the limit. More advanced attacks matching on meaning rather than phrases can still succeed. De-identification must now defend the document's fingerprint, not just its names.
arxiv-2510-06683:
Daoyuan Zhou, Xuchuang Wang, Lin Yang, and Yang Gao study groups of agents that must share options. Their 2025 paper uses the multi-armed bandit model, where each option pays random rewards. Several players pick options at once to maximize their total gains. When two players pick the same option, they collide and earn nothing.

No central coordinator exists, so each player sees only its own picks and collision signals. The authors design a distributed algorithm with a lean communication protocol. Its total communication cost grows extremely slowly with the time horizon. Both group regret and individual regret come out near optimal. Experiments show clear gains over existing baseline methods. Individual regret drops notably compared with the best prior approaches. The team also extends the method to settings where players act at staggered times. For that case they prove a lower bound and give an algorithm with logarithmic regret.
arxiv-2510-06783:
Akshit Singh leads a large team teaching vision-language models to improve while they are being used. Their 2025 paper presents TTRV, a test-time reinforcement learning method. Normal reinforcement learning needs labeled data and a fixed training set. Humans, by contrast, learn from the task in front of them.

TTRV adapts a model on the fly for each test input, with no labels at all. It runs the model several times on the same item. Common answers earn a reward, while a second reward keeps the outputs from collapsing to one guess. Across sixteen datasets, recognition scores rose by up to about fifty-two percent. Visual question answering gains reached about thirty percent. Even stranger, adapting on a single random unlabeled example still helped noticeably. The method beat strong base models across the board in their tests. It even outperformed GPT-4 in the reported comparisons.
arxiv-2510-06883:
Messaoud Guesba, Ismail Lakehal, and Sid Mahmoud introduce a new family of operators in functional analysis. Their 2025 paper works on complex Hilbert spaces, the setting for much of quantum theory and signal analysis. Normal operators are prized because they behave predictably with their adjoints. The authors widen that family using a symmetry called conjugation.

Their class, named 2-C-normal operators, twists the usual condition with a conjugation map. A defining equation ties the squared twisted operator to its partner operation. The paper works out the basic algebraic characterizations of the class. Spectral properties, which describe an operator's fingerprint values, get full treatment. Concrete examples separate the new class from both normal and 2-normal operators. The authors also check how the class survives standard transformations. Relations to other studied operator families are mapped as well. The results feed the growing theory of complex symmetric operators, where conjugation plays the starring role.
arxiv-2510-07083:
Miriam Wanner leads a team showing that fact-checkers for AI text often miss the errors that matter most. Their 2025 paper studies factuality evaluation of language model responses. Methods score every claim in a response as equally important. A wrong key fact then counts the same as a wrong side detail, which misleads users.

The team built VitalErrors, a benchmark of 6,733 queries with sabotaged responses. Each altered answer omits or falsifies one piece of key information. Existing metrics barely noticed these errors in their tests. The authors answer with Vital, a metric family that weights claims by importance. Claims are scored for relevance to the query, not just truth. Vital detected key-information errors better than the baselines. Response-level scoring captured the damage most. The results argue that factuality tools must weigh what a claim is worth. Treating all claims as equal hides the failures users fear.
arxiv-2510-07183:
Zeng and Deng work out the hidden time cost of making quantum operations resist noise. Their 2025 paper studies control schemes that cancel noise by shaping the path of a quantum gate. It stretches the gate beyond the usual speed limits for clean systems. The authors derive firm lower bounds on that extra cost. They assume steady noise and a cap on how strong the control can be.

For one noise source, they prove a universal floor on the time a robust gate needs. They also give a recipe that builds any robust gate just above that floor.Against a whole space of noises, they bound how many segments a control schedule must have. Local control on networked systems adds a further time cost tied to the network's structure. These bounds tell engineers the cheapest price of noise-proof control.No design can go below them.
arxiv-2510-07483:
Stetzler, Garashchuk, and Rassolov implement a trajectory-based method for simulating a molecule whose electrons and nuclei both move quantum mechanically. Their 2025 paper develops FENDy, built on exact factorization of the molecular wavefunction. Nuclei evolve under a complex time-dependent potential that encodes electronic influence. The electronic part is computed on the fly in standard basis sets, without ever solving for electronic eigenstates. That omission is the point: eigenstate methods buckle when states crowd together. A swarm of quantum trajectories represents the nuclear wavefunction, promising gentler scaling with system size than grid methods.

The test case is the hydrogen molecular ion under a femtosecond laser pulse, with real Coulomb interactions. The code reproduced the exact dynamics of a two-state benchmark obtained by a standard split-operator method. Achieving the same result while skipping electronic structure solves entirely is the headline.
arxiv-2510-07683:
Yan, Tao, Franck, and Henann wrote this 2025 mechanics paper on fitting material models to experiments. Hyperelastic models describe how rubber-like materials stretch and recover. Each model carries parameters that must be matched to real measurements. Doing that by hand is slow, and complex models defeat simple fitting. The authors build an automated calibration framework for this task at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

The framework pairs the virtual fields method with a genetic algorithm search. It feeds on displacement fields captured by digital image correlation, together with load cell readings. It accepts uniform or uneven deformation data and rejects parameter sets that behave unphysically. The genetic search handles models with many coupled parameters. Applied to an open-cell elastomeric foam, the framework beat manual fitting in their tests. The authors released two code packages covering both simple and full-field experiments.
arxiv-2510-08083:
Hajdu and Janßen wrote this 2025 physics paper on how one-way behavior emerges from laws that run both ways. Quantum dynamics conserves entropy and can always be run backwards, yet real systems relax to a steady state. Their approach tracks only the degrees of freedom that matter; the rest act as a bath. Observers track it for far less time than full spectral resolution needs. A relaxator appears inside the effective operator and breaks the time symmetry.

The resulting equation carries memory effects and initial correlations. Its steady states turn out generically unique, whatever the starting point, barring degeneracies. Equilibrium states yield a stationary Pauli master equation. It reproduces kinetic equations as special cases and generalizes Kubo's response theory. Under weak coupling, it reduces to bath correlations, and a Markov approximation recovers semigroup evolution. The paper offers a route from reversible micro-laws to observed one-way behavior.
arxiv-2510-08183:
Zenner, Schreiber, and Stellmer wrote this 2025 instrumentation paper reporting the first passive laser gyroscope locked with the Hänsch-Couillaud technique. Large ring lasers measure Earth's rotation and ground motions for geodesy and seismology. Passive gyroscopes with an external laser promise fewer disturbances but need excellent frequency stabilization. This team's alternative was intrinsically limited by flicker noise in its error signal. A simple lock-in arrangement overcame that floor.

The gyroscope reached a rotation sensitivity of a few nanoradians, resolving changes below one ten-thousandth of Earth's rotation rate. That performance matches a similarly sized gyroscope using the established locking scheme. The lock-in enhancement is simple and cheap, so other experiments could adopt it. Drift beyond ten seconds, probably thermal, remains the main limitation. Better environmental control should improve sensitivity substantially.
arxiv-2510-08283:
Cristina Sardón derives a family of special operators from symmetry in a 2025 arXiv paper in mathematical physics. The Dirac operator is a basic tool that mixes derivatives with Clifford algebra, a system for handling directions. Dunkl operators deform it with reflections drawn from a finite symmetry group. Sardón asks whether the deformed operators arise by reducing the plain Dirac operator.

She restricts the flat Dirac operator to one chamber of a Coxeter reflection group. A weight, the Heckman-Opdam measure, changes how functions are averaged on that chamber. She finds the drift and reflection fixes needed to keep the operator skew-adjoint under this weight. Those fixes reproduce the Dunkl operators as the unique match to reflection symmetry. Their contraction gives the Dirac-Dunkl operator, whose square is the Dunkl Laplacian. The scheme extends to other group representations, recovering known particle systems.
arxiv-2510-08483:
Shangqing Tu and co-authors prune redundant reasoning traces in parallel language model sampling, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Parallel scaling runs many chains of thought at once and votes among final answers. The catch is waste: their analysis found over eighty percent of traces reach identical answers. DeepPrune detects that redundancy early and cuts it off.

A specialized judge model predicts whether two partial traces will end with equivalent answers. Trained with focal loss and oversampling, it reached 0.87 AUROC on this prediction task, and the score held across their checks. An online greedy clustering algorithm then prunes duplicate paths while keeping answer diversity. On AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and GPQA benchmarks, token use fell by over eighty percent versus consensus sampling. Accuracy stayed within three percentage points of the unpruned baseline.
arxiv-2510-08683:
Maria Charisi and co-authors combine light curves and gravitational waves to weigh supermassive black hole binaries in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such binaries form in galaxy mergers and shine as quasars with periodic brightness swings. The most massive also emit nanohertz gravitational waves detectable by pulsar timing arrays. Analyzing both messengers together should beat either one alone.

Their joint-likelihood method multiplies the electromagnetic likelihood by the pulsar timing likelihood, treating both as one data stream. They simulated two hundred eight binary signals detectable by both Rubin's ten-year survey and a thirty-year pulsar timing data set. Joint analysis improved parameter estimation, with smaller percent errors than separate analyses throughout. Binary total mass and orbital inclination improved the most among the parameters. The joint approach also beat a pipeline using light-curve constraints as priors for the gravitational-wave analysis.
arxiv-2510-09183:
Jiang and Zhang propose testing educational innovations on simulated students before any real student is exposed to them, in this 2025 arXiv paper. New AI teaching tools may help learners, but they may also cause harm that cannot be undone. Their framework, the student development agent, uses large language models to imitate students with varied traits. The simulated students then live through a proposed learning environment, and researchers watch how they develop.

The team validated the approach in a case study built around MAIC, a multi-agent learning environment. The agents' predicted changes matched the real students' actual outcomes on non-cognitive development, such as attitudes and habits rather than test scores. The authors read the match as early evidence that such simulations can screen new teaching tools efficiently and ethically. They sketch future work: richer student profiles, smaller specialized models, and better ways to interpret simulated data.
arxiv-2510-09283:
Elizebeth and co-authors run a full safety analysis of electric air taxis over the United Kingdom, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They distill hundreds of hazards into a shortlist regulators can act on. Electric air taxis promise quieter, cheaper service than helicopters. But they demand new vertiports, new airspace design, and teamwork among regulators, operators, makers, and pilots. The team applied STPA, a method that hunts unsafe control actions rather than part failures.

The analysis found three hundred seventeen unsafe control actions. A new prioritization extension focused deep analysis on the one hundred ten most critical. Refinement produced one hundred twenty-four distinct high-priority requirements. Fifty-six exposed gaps in existing aviation rules, policies, or procedures, spanning automation, energy management, certification, training, and collision avoidance. The findings hand regulators concrete material for updated rules before air taxis scale up.
arxiv-2510-09583:
Shubham Trehan, Udhav Ramachandran, Akash Rao, Ruth Scimeca, and Sathyanarayanan Aakur present FSP-DETR in a 2025 arXiv paper, a detector for parasite eggs under the microscope. Biomedical object detection struggles with scarce labelled data and with rare or new categories appearing over time. Their target is parasitic ova, the eggs whose naming guides treatment of illness.

Built on a class-agnostic DETR backbone, the framework builds class prototypes from a few support images. It learns an embedding space from augmented views, using a small transformer decoder, trained with prototype matching, separation, and tuning losses. One model then handles few-shot detection, open-set recognition of unknown classes, and new tasks without retraining. The authors add a benchmark of twenty parasite classes with standard scoring rules. Across ova, blood cell, and malaria tasks, FSP-DETR beat prior few-shot and prototype-based detectors, most of all with very few examples.
arxiv-2510-09683:
David Wittman, the sole author, wrote a beginner's guide to the Fisher information matrix in a 2025 arXiv paper. Astronomers use the Fisher matrix while designing experiments to forecast how precisely the experiment will measure what it targets. Many references present the mathematics of the formalism, but few slow down for newcomers.

Wittman's document is pedagogical, meaning it is built for teaching. It works through a few simple examples step by step rather than stating general theorems. The examples are chosen to develop conceptual understanding of what the matrix means and when its forecasts can be trusted. The author notes the tool is used widely in astronomy and presumably in other fields as well. The guide aims to give a beginner the intuition needed before tackling the heavier literature on experimental design and error forecasting.
arxiv-2510-09783:
Dang Nguyen and six co-authors, among them Svetha Venkatesh, use language models to fix imbalanced datasets in a 2025 arXiv paper. When one class is rare, classifiers learn it badly, and oversampling counters this by generating extra minority examples. Classic methods such as SMOTE must first convert categorical variables into numbers, losing information, while recent language model methods generate samples with too little diversity.

Their method attacks diversity from three sides. New samples are conditioned on both the minority label and its features, a new shuffling strategy guides fine-tuning, and the model trains on interpolated samples as well as real minority ones. Across ten tabular datasets, the method sharply beat eight top baselines, and the synthetic samples were judged both realistic and diverse. Theory based on entropy backs the claim, showing the design provably pushes for diversity in what it generates.
arxiv-2510-10083:
Mandal, Zhihan Peng, Yujie Wang, and Praneeth Chakravarthula restore images from metalens cameras in this 2025 arXiv paper on computational imaging. Metalenses are flat arrays of nanoscale scatterers that promise far thinner, lighter cameras than glass optics. In practice their images suffer severe chromatic aberration, strong scattering, narrow bandwidth, and low light efficiency.

The authors tackle in-the-wild imaging from bursts of these badly aberrated frames. A burst gives several flawed views of the same scene, and computation can fuse them into one clean image. Their method aims for high-quality results outside the lab, where lighting and subjects are uncontrolled. Success would bring metalens cameras closer to real products.
arxiv-2510-10383:
Erukude studies bias in convolutional neural networks in this 2025 arXiv paper on machine vision, drawn from his Kansas State thesis work. CNNs now lead most image classification, and their data-driven features are hard to inspect. A network may secretly rely on background, texture, or artifacts rather than the object itself.

Erukude probes that hidden reliance by scrambling images and applying transforms. Scrambling parts of an image destroys some cues while keeping others, so changes in accuracy reveal which features the network truly uses. The method exposes bias that standard accuracy cannot show. Knowing what a classifier looks at is a precondition for trusting it in medicine, security, and other sensitive vision tasks.
arxiv-2510-10483:
Narayan S Iyer and three co-authors improve a neural method for solving partial differential equations in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such equations, called PDEs, describe much of physics and engineering. Physics-Informed Neural Networks solve them without a mesh, but they often suffer from low precision, slow training, and scarce labeled data. The team's method, gST-PINN, adds gradient information and a self training step that generates its own extra training points.

They tested the method on three PDE problems from different fields. On the Burgers equation, a standard network stalled at a mean square error near one thousandth, and on a diffusion sorption equation near one ten-thousandth after many iterations. The new method kept improving instead, reaching an error near one hundred-thousandth after 18,500 iterations on the reported runs. It beat the standard approach in every case, even when no true solution was available for training.
arxiv-2510-10583:
Adrian Langer proves a comparison result for two kinds of fundamental groups in algebraic geometry, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is a surjective map between normal projective varieties over a field of positive characteristic. One group is the étale fundamental group, a standard invariant of a variety's shape. The other is built from F-divided bundles, objects tied to the Frobenius map that defines positive characteristic geometry.

Langer proves that if the map between varieties induces a surjection on étale fundamental groups, then the corresponding map on F-divided fundamental groups is faithfully flat. He proves an analogous result for isomorphisms. This generalizes and strengthens a recent theorem of Sun and Zhang, which itself extended work of Esnault and Mehta and of Biswas, Kumar, and Parameswaran. A key new ingredient is an analogue, for F-divided bundles, of a descent theorem of Bhatt and Scholze.
arxiv-2510-10683:
Hussein Nassar proves a counting rule for how thin shells respond to loads, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A shell held in the hands can be loaded six ways: three from pulling and shearing, and three from bending and twisting. Nassar shows that a simply connected shell, one with no holes and no handles, resists exactly three of these load cases and complies with the other three.

Formally, he studies the space of membrane and bending strains, defined as in plate theory, that can be relaxed into a tiny stretching-free deflection. For any simply connected shell that is periodic, or statistically uniform, that space is three dimensional. The result holds whether the shell is corrugated, creased, or wrinkled. Such rules matter for design: they show which loads a shell absorbs by bending rather than stretching.
arxiv-2510-11183:
Translating sign language automatically is hard because each national sign language has its own grammar and vocabulary. Ali Alhejab and co-authors apply the T5 text model to Saudi Sign Language translation in this 2025 arXiv paper. They work with a new dataset that includes three challenging testing protocols and captures features such as face coverings, which make recognition and translation harder.

The team compared models pre-trained on American Sign Language data from the YouTubeASL corpus against models trained directly on the Saudi dataset. Pre-training on the American data improved performance substantially, roughly tripling the BLEU-4 score, a standard translation quality measure. That gain shows cross-linguistic transfer between sign languages, even though the two languages differ. Their findings argue for leveraging large-scale data from better-resourced sign languages when building translation systems for smaller ones, and their code is publicly available.
arxiv-2510-11383:
Two immiscible compressible fluids, like gas and liquid in a pipeline, share a velocity field but keep a sharp interface, across which the density jumps. Marcel Zodji proves that such interfaces persist for all time in this 2025 arXiv analysis paper. The model couples two hyperbolic equations, carrying the phase fraction and the density, with a parabolic equation for the velocity, and the viscosity depends on the density.

Starting from an interface that is a smooth surface with Hölder-regular density on each side, Zodji constructs a global-in-time weak solution, in an intermediate regularity class, and proves it is unique. Within that solution the piecewise Hölder regularity of the density and the smoothness of the moving interface persist forever: the interface deforms but never loses its regularity class. The result is a well-posedness theorem for the single-velocity Baer-Nunziato two-phase model in three dimensions, .
arxiv-2510-11483:
Systems that reason step by step while retrieving documents can produce confident nonsense, and distrusting them wisely requires measuring uncertainty from both parts. Heydar Soudani, Hamed Zamani, and Faegheh Hasibi propose a method for that in this 2025 arXiv information retrieval paper. Existing methods handle simple queries or single retrieval steps, not multi-step reasoning loops.

R2C perturbs the reasoning process: altering steps in the most likely path changes what the retriever fetches, which changes the generator's next step. Disagreement across these perturbed runs, settled by majority voting, becomes the uncertainty score. Across five retrieval-augmented reasoning systems and question-answering datasets, R2C improved the AUROC measure by over five percent on average against the best baselines. Used as an external signal, it also gained about five percent on abstention metrics and improved exact match in model selection by roughly seven percent over single models.
arxiv-2510-11783:
Richard Dyer and Christopher J. Moore build better error bars for computer simulations of merging black holes. Numerical relativity solves Einstein's equations on supercomputers to predict gravitational-wave signals. Even the best codes carry small numerical uncertainties, which matter when researchers study faint effects near the merger. Their 2025 arXiv paper models those uncertainties with a Gaussian process, a statistical tool that treats errors as smooth random functions.

The model covers every wave pattern in a state-of-the-art catalogue of simulations. It then defines a likelihood, letting standard Bayesian methods, long used on real detector data, run on simulations too. A clever sampling scheme recovers result distributions without slow Markov chain Monte Carlo runs. The authors demonstrate the approach on quasinormal modes, the fading tones a merged black hole rings with. Applied to Cauchy-characteristic waveforms, the uncertainties stay honestly accounted for in the mode measurements.
arxiv-2510-12383:
Ovcharenko and Schelter take a first step toward detecting data errors that span tables and images together, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Large organizations struggle to keep data accurate, and errors often cross modalities: a product table may disagree with its photo. Traditional detection methods examine one modality at a time and miss such mismatches, which are common in e-commerce and healthcare.

The authors benchmark several methods for cross modal error detection in tabular data. Their evaluation spans four datasets and five baselines. Cleanlab, a label error spotting framework, and DataScope, a data valuation method, performed best when paired with a strong automated machine learning framework, achieving the highest F1 scores. Even so, the authors find current methods remain limited, especially on heavy tailed real world data where extreme values are common. They present the benchmark as a spur for dedicated cross modal methods, not a solved problem.
arxiv-2510-12683:
Drouillard and colleagues make a broad rainbow of light in a common alcohol, offering a safer nonlinear medium for ultrafast optics, in a 2025 arXiv physics paper. Supercontinuum generation broadens a laser pulse into a spectrum spanning more than an octave. Solids are often used for this broadening but suffer permanent damage at high intensity. Liquids resist damage while offering similar nonlinearity.

The team generated a supercontinuum in 1-decanol, an alcohol, spanning from the visible into the near infrared. Measuring its nonlinear refractive index, they found a large higher order part. That contribution makes the liquid's nonlinearity match carbon disulfide, a standard reference material, in high intensity regimes. The liquid is far less volatile and toxic. The generated spectrum stayed stable for at least thirty minutes of operation. The authors present 1-decanol as a practical, safer medium for high intensity nonlinear optics.
arxiv-2510-12783:
Eschen and a large international team report two new exoplanets in this 2025 arXiv paper, orbiting a metal-poor star called TOI-2345. The star belongs to the galaxy's thick disk, an older population whose chemistry differs from the Sun's, so its planets test whether star and planet compositions are linked. One planet is a super-Earth on a very short orbit, and the other is a larger sub-Neptune farther out.

The team combined data from the TESS and CHEOPS space telescopes with ground-based velocity measurements to pin down both planets. The inner world proved slightly larger than Earth with a few times its mass, while the outer one was about two and a half times Earth's radius and notably heavier. Modeling their interiors against the star's depleted chemistry, the authors argue the pair challenges current ideas about planet formation around thick-disk stars.
arxiv-2510-13083:
Friedlander, Kubal, Plan, and Scott analyze exact regularization of linear programs on average in this 2025 arXiv paper. Adding a small penalty term, regularization, can make optimization problems better behaved, and sometimes it leaves the original solution completely unchanged, which is called exact. Until now nobody had quantified how likely that happy outcome is on typical instances.

With a standard Gaussian cost vector and a fixed constraint set, the authors bound how the probability of exact regularization succeeding depends on penalty strength. Failure is characterized through the Gaussian measure of inner cones, controlled by new two-sided bounds on shifted cone measures. The results reveal dimension-dependent scaling laws and tie exact regularization to polyhedral geometry through the normal fan of the feasible set and the solid-angle measure of its cones. They obtain computable bounds in canonical settings including regularized optimal transport, and numerical experiments confirm the predicted thresholds.
arxiv-2510-13683:
Ang, Sun, and Yu derive an exact formula linking two parameters that index coupled random trees. Their 2025 arXiv paper belongs to the mating-of-trees approach to random surfaces and curves. Two pairs of correlated Brownian motions describe the coupling. One parameter, p, speaks the language of the motions themselves. The other, theta, speaks the language of the curves drawn on the random surface.

Before this work, their relation was known only at two special points, by symmetry. The authors prove the full relation for all values in closed form. The proof blends mating-of-trees ideas with Liouville conformal field theory. A boundary three-point function from that theory supplies the exact inputs needed. As a demonstration, they compute statistics of the skew Brownian permuton. That object governs scaling limits of certain random permutations. The formula turns curve-side questions into motion-side computations and back.
arxiv-2510-14183:
Zhiyuan Zheng and co-authors measure the cold molecular gas in the host galaxies of seventeen gravitationally lensed quasars, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Molecular gas is the raw material of star formation. Studying it in moderate quasars, rather than the most luminous ones, tests how black hole activity and galaxy growth connect at cosmic noon. Gravitational lensing magnifies these systems, making faint ones observable.

Using the IRAM thirty-meter telescope, the team observed carbon monoxide emission, the tracer of molecular gas, in quasars split into four images. They detected the emission in five of seventeen targets, a detection rate near thirty percent. The detected hosts are gas-rich but show weaker starbursts and lower star formation efficiency than luminous quasars. The carbon monoxide line patterns of two quasars indicate mild star formation rather than extreme starbursts. The authors conclude these quasars live in quieter star-forming environments.
arxiv-2510-14383:
Danish Ali and co-authors present DRBD-Mamba, an efficient three-dimensional brain tumor segmentation model built on state space architectures, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Segmenting tumors in MRI scans is vital for diagnosis and treatment planning, but tumors vary wildly. Mamba models, though efficient in principle, pay heavy overhead here. They scan features sequentially along several spatial axes.

Their dual-resolution bi-directional design captures multi-scale, long-range context with minimal computation, using a space-filling curve to flatten the volume into a sequence while preserving spatial locality, avoiding expensive multi-axis scans. A gated fusion module blends forward and reverse contexts adaptively, and a quantization block improves robustness. The team also proposes five systematic evaluation folds on the BraTS2023 benchmark for rigorous testing under diverse conditions. It also analyzes common failure scenarios, addressing the field's habit of reporting results on a single convenient split.
arxiv-2510-14583:
Rusanovsky, Malnick, and Avidan introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a way for vision and language models to talk about single pixels. Such models can describe whole objects or regions in an image. They cannot explain one exact point, such as the tip of a bird's beak, or find it again from a description. The authors split the job into two cooperating parts.

A Point Descriptor writes a rich description of a keypoint, moving from the broad scene down to local detail. A Point Localizer then turns such a description back into exact pixel coordinates. Because no training data existed, the team built a dataset of over twenty thousand image, keypoint, and description triplets with help from several vision and language models. They tuned the descriptor with reinforcement learning, using the localizer's accuracy as the reward. In their new evaluation, the system beat baselines at recovering the described point.
arxiv-2510-14683:
Graham and Leyton-Brown work, in a 2025 arXiv paper, on tuning an algorithm's parameters to maximize what a user actually values. A utility function can express preferences about runtimes directly: a hard deadline, a per-hour computing cost, or diminishing returns from longer runs. A recent procedure, COUP, chose configurations with strong theoretical guarantees about utility. Its practical performance, though, lagged behind popular heuristic tuners that promise nothing.

The authors close that gap with a series of improvements to COUP. The changes raise its real-world performance without weakening the guarantees it offers. Experiments show the improved procedure now competes with the widely used heuristic configurators. A case study also shows how to probe robustness: the authors vary the utility function and check how sensitive the chosen configuration is. That matters because users rarely know their true utility exactly, and a good choice should not collapse when preferences shift slightly.
arxiv-2510-14783:
Verraest and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a drone racing system that flies from raw camera pixels to motor commands, with nothing in between. Racing drones have reached champion level, but their systems are bespoke. Vision-based end-to-end methods had never combined full simulation-to-real transfer, onboard running, and top performance at once. SkyDreamer aims to be the first.

It builds on model-based reinforcement learning: a learned world model of the drone and its track. During training the model decodes to privileged information, such as exact state, unavailable in flight. At deployment the same hidden state acts as an implicit estimator, making decisions interpretable and resolving what the camera leaves ambiguous. It needs no external aid or camera calibration, so new drones can adopt it without retraining. In real flights it executed inverted loops and split-S maneuvers at twenty-one meters per second.
arxiv-2510-14983:
Triebe and a large team design, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a forecasting system that lets control rooms see tomorrow's electricity demand substation by substation. Transmission operators today forecast load for zones, but renewable growth makes local demand less predictable, and reliability depends on individual nodes. Nodal loads are volatile, differ from each other, and number in the thousands, more than control-room experts can assess one by one.

Working with a transmission operator, the team built a multi-level system for hourly day-ahead forecasting on a dataset of zonal and nodal net loads. Its model is interpretable and scalable, letting operators extend zonal practice to nodal forecasts rather than replacing it overnight. They evaluated approaches to the heterogeneity and volatility of nodal series, which trade off against each other. A parallelized single-model workflow keeps the system manageable. Results improved zonal accuracy and interpretability, and nodal accuracy substantially.
arxiv-2510-15183:
Vicente Vergara develops mathematical machinery for analyzing wave-like operators whose behavior changes from place to place, in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is phase space, which tracks both position and frequency, equipped with metrics that stretch differently in different directions and vary with position. Such anisotropy breaks many standard tools of microlocal analysis, the study of where signals live in space and frequency at once.

Vergara builds a dyadic partition, a slicing of phase space into bands of doubling frequency, adapted to those changing metrics. He proves uniform bounds for Weyl quantization, a standard way to turn formulas into operators. A step-by-step rescaling restores exact scaling inside each band, while an almost-orthogonality argument stitches the bands into global estimates. As applications, he builds an approximate inverse for such operators and analyzes the Radon transform, used in medical imaging.
arxiv-2510-15383:
Chitralekha Gupta and four colleagues release a sound library for drones that listen for people during search and rescue. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that rescue drones mostly rely on cameras, which fail in darkness, smoke, or when victims are hidden. Hearing offers a backup, but a drone's own motors roar loudly enough to mask cries and voices.

DroneAudioset holds twenty-three and a half hours of annotated recordings gathered under realistic conditions. The clips span a wide range of signal-to-noise ratios, several drone types and throttle settings, and varied microphone setups and environments. Because the noise is real, models trained or tested on it face the true masking problem. The dataset supports work on noise suppression and on detecting human presence from sound. It also guides practical design choices, such as where microphones should sit on a drone. The data and code are public under an open license.
arxiv-2510-15483:
Samuel Girard, Aurélien Bibaut, and Houssam Zenati build learning guarantees for experiments that adapt as they go. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that adaptive trials, produce data that depend on earlier outcomes. That dependence breaks the independence assumptions behind classical statistics, so standard risk bounds can badly mislead policy learning.

The core tool is a new self-normalized maximal inequality for martingale processes, the mathematical model of such dependent data. From it the authors derive a variance-penalized training rule that honestly balances average loss against spread for general dependent data. Feeding that penalty into a pessimistic off-policy objective yields guarantees on excess risk. With sequential updates and standard conditions, their estimator converges faster than the usual square-root rate in both parametric and nonparametric settings. Simulations illustrate the practical gains. The work targets safer learning in systems that update their own data stream.
arxiv-2510-15583:
Jixin Zhang and Yong Lai count solutions to logical formulas with a neural network that mimics a classical counting algorithm. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles the #SAT problem, which asks how many assignments satisfy a Boolean formula, a task far harder than finding one solution. Their model builds on iterative join graph propagation, a message-passing method from probabilistic inference.

The method first uses tree decomposition to turn the formula into a join graph of clusters. Messages then pass between clusters iteratively, and the network learns partition functions to estimate the total count. Attention mechanisms are added inside and between clusters. Those let the model focus on the key variables and clusters while cutting redundant computation. Experiments showed the attention-enhanced model beating other neural network approaches on solving accuracy. Zhang and Lai present attention as the ingredient that makes learned counting both sharper and cheaper.
arxiv-2510-15683:
Dense retrieval models embed queries and documents as vectors, but they generalize poorly beyond training domains. Effrosyni Sokli and three colleagues test a leaner mixture-of-experts design in this 2025 arXiv paper. Earlier work inserted expert blocks into every transformer layer, adding many parameters. Their SB-MoE places a single expert block after the final transformer layer instead. Experts are small subnetworks, only some of which activate for each input.

Across seven benchmarks, SB-MoE helps lightweight models like TinyBERT and BERT-Small most clearly. Zero-shot tests on thirteen BEIR datasets, after training on MSMARCO, check broader generalization. Larger base models need more training samples before the expert block pays off.
arxiv-2510-15783:
Haowei Zhu and colleagues introduce ReCon in a 2025 paper. ReCon makes extra training data for object detection. It uses image generation to do this. Hand-labelled data is costly to produce. Generated images often misplace objects. Meaning can also leak between regions. ReCon adds region-level control. A correction step runs during generation itself.

A pretrained perception model inspects the image as it forms. It feeds back corrections in real time. These fix mismatches between content and intended position. The framework strengthens generators that follow a set structure. It also cuts heavy post-processing. Extensive fine-tuning is reduced as well. Detection training is the target use.
arxiv-2510-15983:
Sarah Rebecca Ondraszek and five co-authors lay out a knowledge graph for motor performance data in sports science. Testing strength, speed, and related traits lets researchers compare physical and cognitive capability across populations. The MO|RE repository at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology already publishes and archives such data, above all for motor performance studies.

Their vision roots the graph's ontology in the Basic Formal Ontology, a standard upper framework. The model formally links plan specifications, the processes that carry them out, and the measurements those processes yield. The goal is to make motor performance data standardised and machine-understandable, so studies can be shared and compared cleanly. The idea grows inside a Leibniz Science Campus project on the digital transformation of research, the team notes.
arxiv-2510-16083:
Jaehan Kim works with five co-authors to predict which websites share reused passwords. Credential stuffing risk can then be scored before an attack lands. Attackers replay breached passwords across sites because users reuse them widely. Earlier defences restrict password creation or demand complex account sharing. Those steps hurt usability and block real deployment in practice.

Their framework defines a password reuse relation between two sites. It is the chance that users reuse passwords across that pair of sites. Those relations become edges in a website graph. A graph neural network then performs link prediction to assess reuse risk, and new sites join as nodes from public facts. A federated version keeps user data with each site administrator. On a real data set of hundreds of millions of breached accounts, the federated model reaches a strong F1 score. It beats rival graph models in ablation tests.
arxiv-2510-16183:
Ismail Belgacem and Franck Delaplace work on a first step that can make or break models of gene control. Such models, called Boolean networks, treat each gene as simply on or off. Raw gene data comes as smooth levels, though, so it must be cut into on and off states, a step named binarization.

Plain cutoffs miss much of the biology, since genes play unlike roles and data is noisy and sparse. Their method pairs a cutoff with the known web of which gene controls which. Missing or doubtful values get filled in by following the control rules forward and backward. Checked against detailed cell models, the method sorts genes into on and off states with care. Better binarization means gene models that match real lab results more closely.
arxiv-2510-16283:
Gavin Stewart and Avy Soffer wrote a 2025 maths paper on how waves spread in one dimension over time. They study the Schrödinger equation, the core rule for quantum waves. The setting uses a pull that fades fast far from the centre. A weakly bound part is a wave part that stays near the centre but holds on loosely.

The pair prove each wave splits into a free wave plus a weakly bound part. They then show the bound part has its slope packed near the centre at all times. The result extends past work to the harder one-line case. It helps show which wave states keep their energy close to home.
arxiv-2510-16583:
Nicholas Gismondi and Alexandru F. Radu, working on their own, construct unusual solutions to the stationary surface quasi-geostrophic equation on a flat two-dimensional torus.
