arxiv-2511-14183:
Jingdong Zhang, Lingzhi Zhang, Qing Liu, and twelve co-authors train one foundation model to remove many kinds of soft image damage. Lens flare, haze, shadows, and reflections all half-hide a scene rather than blocking it, yet past work built a specialist for each. Big generalist editors exist, but they lean on detailed prompts and often fail these fine-grained removals.

UniSER exploits the shared nature of soft effects as semi-transparent occlusions. The team curated a dataset of nearly four million image pairs, including new physically plausible examples, and fine-tuned a diffusion transformer with mask and strength controls. The single model aims at robust, identity-preserving cleanup across all soft degradations.
arxiv-2511-14383:
Tony J. Puthenpurakal studies when the blow-up of an ideal inside a nice local ring is itself a complete intersection. The rings in question are excellent local complete intersections, and the construction is the Rees algebra of an ideal of positive height, with an analogous question for the extended Rees algebra. The obstruction is measured using André-Quillen homology and Koszul homology.

He proves the blow-up's projectivization is a complete intersection exactly when two conditions hold. A third André-Quillen homology group must vanish in all large degrees. A first Koszul homology module must also be locally free on the projectivization. For Cohen-Macaulay domains he also computes the rank of that homology module and hence its free locus.
arxiv-2511-14483:
Minami Nakane and seventy-seven co-authors report a strongly lensed galaxy seen as it was in the very early universe. The galaxy, nicknamed Misty Moons, lies behind a massive galaxy cluster that magnifies its light. It was found in a James Webb Space Telescope survey called VENUS. Lensing creates five images of the same galaxy.

Two images are bright and show a sharp break that signals great distance. In its own plane the galaxy resolves into compact star clumps only tens of parsecs wide. Those clumps hold most of its stellar mass. The authors argue this clumped birth of stars was common in faint early galaxies.
arxiv-2511-14583:
The CMS Collaboration searches for heavy resonances that decay to a Higgs or Z boson plus a photon. The Higgs or Z then decays to a bottom quark pair. Data come from proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Events hold a photon and a large jet from the boosted quark pair.

A transformer based tagger reads jet substructure and flavor to flag candidate decays. The photon plus jet mass spectrum is fitted for any excess signal. No significant excess appears above standard model expectations. The team set upper limits on production rates at high confidence. The search narrows where such heavy resonances could still hide.
arxiv-2511-14883:
Bernhard Aigner and Marcus Waurick extend a key existence proof to a broad class of evolving equations with delays that depend on the state itself. In such problems, how long the delay lasts is set by the current solution, which makes the math much harder. The work sits inside the evolutionary equations framework built around material laws and unbounded operators.

The authors prove local well-posedness for weak solutions, given smooth starting histories and a few consistency conditions. They test the result on classic cases such as heat, wave, and Maxwell equations, plus systems with memory effects. The proof gives a shared foundation for many delayed physical models.
arxiv-2511-14983:
Abigale Snortland, Jeff Clerc, and two co-authors measure how wind steers birds and bats over the ocean, a key input for judging turbine collision risk. An all-direction radar on a research barge off the northeastern United States tracked flying animals for five weeks during the autumn migration of 2024. Two lidar instruments on the same barge profiled wind speed and direction at height.

Joining the animal tracks with the wind profiles shows wind driving where animals appear, which way they head, and how high and fast they fly. The team presents this joined analysis as a first method that later studies can reuse. Better behavior models mean offshore wind farms can be sited and run with less harm.
arxiv-2511-15183:
Rishikant Chigrupaatii and eight co-authors present an approach and benchmark for vision language models in Hindi and Telugu with English aligned samples. India holds immense linguistic diversity, yet model evaluation for low resource languages is weak. Past evaluations relied on unchecked auto translations and narrow tasks. Native, culturally grounded question answering was largely missing.

Their semi automated pipeline mixes back translation, filtering, and human verification to build samples. The resulting benchmark draws from diverse sources in both languages. Models can be compared directly against English performance on aligned items. Contributions include the creation approach itself and a broad evaluation resource. The goal is more equitable progress for Indian language vision language systems.
arxiv-2511-15283:
Manuel Asorey and three co-authors test reflection positivity in a higher derivative theory with bound states of ghosts. Higher derivatives are needed for renormalizable quantum gravity, yet they often cause instability and loss of unitarity. Reflection positivity and a spectral representation are standard consistency checks. The authors examine a six derivative scalar theory they proposed earlier.

In that theory a pair of complex mass ghost fields forms a physical bound state. The authors show the two point function satisfies the required positivity and spectral conditions. Physical observables can thus emerge from ghost dynamics in a consistent way. The result supports a unitary reading of the model. It keeps higher derivative gravity approaches alive on firmer ground.
arxiv-2511-15583:
Alberto Bucci, Yuji Nakatsukasa, and Taejun Park settle when a popular shortcut for kernel methods is numerically safe. The Nyström method approximates a large kernel matrix from a small set of columns, helping methods like kernel ridge regression, spectral clustering, and Gaussian processes scale up. Its weak point is inverting that small submatrix, which is often badly conditioned and can wreck accuracy.

Bucci and co-authors give conditions under which the method stays stable. Good column choice and a careful way of computing the pseudoinverse are the key ingredients. Their theory is backed by experiments, giving users both justification and practical guidance for stable large-scale kernel work.
arxiv-2511-15683:
Yao Fu, Raymond Brock, Daniel Hayden, and Chien-Peng Yuan show how to shrink a major uncertainty in searches for new heavy particles at the Large Hadron Collider. Parton distribution functions describe how a proton momentum is shared among its quarks and gluons, and their uncertainty limits searches at high mass. Drell-Yan processes, where a quark and antiquark make a charged or neutral boson, dominate the backgrounds there.

An earlier strategy used neutral-current Drell-Yan data to tighten those functions. The updated program adds charged-current final states and chooses measurable motion variables carefully. The authors demonstrate notable reductions in the assigned uncertainty, which should sharpen limit setting and discovery power in high-statistics collider data.
arxiv-2511-15783:
Po-Shen Hsin and Ryohei Kobayashi study symmetries that arise from automorphisms of a gauge group. Gauge theories describe many physical systems and also underpin quantum computation, and an automorphism is a symmetry of the group itself that permutes its elements while preserving structure. Such maps naturally induce global symmetries of the whole theory, especially when topological terms are present in various dimensions.

They show the automorphism symmetry can extend, become a higher group symmetry acting on extended objects, or become non-invertible, meaning it has no simple reverse operation. Examples span field theory and lattice models. A highlight is new transversal non-Clifford logical gates for topological quantum codes, built from this symmetry for multi-level quantum units.
arxiv-2511-15983:
Siqiao Mu and Diego Klabjan compare two stochastic methods for machine unlearning. Unlearning removes the effect of chosen training data from a model without full retraining. Descent-to-Delete and Rewind-to-Delete are full-batch methods with provable guarantees. The stochastic descent version is widely used as a fine-tuning baseline, despite lacking theory for nonconvex losses.

Viewing unlearning as a disturbed gradient system, they prove certified unlearning guarantees for both stochastic methods. The proof covers strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex losses. Descent gives tighter guarantees in the strongly convex case, while rewinding suits convex and nonconvex cases. Experiments confirm the strengths and limits of each approach.
arxiv-2511-16083:
BESIII Collaboration reports a search for a rare weak decay of the J/psi charmonium particle into an anti-D meson and an anti-K star meson, plus the charge-conjugate process. Weak decays of charmonium are extremely rare, and finding or limiting this channel tests the Standard Model. The search uses a huge sample of J/psi events collected with the BESIII detector at a Beijing collider, at the exact production energy.

No significant signal is observed in the data. The collaboration therefore sets an upper limit on the decay branching fraction at ninety percent confidence. That limit improves the sensitivity of the previous best limit by an order of magnitude, tightening what future theory and experiments must accommodate.
arxiv-2511-16283:
Zhiyuan Li and four co-authors introduce MuISQA, a benchmark for scientific question answering where one question hides several intents at once. A query might ask for a gene mutation and the diseases tied to it, needing evidence from varied sources and several reasoning hops, while standard retrieval systems chase a single intent.

Alongside the benchmark, the team proposes an intent-aware retrieval framework. A language model drafts possible answers, splits them into intent-specific queries, and gathers passages for each intent separately. The fragments are merged and re-ranked with Reciprocal Rank Fusion to balance coverage and cut repetition. On MuISQA and on general retrieval datasets, the method beat standard approaches, with the clearest gains in retrieval accuracy and evidence coverage.
arxiv-2511-16883:
Zhongjie Dai, Tao Feng, and Jiaxuan You present PersonalizedRouter, a system that picks which large language model should answer each user query based on that user's own tastes. Users differ in how they trade off quality, cost, and response style, while existing routers optimize one fixed objective for everyone.

PersonalizedRouter learns preferences from interaction records containing the task context, the query, the candidate models, and the user's actual choice. Those records become a heterogeneous graph linking users, queries, and models, and routing decisions are read off that structure. A new benchmark, PersonaRoute-Bench, simulates a thousand users choosing among ten models. The router beat the strongest existing methods by wide margins under two evaluation strategies and generalized well to new users and new models from few examples.
arxiv-2511-17083:
Sébastien Quistrebert, Elisabeth Gliott, Jean-Sébastien Lauret, and Nikos Fayard study two coupled quantum emitters, tiny sources that can emit light together. When emitters act as one, they can shine brighter or dimmer than alone, effects called superradiance and subradiance. A blurring process in the material can wash those shared effects out, and recent work with tiny dots has kept the contest close.

The team works out, for four signals that labs can actually measure, the exact blurring rate past which the shared effects vanish. Each signal has its own threshold, and the gaps between them are wide. That spread matters: a lab could miss shared behaviour with one signal while another would still show it. The paper gives experimenters a map for choosing conditions and readouts.
arxiv-2511-17283:
Ilja Siroš and three co-authors build ThreadFuzzer, the first fuzzing framework dedicated to the Thread networking protocol. Thread underpins smart-home mesh networks and serves as a core transport layer of the Matter standard, so bugs in its implementations carry real security weight. The framework mutates packets at the protocol's management layer and can test both virtual nodes and physical devices.

Several fuzzing strategies are included, among them coverage-guided fuzzers and a new inserter designed for the type-length-value structure of Thread messages. Running against the OpenThread stack, the framework found five previously unknown vulnerabilities, several reproduced on commercial devices. It also held up well against a strong general-purpose fuzzing baseline. The authors present the tool as both a practical tester and a prompt for more wireless protocol fuzzing research.
arxiv-2511-17483:
M. Nabil Y. Lhachemi, Valentin Crépel, and Jennifer Cano make it cheap to predict when a superlattice, a periodic pattern imposed on a material, creates topologically nontrivial energy bands. Their symmetry indicator scheme needs only data from the parent material before the superlattice is applied, for a weak superlattice field. The results survive beyond that regime as long as the induced gaps stay open. Compact formulas give the key number of the lowest miniband for systems with time-reversal and inversion symmetry, and a Chern number formula covers systems where time reversal breaks.

The authors apply the theory to transition metal dichalcogenides, HgTe quantum wells, and thin films of topological insulators and Dirac semimetals. Topological bands can emerge even from non-topological parents. That widens the pool of options for topological flat bands. The framework tells builders which superlattice pattern and period to choose for a given material.
arxiv-2511-17583:
Chenrui Ma and four co-authors aim for one-step image generation by straightening the paths a generative model travels. Flow matching learns curved trajectories between noise and data, which forces many sampling steps. Earlier attempts to straighten them altered the data coupling or modeled average velocities, and ran into approximation errors, instability, and convergence trouble. The proposed method, Straight Variational Flow Matching, adds a variational latent code that summarizes the generation overview and guides the trajectory toward straightness.

Ideally the generation paths become linear, so a single step can traverse them. Across three challenge benchmarks, the method performed competitively with existing approaches while showing advantages in both training and inference efficiency. The authors present explicit straightness enforcement, rather than indirect encouragement, as the cleaner route to fast flow-based generation.
arxiv-2511-17683:
Lara Hassan, Mohamed ElZeftawy, and Abdulrahman Mahmoud study whether running large language models in Middle East desert data centres can be both workable and sustainable. The region is growing as a hub for AI facilities, but heat and energy supply raise hard questions. The team measures energy use and carbon output for a code-writing model on a standard coding test set.

Runs are compared across the United Arab Emirates, Iceland, Germany, and the United States, using a tracking library that logs power and emissions. The results weigh the desert's hurdles, such as cooling demand, against its possible gains, such as solar supply and new grids. The authors aim for a balanced view of where AI computing should sit as it expands worldwide.
arxiv-2511-17883:
Jiong Lin, Jinchen Ruan, and Hod Lipson introduce ArticFlow, a generative method for mechanisms with moving joints, such as robot bodies and hinged objects. Generating static shapes is now strong, but motion dependent deformation and scarce data make articulated shapes much harder.

ArticFlow uses two linked flow stages: one moves noise to a compact shape code, and the other moves points under an explicit action, guided by that code. One model can cover many mechanism types and generalize across actions. On a standard robot collection it beats object specific simulators in motion accuracy and shape quality, and it can invent new forms by mixing codes.
arxiv-2511-18083:
Md Abdullah Al Kafi, Raka Moni, and Sumit Kumar Banshal ask whether heavy deep learning is needed to classify malaria in cell images. It is a binary task where models are often chosen by default despite high computing needs and opaque decisions. Their alternative extracts just two features per cell: its non background pixel count and its number of holes.

Simple logistic regression on one feature already reaches high test accuracy with a file of about a kilobyte and near instant predictions, and an ensemble with a random forest does better still. Deep networks need tens of megabytes and far longer per image. The authors argue the transparent pipeline suits clinics with limited computing.
arxiv-2511-18283:
Sanskriti Das and five co-authors analyze a deep X-ray observation of NGC 3221, a nearby, highly tilted star forming galaxy, using a long XMM-Newton exposure that combines new and archival time. They study point sources, hot gas, and the galaxy's center together.

They confirm a faint, likely heavily obscured active nucleus. Six very luminous X-ray sources vary in diverse ways over days, and two new soft sources appear, one plausibly a superbubble paired with a compact object. Hot gas above and within the disk needs two temperature phases, with the outer region hotter and thinner.
arxiv-2511-19183:
Carsten T. Lüth and eight co-authors build nnActive, a framework for testing active learning in three-dimensional medical image segmentation. Labeling scans by hand is slow and costly, so active learning picks only the most useful cases to label. In 3D biomedical imaging, though, earlier studies disagreed on whether it truly beats random sampling.

The authors name four flaws in past evaluations, from too few data sets to counting cost only in voxels. nnActive fixes them with a large study, partial annotations inside the nnU-Net tool, foreground-aware random baselines, and a foreground efficiency metric. The setup gives a fairer test of when active learning saves effort.
arxiv-2511-19783:
Osamu Fujino and Nao Moriyama restate a vanishing theorem for algebraic surfaces in a form built for heavy use. Vanishing theorems say certain cohomology groups are zero, and they power much of surface theory. The new statement follows easily from the classic Kawamata-Viehweg theorem, yet the authors show it carries surprising weight.

On its own, the restated theorem is enough for the minimal model theory of log surfaces. Both the minimal model program and the abundance theorem for log surfaces can be carried through without calling on deeper vanishing results. A modest reformulation thus simplifies a whole branch of classification theory.
arxiv-2511-19983:
Pei Zeng, Guo Zheng, Qian Xu, and Liang Jiang design fault-tolerant quantum gates that fit the errors of real hardware. Fault tolerance is needed for reliable quantum computing, but its space and time costs are huge. A sore point is logical rotation gates, which cannot be done transversally and usually need costly magic state factories.

The authors analyze fault-tolerance conditions by mixing perturbative study of realistic dissipative noise with the structure of stabilizer codes. From that, they design one-fault-tolerant continuous-angle rotation gates driven by dispersive-coupling Hamiltonians, needing only nearest-neighbor links. Combined with small-angle state preparation, the scheme suppresses gate error sharply and, for a test simulation task, cuts space-time cost greatly against distillation methods.
arxiv-2511-20483:
Fittipaldi, González Casanova, and Nava Trejo follow gene frequencies in populations that sleep. Their 2025 paper studies a Wright-Fisher process with a seed bank. Some organisms wait dormant in seeds while others reproduce. Offspring numbers can also be heavily skewed in this model. The question: how do frequencies evolve if one type eventually takes over?

Conditioning on eventual fixation changes the process's nature. A change of measure performs that conditioning rigorously. The conditioned process remains a Wright-Fisher type with seed bank. New coordinated mutations appear, driven by a random switching environment. Two tools power the analysis behind the scenes. The lookdown construction builds the process path by path. Sampling duality recovers the conditioned family tree. That genealogy becomes a structured coalescent with coordinated mutations. Skewed reproduction alone breaks classical one-dimensional methods. Dormancy makes the conditioning problem substantially harder still.
arxiv-2511-20683:
Bharadwaj Yadavalli targets a billing quirk of large language models in 2025: output tokens, the words a model writes, cost four to eight times more than input tokens at major providers. Most services answer every question with the same long-winded template, so simple factual questions get padded replies that users pay for. Yadavalli's system, Dynamic Template Selection, instead routes each question to a response template matched to its complexity, trimming cost without hurting quality.

He compared two routers on 1,000 MMLU exam questions: a small MLP network reading pre-computed embeddings, and a fine-tuned RoBERTa transformer. The simple MLP won, reaching 90.5 percent routing accuracy on held-out questions against RoBERTa's 89.5 percent, while using 125 million fewer parameters. Checking through 9,000 live API calls across OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic models, Yadavalli found the same routing accuracy everywhere, with output tokens cut by 33.2 percent on average, a saving that grows quickly at production scale.
arxiv-2511-20783:
A. E. Schwertner and F. N. C. Sobral tackle in 2025 a twist on optimisation: sometimes the goal is to minimise the smallest of several function values, not a single one. This Low Order-Value Optimization problem, LOVO, appears in robust parameter estimation, protein alignment, and portfolio optimisation. In these problems only the best-matching scenario counts. Their setting is harder: the functions are black boxes, smooth but with no derivatives available, and the feasible set is a convex constraint.

They develop the first trust-region algorithm for constrained LOVO that needs no derivatives. The method builds linear interpolation models inside a trust region, adapted to the objective. They prove convergence to weakly critical points, points satisfying a stationarity notion for this nonsmooth problem, and derive a worst-case iteration complexity bound. An open-source implementation accompanies the theory. Extensive experiments against alternatives, they report, show the approach is efficient.
arxiv-2511-21083:
Feiyang Pan and colleagues teach in 2025 a drone's navigation system to spend its computing budget only when it matters. Visual-inertial odometry tracks motion from cameras plus inertial sensors. Optimisation-based versions are accurate but lean on heavy bundle adjustment that embedded hardware struggles to run. The team's answer is two reinforcement-learning agents wrapped around the pipeline. A Select Agent reads only the high-rate inertial stream and decides whether the visual frontend is worth waking.

A Fusion Agent then judges how strongly to trust the visual output when fusing position, velocity, and orientation. On the EuRoC MAV and TUM-VI benchmark datasets, the system posted the best average trajectory error among GPU-based rivals tested. It ran up to 1.77 times faster while using less GPU memory. Against classical optimisation-based systems it kept competitive accuracy at lower computational load, a trade aimed at small flying robots.
arxiv-2511-21183:
Theoretical physicists David Díaz-Guerra, Angel Rincon, and Diego Rubiera-Garcia ask what a black hole without a central singularity would look like, in a 2025 paper. Their model comes from Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity, an altered gravity theory, joined to an anisotropic fluid, meaning matter whose pressure pushes differently in different directions. Such a black hole keeps a single outer horizon almost exactly at the familiar Schwarzschild radius.

The team simulated a thin, glowing accretion disk around the hole and produced images showing its photon ring, the bright loop made by light that circles the hole. They measured the widths of the first two rings and used them to recover the Lyapunov exponent, a number controlling how fast light orbits drift apart. Even so, they find the method cannot separate this exotic hole from an ordinary Schwarzschild one, because modeling and measurement errors are too tangled.
arxiv-2511-21383:
Victor Ziapkoff and colleagues present in 2025 a recipe for measuring films a few nanometres thick, the soap films whose colours have fascinated physicists since Newton. White light reflecting off a film interferes with itself, and the resulting spectrum encodes the thickness, if it can be decoded reliably. Their open-source Python library, optifik, automates that decoding from spectrum to thickness.

The authors walk through three spectral situations: many interference fringes, a moderate number of peaks, and a few identifiable features, with worked examples. They are candid about limits: the spectral range binds, the refractive index must be known, and signal quality matters. History shows the stakes. Newton tied one film colour to about 107 nanometres, Reinold and Rücker reached 11 to 12 nanometres in the 1890s, and Perrin proposed an elementary layer of 5.2 nanometres. It closes with a time-resolved study of a TTAB foam film stretching and thinning.
arxiv-2511-21683:
Yves H. Kwan and five coauthors wrote an invited review and user's guide to mean-field modelling of moiré materials, in 2025. Moiré materials form when atom-thin sheets stack with a slight twist, creating large-scale patterns that reshape electron behavior. The guide centers on magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, two graphene sheets rotated to a special angle where electrons slow dramatically.

The review teaches continuum modelling of the twisted bands, then shows how Hartree-Fock mean-field theory, which replaces electron interactions with an average field, captures correlated states. Three case studies follow. The incommensurate Kekulé spiral order arises from ever-present strain. Collective modes animate broken-symmetry insulators. Alignment with a boron nitride substrate stabilizes the strong-coupling picture. Along the way the authors explain where the idealized chiral-flat limit works and where it fails, giving practitioners a map of the method's reach.
arxiv-2511-22083:
Peng, Li, Lv, and Zheng, physicists, propose a scheme for moving topological corner states across a two-dimensional lattice without losing them, a capability wanted for robust quantum information transfer. Their setting is a two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a standard lattice with alternating couplings that hosts protected states pinned at its corners. The design uses a modular architecture of four topologically distinct subblocks, and transfer happens by coherent tunneling through an adiabatic passage involving corner and interface states.

A multilevel model the authors build describes the pumping mechanism accurately, showing how tuning the lattice couplings steers a topological dark state through the structure. The scheme is compared against a sequential two-stage Thouless pumping protocol, the standard quantized transport method. Their scheme delivers superior performance in both transfer fidelity and efficiency, moving the protected state over long range in one coordinated process rather than two successive pumps.
arxiv-2511-22183:
Zhu, Wu, Lv, Zhang, and Xia, coding theorists, construct error-correcting codes that are simultaneously two things usually traded off. LDPC codes decode iteratively near the Shannon limit but are often found by computer search. MDS array codes have clean algebra and crush burst errors but their standard Blaum-Roth form carries harmful 4-cycles in its decoding graph. The goal is binary codes with the block MDS property and no 4-cycles, built algebraically rather than searched.

Two families result: binary block MDS codes from punctured circulant permutation matrices, and block MDS LDPC codes from heavier circulant matrices, plus a Moore determinant formula and a no-4-cycle condition. They also prove binary block MDS CPM quasi-cyclic LDPC codes cannot exist. Against comparable published constructions at matched parameters, the new codes correct random errors better at similar length and rate, and double as burst-error array codes.
arxiv-2511-22383:
Kitahara, Miyamoto, and Sasaki compute missing corrections in a precision test of particle physics. The CKM matrix describes how quarks mix, and the Standard Model requires it to be unitary, a consistency condition on its rows and columns. Recent data hinted at a violation in its second column. The decays studied are those of the strange-charm meson into a muon or tau plus a neutrino.

For the first time, the team derives the complete one-loop electroweak and quantum electrodynamics corrections analytically. The corrections cover short-distance effects beyond the usual leading-logarithm shortcut. They also cover long-distance soft-photon effects matched to how experiments detect photons. With these corrections included, the second-column unitarity test agrees with the Standard Model again. The limiting factor is now the precision of the QED corrections, and the authors urge lattice simulations including QED for a sharper test.
arxiv-2511-22483:
Lu, Chen, Que, Luk, and Fan ask a neglected question about shrinking large language models: what does compression do to trustworthiness? Quantisation stores weights and activations in fewer bits, cutting memory and compute, and developers usually check only accuracy or perplexity afterwards. The team instead benchmarks quantised models on four trustworthiness measures: adversarial robustness, fairness, machine ethics, and out-of-distribution robustness.

They find 8-bit models usually hold up, but at 3 and 4 bits trustworthiness scores become unstable, diverging across quantisation methods even when ordinary accuracy survives. As a remedy, they propose precision-ensemble voting, combining predictions from several mixed-precision versions of the same model. The ensemble improved trustworthiness scores by up to 5.8 percent across their tests, suggesting compression pipelines for high-stakes uses like finance and healthcare should budget for trust checks, not just accuracy.
arxiv-2511-22883:
Ye and a large collaboration test whether language models can mark schoolchildren's English writing as a teacher does: error by error. Surface corrections and scores miss what learners need, and no taxonomy of writing errors existed to test against. The team defines fine-grained error analysis for English learners and builds FEANEL, 1,000 essays by elementary and secondary students, each error annotated by language education experts.

Every error is categorised by type, severity, and explanatory feedback using a part-of-speech-based taxonomy the experts co-developed. Evaluating state-of-the-art models against this standard exposed significant gaps. They showed foundational ability, but categories applied inconsistently to errors, little of human feedback's pedagogical nuance and conciseness, and swings with prompt engineering, model scale, and reasoning structure. The dataset is released; educational feedback, precise, categorised, and pitched to the learner, is a capability current models have not yet earned, they argue.
arxiv-2511-23283:
Moine and colleagues build the first verification framework for internally deterministic parallel programs. Programs whose parallel steps are arranged to behave as if they ran in one fixed sequential order. Nondeterministic scheduling normally forces verifiers to consider every possible interleaving, but the authors define in this paper schedule-independent safety. The property that checking one terminating execution for safety guarantees safety under all orderings of the schedule.

Two separation logics divide the labor, Musketeer proves a program has the schedule-independent property. And Angelic then verifies just a single, dynamically chosen sequential ordering instead of the whole interleaving space. They prove the soundness of MiniDet, an affine type system enforcing internal determinism with primitives including a deterministic concurrent hash set. And every result in the paper is machine-checked in the Rocq prover using the Iris logic framework end to end.
arxiv-2512-00083:
Large language models need huge amounts of memory while they generate answers, which strains current hardware. Zhongchun Zhou, Chengtao Lai, and Wei Zhang present LLaMCAT in a 2025 conference paper. Their target is the last-level cache, the fast memory layer shared by processors in GPUs and AI accelerators.

LLaMCAT optimizes how that cache is shared and throttled during model inference. Better cache use can speed responses and lower the cost of running large models. The work matters as language models grow and memory, not raw computing power, becomes the main limit on performance. The paper appeared at a major parallel computing conference in 2025. Cache behavior is often where that memory limit bites first.
arxiv-2512-01283:
Haifeng Yang and Lile Wang present a new code for tracking light in space. Light can be polarized, which means its waves line up in a set way. That pattern can reveal the shape of gas, dust, and fields around stars and black holes.

Their code, Kratos-polrad, runs on graphics cards to gain speed. It sends many test rays through a model scene and tracks how each ray bends and twists. The code keeps the twist of the light correct at each step. Fast and correct runs like this help teams test ideas about what a scope should see.
arxiv-2512-01583:
Nicola Fabiano proves a fixed point result in quantum metric spaces. In such spaces, distance between states is set by the L2 norm. Contraction maps shrink distances at each step. In classic spaces, they must hit one fixed point.

Fabiano shows the same holds in the quantum frame. He proves both existence and uniqueness of the point. He also argues the quantum frame has structural gains over fuzzy frames. Fixed point results back iterative methods used across physics, economics, and data science. The proof uses no extra compactness claims, which keeps its scope broad across the quantum spaces where such maps arise in practice.
arxiv-2512-02083:
Domination problems ask how to place guards on a network so every node is covered, and the Roman variant lets some posts count double. Sangam Balchandar Reddy analyzes in 2025 the computational complexity of signed Roman domination, where vertices receive values that can also be negative.

A signed Roman dominating function must give every closed neighborhood a positive total weight while obeying rules at each vertex. Knowing whether finding the best such assignment is easy or provably hard guides algorithm designers. Complexity results like this sort network optimization problems into those worth attacking exactly and those needing heuristics.
arxiv-2512-02283:
Self-driving and other safety-critical machines increasingly explain themselves by recovering the equations that govern them, a technique called model recovery. Bin Xu, Ayan Banerjee, and Sandeep Gupta tackle in 2025 the problem of running that recovery on small edge devices, where memory and energy are tight.

The obstacle is the method's engine, neural ordinary differential equations, whose iterative solving maps poorly onto FPGA hardware. The authors adapt model recovery to survive those resource constraints while staying real-time. Explainable decisions matter most exactly where edge devices operate, in physical systems whose failures are dangerous and whose reasoning must be auditable.
arxiv-2512-02483:
Rozhin Mohammadikian and three co-authors ask whether news and ideas spread through social networks by chance. Online platforms now move posts faster and wider than ever before. If spread followed clear patterns, those patterns could be mapped and perhaps predicted.

Working with real world hashtag data, the team finds that spread is not random at all. Hashtags travel along preferred routes, following specific patterns as they move between users. Findings like these matter for anyone who studies rumors, campaigns, or viral posts, since the path a message takes shapes who sees it. That kind of map helps explain why some posts fade fast and some spread far and wide.
arxiv-2512-02683:
Luiz A. Rodrigues, Elias P. Duarte Jr., and Luciana Arantes build self managing broadcast trees for distributed systems. Sending one message to all processes by direct flood overloads the sender. A spanning tree spreads that load, passing each message along shared branches.

Their autonomic algorithm lets the processes build and maintain the tree themselves. When machines join, leave, or fail, the tree repairs its own shape. Self healing communication backbones keep large systems running through churn, a basic need for cloud services and sensor networks alike. A tree that heals on its own needs no crew on call, which is the whole point for far flung nets.
arxiv-2512-02783:
Björn Þór Jónsson and three co-authors ask what quality and diversity should mean when a computer explores sounds. Digital synthesis opens parameter spaces with millions of possible sounds. Quality diversity algorithms search such spaces well, but only if sounds are measured in the right features.

Handcrafted descriptors and trained classifiers can bias the search toward familiar sonic regions. The team explores definitions of quality and diversity inside sonic measurement spaces. Better measures could help sound designers and musicians discover genuinely new timbres, not just variations on sounds already known. What counts as a new sound is the hinge here. Set the bar by ear, by plot, or by rule, and the hunt takes a new path each time.
arxiv-2512-02983:
Louis McConnell and four co-authors map the neighborhoods of tumors so treatments can be tailored better. The spatial architecture of the tumor microenvironment shapes how cancer grows and responds. ProteinPNet learns from spatial proteomics data, which records many proteins across tissue locations.

Built on prototypical part networks, the framework discovers recurring microenvironment motifs directly. Unlike post hoc explanation tools, it learns interpretable spatial prototypes during supervised training itself. Faithful prototypes could help oncologists read a tumor's layout and choose therapy with the tissue context in view. A map of tumor hoods in plain forms gives drug teams a place to aim. A black box score can not give them that at all.
arxiv-2512-03183:
Heavy grains settle as they move in turbulent flow. Y. Zhang, D. H. Richter, and A. D. Bragg study that settling near walls in this 2025 work. Gravity gives grains a settling speed and also changes how they interact with the flow.

Wall direction matters, the authors explain. When a wall is flat, both effects push grains toward it. When a wall is upright, only the second effect acts. Knowing these rules helps predict dust, ash, and pollutant spread in pipes, rooms, and the atmosphere. Settling rules also affect how ash and dust coat surfaces in homes and factories.
arxiv-2512-03483:
Fluid equations with randomness need careful numerical analysis. Binjie Li and Qin Zhou study two-dimensional stochastic Navier-Stokes equations in this 2025 work. Their system includes transport noise and no-slip boundaries on a convex polygonal domain.

The main challenge is a lack of spatial regularity in the solution. That gap blocks standard error analysis techniques. The authors establish strong convergence rates for the spatial finite element discretization. Proven rates tell engineers how much to trust simulations of turbulent, noisy flows. Transport noise models how flows stir particles, a key effect in environmental fluids.
arxiv-2512-03983:
Networks can carry several kinds of connection at once, each changing over time: messages, calls, and meetings between the same people. Maximilian Baum, Francesco Sanna Passino, and Axel Gandy ask how to test whether those layers genuinely differ in a 2025 statistics preprint. Each layer is a graph generated from positions in a latent space.

The proposed test asks whether all layers share one common latent representation or whether some layer has drifted apart. Its statistic comes from a spectral embedding of the unfolded adjacency matrices stacked together. The authors prove the test detects differences as the networks grow large, and they check its behaviour in simulations. A biological dataset, neural activity in larval fruit flies, serves as a real-world trial. The method can also compare time points rather than layers.
arxiv-2512-05083:
S. J. Paul and a very large collaboration report the first measurement of how pions and slow protons emerge when an electron smashes into an atomic nucleus. The pattern of their relative angles reveals how a nucleus responds when a fast quark tears through it, a process central to electron-nucleus experiments. The team used the CLAS detector, firing an electron beam at targets of deuterium, carbon, iron, and lead.

For heavier nuclei, the pion-proton pairs spread more widely in angle than for lighter ones, and the widening is stronger than earlier two-pion studies found. Heavy targets also yield more protons per pion, though the rise levels off for the heaviest nuclei. Leading simulation programs reproduce these trends in outline, which supports their picture of how nuclei fragment. But the data's precision exposes disagreements in detail, marking where models of cold nuclear matter need work.
arxiv-2512-05183:
Guillermo Alonso-Linaje and five co-authors present a compiler that loads classical data into quantum circuits at the lowest cost. Encoding a data vector as a quantum state is a bottleneck for quantum algorithms, and the loading method depends on the data and on how much error is tolerable. Their framework takes a target vector and an error budget and chooses a strategy by itself, splitting the budget between precision and approximation.

The compiler commands a suite of loaders, from multiplexer schemes and quantum read-only memory to matrix product states and Walsh-based operators. On applications it finds non-obvious, cheaper strategies. In a fluid-dynamics workflow it cuts resource needs by more than ten thousand times over approaches. The project yields a leaner circuit for a class of matrices and an optimized encoding of kinetic energy, arguing that approximation-aware automation is essential for quantum computing.
arxiv-2512-05383:
Mara Downing and four co-authors bring a software-testing weapon to the safety of brain stimulation. Machine learning models generate the electrical patterns delivered by neuroprosthetics such as retinal implants, and a bad pattern goes straight into neural tissue. The authors adapt coverage-guided fuzzing to hunt for stimulation patterns that break biophysical safety limits. Coverage-guided fuzzing is automated stress testing that mutates inputs and watches for failures. The limits cover charge density, current, and electrode co-activation.

The framework treats the stimulus encoders as black boxes and steers the search with coverage metrics measuring how broadly the tests span possible outputs and violation types. Applied to deep encoders for retina and cortex, it uncovers diverse regimes exceeding established limits, and two coverage metrics prove best at finding varied violations. Safety becomes a measurable property of the model, a basis for benchmarking and regulation in neural interfaces.
arxiv-2512-05483:
Yingang Fan, Binjie Ding, and Baiyi Chen forecast low-altitude air turbulence by factorizing the wind field itself. Turbulence near the ground is chaotic and hard to observe; with only wind-profile radar data, traditional predictors struggle to say what the air is doing between measurements. The authors' model treats the three-dimensional wind field as a large, mostly empty table of numbers and learns its hidden low-rank structure with a neural Tucker decomposition.

Two ideas make it work. Continuous wind data are discretized so the decomposition machinery can consume them. A four-dimensional interaction tensor is built to represent every possible interplay among heights and the three wind components across space and time. On datasets with missing observations, the discretized model estimates the gaps better than a range of regression models. For aviation and drone operations, better turbulence reconstruction from sparse radar is a safety gain.
arxiv-2512-05683:
Yong En Kok and six co-authors built ZRNet, a system that repairs microscope images blurred by optical aberrations. When lenses bend light unevenly, the wavefront warps and fine detail smears, worse deep inside a sample. Such warps can be written as sums of Zernike patterns. Older tools treat the job as a black box and handle only mild warps. ZRNet instead puts the physics of the warp inside the model.

A graph module links the Zernike patterns by their physical relations, so corrections respect the physics. The network predicts the warp and restores the image jointly. A new loss works in the frequency domain, keeping the two outputs consistent with each other. On a large public set of cell images, the system set the best scores for both restoration and warp prediction. It also held up on data from a real microscope and under realistic sensor noise.
arxiv-2512-05783:
Maryam Yousefi and Soodeh Bakhshandeh rebuild full three dimensional scenes from depth data that is ninety five percent missing. Depth sensors often return only scattered points, and naive reconstruction leaves shapes warped. Their method adds one geometric rule to a variational autoencoder: a curvature penalty built from a discrete Laplacian, which discourages needlessly wrinkled surfaces. The surprise is how much that single, well chosen term achieves.

Reconstruction accuracy came out about a fifth better than a standard variational autoencoder. The authors stress the wider lesson: stacking several geometric penalties does not beat one good one, and can do worse. Their single term also gives stable gradients and suppresses noise, while adding only a modest training overhead and no cost at all when the trained model runs. For engineers, the paper argues for restraint: pick the constraint that matches the geometry.
arxiv-2512-05883:
Juan Sosa, Carlos Martínez, and Danna Cruz offer a full introduction to Bayesian inference, the approach to statistics that treats uncertainty as probability and learning as updating. The paper opens with Bayes' theorem and the philosophical split from frequentist practice. It then builds the framework: estimation, intervals, hypothesis testing, and prediction. Canonical models show how prior information and data combine into posterior distributions.

Key ideas each get their due: loss functions, credible intervals, Bayes factors for comparing hypotheses, identifiability, and what happens as data grows without bound. The authors favor settings where answers can be computed exactly, which keeps the logic transparent. Modern extensions driven by simulation are sketched, along with the standing difficulties of choosing priors and checking models. The paper closes toward hierarchical models, nonparametrics, and applications in time series, space, and networks. It is a rigorous, welcoming doorway into the Bayesian way.
arxiv-2512-05983:
Eyal Briman, Ehud Shapiro, and Nimrod Talmon ask language models to do the work of a mediator: find the sentence everyone can sign. Coalition formation gathers agents around proposals a majority prefers to the status quo. The hard step is the compromise itself. Their model adds bounded rationality and uncertainty; their algorithms draft compromises for writing text together.

Language processing supplies a semantic space where compromise points can be computed. Simulations show groups forming around the drafts. The ambition is democratic tooling. Writing a constitution, a charter, or community rules is usually slowed by whoever holds the pen and whoever can attend the meeting. AI drafted compromises, tested for majority support before humans ever vote, could let very large groups genuinely co-author their founding texts. What is offered is the pipeline, plus evidence that it behaves.
arxiv-2512-06083:
Yaguang Li and a large collaboration turn one well measured star system into a courtroom for brown dwarf theory. Its companion, about seventy five Jupiter masses, sits where cooling models disagree most. The primary's oscillations give one age; its rotation gives another. Combined, the system is about two and a quarter billion years old, with unusual precision.

Orbit fitting pins the mass precisely. Six cooling models must pass the combined test. One modern model family, with an updated equation of state, agrees with everything. The other five strain at one to three sigma, and some cannot make the companion dim enough at any age for its measured mass. Such benchmarks show theorists which interior physics needs repair.
arxiv-2512-06183:
Lindong Liu, Zhixiong Jin, and Seongjin Choi reconstruct the full speed map of a highway from the five percent of it sensors actually see. Loop detectors leave the speed field sparse and noisy. Its diffusion prior trains directly on sparse fields. Mask aware training teaches the model the shape of missingness.

A physics guided sampler alternates diffusion, observation, and smoothing steps. It beat baselines at five percent visibility, nearly matching full data training. Dense sensing may be unnecessary. Small cities could afford full quality maps. Tests ran on a real interstate dataset.
arxiv-2512-06483:
Elias-Leander Ahlers, Witold Brunsmann, and Malte Schilling test whether large language models can grade how well a person writes German. Schools sort learners into the levels of the Common European Framework, from beginner to near native, so teaching can match the learner. Human grading is slow, so an automatic grader that teachers can trust would help a great deal.

The team built a broad training set by merging several existing graded corpora with synthetic texts. They then compared three routes: careful prompting of a ready model, fine tuning a LLaMA model on the graded set, and probing the model's internal state as a signal for the level. All three beat earlier published methods, they report, with steady gains across the board. The study supports language models as reliable, scalable graders for language level, at least for German texts of the kinds tested.
arxiv-2512-06583:
Jeremy McEntire argues that forced ranking systems in companies misjudge people by design, not by poor execution. In these systems each team must rank its members and fit a fixed spread: a set share at the top for promotion, a set share at the bottom for firing. The stated aim is to force honest differentiation and solve the problem of managers who rate everyone alike.

Through agent based simulation, McEntire shows the mechanism itself scrambles the verdicts. With random team assignment, about a third of firing and promotion calls were wrong, purely because strong and weak teams differ. Under realistic gaps in manager skill, errors passed half, with false calls outnumbering right ones. The usual fix, calibration across teams, turns into a contest of persuasion. Over time, workers play safe, and top performers leave. Firms, the paper argues, should judge the system itself.
arxiv-2512-06883:
Zhongtao Rao and co-authors improve online recommenders that use both product images and text by adapting large vision-language models to the job. Two problems block the way. First, shopping data differs from the general data these models learned on, so their internal maps of items end up misaligned. Second, when one shared adapter is tuned for both image and text, the learning signals clash and blur what makes each view distinct.

Their framework, SDA, attacks both problems with light additions. One part uses structure inside each view as a soft teacher to pull the maps into line. Another part splits the tuning into expert paths with gates, so image and text updates stop fighting. Added to existing recommenders and tested on three public Amazon data sets, SDA lifted ranking quality, with the biggest gains on rarely bought items. It did so while adding little cost at run time.
arxiv-2512-06983:
Eli J Laird and Corey Clark ask how long a world model can remember. Such models let an agent dream ahead, predicting future scenes from past views and actions, but the dream blurs: recently seen places fade as the imagined rollout stretches. The authors sort memory aids into two kinds, ways of encoding what to keep and ways of injecting it back into the model's stream of thought.

Twenty pairings of four encoders and five injectors were tested in a maze environment built for memory research. One encoder, based on a modern recurrent design called mLSTM, beat all rivals on both quality measures. Paired with simple additive injection, it recalled best at a fair price, matching or edging a pure state-space backbone. The study covers one environment; effects on task performance are left for later work.
arxiv-2512-07283:
Sebastian Lundström and co-authors ask how the quantum vacuum's response to strong fields changes when the field lives inside a plasma of real electrons and positrons. Vacuum polarization, the virtual-particle dressing of electromagnetic fields, is usually computed in empty space. In astrophysical and high-intensity laser settings, though, the vacuum is never alone: a sea of real charges shares the stage.

Starting from quantum kinetic equations, expanded for weak fields and slow change. The authors show the Dirac field's evolution can be told through classical-style distribution functions for the real electrons and positrons. Those distributions are coupled weakly by quantum terms, and the coupling reproduces the known vacuum polarization expressions, plus new corrections proportional to the real particle content. Which correction leads depends on the plasma's starting density: sparse plasmas are governed by the virtual dressing, dense ones by their own real particles.
arxiv-2512-07383:
Deepika S N Vemuri and co-authors give concept-based neural networks a sense of logic. In a concept bottleneck model, the network must explain itself: it first names human-readable concepts in an image, then predicts from those names, which makes its reasoning inspectable. The catch is that the prediction is usually a plain weighted sum of concepts, too blunt to express relations like both, either, or not. LogicCBM inserts a module that wires the learned concepts together with differentiable logic operations.

Because the logic steps are themselves learnable end to end, the model can compose concepts into richer rules while keeping its answers readable. On well-known benchmarks and on synthetic data sets, the logic-enhanced models were more accurate than their linear parents.
arxiv-2512-07483:
Daniel Fürst, Matthijs Jansen op de Haar, Mennatallah El-Assady, Daniel Keim, and Maximilian Fischer wrote this 2025 paper on guided data exploration. Interactive tours walk newcomers through a dataset one view at a time. That straight-line format helps beginners, but it locks the path in advance.

In fields like law, a fixed path gets in the way. Lawyers must branch off, test rival readings, and build chains of argument. The authors propose SemanticTours, a model that turns tours into graphs. A domain knowledge graph links data items through meanings the user defines. Tours then wander that graph instead of marching down a line. The team shapes the idea for legal case analysis, with a matching visual design. Aggregated nodes and a semantic lens keep the complex graph readable. Six legal experts judged the graph tours against plain sequences. They found the branching tours fit their reasoning better.
arxiv-2512-07683:
Cong Li and sixteen co-authors wrote this 2025 materials physics paper on a crystal called CrSb. CrSb is a leading example of an altermagnet, with spin patterns but no net magnetism. The team asks what extreme stretching does to it.

Flat bands and altermagnetism both grow out of lattice symmetry and orbital mixing. A huge distortion could merge the two themes in one material. The authors built a strain device with a tailored crystal mount. It imposes a strong tensile strain gradient through the bulk crystal. The near-surface layer ends up far more distorted than the bulk beneath. Photoemission measurements reveal two regimes as strain grows. At moderate strain, flat-band features sharpen reversibly. At larger strain, bonds partly decouple and the surface turns largely insulating. Calculations show the altermagnetic spin texture survives across that whole range. Strain, they argue, can tune correlated and spin-textured states together.
arxiv-2512-07883:
Anupama Ghorai and Jitraj Saha wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on how particles clump together. Aggregation equations track clusters as they merge and grow over time. A condensing version adds the reverse process, clusters breaking apart again.

The authors study the passage from many discrete sizes to a smooth continuum. Their setting is the most general form of that two-way equation. The kinetic kernels driving merging and splitting need not match each other. They approximate the continuous equation by a chain of discrete ones. Weak compactness arguments then carry the chain to the true solution. Existence for the discrete model is proven along the way. Uniform bounds on moments of all orders support the limit passage. Long-time behavior gets its own analysis in the paper. Blowup can mean mass draining away or a gel forming from the clusters. Three numerical experiments confirm the approximations converge as designed.
arxiv-2512-08183:
Sanika Damle and Radhika Krishnan, researchers who study online media, posted an exploratory study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is how climate change is framed on YouTube, and whether the framing splits along the Global North and Global South divide. They analyze hundreds of English language videos tied to major climate negotiation events, plus the comments under them.

Using topic modeling on transcripts and sentiment analysis on comments, they find clear contrasts. Videos from the Global North stress cutting emissions and institutional duty more often. Videos from the Global South put development concerns first. Audience reactions split even more sharply: comments under Northern videos lean toward criticism and conspiracy talk. Comments under Southern videos are more supportive and constructive. The authors argue a gap exists between polished narratives and public feeling on the platform, whose dynamics may deepen or reshape the old divide in climate talk.
arxiv-2512-08283:
James P Vary, Chandan Mondal, and colleagues, nuclear physicists, posted a long review on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the internal structure of the nucleon, the proton and neutron, as computed with basis light front quantization. That framework is a relativistic, nonperturbative way to solve quantum field theory, giving wave functions for the particles inside.

The review traces the method growth from a simple three quark starting sector to richer ones that add a gluon, then sea quarks. With each step, the approach reaches new observables: gluon helicity, orbital angular momentum, and three dimensional images of where quarks and gluons sit. The newest milestone computes wave functions from the quantum chromodynamics Hamiltonian without an added confining potential. Results agree qualitatively with experiment, and the authors argue the framework now offers an increasingly complete, first principles picture of the nucleon.
arxiv-2512-08583:
Jesper Nederlof studies fast exact methods for hard path and subset problems in theoretical computer science. He introduces a data structure called a Dynamic Representative Set that keeps a compact summary of a large family of sets. The structure supports merging families, combining elements, and asking whether a disjoint set of a given size exists.

With that tool, Nederlof gives a deterministic method for the weighted directed k path problem, which asks for the cheapest path through a set number of vertices. The running time is close to the best known bounds and settles a question asked often in the field. The same structure also helps with several other problems, showing how one clean idea can speed up many exact algorithms at once.
arxiv-2512-08783:
Fabio Chalub and Max Souza examine when finite and infinite population models in genetics tell the same long term story. Two standard tools are compared: the replicator equation for large populations and the Moran process for finite ones. Their relationship is rarely discussed, despite wide use of both.

Except for degenerate cases, the authors fully characterize when the two models match in long term dynamics. That match means a one to one link between stable attractors of the equation and metastable states of the finite process. A key step extends the large population formula for fixation probability to almost arbitrary interactions, including multi player games. The authors also solve the inverse problem of building a finite process for a given replicator dynamics. Results connect to the Lewontin paradox and to classic ideas of metastability in stochastic processes.
arxiv-2512-09583:
Alberto Rota leads a team presenting UnReflectAnything, a system that removes specular highlights, the bright glare spots on shiny surfaces, from a single photograph. Highlights distort appearance, hide texture, and interfere with geometry estimation in photos and in surgical imagery alike. Earlier methods needed special inputs or capture setups.

Their framework works from one RGB image. It predicts a highlight map and a reflection-free reconstruction of the scene at the same time. It uses a vision transformer encoder for multi-scale features, a light head to localize the glare, and a token-level inpainting module that repairs corrupted features before the final image is formed. Because paired training examples barely exist, they built a Virtual Highlight Synthesis pipeline that renders plausible highlights on arbitrary photos using estimated geometry, Fresnel-aware shading, and randomized lighting. The system generalizes across natural and surgical domains and reaches competitive results on benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-09683:
Gefei Cai and Zhuoyan Xie compute the probability of a backbone event for a Brownian path in the plane. The question comes from critical percolation theory, where the backbone of a cluster, the part carrying flow between two points, has its own statistics. For Brownian motion, the analogue asks whether the random trajectory contains two disjoint subpaths connecting the neighborhood of its starting point out to a macroscopic distance.

Such connections are rare when the starting neighborhood is small, and the authors determine how the probability decays as that neighborhood shrinks. The decay is governed by a constant divided by the double logarithm of the small scale, with a sharp asymptotic formula including the vanishing error term. Establishing the constant, rather than bounds up to constants, is the paper's improvement over its earlier version. The result quantifies how unlikely it is for a random path to bridge scales twice independently.
arxiv-2512-10483:
Mladen Pavicic disputes a recent claim about the simplest Kochen-Specker set, a geometric arrangement used to prove that quantum measurements cannot all have preset outcomes. A 2025 paper announced the simplest three-dimensional contextual set, with a stated count of vertices and bases. Pavicic argues the discovery is neither new nor fundamental.

He shows the same set had already been produced in a 2023 paper, and that many three-dimensional contextual sets exist with fewer complete bases, undercutting the claim of special status. He further shows that automatic generation from basic vector parts recovers all known minimal sets in any dimension at no real computing cost. The short paper closes by sorting out the varieties of contextual sets and the loose definitions that let such claims arise.
arxiv-2512-10883:
Thomas Donlon, Sukanya Chakrabarti, and Jason Hunt weigh two of the Milky Way's satellite galaxies by feeling their pull on nearby pulsars. Dwarf satellites test galaxy formation and cosmology, but measuring their masses through stellar motions is muddied by the processes that stir the galaxy's stars. Pulsar timing offers a cleaner handle: millisecond pulsars are exquisite clocks, and their timing reveals the acceleration of the solar neighbourhood.

As the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Sagittarius dwarf orbit, they warp the disc. They also offset the dark halo from the baryonic disc. This produces an asymmetry in accelerations above and below the disc plane near the Sun. The size of that asymmetry depends on the satellites' masses. The team matched a grid of simulations to the pulsar data and measured both masses. The results are competitive with earlier values. Yet they are independent of stellar kinematics for the first time.
arxiv-2512-10983:
Merlin Pelz, Skirmantas Janusonis, and Gregory Handy build a mathematical model of how serotonin moves in brain tissue outside cells. Serotonin is a major signalling chemical released from many small sites called varicosities. Its behaviour plays out at tiny distances and brief times, so it stays poorly understood despite its importance for brain flexibility.

Their framework couples spreading and chemical reactions in realistic tissue settings. Using perturbation methods, they reduce the system to a simpler set of linked equations that still capture the spreading. Results cover average steady levels, bounds, and the highest and lowest spike values, backed by a fast solver. The model shows varicosities forming shared local pools of serotonin and helps interpret imaging data and the action of common antidepressant drugs.
arxiv-2512-11083:
Grant Peel and Ersegun Deniz Gedikli compare two sources of sea ice information used for safe shipping in Alaskan waters. Regional ice charts from the Alaska Sea Ice Program are drawn by analysts, while the Copernicus service derives ice concentration from satellites. As climate change reshapes Arctic ice edges, knowing where the two disagree matters for navigation risk.

Aligning more than fifteen years of daily data on a common grid, the team found that the satellite product consistently reports less ice than the regional charts. Gaps were largest near shore and in broken ice zones, including Cook Inlet, where land contamination blurs satellite pixels. Both sources captured the same main patterns of ice change. Using ship tracking data with a polar risk framework, they found many vessel observations fell in elevated risk conditions, supporting combined use of both products.
arxiv-2512-11183:
Alwin Jin, Sean Hendryx, and Vaskar Nath argue that AI benchmarks should measure scientific progress itself, not just scores on fixed problem sets. Today's language model tests use static, already solved problems, and the field keeps answering with bigger static collections. That cycle limits which advances get noticed and rewarded.

Their alternative is a progress oriented benchmark whose target is an open scientific objective, so topping it literally moves the field. As a first example they build an environment around the NanoGPT speedrun, a community race to train a small language model faster. Standardised data, a reference model, detailed telemetry, and anti gaming checks keep runs honest. Evaluation centres on the best loss reached and the cost frontier. Using it, they set a new training time record and saw genuinely new algorithmic ideas emerge.
arxiv-2512-11283:
Yi-Nan Chen, Yong-Kun Zhang, and Zi-Gao Dai use a new statistic to ask whether fast radio bursts come from starquakes on neutron stars or from collisions with passing interstellar objects. The two ideas predict different behaviour: quakes should cluster and relax like earthquakes, while collisions should arrive as an unrelated random stream.

Their tool, the energy structure function, tracks how burst energies change with the time gap between events in active repeating sources. Earthquakes show a clear pattern, with pair energy differences growing over short gaps, but the radio bursts show nothing of the kind. Instead their energy behaviour closely matches a purely stochastic process. The result argues that repeating bursts are not quake driven, favouring a series of unrelated triggers such as impacts on a neutron star. That distinction narrows the search for the bursts' long mysterious origin.
arxiv-2512-11483:
F. Javier Cardama and Tomás Pena bring a programming style that supercomputing programmers already know to distributed quantum computing. Running a quantum method across several networked machines could overcome the limits of today's small, noisy devices, but developers currently hand manage entanglement links and standard synchronisation in verbose, error prone code.

Their NetQMPI library mirrors the classic Message Passing Interface, letting one program run across many quantum nodes with a shared communicator abstraction. Point to point operations are joined by new collective operations designed around the no cloning rule of quantum mechanics, using multipartite entanglement to distribute data. Code for building a shared entangled state across any number of nodes shrinks from quadratic complexity to constant. The setup runs on physical simulators today and aims at future hardware following the same standards.
arxiv-2512-11683:
Qiushi Guo proposes Depth-Copy-Paste, a way to fake more training photos for face finding systems. Face detectors fail more under blocked views, odd light, and busy scenes, so they need varied practice data. Plain copy and paste tricks often look fake, with bad edges, wrong scale, or clashing backgrounds.

The new method pairs whole people with scenes that fit in meaning and depth. BLIP and CLIP scores pick good backgrounds, SAM3 cuts clean body masks, and a depth tool trims hidden parts. A sliding search then sets each person at a spot with smooth depth and right scale. Detectors trained with these fakes did far better on hard test sets.
arxiv-2512-11883:
Wenqi Marshall Guo and co-authors argue that pushing image generators toward one shared idea of beauty harms art. When users ask for ugly, raw, or low quality images for artistic or critical aims, aligned models often refuse in effect, defaulting to pretty output. That habit puts developer taste over user intent.

The team built a wide spectrum aesthetics data set and tested top generators and reward models. Aligned generators repeatedly beautified what should stay rough. Worse, reward models scored down anti aesthetic images even when they matched the prompt exactly. Editing tests and real abstract art checks confirm the bias. The paper defends plural taste in image tools.
arxiv-2512-11983:
Nat Sothanaphan questions a long held guess about the growth of certain number sequences. Stanley sequences start from a small set and grow by always adding the smallest number that avoids three term arithmetic patterns. Starting sets split into regular types with known growth and irregular types thought to grow like n squared over log n.

The case starting from 0 and 4 is the flagship irregular candidate, yet nothing is proven. Sothanaphan numeric evidence now pushes against the guessed rate. The upper bound may hold, but the lower bound looks too strong, likely of the form n to the 2 minus delta. The sequence seems less random than assumed, a subtlety the paper probes with care.
arxiv-2512-12083:
Guanfang Dong and co-authors present RePack then Refine, a way to feed rich vision features into image generators without slowing them down. Vision foundation models supply meaning rich features, but those features are bulky and redundant, which makes diffusion transformers slow to train.

The RePack step squeezes the features onto a compact manifold, keeping structure and dropping waste. A diffusion transformer then learns generation in that small space. A final Latent-Guided Refiner restores fine detail lost in the squeeze. On ImageNet, the large model reached an FID of 1.82 in just 64 training epochs, and 1.65 with the refiner added. That is far faster convergence than rival latent diffusion models.
arxiv-2512-12483:
Lily Erickson explores using transformer models to attack elliptic curve cryptography in a 2025 paper. Elliptic curve methods, such as the secp256r1 curve, protect much of modern web traffic and systems like Bitcoin. They rest on the gap between easy key creation and hard reversal: given a public key, finding its private key should be infeasible.

Erickson tests whether a language model style architecture can learn to reverse the key generation process, effectively solving the curve. A second test asks how well models can memorize public and private key pairs. The paper frames both proof for and proof against as valuable outcomes, and closes with thoughts on where the field may head.
arxiv-2512-12583:
Safwan Shaheer and five co-authors train classifiers to detect prompt injection attacks in a 2025 paper. Prompt injection tricks an AI integrated app into following attacker instructions hidden in user input, a risk for large web systems. The team curated and augmented a prompt injection data set based on the HackAPrompt Playground Submissions corpus, a public collection of attack attempts.

They trained several classifiers on that data, including LSTM networks, feed forward neural networks, Random Forest, and Naive Bayes, to flag malicious prompts. The approach improves detection and mitigation of such attacks, the authors report, helping protect targeted applications and systems that embed large language models.
arxiv-2512-13183:
Alfredo Gonzalez-Calvin, Juan Jimenez, and Hector Garcia de Marina present a method that turns rough planned routes for mobile robots into smooth, drivable paths. Planners often output straight segments joined at corners. Tracking algorithms, though, need paths with well-defined curvature, above all for robots that cannot turn in place.

Their method uses mollification, a smoothing technique that can approach the rough path as closely as desired while staying smooth. They give a systematic way to bound the curvature of the paths produced. The approach is shown to be faster than standard interpolation methods, fast enough for microcontrollers, and compatible with common tracking and following algorithms.
arxiv-2512-13783:
Federico Sestito and Chiaki Kobayashi use Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument data to confirm members of Local Group dwarf galaxies. They cross-match DESI targets with candidate members picked from Gaia proper motions, positions, and photometry. Adding DESI radial velocities secures membership in 15 systems.

Their results confirm Gaia-based selection keeps foreground contamination low. Two stars may belong to DES J0225+0304, which would give its first systemic radial velocity, minus 150.0 plus or minus 7.0 kilometers per second. In Sextans, they trace stellar motion out to about 10 half-light radii. Metal-poor stars there are hotter in velocity and more spread out than metal-rich ones. They also flag 8 ultra metal-poor candidates needing higher quality spectra.
arxiv-2512-13883:
Philipp Fleig proposes a renormalization group approach to collapse eigenvalue spectra of random matrices across system sizes. Random matrix models describe complex systems, but spectra at different sizes are hard to compare directly. His fix is to let the model normalization run with size, setting a natural spectral scale.

That running turns raw spectra into comparable, collapsed density curves. He demonstrates the method on generalized Wigner and Wishart ensembles with power-law variance profiles. Self-consistent fixed-point equations give the eigenvalue densities, and a decimation scheme defines the flow and its Beta function. Spectral collapse is confirmed in simulations and in solutions of the fixed-point equations. Fleig expects the approach to carry to other ensembles and complex system data.
arxiv-2512-14083:
Sungnyun Kim's PhD thesis builds scalable frameworks for audio-visual speech recognition in real-world settings. Such systems read both sound and lip movement, but real settings degrade them with noise and visual interference. Kim argues a layered approach is needed to reach robust scale.

At the feature level, the work builds a unified model whose audio-visual features resist diverse corruptions and carry to new settings. At the architecture level, it expands model capacity and allocates compute by input traits. At the system level, modular links with large foundation models add their strength to raise accuracy. Together, the three levels aim at a reliable next-generation system.
arxiv-2512-14283:
Hao Zhao, Qianjun Zheng, and Peng Yan show how curved films can create magnon frequency combs in a 2025 paper. Magnons are waves of magnetic spin, and a frequency comb is a set of evenly spaced tones. Making one from a single drive tone usually needs complex spin textures like skyrmions.

In curved ferromagnetic thin films, curvature turns the flat resonance into a localized, redshifted magnon bound state. Under off resonant driving, that state triggers step by step three magnon scattering, aided by curvature driven anisotropy and Dzyaloshinskii Moriya interaction. The result is a robust comb whose spacing is set by the bound mode frequency. Simulations confirm the effect, and a curvature gradient even mimics an event horizon.
arxiv-2512-14383:
Tiago Pernambuco and Lucas Céleri recast quantum thermodynamics in geometric language, building on a recent gauge theory where redundant information comes from a set of changes called the thermodynamic group. Classical thermodynamics discards microscopic detail, but quantum systems can be controlled closely, so information plays a central role in their thermal behavior.

The authors construct the principal fibre bundle behind the theory and show that two distinct but related geometric structures arise from it. Putting thermodynamics into the same geometric language as other fundamental theories lets its basic features be studied through shape and topology. Readers gain a formal map of how the gauge picture is organized.
arxiv-2512-14583:
A quantum computer is only as good as its readout: the starting configuration of its qubits must be inferred, often from a weak measurement record that changes over time. The catch is that the measurement process and the system's own dynamics can scramble that starting information.

Five researchers examine how much of the initial state can still be recovered from such sequential weak measurements, and where the loss becomes permanent.
