Their limits tell experimentalists when a readout scheme can work in principle and when no clever processing can rescue the data. That guidance matters for building reliable qubit readout in real devices.
arxiv-2512-14783:
J. Alfonso L. Aguerri and a large team of coauthors argue that the Northern Hemisphere needs a telescope 30 to 40 meters wide. Their case here centers on the smallest galaxies known, with stars totaling just 100,000 to 10 million times the mass of the Sun. Such dwarfs feel feedback, early radiation, and their surroundings more strongly than big galaxies do.

With a spectrograph that samples many points at once on such a telescope, the team would survey dwarfs in the Coma Cluster and in groups, filaments, and empty regions. The data would map how their stars formed, what their gas holds, and how the galaxies move inside. That would test ideas about dark matter, early feedback, and how surroundings shut down star birth in the smallest systems.
arxiv-2512-14983:
Roberto Vila and a coauthor study the Gini coefficient, a standard measure of inequality, and the bias in how it is estimated from samples. An estimator is biased when its average value misses the true value. The authors find a general formula for the expected estimate, built from the Laplace transform of the underlying distribution and a tilted version of it.

That formula yields a fresh characterization of the gamma family of distributions, based on how it behaves under exponential tilting. It also proves the Gini estimator is biased for Poisson and geometric populations, and unbiased for gamma ones. The team then builds bias corrected estimators and tests them in Monte Carlo simulations. The corrected versions improve sharply on the original in small samples, and the whole approach rests on scale invariance rather than case by case algebra.
arxiv-2512-15083:
Yifei Li and four coauthors rebuild elastic simulation as a set of neural modules that mirror classic solvers. Learned simulators usually train one big network end to end, which is fast but can lose physical reliability and clarity. Classical simulators, by contrast, work in stages with clear physical quantities between them.

Neural Modular Physics splits elastic dynamics into neural modules joined by those in between quantities. That split allows direct supervision of intermediate values and physical constraints during training. In tests, the system generalized better to new starting conditions and resolutions than rival neural simulators. It stayed stable over long runs and preserved physical properties more faithfully. It also handled cases where the true dynamics are unknown better than classic solvers did, blending learning's flexibility with a solver's discipline.
arxiv-2512-15183:
Mika Hämäläinen and a coauthor draw a pointed parallel between grading AI generated text and grading students in the age of ChatGPT. Both fields, they argue, suffer the same Great Misalignment Problem. At their Finnish university, as in natural language generation research, judges score final products while the process that made them stays hidden.

When students can produce polished work with tools like ChatGPT, product based grades lose their validity as proof of learning. The authors propose Pedagogical Multi-Factor Assessment, or P-MFA. Borrowed from multi factor authentication, it gathers several kinds of process evidence instead of one final artifact. The model aims to restore trust in assessment by checking learning as it happens, from many angles at once.
arxiv-2512-15383:
Yunjie Fan and Matteo Sesia present a conformal prediction method for several related outputs at once in a 2025 paper. Conformal prediction wraps a model forecast in an interval that covers the true value with a stated chance. Making tight intervals for many outputs from one input, with a firm coverage promise, is the hard part.

Their key idea is a coordinate wise scaling step that makes errors across outputs directly comparable, using the calibration data itself to set the scales. It needs no model of how outputs depend on each other and no extra data split. Tests on simulated and real data give tighter intervals than prior methods while keeping valid coverage.
arxiv-2512-15483:
Luca Torresi and Pascal Friederich extend Bayesian optimization for self driving labs in a 2025 paper. Such labs use robots and machine learning to run experiments with little human help. The usual search method assumes a fixed workflow where only the final measurement counts, which forces many real experiments to be simplified.

Their multi stage version allows flexible sampling of staged workflows and uses intermediate readings, called proxy measurements, to guide decisions on the fly. Across a wide range of test scenarios, using proxy readings finds good solutions faster and reaches better final results than standard Bayesian optimization. The approach also opens a path to mixing simulations and real experiments in one lab loop.
arxiv-2512-15583:
Sabri El Amrani and co authors design a market based charger schedule for flexible electric vehicles in a 2025 paper. Vehicle batteries could back up a grid strained by variable renewable power. Drivers, though, tend to unplug just when that backup is most needed, and busy charging stations face congestion.

Their scheduler pays drivers to delay disconnection and uses their time flexibility to ease station crowding. Finding the best flexible schedule is cast as a mixed integer quadratic problem, solved approximately with a standard splitting method. A Vickrey Clarke Groves payment scheme rewards honest reporting of charging needs. A simulated case study with real world data measures the gains.
arxiv-2512-15683:
Harry Lane and co authors explain anisotropic band split magnetism in cobalt ferrite in a 2025 paper. The spinel compound CoFe2O4 has the largest room temperature saturation magnetostriction among non rare earth compounds, plus a high Curie temperature near 780 kelvin. Those traits suit industrial and medical uses, but the mechanism behind them was unclear.

Neutron spectroscopy reveals a large splitting, about 60 milli electron volts, between two ferrimagnetic magnon branches, driven by site mixing of cobalt and iron ions. Magnetocrystalline anisotropy is far weaker, near 3 milli electron volts. Competing molecular fields lock moments inside each structural domain. Switching domains then beats rotating spins under a field, which amplifies the magnetostriction.
arxiv-2512-17083:
Michael H. Coen argues that dialogue topic segmentation is graded the wrong way. Strict boundary matching and F1 scores dominate, yet modern chat systems use segmentation to manage history past a fixed context window, where the grain of segments matters as much as their spots.

His frame reports boundary density plus purity and coverage diagnostics next to a window-tolerant F1 score, splitting boundary scoring from boundary selection. Across eight dialogue data sets, score gaps often trace to annotation grain mismatch, not placement skill. Threshold sweeps moved scores more than switching methods did. He recasts segmentation as a grain choice problem, not a hunt for one true boundary set.
arxiv-2512-17383:
N Kabeya and four co-authors report heat-based proof that a quasicrystal can superconduct with a full energy gap. Quasicrystals have ordered patterns that never repeat, unlike normal crystals. Their sample is a layered material, copper-doped Ta1.6Te, whose pattern has twelve-fold symmetry. Measuring its faint electronic heat signal took a trick to strip out a huge nuclear background.

Cooled to 60 millikelvin, the material showed a clean gap of 1.43 kelvin in the paper's units, with stray excitations strongly suppressed. Both the gap and the heat jump at the transition came in below what standard BCS theory predicts. Magnetic tests added a high critical field and strong direction effects. The work gives the first heat-based evidence of a full gap in such a material.
arxiv-2512-17583:
Vignesh Sundaramurthy and coauthors compare the Raman spectra of layered nickel oxides in the Ruddlesden Popper family. Some members of that family turned out to superconduct, which drew wide attention. Crystals of these materials tend to grow with rival phases mixed in and uneven oxygen content, which has muddied reports of their basic traits.

The team works with high quality crystals of the monolayer trilayer polymorph, a member built from single and triple layer blocks. With samples tuned to the best oxygen content, they map both the lattice and the electronic Raman response. They pin down spectral features that identify each phase without doubt, and they find traits in the mixed polymorph that neither parent compound shows. They trace those traits to electrons doping themselves and being confined by the single layer block inside the stack.
arxiv-2512-17683:
Shihan Kanungo tightens bounds on a quirky sequence game. A sequence is saturated for a pattern u when it avoids u as a scattered subsequence, yet adding any new letter anywhere creates u. The cheapest such sequence over an n-letter alphabet has a cost, Sat(n,u), and a 2021 paper proved that cost grows at most linearly for two-letter patterns, guessing the same for all patterns.

Kanungo gives a construction algorithm that builds saturated sequences cheaply. With it, linear growth is proven for several wide families, including endlessly repeated triples and long two-letter runs. For most patterns, an infinite saturated sequence exists at all. A linear program in the paper computes exact costs for small cases, anchoring the theory.
arxiv-2512-17783:
Lei Zhu and seven co-authors film living embryos a thousand frames per second by splitting each laser pulse into a train of smaller ones. Two-photon microscopy watches glowing molecules inside live tissue, but speed is capped: push the laser and the specimen cooks, starve it and the image dims. Their light-sheet design already spreads the light thinly across a plane.

A stack of birefringent crystals now chops every pulse into an adjustable burst of sub-pulses, tuning the timing without touching the laser's wavelength or power. On live zebrafish embryos, the team imaged the beating heart and brain calcium waves at kilohertz frame rates, over 150 million pixels per second, with healthy brightness and modest power. Developmental biology gains a camera fast enough for the heart's own tempo.
arxiv-2512-17983:
Irina Seregina, Philippe Lalanda, and German Vega test cheap ways to adapt big activity spotting models to new data. Human activity recognition powers many health and home tools, yet full retraining of a large model is too heavy for small devices. They try two light add on methods, LoRA and its compressed cousin QLoRA, on a transformer backbone.

Across five public data sets, each tested as the held out newcomer in turn, both methods matched full fine tuning scores. They used far fewer trained parts, less memory, and less time. The size of the add on gave a clean dial between accuracy and cost. QLoRA squeezed the frozen weights further with little loss in quality.
arxiv-2512-18083:
Ashley Zhang reframes a classic question: how to judge the average effect of a treatment from messy real world data. Standard tools blend outcome models with weights tied to each person's chance of treatment. Zhang shows these tools are really a form of domain adaptation, the machine learning craft of shifting a model between groups.

From that view, a trusted workhorse estimator turns out to be a narrow special case of a broader one. Zhang then argues that the two outcome models need not each be unbiased; their errors only need to cancel. Her Joint Robust Estimator trains both models together while tracking doubt in the treatment scores. In tests with flawed outcome models it cut squared error by up to 15 percent.
arxiv-2512-18483:
Rahul Yumlembam and four co-authors build a system for spotting insider threats, harmful acts by trusted users inside an organization. Such acts are subtle and well hidden, so the team models user behavior as graphs plus time sequences. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, combines two graph views of the same activity data.

One graph is built from set organizational rules; a second is learned from feature similarity, so hidden links can surface. Graph convolutional networks process both views, an attention step stresses the most threat-relevant features, and a bidirectional LSTM reads the order of events. On the CERT r5.2 dataset the system scores an AUC of 98.62 with a 100 percent detection rate. On the harder r6.2 set it reaches an AUC of 88.48.
arxiv-2512-18783:
Shuo Liu, Shao-Kai Jian, and Shi-Xin Zhang review a fast-growing framework: quantum circuits that are watched while they run, and corrupted by noise while they are watched. Such noisy monitored circuits link many-body physics, quantum information, and computation. Their review, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in the Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter, surveys the field's recent advances.

A central trick maps the quantum dynamics to classical statistical models, showing how noise reshuffles the dominant spin patterns. That view explains universal scaling, including entanglement growing with noise probability to the minus one-third power, and separate timescales for protecting information. The review ranges over applications from variational algorithms and classical simulation to mixed-state phases and quantum error correction. It presents monitored circuits as a practical lab for quantum dynamics in realistic, decohering conditions.
arxiv-2512-19383:
Abdelmadjid Benmachiche, Khadija Rais, and Hamda Slimi survey machine learning for spotting anomalies on tiny embedded devices. The Internet of Things spreads sensors that must flag trouble on the spot, with strict limits on delay, memory, and power. Cloud help is often too slow or too far away.

Lightweight methods are compared head to head: isolation forests, one-class support vector machines, recurrent networks, and plain statistics. Each trades detection accuracy against compute cost in its own way, and hardware limits end up dictating the choice. The survey closes with practical picks by device profile, plus trends in TinyML that may narrow the gap for safety-critical edge work.
arxiv-2512-19683:
Mingrui Wu and five co-authors built a benchmark to find out whether AI models truly understand space outdoors. Multimodal language models shine on indoor tests, but indoor data is tidy and metric ground truth is rare outside. Their dataset comes from pedestrian-perspective video recorded with synchronized stereo cameras, LiDAR, and motion and GPS sensors, giving precise three-dimensional truth for automatically generated questions.

Questions range from simple relations to metric and motion judgments. The headline finding is a gap: gains models show on structured indoor benchmarks evaporate in open-world scenes. Synthetic abnormal scenes and blinding tests, where images are hidden, suggest models lean on language habits rather than what they see. The benchmark aims to guide work toward physically grounded spatial intelligence.
arxiv-2512-19883:
Phong Nguyen, Anh Bui, and Phuong Nguyen dispute a claim about code comments. The claim is that catching stale comments takes the biggest language model on hand. Comments go stale when code changes and the notes do not. Stale notes mislead those who read the code later. Past detectors lean on large models. Those models read meaning well, but skip how the code evolved. They also raise privacy and cost worries.

Their detector, built on the smaller CodeT5+ model, works just in time. It reads a change as an ordered list of acts. The acts are swaps, deletes, and adds, not one blob. On the JITDATA and CCIBENCH test sets, it beat the best past systems. Its F1 score rose by up to about thirteen and a half points. It also beat fine-tuned coder models by a clear margin.
arxiv-2512-20083:
Wenzhao Wu and five co-authors test embodied agents for how well they finish, not just whether they finish. An agent can succeed in a wasteful way. It can take detours and extra steps, and standard checks never notice. The team names such flaws non-optimal decisions. Their framework, NoD-DGMT, hunts them with metamorphic testing. Sound planners should act the same under set transforms of a task.

Four relations encode those optimality traits. They cover detours, action completeness, refinement, and scene changes. A diversity-guided selector picks test cases across flaw types. It avoids checking the same flaw twice. On the AI2-THOR simulator, with four top planning models, the tool found flaws in about a third of cases. It beat six baselines, and its diversity filter raised the hit rate further.
arxiv-2512-20483:
Steven Creech, Henry Twiss, Zhining Wei, and Peter Zenz average a central quantity in number theory over a whole family of modular forms. The forms have half-integral weight and are eigenfunctions of every Hecke operator. The quantity is the squared central value of each form's L-function, weighted by Hecke eigenvalues and Petersson norms.

Using the relative trace formula, the authors derive an asymptotic formula for this second moment. Amplification then converts the moment bound into subconvexity: central values grow strictly slower than the convexity bound predicts, the first such result for half-integral weight forms in the weight aspect. A further application gives quantitative simultaneous non-vanishing, showing many central values in the family are provably nonzero at once.
arxiv-2512-20583:
Kyle Hogan and co-authors model online advertising end to end and find its privacy story does not add up. Proposals for private advertising treat targeting and engagement measurement separately. Privacy guarantees that look fine for each piece in isolation can fail when the pieces compose, letting advertisers extract new information about their audiences.

The authors then prove a sobering limit: perfect privacy is impossible for any even minimally useful advertising ecosystem, because advertisers expect market research from the results. Leakage is inherent, so the question becomes what privacy should realistically mean. Building on the notion of sensitive data in context, they argue that advertising subsystems need fundamentally new designs. Only end-to-end thinking keeps the whole system's promises aligned with people's actual privacy desires.
arxiv-2512-20683:
Boyu Jiang, Jiawei Shen, and Kexue Li study how solutions of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation fade over time in three spatial dimensions. Their regime is inter-critical: mass-supercritical yet energy-subcritical, a middle zone where neither conservation law alone controls the dynamics. Initial data are taken in the critical homogeneous Sobolev space, the natural scaling-invariant setting.

The authors prove a uniform decay estimate for the long-time behaviour of solutions starting from that critical data. Uniformity matters: the bound does not deteriorate with the particular solution chosen. The result extends earlier decay theorems into this critical regularity setting. Dispersive decay estimates are the workhorse behind scattering theory, so sharpening them widens the class of waves whose eventual spreading is fully understood.
arxiv-2512-20783:
Raja Mallina and Bryar Shareef target breast ultrasound, where software must outline lesions so doctors can plan diagnosis and treatment. Prompt-guided tools can draw better outlines when text or location hints exist. Many public scan collections, though, lack trustworthy reports, so training data with prompts stays small.

Their system, NullBUS, learns from scans with and without prompts inside one model. Learnable null placeholders stand in when text is missing, letting the model fall back on the image alone. Tested on three public datasets pooled together, NullBUS posted the best overlap scores reported under mixed prompt availability. The approach fits real hospital data, which is often incomplete.
arxiv-2512-20983:
Oleksii Proniakin, Razvan Marinescu, and two co-authors automate the hunt for medical mistakes by language models. Checking whether a model's specific error recurs in other models normally takes manual work. Their pipeline, MedMistake, stages conversations between a model patient and a model doctor. A two-judge committee grades the exchanges across reasoning, safety, and patient-centeredness. Each failure is then distilled into a single-shot question.

The full release holds 3,390 question pairs that two frontier models currently fail, and medical experts validated a 211-question subset as the benchmark proper. Twelve leading models were run against it, with the GPT, Claude, and Grok families performing best. Both datasets are public, giving clinical-AI evaluators a ready-made stress test built from real conversational failures rather than exam questions.
arxiv-2512-21383:
Ravi Kumar, Yuval Ronen, David F. Mross, and their co-authors report an experiment on bilayer graphene placed in a strong magnetic field. They study composite fermions, which are electrons bound to magnetic flux, in a half-filled Landau level. By tuning an electric displacement field, they change the orbital character of the level and watch the composite fermions switch behavior.

At the filling factors studied, transport measurements show conductive states giving way to well-developed plateaus as the displacement field grows. The new states ignore an in-plane magnetic field, which points to single-component ground states and possible non-Abelian order. Computer calculations using displacement-dependent wave functions support the orbital explanation and suggest Moore-Read or anti-Pfaffian ground states. The work shows orbital tuning is a practical knob for steering a quantum Hall system between a metal and a paired phase.
arxiv-2512-21483:
Khanh Chau Le reduces the three-dimensional theory of elasticity for slender rods to a one-dimensional rod theory, with a guarantee that the reduction is exact in the limit. The rods are functionally graded, meaning material properties change gradually through the cross-section, and generally anisotropic, so stiffness differs by direction. Simulating the full body is expensive.

Le applies the variational-asymptotic method, which derives the simpler theory step by step. A distinctive step solves dual cross-sectional problems numerically, bracketing the true average transverse energy density between rigorous bounds. An error estimate based on the Prager-Synge identity certifies the model's accuracy in the energy norm. The estimate extends to low-frequency vibrations, and wave dispersion relations match exact solutions. In benchmarks, a naive rod theory errs by up to twenty percent in deflections, while the new one stays below three percent.
arxiv-2512-21583:
Zelin Zang, Guohui Fan, and their co-authors build a medical diagnosis system that combines medical images with clinical text. Simply feeding both into a vision-language model does not guarantee sound reasoning: models hallucinate or produce inconsistent chains of thought, which limits trust in clinical settings.

Built on LLaVA, their framework adds a reasoning controller that breaks a diagnostic task into steps. A logic tree generator then assembles the stepwise premises into conclusions that can be checked. An input encoder and a projection module handle the alignment of text and image features. On MedXpertQA and other benchmarks, the method improves diagnostic accuracy on multimodal tasks and produces more interpretable reasoning traces. It stays competitive on text-only tasks. The authors present the system as a step toward medical AI that clinicians can audit.
arxiv-2512-21683:
Yuntian Bo, Tao Zhou, Zechao Li, Haofeng Zhang, and Ling Shao segment medical images in a hard setting: few labels, and a target domain different from the training one. Clinics need organ and lesion outlines, but annotations are scarce and scanners differ. Earlier methods improved transfer by filtering out domain-specific information, which hurt accuracy in the source domain.

Their framework, C-Graph, instead leans on a transferable prior: the structural consistency of medical images. Features become a graph, with pixels as nodes and semantic affinities as edges. A structural prior graph layer models dependencies among target-category nodes. A subgraph matching decoder uses relations among nodes to guide the predicted outline. A contrastive loss reduces node ambiguity and subgraph mismatch by making nodes more distinguishable in graph space. Across cross-domain benchmarks, C-Graph beat earlier approaches while keeping strong source-domain accuracy, a combination previous methods traded away.
arxiv-2512-22583:
Miguel J. Torrejon, S. Blazquez, Jesus Algaba, M. M. Conde, and F. J. Blas compute when hydrogen hydrate falls apart, and how badly it wants to form. Hydrogen hydrate traps hydrogen molecules inside water cages, and its multiple-occupancy variant lets several guests share a cage. Using molecular simulations with known water and hydrogen models, the team finds the dissociation temperature two separate ways, both resting on dissolving curves.

At a pressure of 185 MPa, the dissolving curves for hydrate-contacted and hydrogen-contacted water cross exactly at the three-phase coexistence temperature, matching published values. Cage occupancy barely moved that temperature. Extra bulk simulations then yielded the nucleation driving force as a function of supercooling and occupancy. The favored arrangement puts one hydrogen molecule in each small cage and three in each large cage.
arxiv-2512-22683:
Anumanchi Agastya Sai Ram Likhit and Rajib Saha use a diffusion model to recover the faint traces of the universe's first gravitational waves. The primordial B-mode polarization of the cosmic microwave background would directly evidence inflation, but the signal is buried under lensing distortion, instrument noise, and galactic foregrounds. Their score-based method, built on variance-exploding stochastic equations, learns what clean low-multipole B-mode power spectra should look like.

The score model trained only on mock primordial spectra at one fixed tensor-to-scalar ratio. At inference, a reverse diffusion process pushes, step by step, a dirty observed spectrum toward that learned family, effectively cleaning and delensing it. Tests used mock observations with lensing, complex foreground mixes, and noise modeled on the proposed ECHO mission. The learned prior can also generate fresh consistent signal samples.
arxiv-2512-22883:
Tao Li and Quanyan Zhu contribute a book chapter arguing that security built around foundation-model AI needs a new organizing idea: agentic cyber resilience. Large language models can now plan, use tools, and adapt on their own, which strains defenses built on fixed rules, perimeter walls, and human-paced workflows. Rather than promising perfect prevention, resilient systems should expect disruption, keep essential functions running during attacks, recover quickly, and keep learning.

The chapter places this shift in the history of security paradigms, ending with an AI-augmented era where autonomous agents join sensing, reasoning, and response. A system-level framework follows, with attacker and defender workflows treated as coupled adaptive processes. Game theory supplies the design language for dividing work between humans and agents and for ordering actions in time. Case studies on automated penetration testing, remediation, and cyber deception show the framework in action.
arxiv-2512-22983:
Shuanghao Bai and a large team survey how foundation models are changing robot manipulation, the task of getting robot arms to handle objects reliably. Manipulation is among the hardest embodied skills because it fuses perception, language understanding, task reasoning, and physically grounded action. The survey organizes recent learning-based work through one abstraction: high-level planning on top, low-level action modeling underneath.

At the planning level, the classical idea of task planning is widened to cover language, code, affordances, geometric constraints, and three-dimensional scene models. At the action level, approaches are sorted by how they model inputs, latent variables, and policies. Foundation models enter either by producing structured planning artifacts that controllers must respect, or by directly generating actions and trajectories. The survey closes with open problems in scale, generalization, data efficiency, and safety.
arxiv-2512-23083:
Amina Halima Arrouche and Benharrat Belaïdi study how fast solutions of complex differential equations can grow inside the unit disc. The equations are linear and of higher order, with analytic coefficients whose own growth is measured by a generalized notion called (alpha, beta, gamma)-order. Growth questions of this kind matter because they classify which equations admit tame solutions and which force explosive ones.

Working with the concepts of order and type for the solutions, the authors establish new results describing the growth of solutions when the coefficients have finite generalized order. The theorems extend and generalize earlier work by Belaïdi and by Biswas, placing their estimates inside a flexible three-parameter scale. As is typical for this branch of complex analysis, the contribution is a sharper classification framework rather than a closed-form answer. Researchers gain tools for comparing solution growth across families of equations.
arxiv-2512-23183:
Shiwen An, Jiayi Wang, and Konstantinos Slavakis built LogosQ, a quantum computing library written in the Rust language. Most quantum software lives in Python frameworks, whose dynamic nature invites runtime errors and scaling bottlenecks. LogosQ instead leans on Rust's compile-time type checking to rule out classes of mistakes before a program runs, and it stays independent of any hardware backend.

The engineering pays off in speed. Direct state-vector manipulation, adaptive parallel processing, and an FFT-optimized quantum Fourier transform deliver reported speedups. State preparation runs up to nine hundred times faster than in Python frameworks. Gains over Julia tools are smaller but real, and performance against Q# is competitive. A special target is the parameter-shift gradient computations used by variational algorithms, where type safety removes silent errors. Variational eigensolver tests on molecular hydrogen and Heisenberg models reached chemical accuracy, including edge cases other libraries failed.
arxiv-2512-23383:
Hakan Yildiz and Axel Küpper present interID, a tool for checking digital credentials across competing self-sovereign identity ecosystems. Self-sovereign identity gives people control of their own records, but the field has fragmented. The European Digital Identity framework, the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure, and Hyperledger-based networks each verify them their own way, with different rules. A service provider wanting to accept all of them must build three separate links.

interID hides that split behind one layer. Ecosystem-specific verifier services sit underneath, while providers call a single unified API that abstracts the protocol differences away. The system bridges the three named ecosystems, and tests showed checking worked across all tested wallets with minimal overhead. The design is built to extend, so further ecosystems can be added. The authors offer interID as both a working tool and a reusable pattern for joint checking.
arxiv-2512-23483:
Long videos defeat today's video language models: their viewing window is short, and they miss slow changes of meaning spread over many minutes. Zongsheng Cao and five co-authors present TV-RAG, a retrieval framework that helps such models find the right moments before answering. It requires no retraining of the underlying model.

Two mechanisms do the work. A time-decay retrieval module scores candidate clips with their true position in the video, not just word overlap, while an entropy-weighted sampler picks evenly spaced frames that carry the most information. Together they let the model reason over visual, audio, and subtitle channels across the whole video. TV-RAG beat most leading baselines on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench.
arxiv-2512-23583:
Paolo Restuccia and four co-authors simulate how phosphorus-based lubricant additives behave on iron surfaces at the molecular scale. Such additives protect metal contacts under boundary lubrication by forming surface films, but why one additive beats another, most of all among phosphate esters, is not well known.

They ran atom-level simulations of three additives and of variants with changed ester groups and chain lengths. One phosphite additive gave the lowest friction and the widest separation between surfaces, thanks to a bulky shape plus a strong grip at the surface. Monoesters guarded the metal less well and partly lost cover in harsh use. Multi-ester, longer-chain types kept the faces apart and cut friction. The results suggest designing additives that combine firm surface anchoring with bulky, space-filling structures.
arxiv-2512-23683:
Guillermo Lara, Georg Trenkler, and Leonardo Trombetta study black holes in a modified gravity theory where a scalar field couples to the Gauss-Bonnet invariant. The field also carries its own nonlinear kinetic term, a K-essence term. In such theories a black hole can carry a scalar charge induced by the coupling, and that charge changes how the hole interacts with its surroundings.

Working in a test-field approach, the authors first examine static solutions, flat far away, where the kinetic term screens the scalar charge. They then turn to cosmologies where the same kinetic term drives self-acceleration. There the scalar's time dependence opens the parameter space, promoting the black-hole charge from a secondary by-product to a primary quantity. A stability analysis and a screening-intensity measure, read off from how mixed scalar and gravity waves spread, complete the study.
arxiv-2512-23783: Zhuang Li submitted this comment on a paper about regular magnetically charged black holes in nonlinear electrodynamics, addressing its thermodynamics, light deflection, and orbital dynamics. The submission no longer stands as normal research: arXiv withdrew it by an admin action, stating that authorship and affiliation were disputed and unverifiable. The record now consists of that withdrawal notice, and the paper should not be cited as standing work.
arxiv-2512-23883:
Achyut Tiwari and five co-authors probe how charge moves in tantalum disulfide, a layered material famous for its charge-density-wave phases. In its cold commensurate phase, the tantalum atoms shift into star-of-David clusters tiled in a repeating pattern, and the material turns from metal to insulator. What drives that switch, electron correlations or the new structure itself, has long been debated.

Using infrared light at many temperatures and polarizations, backed by density functional calculations, the team split charge motion along the layers from motion across them. Along the layers, the response tracks the rebuilt electronic structure of the shifted layers. Across them, it is ruled by a Peierls-like pairing of the star-of-David layers along the stacking direction. That pairing turns out to drive the metal-insulator switch in both directions, while electron correlations play no significant part. The verdict settles a long argument.
arxiv-2512-24083:
Miklos Eper and Szilard Szabo study rank-three representations of Painlevé systems. These systems are differential equations with deep ties to geometry. The language of the work is D-modules. The authors apply formal microlocalization to the problem.

They describe the Fourier-Laplace transformation for these representations. It connects the rank-three case to the rank-two case. They then establish a matching result. The corresponding de Rham complex structures correspond under a morphism. That morphism is regular in both directions. The note is brief and highly technical. It forms the second part of a series. Specialists in Painlevé systems and D-module theory are its audience.
arxiv-2512-24283: Alexander Bufetov and Ilya Zavolokin write a short note on a classic proof in analysis. The Picard-Lindelöf theorem promises solutions to differential equations under mild conditions. Its proof applies an operator again and again until the results settle. A fixed point principle powers that settling. The note shows that a slightly sharper form of the principle gives back the exact rate at which the theorem's iterates converge.
arxiv-2512-24483:
Liyuan Liang, Yilong Song, and Kun Yuan solve a long-standing problem in decentralized optimization. Many nodes optimize together over a directed network. Robotic swarms, sensor networks, and distributed learning all fit. In broadcast networks, out-degrees are unknown. Only row-stochastic mixing matrices can be built. Exact convergence there stayed open for years.

Row-stochastic mixing settles to a weighted average set by a limit vector. That vector depends on future graph realizations. It cannot be estimated in advance, so bias correction fails. Their protocol, PULM, controls the vector instead. Gossip rounds interleave with a communication-free adjustment. Each node anchors its initial weight at one over n. Average consensus then converges exponentially for every admissible graph sequence. A gradient method on top reaches the target accuracy in a stated number of rounds.
arxiv-2512-24883:
Crispin and Talebi develop a quantum theory of free electrons coupled with quantum emitters, driven by time-resolved cathodoluminescence that now reaches femtosecond detail on single emitters. Emitters may start in any states, including coherent superpositions. Their analysis shows a passing free electron can induce transient coherent wiggles in emitter groups when that superposition is present.

The electron energy spectrum carries a clear sign of the unity and is precise to the change rate of the emitter. Electron microscopy readers get a theory basis for reading quantum unity from electron spectra. Free electrons thus become probes of coherent motion in quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-00083:
Leticia Guedes, Gabriela Hoff, Farinaldo S Queiroz, Y M Oviedo-Torres, and Y Villamizar study the hunt for scalars that carry two units of electric charge. Such particles appear in many extensions of the standard model, often in ideas meant to explain why neutrinos have mass. Their clean decays into charged leptons make them attractive targets for collider searches. Their 2026 paper weighs the reach of current and future machines.

The team considers the full second run of the Large Hadron Collider, including collisions of photons, and the future FCC-hh collider. They assume the scalars decay at once and only into charged leptons, whether or not lepton flavor is kept. The FCC-hh, at much higher energy, could probe masses up to seven TeV.
arxiv-2601-00183:
The CMS Collaboration reports a search for an exotic way for the Higgs boson to decay. The Higgs might split into two lighter hypothetical particles. Each of those would then decay into two photons. The team hunts events with a semi merged shape. One pair blends into a single photon like object. The other pair stays resolved as two photons.

Data come from proton collisions at the CMS detector. The sample covers a large integrated luminosity at top energy. What the data show matches standard model background alone. No exotic signal stands out. The team therefore sets upper limits on the decay rate. Limits vary across the light particle mass range. In the lowest mass stretch, they are the tightest yet. Null results still guide theory here. Allowed room for this Higgs path keeps shrinking.
arxiv-2601-00283:
Eduard Emelyanov and coauthor Svetlana Gorokhova study when maps between ordered and topological vector spaces must be continuous on their own. Some operators are only assumed to respect bounds. Others are assumed continuous in an order to topology sense. The question is whether plain continuity then comes for free. Such results are called automatic continuity theorems.

Several results here start from ordered Fréchet spaces. Those spaces carry both an order and a complete metric style topology. Two special operator classes get close attention. Levi operators and Lebesgue operators each tie order convergence to output behavior. Knowing when they must be continuous sharpens functional analysis tools. Order structure alone sometimes forces analytic control. The paper maps where that forcing holds.
arxiv-2601-00383:
Xian Shi, the sole author, studies entanglement distillation, a process that extracts clean, strongly entangled pairs from many noisy ones. Recent work has mapped the limits of such conversions when they are allowed to fail sometimes. His 2026 paper tackles a gap: no analytic formula was known for how fast the error falls in this probabilistic setting, under operations that almost never create entanglement.

Working at finite block length and at zero rate, Shi connects distillation to a form of quantum hypothesis testing done after selection. The test asks whether a state could be separable, meaning unentangled. From that link he derives an analytic formula for the error exponent under the stated operations. The result ties a basic task in entanglement theory to a testing problem.
arxiv-2601-00483:
Long Ma and four co-authors report, in 2026, a way to steer a tiny force between close surfaces. The force is the Casimir force, a quantum effect that can pull two surfaces toward each other. Here one surface is a kind of plastic, and the other is a coated metal plate. Both sit in a fluid of toluene mixed with tiny bits of magnetite, a magnetic mineral. The mix lets the force flip from pull to push.

That flip lets a surface float at a set gap, held by the force alone. The authors trace how the choice of metal and fluid brings this trap about. They weigh the parts played by heat and by quantum effects. A tunable trap of this kind could help build very small machines. It also gives a clean test bed for a force that is hard to measure.
arxiv-2601-00683:
Simon Gritschacher is the sole author of a 2026 math paper on pairs of commuting matrices. A matrix is a grid of numbers, and some pairs can be swapped in a product with no change. The set of all such pairs, for grids of a fixed size, forms a shape with rich structure. Gritschacher studies a ring that counts holes and twists in that shape. The ring is read while a group of grid changes acts on the shape.

He gives a full recipe for that ring over the whole numbers. It is built from a base ring by just three times the grid size in new parts. The rules that link those parts come from one small set, stretched by powers of a known polynomial. He also gives the plain ring, with no group action, for most number fields. The result gives algebraists a firm grip on a classic space.
arxiv-2601-01483:
Seven authors led by Xinyu Qiu train one vision-language model to both answer questions and check its own answers. The usual route trains a separate verifier, which doubles cost at training and at run time. Their method, ADPO, folds verification into the same reinforcement learning policy that generates answers.

Two ideas drive it. A verification reward uses the average scores of right and wrong samples as a threshold, rewarding the model when its judgment matches the truth. A decoupled advantage then optimizes generation and verification separately, with token masks keeping their gradients apart. The reported gains are large: verification quality up by about a third, inference time cut by more than half, and accuracy up on math, general, and interface benchmarks. One model that grades itself is cheaper to run and, the authors argue, better calibrated about its own limits.
arxiv-2601-01583:
Caner Tanış introduces a new family of probability distributions built from lower record values and a cubic change of form. Distributions give the math for how random measures spread out, and a good new family can fit real data that older curves miss. One special case is offered as a rival to the well-known exponential distribution.

Tanis works out the family's main statistical features and tries nine ways to estimate its settings from data. Large computer simulations compare those methods, and a distance-based method stands out as a sound rival to the standard best-fit method. Two real data examples show the new model fitting better than its competitors.
arxiv-2601-01683:
Solid-fuel ramjets are simple, rugged engines for fast flight, but steering their thrust is tricky because the fuel burns on its own schedule. Parham Oveissi, Ryan DeBoskey, Venkateswaran Narayanaswamy, and Ankit Goel apply a data-driven adaptive control method, called DMAC, to hold a ramjet's thrust on target by adjusting its variable-geometry inlet.

DMAC first learns a local model of the engine's behavior from data, using dynamic mode decomposition, then builds a tracking controller around that model. In simulations driven by a one-dimensional engine model, thrust followed a range of commanded profiles accurately across operating conditions. Notably, the controller needed no hand-derived equations for the engine itself, which suits systems that resist exact modeling.
arxiv-2601-01883: Takuma Aihara studies maps between differential graded algebras called homological epimorphisms. He proves the following result. If the source algebra is finite dimensional and piecewise hereditary, the target is derived equivalent to one of the same kind. The note adds a constraint to the theory of derived equivalence. That theory covers this well-studied class of algebras.
arxiv-2601-01983:
Turbulence in a wide channel, flow dragged between moving walls, organizes itself into striking large-scale streaks and rolls. Brian Farrell and Petros Ioannou show the pattern is no accident of simulation. It is a fixed point of the Navier-Stokes equations. The view comes through statistical state dynamics. That framework tracks the flow's statistics directly.

The fixed point has rank three. One roll-streak structure carries the mean. Two more modes support the fluctuations. Both are found in analytic form. Everything else contributes negligibly. Other Couette regimes, limit cycles and chaos, then appear as extensions where those two modes are replaced by Floquet modes or Lyapunov vectors. The result is a rare analytic handle on a turbulent flow's structure and mechanism.
arxiv-2601-02083:
An observer who speeds through empty space sees a horizon. A bath of thermal radiation appears as well. The one-way nature of that setup echoes renormalization group flows. G. Prokhorov shows the link is real. The unitarity of quantum field theory forces it. Positivity of spectral functions is the key.

Prokhorov computes two viscosities for thermal radiation in Rindler space. Rindler space is the geometry of accelerated frames. He calls the pair entanglement viscosities. The formulas tie shear viscosity under acceleration to the conformal anomaly of curved space. That hints at a new probe of the anomaly in systems under extreme acceleration. For conformal theories, the entanglement viscosity reaches the famous Kovtun-Son-Starinets bound.
arxiv-2601-02483:
D. C. Smolinski and co authors study the radio halos of sixteen edge on galaxies from the CHANG-ES survey, asking how thick the radio glow is at different frequencies. Radio continuum light traces cosmic rays and magnetic fields above a galaxy's disk. As cosmic ray electrons age and cool, the halo thickness should change with frequency, an effect called spectral aging.

They combine maps at a low frequency from LOFAR and at a higher frequency from the Jansky Very Large Array, at matched resolution. Vertical profiles are fitted with two component exponential models to separate thin and thick disks. For thick disks the mean ratio of low frequency to high frequency scale height is only modestly above one, lower than simple expectations. The team tests how that ratio and the spectral index vary with star formation rate, mass, and size.
arxiv-2601-02683:
Dongyu Chen and six co authors optimize the prompts given to large language models in a structured way, rather than by hand or from scratch. Prompt design is an optimization problem, but current automatic methods suffer prompt drift, where a new prompt fixes old failures while quietly breaking cases that used to work. Prompts generated from nothing can also be hard to interpret. Their framework, hierarchical attribution prompt optimization, is designed to learn from the prompt itself.

A dynamic attribution mechanism first targets the error patterns showing in training data, assigning blame to specific parts of the prompt instead of rewriting blindly. Further components of the framework then revise the prompt in a hierarchy, keeping what already works. The aim is a prompt improvement process that is automated, less wasteful of earlier gains, and interpretable enough for a human to audit.
arxiv-2601-02983:
Yuankun Xie and eight co-authors build a detector for audio deepfakes that works across speech, environmental sounds, singing, and music, and can explain its calls. Audio language models now make realistic fake audio easy to produce, so detection has to generalize and stay interpretable. Training such a model on bare real-or-fake labels turns it into a black box, while plain reinforcement tuning can produce made-up reasoning.

To fix that, the team built an automatic pipeline that writes structured frequency-time reasoning traces, producing about 340,000 training demonstrations. Their two-stage method first fine-tunes the model on those traces, then applies a group-relative reinforcement method under frequency-time rules. The result is an all-type detector whose decisions come with grounded, checkable explanations.
arxiv-2601-03483:
Lingzhi Shen and five co-authors introduce CALM, a framework meant to give language models cultural self-awareness. Most systems treat culture as fixed background facts, but cultures shift and overlap, so static knowledge can make answers unreliable in sensitive tasks. CALM instead separates a task's meaning from explicit cultural concepts and subtler cultural signals in the text.

Contrastive learning shapes those signals into structured cultural clusters. Cross-attention links related features, and a mixture-of-experts step blends them along culture-specific lines. The result merges with the model's own knowledge to form a culturally grounded internal state. Reflective self-prompting then helps the model keep adapting. The aim is AI that notices cultural context instead of flattening it.
arxiv-2601-03583:
Yong-Chang Lau and four co-authors clear up a factor-of-two dispute in how physicists measure current-induced torques in magnetic materials. These spin-orbit torques matter for next-generation memory devices, and labs estimate them from harmonic Hall voltage signals. Different groups have used fitting formulas that disagree by a factor of two, especially for signals taken under a rotating in-plane magnetic field.

By deriving the relations explicitly, the authors trace where the discrepancy enters and give the correct fitting form. They also discuss how to read the sign of the field-like torque, which depends on the assumed form of the torques themselves. A short comment paper like this one protects the field from quiet measurement errors that could mislead device design across many laboratories.
arxiv-2601-03683:
Xin Lai and five co-authors rethink recurrent neural networks for forecasting time series such as demand, traffic, or sensor readings. Classic recurrent predictors slide a window of past values forward and treat every time step and hidden state as equally important, which wastes signal. Their method wraps the recurrent encoder in a reinforcement learning loop.

The reinforced encoder treats internal adaptation as a decision process. A prediction-focused tuning method then adjusts the network toward forecast accuracy rather than generic fit. The design aims to raise both modeling capacity and final accuracy over conventional recurrent predictors. For firms that plan stock, energy, or staffing from forecasts, even modest accuracy gains add up to real savings across thousands of repeated calls.
arxiv-2601-03983:
Christophe Hurlin, joined by Quentin Lajaunie and Yoann Pull, sets out a formal way to reverse stress test company loan portfolios for political risk. Normal stress tests start from a set scene. Reverse tests start from a bad outcome and ask which scene could cause it.

Their method adds a clear political risk factor to a joint scene of economic and financial variables. That scene is mapped to missed payments and losses, then to a bank capital ratio. The search is framed as a constrained likelihood problem, which yields the most likely breaking scene. Neighbouring scenes support checks on how sensitive the answer is. The method fits rating-based bank models and can run by loan or by sector.
arxiv-2601-04083:
Marvin Illian, Ramin Khalili, Antonio A. de A. Rocha, and Lin Wang ask whether a learning agent can tune how phones pick mobile cells. With 5G and 4G side by side, devices face many candidate cells. Today the settings that guide choice are fixed by hand from operator experience and rarely adapt.

Their framework, CellPilot, uses reinforcement learning to adjust reselection settings by learning patterns in space and time. In tests with real-world data, even a light agent beats standard hand-tuned resets by a large margin, with gains reported up to well over double. The agent also transfers across different network scenes. The four authors present the result as evidence that data-driven tuning can lift everyday mobile performance.
arxiv-2601-04283:
Nikolay Yudin studies a quiet failure of small language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Character-level Transformers that learn modular addition from text can score highly on familiar formats yet collapse when the same sum appears at different character positions or in new wording. His tests use modular addition with a data split that keeps the tested pairs unseen during training.

His training recipe combines boundary markers around expressions, a curriculum that widens where expressions may sit, varied natural-language templates, and consistency training across versions of each example. Across three random seeds the recipe sharply improves robustness to shifted positions and unseen templates while keeping ordinary accuracy high. A comparison variant using a popular position scheme fails to learn the task under his setup, suggesting such invariances must be taught directly.
arxiv-2601-04383:
Paul Breiding and eight co-authors find the regions where a geometric surface is not, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Many key surfaces in algebraic geometry, such as discriminants, are shadows — projections of other varieties — and the real space around such a surface splits into linked regions worth mapping. Older methods need the surface's defining formula, but eliminating variables to get that equation can be impossibly costly.

Their method never works out the formula. Instead it slices the surface with a line, finds the intersection points using pseudo-witness sets, and rebuilds the picture of the real complement from those slices by interpolation. Implemented in a forthcoming Julia package, the algorithm recovered every component correctly on the cases tried. The approach opens complement computations for surfaces whose equations were earlier out of reach.
arxiv-2601-04583:
Saad Alqithami surveys what happens when agents are handed the keys to a blockchain, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Language-model agents can now plan multi-step work and use tools, while public blockchains offer programmable money and verifiable state. Joining them means designing interfaces that let an agent read chain state, form transaction intentions, and get them executed without unacceptable security, governance, or economic risks.

From an initial pool of over three thousand records, the review keeps three hundred seventeen works and organizes them into a five-part taxonomy of integration patterns. From read-only analytics through delegated execution and autonomous signing to multi-agent workflows. A tailored threat model covers prompt injection, policy misuse, key compromise, and collusion, and a matrix compares more than twenty systems across thirteen dimensions. The roadmap proposes two standard abstractions — a transaction intent schema and a policy decision record — plus a shared evaluation suite.
arxiv-2601-04783:
Rostyslav Kozhan and 1 co-author study a family of polynomials on the unit circle in a 2026 math paper. The polynomials must meet a set of balance rules at the same time, rules tied to more than one weight on the circle. The family they use is of Laurent type, built from powers that run both ways around the circle.

They show that these polynomials solve a two-point fitting task, in which one set of rules fits more than one function at once. They also find step-by-step rules that build each new polynomial from the last ones. New formulas link this case to close cousins in the same field. The work gives other researchers a fuller set of tools for this type of problem.
arxiv-2601-05083:
Ellington Kirby and 13 co-authors present DrivoR, a transformer design for driving a car end to end, in a 2026 paper. Their design builds on pretrained vision transformers and adds camera-aware register tokens, extra tokens that compress features from several cameras into one compact scene representation. That compression cuts downstream computation sharply without sacrificing accuracy, a practical concern for vehicles that must decide in real time.

Two lightweight transformer decoders first generate candidate trajectories and then score them. The scoring decoder is trained to imitate an oracle, an ideal judge, and predicts interpretable sub-scores for aspects such as safety, comfort, and efficiency. Interpretable scoring matters because engineers and regulators need to know why a car preferred one path over another.
arxiv-2601-05183:
Dadi Ni and Kaichuan Qi give an explicit construction of circle gerbes over a quotient stack in a 2026 mathematics paper. A gerbe is a higher geometric object used in modern geometry and string theory, and the stack in question encodes a compact, connected Lie group acting on itself. The construction is framed through circle central extensions of Lie groupoids, the machinery that makes such stacks concrete.

Their work completes a proof of a construction outlined earlier by Behrend, Xu, and Zhang, including a differential-form identity stated there without proof. For simple, simply connected groups, the resulting class is the canonical generator of the relevant cohomology group. Explicit models matter because abstract existence proofs cannot be used in calculations.
arxiv-2601-05283:
Alain Blondel and 3 co-authors give first comments on a descoped version of CERN's planned Future Circular Collider in a 2026 note. A strategy group had recommended the electron-positron collider as the preferred next flagship machine, with a descoped variant as the fallback if the full version proves infeasible. The fallback would use reduced synchrotron radiation power, skip a run at the top-quark threshold, and operate only two interaction regions instead of more.

At the strategy group's request, the authors compare what the descoped option could still deliver in physics against the baseline design. Their short note offers the first assessment of what science would be lost. The comparison feeds a real funding and strategy decision about Europe's flagship physics facility for decades.
arxiv-2601-05383:
Prakash Gawas, Antoine Legrain, and Louis-Martin Rousseau sort the roles a teacher can play when a model learns by copy in a 2026 paper. The field is imitation learning for hard pick-and-path tasks, where exact tools cost too much time to run. A learner apes the acts of a pro, the expert, on tasks played out step by step, each call made with doubt in the air. The pro's build is core to the end skill, yet it had no shared frame.

Past work used pros of all kinds, with no shared terms for their traits, costs, or pull on the end score. The team set out a clean sort of pro builds. A shared tongue lets teams pick a pro with open eyes. Since a learner can top its pro by a hair at best, the pro's build is the base of the whole art.
arxiv-2601-05783:
Sigmund Kohler and Jesus Casado-Pascual uncover in 2026 a hidden symmetry behind exact level crossings in a driven two-level quantum system. They study the Floquet spectrum, the energy-like levels of a system under periodic driving, with a detuning between the system and the drive.

Crossings appear exactly when the detuning is a whole multiple of the drive's energy quantum. A hidden time-nonlocal parity explains this: Floquet modes split into even and odd classes, and levels of different parity may cross exactly. The authors prove the symmetry exists through a scalar recurrence relation. They also give a general numerical scheme for computing it that applies beyond two-level systems, and illustrate the analytical results with numerical data.
arxiv-2601-06083:
Xiuqing Huang predicts a ceiling for superconductivity in nickelate materials in a 2026 theory paper. Under high pressure, a lanthanum-samarium nickel oxide reaches a record transition temperature near the top of its class. That result raised the question of how high nickelate transition temperatures can go.

Huang argues two crystal forms of the material share a quantum-well structure that also governs a famous copper-based superconductor. A scaling law based on the depth of that well reproduces the measured temperatures closely. Further calculations give a universal limit near 100 kelvin for rare-earth nickelates, whatever the layer stacking. The paper also links broken mirror symmetry in paired quantum wells to Fermi pockets and to superconductivity at normal pressure.
arxiv-2601-06983: Ji Tong Wang and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers hybrid bound states in the continuum beyond diffraction limit. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Bound states in the continuum (BICs) have greatly impacted our ability to manipulate light-matter interaction at the nanoscale. However, in periodic structures, BICs are typically realized below the diffraction limit, thus leaving a broad spectral domains largely unexplored. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07183: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Zehai Yang and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers RAIRS. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. IVF is one of the most widely used ANNS (Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search) methods in vector databases. The idea of redundant assignment is to assign a data vector to more than one IVF lists. For reducing the chance of missing true neighbors in IVF search. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07383:
Research by Fabian Schnelle and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with igusa stacks for certain abelian-type shimura varieties. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors construct Igusa stacks for the good reduction locus of.

A class of abelian-type Shimura varieties that can be defined in terms of a PEL datum. Under the assumption that it is of type (A even) or (C) and unramified at a prime p p. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07683:
Akash Halder, Amlan K. Roy, and Debraj Nath study hydrogen-like ions inside a deformed version of quantum mechanics. They solve the Schrödinger equation for a Coulomb potential with a Dunkl reflection operator present. The Dunkl framework adds reflection terms to standard calculus. The authors give formulas for eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, and radial densities for ions with atomic numbers one to three.

They also discuss how energy degeneracy changes with and without the reflection. Degeneracy means several states sharing one energy, a hallmark of hydrogen-like systems. Tracking it shows exactly what the Dunkl deformation alters. Quantum information measures and statistical complexity of these ions are part of the study. The paper speaks to mathematical physicists testing how far standard results survive deformation.
arxiv-2601-07783:
Chaoyi Lin Yang, Gabriele Dessena, and Oscar Bonilla-Manrique build a cheaper way to record vibrations from unmanned aircraft on the ground. Structural vibration testing checks dynamic behavior, reliability, and structural integrity. Such tests need accurate data acquisition systems to capture acceleration well. Commercial systems with the right performance are often expensive and complex. Their 2026 preprint presents an affordable alternative for UAV taxi vibration testing.

Taxi tests roll the aircraft on the ground to excite its structure. Small research teams need data quality without aerospace-level budgets. A low-cost system widens who can run these tests. The design targets small-scale and experimental applications that commercial gear prices out. Aerospace engineers and university labs are the readers. The paper treats cost as an engineering requirement, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-07883:
Indrajit Sen and Matthew Leifer draw testable predictions from an alternative formulation of quantum theory. The formulation is local, scale invariant, and non-Hermitian, built on pilot-wave ideas. Pilot-wave theory guides particles with a wave, in the de Broglie-Bohm picture. Sen and Leifer use Weyl's definition of the gravitational radius of charge. From it they obtain a fine-structure constant for non-integrable scale effects. Their 2026 preprint explores the experimental predictions that follow.

Alternative formulations matter when they predict something different from standard theory. A concrete prediction gives experimenters a target. Scale effects that cannot be integrated away would leave specific signatures. The authors work out where those signatures should appear. The paper serves scholars in quantum foundations. It moves a new formulation from formalism toward the laboratory.
arxiv-2601-07983:
A 2026 preprint models how Earth's radiation record would change if the Sun met a cold interstellar cloud. Geologic records of cosmogenic beryllium-10 are sensitive to the radiation environment over time. Recent work suggests the Sun sometimes encountered massive cold clouds. Such clouds could compress the heliosphere to within Earth's orbit. Earth would then face increased galactic cosmic rays and energetic particles of heliospheric origin.

Beryllium-10 in ice and sediments is a natural archive of past radiation. Modeling the cloud encounter tells scholars what spike to look for. A confirmed spike would date a dramatic event in the Sun's recent travels. It would also test models of the heliosphere's protective bubble. The paper serves space physicists and paleoclimate scholars. It connects deep-space conditions to traces readable in Earth's own records.
arxiv-2601-08283:
Heba Shakeel and three co-authors present AgriLens for searching agricultural texts by meaning. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses the growth of unstructured text across domains. Large text collections need scalable ways to organize, summarize, and retrieve what they hold.

AgriLens unifies three tasks: interpretable topic modeling, zero-shot topic labeling, and topic-guided semantic retrieval. It uses BERTopic to extract semantically coherent topics from agricultural corpora. Zero-shot labeling names topics without hand-built training sets for each theme. For farmers' advisors, researchers, and extension services, topic-guided search could surface the right guidance faster. The framework keeps topics readable, so users can judge what a search result covers.
arxiv-2601-08383: Bo Wang and five co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on where a model gains its facts in pre-training. The paper sets dense designs, where all parts work on each token, next to Mixture-of-Experts designs, where a few parts work on each token. That split lets size grow past dense caps, yet how it shapes the gain of facts was not known. The team sets out Gated-LPI, a neuron-level score based on log-probability increase, which splits gains across neurons.
arxiv-2601-08783:
Eline Kempkes and Alberto Perez de Alba Ortiz work on ways to map the energy hills of small scale systems. Such maps show which states a molecule likes and how it moves. Biased runs can cross hills that plain runs can not cross in time. But each new system tends to need fresh hand tuning of the bias.

The team boosts a known bias method called umbrella sampling. They add a math tool that sums the biased runs with less waste. The aim is a method that works well on many kinds of systems with less fuss. A reader who runs molecule sims gets a more firm path to energy maps. Less hand tuning means more time on the science.
arxiv-2601-08983:
Yinon Spinka and Oren Yakir study fair matches between random points and grid points on a vast graph. The graph is of a type that spreads fast, called non-amenable. Points fall at a set rate, at random. A match pairs each random point to a grid point. A good match keeps most pair spans short, and looks the same from each node.

The pair ask when a best such match can be built, and how short its spans can be. Past work left gaps for this fast spread graph type. Their work fills part of that gap with firm bounds. A reader in chance and graphs gets a new base case. It helps work on fair load share in vast nets.
arxiv-2601-09183:
Takahito Kashiwabara bounds how fast the flow strength can grow for the sea and air flow rules used in weather work. Those rules are the primitive equations. They run in a box that wraps round in the flat ways, with set rules at top and base. Full drag terms are kept in the rules, as in real flow.

He proves the strength gauge can grow at most by a single exponential in time. That bound is more sharp than past double bounds for this case. It rests on care with the top and base rules. A reader in flow math gets a firm growth cap. Such caps help prove that weather sims stay sound over long runs.
arxiv-2601-09583:
Berke Ates, Philipp Schaad, Timo Schneider, Alexandru Calotoiu, and Torsten Hoefler build tooling for people who design compiler languages. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents MLIR-Forge, a modular framework for language smiths. Domain-specific languages rely on custom middle forms inside their compiler pipelines.

Each new form adds power but also bulk, so it must be tested with care. MLIR-Forge aims to make building and testing such forms easier within the MLIR project. Good compilers sit under most computing in science, so better tooling lifts many fields at once. The framework targets the gap between a language idea and a reliable compiler.
arxiv-2601-09683:
I. F. Herrera-González computes how heat flows through a disordered chain of atoms. The 2026 arXiv paper studies one-dimensional harmonic chains with mass disorder and weak bond disorder. The chain's ends touch heat baths through weak, mismatched links.

The model includes correlations within the mass disorder, within the bond disorder, and between the two. An analytical approach, rather than pure simulation, reveals how those correlations steer thermal conductivity. Tiny chains are testbeds for the physics of insulation at small scales. The results inform how disorder can be used to block or guide heat.
arxiv-2601-09883:
Xinxing Ren and seven co-authors, from the CORAL project, replace fixed workflows for agent teams with information flow. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes an orchestrated multi-agent paradigm built on agent-to-agent communication. Most current systems follow workflows that engineers enumerate in advance.

In rule-based designs, humans must predefine task states, routing rules, and what context each step receives. That rigidity breaks on open-ended work. Letting agents pass information directly to each other promises teams that can adapt as their tasks unfold step by step. The new paradigm targets the brittle middle layer of today's agent frameworks, where most designs tend to break first.
arxiv-2601-10083:
Shayan Hamidi Dehshali, Tzu-Hsuan Liao, and Shaileshh Bojja Venkatakrishnan lay out links for vast fleets of low orbit craft. Such fleets can form a fast web with wide reach. Laser links let craft talk at high speed with low lag. But which craft should link to which is a hard call.

The team shapes the link web by demand. Places with more need get more links. The plan uses shape math and graph tools. It is tested in sims of the fleet. The aim is a web that serves real need, not a plain grid. That should lift speed where users are.
arxiv-2601-10283:
Dmitrii Kolotkov, Anne-Marie Broomhall, Laura Jade Millson, and Sergey Belov track sun waves past a cut off tone. The sun rings with sound waves from its core. Past a set tone, waves can leak to the air. Their hues show a fine comb of peaks and dips.

That comb comes from waves that clash as they rise. The team ask if the comb shifts with the sun's cycle. The cycle is the slow swing in sun spots and flares. They use both sun data and like data from far stars. A shift would tie deep waves to the cycle's pull.
arxiv-2601-10383:
Marcel Gohsen and co authors test if a busy mind misses fake voices. Fake voice tools can forge a speech with ease. Such fakes can spread false tales on social feeds. How well a hearer spots them sets how far a fake can go. Past tests used calm hearers with full focus.

Real hearers are oft busy or tired. The team ask if that load cuts spot rates. They test hearers under set loads as they judge clips. A drop would mean fakes gain when minds are taxed. The work speaks to how feeds and news rooms should flag voice clips.
arxiv-2601-10583:
Maximilian Schiffer, Heiko Hoppe, Yue Su, Louis Bouvier, and Axel Parmentier survey a young field that joins two older ones. The field mixes machine learning with combinatorial optimization, the math of choosing the best option from a huge set. It goes by the name COAML. The authors map its base ideas, its uses, and its open fronts.

In COAML, an optimization oracle sits inside the learning pipeline. The learned rules stay data-driven, yet they respect hard limits on what counts as a valid choice. The survey ties the field to machine learning, operations research, and stochastic optimization. It gives new readers one place to see the whole landscape and where work is still needed.
arxiv-2601-10883:
Andrea Rondelli designs a public-key cryptographic algorithm meant to stand against quantum adversaries. In antiquity, a seal stood for trust, secrecy, and integrity in letters. Modern public-key systems play that role for digital messages. Quantum computers threaten many of them, since they can break the math that current keys rest on.

Rondelli's design draws on differential geometry and algebraic topology for its hard problems. Geometry-based hardness is a less worn path than number theory. The paper frames the scheme as a bid to keep the old seal's promise in an era of quantum machines and strong AI. Cryptographers get a fresh candidate to test, attack, and judge.
arxiv-2601-11383:
S. Giappichini, M. Klute, M. Presilla, X. Zuo, and M. Cepeda plan Higgs measures at FCC-ee. Their 2026 preprint studies the Higgs decay to tau pairs. The Future Circular Collider is CERN's planned flagship machine. Its electron-positron arm is called FCC-ee in the plan.

The tau-pair decay has a large share of Higgs decays. It is clean to spot in the FCC-ee setting. Tau polarization can also be rebuilt from the decay. Polarization adds a handle on the Higgs's traits. The team measures the cross-section for that channel. Such measures test if the Higgs acts as theory says. The work feeds the case for the future collider.
arxiv-2601-11483:
Lukas Vierus and coauthors extend tensor field tomography to moving fields. Their 2026 preprint handles attenuation and refraction at once. Tomography rebuilds inner fields from rays that cross them. Tensor fields carry direction as well as size at each point.

The model uses attenuated ray transforms of the fields. Rays bend along geodesic curves set by refraction. The bending follows a Riemannian metric from the refractive index. Time-dependence adds a dynamic case to the classic setup. The team derives adjoint operators for that dynamic case. Adjoints are the key step toward rebuilding the fields. Numerical experiments test the theory on synthetic data.
arxiv-2601-11683:
Zhuoyi Shang and five coauthors attest model lineage after fine-tuning. Their 2026 preprint tracks knowledge evolution along the tuning path. Fine-tuning creates lineage links among deep learning models. A tuned model descends from its base in a clear line.

Lineage could answer pressing security concerns in open libraries. Unauthorized redistribution of models is one such concern. False claims of model provenance are another live risk. Open-weight libraries often lack robust lineage checks. The team uses the fine-tuning trajectory as evidence. Consistent knowledge evolution along it attests true descent. Proven lineage helps owners prove what is theirs.
arxiv-2601-11783: Murtuza N. Shergadwala tests a common way to audit AI systems in firms. In fields such as hiring, firms must show that AI tools obey set rules. A quick route is to let a large model judge if outputs obey the rules. That route scales well, but its steadiness was not checked. He calls the risk the stability trap. A judge that shifts its calls from run to run can hide real faults.
arxiv-2601-12183:
Davide Rinaldi, Radim Filip, Dario Gerace, and Giacomo Guarnieri chase max precision in charging multi-qubit quantum batteries. Precision, robustness, and efficiency all matter in quantum tech design. A charger must hit a set charge level, hold it under noise, and waste little energy.

They show that true quantum traits, plus non-Gaussianity, can give the best of all three at once. Their setup draws on a light-matter model. A precise quantum battery would help small quantum devices. The work maps how to reach that charge point.  Three goals at once is the hard core of the claim.
arxiv-2601-12383:
Ahmad Mousavi and three co authors work on a hard class of optimization problems. The task is to shrink a smooth function, which may be nonconvex, over a sparse symmetric set. Sparse means most values in the answer should be zero. Sets of this kind show up in tasks where one wants a compact, clean solution.

The team put forward an improved penalty decomposition algorithm. It uses a quasi Newton method to solve a chain of penalty subproblems. The chain splits into two blocks with distinct traits. The first block has a closed form answer with no sparsity rule. The second block is handled by a fast sparse projection onto the feasible set.
arxiv-2601-12583:
The CMS Collaboration combines many searches for heavy new particles at the Large Hadron Collider. The quarry is a heavy vector boson resonance, a short lived particle with spin one. The data come from proton proton collisions at an energy of 13 TeV. Single searches each cover one decay path, and each has limited reach on its own.
