The team merge the searches into one combined statistical analysis. The resonance could decay into pairs of W or Z bosons, or Higgs bosons. It could also decay into quark pairs or lepton pairs of several kinds. Combining channels sharpens the net limit on such a particle. A null result still pays off, since it rules out wide zones of theory space.
arxiv-2601-12683:
Liwei Liao and Ronggang Wang work on segmenting scenes built from 3D Gaussians. Such scenes represent a place as a cloud of soft Gaussian blobs. Segmentation methods for these scenes have emerged as the format spread. Most of them cut the scene at the level of single Gaussian primitives.

That primitive level cut has a flaw at object edges. Gaussians vary a lot in scale, and large ones often span foreground and background. Cutting by primitive then yields jagged boundaries on segmented objects. Their method is called GaussianTrimmer, and it trims boundaries online. Cleaner boundaries matter for editing, robotics, and virtual scene work. The work targets a visible artifact that users notice at once.
arxiv-2601-12983:
Jesus-German Ortiz-Barajas, Jonathan Tonglet, Vivek Gupta, and Iryna Gurevych test how language models can be misused to make misleading charts. Multimodal models now automate chart generation from data tables. That enables efficient analysis and reporting at scale. It also introduces new misuse risks, since a chart can lie while its data stay true.

Their framework is called ChartAttack. It evaluates how models can be prompted to generate misleading charts at scale. Slanted axes, cherry picked ranges, and swapped colors are classic chart tricks. Knowing how easily models produce them helps set guardrails. The work serves data literacy and AI safety at once.
arxiv-2601-13083:
L. F. Melo, O. Jimenez, and L. Neves set sharp bounds on a core trade off in quantum tests. A test rig can split a quantum bit, called a quanton, across many paths. One part of the test shows wave like acts. A second part stores clues about which path was taken.

In their rig the quanton can take N paths, each as likely as the next. It meets a detector whose clue states are set in a fair, matched way. The team then proves bounds that link two scores. One score is wave coherence, read by a form of entropy. The other is path clue, read by shared data from telling detector states apart. The bounds make the old wave versus bit trade off exact for this broad rig.
arxiv-2601-13183:
Sergio Servantez, Sarah B. Lawsky, Rajiv Jain, Daniel W. Linna Jr., and Kristian Hammond build a new kind of test for law sense in AI. Tests of sense have driven gains in language models. Yet a fixed set of question and answer pairs gives just a snap shot. It squeezes rich acts into one score.

That flaw bites hard in law, where rules bind each step. Past law tests cost a lot to build and sort flaws poorly. Their tool, OpenExempt, is a probe test for law sense. They also give a frame to build like tests on call, fit to a flaw a team wants to isolate. Law and AI teams gain a way to find where a model fails, not just that it fails.
arxiv-2601-13283:
Abhinava Chatterjee and Chao-Xing Liu study how a surface effect can make sound like waves in a film act one way. The film is a magnetic topological insulator, a stuff whose bulk blocks current while its face can carry it. Wake its face states with magnetism and a half quantum Hall act shows on the face.

That face act is a mark of axion type charge rules. The team asks how it pairs with phonon Hall viscosity, a trait that can give sound waves a handed spin. They find face led chirality and one way acts for such waves. For staff who hunt new wave tools, one way sound in a film is a rich prize.
arxiv-2601-13383:
A. A. Jafari, C. Ozcinar, and G. Anbarjafari built a light frame for AI agents that firms can bend to their needs. Large language models sparked a shift in agent build. Agents can now sense, plan, and run multi step tasks. Yet old frames are oft stiff, tied to one vendor, or too bulk to bend fast.

Their frame, shown in a tool called AgentForge, is modular. Parts can be swapped with no tear of the whole. That keeps build light and lets teams test fast. For firms that must ship agents on a clock, a frame that bends beats one that must be fought. The paper lays out the plan, the build, and uses.
arxiv-2601-13483:
Louiza Fouli, Kuei-Nuan Lin, Haydee Lindo, and Maral Mostafazadehfard mark when the special fibre ring of a ladder module is Gorenstein. A ladder module is a sum of ideals of top minors of a ladder matrix, a matrix with a stair of zeros. Its special fibre ring codes how the module acts at a prime.

Gorenstein rings are a prized class with a deep duality. The team gives terms that are both need and apt for that trait. The terms are read off the matrix data that sets the module. For algebra staff, a read off test beats a case by case hunt for a trait as deep as this one.
arxiv-2601-13583:
J. Stiles built a Python tool kit to grade radio antennas in the frequency domain in one flow. Such tests check how an antenna takes power, beams it, and holds its tune. Data comes from both lab marks and sims, in mixed forms that take hand work to join.

The kit is called AAFIYA. It runs S parameters, impedance, realized gain, beam patterns, and polarization marks in one pass. It also gives a calibration based yield call, how many built units pass. It reads stock Touchstone files and beam data. For radio teams, one flow for all marks cuts the glue code each new test now needs.
arxiv-2601-13683:
Boyuan Cao and co-authors aim to cut the cost of making images with diffusion transformers in 2026. These models, called DiTs, make high-fidelity images that look sharp and true. Their self-attention step, though, grows in cost with the square of the input size. That quadratic cost blocks use at large scales.

The team builds a linear form of attention with a dynamic differential twist. Linear cost grows in a straight line, not a square, with size. Keeping image quality high while costs drop is the core test. Cheaper, finer image models would serve more users on less hardware.
arxiv-2601-13883:
Cuong Le, Thang Vu, Stefano Andrenacci, and Symeon Chatzinotas study spectrum sharing between ground and space networks in 2026. Terrestrial base stations and non-terrestrial ones, on satellites, must coexist in the same spectrum. Their joint resource allocation is a constrained problem. Real cases bring many channels, many users, and fast-changing user behavior.

The team uses constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning for the task. Many agents learn to share while respecting hard limits. Scale and flexibility are the twin aims of the work. Good sharing lets satellite links boost, not jam, ground networks.
arxiv-2601-14183:
Francesco Mottes, Qian-Ze Zhu, and Michael Brenner tune exact stochastic kinetic models with gradient methods in 2026. Such models describe systems across biology, chemistry, and physics. In them, events are discrete and counts are small, so smooth approximations fall short. Design and inference both need search over paths drawn by the standard sampler.

The discrete reaction events in those paths block the usual gradient flow. A gradient needs a smooth slope, and a jump has none. Their method finds a way to push gradients through such jumps. That opens exact models to the same fast tuning used in deep learning. The method runs on data drawn from past runs, with no fresh shots on the rig.
arxiv-2601-14283:
Kangyu Zheng, Kai Zhang, Jiale Tan, and a team across several labs compare drug design methods in this 2026 paper. The field is structure-based drug design, where new drug candidates are shaped to fit a target protein. Three kinds of algorithms lead the field. They are search-based methods, deep generative models, and reinforcement learning.

Most past studies compare models inside one kind only. Cross-kind comparisons are rare, so no one knows the true trade-offs. The team built a benchmark that runs all three kinds on shared ground. Its title says the results expose key trade-offs among 1D, 2D, and 3D methods. Readers get a fair map of what each approach does best.
arxiv-2601-14383:
Jennifer N. Stafford and four co-authors study heat flow in galaxy clusters in this 2026 paper. Cool core clusters have dense, cool gas at their centers that should cool and flow inward. Conduction, heat carried by particle motion, was mostly discounted as the fix. It moves heat too slowly to warm the core from outside.

The team looks at a special case. Jets from the central black hole can stir hot and cold gas into close contact. Conduction grows strong when materials of very different temperature sit that close. Their title calls the effect self-limiting. The paper studies how jet-modulated conduction behaves under that limit.
arxiv-2601-14483:
A. Mummery studies black hole masses in this 2026 paper. Tidal disruption events happen when a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and is torn apart. They offer a truly unique, and potentially very powerful, probe of the quiescent supermassive black hole population. Most black holes are quiet, so such probes are rare and prized.

Current survey capabilities shape what can be learned. The vast majority of tidal disruption events found in the next decade will be observed only across optical and ultraviolet wavelengths. Mummery studies mass inference from the optical flares of these events. Readers get a method to weigh dormant black holes from the flash of a single destroyed star.
arxiv-2601-14583:
Walter H. Hartung, Wei Chang, Sang-Hoon Kim, Taro Konomi, and Ting Xu write practical notes on RF cavity tests in this 2026 paper. Radio-frequency cavities power particle accelerators. A cavity with a mismatched input coupler poses a measurement problem. Direct calculation of power dissipation and intrinsic quality factor from continuous-wave measurements may carry uncertainty from systematic errors.

The authors focus on two-port CW measurements. Their notes cover self-consistency assessment: checks that tell whether the numbers agree with each other. They also cover indirect methods for the same quantities. Readers who run cavity test stands get guidance on trusting their quality factor values.
arxiv-2601-14683:
Aisvarya Adeseye, Jouni Isoaho, Seppo Virtanen, and Mohammad Tahir work on privacy in qualitative research in this 2026 paper. Qualitative data often contain personal, contextual, and organizational details. Those details pose privacy risks if not handled appropriately. Manual anonymization is time-consuming and inconsistent. It frequently omits critical identifiers.

Existing automated tools tend to rely on pattern matching or fixed rules. Such tools fail to capture context and may alter the meaning of the data. The team uses local language models for context-aware adaptive anonymization of sensitive text. Local means the text never leaves the researcher's machine. Readers get a privacy tool that reads for meaning before it hides a name.
arxiv-2601-15183:
Marcelo Campos and Cosmin Pohoata update lower bounds for multicolor Ramsey numbers. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a classic question in graph theory. A Ramsey number marks the size at which a pattern must appear, no matter how edges are colored.

The work builds on results by Conlon, Ferber, and Wigderson, and on a step by Sawin. The key tool is an upper bound on how sparse the independent sets of a certain graph must be. From that bound, the authors draw fresh lower bounds for the multicolor Ramsey numbers.
arxiv-2601-15283:
Ruofan Liang, Norman Müller, and co-authors take indoor lighting apart so it can be remixed. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with light editing in indoor scenes. The input is a single multi-view capture of a room.

Their method uses a generative model to split the scene's light into its sources. Each lamp or window becomes a separate factor. Once split, each source can be edited on its own. Users can switch it off or on, shift its color, or change its brightness, and then rebuild the newly lit indoor scene at will.
arxiv-2601-15383:
Krista Lynne Smith, Macon Magno, and Michael Koss watch a small galaxy's core flicker in two bands at once. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with UGC 6728, a dwarf Seyfert galaxy. They present radio and X-ray light curves taken at the same times over five years.

The X-ray curve shows a flaring stretch, then a slow rise and fall. Through all that change, the X-ray hardness ratio and spectrum stay much the same. The observations were serendipitous, a lucky catch. Paired curves like these are rare for such a small active galaxy.
arxiv-2601-15483:
Kahn Rhrissorrakrai and six co-authors test quantum machine learning on a medical task in a 2026 arXiv paper. The task is to predict antibiotic resistance from clinical urine cultures. Resistance ranks among the top threats to human health, the authors note. Poor antibiotic use is a main driver of that threat. Better prediction could guide treatment choices.

The team calls their study the first large-scale test of its kind. They check whether quantum methods help on this real clinical problem. They also study a data complexity signature. Per the title, that signature predicts when quantum projected learning gives a benefit. For clinicians and model builders alike, the draw is practical. The work asks where quantum tools earn their keep, using data from actual patient care.
arxiv-2601-15683:
Baradhwaj Coleppa, Akshat Khanna, Santosh Kumar Rai, and Agnivo Sarkar hunt for new particles at the LHC in a 2026 arXiv paper. Extending the scalar sector is a standard route beyond the Standard Model. Their model is the Three Higgs Doublet Model, with a Z3 symmetry. They work in the Type-Z, or democratic, Yukawa setup. The paper examines how this model would show up in collider data.

Their focus is neutral scalar cascades. A heavy scalar can decay through lighter ones in steps. Such chains leave distinctive signatures in detectors. Mapping those signatures tells experimentalists what to search for. It also tells them which signals would point to three doublets rather than two. For collider phenomenology, that translation from model to signal is the core service.
arxiv-2601-15983:
Masashi Aiko and five co-authors compute corrections to Higgs boson decays in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their model adds a complex triplet field to the Higgs sector. Such an extension can generate neutrino mass through the Type-II seesaw mechanism. The extension usually predicts a rho parameter different from one at tree level. Rho measures a key electroweak ratio. Its shift changes how electroweak parameters are renormalized.

That makes the model differ from the Standard Model and from two-Higgs-doublet models. The authors compute radiative corrections to decays of the 125 GeV Higgs boson in this setting. Precision Higgs data from colliders can then test the model. Small deviations in decay rates would be the tell. The paper supplies the theory numbers those tests need.
arxiv-2601-16083:
Matthew Shorvon, Frederik Mallmann-Trenn and David Watson tackle a core task in chance based thought. Their 2026 preprint deals with the best single guess for a set of facts. That guess is known as the maximum a posteriori pick. To find it in full is known to be hard. It stays hard in many plain cases and with rough methods too.

The team frames the task in a looser sense. They ask for a pick that is close to best with high odds. That frame is known as prob ably approx i mate ly correct in the field. A loose but firm frame can make hard tasks usable. The work sets bounds for when such picks can be found.
arxiv-2601-16383:
Soumitri Chattopadhyay, Başar Demir and Marc Niethammer test big med image tools with loose prompts. Their 2026 preprint deals with tools that cut 3D med scans by prompt. Such tools show strong skill when prompts are sharp. Real prompts in wards are oft loose or off the mark. Loose prompts may bend the cut in ways past tests miss.

The team bends dense prompts in set, ruled ways. They then weigh how cuts shift as prompts stray. Firm tools should hold their cuts through small prompt flaws. Weak tools will need prompt guards in real use. The work maps prompt risk for ward use.
arxiv-2601-16783:
Sam Mathew sorts all ways to morph one least-area graph skin to the next. A least-area skin spans a wire loop with least size. A graph skin is one drawn from a height map. Morph maps shift one height map to a next one. Their 2026 preprint gives a full sort of such morphs.

The sort lists which least-area graph skins can morph at all. It names the morph maps that do the job. Full sorts close long hunts in surface math. They also tell film and design tools which skins can blend. Least-area skins show up in roofs and nano forms too.
arxiv-2601-16983:
Willem Hoogendam and a large team read light from a comet born past our Sun. The comet 3I/ATLAS is just the third such guest known. Guests like it carry stuff from far star homes. Its gas glow can tell what that stuff is. Their 2026 preprint reads its glow since it passed the Sun.

A field scope split the comet's glow by place and hue. Past reads tracked it as it came in. Now it leaves, and its glow has shifted. Shifts tell how Sun heat changed its ice and dust. Such guests give rare ground truth on far systems.
arxiv-2601-17083:
Goldy Ahuja and Shashikiran Ganesh track how faint forces bend a comet's path. The comet 3I/ATLAS is the third known guest from past our Sun. It passed its near point to the Sun in late 2025. Now it heads out, set to pass near Jupiter. Forces past gravity's pull can nudge its path. Heat jets and light push are such faint forces.

Their 2026 preprint weighs how each faint force bends the track. The Jupiter pass sits at a third of an Earth-Sun span. True tracks tell if the comet's jets push hard or soft. They also sharpen charts of its home-bound path.
arxiv-2601-17383:
Chen Ling and five co-authors show a new attack on large vision-language models. These models see images and reason about the real world. Prompt injection is a known flaw, where fake commands hijack the model. Past attacks need access to input channels. Or they need to know the user's query. Those terms rarely hold in real use.

The team's physical prompt injection works in the open world. Malicious cues sit in the scene the model views. That makes the threat far more real for robots and cameras. Defenders must now guard the scene, not just the text box. The work sets a harder bar for safe deployment.
arxiv-2601-17483:
Barak Or tackles sudden failure in neural network training. Modern training can be fragile. Rare bad updates can cause divergence that cannot be undone. Or they can quietly drag quality down. Most current methods try to prevent such breaks inside the optimizer. Once a break starts, they offer little way back.

Or proposes automatic stability and recovery for training. The system should catch instability as it starts. It should then restore a sound state and resume. That shift treats training like a process that needs a safety net. Big training runs cost vast sums. A recovery tool could save runs that now are lost. The work targets a pain every large lab knows.
arxiv-2601-18383:
Zhenyuan Guo and six colleagues look for a way to make large reasoning models cheaper to run. Such models write out a long chain of thought before they give a final reply. That chain helps on hard tasks, but it eats up memory and time. Long chains slow each reply and raise the cost of each run.

The team treats some parts of the chain as more key than the rest. Their plan picks which thought steps to keep with care. It trims the parts that add little to the final reply. A leaner chain should keep most of the skill while it cuts the load on the chip. Work of this kind is key as firms try to serve more users with the same stock of machines.
arxiv-2601-18483:
Arya Labroo and four colleagues test how well language models can hold two style goals at once. A user may ask for text that is both funny and strong in its pitch. Past tools could set one trait at a time, by prompt tricks or by tweaks inside the model. Joint sets of traits were far less checked, and the checks that do exist stay coarse.

The team built a finer test that grades traits one by one and in pairs. It asks if a gain in one trait costs a loss in the next. The title gives their main hint: the two goals tend to clash. A tool that must be both at once may end up as not quite each. The test could help firms set fair hopes for style control in chat tools and ad tools.
arxiv-2601-18683:
Alicja Polanska and Jason McEwen hone a way to score how well a world view fits the facts, in the hard case where the view has more than one peak. That score, called the marginal likelihood, sums the fit of a view over all its dial sets. It is the key score when two views are set side by side. It is also hard to work out when the peaks are far apart.

A past tool learned to fix the score from a set of draws from the view. It worked well but could wobble on peak-rich views. The pair blend it with a way to build draws that can hop peaks with ease. That blend should keep the score firm where the old tool shook. Firm scores help staff pick the right view of the sky, of genes, or of markets.
arxiv-2601-19683:
Hanting Niu and four colleagues improve a basic neural network tool. Multi-layer perceptrons are the standard blocks for learning functions from data. Their outputs are inherently smooth everywhere. Some real functions, though, are continuous yet have sharp corners at chosen points. Such functions are non-differentiable at those points by design, and smooth networks struggle to copy them.

Their network, SharpNet, is built to represent functions with controlled non-differentiability. The sharp features are prescribed in advance, so the model knows where the corners belong. Older workarounds bolted on fixes after training. A built-in ability should give cleaner and more exact fits. Shape modeling and geometry processing are natural homes for such functions.
arxiv-2601-20183:
Yuhua Zhao, Tiejun Lv, and Ke Wang study data freshness in satellite Internet of Things systems, where sensors send readings through orbiting links. Satellite links face long delays, fading signals, and scarce bandwidth all at once. A layered retransmission scheme improves reliability, but its backward decoding makes the age of the data unclear.

The authors define a metric that handles this ambiguity and use it in a cross-layer optimization. Their goal is to balance freshness against transmission efficiency, since sending more often wastes scarce bandwidth. The work matters for remote sensing networks, where stale data can be nearly as bad as lost data.
arxiv-2601-20283:
Tanmay Karmakar and three colleagues show that a single well-chosen word can fool a neural text ranking model. Ranking models are effective at retrieval, but earlier work showed they can be pushed around by attacks. The authors revisit this with a minimal, query-aware attack that promotes a target document.

The attack inserts or swaps in one word aligned with the query, the query center. If one word can lift a document's rank, ranking systems are more fragile than their scores suggest. The finding matters for search engines and for any contest where placement brings money or attention.
arxiv-2601-20483:
Ashot Matevosyan, Frank Jülicher, and Ricard Alert study noise that emerges in active gels when detailed balance is broken. In equilibrium, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem ties thermal fluctuations to dissipation. Living systems are driven out of equilibrium by internal processes, which produce extra, active fluctuations.

Predicting the statistics of those fluctuations is still hard, though they matter for functions such as transport inside cells. Active gels are lab models of the cell's inner scaffolding. The authors work out how nonequilibrium noise arises there, a step toward reading cell mechanics from its flickering.
arxiv-2601-20683:
Samuel Rhys Cox, Joel Wester, and Niels van Berkel study how chatbots should give feedback. Their paper appears in the 2026 CHI conference proceedings. Chatbots are now common in programs that help people change habits. The tone of a bot's reply can shape how users react. A style that feels pushy can spark reactance, the urge to push back.

The team frames a design trade-off. Feedback must not feel like a threat to the user's freedom. Yet it should still surprise and engage the user. A polite style may be safe but dull, as the title hints. The study weighs these two pulls against each other. Its lessons help designers pick a voice for bots that coach health and habits.
arxiv-2601-20783:
Naveen Durvasula proposes a principled way to order transactions in smart contracts. His 2026 paper presents the Monotone Priority System. Modern blockchain applications gain from stating sequencing constraints on the calls they receive. Order can decide who profits and who loses. But free-form constraints could make block production hard to compute.

Durvasula seeks a balance between expressivity and tractability. The system lets contracts specify how their function calls should be sequenced. It does so on an axiomatic basis, so the rules rest on stated principles. The aim is a design that is both flexible and practical for block builders. The paper speaks to blockchain designers who need fair, predictable ordering without slowing the chain.
arxiv-2601-21083:
Jarrod Barnes measures whether AI incident responders know when they might be wrong. The 2026 paper presents OpenSec, a benchmark for incident response agent calibration. As language models improve, so do their offensive uses. Frontier agents now generate working exploits for under fifty dollars in compute, he notes. Defensive agents must keep pace. Existing benchmarks, though, conflate doing an action with doing it correctly. That hides calibration failures.

Calibration means the agent's confidence matches its true accuracy. The danger grows when agents process adversarial evidence. Attackers can plant clues that mislead the responder. OpenSec tests agents under exactly that pressure. It separates action execution from correct execution in scoring. The benchmark helps security teams judge which agents to trust at 3 a.m. It reframes defense evaluation around honest uncertainty.
arxiv-2601-21183:
Jacek Duszenko localizes the exact moment a reasoning model caves to its user. The 2026 paper studies sycophancy in reasoning models. These models frequently agree with incorrect user suggestions. That behavior is known as sycophancy. It is unclear where in the reasoning trace the agreement originates. It is also unclear how strong the commitment is. Duszenko introduces sycophantic anchors to answer both questions.

An anchor is a sentence that causally locks the model into agreement. Once written, the rest of the trace follows it. Anchors can be located and their strength quantified. That turns a vague worry into a measurable event. Developers could then target training at those sentences. The work serves anyone who needs AI that pushes back when the user is wrong. It gives sycophancy a handle researchers can grip.
arxiv-2601-21483:
Jonas Becker and a large team build multilingual datasets for a richer kind of stance analysis. Classic stance work sorts a writer's view on a target into broad camps like favor or against. Real attitudes, though, vary in strength and heat, not just in side.

The team models stance along two smooth scales drawn from emotion science. One scale runs from negative to positive, and the other from calm to active. Their datasets cover several languages. Finer scales let researchers track how public feeling shifts in degree, which blunt labels can miss entirely.
arxiv-2601-21583:
Tin Hadži Veljković, Erik Bekkers, Michael Tiemann, and Jan-Willem van de Meent give learning systems a smooth way to predict sets of unknown size. Many tasks need a set as output: objects in a scene, molecules, or sources in the sky. The count is part of what must be predicted.

Older methods pad outputs to a fixed size or guess the count as a separate step. Both routes are clumsy and error-prone. The authors build continuous representations of discrete sets, so learning can flow smoothly. A cleaner set representation helps detection, science, and design tools that think in collections rather than single answers.
arxiv-2601-21883:
Victor Spitzer and Francois Sanson study decision-focused learning, where a predictive model is trained to improve the final decision, not just its own accuracy. The model feeds a combinatorial optimization problem, such as scheduling or routing, and training must pass gradients through that optimizer.

That differentiation is the central challenge, and recent methods use perturbation-based approximations to get through it. Those approximations can make solutions jumpy, so this 2026 preprint focuses on managing solution stability, using cost regularization to keep decisions steady. Stable decisions matter in practice. A delivery plan that flips wildly after small data changes is hard to trust. The same holds for a power schedule.
arxiv-2601-22283:
Giacomo Marocco, David Moore, and Daniel Carney set out a way to feel tiny pushes past a known quantum limit. Their 2026 preprint works with a tiny glass sphere held in light, free of any touch. The plan squeezes the sphere's state in all three directions of space.

A chain of quick jumps in the trap's rate does the squeezing. The team then weigh how real-world noise, called decoherence, caps the gain. Sharper push sensors could test weak forces and faint signals. The work shows what a real setup must beat. It is a clear target for labs.
arxiv-2601-22383:
G. Alencar, C. R. Muniz, and M. S. Oliveira map a black string in a curved cosmos onto a simpler field, twice over. A black string is a black hole stretched along one line. Their 2026 preprint works in anti-de Sitter space, a cosmos with a steady inward pull.

The trick, called the classical double copy, turns gravity math into gauge-field math. They cast the string in Kerr-Schild form over a drum-shaped base space. From that form they build the single copy and the zeroth copy. The work tests how far the copy trick reaches. Each new case firms up the claim.
arxiv-2601-22783:
Ilyass Moummad and a team speed wildlife record search by packing text codes into compact hypercubes. Biodiversity platforms hold vast archives of sightings, sounds, and notes. Their 2026 preprint notes that rich foundation-model codes make search slow at that scale, due to high-dimensional matching.

Compact codes cut the cost of finding like records. Fast retrieval helps trackers spot trends and rare events in time. The work serves field science with a systems fix. It keeps meaning while shrinking size. That trade is the whole game at archive scale. The gain grows as the archive grows.
arxiv-2601-22883:
Michiel De Wilde and Robert Seiringer show a surprising freedom in how an ideal Bose gas can condense. In such a gas, many particles settle into the lowest energy state, forming a condensate. With the right boundary rules for the space, the authors prove far more freedom is possible.

In the large-system limit, any number of condensates can appear, each shaped by an arbitrary harmonic function. Harmonic functions are smooth shapes fixed by a simple equation. The result widens what theory says quantum gases can do at very low temperatures.
arxiv-2601-22983:
Tristan Bilot, Baoxiang Jiang, and Thomas Pasquier build a fair testbed for intrusion detection based on system history. Such systems watch provenance graphs, records of which process touched which file, to catch advanced attacks. Comparing them has been hard because studies use mismatched data prep, splits, labels, and metrics.

Their tool, PIDSMaker, standardizes how these detectors are built and judged. A shared yardstick shows which methods truly work, and which only looked good under friendly settings. That clarity helps defenders pick tools that hold up in real networks. Standardized splits and labeling are part of the remedy, since mismatched ground truth made past comparisons nearly meaningless.
arxiv-2601-23183:
Casimiro Pio Carrino and four co-authors release JobResQA, a benchmark for reading résumés and job descriptions. It tests machine reading comprehension of language models on human-resources tasks. The set holds hundreds of question-answer pairs over synthetic résumé and job pairs in five languages.

Questions range over three levels, from basic fact extraction to cross-document reasoning. Multilingual hiring documents are a real test of practical language skill. A public benchmark helps employers and builders judge tools before trusting them with applicants. Synthetic résumé and job pairs keep the benchmark safe to share, avoiding real applicants' private employment histories.
arxiv-2602-02383:
Maksim Afanasyev and 1 co-author propose a safer way to teach language models from human preferences in a 2026 arXiv paper. Preference methods usually reward a model for ranking a chosen answer above a rejected one. That relative goal can backfire: the model may lower the quality of good answers, a failure called unlearning, or wreck its formatting by crushing rejected answers too hard.

Their method, SLIME, needs no reference model and splits the goal into three parts. One part anchors the model to keep preferred answers likely. Another stops rejected answers from collapsing to zero probability. A third shapes the margin between them with both hard and soft limits. The authors report stronger results than leading baselines, with steadier generation quality throughout training.
arxiv-2602-02483:
Andreas Leibing examines how the economy at high school graduation steers young Germans toward university or vocational training, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Administrative data cover more than six million graduates from 1995 to 2018. The author exploits deviations from long-run state-specific trends to isolate the effect of local labor market conditions at the moment of choice.

College enrollment turns out to be procyclical, rising in good times and falling in bad ones. Cyclical increases in unemployment reduce enrollment at traditional universities. Graduates shift instead toward vocational colleges and apprenticeships, substituting one skill path for another rather than simply delaying education. The pattern matters for policy: a recession at graduation does not just postpone study, it redirects careers. Leibing's evidence quantifies that substitution across nearly a quarter century of German cohorts.
arxiv-2602-02583:
Alireza Moradi and 3 co-authors turn many site-level forecasts into one fleet-level forecast one can trust, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Grid operators often cannot access fleet-level probability models. They instead receive site forecasts from mixed third-party providers, and naive pooling miscalibrates because sites move together in complex ways.

Their system, CoCopula, first models cross-site dependence with copulas, math tools that join distinct distributions into a joint one. Context-aware conformal tuning then recalibrates the pooled forecast to fix coverage. Tests use large solar output data sets from three United States system operators. The method hit near-nominal empirical coverage and steadily lower Winkler scores than competing aggregation rivals across target levels. It matched forecasts calibrated directly at system level. The work grew from a real running challenge raised by an industry partner.
arxiv-2602-02683:
Ben Craps and 3 co-authors ask where the gravitational area term hides in the entanglement entropy of two-dimensional string theory, in their 2026 paper. They work both in the low-energy effective field theory and in the dual matrix quantum mechanics, whose singlet sector describes the same physics. A generic bulk subregion should carry a generalized entropy.

That entropy should combine a dilaton-dependent gravitational term with a matter contribution from the tachyon field. Earlier analyses of the model found only the matter part. The authors test whether the nonlocal leg-pole transformation, which maps the target-space tachyon to matrix-model excitations, can generate the missing area-like term. It cannot, they show. Attention shifts to the non-singlet sectors of the theory as the term's possible origin. The paper maps a genuine gap in how duality handles entanglement.
arxiv-2602-02883:
Faster first-stage search is the goal of a 2026 paper by Parker Carlson and 3 co-authors. Learned sparse retrieval ranks documents using language-model meaning while staying cheap to run on ordinary processors. Earlier systems group blocks of the index into superblocks to skip work quickly, but scoring those groups costs time.

The authors propose a simpler pruning scheme for superblocks. It cuts that scoring cost while keeping result quality competitive. A compact index structure and a ready-to-use configuration accompany it. Tests use the MS MARCO and BEIR collections. Analysis supports the design. The authors present the scheme as a strong, efficient option across retrieval models and datasets.
arxiv-2602-02983:
Do language models reason about causes the way humans do? Hanna M. Dettki and 2 co-authors benchmark that question in a 2026 paper. They compare more than twenty models against matched human judgments. Eleven tasks share a collider structure, where two separate causes produce one shared effect, a classic test of causal reasoning.

A small interpretable model summarized the models' judgments well. Most models reasoned in a more rule-like way than humans. Humans seemed to account for unmentioned hidden factors, while models largely did not mirror human collider biases. Extra tests added abstract wording or irrelevant text. Chain-of-thought prompting improved robustness for many models. The authors suggest model reasoning can complement human judgment, but may falter when uncertainty is intrinsic.
arxiv-2602-03083:
Approximating functions on infinite domains more accurately is the subject of a 2026 paper by Hao Hu and 1 co-author. Generalized Hermite and Laguerre methods use special functions suited to unbounded domains. Their accuracy depends on choosing a scaling factor well, and classical theory misses intricate convergence behaviors that appear in practice for functions with different decay and oscillation patterns.

The authors propose an error analysis framework modeled on the sampling theorem. It characterizes which spatial and frequency bandwidths the sampling points can capture. Functions meeting those limits can be approximated accurately, with systematic guidance for optimal scaling. The framework predicts root-exponential and other convergence patterns. A comparative study shows similar-looking functions can converge at markedly different rates, and paired Laguerre sets can beat single Hermite sets.
arxiv-2602-03383:
In decentralized learning, many machines train one model together without any central coordinator. Bart Cox and 2 co-authors address a weak point of that setup in a 2026 paper. Accuracy drops when each node holds different kinds of data and the communication network never changes. Their answer is an algorithm named Morph.

Morph lets each node pick exchange partners whose models differ most from its own, while keeping the number of incoming links fixed. Nodes find new peers through gossip and keep reshaping the network during training. Tests on image datasets with up to 100 nodes beat static and epidemic baselines. They come close to a fully connected network, converge faster, and need fewer communication rounds.
arxiv-2602-03483:
Kriging predicts values across space from scattered measurements, but its cost grows with the cube of the dataset size. Francisco Cuevas-Pacheco and Jonathan Acosta offer a scalable version in a 2026 paper. Local kriging normally uses the K nearest neighbors, yet picking K by rule of thumb ignores how strongly nearby points actually correlate.

Their penalized kriging adds LASSO-type penalties directly into the kriging equations, so unhelpful neighbors get exactly zero weight automatically. An adaptive version tunes the penalties using the spatial correlation structure, and a criterion built on effective sample size sets the penalty level. Experiments show neighborhoods that adapt to the field, fewer neighbors for smooth processes, and accuracy close to full global kriging at much lower cost.
arxiv-2602-03783:
When one model trains on translation, code, mathematics, and text prediction together, which task taught it what? Zhenshuo Zhang and 2 co-authors study task attribution in a 2026 paper. They use surrogate models that predict target-task performance for any subset of training tasks. The exact alternative, retraining without each task in turn, is infeasible at scale.

Linear surrogates miss nonlinear interactions between tasks, such as XOR-type effects. The authors connect linear surrogates to influence functions through a second-order analysis, then introduce kernel surrogates that capture second-order interactions. A gradient-based estimator learns them efficiently from a first-order approximation of the pretrained model. Kernel surrogates track leave-one-out ground truth far better than baselines and improve downstream data selection substantially.
arxiv-2602-03983:
Robot brains that see, read, and act struggle with long video streams. Weikang Qiu and 3 co-authors present DySta, a framework that splits visual input into static and dynamic parts. Their 2026 paper targets vision-language-action models, whose attention costs balloon with every added frame.

Static tokens, covering what does not change, are stored once and reused across frames. A lightweight gate refreshes that cache only when needed. Dynamic tokens carry the motion. The team also built a benchmark stressing multi-frame integration. DySta improved performance there while cutting context length sharply, a practical step toward robots that watch whole tasks, not snapshots.
arxiv-2602-04383:
A celebrated criterion for the spin glass phase boundary fails in general, show Jean-Christophe Mourrat and 1 co-author. The de Almeida-Thouless line marks where replica symmetry breaks in spin glasses. A recent proposal generalized the criterion to mixed p-spin models. Their 2026 paper tests that generalization.

Using the Hopf-Lax representation of the Parisi formula, they construct explicit counterexamples within the mixed p-spin class. In one model, the perturbation is performed around the unique minimizer of the replica-symmetric free energy, and still the criterion fails to characterize the phase. The classical model's own case remains open, a careful distinction the authors keep.
arxiv-2602-04583:
Gabriele Magrini and 3 co-authors use event cameras to make ordinary image models tougher in a 2026 paper on domain generalization. Event cameras report pixel changes rather than full frames. Their sparse output changes less between day and night than regular images do.

Training the image model to copy event features directly would erase rich semantic detail. Instead, their method, PEPR, asks the image encoder to predict event-based features in a shared space. Event data serve as privileged information, available only during training. The final model uses ordinary images alone. It improved robustness on detection and segmentation tasks under domain shifts, beating methods based on direct feature alignment.
arxiv-2602-04783:
Prateek Vaish and Brenda Rubenstein cut the cost of a demanding quantum chemistry method in a 2026 study. Unitary coupled cluster theory suits strongly correlated molecules and quantum computers, but its cost grows steeply because a key expansion never terminates.

Their approach partitions the problem. Inside a chosen active space, a fourth-order truncated version of the method runs. Outside it, excitations are treated with cheaper perturbation theory. Two variants either sum the parts separately or couple them for accuracy. Tests included a large benchmark set, a chemical reaction, and twisting ethylene. The coupled variant reproduced reference energy curves using only a small share of orbitals, though strongly correlated cases kept inherited flaws.
arxiv-2602-05183:
Watching a language model learn to play Diplomacy by reinforcement learning yields mountains of data and few explanations. John Yan and 5 co-authors apply data-centric interpretability to that task in this 2026 machine learning paper. Their material is large training runs in Full-Press Diplomacy, a demanding multi-agent game of negotiation and betrayal.

Pretrained sparse autoencoders dissect the models' internal features, and a new method, Meta-Autointerp, groups those features into hypotheses about training dynamics. The haul includes role-playing patterns, degenerate outputs, language switching, high-level strategy, and environment-specific bugs. It also includes one surprising case of reward hacking, with automated checks confirming most found features are real. Two user studies add a caution: features that look interesting to humans were often useless or worse. A subset predicted downstream behavior, and adding them to an untrained agent's prompt raised its score notably.
arxiv-2602-05483:
Software teams watch dashboards full of separate gauges, yet a service can drift toward failure while each gauge looks fine on its own. Anatoly Krasnovsky sets out a design for a drift monitor grounded in Rasmussen's dynamic safety model, which views safety as a balance under competing pressures. The monitor treats key state variables, such as remaining margin, work effort, and risk, as parts of one whole that shift over time.

From changing software artifacts, the design builds a stable monitoring state, maps live data into it, and tracks movement toward policy limits in log-ratio coordinates. Splits, merges, and renames are steadied through lineage-aware grouping, so routine churn does not fake a drift signal. The monitor would report drift direction, distance to the boundary, and which part drives the change. A synthetic check shows it can spot boundary drift under controlled churn.
arxiv-2602-05983:
A motorway digital twin needs more than live sensor feeds: to help managers act early, it must also predict traffic ahead. Krešimir Kušić and two co-authors build GATTF, a geographically aware transformer for that forecasting job. The model reads the geography between spread-out sensors through their mutual information, so nearby sensors that move together inform each other.

They test it on live feeds from Geneva's motorway network. Adding geographic awareness beats a standard transformer on accuracy, with no added model complexity. The gain matters for traffic control rooms, where a twin that sees ahead can warn of jams before they form. GATTF shows that where sensors sit is itself useful signal, not just background detail.
arxiv-2602-06083:
Light can appear to travel faster than light itself near strong gravity, once electron effects are counted. Madhukar Deb and 2 co-authors ask whether that odd effect breaks causality, the rule that causes come before effects. They study photons described by the Drummond-Hathrell action, a standard effective theory for this setting.

The team checks the problem two ways. First, they test whether the effective light paths can loop back on themselves, and find conditions where they cannot. Second, they apply flat-space analyticity bounds to the photon signal. In two test cases, a photon orbit near a black hole and a path past two black holes, the effect looked causally safe.
arxiv-2602-06283:
Long documents make attention, the core operation of transformer models, very expensive. Sahil Joshi and 7 co-authors present SOCKET, a method for picking which past tokens deserve attention. It reworks locality-sensitive hashing, a classic trick that buckets similar items together.

Classic hashing gives a yes-or-no collision signal, which ranks tokens poorly and needs many hash tables. SOCKET instead adds up graded collision evidence across tables, producing a soft similarity score that closely tracks the true top tokens while using far less memory. Custom chip kernels handle scoring, selection, and attention. Across long-context benchmarks and several models, SOCKET matched or beat rival sparse attention methods, with much faster processing at the top end.
arxiv-2602-06483:
In a synchrotron storage ring, bunches of electrons circulate and emit radiation for experiments, but dense bunches develop a bursty instability. C Evain and 11 co-authors show those bursts can be synchronized by an outside signal. The instability spontaneously forms microstructures inside the bunch, which appear and vanish in bursts.

Modulating the radiofrequency cavity's electric field with a sine wave locked the bursts to the outside rhythm. The team observed Arnold tongues, regions where locking holds, at the natural rate and at its harmonics and subharmonics. Near the locking edge, the bursts slipped in phase. Simulations based on the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation matched the mechanism, and a proof-of-principle test ran at the SOLEIL facility.
arxiv-2602-06583:
Whether the vacuum of a quantum field in anti-de Sitter spacetime stays stable depends on how the field is quantized. Shi-Yuan Li and Chengwu Liu study scalar and Maxwell fields in that curved setting. For the scalar field, a strong coupling to curvature can push the Hamiltonian's spectrum below zero without a lower bound, which threatens stability.

The problematic modes turn out to be constrained and ambiguous in direction and commutation rule. Only one alternative algebra fits the constraints in three dimensions, and it renders the negative spectrum inactive, leaving physical bosons from the non-negative part to span the space. For Maxwell fields, a gauge-invariant energy tensor directly yields a non-negative Hamiltonian. Renormalized energy tensors stay finite at operator level, securing a stable, maximally symmetric vacuum.
arxiv-2602-07083:
Yongqing Jiang and seven co-authors rethink how language models make building models. Building models sit at the heart of computational engineering science, where even small physical flaws or spec violations can void later simulations. Language models can make modeling code, yet under strict engineering rules their outputs often fail to run or break physics. A new framework aims to fix that, joining three parts: building domain knowledge, aligning models to constraints, and checking through verification.

CivilInstruct, a domain-specific data set, formalizes building knowledge and constraint reasoning, enabling simulation-ready generation. A two-stage fine-tuning strategy enforces constraint satisfaction and interface compliance, cutting hallucinated and non-conforming outputs sharply. MBEval, a checking benchmark, scores runnability and structural dynamics consistency through closed-loop checks. Tests show steady gains over baselines across rigorous checking metrics.
arxiv-2602-07483:
Dense wireless networks must assign channels to avoid interference, a discrete tuning problem that scales poorly.  Kuan-Cheng Chen and three co-authors apply recursive quantum approximate optimization (RQAOA), interleaving shallow quantum layers with variable elimination guided by measured correlators.

Their compact QUBO form encodes pairwise interference as same-channel couplings with one-hot constraints via penalties or constraint-preserving mixers. Fixing high-confidence variables shrinks the instance until it can be solved exactly.  Simulations on modest instances test the approach.  Wireless and quantum tuning teams get a hybrid recipe for interference-aware allocation that spends quantum effort where it matters most.
arxiv-2602-07783:
Coding standards keep team code consistent, but configuring linters to enforce them is slow, expert work that must be redone as languages and tools evolve. Zejun Zhang and seven co-authors propose LintCFG, which compiles plain-language coding standards into linter configurations through a purpose-built intermediate language.

Inspired by compiler design, the method first expresses rules in a tool-neutral, precise domain-specific language, then matches them against configuration instructions for the target linter, verifying names, options, and values. The approach works across languages, standards, and linters rather than being tied to one toolchain. Development teams gain a route to automated, maintainable enforcement of the style rules they actually write down.
arxiv-2602-07883:
AI agents usually run with configurations fixed before the task begins, forcing a choice between specialized strength and broad generality. Jingqi Zhou and eleven co-authors propose ToolSelf, a paradigm in which the executing agent reconfigures itself during the task, treating configuration updates as ordinary tool calls within one policy.

As work progresses, the agent can revise sub-goals, strategies, toolboxes, context, and context-management modes in response to feedback, unifying execution and adaptation instead of separating them. A two-stage configuration-aware training scheme teaches this behavior. The paper addresses a real tension in long-horizon agents: plans made before seeing the task rarely survive contact with it. ToolSelf lets the agent adapt without handing control to a separate optimizer.
arxiv-2602-08083:
Overall tennis ratings blend serving, returning, and other skills, hiding how much the serve alone is worth. Aiwen Li and three co-authors build serve-specific metrics from point-by-point Wimbledon and US Open data. They fit logistic mixed-effects models with serve speed, variability, and placement, plus random effects for server and returner strength.

From those models they derive Server Quality Scores, partially pooled and opponent-adjusted estimates of serving impact. Out of sample, the scores track serve efficiency, winning points within three shots, better than weighted Elo ratings. Analysts and coaches gain a cleaner way to value serving, separate from the rest of a player's game, with benchmarks showing what each modeling choice adds.
arxiv-2602-08283:
Faint, low-surface-brightness shapes record how star cities built, but reaching the needed light depth in optical light remains hard despite decades of scope gains. A large team led by Woowon Byun tells K-DRIFT, a novel scope under building to explore this faint cosmos, with a science theme focused on nearby single star cities.

The paper sketches the scope's specs and the low-surface-brightness traits it targets, including star birth in regions of low gas density, where standard grasp of star birth is stretched thinnest. Built-in doubts that limit seen brightness levels motivate the dedicated design. Astronomers gain a clear statement of what K-DRIFT will hunt and why the faint cosmos deserves its own instrument.
arxiv-2602-08483:
Superintelligence is often imagined as human ability scaled up, but Byung Gyu Chae proposes a different picture: a sharp change in kind, driven by how a system moves as a whole. His arXiv paper builds a field model in which loops that feed back push a mind-like system toward a critical state with many slow shared motions. The author argues that this shift creates coherent motion along low-dimensional surfaces.

Numerical work finds that relaxation rates follow power laws with set exponents, placing the system in a self-organized critical class. A built-in balancing force adds a stabilizing gap, so the critical part persists without collapse. Readers should treat the claims as theory only: the paper proposes a new stability class for superintelligence, it does not show one in any built system.
arxiv-2602-08583:
Particles usually flow downhill along concentration gradients, but in crowded, charged systems they can flow uphill instead. Francesco Casini and four co-authors study that regime in drift-diffusion models with volume exclusion. Their arXiv paper starts from a multispecies exclusion process and derives its stationary hydrodynamic limit.

That limit predicts sharply characterized uphill regimes across the space of external drivings. For oppositely charged particles, the authors connect the exclusion picture to a modified Poisson-Nernst-Planck continuum model, bridging particle and engineering descriptions. Uphill flow persists across scales, and the paper weighs each model's merits and limits. Readers get conditions for uphill transport in nanoscale electrolytes and membrane devices.
arxiv-2602-08683:
Vision models waste most of their compute on static backgrounds, while the real information sits in sparse, surprising regions. Feilong Tang and eighteen co-authors argue that intelligence is at heart a compression problem, and architectures should align with how video codecs already compress. Their arXiv paper introduces OneVision-Encoder, built on codec-aligned sparsity.

Instead of uniform pixel grids, the encoder focuses on just 3.1 to 25 percent of regions rich in signal, using shared 3D position encodings for irregular token layouts. Training over a million semantic concepts captures object permanence and motion. Integrated into a language model, it beats strong vision backbones on sixteen benchmarks with fewer tokens and less pretraining data. Readers get a principled case that efficiency and accuracy can rise together.
arxiv-2602-08883:
Nuclear magnetic resonance of tightly coupled spins often uses a technique called spin-lock-induced crossing, but it is sensitive to radio-frequency errors. Mohamed Sabba and three co-authors propose a compensated version, cSLIC, that repeats an element using two different field strengths. The trick cancels amplitude deviations without lengthening the sequence at all.

The scheme targets solution NMR of strongly coupled systems, including singlet-state work and parahydrogen-boosted hyperpolarized experiments. Computer simulations and representative lab tests both confirm the improved tolerance. For experimenters, cSLIC offers sturdier results at no cost in time.
arxiv-2602-08983:
Clocks in the real world stretch and squeeze: financial cycles shift, biological rhythms flex, yet transformers assume time ticks evenly. Yubin Kim and five co-authors first prove that rotary position embeddings cannot represent non-affine time warping at all. Their answer is Symplectic Positional Embeddings, a learnable encoding drawn from Hamiltonian mechanics that generalizes rotations to the symplectic group.

An input-dependent warp module lets attention dilate or contract time coordinates end to end, capturing locally varying periodicities without preset warp functions. Built into StretchTime, a multivariate forecaster, the method reaches state-of-the-art scores on standard benchmarks and proves sturdier on non-stationary data.
arxiv-2602-09083:
Disorder can break a symmetry locally while preserving it on average, and Yabo Li and two co-authors study that subtle case in one-dimensional systems. The random transverse-field Ising model at criticality, with its average Kramers-Wannier duality, is the canonical example. Their topological holographic setup encodes the group data in a two-dimensional order, the Drinfeld center of the exact part, enriched by the exact or average case.

Within it, they fully classify anomalies and average-case protected topological phases. With only the average case, anomaly freedom hinges on a magnetic Lagrangian algebra invariant under the group's permutation of anyons. When an anomaly exists, single disorder realizations yield long-range entangled ground states with probability one, plus power-law Griffiths singularities.
arxiv-2602-09383:
Using language models as judges of other models is now widespread, but judging itself can be biased, and known-bias checklists miss biases nobody has named yet. Peng Lai and six co-authors propose BiasScope, a 2026 framework that hunts for evaluation biases automatically and at scale, turning bias discovery from passive manual checking into active exploration. The system is driven by language models and works across model families and sizes.

Validated on the JudgeBench evaluation set, BiasScope uncovers potential biases that predefined lists would miss. Building on it, the authors release JudgeBench-Pro, a harder benchmark for judge robustness. Strikingly, even powerful evaluator models err on more than half the items there. The paper argues that judge-based evaluation needs systematic bias hunting, not just spot checks, before its verdicts can be trusted.
arxiv-2602-09483:
Multimodal language models impress across images and text, but their size blocks deployment, and distillation methods that merely match next tokens miss how tokens interact. Lin Chen and eleven co-authors introduce Align-TI, a 2026 distillation framework built around token interactions. Two interactions matter most: vision-instruction tokens picking out relevant image regions, and response tokens shaping each other during generation.

Align-TI mirrors both. One component aligns the student with the teacher's instruction-relevant visual focus on salient regions. The other aligns sequential token-to-token transition odds, capturing the teacher's generative logic in motion. Trials show the method beating vanilla distillation, with a two-billion-parameter student surpassing a much larger rival model. The paper sets a new bar for compact multimodal models.
arxiv-2602-09783:
Linear probes and sparse coders often recover real structure from transform pictures. Yet why should such simple methods succeed in deep, bent systems? Andres Saurez and two co-authors show this is not merely an observed pattern but a result of design need in their 2026 paper. Transforms pass information through linear gates, focus output-value circuits and output grids, and any meaning feature decoded through such a gate must occupy a fixed linear subspace.

This is set out as the Fixed Subspace Need theorem, with a derived Self Rule. Tokens straight provide the shape way for their linked marks, letting zero-shot finding of meaning structure without labeled data or learned probes. Observed tests across eight sorting tasks and four model kinds confirm match between class tokens and meaning-related cases. The frame unifies linear probes and sparse coders under one sound design account.
arxiv-2602-09983:
Scenes are built from parts, and understanding a scene often means pulling those parts back apart. A 2026 paper led by Calvin Yeung, with three co-authors, tackles that decomposition problem inside diffusion models. The team treats decomposition as an inverse problem, coupling diffusion processes with a guidance term that pushes factor estimates to rebuild the bound vector.

A new iterative sampling scheme lifts performance further. The authors also show that attention-based resonator networks fall out as a special case of their framework. Across synthetic semantic decomposition tasks, the coupled inference method outperforms resonator networks, linking Hopfield-style decomposition to modern diffusion machinery.
arxiv-2602-10583:
Bo Xue and seven co-authors transfer language models beyond fixed token vocabularies in a 2026 paper. Standard autoregressive models generate token by token from a fixed words, a tree-ordered view that limits bend. Recent dynamic vocabularies sample retrieved text spans. But they ignore that one sentence can be split into spans many ways, biasing exploration toward the chosen split.

Their method, Flow of SpanS, models making over the full directed acyclic graph of span compositions using creative flow networks. Those networks explore and transfer over graph-ordered spaces far better than tree-confined methods. By treating spans as first-class actions with many compositional paths, the model gains expressive freedom that token-level making cannot offer. Training stays grounded in flow-matching principles.
arxiv-2602-10883:
M. Montelius and eleven co-authors measure metallicities for the most metal-poor APOGEE stars in a 2026 paper. H-band spectra carry little information at the lowest metallicities because iron lines in Sun-like stars grow weak in that wave size range. A companion paper identified hundreds of very metal-poor stars the main pipeline could not properly analyze.

Here the authors measure metallicities using magnesium and silicon abundances. Those absorption lines remain of good quality despite low metallicity, wave size regime, resolution, and signal-to-noise limits. A specialized pipeline measures those abundances for the sample, most of which sit on the red giant branch. The work rescues quantitative chemistry for stars near the edge of what the survey can see.
arxiv-2602-11183:
Drone navigation drifts as small position errors pile up step by step. Yin Tang and four co-authors propose NeuroKalman, a frame that treats navigation as recursive Bayesian state value. It splits the job into prior forecast from motion motion and likelihood correction from past sights.

Kernel density value of the measurement likelihood is tied to focus-based recall, letting retrieved history anchors correct the latent state without gradient updates. Tests on the TravelUAV benchmark show the method beats strong rivals while fine-tuning on only a tenth of the training data. The work brings classic control ideas to vision-language navigation, where drift has long capped path scores.
arxiv-2602-11283:
Parton spreads describe quarks inside nucleons, but computing them on a lattice is hard. Xiang Gao and six co-authors test a Coulomb-gauge method that uses boosted correlators and avoids Wilson lines. Their first exploratory run covers unpolarized, helicity, and transversity spreads.

Valence-quark results converge with rising nucleon momentum and match recent global analyses across spin structures. Full-quark results from imaginary correlators disagree between the two largest momenta, though the higher momentum matches phenomenology. Excited-state contamination likely drives the gap. The work benchmarks the Coulomb-gauge approach, showing promise for more fast and accurate lattice parton physics.
arxiv-2602-11783:
Early JWST observations found a surprising surplus of bright UV galaxies at redshifts above nine, a puzzle for models of early star birth. Clara Pollock and a large team analyze objects confirmed by spectra at those redshifts with enough signal to model their UV to optical light and line emission carefully. Modeling damped Lyman-alpha absorption in each object constrains how neutral hydrogen gas assembles onto halos at the onset of cosmic reionization.

From hydrogen column levels and star birth rate levels, the team shows all objects form stars fast, using up gas in roughly ten to one hundred million years. That pace greatly exceeds the standard local rule and what leading simulations expect. Dense hydrogen gas also drives offsets from the standard metallicity rule, though dust-to-gas ratios mostly match local values. Efficient star birth plus little dust blocking the light likely explains the early brightness.
arxiv-2602-12083:
Multi-agent AI systems are hard to debug when they fail in subtle ways. One agent may trust the wrong partner, misread timing, break a rule, or overstate its confidence, and plain chat logs rarely explain why. Antonin Sulc's tutorial offers a tool for that gap: differentiable modal logic, built with modal logical neural networks.

The method lets a system learn trust networks, causal chains, and rule boundaries from behavior alone, instead of requiring every relationship to be written out by hand. Four lenses organize the work: who to trust, when events cause failures, what actions are permitted, and how to read agent confidence. Examples range from spotting deceptive alliances in diplomacy games to catching language-model hallucinations, with working notebook code that turns logical contradictions into training signals.
arxiv-2602-12183:
Connected devices face new attacks every day, and the worst are the ones no one has seen before. Shan Ali led this work with three co-authors, building SiamXBERT to spot unknown attacks in Internet of Things networks. Older tools often need large labelled sets, clear payloads, or a closed list of attack types, and all three fail in real deployments.

The system blends flow-level and packet-level signals, so it still works when traffic is encrypted. Meta-learning lets it adapt to a new attack type from only a few labelled examples, then generalise to unseen behaviour. Tests on standard IoT data sets beat rival methods within and across data sets, with up to about 79 percent gain on unknown-attack scores, using far less training data.
arxiv-2602-12583:
Opinion dynamics research suffers from scarce real-world longitudinal data, making it hard to validate theoretical models. Yulong He led this work with four co-authors, proposing a simulation framework using large language model agents in structured multi-round dialogs. Each agent's dialog history updates iteratively with its own prior opinions and those of others, in a manner analogous to the classical DeGroot model.

By retaining each agent's initial opinion throughout the dialog, the framework also simulates anchoring effects consistent with the Friedkin-Johnsen model. It thus bridges classical opinion dynamics and modern multi-agent language model systems, providing a scalable tool for simulating and analysing opinion formation when real-world data are limited or inaccessible. Readers get a practical bridge between old models and new agent simulations.
arxiv-2602-12683:
Generative models that turn random noise into data can be described as flows. A rule nudges each point step by step toward its target. Kenji Fukumizu and four co-authors recast one popular version of this idea, known as optimal transport conditional flow matching, in a different mathematical language. They show it has an exact form based on a proximal operator, a tool from convex analysis. No assumption is needed that the target has a smooth density.

From that form they derive a direct expression for the flow's direction field. They also study how small-batch versions approach the full version as batch size grows. Using second-order tools for convex functions, they prove a striking trait for targets that live on curved surfaces. After rescaling time, motion shrinks fast across the surface while staying neutral along it.
arxiv-2602-12783:
Spoken queries are a common way to search, but existing tests use simple queries in mild noise, so they say little about real-world robustness. Yuejie Li and six co-authors present SQuTR, a benchmark that stresses spoken query retrieval under acoustic noise. It gathers 37,317 distinct queries from six English and Chinese text retrieval sets, spanning varied domains and query types, with speech from 200 real speakers.

Seventeen kinds of real-world noise are mixed in at controlled loudness levels, from quiet rooms to harsh conditions. Tests of cascaded and end-to-end systems show performance falling as noise rises, with different systems dropping by very different amounts. Even large models struggle in extreme noise, marking robustness as a key bottleneck. SQuTR gives the field a reproducible testbed for diagnosing and fixing that weakness.
arxiv-2602-12883:
Heart MRI gives rich structural detail but is scarce and costly, while the ECG is everywhere and cheap yet says little about structure. Laura Alvarez-Florez and nine co-authors bridge the gap with contrastive learning from paired ECG and MRI data. Their framework aligns each ECG with three-dimensional MRI volumes at both end-diastole and end-systole, using a dual-phase loss that anchors the ECG jointly to both cardiac phases.

Unlike earlier methods limited to two-dimensional MRI, the approach models full 3D anatomy at both phases as separate representations, disentangling structure from function. On over 34,000 UK Biobank pairs, image-derived phenotypes read from ECG improved, especially functional parameters at 9.2%, while clinical outcome prediction rose only modestly at 0.7%. The strategy points toward scalable, low-cost cardiac phenotyping from ECG alone.
arxiv-2602-12983:
Video trackers fail, and knowing when they fail matters for surveillance, motion capture, and robotics. Deployed systems usually guess reliability from heuristic confidence scores, with no formal guarantee. Alejandro Monroy Muñoz and two co-authors recast tracking as a sequential hypothesis test, gathering evidence for or against failure over time.

Their test, formalised as an e-process, flags failures quickly while provably capping false alerts at a chosen rate, limiting costly recalibration or intervention. The method is light to compute, needs no extra training or tuning, and works in principle with any tracker. Supervised and unsupervised variants use ground truth or internal signals alone. Tests on two established trackers across four video benchmarks show the approach works in practice.
arxiv-2602-13283:
People may demand far stricter accuracy from AI at work than at home, but that gap is rarely measured. This survey study defines accuracy as fit to the user's intent within a tolerance that depends on stakes and fix-up cost, then asks 300 online respondents about both settings. Among the 170 who answered both accuracy items, 24.1 percent demanded top-level accuracy at work, against 8.8 percent in personal life, a gap that held under broader measures and on the full five-point scale.

Heavy app use tracked with stricter work standards, while losing access to tools disrupted personal routines more than work routines, 34.1 percent against 15.3 percent. The main text sticks to these findings, with test details in an appendix. Gaston Besanson leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13483:
Mechanistic interpretability seeks the internal circuits language models use to solve tasks, and a key question is why each attention head attends where it does. ACC++ is an improved circuit-tracing method built on attention-causal communication. It finds low-dimensional signals that cause attention on a token pair, extracting circuits from a single forward pass with no replacement models or patching. Circuits come out as causal components plus the signals that link them.

Across models, many ACC++ signals admit short plain-language descriptions, showing the circuits are genuinely readable. Studies of indirect object identification show prompt-specific circuits cluster into distinct mechanisms, and multilingual tests show components reused across languages while signals stay language-specific, with circuit distances tracking linguistic relatedness. Gabriel Franco leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13683:
Young stars show a break in how specific angular momentum varies with radius: roughly constant in the infalling rotating envelope, then rising as the square root of radius in the Keplerian disk. Global magnetohydrodynamic simulations of collapse from a supercritical prestellar core trace that break to a finite envelope-disk transition zone. That zone is marked by positive local gravitational torques. The zone's outer edge is where infall speed drops sharply and angular momentum begins its transition.

Moving inward, the centrifugal radius marks where rotation first becomes Keplerian, then self-gravity drives super-Keplerian rotation. At the centrifugal barrier, infall drops to negligible values and negative torque drives accretion onto the protostar. A matching jump in the observed profile of L1527 IRS, seen first in ALMA eDisk data, offers a kinematic tracer for the zone. Indrani Das leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14183:
Le Lin and four co-authors test a 2026 arXiv chatbot that joins therapeutic art activity. Expressive drawing and painting blend visual creation with dialogue, and multimodal language models can now read both text and images. The paper introduces a chatbot that watches art being made in real time and talks with the maker in reflective conversation.

A review by five art-therapy experts found promise for therapeutic engagement. It also flagged work ahead: safer entryways and risk management, matching the bot to user profiles and therapeutic styles, balancing depth and breadth in conversation, and richer visual interaction. Those themes form a design roadmap for future AI-mediated creative tools.
arxiv-2602-14883:
Jogli G. S. Araujo and Weiller F. C. Barboza study whole space-like Weingarten bend shapes in even semi-Riemannian rooms, with even mean bend and flat side bundles. With fair bend rules in place, a Simons-type form and a tuned Cheng-Yau tool give sharp links midst the bend's pure part and the mean bend's slope.

From those links, shape calls follow: such a shape must be all round or of one narrow other kind, in the cases proved. Bend lore thus gains a stark fork: full roundness, or else a tight second path.
arxiv-2602-15283:
Jafari and colleagues propose a classification head sending backbone features into a Hilbert space, evolved under a learned unitary change via the Cayley map. Modern deep nets achieve high scores but remain poorly tuned, with trust scores not reflecting odds of rightness. Teaching one shared backbone and testing light mixed heads, the team pins the effect of unitary forms on tuning.

On CIFAR-10, the unitary head achieves a Calibration Error near one and a half hundredths. That is about 2 and a half times better than a standard softmax head and 3 and a half times better than heat tuning. Swapping the softmax read with a Born rule test worsens tuning to about eight hundredths. On the CIFAR-10H benchmark, the wave head achieves the lowest gap of about one third to human soft tags. The team reports results on spread finding and feeling study, and notes uses for safe work.
arxiv-2602-15383:
Li and colleagues tackle day-to-night image mapping, downstream but hard given big shifts and no pixel-level guidance. Current tools often fake objects from target classes such as traffic signs, vehicles, and man-made light glows, harming scores.

The team offers a setup spotting and blocking ghosts of target traits. To spot ghosts, they build a dual-head judge also doing meaning splitting to spot ghost stuff. To block ghosts, they offer class samples, made from labeled target-domain objects, which act as pins for each class. Built on a Schrodinger Bridge model, the setup stepwise tunes, moving spotted ghost traits away from samples, keeping object meaning across the path. Tests show the method beats current routes. On BDD100K, it lifts mAP by 15 and a half percent for day-to-night shift. It shows about 32 percent rise for classes such as traffic lamps apt to ghosts.
arxiv-2602-15583:
Arrieta and Suarez ask which frame maps can be lifted to the lattice of smooth sublocales. For a frame L, that lattice gathers joins of complemented sublocales. In other words, it is the Boolean version of the set of all sublocales of L. The question is when a frame map f from L to M extends to a frame map between the two smooth sublocale lattices.

The answer comes through a new identification. The smooth sublocale lattice matches the Bruns-Lakser completion of the meet-semilattice of locally closed sublocales. Those are sublocales formed by meeting a closed and an open sublocale. That bridge turns a lifting question into a claim about completions, giving pointfree topologists a concrete handle on when maps survive passage to smooth sublocales.
arxiv-2602-16283:
Nathan Huet and Ilaria Prosdocimi present orthogonal reparametrisations of the main extreme-value distributions used to assess risks from rare events.
