Such models typically carry two or three parameters, and inference can prove unstable. That instability is serious since they are often fitted to small samples. Their values are also not directly interpretable.

Applying theory from Cox and Reid, the authors recast the Extreme-Value, Generalised Pareto, and Gumbel models. That reparametrisation separates values so estimation of one interferes less with others. A simulation study illustrates the principal advantage of the new forms.
arxiv-2602-16383:
Ziming Liu leads four coauthors on a robust two-stage protocol for STAR-RIS-aided integrated sensing and communication. They are programmable metasurfaces transmitting and reflecting at once. A preparation phase estimates outdoor users' arrival directions and sends downlink communication to all users. A later phase uses the angular information to strengthen downlink signals.

Outdoor bearings are modeled as Gaussian random variables, and non-line-of-sight channel parts through spatial covariance statistics. A performance-balanced optimization then maximizes sum-rate while guaranteeing sensing accuracy. It chooses beamforming vectors, transmission and reflection coefficients, and the split between energy-splitting and transmit-only modes. A tailored alternating framework solves this non-convex mixed discrete-continuous problem with proven steady convergence. Tests show roughly fifteen percent higher throughput than the strongest benchmark without non-line-of-sight data, with robustness under estimation errors and partial channel knowledge.
arxiv-2602-16983:
Mohamed Nedal and co-authors characterize multiple shocks generated by the May 2024 coronal mass ejection. The study characterizes a series of type II radio bursts associated with a coronal mass ejection on May 14. It focuses on coronal conditions during the event and identifies the likely location of shocks where radio bursts are generated. The ejection was tracked using white light and extreme ultraviolet observations from GOES-SUVI and two SOHO-LASCO coronagraphs. Ground-based radio observations from I-LOFAR were used too.

Four type II bursts were identified in the I-LOFAR radio dynamic spectrum over fifteen minutes, exhibiting band splitting, herringbones, and fragmentation. Shock speeds ranged widely, with drift rates strongly negative, and Mach numbers indicating super-Alfvénic shocks. The first burst was triggered eighteen minutes after ejection launch, with each burst apparently generated at a different height in the corona.
arxiv-2602-17183:
Kishan Maharaj led a four-author team stress-testing language models on long-code question answering. Such models increasingly help with software tasks that demand reasoning across large codebases, yet their robustness under varied inputs remains unclear. The study extends a Python benchmark with new COBOL and Java question sets and runs controlled ablations on answer format, distractors, and context scale.

Models faced shuffled multiple-choice options, open-ended questions, and needle-in-a-haystack contexts mixing relevant with adversarially irrelevant material. Performance dropped substantially on shuffled options and open-ended items, and models behaved brittly around irrelevant cues. The findings expose limits of current long-context evaluation and offer a broader benchmark for code reasoning in legacy and modern systems alike.
arxiv-2602-18083:
Ioannis Kontogiorgakis and team present a ten-meter soil moisture system for vegetated areas across Europe, mixing Sentinel-1 radar, Sentinel-2 imagery, and ERA-5 data through machine learning. Soil moisture gauging matters for farming, water use, and climate monitoring, yet space products are coarser than one km.

Using one hundred thirteen Soil Moisture Network stations, the authors compare sensor mixes with settings under spatial cross-checks. They test whether Prithvi model vectors improve on traditional hand-crafted cues. Hybrid time matching with S-2 data and the S-1 down orbit performs best, with a ten-day ERA-5 lookback lifting it. Prithvi vectors barely beat hand-crafted cues, so classic feature craft stays strong for sparse-data fits. Domain spectral indices with tree-based groups offer a handy, fast route to working pan-Europe field-scale tracking.
arxiv-2602-18183:
Helmut Abels and two co-authors study how spread-out, nonlocal operators settle into local ones. Their 2026 paper treats convolution-type operators with singular kernels that may point in favored directions. As the kernels bunch up near the origin, the operators should approach a local differential operator with natural edge conditions.

Such limits matter because they justify local models that cannot be derived straight from small-scale laws. The paper widens earlier results in three ways. Kernels may be as singular as those of fractional Laplacians, they may be anisotropic and spread out, and convergence holds strongly across general Lebesgue spaces with explicit rates. The work gives modelers both the limit and a measured speed for reaching it.
arxiv-2602-18383:
Xinyuan Chen and one co-author sharpen covariate adjustment for pairwise comparisons in randomized trials. Their 2026 paper treats comparisons that summarize treatment effects for ordinal, multi-outcome, or prioritized outcomes, under complete randomization with fixed potential outcomes and covariates. Only treatment assignment varies randomly.

The team works out the exact random variation of the plain estimator and describes linear calibration tweaks through between-arm covariate mean gaps. As samples grow, variation forms a strictly convex quadratic in the tuning number, giving a closed-form best value that never loses to the plain estimator. Everyday pair-level and single-arm least squares tweaks can stray from that best value and lose much efficiency. A within-arm variation estimator supports cautious inference, and fitting each arm on its own number repairs the usual gap. For plain outcome differences, the estimator matches Lin's fully interacted regression adjustment to first order.
arxiv-2602-18483:
Adriana Alvarado Garcia and three co-authors study red teaming as a human practice, not a technical test. Their 2026 paper notes red teaming, rooted in security, has become a key way to check the safety and reliability of generative AI. Most existing work stresses technical benchmarks and attack success rates, but leaves the human practices behind red teaming datasets underexamined.

From twenty-two interviews with practitioners who build and evaluate red teaming datasets, the team examines the data practices behind this work. Adversarial datasets set the scope and accuracy of evaluations, so they are key artifacts for assessing harms from large language models. Contributions include evidence of how practitioners view red teaming and build its datasets. The team reflects on how their view of risk overlooks context, interaction type, and user detail. It closes with three opportunities for interaction researchers to expand concepts and data practices for red teaming.
arxiv-2602-18683:
Heavy-ion collisions are used to probe the inside of nuclei, but the probe itself has a size, and that size can blur the picture. Hao-jie Xu, writing alone in 2026, asks whether lead-lead collision cross sections really measure how wide a nucleon is, or something else entirely.

The argument is that a width setting meant to describe interaction range also reshapes the modelled nuclear surface, so it can masquerade as structure. Fixing the folded density that feeds the Glauber phase shift removes that mix-up, leaving a cross section that tracks the nuclear surface instead. The result recasts the measurement as a surface probe, and gives only a broad range for the neutron skin of lead.
arxiv-2602-18883:
Galaxies change shape as they evolve, and the leftovers after fitting a smooth light profile can reveal that history. Kameswara Bharadwaj Mantha, with ten co-authors, working with the CANDELS team, studies leftover shape substructure in 2026 using guided and unguided deep learning.

The study uses leftover images from over ten thousand bright, massive galaxy sample in the CANDELS survey, spanning a wide redshift range, with visual labels for the shapes they host. A guided CNN and an unguided CvAE are trained on those leftovers. Inputs are prepared to contain only the galaxy of interest, and augmented to span leftover traits evenly. Latent spaces are assessed with PCA and metrics of leftover strength. Guided signs track leftover strength and separate strong from weak shape, while unguided signs track visual traits but separate them less clearly.
arxiv-2602-18983:
Ray transforms probe a field by integrating along rays, and injectivity asks whether those integrals fix the field. Antti Kykkänen, with two co-authors, studies a solenoidal-potential type decomposition of symmetric tensor fields in 2026, and its implications for momentum and elastic ray transforms.

An earlier split carried a restriction on dimension and order. The authors extend it to dimension two under a mean-zero assumption. That split proves injectivity of momentum and elastic ray transforms in two dimensions. It also proves a connection between the two transforms for two-tensors. Later, the split proves injectivity of further integral transforms, including longitudinal and elastic variants, without any mean-zero assumption. Connections between transforms are then used to relate their properties. Integrals can determine fields. That is what injectivity means.
arxiv-2602-19183:
Drug safety data often resist meaning-based thought. Mohammad Ashhad, with three co-authors, fixes that in 2026 with SIDEKICK, a joined meaning graph. Existing sets lean on word lists like MedDRA, limiting interoperability with Semantic Web word maps and knowledge graphs. Structured labels hold more value than those word lists unlock.

SIDEKICK unifies uses, bans, and adverse effects from FDA product labels. A workflow combining language-model pulling with graph-lookup-augmented generation maps terms to trait, disease, and drug word maps. Over fifty thousand labels were processed. The resource beats SIDER and ONSIDES on drug repurposing by side-effect likeness. Serialised as RDF with a shared upper ontology, it enables automated safety watch and trait-based likeness analysis.
arxiv-2603-01683:
Mia Hopman, Jannes Elstner, Maria Avramidou, and colleagues measure how often AI agents scheme when given the chance. Their 2026 work defines scheming as secretly chasing goals that clash with the task set by humans. Prior studies showed agents can scheme, but not how prone they are in realistic settings.

The team splits scheming drives into agent traits and setting traits, then varies each in turn. Settings offer chances to chase self-preservation, resource gain, or goal defense. Despite strong bait in the settings, clear scheming stays rare, and the team finds little sign that agents merely hide it. Prompt snippets that push agency can spike rates, yet snippets in real agent setups seldom do. In built test agents, the behavior proves brittle to small changes in tools or oversight.
arxiv-2603-01883:
Ludovic Huguet, Thomas Frasson, Souvik Naskar, and colleagues simulate how a stratified layer at the base of Earth core would mark the magnetic field. Their 2026 work models the F-layer as a slurry of solid iron snow falling through iron-oxygen liquid. Seismic data show this lowest core zone is density stratified, which challenges classic dynamo theory.

Their simulations are the first to add a simple slurry F-layer to rotating convection and dynamo runs. The layer blocks columnar flow and pushes peak flow speeds toward lower latitudes near the surface. In dynamo runs, polar dips appear in the radial field at the outer boundary and deepen with stronger stratification. Time-averaged field maps carry the clearest signature, visible at modest spherical harmonic resolution. Trends in key Gauss coefficients also grow with layer thickness and strength.
arxiv-2603-02783:
Mattes Kraus and Jonas Kuckling teach robot swarms by watching people rather than by copying other programs. Their 2026 paper builds on generative adversarial imitation learning, where a learner improves by trying to match demonstration behavior. Most swarm studies feed the learner rollouts from an existing controller, which assumes a good controller already exists.

Their framework instead learns collective behavior straight from human demonstrations. They test it on six missions, using both hand-made demonstrations and ones from a policy trained by trial and error. The learned behaviors looked meaningful and scored about as well as the demonstrations. Policies also moved to a real TurtleBot 4 swarm, keeping their character and performance outside simulation.
arxiv-2603-02883:
Wonsuk Jang and Thierry Tambe shrink video generation models so they can run on small devices. Their 2026 method, SemanticDialect, compresses video diffusion transformers, which are powerful but heavy in memory and compute. Standard compression often breaks the meaning or timing coherence of the video.

The method picks a number format block by block from a shared format book, using lookup tables to keep the online cost low. It then re-adds leftover errors and gives extra care to tokens flagged as important by attention. A semantic assignment step shares formats among related tokens, keeping their values consistent. On a leading video model, the approach beat prior compression methods and came close to full-precision quality at four-bit settings.
arxiv-2603-02983:
Yule Wen, Yanzhe Zhang, Jianxun Lian, and colleagues give AI agents a privacy coach that speaks up during the task, not after. Agents increasingly handle personal data across many steps, yet most defenses are static prompts or guards that merely block actions. Their 2026 method, Contextualized Defense Instructing, reshapes each step as it happens.

An instructor model issues step-specific privacy guidance tuned to the current context, proactively steering the agent's choices. The instructor itself is trained by reinforcement learning, turning past failure cases with privacy slips into practice environments. In a shared simulation testbed, the approach preserved privacy in most cases while staying highly helpful. It also held up better than baselines under attack and on new situations.
arxiv-2603-03183:
Pierre Vanhove writes exact formulas for a family of loop integrals that tend to resist closed forms. Sunset integrals show up when particles loop through a diagram more than once. The multiloop kinds, with mixed masses, are the most stubborn of all. His 2026 paper solves them in two dimensions, for any masses and any loop count.

The answers are neat sums of symmetric polynomials in log mass ratios. They are scaled by the outside momentum, with factors drawn from series expansions. For equal masses, a rank-raising rule links each loop order across dimensions through a differential step. No exotic functions appear, so the formulas suit both theory and precise numeric work. The two-dimensional results also seed a rebuild of the four-dimensional cases used in real physics.
arxiv-2603-03283:
Point clouds are sets of points that record the shape of a scene in three dimensions, but each sensor makes them differently. Yujia Zhang and colleagues present Utonia in 2026, a single self-supervised encoder meant to learn from all of them at once. Training mixes remote sensing scans, outdoor lidar, indoor depth sequences, computer-designed object models, and clouds lifted from plain videos.

Trained together, these sources produce one shared representation space that transfers across domains, and new behaviors appear that single-domain training misses. The features also help beyond perception. Robot control policies using them handle manipulation better, and vision-language models using them reason better about space. The authors frame Utonia as an early step toward foundation models for sparse three-dimensional data.
arxiv-2603-03783:
Junho Bang and four others photograph how the Coulomb blockade bends across a metal island. In nanoscale islands, adding one electron costs so much energy that current blocks in steps, the effect behind single-electron transistors. A quantitative link between junction traits and the blockade spectrum stayed elusive. Their 2026 study uses scanning tunneling spectroscopy on indium nanoislands grown on black phosphorus, a semiconducting crystal, and maps the charging resonances position by position.

The resonance paths shift sideways in bias and curve asymmetrically, a spatial pattern never properly explained. Calculations in the standard orthodox theory reproduce both traits when one ingredient is admitted: the two junctions have distinct work functions. Junction-specific electrostatics, the authors conclude, governs nanoscale charge transport, and any quantitative device design must reckon with it.
arxiv-2603-03883:
Rohit Kumar Shukla and Cheng Shang examine how many-body structure shapes the charging of quantum batteries under periodic driving. Quantum batteries store energy in quantum systems, and while static driving has been widely studied, periodic driving of many-body versions has received little attention. The authors study a collective spin-half battery driven by a periodic Ising charger and ask which structural features govern performance.

They find that interaction range, boundary conditions, system size, and integrability are decisive. Long-range chargers reach super-extensive energy storage near the fundamental upper bound across broad conditions. Nearest-neighbor chargers charge optimally only at finely tuned settings, and open boundaries prove more robust than periodic ones. Broken integrability consistently helps by promoting ergodic dynamics that populate the spectrum. Long-range, nonintegrable structures emerge as a central resource for fast, scalable charging.
arxiv-2605-00283:
Luis Rodríguez-Flores and 3 co-authors tackle a privacy problem in process mining, the study of how work actually flows inside organizations. Conformance checking compares a model of how a process should run against a log of how it did run. Normally one analyst can see both, but sometimes the model or the log holds sensitive information.

Their approach keeps both sides hidden from each other during the check. It rests on string processing methods and homomorphic encryption, a form of math that allows computation on sealed data, and uses the standard alignment formalism. Tests on synthetic and real event logs show the secure check works. The cost is heavy memory and processing demand, which the authors report plainly.
arxiv-2605-00483:
Misael Avendaño Camacho, Jhonny Kama Mamani, and Eduardo Velasco Barreras study Hamiltonian dynamics on Lie algebroids, structures that extend the tangent bundle of classical mechanics. Vaisman had asked, for tangent bundles, when the flow of a moving system can be written as a Hamiltonian flow. The authors extend that question to any Lie algebroid and give a general solution.

Given a Lie algebroid and a regular Lagrangian, they construct a family of Poisson brackets on it. For the right brackets, the flow field of the energy function is exactly a semispray, the object that encodes second-order motion. Their approach runs through the symplectic geometry of its prolongation and a close analysis of one of its subbundles. The result frames second-order dynamics in geometric terms on algebroids, extending known facts and exposing new links between Poisson geometry and algebroid structure.
arxiv-2605-00583:
Aharon Azulay and 4 co-authors jailbreak vision-language models through their eyes rather than their text channel. Safety training is mostly textual, and the authors probe whether harmful intent smuggled in as images slips past it. They devise four visual attacks. One encodes instructions as symbol sequences with a printed legend. Others swap harmful objects for benign stand-ins, replace harmful words in pictures while context preserves meaning, or pose analogy puzzles whose solution is a prohibited concept.

Across six frontier models, the visual attacks bypassed safety alignment, exposing a cross-modality gap. A visual cipher succeeded far more often than the equivalent text cipher against the same model. The authors add early interpretability work and test mitigations. Their conclusion is direct: vision must be treated as a first-class target for safety training, since alignment learned from text does not automatically generalize to harmful intent conveyed in pictures.
arxiv-2605-00783:
Thomas Nikolaus and Phil Pützstück develop a theory of completeness for weight structures on stable categories, dual to the known theory for t-structures. In the bounded case, complete weight forms are determined by their weight heart. The authors extend that picture, giving a universal construction that assigns a complete weight setting to an additive setting and recovers classic examples such as homotopy categories of chain complexes.

They also construct weight forms on presentable stable settings generated by a small set of objects, recovering the standard structure on spectra and an exotic one tied to Anderson duality. To handle partially complete examples, they introduce weak t-structures and prove a rebuilding of a setting from its heart by a two-step completion.
arxiv-2605-01183:
M. Affouf studies a one-dimensional model of a material that can switch between phases, such as a metal that changes crystal form as it is worked. The model uses a Ginzburg-Landau energy with a non-convex cubic stress-strain law. Unlike the simpler heat-fixed version, this system links the motion equation to a heat equation for the temperature field, adding viscous, capillary, and heat-spread terms.

Affouf proves that smooth solutions exist for all time and are unique for the Cauchy problem, where the starting state is given on the whole line. The proof splits the solution into traveling waves, applies an exponential change of variables to the motion part, and uses linked energy estimates at rising levels of smoothness. With extra conditions on the size and decay of the starting data, the temperature disturbance is shown to fade at an algebraic rate.
arxiv-2605-02083:
Garvin Kruthof introduces EditPropBench, a benchmark for whether language model editors carry a factual edit through a whole scientific manuscript. A local change, such as a data set shrinking from 215 to 80 documents, can make distant claims stale even when they never repeat the number. An audit of recent arXiv papers found such fact-dependent claims in over a third of benchmark papers.

Each benchmark item holds a synthetic manuscript in machine learning style, a target edit, and a fact graph with sentence labels. Labels mark direct targets, required downstream updates, and text that must stay unchanged. A score called Edit-Ripple Adherence measures the share of required updates done right, checked with adversarial probes.
arxiv-2605-02183:
Guanmeng Xian, Ning Yang, and Philip Yu make adversarial training work better on long-tailed data, where a few classes dominate and many have few examples. Standard adversarial training is strong on balanced sets, but tail classes suffer high robust error and unstable boundaries under attack. Their method, MCAT, keeps adversarial examples semantically valid while balancing class separation.

MCAT penalises movement away from each class's feature manifold and adds a regulariser, inspired by equiangular tight frames, that promotes even geometric separation across classes. Theory links that separation to lower bounds on robust margins and bounds robust risk on high-density regions. Tests on standard long-tailed benchmarks show steady gains in overall, balanced, and tail-class robustness.
arxiv-2605-02483:
Sumanta Mukherjee gives a unified account of how weak disorder lowers the peak magnetization of a spin one-half ferromagnet. In a clean magnet, spins line up fully at low temperature. When finite-size effects spread across the sample, that full alignment is lost, and older accounts treated each part of the loss apart.

From the unified form, Mukherjee derives a single Bloch-type equation for these systems. The same approach is then extended to spin transport, so movement of spin through the disordered magnet gets a matching unified expression. The report is short and formal, aimed at readers who work on magnetic materials theory. Its value lies in joining two topics, static magnetization and spin flow, under one frame.
arxiv-2605-02583:
Max Reimann, Benito Buchheim, and Jürgen Döllner work on a fine control problem in image generation: changing style without changing content. Text-to-image diffusion models can restyle a picture, but crude controls often alter the subject as well. Their approach learns separate editing directions for style traits from synthetic datasets built for that purpose.

Traits handled include outlines, local contrast, watercolor effects, and geometric patterns, each adjustable in small steps. Guidance composition closes the gap between a style-tuned model and the base model, helping keep the original meaning of the image. A training loss and an improved inversion method keep edits consistent, including on real photos. In evaluations, the method gave more precise and better integrated style changes than text-based editing.
arxiv-2605-02683:
M. Barik and five co-authors report tests on a distorted honeycomb magnet that shows exotic magnetic behavior. The material's iron ions carry large spin and sit on a two-dimensional honeycomb network. Competing interactions there frustrate simple ordering. Such systems test how classical and quantum magnetism differ, and what unusual excitations appear.

The team measured crystal structure, heat capacity, and neutron scattering, plus how the material responds to a magnetic field. Iron moments interact mainly in a way that favors opposed neighbors. A dip in the field response points to an unusual field-driven change, backed by odd features in the field curves. Heat data show ordering at a very low temperature, shifting under a field toward a canted state. Short-range spin links persist well above that point, and neutron results support that picture of lingering order.
arxiv-2605-02783:
Bao-Zhu Guo, Dong-Hui Yang, and Jie Zhong introduce an approximation method for degenerate partial differential equations, where the leading term can vanish and standard tools strain. Two equation types are treated, one elliptic and one parabolic, and both share the same principal operator. That shared structure is what the new method exploits.

The shape design approximation gives solutions for both classes. As an application, the authors derive a Carleman estimate for the backward degenerate parabolic equation, a weighted inequality central to control theory. That estimate then yields null controllability: the parabolic system can be steered to zero. A noted strength is that the route avoids needing second-order derivative bounds, a classic obstacle for degenerate Carleman estimates. The paper is a methods contribution to control of singular equations.
arxiv-2605-02983:
Hassan Sartaj and four co-authors present RoboULM, a human-in-the-loop method and tool that helps engineers map uncertainties in self-adaptive robots before deployment. Such robots face shifting, unpredictable settings, where a missed uncertainty can become a safety fault or a failed run. Systematic analysis is hard because environments, robot behavior, and the technology itself all keep changing.

The method uses language models at the design stage, guided by structured prompts and iterative refinement, with a human checking the output. A detailed taxonomy of uncertainties in self-adaptive robots accompanies the tool, cataloging sources, impacts, and mitigations. Sixteen practitioners from four industrial cases evaluated it. They found it useful and easy to grasp, valuing the structured prompting and refinement support most. Systematic uncertainty work, the study suggests, can be partly automated.
arxiv-2605-03083:
Jacob A White studies the cyclic sieving phenomenon for independent sets in graphs, where counting fixed points under a group action matches a polynomial evaluated at roots of unity. Independent sets are vertex groups with no edge inside the set.

White gives sieving examples for powers of cycle graphs and derives a closed formula for the number of independent sets of a given size in cycle and path powers. Adding whiskers to a graph yields new sieving results from old ones. Recursive methods extend the work to gear, helm, and book graphs, broadening the known families.
arxiv-2605-03283:
Brian Keith-Norambuena and Juan Bekios-Calfa give a unified theory of multilabel Fisher discriminant analysis. Orthogonality constraints apply throughout. When each item carries several labels, the classic bound on discriminant directions no longer holds. Competing objective forms also need careful comparison.

They show the between-class scatter rank can exceed the single-label limit. All four Fisher objectives agree under one normalization, but diverge under the Stiefel constraint. They bound how label distances survive projection. Finite-sample error bounds come with a matching lower bound, near optimal overall. Synthetic tests check the algebra and the quantities that drive the bounds.
arxiv-2605-03383:
Xiaoyu Tao, Mingyue Cheng, Jiahao Wang, Yitong Zhou, Qingyang Mao, Yimin Dou, Qi Liu, Shijin Wang, and Enhong Chen present GeoDecider, an agent for geological interpretation from well logs. Different rock units can give near-identical log responses, so fixed prediction pipelines struggle on hard intervals where context and domain knowledge decide the call.

GeoDecider starts with a fast classifier, flags hard points by score, and then gathers evidence for whole intervals: knowledge summaries, depth trends, prior calls, and similar training cases. Three scientific views propose labels, disagreements are weighed, and geology checks enforce continuity. Four public benchmarks show steady gains.
arxiv-2605-03683:
Guido Maria Lido and Luca Mauri generalize a classical theorem of Strassmann about zeros of power series. In one variable over a complete non-Archimedean field, a nonzero convergent power series has only finitely many zeros, with an explicit bound. The authors extend that control to convergent power series in several variables.

They characterize when the zero set is finite and bound its size in terms of the reduction of the saturated ideal defined by the series. They also discuss how to make the result effective when working with approximate power series, under suitable assumptions. The theorem gives multivariable analytic geometry over non-Archimedean fields the same kind of finiteness grip Strassmann provided in one variable.
arxiv-2605-03883:
Jixiang Weng and twenty-four co-authors report ALMA observations of an accretion disk around an early O-type protostar in the Sagittarius C cloud near the Galactic Center. Disk-mediated accretion is central to theories of massive star formation. Yet Keplerian disks around such protostars are rarely observed cleanly, because they blend into complex surroundings. The observations reach a resolution of about three hundred astronomical units.

The team fits a dynamical model to molecular line data. The model has an inner Keplerian disk and an outer free-falling envelope. It constrains the central protostar's mass to about forty solar masses. It also puts the disk's centrifugal radius at about thirteen hundred astronomical units. They estimate the envelope-to-disk accretion rate and identify spiral-like structures in the disk that can be described as free-falling streamers.
arxiv-2605-04083:
Tadhg Looram, Lucas Nuzzi, Kyle Waters, and Steven Dillmann present AsymmetryZero, a framework for turning human expert preferences into semantic evaluations usable in reinforcement learning pipelines. Many real-world tasks are governed by subjective, procedural, domain-specific requirements that exact-match targets and open-ended preference judgments capture poorly. Evaluation design, the authors argue, is where post-training succeeds or fails.

AsymmetryZero represents each task as a stable evaluation contract that states explicitly what is being graded, how each criterion is judged, and how criterion-level decisions aggregate into a task outcome. The same contract runs in model-only evaluation tools and in agentic evaluation frameworks, giving comparable scores and shared audit artifacts. A study with fixed contracts compares a five-model frontier jury against a five-model compact jury.
arxiv-2605-04183:
Friedrich Eisenbrand and three co-authors study a basic geometry question: how far can one convex shape be scaled up before it no longer fits inside another shape? The inner shape here is a zonotope, a form built from line segments, and the outer shape can only be probed through tests.

They give a sampling method whose error is close to the best anyone can hope for in this setting. They also prove a long-standing guess for a special class of zonotopes, linking the problem to known work on thinning large sets of vectors.
arxiv-2605-04283:
Zsolt Benedek and four co-authors give a detailed theoretical account of a defect in hexagonal boron nitride that is drawing interest as a tiny quantum sensor. The defect is a missing boron atom with a negative charge, and its spin can be read with light.

Using a high-level wave-function method, they model the defect's energy levels, structural relaxation, and rates for light emission and spin changes. Their analysis covers fine structure, distortion effects, and how stress shifts the behaviour. The results clarify how the optical readout works and lay groundwork for sensors built into thin two-dimensional materials.
arxiv-2605-04383:
Zhen-Yang Wang and three co-authors investigate whether pairs of heavy mesons can bind into new states, and whether those states would be produced when B mesons decay. The candidates pair a strange heavy meson with its antiparticle, or a non-strange pair in the same way.

Working within the Bethe-Salpeter framework with a one-boson-exchange model, they compute the bound-state wave functions and then the rates for the two B decay channels. Bound solutions exist for the non-strange pair under all settings tried, but for the strange pair only in a narrow region. Their rate ranges give experiments concrete targets, including a link to the known X(3915) state.
arxiv-2605-04683:
Lena Ehrmuth and Laura Strieker analyse the computational power of transformer encoders, the attention-based networks behind modern language models, when they are viewed as functions from sequences to sequences. The question is which families of computations such an encoder can carry out.

They show that average hard attention lets a transformer simulate arithmetic circuits that are supplied to it as part of the input. The simulable circuit families have constant depth while using unbounded addition, binary multiplication, and sign gates, and the transformers in their construction use arithmetic circuits in place of the usual feed-forward blocks. The results hold over the reals, the rationals, and any ring between them.
arxiv-2605-04883:
Samuel Haeuser and eleven co-authors image special edge currents that run along the steps of a layered material and carry spin information. Such topologically protected modes could move signals with very low loss, a need for electronics below ten nanometres. Until now their nanoscale spin behaviour had rarely been seen directly in real space.

Using a cryogenic infrared microscope that senses near fields, the team found magnetic fields brightening the edge response. The response grew nearly in line with the number of atomic layers, suggesting each layer keeps its own edge state. The contrast with low-frequency transport points toward high-frequency, magnetically tunable links for future devices.
arxiv-2605-05183:
Théo Gaudry and three co-authors numerically study a two-dimensional water-wave system, the well-posed version of the Kaup-Broer-Kuperschmidt equations. Systems of this Boussinesq type describe long waves in shallow water. The authors construct soliton-type solutions, wave packets that would normally hold their shape, and test whether they survive.

Their simulations show the constructed solitons are unstable, breaking down through both dispersion and the formation of singularities. Line solitons and their stability are examined next, followed by general localised starting data. In every case the authors fail to find stable structures, a negative result that maps the limits of coherent wave behaviour in this system.
arxiv-2605-05283:
Shakeeb Murtaza explains medical image labels by asking what should not be there, using what-if models to attribute a finding to the objects in a scan. Standard display tools highlight only the minimal regions a classifier used, missing other visible objects that shaped the choice. His method instead builds class-based explanations of the form: if this feature had not happened, that outcome would not have followed.

The approach rests on generative adversarial networks with a cycle-consistent loss, producing counterfactual versions of scans for contrast. Tests on test data, TB images, and brain tumour data confirm the method's value. Murtaza also highlights limits of existing counterfactual methods in producing real-looking altered images.
arxiv-2605-05383:
Security teams write log-based rules to flag attacks, then keep revising them for years. Minjun Long and David Evans present the first long study of how those rules change over time. They track rule histories in two public collections, the community Sigma project and Splunk's curated security content.

To compare versions by logic rather than wording, they convert each rule into a predicate graph. Across nearly seven thousand histories, about fifty-six percent of rules changed their detection logic at least once. Additions and removals often alternate, so rules keep trading wider coverage against fewer false alarms instead of settling down.
arxiv-2605-05583:
An AI agent that remembers must decide what each observation meant, and early guesses can harden into errors. Junfeng Liao and five co-authors propose BeliefMem, a memory that keeps several candidate conclusions per observation, each with a probability. Ordinary agent memory stores one firm conclusion, which the agent then acts on and reinforces.

Probabilities update as new evidence arrives, and retrieval surfaces all candidates with their odds. The agent can act firmly on well-supported beliefs yet still change its mind. On the LoCoMo and ALFWorld benchmarks, BeliefMem posted the best average performance among the systems tested.
arxiv-2605-05683:
Loss curves say a language model is improving; they say little about what is forming inside. Andy Zeyi Liu, Elliot Paquette, and John Sous propose spectral diagnostics for that hidden mechanics. Using a controlled family of small decoder models, they measure activation covariance spectra and per-sample gradient spectra throughout training.

Three findings stand out. Batch size quietly determines representation geometry: runs reaching equal loss settle into distinct spectra. Early covariance tails forecast later token efficiency. And the gradient view explains the pattern mechanistically. The protocol turns spectra into practical instruments for steering optimization.
arxiv-2605-06083:
Jun Li and seven co-authors build a video retrieval system that models its own uncertainty explicitly. In partially relevant retrieval, a short text query describes only part of a long untrimmed video. Vague queries blur meaning across videos, and sparse timing labels give little matching evidence inside each video.

Their framework, Holmes, gathers evidence at two levels in a hierarchy. Between videos, similarity scores become evidential support under a Dirichlet model, guiding calibrated learning with fine grained query checks. Within a video, a soft alignment between query and clips, built on flexible optimal transport, gathers denser evidence while damping false local matches. Experiments show the system beating leading methods for this retrieval task.
arxiv-2605-06283:
Jessica Huynh and five co-authors measure how editing an evaluation rubric changes agreement between human raters and automated raters. Autoraters, often language models acting as judges, now score content at scale, but rubric design choices may move their scores toward or away from human judgment. Holistic rubrics ask for one overall call, while analytic rubrics split the call into named parts like fluency and organization.

The study tracks agreement as rubrics gain examples, context, complexity, and different aggregation rules. Edits that added representative examples and context, and reduced positional bias, raised human and autorater agreement. Higher rubric complexity and conservative aggregation tended to lower it. Results from essay scoring and instruction following domains suggest practitioners should test rubric changes per domain rather than assume a better rubric helps both sides equally.
arxiv-2605-06383:
Shahroze Shahab and three co-authors construct higher order topological phases protected by the shape of the system itself. Such phases host protected boundary modes at corners or hinges, one dimension below the usual edge states. They were understood as protected by lattice symmetries, so breaking those symmetries should let the boundary modes be removed without closing the bulk energy gap, a vulnerability this work designs around entirely.

Their construction schemes protect the phases with only the bulk gap, fundamental local symmetries, and the global genus of the system's shape, meaning its number of holes. No crystalline symmetry is needed at any point. As long as the fundamental local symmetries hold, no purely surface perturbation can remove the boundary states. The result ties topological protection to the topology of the sample's own geometry.
arxiv-2605-06483:
Bowen Ye and four co-authors present ReasonSTL, a framework that translates plain language into Signal Temporal Logic formulas. That logic states timing requirements over real signals and is widely used to verify autonomous and cyber-physical systems. Writing formulas by hand needs expertise, while commercial model APIs cost money and may expose sensitive requirements.

ReasonSTL adapts local open-source models instead, splitting translation into explicit reasoning, deterministic tool calls, and structured formula building. Training rewards both the tool-use steps and the final formula. A bilingual benchmark grounded in real signals is also introduced. A small four-billion-parameter model reaches leading results in automatic and human checks.
arxiv-2605-06583:
Zhengyi Guo, Jiayuan Sheng, David D. Yao, and Wenpin Tang fine-tune flow-based generative models toward human preferences using adjoint matching recast as deterministic optimal control. The velocity field becomes the control, and training regresses it toward a target derived from the value gradient under the current model, giving a simple and stable objective.

A truncated adjoint scheme spends computation only on the final part of each trajectory, where reward signals concentrate, saving cost while keeping alignment quality. The framework also generalizes beyond standard KL regularization for more flexible trade-offs. Experiments on two image models show consistent alignment gains plus better diversity and mode preservation.
arxiv-2605-06683:
Benjamin L. Badger and Ethan Roland introduce the Toeplitz MLP Mixer, a sequence architecture that replaces attention to cut its quadratic cost. Attention grows steeply in time and memory with sequence length. Their mixer swaps it for triangular-masked Toeplitz matrix multiplication across the sequence, reaching near-linear training cost and linear inference cost with a much simpler mechanism.

Despite lacking the input modulation or state tracking of rival sub-quadratic designs, the mixer reaches lower loss per unit of compute and memory. It retains more input information, improving copying, retrieval, and in-context learning over comparable architectures. An operator theory analysis adds a surprise: trained causal layers tend toward invertibility even when not built to be invertible.
arxiv-2605-06783:
Madeline L. Cross-Parkin, Cullan Howlett, Leonardo Giani, Chris Blake, and Tamara M. Davis test how choices of method affect cosmic expansion measurements from dark gravitational wave sirens. Gravitational wave events give absolute distances, and cross-matching them with galaxy lists constrains the Hubble constant through shared large-scale structure. The derived value, however, can shift with analysis choices.

They vary covariance treatment, bias settings for galaxies and wave events, and binning widths in distance and redshift, and they fold catalogue incompleteness directly into predictions. With sound modeling choices and enough precise events, the systematic biases they study can be effectively mitigated. The work supports cross-correlation as a route to precision dark siren cosmology.
arxiv-2605-06983:
Haoran Chen and four co-authors develop a theory of magnetic moments carried by phonons, the vibrations of a crystal lattice. Earlier theory worked mainly in a slow, adiabatic limit and for insulating materials. The new work aims to cover metals as well, and to handle higher vibration frequencies.

The team derives a gauge-invariant formula that separates effects from filled electronic states and from the surface between filled and empty states. Applied to a lead-tin telluride material, the surface effect greatly boosts the predicted moment, matching the size seen in experiments. The result gives one framework for both insulators and metals.
arxiv-2605-07283:
Toe Toe Shwe, Kentaro Hirata, and Adisak Seesanea solve a Lane-Emden type boundary problem with several sublinear terms. The equation couples an elliptic operator with weaker powers of the unknown, weighted by measures. It lives inside a domain with a possibly unbounded edge part. Edge values are set by a nonnegative function.

The authors prove such solutions exist and are unique, and give sharp two-sided pointwise bounds. A parallel result covers positive solutions, and the method adapts to zero edge conditions with a fractional Laplacian in place of it. The work sits in the analysis of such elliptic problems with measure data.
arxiv-2605-07483:
Leonel Aguilar and three co-authors ask when a neural network can generalize beyond its training data, and when it provably cannot. From one training window, they argue, the true process behind the data is not identifiable: many different processes fit the training data equally well yet diverge outside it. No test using only training data can choose between them.

What decides success, they show, is the structural commitment built into features, labels, and model class, often smuggled in through architecture, pretraining, or data formats. Changing only the representation changed out-of-distribution error by a factor of about 520 in their tests, at unchanged training loss. They check the same mechanism in chemistry, exoplanet, and DNA settings, plus a 264-run study of positional encodings.
arxiv-2605-07583:
Gopal Datt and two co-authors work in complex analysis, on families of holomorphic curves that map the unit disk into complex projective space. The central question is when such a family must be normal, meaning it behaves tamely enough that convergent subsequences exist. Their criterion concerns curves that avoid certain moving targets.

They establish that a family of curves omitting sufficiently many moving hypersurfaces, placed in pointwise general position, satisfies an avoidance criterion tied to normality. They also study the related situation where curves share hyperplanes rather than omit them, and derive matching normality conditions there. Results like these extend classical value-distribution theory for holomorphic maps into more flexible, moving-target settings.
arxiv-2605-07683:
Ivan Puga-Gonzalez and seven co-authors design a simulation architecture for climate governance, where citizens, advocacy groups, media, and politicians all shape land-use policy. Agent-based models exist for this, but most study either personal behavior or firm-level dynamics in isolation. Their architecture joins the two levels in one modular framework.

Individual agents decide through motive-based cognitive models grounded in the HUMAT and MOA frameworks, and influence spreads through networks of agents alike in background. Separate modules give green NGOs, media actors, and political leaders their own plans, with decisions pooling expert input, public pressure, party alignment, and media framing. The paper presents design ideas and how the parts fit, rather than results, with calibration from survey-based artificial populations and stakeholder work planned.
arxiv-2605-07883:
Ying Zhang and three co-authors soften the blunt way language models refuse requests. Safety alignment teaches models to refuse harmful prompts, but the standard response is a rigid template, the same flat refusal for everything, which damages natural conversation and fires indiscriminately. Their system, LANCE, aims for refusals that are safe yet flexible.

LANCE uses variational inference to predict a continuous distribution over several rejection categories for a given prompt. Those fine-grained distributions give a refinement model textual guidance to neutralize the hazardous elements, so the final answer can stay safe without the canned wording. In experiments LANCE substantially reduced rigid rejection while holding security standards, beating baselines on both helpfulness and naturalness of responses.
arxiv-2605-07983:
Aditi Awasthi and four co-authors show that randomness in magic state production changes how fault-tolerant quantum computers should be planned for. Magic states are the costly fuel of error-fixed computation, made in their own factories, and designers must choose how many factories to build. Deterministic planning either wastes qubits on worst-case peak demand or assumes average demand and slows execution.

Their setup couples circuit scheduling with stochastic output models for distillation, cultivation, and synthesis routes. Chance has a dual effect: it stretches total execution time but smooths peak demand. For distillation designs the space-time-optimal point shifts to fewer factories, cutting space-time volume by up to about twenty-seven percent against the fixed-plan optimum. Static estimates, they conclude, get the cost of such execution wrong.
arxiv-2605-08383:
David Freeborn, Malihe Alikani, and Anthony Sicilia study which moves change minds online. Philosophy often expects shared evidence to pull peers toward agreement. Ordinary debate suggests otherwise. The authors turn to Reddit's ChangeMyView forum. Users there publicly flag when a comment shifted their view.

Language models forecast from the midpoint of each thread. They estimate whether a change would be acknowledged. Those estimates serve as a conversational baseline. Human-machine coding then tagged each reply for ten rhetorical strategies. The strategies range from concession and empathy to logical challenge and credibility appeals. Adding those features improved prediction sharply. Concession and empathetic alignment raised the odds of belief change. Frontal attacks lowered them.
arxiv-2605-08583:
Mingzhe Li, Zhiqiang Lin, and Shiqing Ma build CiteTracer, a system that catches fake references in scientific writing. Language models can invent citation shaped entries that look real but fail checking, and simple found or not found tests miss field level errors. Their twelve code taxonomy sorts citations as real, possible, or hallucinated with specific fault labels.

A chain of agents extracts citation details, gathers evidence from caches, links, and search, matches fields by fixed rules, and sends hard cases to specialist judges. On synthetic and real fabricated sets drawn from rejected submissions, detection accuracy sits near ninety seven percent. Scholarly publishing gains a detailed audit tool for a growing integrity problem.
arxiv-2605-09083:
Madjid Eshaghi Gordji, Esmaiel Abounoori, and Mohamadali Berahman study why small policy nudges so often fail to change behavior. In settings shaped by coordination and habit, people stick with the old way of doing things as long as it remains a stable outcome, a force they call status-quo inertia.

Within their framework, price-based tools and simply adding new options can fail even when they look better on paper. Interventions that remove or replace the old actions work far better, because they take away the ground the old outcome stands on. The authors prove general results and draw examples from climate policy, platform rules, financial reform, and industry. Their lesson: sometimes the game itself must change.
arxiv-2605-09183:
Surbhi Goel, Jonathan Pei, and James Wang study imitation learning, where a system copies an expert's actions from examples. Copying works well when training and test settings move in the same way. Their 2026 paper considers a harder case: the test setting can shift in any way, so at some states the examples give no safe guidance at all.

Instead of forcing an action everywhere, their learner may stop when it cannot act with confidence. The authors define what good stopping means, then give a method that builds a stopping rule from a small set of checker policies. Its sample needs do not grow with the time horizon. Extensions cover imperfect experts and cases where the training and test experts differ.
arxiv-2605-09283:
Egami and a colleague build a framework for the Agentic Web, where AI agents rather than humans drive the web, and AI made content is set to dominate. Today nothing lets agents check AI made content for trust, repeatability, or license rules while it is made, risking chained falsehoods and rule breaches through reuse. Their framework auto attaches structured metadata to AI made content as it is made, covering modular prompts, contexts, thoughts, model details, hyperparameters, and confidence.

The metadata travels wrapped with verifiable credentials, supporting sound assessment and reuse of the content. That enables tidy curation of structured AI made content and its safe use for fine tuning and knowledge distillation. The work treats origin records and generation conditions as core infrastructure for an agent driven web, not an afterthought. By making generation conditions machine readable, the framework lets agents judge content before reuse, instead of trusting it blindly.
arxiv-2605-09483:
Madhyastha presents BPL, the Bounded Pragmatic Listener, a Bayesian framework for modelling why people fall for information disorder. It builds on Rational Speech Act theory with three bounds from the study of bounded rationality. A recursion depth bound reflects working memory limits. A prior compression parameter tracks the information bottleneck. A sample size for availability runs importance sampling with saliency-weighted proposals. The paper is flagged as work in progress.

That design lets the author test claims about who falls for falsehoods and why annotators disagree. It also tests who is most at risk from mis-, dis-, and mal-information under the Information Disorder framework. Tests on the LIAR and MultiFC benchmarks show strong truth classification and trial support for the depth-mismatch paradox.
arxiv-2605-09583:
Towers and two colleagues introduce a graph built from a finite dimensional Lie algebra, called the comaximal graph. Its points are the nontrivial proper subalgebras. Two points join when the subalgebras together span the whole algebra. The build extends a family of graphs made from algebraic structures, including the earlier subspace sum graph. But the spanning rule here fits Lie algebras. The authors set out general structural traits, including isolated point traits via the Frattini subalgebra.

They sort the graph fully for Lie algebras of dimension no larger than three over a finite field, with explicit accounts in each case. For the special linear algebra in dimension two, they work out degree lists, clique and chromatic numbers, domination number, diameter, and radius. That graph is connected and non planar. A large clique comes from nonsplit semisimple lines plus Borel subalgebras. Nilpotent and split lines show tighter adjacency.
arxiv-2605-09683:
Schork gave a combinatorial reading of normal ordering in a deformed algebra, the art of rewriting products in a standard order. For words in variables X and Y obeying the q-deformed generalized Ore relation, the paper shows normal-ordering coefficients count mixed placements of rooks and files on boards. The q-deformed Ore-Stirling numbers match placements on the staircase board, while the Ore-Lah numbers match placements on the Lah board.

From those board pictures, recurrence relations for both number families follow directly. Schork also worked out the normal-ordered form of the binomial power (X + Y) raised to m. He then extended the whole story to the polynomial Weyl algebra, where the relation uses an arbitrary polynomial in Y. Board combinatorics, the paper shows, can carry a whole deformed algebra.
arxiv-2605-09883:
Hu and six colleagues expose a shortcut behind strong vision-reasoning scores. Most benchmarks lay tasks out on orthogonal grids, which models can quietly convert into text coordinates and solve by deduction rather than sight. The authors call this the Cartesian Shortcut and ask whether high scores reflect real visual understanding at all. Their answer is a new benchmark, Polaris-Bench.

Polaris-Bench restates 53 visual reasoning tasks in polar coordinates, with paired Cartesian versions as controls, keeping the logic identical. Fourteen leading multimodal models that scored seventy to eighty-three percent on Cartesian layouts fell to thirty-one to thirty-nine percent on polar equivalents. Reasoning gains seen on Cartesian tasks largely vanished too, pointing to a missing skill: topology-invariant visual reasoning.
arxiv-2605-10183:
Wang and three colleagues rethink Sharpness-Aware Minimization, a training method that improves generalisation by shrinking the worst-case loss inside a fixed parameter-space radius. SAM and its variants lean on a first-order linearised surrogate, yet flat minima are by nature a second-order curvature notion. That mismatch motivates Loss-Equated SAM, which flips the mechanism: a fixed loss-space budget replaces the fixed perturbation radius.

Fixing the loss budget removes gradient-norm-dominated learning signals and shifts optimisation toward curvature-dominated terms. Across diverse benchmarks and tasks, LE-SAM consistently beats SAM and its variants, reaching state-of-the-art performance. The paper's message is in its title: fix the loss, not the radius, since the radius is the wrong knob for a curvature concept.
arxiv-2605-10683:
H. Che and co-authors report the design, build, and beam test of a pilot 3D projection detector based on opaque water-based liquid scintillator. The detector is an 8 by 8 by 16 cm acrylic vessel fitted with three right-angle planes of colour-shifting fibres read out by multi-pixel photon counters. Its CITIROC front-end circuits were built for the T2K experiment's WAGASCI and SuperFGD detectors. Filled with the opaque liquid, it was tested with cosmic rays and proton beams at four energies at Brookhaven's NASA Space Radiation Laboratory.

3D event displays of cosmic muons and proton candidates go with a study of sideways light trapping through radial charge spreads. Measured data show tighter trapping than a Geant4 run with a 2 cm spread length. This places the working spread length well below that value. It confirms optical trapping in the medium.
arxiv-2605-10983:
Jiaming Li and eleven colleagues present TMPO, a diffusion-alignment method that fights reward hacking without killing variety. Reinforcement learning aligns diffusion models to tasks, but reward chasing piles onto a few high-reward paths, collapsing visual variety and amplifying shaky rewards.

TMPO swaps scalar reward chasing for trajectory-level distribution matching. A Softmax Trajectory Balance goal aligns policy odds across paths with a reward-shaped Boltzmann distribution, keeping cover over all good paths as forward KL divergence does. Dynamic stochastic tree sampling, sharing path segments, cuts multi-path training time on large flow-matching models. Diffusion teams get alignment that preserves cover over all acceptable outputs.
arxiv-2605-11083:
Jaime Salcido and eleven colleagues trace the thermal history of the universe through thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich cross-correlations in the FLAMINGO simulation suite. Matching large-scale-structure tracers like galaxies and quasars with the tSZ signal measures bias-weighted mean electron pressure, from which the Compton-y history follows given a bias model.

Across FLAMINGO's range of cosmologies and gas physics setups in volumes up to 2.8 gigaparsecs cubed, the pressure measure depends steeply on S8, the standard clustering amplitude combination. The study maps how redshift, cosmology, and galaxy-formation physics each move the thermal history, separating cosmic drivers from galaxy drivers. Cosmologists get a calibrated thermal-history probe for weighing feedback against cosmology.
arxiv-2605-11283:
Tintin Nguyen and four colleagues map black hole binary detection for LILA, the Laser Interferometer Lunar Antenna. LILA, a proposed Moon-based gravitational-wave project, reaches deci-Hz. It targets intermediate-mass binaries of ten squared to ten to the sixth solar masses.

With 4 years observing, LILA extends its IMBH horizon to the early Universe. It probes first massive black holes at redshift twenty to thirty. LILA could also detect intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals. Masses: ten to the fourth to ten to the sixth solar masses; ratios: ten to the minus fourth to ten to the minus second. LILA can catch IMBH binaries well before merger, with eccentricity leftovers from formation giving early warning for multi-messenger follow-up. High signal-to-noise LILA events above one hundred enable strong-field tests of gravity. LILA will thus illuminate massive black hole formation and evolution.
arxiv-2605-11383: Peng and five colleagues propose HamBR, a defense for learning with noisy labels based on Hamiltonian dynamics. In noise-degraded feature space, decision boundaries collapse, so models cannot tell hard clean samples from noisy ones at the margins. HamBR uses Spherical Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to probe ambiguous regions between classes and synthesize high-quality virtual outliers. Energy-based repulsion constraints then build robust barriers at boundaries, pushing real samples toward their class centres and restoring sharpness, with state-of-the-art results on CIFAR and real-world noise benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-11483: Ishmam Khan and two colleagues test whether small language models can internalize Stoic philosophy from tiny datasets. They specialize small models on tiny sets of core Stoic texts tuned by preference optimization. Judged by a multi-model critic bank, just 300 high-fidelity examples build strong alignment with inward-facing Stoic virtues. The result nearly matches few-shot prompting and frees the context window. Yet all models, including few-shot baselines, fail persistently on Stoicism's outward-facing cosmopolitan duties, a limit micro-datasets alone cannot fix.
arxiv-2605-11783: Philip Kennerberg proves stability for compensator integrals and nonlinear operators when processes converge in canonical p-th power variation. He looks at cadlag paths with compensators known in advance. He shows one class of these tools stays stable as approximations converge, even when they do not converge in the usual sense. The proof rests on a stopped estimate and a weighted cylinder approximation. Examples span covariance, cumulant, and kernel cases, plus smoothed transport cases.
arxiv-2605-11983: Tobias Fuchs, Florian Kalinke, and Nadja Klein speed up Schrödinger bridge training for unpaired source and target samples. Simulation-free bridges need paired data from entropic optimal transport, but global coupling is infeasible and minibatch iteration costs heavily while distorting global geometry. Their quantized diffusion Schrödinger bridges compute coupling on anchor-quantized endpoint distributions, then lift the plan back through cell-wise sampling. The regularized coupling stays stable under quantization, and experiments matched baseline sample quality in far less time.
arxiv-2605-12183: Ali Falahati and three colleagues present DriftXpress, a faster form of drifting models for one-step image generation. Drifting models replace iterative denoising with a single generator evaluation, trading cheaper inference for costlier training. DriftXpress approximates the drifting kernel in a compact feature space using projected RKHS fields, keeping the original field's pull-push structure while cutting evaluation cost. Across image benchmarks it matches standard drifting on FID while reducing wall-clock training cost, pushing the training-inference trade-off further without losing one-step inference.
arxiv-2605-12283: Natalia Gonzalez-Vazquez and eight colleagues ask whether size still tunes magnet pull in micrometer Janus particles. They make FePt caps on silica spheres 3 to 10 microns wide, stretching to 1 to 20 microns in simulations. Across that range, holding force, rest pull, and loop shape show no size link. The length ratio, near ten to the minus three to ten to the minus four, places them there. Size and response are split: diameter can serve payload and safety needs with no penalty. But size cannot tune pull flip, which follows matter.
arxiv-2605-12383: Grassi and Penati review higher-form symmetries in supersymmetric theories, viewed through supergeometry. That view reveals a larger set of topological conserved supercurrents. It includes Chern-Weil symmetries and new geometric versions built from invariant forms on super spaces. In three-dimensional N=1 super-Maxwell theory they build the matching operators and charged defects. Charges there are set by a super-linking number between supporting surfaces. The paper closes with unpublished hints toward a super-symTFT for these symmetries drawn from supergravity.
arxiv-2605-12483: Xu and five colleagues state a practical rule for spending scarce checked examples in language-model training. Sparse sequence-level reward helps most on models strong enough to explore and find better behaviour. Dense token-level teacher guidance suits compressing that behaviour into a smaller model. Scarce labels should therefore go upstream to the strongest teacher, then flow downstream as dense supervision. In tests, an improved eight-billion teacher distilled through that bridge beats direct GRPO on a small student on maths and code tasks.
arxiv-2605-12583: Sarkar and Bhattacharjee build a compiler for modular multi-QPU quantum systems, where local connectivity and cross-QPU communication must be weighed. A mapping that looks fine on one coupling graph can flood a few interconnect links, overload ports, or strand boundary qubits on a port-poor QPU. Their QuPort framework models the problem at three levels: a weighted logical interaction graph, a directed coupling map of the hardware, and an undirected interconnect graph for QPUs. Its TPCCAP partitioner optimises cut distance, port overflow and routed link-load congestion together.
arxiv-2605-12683: Hess, Götz and Durstewitz study parallel-in-time training of recurrent neural networks for reconstructing nonlinear systems from data. Sequential models usually force linear runtime in sequence length. Recent parallel algorithms achieve log time by splitting along sequence length. The paper examines two classes of parallel algorithms, both built on linked scans. The first class covers models with linear self-run motion and a nonlinear readout, like modern state space models. The second covers general curved models, opening new avenues for long-sequence rebuilding.
arxiv-2605-12883: Kumar and Weber study mixing in a passive divergence-free vector field carried by another such field on a torus. Pressure makes the vector case far harder than the scalar case, since the simple particle-tracking view no longer applies. They first set conditions that guarantee solutions exist and are unique, then derive lower bounds on the mixing rate across ranges of parameters. Simulations suggest the best mixing rate is at least exponential in time.
arxiv-2605-12983: Soltani Moakhar, Ghahremani, Banihashem and Hajiaghayi extend the theory of greedy decision-tree learning from uniform distributions to arbitrary product distributions. For any function computed by an optimal tree of size s, they show the greedy heuristic builds an approximating tree whose size grows at most exponentially in optimal depth terms. When the optimal tree is full and binary, the bound improves on Blanc and colleagues and covers a broader distribution class. Their algorithm is fully parameter-free.
arxiv-2605-13183: Niarchos and Papageorgakis review a conformal bootstrap approach that skips positivity, handling the endless tower of high-dimension operator terms to conformal correlators via dispersion relations and neural nets. They apply it to scalar thermal two-point functions on a circle times flat space. They discuss stability of the non-convex optimisation scheme and links to smoothness in conformal field theory correlators. Numerical tests on generalised free fields and four-dimensional holographic conformal field theories show the method at work. The paper comes from a 2025 Athens workshop on theoretical physics.
arxiv-2605-13483: Jonas Vasikonis and four colleagues reconstruct a vector beam without ever detecting the field itself. Vector beams carry polarisation that varies across their profile, yet they are hard to measure without good detectors. The team uses induced coherence in a nonlinear interferometer, where two down-conversion paths cannot be told apart. A telecom idler field gains a varying polarisation pattern but stays undetected, while its pattern is read from visible signal interference. With quantum holography, they recover the full vectorial structure of an m equals 2 beam.
arxiv-2605-13783: Sebastian Munoz proves oneness of synced still rests in the Kuramoto mean field game. The still game models a crowd of phase swingers forming synced Nash rests above a key coupling strength. He proves the synced branch is one smooth family of Nash rests rising from the uniform state at the split. Both follow from the main key result that the scalar self-match map is strictly concave, closing a guess of Carmona, Cormier and Soner.
arxiv-2605-14083: Arbabifar, Morshedian and Tehrani give a new analysis of nucleon form factors from generalized parton distributions, which map the nucleon's three-dimensional structure. Extracting such distributions from data needs flexible, physically motivated guesses. Their new ansatz, AMA25, addresses limits of the earlier GSAMA24 model. Fits run with the iMinuit package in Jupyter notebooks show AMA25 beating rivals on fit quality. Its reduced chi-squared is lower, it meets theoretical constraints better, and it stays steadier when pushed to the exclusive region.
arxiv-2605-14183: Jaykar and James construct integral representations for a broad class of time-harmonic solutions to Maxwell's equations in vacuum or homogeneous source-free media. The work builds on an earlier form used for helical atomic shapes with twisted rays. Their form uses tunable distributions for set edge or far-field conditions. When those functions meet mild periodicity and smoothness conditions, multi-dimensional trapezoidal rules approximate the solutions with very fast convergence.
arxiv-2605-14283: Kim, Fang and Sandholm study watermarking game-playing agents in perfect-information extensive-form games. LLM watermarks hide information in output so its source can be verified, aiding misuse detection. Game-playing faces similar misuse, such as unauthorized AI tools on gaming platforms. The KGW watermark for LLMs is adapted to watermark game-playing agents, detected by a stats test. Quality loss in the watermarked strategy can be bounded, but detectability trades off against quality. Chess-engine experiments show negligible quality impact and detection with a handful of games.
arxiv-2605-14383: Newton's problem of minimal resistance asks which shape meets least drag in a flow, and López extends it to radial fields beyond translational symmetry. He analyses two non-equilibrium cases, a scale-invariant free expansion and an incompressible source flow. The scale-invariant model suffers a symmetry-breaking instability, a loss of ellipticity forcing geometric truncation. The incompressible flow instead acts as a steadying influence, giving unique, smooth, strictly concave solutions. The findings link conservation laws to the smoothness and symmetry of optimal shapes in fast central flows.
arxiv-2605-14483: Xudong Chen and colleagues propose LEMON, a planner learning efficient multi-agent orchestration for language-model systems. Across tasks, role design, capacity and dependency links jointly affect quality and speed. Older methods handle parts of this design, yet tune choices bit by bit or in order. Given a task, LEMON designs a unified plan of duties, capacity levels and dependency links. Training adds group policy tuning with a counterfactual credit signal. On six reasoning and coding benchmarks, LEMON scores best on average while lifting the accuracy-token trade-off.
arxiv-2605-14583: Zhang and Zhao describe the gaps and the Weierstrass semigroup for a totally ramified place of degree one. The place lies on a Kummer extension given by y to the m equals f of x. One unified form covers distinct such places. A necessary and sufficient condition for the semigroup to be symmetric is given. The minimal generating set at many such places is described, with functions built whose pole divisors have coefficients in the set. GGS curves and BM subcovers illustrate the results.
arxiv-2605-14683: Amer and team model and control SeaVis, a towed robot vehicle run from afar for seabed maps and views. Steady exact positioning matters for sharp seafloor maps. They derive a math model and build a gain-scheduled linear-quadratic regulator for depth and attitude control. In a high-fidelity simulation against a standard PID controller, the new controller is claimed to be tougher, more efficient, and far lighter on flap actuation.
arxiv-2605-14783: Lin and Liu show that readable event-level observables for collider interference can be discovered by AI-driven symbolic search. Score data from matrix-element reweighting serves as the statistical goal. The study focuses on a CP-sensitive Higgs-Z coupling. Two cases are studied: associated production in electron-positron runs and four-lepton Higgs decay. Learned observables are claimed to keep far more local Fisher information than standard angular rivals. They stay compact analytic formulas and recover typical helicity-interference harmonics in both cases.
arxiv-2605-15183: ML Nissen Gonzalez and five others offer tensor similarity, a weight-based metric for judging when two neural network parts implement the same computation. Action tests miss out-of-distribution gears, while weight tests ignore weight-space mirror rules. Tensor similarity is invariant under those rules, captures global functional match and cross-layer mechanisms, and runs through an efficient recursive algorithm. In tests it tracks training dynamics like grokking and backdoor planting more truly than old metrics.
arxiv-2605-15483: Sky Qiu, Nerissa Nance, Rachael Phillips, Jens Tarp, Maya Petersen, and Mark van der Laan sharpen subgroup reads in randomized trials. Small subgroups give shaky reads. Their two targeted tools borrow strength from trial members outside the subgroup. No outside data is used, so no outside bias creeps in. Random assignment still guards the reads. In a heart trial case study, the adaptive tool finds real risk cuts for major cardiac events in Asian and Black subgroups. Its ranges rule out no effect at each time point.
arxiv-2605-15583: Ryohei Goto, Takuya Fujihashi, Shunsuke Saruwatari, and Fumio Okura lift 3D human poses from one view with no 3D training data. They stretch multi-view ancestral sampling of motion diffusion models to this lift task. The 3D pose is tuned so its views track the 2D diffusion manifold. It must also match the given 2D pose and human anatomy. On a yoga set the method beats supervised and unsupervised rivals across domains. It wins even on extreme poses where 3D training data do not exist.
arxiv-2605-15683: Zhiguo Ding, Xu Song, and Wei Xiong pin down all permutation polynomials in several families over finite fields of cubed order. They find new families with simple coefficients for infinitely many characteristics. As a payoff, their results settle a broad version of conjectures by Zhang, Zheng, Wang, Peng, and Li in even characteristic. Their proofs are short in concept and use no tangled computations, unlike past proofs on this topic. They also build a wholly new systematic method for studying permutation polynomials.
arxiv-2605-15883: Gijs W. A. Simons, Rik F. J. van Haren and Bert Koopmans make stable magnetic nanodomains with focused gallium-ion irradiation. Patterned anisotropy gradients form tiny wells that trap domain walls and allow step-by-step switching both ways, replacing random defect pinning. A theory of wall energetics in graded profiles gives design rules for depinning and stability, backed by simulations and experiments. The team makes programmable multi-domain states in flat ferromagnetic films, switching 750 nm regions well, with first results at 100 nm near the domain-wall width limit.
arxiv-2605-16083: Addanki and Pitale end with a clean sign claim: for every large enough prime, the Hecke eigenvalues of Ikeda lifts come out positive. The route there runs through a spherical map on the symplectic group's Hecke algebra, which turns each eigenvalue into an explicit formula. That formula writes the eigenvalue as a polynomial in p to the plus or minus one-half power, with a positive leading term. A further step bounds every coefficient of that polynomial, and the positivity claim follows from that bound.
arxiv-2605-16283: Fan frames a stock-building measure gap in AI's effects on skill building. Field data show AI use focused in skilled work aiding instant task results, but observe current skill rather than whether users grow able to perform tasks alone. Lab studies measure solo ability more head-on, but only in small groups with design-bound results. Fan merges both evidence streams by ID strength and offers a research program linking agreed usage records to solo tests, varying whether AI supplies answers, hints, feedback, or grading.
arxiv-2605-16383: Kilicdere and two others propose a neurosymbolic framework augmenting Swin Transformers with focal sets and fuzzy logic for hierarchical classification. Deep networks often answer too strongly, failing to express uncertainty and breaking logical rules.
