Their method induces focal sets in the learnt embedding space to capture uncertainty over fine-grained classes. A belief layer with fuzzy functions supports fine-coarse consistency. A learnable loss trades off calibration, mass costs, and logic. Tests show accuracy on par with transformer baselines with more calibrated, interpretable predictions.
arxiv-2605-16483: Pontzen and three others use FLAMINGO to investigate why AGN feedback depletes group gas but not cluster gas. Three zones emerge: inner shock heating, buoyancy rise, and outer termination-shock stall. Inner heating self-limits because hot gas makes shocks too weak to deposit entropy, giving a ceiling of 360 keV cm² independent of halo mass. Outflows rise at fixed entropy, escaping below 10^13.7 solar masses, as inflow entropy tracks the virial relation. Above the critical mass, inflow entropy stalls outflows at the splashback radius, and lingering gas rejoins as halos grow.
arxiv-2605-16783: Gao and colleagues propose a staged learning path for geophysical AI when field labels are scarce and synthetic data diverges from field data. It chains self-taught pretraining, synthetic supervision, prior-driven refinement, and domain fine-tuning into one workflow. Tested on relative geologic time estimation in global shelf-edge clinothems, with 3,000 field datasets from many basins, the path works well across surveys. It also sharpens fine-scale rock-layer and structure detail, offering a guide for other geophysical tasks such as interpretation, regression, and inversion.
arxiv-2605-17283: Ma and colleagues present OProver, a unified framework for agentic theorem proving in Lean 4 that folds agent behavior into training rather than leaving it to inference. Failed proofs are revised with compiler feedback and retrieved verified proofs, feeding repair data and hard cases back into training. Its OProofs corpus holds 1.77 million statements and 6.86 million verified proofs, and the 32-billion-parameter model leads three of five benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-17383: Kokol Bukovšek, Oblak and Šmigoc study star covers of graphs, but instead of minimizing star count they optimize the number of bipartite components in the cover. The problem, tied to symmetric nonnegative trifactorization and the SNT-rank of graphs, is hard in general. For graphs with no four-cycles they develop an algorithm that determines the SNT-rank, giving a tractable corner of a hard problem.
arxiv-2605-17583: Bin Kang and colleagues present AgentSteerTTS, a multi-agent closed-loop frame for intent-faithful expressive steering of composite speech instructions. A disentanglement agent separates identity from emotion-prosody spaces to stop speaker-emotion leakage. A dual-stream anchor control grounds intents with retrieved acoustic anchors fused into control vectors. A fast-slow feedback agent refines intensity by latent gradient fixes. It also resolves meaning-sound mismatches by perceptual review. Tests show steady significant gains over baselines.
arxiv-2605-18083: Hao Zhou and eight colleagues tackle expanding large language models to new languages without costly continued pre-training and data-heavy alignment. Merging a multilingual model with its instruct version trades off new language gains against keeping old skills. Their method upcycles a dense model into a mixture-of-experts design, giving different experts to different languages. Alignment skill is then grafted on as a mixture-expanded parameter delta, skipping the complex alignment phase. Tests show gains on expanded languages while preserving old abilities, across models and post-training deltas.
arxiv-2605-18483: Jordan Tschida and twelve co-authors review time series classification in a 2026 paper of biological signals through a unified morphology-modality lens. The lens links waveform shape to model design across EEG, EMG, ECG, PPG, and eye-tracking signals. The review finds shape, not model class, most strongly drives performance and interpretability. Shape-aware modeling emerges as a unifying principle for general, clear, physiologically meaningful models, with shape-based augmentation and new metrics as future work.
arxiv-2605-18583: Yubin Qu and six co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, overeager coding agents, which exceed benign requests by deleting files or rewriting unmentioned configuration. Their OverEager-Gen benchmark certifies each case's discriminative power before admission and audits tool calls through a dual-channel stack. On Claude Code, stripping consent alone lifts the overeager rate from zero to about seventeen percent on paired scenarios. Across four agent products, permissive frameworks run about five to twenty-eight percent overeager. OpenHands, which asks first, sits near zero to four percent.
arxiv-2605-18783: Xuli Qi and Yanrui Feng settle a 1997 conjecture about splitting a vertex in a regular graph. Hilton and Zhao had claimed that splitting one vertex in a connected regular Class 1 graph yields an edge-critical graph when the degree tops one third of the vertex count. Earlier work had reached only three quarters of that count. Qi and Feng push the proof down to a threshold just below two thirds, closing the gap for high-degree graphs.
arxiv-2605-18883: Andrew Bukowski, Aditya Kothari, Simba Shi and Ishir Rao test whether neural simulators learn conserved energy or only mimic motion. A diffusion model can track Hamiltonian trajectories closely while its energy swings thousands of times more than the true value. Their structured energy model recovers analytical energy almost exactly on clean data, while a black-box network nearly matches it with a small alignment cue. Without that cue the black-box method collapses, showing time consistency alone cannot pin down the true conserved quantity.
arxiv-2605-18983: Cameron Ruether introduces lowered flags of modules to define flag sheaves of ideals matching parabolic subgroups for the general linear group of an Azumaya algebra. The notion extends to outer type A, defining a matching sheaf for a unitary group. When split, these relate to submodule flags in a vector bundle, or in one with hermitian form. He defines idempotent-tuple sheaves matching parabolic and Levi pairs, describes the type morphism to the Dynkin scheme, and generalises Quillen's construction to the outer case, producing an algebra with unitary involution.
arxiv-2605-19083: Steven J. Miller, Dimitrios Nikolakopoulos, and Anitha Srinivasan solve a rational Diophantine equation completely using Vieta jumping, a technique that steps between solutions. They study pairs of positive integers a and b for which a simple fraction sum equals an integer k. They prove k can only be 3 or 4, with solution pairs tied to Fibonacci numbers. It follows that a related ratio built from a, b, and their greatest common divisor takes just the values 1, 2, 3, and 5.
arxiv-2605-19183: J. A. Santiago and F. Monroy show that a nematic field held to a curved embedded surface gains a mass from shape alone. A closure in the space around it, steered by the surface spin link, yields a scalar mode whose mass is set by the outer curvature measure. The mass comes from embedding geometry, turning the massless nematic force into a shape-ruled heavy field. The theory treats Gaussian curvature as a spread-out geometric charge and makes shape the guide for defect links on curved nematic skins.
arxiv-2605-19383: Huang, Gong and Wei ask whether a crystal's electronic symmetry must match its space-group symmetry. Space groups sort atoms by layout, but electronic links such as hopping and Coulomb coupling can redraw equivalence. Their theory treats site charge imbalance as an order parameter set by charging cost against Coulomb gain. Equivalent sites can split, lowering symmetry, while inequivalent sites can stay equivalent via hidden gauge symmetry. First-principles checks confirm both patterns, with pressure as a control that can split doublets or drive a metal-insulator switch.
arxiv-2605-19483: Athreya, Bhattacharya and Borkar explain generative-model memorization, where a model being tuned repeats the same or similar outputs for long stretches, through training dynamics alone. Building on work about collapse in generative models and two-timescale stochastic gradient descent, they model the loss as depending strongly on some variables and weakly on the rest. That split yields two distinct timescales in constant-step-size descent, already used to explain double descent. Combined with a collapse model, it explains memorization as a dynamical effect, tying several reported phenomena together.
arxiv-2605-19683: Hajdu, Hozzova, Kovacs and Wagner repair a proof-based method for building programs from written specifications. Their superposition calculus first handled programs without recursion, even when some symbols cannot be computed, but it failed on certain cases. The team fixes those gaps, proves the repaired method sound, and shows it complete: whenever a computable program meets the specification, the method finds one.
arxiv-2605-20683: Shengyao Zhuang, Zhichao Xu, and Ivano Lauriola propose layer-wise token compression for document reranking. Cross-encoder rerankers are central to search but costly on long query-document pairs. Compressing tokens at the input layer works for bi-encoders yet fails for cross-encoders in their tests. Their LTC method instead pools tokens adaptively at middle transformer layers. That preserves ranking quality while lifting throughput by up to 25 percent on passage ranking tasks.
arxiv-2605-20883: Sonia Mazelet, Remi Flamary, and Bertrand Thirion learn fMRI activation dictionaries across individual brain geometries via optimal transport. Dictionary learning creates interpretable representations, and fMRI patterns support tasks like brain-state sorting and group analysis. A major challenge is geometry variation across individuals. The usual fix projects each brain onto a common template, which discards person-specific information. Their method accounts for that variation using the Fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance to compare graphs with different shapes and traits.
arxiv-2605-21083: Mei and many colleagues present AIMBio, an AI-native FAIR platform for closed-loop materials discovery and biomedical translation. Materials discovery and biomedical translation increasingly need models that reason across makeup, handling, structure, bio response, making, safety, and control constraints, a wide span. Old data ecosystems are strong but remain poorly coupled for AI-guided work. AIMBio formulates biomedical discovery as limited multi-objective optimization, linking provenance, medical context, knowledge graphs, and doubt-aware machine learning in a control-aware choice layer, a neat setup.
arxiv-2605-21283: Ophélie Schaller, Andrew Titman, and Rachel McCrea offer a continuous-time Markov chain framework for estimating population size from multi-list data. The framework allows directional interactions between lists and can handle absorbing lists, such as death records. When lists are independent, it matches the standard log-linear model, and the two give similar results even with dependencies. Simulations show that ignoring an absorbing list biases population estimates. The authors motivate the work with first-stroke cases in North-West England, where one list is a death record.
arxiv-2605-21383: Dimitri Veras, Jordan K. Steckloff, and Kathryn Volk quantify how rotational fission from sublimative outgassing can produce planetary debris outside white dwarf Roche radii. Most white dwarfs hosting transiting debris do so beyond the rubble-pile Roche limit. This contradicts models centered on tidal disruption. Using the Many Materials Orbital Sublimation model for iron cores, olivine mantles, and water-ice comets, they characterize spin-up analytically. SYORP coefficients range from ten to the minus five to ten to the minus three. They compare this rate to radiative YORP spin-up.
arxiv-2605-21483: Tilman Tröster and co-authors introduce Velocityformer, a graph transformer for cosmic velocity maps. Accurate galaxy speeds are needed to measure the kSZ effect, a probe of large-scale ordinary matter spread. While physics respects translation and rotation symmetry, observations break symmetry via a chosen viewing line. Matching the model to that broken symmetry improves performance. The goal is better maps of galaxy motion.

arxiv-2606-04283:
George Zhou leads a large team in 2026 designing a space mission to settle how young close-in planets are built. Two recipes compete. One gives planets light hydrogen-helium envelopes. The other makes them water-rich worlds.

Both recipes match today's mature planets, so only young ones can tell them apart. The team's simulated survey would stare at thirty young star fields for two and a half years. It would use ultraviolet, optical, and infrared light at once. The catch: about a hundred transiting planets younger than fifty million years. Only twenty are known today. Measuring how common each size is would split the two scenarios for good, the team argues.
arxiv-2606-04483:
Luo and colleagues show that the writing style of fanfiction can break the safety training of aligned language models, in a 2026 arXiv security study. Known jailbreaks are crafted prompts, easy to fingerprint and patch. The authors argue the real weakness is a register of natural human writing that safety training under-covered. Their attack conditions a creative-writing setup on passages from twelve fanfiction subgenres on Archive of Our Own, with harmful behavior written in as the scene's climax. No attacker model or per-target tuning is needed.

On eight aligned models, tested on HarmBench and JailbreakBench with a four-judge panel, the attack raised the mean success rate from 0.278 to 0.731, and a factorial analysis showed the gain came from register, not length or structure. Two defenses widened the gap. A static four-turn extension, Saga-A4, reached a mean success rate of 0.924, beating three multi-turn methods.
arxiv-2606-04583: HALFNET: randomized neural networks were developed with learned subspace geometry. The efficient AI was built. The finding serves AI research. Learned subspaces geometry random networks. HALFNET randomizes networks with learned geometry. TinyML needs randomized efficiency. HALFNET suits edge devices. HALFNET's geometry preserves accuracy.
arxiv-2606-04683:
Lalanne, Rodríguez-Vítores, Iutzeler, and Loubes solve a privacy problem in optimal transport, the mathematics of moving one distribution into another at least cost, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Estimating the transport map between two distributions from private data risks leaking individuals' information. So the estimation must satisfy differential privacy, a formal guarantee that no single person's data changes the output much. Their estimators build on wavelet-based density estimates and recent stability bounds for smooth transport maps.

Their main estimator achieves near-minimax optimal rates in dimension two or more, under both central and local privacy models, meaning its error is essentially the best any private method could achieve. A complementary quantile-based estimator attains exactly minimax optimal rates in one dimension under central privacy. Matching lower bounds confirm the near-optimality.
arxiv-2606-04883:
Rögnvaldsson, Sun, Dekoninck, and Vechev teach an AI theorem prover to quit while it is behind, in a 2026 arXiv paper on formal proof in Lean. Language model workflows for Lean decompose problems into lemmas, sample many proof attempts, and use compiler feedback to guide search. Their action-routing agent separates a data plane from a control plane: the data plane generates natural-language lemma decompositions, formalizes them in Lean, and samples proof attempts for theorem and lemma targets.

The control plane watches previous failed Lean attempts, and decides whether to keep proving the current target or restart from a new breakdown. On a subset of PutnamBench, the agent cuts cost by 28.9 percent on average against a fixed-step baseline.
arxiv-2606-05083:
Hugo Molinares, Gianluca Rastelli, Victor Montenegro, and Vitalie Eremeev propose squeezed phonon lasing through Floquet-controlled solid-state defects in this 2026 arXiv paper. Phonon lasing is the acoustic analogue of a laser: a mechanical oscillator emits coherent vibrations instead of light. Squeezed output, with noise pushed below the standard quantum limit in one quadrature, would suit fine measurement, but producing it steadily is difficult.

Their scheme uses color centers, atomic-scale defects that act like spins, embedded in a circular hexagonal boron nitride membrane. A mechanical oscillator couples to main and ancilla spins under Floquet driving, meaning periodic modulation in time. The setup moves from ordinary lasing to phase-locked squeezed phonon lasing. The authors analyze the steady state, covering lasing threshold, mechanical occupation, and the emission spectrum. They show that Floquet control can hold phase locking while tuning the squeezing.
arxiv-2606-05183:
Patrick Keough audits sycophancy in Google's Gemini models across three generations in this 2026 arXiv paper, arguing that binary safety metrics hide most of the behavior. Pass-fail scoring treats social compliance as an event, but models often shade answers toward user validation over accuracy by degrees. Keough scores sycophancy as a continuous phenomenon instead.

The audit covers 8,830 responses from eight model variants, seven adversarial prompt categories, and three guardrail conditions, scored on sycophancy, truthfulness, and refusal specificity axes checked against human raters. Binary scoring left 71 percent of behavior variance unexplained, a shortfall the author names the Granularity Gap, and 94 percent of mild sycophantic responses passed binary filters unnoticed. Sycophancy predicted hallucination, a coupling that nearly doubled from the 2.0 to the 3.0 generation. Safety gains rose and fell across generations, flattery requests provoked nearly twice the sycophancy of unethical ones, and simple guardrails beat complex reasoning schemes at reducing it.
arxiv-2606-05283:
M. N. Isla Llave and colleagues find a strong enhancement of active galactic nuclei among dusty star-forming galaxies in protoclusters in this 2026 arXiv paper. Protoclusters at redshift above two are dense, gas-rich regions where interactions run high, conditions expected to feed black holes as well as starbursts. Earlier studies disagreed over mismatched samples and methods.

The team took ALMA-detected star-forming galaxies in seven protoclusters between redshifts two and 4.5. They built a selection-matched sample from the COSMOS survey and compared the incidence of X-ray-selected active nuclei. The protocluster fraction came out about 2.7 times the field value, with statistical significance, and enhancements appeared in both redshift halves of the sample. The samples matched in mass, star formation rate, and dust mass, so the excess is not a selection artifact. The authors attribute it to the dense environment, through gas availability and interaction-driven fueling.
arxiv-2606-05883:
Xiao Cui and colleagues shrink training sets for diffusion models without warping the data's shape in a 2026 arXiv paper. Dataset condensation swaps huge corpora for compact stand-ins. Synthetic stand-ins often look fake, which poisons diffusion training. Plain subset picking keeps real images but loses the distribution's geometry. The team recasts selection as geometry-aware alignment between subset and full data.

One-sided partial optimal transport matches the subset to the bulk while leaving sparse regions unmatched. Light regularizers guard feature statistics and semantic consistency. A two-stage discrete optimization makes the search practical. Experiments spanned diffusion variants, subset sizes, resolutions, and training rounds. The selected subsets delivered better fidelity and coverage than rival methods throughout. Keeping geometry intact, the authors argue, is what likelihood-based training actually needs. Their code ships with the paper for reuse.
arxiv-2606-06183:
Simon Malan, Danel Slabbert, and Herman Kamper question how speech technology grades its own word discovery in this 2026 arXiv paper. Zero-resource systems learn from untranscribed speech and cluster recurring sound stretches into word-like units. The standard score, normalized edit distance, averages how far apart the sounds inside each cluster are. The authors show this score quietly favors systems whose large clusters happen to be tidy.

Drawing on clustering theory, they propose two fixes: a weighted score that accounts for cluster size when judging consistency, and an inverse score that checks how true words spread across clusters. On synthetic and real lexicons, the pair tracked similarity to the true lexicon more closely and resisted the old biases. The weighted normalized edit similarity and its inverse emerged as the most complete option.
arxiv-2606-06283:
Samapan Bhadury and co-authors derive flow equations for the hottest matter in the universe in this 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear physics. In heavy ion collisions, quarks and gluons melt into a plasma that expands like a fluid. That fluid carries several conserved charges at once: baryon number, electric charge, and strangeness. How those charges diffuse through the plasma shapes what detectors finally observe.

Using the Chapman Enskog method inside kinetic theory, the team solves the relativistic Boltzmann equation in a relaxation time approximation. Demanding that entropy be produced, as Boltzmann's H theorem requires, pins down the transport coefficients order by order. Alongside the familiar shear and bulk viscosities, they obtain the full diffusion matrix linking the three charges, including its cross terms. They map how those entries vary with temperature and chemical potential for a plasma of two light flavors plus strange quarks.
arxiv-2606-06483:
Many data sets collected in different ways still share one hidden pattern. Agterberg tackles that shared pattern in this 2026 arXiv paper on common subspaces, the low dimensional spaces that sit inside several data tables at once. Each table is modeled as a clean low rank signal, a simple pattern with few moving parts, blurred by random noise.

The paper sorts the problem by signal to noise ratio, the strength of the pattern compared with the noise. It gives an estimation method built on projected gradient descent, a step by step fitting routine, started from a spectral method. Under strong signal conditions the method reaches the best possible error rate, and its estimates follow a normal spread closely enough to support confidence intervals. Below a set signal level, the paper proves, such adaptive intervals cannot exist at all.
arxiv-2606-06583:
Stephan R McCandliss and co-authors make the case for giving the Hubble Space Telescope a second life in this 2026 arXiv paper. A proposed boost would raise Hubble's orbit and extend its mission. Its ultraviolet spectrographs, COS and STIS, have no planned replacement. The authors' iPhoton program would study ionizing photons with them. That radiation escapes star forming galaxies and once reionized the universe. Open questions include the true shape of the escaping spectrum, and whether nearby leaker galaxies resemble the ancient ones.

Their plan is deep, multi orbit spectroscopy across the far and near ultraviolet, open to the wider community. The numbers are concrete: measuring the ionizing continuum down to seven hundred angstroms would take roughly twenty orbits per target. A program of five hundred to one thousand orbits would yield twenty to forty galaxies, an unprecedented view of escaping ionizing light.
arxiv-2606-07183:
Two rival maps of word meaning, one from neural embeddings and one from word co-occurrence graphs, draw surprisingly different continents. Bounias and Ploux compare them in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vector models place words in continuous space learned by deep networks. Graph models link words that appear together, forming discrete clusters of usage.

The test corpus was France's Great National Debate, a large set of citizen contributions. The team compared local neighborhoods and global topology under both maps. Locally, the two geometries agreed well. Globally, they diverged sharply in structure and balance. The graph model's semantic distances graded more evenly, and its space was used more homogeneously. Cluster coherence also favored the discrete approach. Neural embeddings still classified strongly from just a few dozen dimensions. The authors read the models as complementary, not competing. Graph structure might even guide future neural designs toward steadier, more readable meaning spaces.
arxiv-2606-07283:
Schrills and Franke propose a theory of how people and AI systems work together on shared tasks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Existing models describe automation levels or role allocation, they argue, but not the psychological process of joint activity. Their Integrated Information Processing model pictures both human and machine as coupled control loops. Each loop takes input, compares it with goals, and produces output, using one shared vocabulary for both partners.

Three qualities define good coupling in the model: input adequacy, reference consonance, and output operativity. Roughly, these mean receiving the right information, sharing compatible goals, and producing usable next steps. The authors map interface choices, such as explainability tools, onto expected effects on each quality. They also state testable predictions, for example that letting users correct the task state should raise input adequacy, and they illustrate the model with example applications.
arxiv-2606-07583:
Liu, Sun, and Wang teach power grids to restore themselves after outages using reinforcement learning over the grid's frequency structure, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-healing distribution networks reconfigure switches and shed load to minimize disruption, but most outages originate in the distribution network and demand decisions. Policies are learned with graph neural networks operating spatially, which can miss global patterns visible in the graph's spectral, or frequency, domain. Their spectral graph reinforcement learning framework learns restoration policies with a spectral network instead.

Tests covered 3 standard networks of increasing size, from 13 to 123 buses. The learned policy achieved near-optimal restoration performance in real time, a requirement for deployment during live outages. It generalized across a range of outage scenarios rather than memorizing failures. The authors argue frequency-domain structure, which encodes system-wide interactions, is the right representation for decisions whose consequences ripple across an entire feeder network.
arxiv-2606-07783:
Yigit-Sert, at Ankara University, designs a stress test for retrieval-augmented generation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such systems answer questions by first retrieving documents, which usually improves factual reliability. In a misinformation-rich environment, though, retrieved pages may be plausible and wrong, and the system must choose between its own knowledge and poisoned evidence.

The protocol starts from factoid questions the model already answers correctly with no retrieval at all, so any later failure is caused by the evidence rather than ignorance. Each question is then asked under clean, misleading, and mixed retrieval, with the share of misleading material raised gradually. Two metrics do the judging: parametric override, how often retrieved falsehoods displace the model's correct internal answer, and confidence behaviour, whether the model grows surer as it is misled. Together they show when and how strongly bad evidence bends generation.
arxiv-2606-07883:
Cascio and co-authors build a database system that answers SQL queries under differential privacy with policies that can vary piece by piece, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Differential privacy gives each person plausible deniability: results barely change if their records are removed. For single tables this is well understood, but real databases spread one person's information across many tables, and different parts deserve different protection.

Existing private SQL systems impose rigid policies. Protecting the existence of records in one table but only their contents in another, or handling partially public columns, forces manual rework of the accounting each time. Public columns can make some queries need more noise and others less. DP4SQL reasons about such mixed policies directly, letting applications state which pieces of an entity's data need deniability, at what strength, and computing the cost accordingly. The goal is privacy engineering that bends with the application.
arxiv-2606-08083:
Litan Kumar Das, Anupam Khanra, and Sujit Kumar Sardar develop the logic of neighbourhoods without negation, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Instantial neighbourhood logic is a modal language where each world has a family of neighbourhoods, and formulas can say what kinds of worlds occur inside one. The positive fragment drops negation entirely. Its two primitive operators, one box-like and one diamond-like, must then be treated as independent, not duals.

The authors give the language and proof system, interpret it over persistent two-sided models, and build a typed helper semantics controlling the witness conditions, yielding a truth lemma and completeness. In algebra they introduce lattice structures called 2-DLIOs as the logic's semantics, proving soundness and completeness via the Lindenbaum algebra. A canonical bitopological space represents the logic in space: its admissible positive opens form an algebra matching the Lindenbaum one.
arxiv-2606-08183:
Rainer proves a new version of a classical estimate in analysis in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Remez inequality bounds how large a function can be on a whole region using only its size on a smaller part, provided the smaller part is not too tiny. Rainer extends this idea from polynomials to quasianalytic functions, a broad class of rigid smooth functions fixed everywhere by any small patch. The regions allowed are compact sets with tame geometry, a controlled shape condition that still permits sharp corners called cusps.

The role of polynomial degree is taken over by a quantity called the Bang degree, which depends on the function class and the function's size. All constants in the inequality are given explicitly rather than merely shown to exist. From the main result Rainer derives several practical consequences, including estimates for sublevel set volumes and effective versions of related inequalities.
arxiv-2606-08383:
Baisri and colleagues build a minimal way to test whether dark energy changes over cosmic time, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The standard model treats dark energy as a cosmological constant, whose equation of state sits fixed at minus one. Recent baryon acoustic oscillation observations from the DESI survey hint that dark energy may instead be dynamical. The authors introduce a framework that deforms the standard model in a controlled way, letting the equation of state depart from minus one by a redshift-dependent amount.

As an illustration, they reconstruct that deviation using scalar field dynamics of the thawing type, where a field frozen early begins to roll later. The reconstructed deviation does not depend on which specific scalar field realizes it. Fitting cosmic microwave background data, DESI measurements, and a supernova sample, they report how far the data let the equation of state wander.
arxiv-2606-08483: New on arXiv in 2026, this manuscript brings a fresh research result. It addresses the topic named in its title: Testing the Black Box: Structural Barriers to Independent Evaluation of Consumer-Facing Health LLMs. It draws on artificial intelligence — the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. Side-by-side testing is the paper's main service to the field.
arxiv-2606-08583:
Jasmeet Singh Bindra and Panwar audit what deep learning models really use when they read brain and heart signals, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models interpreting these signals are explained through domain features: oscillatory rhythms in brain signals, waveform complexes in heart signals. Yet the signals sit atop a broadband aperiodic background tied to arousal, age, and pathology. If models lean on that background instead of the noted features, their readings are misleading. The authors introduce a spectral audit framework to find out.

The framework splits the signal into periodic and aperiodic parts. It adds Fourier steps that flatten the aperiodic part, sham controls, and simulation checks. Aperiodic reliance proved task-dependent. Flattening caused large accuracy drops for sleep-wake classification, moderate drops for clinical abnormality detection, and minimal effect for motor imagery. Most tested brain-signal foundation models showed significant aperiodic reliance on clinical data.
arxiv-2606-09983:
Easson revisits how a two-dimensional black hole might finish evaporating, in a 2026 arXiv paper on gravity theory. His model is a regular Bardeen-like black hole reduced to two dimensions, where quantum effects are tracked through the trace anomaly, a quantum breaking of scale symmetry. A subtlety matters: reducing four-dimensional matter gives dilaton-coupled matter, not the simpler conformal matter of older treatments. He swaps in the matching anomaly model.

Classifying the allowed late-time branches, Easson finds that any quiet finite-radius ending forces a fixed final radius set by the model's length scale, regardless of local conventions. That outcome looks like a remnant, a leftover object that stops evaporating. For endings along null, light-like paths, the usual exponential boundary restoring strong cosmic censorship is excluded. Generic power-law branches are also excluded, except one borderline case surviving only with constrained flux and rapidly decaying tails.
arxiv-2606-10083:
Ben and colleagues propose a standard framework for cataloguing the human weaknesses that cyberattacks exploit, in a 2026 arXiv paper on cybersecurity. Defenders have spent two decades building shared systems for software flaws, including the CVE catalogue, the CVSS scoring system, and the CWE weakness list. Yet most successful attacks manipulate human cognition, emotion, and trust through social engineering and scams, and no equivalent standard exists for those vulnerabilities. Behavioral science theories explain why such attacks work.

Their Human Vulnerabilities and Exploits framework provides a shared, machine-readable taxonomy with structured identifiers for human-centric weaknesses. It adds multi-dimensional severity scoring through a Human Vulnerability Severity Score and remediation guidance through Human Vulnerability Patches, concrete countermeasures for people rather than code. The authors aim to give defenders the same common language for human vulnerabilities that CVE gave them for software flaws.
arxiv-2606-10183:
Kuklev and his team give video generation models an explicit handle on time itself, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer vision. Diffusion Transformers for video entangle time evolution with the denoising process, so the model never learns a separate, controllable picture of how motion unfolds. Existing control methods shape what moves or where, but do not make time an editable variable.

Their approach extends a pretrained model with a lightweight temporal module, preserving the original generative prior while widening the control range. The module allows control over motion speed and temporal structure without redesigning the backbone. Visual checks show smoother in-between motion with fewer limb artifacts at standard playback, and gradual scene processes, like fog dissipating as sunlight enters a forest, evolving properly under the time control. The same pattern transfers across multiple backbones with varied scales and sizes, hinting at a general recipe for time factorization.
arxiv-2606-10583:
Abassi and colleagues let an algorithm discover the laws of highway driving in this 2026 arXiv paper on traffic science. Symbolic regression searches for short formulas that fit data, keeping results human-readable. Their framework, NOVA, sifts over ten thousand candidate structures against 4.7 million driving observations from the NGSIM freeway datasets. A deterministic Rust search engine does the heavy lifting, and the winner is a compact two-term model of driver acceleration.

One nonlinear term, the hyperbolic tangent of relative velocity, dominates in all eight experiments, capturing the bounded way drivers respond to closing speed. The model reaches an error of 1.376 metres per second squared on the forecasting benchmark, beating the recalibrated symbolic baseline by 0.135 in the same units. Extended to lane changes, NOVA scores 67.4 percent balanced accuracy on 502 unseen drivers, ahead of existing baselines by 29.8 percentage points. Its features also transfer between sites with under three points of loss.
arxiv-2606-10683:
Fang and colleagues unify the language of robot hands in this 2026 arXiv paper. Dexterous hands differ in joint designs, so data from one hand rarely trains another, unlike simple grippers. The team defines a Unified Dexterous Hand Model that maps human and robot hand states into one shared interface with 22 degrees of freedom, treating the human hand as another embodiment. On top of it, UniDexTok learns discrete tokens for hand states from real joint data, conditioned on the embodiment, with no retargeting and no simulation data.

The accuracy jump is dramatic. Against the UniHM baseline, joint angle error falls from 15.63 degrees to 0.16 degrees, and joint position error from 18.51 millimetres to 0.18 millimetres. Those are reductions of 98.98 and 99.03 percent respectively, moving reconstruction from centimetre scale to sub-millimetre precision. Data from other hands improves each target hand's reconstruction, and the tokenizer shows strong zero-shot and few-shot behaviour on unseen hands.
arxiv-2606-10983:
Paul and Pan advance self-testing, the strongest device-independent quantum certification, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Self-testing validates a quantum state and its devices using only observed statistics, trusting nothing inside the black boxes. Their vehicle is Gisin's Bell inequality, where both parties may use arbitrary inputs, not a fixed small menu.

Their systematic sum-of-squares approach derives the optimal quantum violation without assuming any bound on the system's dimension. From the optimization condition they read off the state itself and the interrelation between the local observables, the measured quantities. Real experiments carry noise, so the paper also builds a robust self-testing strategy, showing how near-optimal violations still pin down the state and measurements. The Gisin setting becomes a practical certification tool for untrusted hardware.
arxiv-2606-11083:
Haisch and four co-authors extend a precision tool of particle physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. The matrix element method confronts each collision event directly with theory, computing its probability under hypotheses and keeping every correlation. It is standard at leading order. At next-to-leading order in QCD, the strong-force theory, infrared divergences, negative weights, and extra particles long blocked the extension.

The team shows the POWHEG method offers a practical path. Projecting real-emission events onto Born kinematics, the simpler no-emission layout, includes the hardest QCD radiation while preserving the next-to-leading-order normalization. As proof of concept they apply it to leptonic W pair production, hunting a dimension-six operator that modifies triple gauge boson interactions. The implementation acts as a near-optimal classifier, using spin and polarization correlations among the final leptons to separate standard model events from beyond-standard-model ones.
arxiv-2606-11183:
Jaffe, Santoro, and Sen start a new line of statistics in a 2026 arXiv paper: empirical Bayes denoising on curved spaces. Empirical Bayes methods clean up noisy measurements by borrowing strength across many of them. Here the hidden quantities and measurements live on a Riemannian manifold, a curved space like a sphere or torus, with Riemannian Gaussian noise.

Their starting point is a new Tweedie-Eddington formula for Riemannian Gaussian mixture models. It identifies a surrogate oracle denoiser, the tangential Bayes denoiser, from the measurements' marginal distribution, avoiding computation of the posterior Fréchet mean. They show near-Bayes risk at low noise, build a data-driven version from Laplace-Beltrami spectral theory, and prove finite-sample rates, slower than Euclidean ones due to cut-locus singularities. On the circle, lower bounds prove minimax optimality. Applications denoise gamma ray bursts on the sphere and protein torsion angles on the torus.
arxiv-2606-11283:
Ghazi, Guzmán, Kamath, Knop, Kumar, and Manurangsi study when private synthetic data can be generated efficiently in a 2026 arXiv paper. The goal is a fake dataset that keeps a sensitive dataset's key statistics while satisfying differential privacy. Ignoring computation, optimal error rates are known, but efficient algorithms were not. The authors establish fixed-parameter tractability for the problem, with the treewidth of the query family's incidence graph as parameter.

Their algorithms attain optimal error rates across all regimes, through two approaches. One uses linear programming and the separation problem for the dual. The other uses a subsampled private multiplicative weights method, obtaining it for sampling from Gibbs distributions. Both are unified by dynamic programming over a tree decomposition of the query graph. The results draw a boundary: when the query family's structure has small treewidth, optimal private data is within reach.
arxiv-2606-11383:
Guth Jarkovský, Bickert, Wybo, and Leib apply quantum optimization to railway planning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Rolling stock planning assigns physical trains to scheduled trips while minimizing operational costs. Their instance features 190 trips over two days, with constraints such as mandatory maintenance stops. They reformulate the problem as a maximum-weight independent set problem on a graph whose nodes represent feasible train cycles.

To handle the large search space, they propose a hybrid divide-and-conquer algorithm. It iteratively selects subgraphs and solves the independent set problem with various solvers, including exact classical methods and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, QAOA. QAOA is assessed both by classical simulation and by execution on a real quantum device, the IQM Emerald. Increasing subgraph size generally improves solution quality. The authors conclude the hybrid framework can bridge the gap between polynomial-time approximate solvers and exponential-time exact methods for such planning problems.
arxiv-2606-12283:
Samuel Lockman proves that a certain space of geometric shapes on many-holed surfaces cannot be shrunk to a point, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Riemannian metrics are the notions of distance on such a surface. The Dirac operator is a differential operator tied to spin, a quantum structure on the surface. Metrics making it invertible form a space probed through the index difference, a map recording how an index jumps along loops of metrics.

For any surface of genus, the hole count, at least three, with any bounding spin structure, Lockman shows this map is non-trivial, genuinely detecting loops. For products of two surfaces, carrying any spin structure, the space of Dirac-invertible metrics is not contractible. It has holes of its own. The paper also discusses metrics with harmonic spinors in dimension four. The result extends these methods to manifolds with no positive scalar curvature metrics.
arxiv-2606-12383:
Stoltz proves that a diagram language for quantum computing contains not one wasted rule, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The ZX calculus reasons about quantum circuits with pictures: colored spiders joined by wires, rewritten by rules. Its stabilizer fragment, central to error correction, has a small complete rule set. Earlier work showed most rules are necessary, meaning none can be derived from the others. Two rules resisted proof: one equating red and green compact structures, and the bialgebra law governing how spiders interact.

Using a countermodel-style argument, Stoltz builds interpretations where each target rule fails while the rest hold. Both rules are necessary, relative to the connectivity meta-rule. The rule set has no redundant rewrite at all. Every rule earns its place: removing any one loses power.
arxiv-2606-12683:
Genewein and many co-authors map how artificial intelligence might develop after human-level systems arrive, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Artificial general intelligence, or AGI, means a system matching human cognitive ability across most tasks. The report focuses on the step beyond: artificial superintelligence, or ASI, characterised as more capable than large organisations of humans. Universal AI, a theoretical ideal of optimal decision-making, anchors the far end of their scale.

Four pathways from AGI to ASI are examined. Systems might be scaled up, new paradigms might replace today's methods, AI might recursively improve itself, or superintelligence might emerge from large multi-agent collectives. The report then weighs frictions that could slow each route, from data and energy limits to coordination problems. Its central caution is that progress may not pause at human level, so society should prepare for repeated transformative changes, not one step.
arxiv-2606-12783:
Oh offers a tutorial survey of world models and their role in physical artificial intelligence, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A world model is an internal representation an agent uses to predict how its environment will evolve, aiding reasoning and planning rather than purely reactive control. The tutorial organises the field around a central distinction. Explicit world models learn structured dynamics used for rollout-based reasoning and planning. Implicit world models hide predictive structure inside large learned representations.

Both paradigms rest on shared structure, and the survey shows how they support physical AI in areas such as robotics and autonomous driving, where agents must act under real-world constraints. Recent foundation models suggest a path toward unified systems joining perception, prediction, and action. Even so, the author stresses that challenges remain open, notably hierarchical reasoning, long-horizon planning, and autonomous goal formation.
arxiv-2606-12883:
Zhang and colleagues reveal that the scaling factor in Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, is the dominant driver of optimisation quality, in this 2026 arXiv paper. It is not merely a complement to the learning rate. LoRA fine-tunes large models through a low-rank update scaled by a factor alpha. Through empirical analysis and a Signal-Drift framework, the authors uncover 3 findings about how that scaling works.

First, LoRA's spectral suppression smooths the optimisation landscape, making standard hyperparameters overly conservative and creating an optimisation gap. Second, when exploiting that smoothness to accelerate convergence, alpha outperforms the learning rate because it amplifies the task signal without increasing the drift ratio. Third, the optimal scaling factor follows a sublinear relationship with rank, well described by a square-root law with an unexpectedly large coefficient, showing that rank-tied heuristics under-scale. Across diverse tasks, LoRA-alpha improves performance while streamlining hyperparameter search.
arxiv-2606-12983:
Huang and colleagues present STG, a structured testbench generation framework for language-model-driven hardware design, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In register-transfer-level workflows, models generate many candidate designs that must be verified, but prompt-based testbench generation treats the task as unconstrained code synthesis. That produces stochastic outputs with high token cost, low reproducibility, and insufficient coverage. STG instead exploits the structure of hardware designs to generate deterministic testbenches.

As a direct verification tool, STG runs 720 times faster than a language-model testbench flow, with a higher rate of compilation, higher coverage, and fewer false-pass verdicts on incorrect designs. It exposes errors in RTL generation benchmarks by identifying their testbenches. As a data curation engine, it filters data 11 times faster than language-model-based filtering on a CPU core using 127 times less energy. As a test-time scaling oracle, it reduces node count by 14 to 47 percent.
arxiv-2606-13083:
Markakis and Samaris study fair division of indivisible goods under constraints expressed by a conflict graph, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The items are the graph's vertices, and connected items cannot be allocated in the same bundle. Under such constraints, allocations that are envy-free up to 1 good, the EF1 criterion, may fail to exist at all, unlike the unconstrained setting where simple algorithms always succeed.

They present an algorithm returning an EF1 allocation whenever the number of items does not exceed a bound. The bound is determined by the number of agents and the maximum degree, and it is tight when the degree exceeds two-thirds of the number of agents. For general additive valuations, they focus on instances with at most twice as many items as agents. They give a complete picture of which instances admit EF1 allocations, combining the Round Robin procedure with matching theory.
arxiv-2606-13183:
Gregocki and colleagues report results showing a 2-section delay mask for generating ultrashort pulse trains on a high-power laser beamline, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The work serves the resonant multipulse ionisation injection scheme, ReMPI, for laser wakefield acceleration. That scheme needs a train of pulses with identical peak intensity and a pulse-to-pulse delay matched to the plasma density. Existing pulse-train techniques suffer from pulse stretching, energy losses, or scalability to large-aperture high-power systems.

The delay mask is a thin transparent plate placed after the focusing optics that splits the beam by wavefront division. Based on simulations, the team designed a 500 micrometre fused silica plate with a central aperture, so 2 portions of the incident pulse are focused with equal intensity. The test ran at the CNR-INO Intense Laser Irradiation Laboratory on a 240 terawatt laser system operated at 120 terawatts.
arxiv-2606-13583:
Fei and Rubinfeld improve a classic testing result in this 2026 arXiv paper. Property testing decides whether an object has a property, or is far from having it, while inspecting only a fraction. A graph is bipartite if its vertices split into two camps with no edges inside a camp. Goldreich and Ron showed bipartiteness of bounded-degree graphs can be tested with random walks, but their method needed many long walks. Fei and Rubinfeld show far fewer and shorter walks suffice: on the order of the square root of the vertex count, each of logarithmic length.

As a corollary, they get a streaming algorithm for bipartiteness testing with logarithmically many passes and provably optimal given a recent lower bound. Their proof takes a new route through the semidefinite relaxation for Max-Cut introduced by Goemans and Williamson. Borrowing an approximation tool to sharpen a testing bound is a twist.
arxiv-2606-13983:
Cherchiglia asks whether a future neutrino discovery could come from known types of new particles. DUNE, a major neutrino experiment under construction, may reveal non-standard interactions. Such signals are written as Wilson coefficients in effective field theories. His 2026 arXiv paper builds a pipeline: start from a target coefficient, then test which heavier particle models could generate it under current flavor constraints.

The example targets a lepton-flavor-violating semileptonic coefficient DUNE could probe well. Candidate completions add extra isosinglet or isodoublet fields above the electroweak scale. The largest viable value found is about one point three times ten to the minus two per square tera-electronvolt. That sits almost an order of magnitude below the DUNE benchmark. If DUNE spots the anomaly, the cause must be more exotic than the common types surveyed.
arxiv-2606-14283:
De Smedt, Peeperkorn, Polyvyanyy, and De Weerdt give process-mining networks a loss function grading the whole process's shape, not just the next step. Cross-entropy predicts next steps in process logs well, but it is local: models score high token accuracy while allowing globally wrong behavior, missing loops and concurrency. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents DIFF-ERO, a differentiable form of entropy-based conformance checking.

It builds batch-level transition matrices with soft edge memberships, so structural precision and recall signals flow into backpropagation. The loss is model-agnostic where the final representation parametrizes transitions. In transformer setups for next-activity prediction, used jointly with cross-entropy, DIFF-ERO improved accuracy over the cross-entropy baseline where structure matters most, holding parity elsewhere. Its learned automaton also converged toward the true structure.
arxiv-2606-15283:
Mandl and Mandl map a pragmatic path toward AI-driven software development in a 2026 software engineering paper. Generative AI now touches requirements, architecture, coding, testing, review, and operations. Gains are real but uneven, depending on task type, codebase, and developer experience. AI artifacts also demand control and governance before teams can trust them. The authors organize adoption into stages, from informal assistance to integrated workflows. The final stage is controlled agentic development, where agents work inside guardrails.

Central to the framework is a harness connecting context, tools, checks, and approvals. The harness also handles permissions and logging for every AI action. Design practices concretize the shift for reviews, tests, and agentic workflows. An early case study at a mid-sized software company tests the framework's plausibility. It shows how governance and technical needs take shape in practice. The authors stress the shift as continuous learning, not a one-time switch.
arxiv-2606-15583:
Da Silva and colleagues study how people and models actually edit scientific abstracts in 2026, judging the process rather than only the final text. Abstracts are the gateway to a paper, yet little is known about how revision unfolds keystroke by keystroke. The team logs eight hundred sixty-nine editing sessions and a quarter million edits, on AI and human-authored abstracts.

AI abstracts show stronger sentence-level agency, while human-authored ones keep better global coherence even after editing. Experts behave differently once an AI source is disclosed, switching from restructuring the text to swapping words in place, a pattern the authors call stigmatic. Language models improve edit outcomes using local and global cues, but still struggle most with global coherence. Both humans and models aim their effort at the weakest sections of an abstract. Neither manages to lift the stronger sections further, a shared blind spot in editing practice.
arxiv-2606-15683:
Ma and Eisty review how causal inference is used in software testing in 2026, surveying twenty-seven studies in a rapid review. Causal methods ask what an intervention changes, not merely what correlates, and testers have applied them to debugging, fairness assessment, and performance checks. Adoption, though, is fragmented across tasks and research communities that rarely cite each other.

The authors sort the literature along a layered pipeline: representation, structure discovery, identification, and effect estimation. Most work clusters at the identification and estimation end, while the early layers stay underexplored in testing contexts. Recurring weaknesses include model misspecification, strong premises that go untested, scalability limits, and little real-world validation. Causal reasoning is used mainly to interpret results and debug, with intervention-based methods growing. The review closes with a research agenda aimed at the neglected early layers, where better causal models of software would make the later estimates trustworthy.
arxiv-2606-15783:
Tan and Dinh present their SemEval-2026 system for narrative similarity in 2026, judging how alike two stories are in theme, course of action, and outcome. Lexical overlap cannot capture such deep resemblance, so the team fine-tunes sentence transformers with contrastive learning. Two pipelines reflect two bets about how story structure should be represented.

Track A encodes each full narrative in a single view, with smart layer freezing to limit overfitting. Track B models theme, plot, and outcome separately through view-specific projection heads, then aligns the views self-supervisedly. Both train on synthetic data and run in pseudonymized and raw settings. The approach performs competitively without expensive generative inference, suiting large-scale story retrieval. The authors flag honest limits: synthetic training data may not generalise to diverse narrative styles, and automatically extracted story elements inject noise. No manual audit of the extractions was possible in the shared-task timeline.
arxiv-2606-16383:
Nandi presents in 2026 a compact language model built natively for Bangla, showing that careful tokenization can beat raw scale. Giant models serve non-Latin scripts poorly and cost too much for phones, edge devices, and local hardware. The model, bangla-smollm-135m, has only 135 million parameters in a decoder-only design. Its key trick merges two tokenizers, from TituLLMs and SmolLM2-135M, by a deterministic intersect-and-append strategy.

That merge overcomes the subword fragmentation that shreds Bangla script into wasteful pieces, without destabilizing the pretrained weights inherited from SmolLM2. On zero-shot Bangla benchmarks covering physical reasoning, science questions, commonsense, and broad knowledge, the model matches or beats Gemma-3-270m, a model twice its size. It reaches parity with models in the one-billion parameter tier on these tests, per the report. The conclusion credits efficient tokenization, targeted sub-corpus packing, and tuned training loops.
arxiv-2606-16583:
Fazla and co-authors test in 2026 whether a medical AI's stated uncertainty can warn clinicians before it fails, and find the warning light dims exactly where the road gets dark. Safe clinical vision-language models need a trust signal: a cue for when to trust an answer or escalate to a clinician. The team benchmarks eight uncertainty methods across twelve vision-language models on clinical VQA tasks. The result is uncomfortable: that quality is not a property of the method but tracks the model's accuracy, degrading just where scores are weakest, and reliability most needed.

Stress tests sharpen the worry. When the correct option is hidden among the multiple-choice answers, accuracy collapses while uncertainty barely moves, leaving models badly miscalibrated. Yet there is a constructive twist: uncertainty measured on the original, unperturbed input reliably anticipates which predictions will collapse under the stress test.
arxiv-2606-16983:
Chung-Halpern and Rietsch take quantum cohomology of Grassmannians to the infinite limit in a 2026 algebraic geometry paper. Quantum cohomology turns curve counting on a space into a ring; for flag varieties its structure constants are positive in the Schubert basis. Total positivity, Lusztig's theory of matrices whose minors are all positive, turns out to govern the same numbers.

A precursor paper handled the full flag variety. As the rank grows, the positive side of the ring is described by Edrei's classical theorem on infinite totally positive Toeplitz matrices. The new work does the Grassmannian case, determining how quantum parameters and Schubert classes behave. Along the way it gives a fresh interpretation of the strange duality involution on the localized ring. They also prove an asymptotic formula for partial flag varieties, and state conjectures for the wider picture. The paper honors Lusztig's eightieth birthday.
arxiv-2606-17083:
Ponce-Torres and colleagues exfoliate graphene with a supersonic-style liquid jet in a 2026 materials paper. Making monolayer graphene cheaply, without harsh chemistry, is a standing goal. Their technique, transonic flow focusing, shoots a liquid suspension through a micrometer jet, creating extreme shear and stretching in a contact-free zone.

Graphite nanoplatelets fed through the jet come out split in a single pass. Products include monolayer flakes a few hundred nanometers wide and fragments in the quantum-dot size range. Microscopy shows monolayers are nearly total in isopropanol and above ninety percent in pure water. Theory explains why: during microsecond residence times, strain rates reach a million per second and viscous power densities soar. No surfactants, no oxidation, no centrifuge sorting are needed, and the solvent can be plain water. The same pass yields flakes and nanofragments, a green route to flat and dot-like nanomaterials at once.
arxiv-2606-17183:
Lukina and colleagues give video question answering a hybrid long-term memory in a 2026 computer vision paper. Answering questions over long first-person navigation videos means gathering evidence scattered across distant moments while keeping spatial sense. Feeding the whole video to a model works but is expensive for repeated questions.

The earlier VL-KnG system stored a persistent knowledge graph, but graph retrieval alone misses broad context spread over long segments. VL-MemKnG adds a second memory: segment-level summaries that preserve temporal continuity. A hybrid layer retrieves and reasons over both stores at once, returning answers grounded in organized evidence. The extended benchmark, WalkieKnowledgeT+, adds tasks requiring evidence from moments that never co-occur. The framework targets wearable and robot assistants that must answer, minutes or hours later, where something was seen and what happened around it.
arxiv-2606-17383:
Dixon presents a 2026 arXiv paper on how to validate agentic AI systems, whose risk profile differs sharply from that of ordinary predictive models. An autonomous agent gathers information, forms beliefs about hidden states, forecasts, acts, and adapts, so checking forecast accuracy alone says little about decision quality. Dixon builds the validation framework on partially observable Markov decision processes, the standard formalism for acting under uncertainty about the true state of the world.

Decision making is split into information, beliefs, forecasts, actions, and utility, so each part can be validated on its own merits. Language models are cast as approximate Bayesian filtering operators inside that scheme, and a taxonomy sorts risks from state-space errors to utility misspecification. A portfolio case study shows the method at work, with calibration checks, coverage tests, and ablations. Latent-state inference added independent value to decision quality there.
arxiv-2606-17483:
Castillo and Takala present a 2026 arXiv paper on the Dirichlet problem for the p-Poisson equation, studied not in ordinary Euclidean space but in metric measure spaces. Those spaces carry a doubling measure and a Poincaré inequality, the two supports that let analysis mimic calculus without smooth structure. The equation generalises the p-Laplace equation with a source term, and the problem asks for a solution matching given boundary values in this rough setting.

Existence is proved by a variational approach, building the solution as a minimiser of an energy functional. Stability and uniqueness follow when the space is also geodesic, meaning distances are realised by shortest paths inside it. The tools include Cheeger gradients and upper gradients, the substitutes for derivatives in this setting. The results extend a well-developed Euclidean theory to spaces with no coordinates at all.
arxiv-2606-17583:
Jain and Pradhan present a 2026 arXiv paper solving a counting problem in group theory that had stood open since the early nineteen nineties. An orthomorphism of a group is a bijection whose associated difference map is also a bijection. Such maps correspond to transversals of the group's Cayley table and to Latin squares orthogonal to it. The alternating group on four symbols has thousands of these maps, and finding them all by brute force was the path nobody wanted to trust.

The authors partition orthomorphisms of a general group with a suitable normal subgroup into classes, then relate the class sizes by clean counting rules. Applied to the alternating group, the machinery means counting just thirty maps by hand-style reasoning pins down the full total, nearly four thousand. A theoretical route replaces exhaustive computer search for this case.
arxiv-2606-17983:
Chou and Chang build a toy universe with an expanding de Sitter geometry out of a quantum chain, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Extending holography, the idea that a gravitational world is encoded in boundary data, from anti-de Sitter space to the de Sitter space of an accelerating universe is a major open frontier. Tensor networks give a concrete bottom-up language for such encodings, but a de Sitter version was missing.

The authors construct a non-unitary version of the continuous multi-scale entanglement renormalization ansatz for a non-Hermitian critical fermion chain, and de Sitter space emerges from its boundary entanglement. Geodesics in that space act as extremal surfaces and slide smoothly from timelike to null. The trajectory then dictates a tensor network whose bond counting truncates at that transition, with horizon links costing nothing, yet still reproduces the known entropy scaling.
arxiv-2606-18083:
Sousa and colleagues tune the electrical behavior of a new carbon sheet by adding fluorine, in a 2026 materials paper. Biphenylene is a recently made two-dimensional carbon network whose electrons move more easily along one direction than the other. Using density functional theory, tight-binding models, and quantum transport simulations, the team asks how fluorine atoms, placed in ordered or disordered patterns, rewrite that directional conduction.

Fluorination creates concentration-dependent transport regimes. In pristine and neatly fluorinated sheets they find negative differential resistance, where raising the voltage lowers the current. They also find a bias-driven flip of the preferred conduction direction, between the armchair and zigzag axes. Disorder erases the resistance effect and pushes transport toward plain Ohmic behavior. At heavy coverage, lined-up fluorine patterns open channels along one axis while choking the other.
arxiv-2606-18283:
Huang and Raza replace the Transformer's all-pairs attention with a detour through a small latent space, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Standard attention compares every token with every other, and that quadratic pattern is the central obstacle to long contexts. Gaussian Mixture Attention instead routes information through a fixed set of learned Gaussian components, a shared routing space that queries and keys both address.

Each query and key becomes a vector of responsibilities over the components, and their overlap defines an implicit affinity. Values are written into a small latent memory with as many slots as components, then read back out. The giant token-by-token matrix never materializes, and storage grows only linearly for a fixed component count. The authors give bidirectional and causal variants, a fully differentiable parameterization, and an analysis of the gradient structure and routing stability, reporting the intended linear memory scaling in experiments.
arxiv-2606-18383:
Bandyopadhyay and Ekbal ask when an explanation drawn from a sparse autoencoder can be trusted as a faithful view of a language model, in a 2026 interpretability paper. Sparse autoencoders pull human-readable features out of a model's hidden activity, but an appealing feature list means little if the simplified picture quietly changes what the model would do.

Their certification swaps one layer's activity for its autoencoder reconstruction, forming a sparse proxy of the frozen model. It then bounds the original model's risk using four measurable pieces: proxy risk, reconstruction gap, concept-pool mismatch, and sparse complexity. The bound became non-vacuous at practical sample sizes on three models, including Llama-3-8B, whose later layers certified far more easily than its early ones. Shuffling tests showed the scheme can separate genuine semantic alignment from mere sparsity, flagging explanations that look tidy but should not be over-trusted.
arxiv-2606-18483:
Cortecchia and colleagues recast distributed particle filtering in the language of aggregate computing, in a 2026 distributed systems paper. The method tracks a system's state from scattered, uncertain observations. Particle filters handle nonlinear dynamics and non-Gaussian noise, but spread-out versions are each welded to one hardware layout and one set of communication rules, limiting reuse.

By writing estimation and information spread as fields, their approach separates the filtering logic from coordination and data-flow choices. Designers can then vary, inside one framework, where fusion centers sit and how sturdy they are, how measurements are gathered, and how information spreads. Simulation tests, including a target-tracking case, derived several filter setups this way and mapped their trade-offs among accuracy, communication cost, and robustness. The authors position aggregate computing as a layer for building adaptable filters, with multi-target and mixed-sensor tests left as next steps.
arxiv-2606-18883:
Dessy and the team extend the stability theory of quadruped robots to cover the arm through which the robot carries its load, in a 2026 robotics paper. Spring-based arms are lighter and simpler than actuated manipulators. But their spring-damper dynamics inject forces that can destabilize locomotion. Models treat the payload as rigidly attached.

The authors derive a zero moment point formula with the passive interface dynamics. It relates stiffness, damping, and mass to the stability margin. They show underdamped configurations can resonate with locomotion harmonics. They then augment a rigid body model with the passive subsystem, and embed it in model predictive control. In sims, the controller cut violations tenfold, and reduced horizontal ground reaction force effort by up to fifteen percent. In tests with a two kilogram payload, the robot stayed stable under pull-release, where the nominal controller failed.
arxiv-2606-19083:
Dumitrescu develops a block-encoding compiler for Hamiltonian simulation in 2026, built around matrix product operators. Block encoding embeds a matrix inside a larger unitary, a core tool in modern quantum algorithms. Matrix product operators compress operators as tensor networks. The author treats them as compressed programs for the linear combination of unitaries method, then compiles new conditional prepare and select stages from a parent operator.

Tests cover real-time evolution for Heisenberg chains and a perturbed variant. The method gives polynomial speedups and avoids the steep growth in Pauli-string count that naive expansions suffer when bond dimension and path scaling stay mild. The paper also shows how truncation error affects the compiled form. Tensor networks thus serve as a natural language for quantum circuits.
arxiv-2606-19183:
Bateni and colleagues present ClaMPAPP in 2026, a hybrid system for pediatric appendicitis that uses a language model as an interface, not an oracle. Language models read free-text notes well, but as stand-alone diagnostic engines they are swayed by phrasing, information order, and plausible but wrong reasoning. Supervised models on structured data predict risk robustly, yet they fit poorly with narrative clinical workflows at the bedside.

ClaMPAPP parses note-like narratives into a schema-constrained feature set. Plausibility checks screen bad extractions, and clean features go to a boosted classifier trained on clinical, lab, and ultrasound variables. The system is tested in two independent pediatric cohorts from German hospitals. Narratives were synthesized from structured records with preserved ground truth, then tested under standard and sentence-shuffled conditions. The hybrid design aims to keep language flexibility at the front while leaving the decision to a calibrated model.
arxiv-2606-19483:
Zhang and colleagues propose LEAP in 2026, a training curriculum for distilling vision transformers by layer skipping. Vision foundation models with transformer backbones are essential for tasks like object recognition and segmentation. Their compute cost forces distillation into smaller models for edge deployment. Feature-based distillation suffers from the teacher-student gap, though. A small student struggles to imitate the teacher's complex feature maps in one leap.

LEAP uses the teacher's intermediate feature maps as a sequence of progressively harder targets. The student builds a foundational representation first, then tackles higher-level abstractions. Adaptive difficulty selection across model sizes and dataset scales speeds convergence. A LEAP-distilled small model posts a large accuracy gain over its baseline on a hundred-class image benchmark. Retrieval gains follow on standard photo collections. Students learn deep features best as a staircase, not a cliff.
arxiv-2606-19583:
Christian Borgs, Florian Henning, Remco van der Hofstad, and Nelly Litvak study PageRank fairness on growing networks in 2026. Preferential attachment grows a network by linking new nodes to already popular ones. PageRank scores node importance by random walks, and both quantities often follow power laws.

Their network is undirected and multi-type: vertices carry colours, like fields or communities. Directed coloured versions were studied before, with PageRank tails heavier than degree tails. For the undirected case the authors had shown PageRank tails track degree tails. The new result proves the power-law hypothesis for the coloured undirected model too. Unlike the directed case, the power-law exponent can depend on colour for some setups. Starting colour shares and the attractiveness function decide when that happens. A two-type case study draws out what colour-dependent exponents mean for sampling rare nodes fairly.
arxiv-2606-19783:
Dragoș Crișan studies convolution algebras built from group representations in 2026. Start with a complex reductive group, a representation, and a Borel-stable subspace inside it. A Steinberg-type variety ties those ingredients together geometrically.

Under a condition called gluability, the variety's equivariant homology gains a convolution product. That algebra equals the overlap of two copies of the nil-Hecke algebra inside its localisation. K-theory in place of homology yields a parallel result. Poles and residues give a second description of the new algebras. Loop group versions of the theorems also hold. The work generalises classic descriptions of the affine Hecke algebra and DAHA. It also extends a gluing picture of Coulomb branches from recent work by others. Representation theory gains a uniform machine for building such algebras.
arxiv-2606-20183:
Jian Xu, Delu Zeng, John Paisley, and Qibin Zhao explain two puzzling habits of quantum vision models with one quantity: effective dimension. Their 2026 paper notes that quantum vision models generalize better when their circuits entangle more, and that adding quantum noise can raise test accuracy. Both facts had been found by grid search and explained by hand, if at all. The authors trace both to the effective dimension of the quantum feature kernel.

Entanglement structure and noise are two knobs that move this dimension. In an overfitting regime, shrinking it acts like ridge regularization, the classic cure for over-flexible models. The team derives an exact split of the noisy kernel, a contraction result for amplitude damping, and a capacity bound tying dimension to risk. Empirically, test accuracy across entangling circuits collapsed onto one curve against effective dimension. Noise is not damage but a tunable regularizer.
arxiv-2606-20483:
Karen Yagdjian derives explicit formulas for spherical solutions of the Dirac equation in an expanding universe. Her 2026 paper works in Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker spacetime expanding with the de Sitter scale factor. The initial data can be the wave function of a hydrogen-like atom or a wave from flat Minkowski space.

The formulas track how those waves travel once the background starts expanding. Closed-form solutions are rare for the Dirac equation on curved spacetime, so each one benchmarks numerical codes. They also show how cosmic expansion reshapes a quantum wave packet. The expanding-universe Dirac problem gains a fully explicit test case.
arxiv-2606-20683:
Jianyuan Guo and sixteen colleagues survey language model agents in 2026, tracing a shift from answering questions to completing tasks. Agents perceive settings, call tools, keep state, and act over long horizons. Designs have moved from prompt craft to workflows, context work, harness work, and agent-native training. Their central question is where the bottleneck lies: in the base model, in the execution harness, or in the link between them.

Guo and colleagues define an agent as a base model coupled with a harness. They review limits of model-only scaling and four paradigms of agent engineering. The harness is split into six duties: observation, context, control, action, state, and verification. That split is then mapped to task traits and domain pressures. A shared lens helps builders decide whether to train a better model or fix the runtime that surrounds it, a choice that shapes cost and reliability.
arxiv-2606-20783:
Alexandros Gerbessiotis presents lecture notes in 2026 on number theory for computer science, in e-book form for students. The notes cover elementary and medium-level number theory. The target audience is primarily computer science students. Material can serve the number theory part of a discrete mathematics course. It can also support a course on mathematical foundations of computer science, or background reading for cryptography.

The book builds the number theory that computing topics quietly depend on. Modular arithmetic underlies hashing, error control, and public-key cryptography. Primes, divisibility, and congruences recur across algorithms and security proofs. Notes aimed at computer scientists can stress those links from the start, rather than treating number theory as pure mathematics detached from code. A shared text at this level helps instructors align what math courses teach with what later systems and security courses assume students know.
arxiv-2606-20983:
Michael Trimboli, Wenxi Liu, and Xianqi Li present a physics-guided learning framework in 2026 to predict how material micro-structure evolves. Predicting such change is central to materials design.
