A Communist New 4th Army division was trained by Russians at Falu.
cia-03009183: December 16, 1954: the daily intelligence bulletin went out as usual. Analysts tracked global developments for Washington's leaders. The quiet machinery of the Cold War. Tomorrow's readers will find it. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-03179283: January 28, 1960 opened with this intelligence bulletin. The daily summary reached the leadership's desks. Another Cold War morning. Time has kept the file intact. This file preserves that declassified paper. Kept for readers. Kept for readers.
cia-03192683: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/11/21, a CIA publication. The 1957 briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
cia-06052383: AWARD/CONTRACT, a CIA document. The contract file. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-06541083: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE WEEKLY REVIEW - CONGO, a CIA publication. The Congo review. This file preserves that declassified summary. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06769983: AFTER-ACTION REPORT <SANITIZED>, a CIA document. The redacted report. This file preserves that declassified paper. It awaits future readers. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive guards it with care.
cieza-travels-peru-markham-part-2-1883:
Part Two of Cieza de León's Travels, in Markham's translation of 1883, bears its own title: the Señorío de los Incas, the dominion of the Incas. Pedro Cieza de León had marched through Peru in the years after its conquest, from 1532 to 1550. Where Part One follows journeys and wars, this part steps back to describe the Inca state itself.

Cieza explains how the Incas ruled: their roads, storehouses, taxes in labor, worship, and laws. He had questioned men who remembered the empire whole, before the Spanish broke it. The result is the fullest early account of Inca institutions by a European witness. This volume is the natural companion to Part One, and just as prized.
crabbe-village-1783:
Crabbe's Village, issued in 1783 with The Newspaper beside it, was the poem that made his name. He wrote it as a direct reply to pretty, false pictures of country life in the verse of his day. Dr. Johnson himself helped polish the draft before it reached print, by the v1 account.

In place of singing shepherds, Crabbe shows poverty, grinding labor, sickness, and early death among the poor. The companion piece turns the same blunt eye on the press and its habits. Side by side, the two poems announced a new kind of poet, one who insisted on telling the truth.
dariot-breefe-introduction-1583:
Claude Dariot taught Europe to judge the stars, and Fabian Wither's 1583 English version made his Briefe Introduction the earliest astrology manual in English. Dariot, a French physician, wrote for learners who wanted method, not marvels. Elections, the choosing of lucky times, and nativities, the reading of birth charts, form the core.

Rules, tables, and worked examples guide the student step by step through a judgment. The book seeded the English astrological tradition that William Lilly would inherit a century later. Its plain Tudor English and homely cases show astrology as a working craft of the age, not a courtly game.
davidis-von-der-becke-mindani-experiment: Davidis von der Becke Mindani, Experimenta et meditationes, 1683. The experiments. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
dilthey-einleitung-1883:
Wilhelm Dilthey published his Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften in German in 1883. The title means an introduction to the human sciences. Dilthey argued that fields like history, law, and the study of culture need their own ground. They cannot just borrow the methods of physics or biology.

He drew a firm line between the natural sciences and the human sciences. Nature, he held, we explain from outside, while human life we understand from inside. That split shaped how later scholars defended history as its own kind of knowledge. The book became a founding charter for the human sciences. Standard English versions came much later.
donnelly-ragnarok-1883:
Ignatius Donnelly followed his Atlantis book with a tale of fire from the sky in 1883. Ragnarok: The Age of Fire and Gravel argues that a comet struck the earth in ages past. Donnelly was a Minnesota congressman with a hunger for vast, lost chapters of the past.

The comet, he says, scorched the world, dropped the gravel beds geologists puzzled over, and stamped myths of world fire on every land. He reads the Norse Ragnarok and like tales as garbled news of a real crash. Later writers from Velikovsky on took up his line. The book founded the modern school of comet doom.
europmc-pmc10000783:
Issa and colleagues survey the many types of adeno-associated virus, or AAV, used to carry new genes into the body, in a 2023 overview. Gene therapy aims to treat disease by fixing or replacing faulty genes. AAV carriers are a favored tool because they can reach many tissues and rarely cause disease themselves.

The paper walks through the main AAV types and what each does best. It covers the tissues they target, how long they act, and the hurdles that remain. Readers new to gene therapy get a clear guide to the carrier menu doctors choose from.
europmc-pmc10014083:
Bobrovitz and a large international team review how well past COVID infection protects against the Omicron variant, in a 2023 study. They also review hybrid immunity, the mix of protection from both infection and vaccination. The review looks at how strong that protection is and how long it lasts.

The authors pool past studies and use a method that tracks change over time. They focus on protection against Omicron infection and against severe disease. The results matter for vaccine timing and for public health planning, and the paper states its methods in careful detail.
europmc-pmc10133283:
Gao and colleagues test whether ChatGPT-written research abstracts can be told apart from real ones, in a 2023 study. They gathered abstracts from five leading medical journals and asked ChatGPT to write new ones on the same topics. The question was whether detectors and human experts could spot the fakes.

Blinded reviewers and detection tools each tried to sort real from generated text. The study reports how often each method was fooled. The results feed a wider debate on trust and honesty. They also bear on AI use in science writing.
europmc-pmc10373083:
Gu and Hübschmann built a software package in 2023 to tame long gene result lists. A common gene test returns the shared themes in a list of genes. The output can run to scores of terms with much repeat content. Past tools grouped the terms, but left repeats or uneven groups.

Their new method, called binary cut, splits a term map step by step. Gu tested it on fake and real data sets. Terms inside each group stayed close kin, while groups stayed apart. Meaning-based scores worked best with the method in their tests. The package, simplifyEnrichment, also draws charts and sums up each group. It is free through the Bioconductor store for the R language.
europmc-pmc10987683:
Wang, Gessler, Zhan, Gallagher, and Gao review a virus used to ferry genes into patients in this 2024 paper. Adeno-associated virus is a small virus that rarely causes illness. Rebuilt forms of it can carry a healthy gene into tissues and keep it active for years. Seven such gene therapies have won approval so far.

The review explains the virus's biology and how engineers tune it to hit chosen tissues. It surveys trials across eye, brain, metabolic, blood, muscle, and heart diseases, plus cancers. High doses bring risks, the authors stress. These include immune reactions, liver harm, and a clotting disorder of small vessels. Making enough virus is also a bottleneck. The paper closes with ways to blunt immune attacks and cut side effects.
europmc-pmc1247383:
Patz and a working group warned that land use change spreads infectious disease in 2004. Farming expansion, logging, roads, dams, and irrigation all reshape habitats. Mining, wetland loss, and city growth add pressure. Each change can spark outbreaks or shift steady infections.

Side effects include forest fragmentation, pollution, poverty, and migration. Together they ease disease emergence in clear chains. The group built a systems model linking land choices to disease. They also ranked diseases most tied to ecological damage. Patz offers policy steps that treat land and health as one problem.
europmc-pmc1247483:
Inoue and co-authors measured fluorinated compounds in mother and cord blood in 2004. PFOS and kin coat plastics, electronics, textiles, and leather goods. They had been found in human blood before. Rodent work hints they may disturb development through thyroid effects.

Fifteen mother and cord blood pairs were analyzed with precise methods. Detection limits reached 0.5 nanograms per milliliter for PFOS and PFOA. The method paired liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry and online extraction. Inoue focuses on pregnancy as a sensitive window. Measuring both sides of the placenta shows what reaches the fetus.
europmc-pmc1281283:
Oken and co-authors studied fish eating, mercury, and infant cognition in 2005. Fish carries mercury but also brain-building fatty acids. The cohort held 135 mother and infant pairs in Project Viva. Mothers averaged 1.2 fish servings weekly in mid-pregnancy.

Mean hair mercury was 0.55 parts per million at delivery. Ten percent of mothers topped 1.2 parts per million. Infants took a visual memory test at six months. Higher fish intake tied to higher infant scores. The link grew stronger after adjusting for hair mercury. Each extra weekly serving added 4.0 points to the score.
europmc-pmc1434783:
Curcumin, the yellow pigment in turmeric spice, may help prevent cancer, but its safety at high doses was untested. Lao and co-authors ran a dose trial in 2006 with healthy volunteers. Each person took one dose of a standard curcumin extract. Doses rose from 500 to 12,000 milligrams across groups.

Seven of 24 people had mild side effects, with no clear link to dose size. Blood tests found no curcumin at doses up to 8,000 milligrams. Trace amounts showed in two people at the top doses. Lao concludes that even large single doses are well borne, and backs longer trials for cancer prevention.
europmc-pmc1435883:
Stem cells from bone marrow hold promise for therapy, but labs must grow them first. Bonab and co-authors asked in 2006 whether long growth in a dish ages these cells. They kept mesenchymal stem cells, a marrow type that can form bone and fat, for about 118 days.

Growth slowed with each round of copying. Telomeres, the caps on DNA ends, shrank from 9.19 to 8.7 thousand base pairs. The power to change into other cell types faded after the sixth round. Bonab concludes the cells age from the start of culture. Teams should use them early, while their stem traits last.
europmc-pmc1550283:
Gene activity webs can reveal which genes drive body weight. Ghazalpour and co-authors built such a web in 2006 from liver data of crossed mice. They grouped co-active genes into modules, then tied modules to 22 body traits.

Some chromosome spots, dubbed module QTL, perturbed whole modules at once. For a weight-linked module, the team modeled which genes matter using both those spots and each gene's web centrality. Genes that were both central and under a spot's sway predicted weight best. Ghazalpour argues that joining genetics with network maps can pinpoint the genes that steer complex traits.
europmc-pmc1634883:
Cells under mild protein-folding stress choose survival over suicide, and the choice is timed. Rutkowski and co-authors explained how in 2006. Stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's folding workshop, triggers the unfolded protein response, which opens both rescue and death paths.

Mild stress switched on all sensors of the response. But the death-promoting messages and proteins are intrinsically short-lived, while folding helpers persist. So death signals fade as the cell adapts, and rescue wins. Rutkowski found the same pattern in a genetic case of such stress. Timing of decay, they argue, structures the verdict.
europmc-pmc1877083:
Hall, Crosier and colleagues built in 2007 zebrafish that glow in one branch of their immune system. Watching immune cells interact inside a living vertebrate had been near impossible. Zebrafish larvae are transparent, so labeled cells can be filmed in real time as inflammation unfolds.

The team took the control switch of the zebrafish lysozyme C gene, which is active in myeloid cells, and wired it to green and red fluorescent proteins. The glowing pattern in the engineered fish exactly matched the gene's natural activity. Sorting and co-staining showed the lit cells were a subset of macrophages, the large eater cells, and likely some granulocytes. In larvae the marked cells migrated toward inflammation sources and behaved like true myelomonocytic cells, giving researchers a live window on early immune responses.
europmc-pmc1885283:
Turck, Colot and co-authors showed in 2007 that a plant repressor protein homes in on one specific chemical mark on DNA packaging. The protein, TFL2/LHP1, silences many genes in Arabidopsis, including ones that time flowering and shape flowers. It was proposed to steady the Polycomb complex, which places a silencing mark called H3K27me3.

Mapping its binding on a chromosome-wide chip found hundreds of small domains, nearly all on genes in open, active chromatin regions. In test tubes the protein could grip two different marks, the classic heterochromatin mark and the Polycomb mark. Inside living plants, though, its binding matched almost exclusively the Polycomb mark, H3K27me3. Genes carrying that mark were the ones it sat on. The finding redefines the protein as a reader of the Polycomb system rather than of classic heterochromatin.
europmc-pmc2074083:
MAGEE and BARNES fed rats a chemical called dimethylnitrosamine in 1956 to test its long-term effects. Earlier work showed the compound, shortened to DMN, causes severe liver damage at doses near 25 milligrams per kilogram. That damage centred on the lobules of the liver and bled heavily. Similar plant alkaloids produced liver tumours with longer dosing. The team asked whether this simpler molecule would do the same.

Rats received DMN mixed into their diet over a long period, and a smaller rabbit experiment ran alongside. A very high share of rats developed malignant primary liver tumours. Many of those tumours had spread to other sites. No tumours appeared in the rabbits. In rats, no primary tumours arose in any organ other than the liver.
europmc-pmc2124983: A medical paper on epinephrin in the circulation and its relation to blood pressure. The adrenaline. This article preserves that physiology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2125483: A medical paper on changes in pigment epithelium cells and iris pigment cells of Rana pipiens. The frog's eye pigment. This article preserves that histology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2125783: A medical paper on the distribution in the human body of Spirochaeta icterohaemorrhagiae. The spirochete's spread. This article preserves that pathology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2128083: A medical paper on experimental syphilis in the rabbit, affections of the eyes. The rabbit eyes. This article preserves that venereology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2128183: A medical paper on migration of lymphocytes in plasma cultures of human lymph nodes. The wandering cells. This article preserves that immunology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128283: A medical paper on experimental syphilis in the rabbit, mucous membrane affections. The rabbit membranes. This article preserves that venereology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131083: A medical paper on the problem of the etiology of herpes zoster. The shingles cause. This article preserves that virology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2131183: A medical paper on experimental glomerulonephritis induced in rabbits with endotoxic principle. The rabbit kidneys. This article preserves that nephrology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131383: A medical paper on the role of carbohydrate haptens in bacterial anaphylaxis. The sugar triggers. This article preserves that immunology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2131483: A medical paper with biometry of calcium, phosphorus, cholesterol, and lipoid phosphorus. The body's minerals. This article preserves that biochemistry. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The text survives intact.
europmc-pmc2131583: A medical paper on reactions of rabbits to non-hemolytic streptococci, skin reactions. The rabbit skin. This article preserves that immunology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2140383: Another biology paper on the effect of temperature upon facet number in the bar-eyed mutant. The fly's eyes again. This article preserves that genetics. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place.
europmc-pmc2140583: A biology paper on valency rule and alleged Hofmeister series in the colloidal behavior of proteins. The protein salts. This article preserves that biochemistry. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2140783: A biology paper on physiological ontogeny, chicken embryos, catabolism and chemical changes. The chick's chemistry. This article preserves that embryology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2140983: Two cyanide salts hit the body's air-use gear, and this paper measured the harm to the breath enzymes. The tests caught the cells choking. The poisoned breath, noted. The article keeps that poison study.
europmc-pmc2270283:
Ogilvie and co-workers introduced the harvest plot in 2008, a graphical method for synthesising evidence about interventions' unequal effects. Meta-analysis and its forest plot do not suit questions about how population-level interventions affect social inequalities. As part of a review of tobacco control interventions and smoking inequalities, the team coded 85 studies by design suitability and execution quality. Effects were extracted across up to six inequality dimensions, from income to age.

Each study was judged against three competing hypotheses: a positive, negative or absent social gradient. Results were plotted on a matrix per intervention type, with studies weighted by quality. One clear pattern emerged: raising tobacco prices may discourage smoking more among lower-income and lower-occupation groups. The visual display aided both the synthesis process and readers' grasp of the findings.
europmc-pmc2547983:
Ben-Hur, Ong, Sonnenburg, Schölkopf, and Rätsch wrote this 2008 guide to support vector machines, a leading machine learning method, for biologists. Support vector machines sort data into classes by drawing the widest possible boundary between groups. They had become a workhorse for biology's prediction problems. These range from gene structure to protein function and disease. But the maths deterred many researchers.

The guide explains the core ideas in plain terms: large-margin separation, soft margins that tolerate errors, and kernels, which let the method compare complex objects such as DNA sequences. It covers kernels built for sequences and for other data types. It also covers practical points: normalising data, handling unbalanced classes, and choosing software. The authors aim to give bench biologists enough grounding to use the tools well.
europmc-pmc2571983:
Saint-Geniez and colleagues asked in 2008 whether the adult retina needs its own supply of VEGF, a growth factor famous for driving blood vessel growth. Anti-VEGF drugs are widely injected into eyes and given for cancer, yet VEGF also appears to act on non-vessel cells. Using reporter mice and staining, the team showed the factor is made across the adult mouse retina. Its receptor sits strongly on Müller cells and photoreceptors, the light-sensing cells.

Blocking VEGF throughout the body for two weeks left retinal vessels untouched but increased death of retinal neurons. By four weeks the cell layers had thinned and electrical responses of the retina had declined. Silencing VEGF in cultured Müller cells also threatened their survival. The authors caution that anti-VEGF therapy may carry retinal risks.
europmc-pmc2579683:
Potenta, Zeisberg, and Kalluri reviewed in 2008 the role of endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, or EndMT, in cancer progression. EndMT is a process first studied in heart development, where cells lining blood vessels peel away and take on a mobile, connective-tissue character. The authors assembled evidence that the same switch happens in adult disease, including cardiac fibrosis and tumours.

During EndMT the vessel cells lose their junctions and endothelial markers, gain mesenchymal markers, and become invasive and migratory. In tumours these converted cells act as fibroblasts. They form an important source of cancer-associated fibroblasts. Those support cells are known to help tumours grow and spread. The authors argue that blocking EndMT could become a treatment strategy reaching beyond cancer to fibrotic diseases as well.
europmc-pmc2604883:
Hanson and Frey reviewed in 2008 intranasal delivery, a route for sending drugs up the nose straight into the brain. The blood-brain barrier blocks most medicines from reaching the brain, forcing systemic doses with side effects. Nose-to-brain delivery exploits the olfactory and trigeminal nerves, the only direct connections between the outside environment and the central nervous system.

The method delivers even large molecules within minutes and needs no chemical modification of the drug. In animal studies, intranasal growth factors, deferoxamine, and erythropoietin protected the brain against stroke, and one treatment reversed degeneration and rescued memory in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Nasal insulin improved memory and attention in patients with Alzheimer's or mild impairment, and even in healthy adults. The authors see a route to treating many brain disorders.
europmc-pmc2668183:
He and colleagues mapped in 2009 how the resting human brain organizes itself into modules. Even at rest, the brain hums with slow waves of activity that rise and fall in step across linked areas. Brain scans can catch these waves, but the rules behind their pattern were poorly understood.

Applying network analysis, the team found the resting pattern splits into tight-knit modules. Links inside each module run far denser than links between them. The modules matched known brain systems: movement and touch, hearing, vision, attention, deep brain centers, and the default system active during daydreaming. Each module also had its own internal wiring style, which whole-brain averages would blur away. A few key bridge areas, mostly in the association cortex, held the modules together and kept signals flowing across the whole brain.
europmc-pmc2691583:
Vader, Kabla, Weitz, and Mahadevan studied in 2009 how collagen gels line up their fibers when stretched. Collagen is the body's most abundant structural protein, and its knack for remodeling under load gives tissues their toughness. The team built tools and a stretching rig that deforms gels the way cells deform their surroundings in the body.

As strain rose, fibers swung into line with the pull and packed denser, in both plain and chemically crosslinked gels. In plain gels the new order stayed after release, stamped in permanently. Crosslinked gels aligned just as much but sprang fully back. Stamping-in, then, is not the cause of alignment. The lining up is a built-in, nonlinear property of fiber networks themselves. The finding gives a simple physical route by which tissues could organize their own scaffolding at small scales.
europmc-pmc2722083:
Punjabi and co-authors followed a large cohort in 2009 to test whether sleep-disordered breathing, repeated airway collapse in sleep, raises the risk of death. The condition causes oxygen dips and broken sleep and affects many adults who stay undiagnosed. Clinic studies had hinted at higher deaths, but small, selected samples left the picture unsure.

Among six thousand four hundred forty-one volunteers followed for about eight years, worse breathing in sleep predicted higher death rates even after accounting for obesity, blood pressure, and heart disease. Risk rose with severity, and low oxygen in sleep was a key part of the link. The work came from the Sleep Heart Health Study, a population cohort rather than a clinic sample.
europmc-pmc2801183:
Reid and colleagues mapped which United States communities are most at risk during heat waves in 2009. Heat waves raise deaths and illness, and climate change is making them a growing worry. Knowing who is exposed lets cities aim cooling help where it counts most.

The team combined ten factors for nearly forty thousand census tracts, covering income, schooling, green cover, air conditioning, isolation, age, and diabetes rates. Four grouped factors explained most of the pattern across the ten inputs. Risk ran highest in the Northeast and along the Pacific Coast, and lowest in the Southeast. Inside cities, dense inner neighborhoods stood out as most exposed, giving planners a template for local maps.
europmc-pmc2826283:
Geiser and Kreyling reviewed in 2010 what happens to nanoparticles after they are breathed in, comparing their fate with that of particles a thousand times larger. Knowing where inhaled particles land, linger, and travel is the first step in judging their hazard, yet engineered nanoparticles behave unlike the bulk materials they are made from.

The review covers landing chances in the airways and how long particles stay. It also tracks the routes by which some cross into the blood and pile up in other organs before the body clears them. Whole-body measures give dose estimates for safety testing, while microscope work at single-particle level shows which cells and cell parts actually meet the particles. Real-world dose numbers anchor the whole account.
europmc-pmc2843083:
Clegg, Hankey, Tiwari, Feuer, and Edwards proposed a fairer summary in 2009 for how fast disease rates change over time, aimed at cancer trend reporting. The standard figure assumes one steady yearly percent change across a whole period. Real trends bend at turning points, and groups like racial subpopulations bend at different years, so single-figure and segment comparisons clash.

Their average annual percent change blends the segment figures across any chosen window, honoring the bends instead of hiding them. When a trend truly runs straight, the new figure collapses neatly to the standard one. Because it builds on the full data series, it stays stable when a sub-window is picked. The measure was folded into the Joinpoint software registries worldwide use.
europmc-pmc2848183:
Mokkink and colleagues explained in 2010 the reasoning behind the COSMIN checklist, a tool for judging studies that test health questionnaires. Questionnaires asking patients to report their own health drive treatment and research decisions, but weak test studies make their scores untrustworthy. COSMIN was built by forty-three experts through a structured Delphi process, where panelists vote in rounds toward consensus.

The paper walks through the contested choices: how internal consistency differs from unidimensionality, how to judge whether questions cover what matters, and why responsiveness counts as a validity issue. It also explains why strict criterion validity fits patient reports poorly. The authors hope spelling out the rationale wins wider, more consistent use of the checklist.
europmc-pmc2885083:
Pearson, Mihali, Moffitt, Kellmann, and Neilan reviewed in 2010 four notorious toxins made by cyanobacteria, the blue-green algae that bloom in lakes and reservoirs. The toxins attack different targets: some poison the liver, some the nerves, some cells broadly, and some the skin. Over the previous decade researchers had worked out the gene clusters and chemical steps that build each one.

For the liver toxin microcystin and its cousin nodularin, plus the nerve toxin saxitoxin and the cell toxin cylindrospermopsin, the review traces each assembly line gene by gene. It pairs that genetics with the chemistry of each molecule and its toxic action in animals and people. Knowing the blueprints lets water managers detect toxin genes in a bloom before the poison itself peaks.
europmc-pmc2952083:
Bouayed and Bohn reviewed the two-sided nature of dietary antioxidants in a 2010 article. Compounds from food such as vitamin C, vitamin E, plant pigments, and polyphenols top up the body's own defences against reactive oxygen species.

At normal food-level doses these compounds help keep the balance between oxidation and protection. At high doses of isolated supplements, though, they can turn harmful by driving oxidation themselves or by wiping out the modest reactive oxygen levels cells need to work well. The review weighs enrichment strategies and urges respect for dose when judging benefit.
europmc-pmc2978683:
Baxter and co-authors traced a coastal pattern of salt build-up in leaves of the weed Arabidopsis to one transporter gene in a 2010 study. Plants worldwide face varied soils, and local adaptation to salty coastal ground was a prime test case.

Genome-wide mapping, gene complementation, and expression work pointed to regulatory variants at the AtHKT1;1 sodium transporter. A weak version of the gene lets more sodium reach leaves and had earlier been tied to salt tolerance. That weak version clusters strongly in coastal and salty-soil populations across Europe, genetic proof of adaptation to place.
europmc-pmc3022183:
Brunet, Murray, and Michel introduced their CARTOOL software in this 2011 methods paper on brain recording. Electroencephalogram tests, called EEG for short, record electric fields from the scalp with many sensors at once. The authors focus on the shape of those fields across the scalp, rather than on single sensor traces alone.

Topography, meaning the pattern of voltages over the head, can show when different groups of brain cells become active. The paper walks through measures of field strength, ways to split recordings into stable map segments, and methods to locate sources inside the brain. CARTOOL was released free for academic use. Its three-dimensional displays let users rotate and animate results quickly.
europmc-pmc3033383:
Nica and the MuTHER consortium explored in 2011 how gene control differs across human tissues. They studied healthy female twins and took fat, skin, and blood cell samples from the same women at the same time. The question was whether DNA variants that tune gene activity act the same everywhere, or switch roles from tissue to tissue.

Thousands of tuning variants were found in each tissue. A statistical cleanup that removes hidden noise more than doubled the discoveries, and twin checks confirmed nearly all of them. About three in ten variants acted across all three tissues, while a similar share acted in only one. Even shared variants often changed strength between tissues. The authors argue that judging tissue specificity needs effect sizes, not just significance cutoffs.
europmc-pmc3047583:
Yuan and a large team sorted in 2011 human stem cell offspring into pure batches of nerve stem cells, support cells, and neurons using surface tags. Stem cells grown toward nerve fates produce messy mixes that spoil careful comparisons. The team screened nearly two hundred antibodies against surface proteins on stem cells and their partly grown descendants to find tag patterns unique to each cell type.

One tag pattern picked out nerve stem cells that could be grown for many rounds and still mature into neurons and support cells, in dishes and in animals. Further patterns separated working neurons, which fired electrical signals, from support cells that matured into star shaped astrocytes. Pure batches let drug tests and disease models start from known cells. The screens also give other labs a tested recipe for cleaning up their own cultures.
europmc-pmc3100083:
Son, Cheong, Kim, Chung, Kang, and Pae reviewed in 2011 the puzzle of how corrosive oxygen molecules switch on a major family of cell signaling enzymes. These enzymes, called MAPKs in short, relay signals from the cell surface to the nucleus through a three step chain, controlling growth, stress responses, and death decisions. Oxidative stress reliably activates them, yet the connecting steps were murky.

The review weighs two main explanations. Oxygen molecules may chemically modify the signaling proteins themselves, changing their behavior directly. Or they may disable the phosphatases, the off switches that normally strip the activation tags and shut the chain down, letting signals run longer. Both routes likely operate, in different proportions for different family members. Sorting them out matters because these pathways are drug targets in cancer and inflammation, where oxidative stress is rampant.
europmc-pmc3156683:
Kabir Sheikh and colleagues opened a three-part series on building health policy and systems research in a 2011 paper in PLoS Medicine. The young field studies how health systems and policies work at every level, especially in poorer countries, and recent attention after a first global symposium brought both chance and risk. This first paper frames the questions the field must answer.

The authors warn that fashionable topics may crowd out basic exploratory work, and that dominant research traditions may capture the field before it defines itself. They call for more fundamental and explanatory studies, for research capacity built inside low- and middle-income countries, and for wider use of methods across the social and health sciences.
europmc-pmc3176283:
Brian Pierce, Yuichiro Hourai, and Zhiping Weng sped up a protein docking program in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The program searches how two proteins fit together using a mathematical shortcut, and a sharper scoring system had recently made it accurate but slow. The team plugged in an advanced three-dimensional convolution library and taught the program to orient proteins for leaner computation.

The fresh benchmark covered well over a hundred and fifty known pairs. On it, the upgraded program ran more than eight times faster on average and used much less memory, with no loss of accuracy. An older, simpler scoring version also sped up several-fold. The gains open heavier jobs, such as docking flexible proteins and mapping whole interaction networks, to labs with modest computers.
europmc-pmc3183083:
Jonathan Bradfield and colleagues combined six study groups to hunt new type one diabetes genes in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Genome scans had already found dozens of risk regions for this autoimmune disease, in which the immune system destroys insulin-making cells. Pooling nearly ten thousand cases and seventeen thousand controls gave the largest search of its kind.

Follow-up testing in family trios confirmed three new risk regions at strict significance. One sits inside a gene shaping cell structure and signalling. Another sits in a crowded gene neighbourhood, and the third in a gene-rich stretch tied to immune function. None had been firmly linked before. The additions extend the network of genes predisposing to the disease and offer fresh entry points for tracing how the immune attack begins.
europmc-pmc3184083:
Cheryl Stetler and colleagues produced a guide for applying a revised health-care improvement framework in a 2011 paper in Implementation Science. The framework explains successful uptake of proven practices through three interacting elements: the evidence itself, the setting, and the help provided to change. A review by an outside team had exposed fuzziness in how to use it.

Each author pulled key terms, strengths, and complaints from every reviewed paper onto a shared form, and the group agreed revisions that keep the framework's spirit while sharpening its parts. The companion guide packages reference tools built on the framework's core and on current implementation science. The authors invite trial teams to apply it going forward and report back, so the framework keeps evolving on evidence rather than habit.
europmc-pmc3198983:
Martin Hoyle and William Henley addressed a costing problem in this 2011 paper in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Analysts judging whether a health technology is worth its price need average survival times, usually taken from published survival curves. Patient-level data are rarely shared, so analysts fit curves to summary graphs, which can be inaccurate.

Their method first rebuilds approximate patient-level data from the published curve and the numbers of patients still at risk, then fits the curve by maximum likelihood. In thousands of simulated trials it beat the older regression and least-squares approaches and nearly matched analysis of the true data. Reassessing one cancer drug comparison changed its cost-effectiveness result substantially. A spreadsheet implementing the method is included.
europmc-pmc3323383:
Keawcharoen and a large team reported that bird flu jumped into zoo tigers and leopards in Thailand, in a 2004 paper. Until then, influenza viruses were not known to infect wild cats. During the regional outbreak of deadly H5N1 bird flu, two tigers and two leopards at a zoo in Suphanburi province fell ill. They developed high fever and breathing trouble and died suddenly.

All four had eaten raw chicken carcasses supplied by a local slaughterhouse while poultry around them were dying of the same virus. Autopsies showed severe lung damage and bleeding in several organs. Tests found H5N1 genetic material in lung tissue from all four animals, and staining confirmed the virus inside lung cells. The authors warn that the virus's host range is wider than assumed, with consequences for outbreak tracking and wildlife protection.
europmc-pmc3342883:
Haslehurst and colleagues linked a cell shape changing program to drug resistance in ovarian cancer, in a 2012 study. Ovarian cancer kills more women than any other cancer of the reproductive system, largely because tumors stop answering to the platinum drug cisplatin. The shape change program, known as EMT, normally helps embryos form tissues, but cancers borrow it to spread.

Comparing drug sensitive ovarian cancer cells with a resistant line grown from them, the team found the resistant cells had taken on the mobile, spindle shaped form. Their gene and protein profiles showed a surge in the program's master switches, including two called snail and slug. Silencing those two switches largely restored the original cell form and made the cells sensitive to cisplatin again. Tumor samples from patients showed the same program switched on in resistant cancers, hinting at new markers and drug targets.
europmc-pmc3381683:
Sun and colleagues wrote to the editor in 2012 about a pig diarrhea outbreak that swept southern China from late 2010. The coronavirus disease struck newborn piglets hardest, killing more than a million animals across over ten provinces. Nearly every piglet fell ill within days of birth, and most died, while adult pigs stayed mostly well.

Testing found the virus in most stool samples and in many sows' milk samples, a possible new route of spread. The outbreak strain's spike gene clustered with Thai strains and sat far from the vaccine strain in use. Nine changes in the spike protein may explain why vaccinated herds still suffered. The letter warns pig producers that the virus had shifted.
europmc-pmc3399483:
Savjani, Gajjar, and Savjani reviewed in 2012 why drug solubility matters and how to raise it when it falls short. A drug must dissolve at its absorption site before the body can take it up. Over forty percent of new drug candidates in industry barely dissolve in water, making solubility a central headache for formulators.

The review catalogs the toolbox: shrinking particles, engineering crystals, forming salts, spreading the drug in solid carriers, adding wetting agents, and trapping molecules in ring-shaped helpers. Chemical tweaks to the drug itself are covered too. Choosing among methods depends on the drug's properties, where it is absorbed, and the dose form wanted. The survey guides that choice.
europmc-pmc3441783:
Teixeira, Carraça, Markland, Silva, and Ryan reviewed in 2012 what self-determination theory says about why people keep exercising. Motivation decides whether activity lasts, and health follows. They gathered sixty-six studies measuring the theory's building blocks, from feeling self-directed and capable to the kind of goals people chase.

Freer forms of motivation reliably went with more exercise. Wanting the benefits, called identified regulation, best predicted starting out, while exercising for its own joy best predicted sticking with it over years. Feeling competent and holding intrinsic goals also helped across many settings. Evidence on appearance-driven motives stayed mixed. Studies of every design agreed on the main story, giving program designers clear levers to pull.

fo-sho-hing-tsan-king-beal-1883:
Samuel Beal translated the Fo-Sho-Hing-Tsan-King into English in 1883. It appeared as volume nineteen of the Sacred Books of the East. The text is a verse life of the Buddha by Ashvaghosha.

Ashvaghosha's Sanskrit Buddhacarita survives complete only in its Chinese translation. Beal rendered the Chinese version into English, restoring the poem to the West. The narrative runs from palace luxury to the night of enlightenment. Prince Siddhartha's renunciation, temptations, and awakening unfold in verse. Beal was a pioneer of Chinese Buddhist studies in Britain. His translation let Victorian readers follow the classic poetic life in full.
frus-1861-d183:
Carl Schurz sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 October 1861. It is document 183 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Schurz's third October letter in the file keeps the pace of a post in full swing. Madrid's stance held steady, and he could report it plainly. Such steady word from Spain freed Seward to spend his care on London and Paris. Steady word from Spain let the cabinet spend its fear where fear was due. Fear spent where it was due was the cabinet's goal through that hard autumn.
frus-1861-d283:
From abroad on 28 July 1861, Mr. Haldeman sent Seward his latest account. It stands as Document 283 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d83:
On 14 September 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London.

The crossing letters of 14 September are a neat emblem of the whole run. Chief and envoy each pushed his view of the week across the sea. Their two files, read side by side, show a partnership built on trust and ink. Few chief and envoy pairs in the record match their trust and pace. Their pace that autumn never slackened, though the news gave them little cheer. Their paired pages remain a neat emblem of trust built by mail.
frus-1862-d183:
The second of three Seward letters dated 4 November 1862 stands as Document 183 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Its destination was the London legation, where Charles Francis Adams served as American minister to Britain.

Historians value these dense clusters of mail because they expose how orders were built, topic by topic, before a steamer sailed. A single short dispatch may look slight on its own. Set among its mates, it helps show the full brief Adams carried into his talks with Earl Russell that month. Cotton hunger in British mill towns kept the war a kitchen-table topic across the North of England.
frus-1862-d283:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch on 3 June 1862, printed as Document 283 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It answered into the steady stream of Paris reports.

Seward wrote as the siege of Richmond settled in and the North waited for a decision in Virginia. His guidance to Dayton balanced patience with warning: France should not mistake a long war for a lost one. Letters of this kind, calm in tone and firm in substance, were the Secretary's chief tool in Europe that summer. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d383:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to Simon Cameron on 23 July 1862. In a dispatch printed as Document 383 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron had succeeded Cassius Clay as American minister in Russia.

The same date carries a Cameron report, so the two papers likely crossed in transit. Cameron, a former secretary of war, took the St. Petersburg post in mid-1862. Seward's July dispatch belongs to the channel's change of hands, when Washington refreshed its instructions for a court whose friendship it prized. The legation's quiet year was the exception in a volume full of friction.
frus-1862-d483:
James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands, opened the Dutch file with this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 January 1862. It is Document 483 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Pike was a Maine journalist and antislavery man whom Lincoln sent to The Hague. The Netherlands was a trading nation with colonies in the East and West Indies, and its ports and insurers felt the war's effects at once. His January report told Washington how the Dutch government and press read the conflict after the Trent affair. The letter begins one of the volume's fullest small-country files.
frus-1862-d583:
On 20 March 1862 Thomas Corwin reported from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 583 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

By March the allied expedition in Mexico was splitting apart, as France's larger aims showed through the debt-collecting cover. Corwin, living in the capital of the threatened republic, sent Washington the view from the ground. His sympathy for Juárez's government was open, and his reports argued the American interest in keeping Mexico independent. For readers, the Corwin file is the volume's most dramatic American correspondence, written from a neighboring capital while European armies operated on its soil.
frus-1862-d683:
On 26 November 1861, William Sydney Thayer sent this report from Egypt to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Thayer served as the American consul general there. The dispatch is document 683 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Egypt's cotton had shot up in worth once the war cut off the South's crop, and ports like Alexandria felt the change fast. A consul's letters tracked prices, ships, and the acts of the viceroy's government. Thayer's dispatch is part of that watch. It shows how a trade post at the edge of the war still fed facts that mattered in Washington.
frus-1862-d83:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 23 June 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 83 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d183:
From Washington on 5 May 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 5 letters between the same men dated that day.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d283:
Washington's orders to London on 5 September 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 283 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d383:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 February 1863. His note is document 383 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Under the formal courtesy sits real tension: a neutral Britain trading with both sides, and a Union government sure that trade kept the South alive. This exchange is where the two views met. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d483:
Document 483, dated 28 April 1863, records a letter from the State Department's chief clerk, W. Hunter to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d583:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington received a letter dated 2 July 1863 from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d683:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to London on 15 December 1863, near the end of the year. His letter to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in Britain, is document 683 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume.

Year-end letters often took stock, and Washington had much to weigh. The Union held more ground, but the war was far from over, and Britain's stance still counted. Seward kept the flow of news and orders steady so Adams would not have to guess. For the reader, this note marks where the long exchange stood as 1863 closed. It gains force when read with the notes around it.
frus-1863p1-d83:
On 14 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. A second letter to Adams in the volume bears the same date. An older one of the same day and month sits just before them. This letter is document 83 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Seward's mid-February mail kept the London brief in motion. The standing work was to hold Britain to fair dealing and to choke off the warships rising in its yards for the South. This letter is one of the day's pair on that work. It shows the secretary's steady hand, writing the same claims in fresh forms as the news changed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d183: Hull wrote to Roosevelt again on November 2, 1943, and the letter is Document 183, the last in this run of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two Hull letters in two days closed the Moscow story as the secretary turned for home and the president turned toward Cairo. The record names the parties and the date and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series, at the end of the section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d283:
John Paton Davies, political adviser to General Stilwell, wrote a memorandum at Cairo about 22 November 1943 on the political side of the China and Southeast Asia theaters. A copy reached Secretary Hull in Washington at the end of December, and the paper appears to have been prepared for Roosevelt's use.

Davies warns that fighting under the Southeast Asia Command drags America into the colonial problems of the British, Dutch, and French. It invites the charge that American boys die to rebuild other nations' empires. He urges the main Asiatic effort in and from China instead, where the cause is popular and Stilwell's plan gives the Chinese their own land to fight for. North Burma must still be retaken with the British to reopen the land route, but after that, he argues, the ways part.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d383:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a secret telegram from Washington on 27 November 1943 about staffing the European Advisory Commission. The three-power body, agreed at the Moscow Conference, will handle European questions as the war ends, and Britain and Russia have already named their men.

Britain has named Strang and Russia Gusev as their principal representatives. Washington, Hull argues, should not play up the body's importance, but its American member will hold a full-time job and must be fully capable of guarding American interests. He offers three names for Roosevelt's choice: Joseph Grew, Jefferson Caffery, and Herschel Johnson. One doubt is attached: Caffery, ambassador in Rio, may not be spareable from Brazil at this time. Hull asks for the President's instructions.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d483:
A formal report by the Combined Chiefs of Staff, dated December 5, 1943, comes from the heart of the Second Cairo Conference. The chiefs, the senior American and British officers, reported upward to Roosevelt and Churchill as the conference neared its end. The State Department printed the report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Reports of this kind gathered the chiefs' joint conclusions into one paper the two leaders could approve. They are among the most important documents a summit produces, because they state what the military advisers of both nations could jointly recommend. For readers, this report shows the combined command speaking with one voice near the close of Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d83: Hull wrote to Stettinius, his acting deputy in Washington, on October 31, 1943, and the letter is Document 83 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Secretary-to-deputy letters of this kind handed the department's work back and forth across the Atlantic during the Moscow trip. The record names the two men and the date. Its contents are stated only in the printed text of the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d183:
The Combined Chiefs met at 10 a.m. on September 14, 1944, approved the previous meeting's conclusions, and settled the directive on control of the strategic bomber forces in Europe. The long item was British participation in the Pacific. Brooke said the British chiefs were disturbed by an American paper on the subject, which predated the plenary session and did not match what the president had accepted there.

The argument narrowed to words and fleets. Words confining the British force's first use to the Southwest Pacific's western flank were deleted by agreement. Cunningham described the balanced force Britain had in mind: some four battleships, five or six large carriers, and about twenty light carriers, self-supporting with its fleet train. King insisted the force must be self-supporting, and asked the British to propose its employment.
frus-1944-quebec-d283:
The memorandum initialed by Roosevelt and Churchill on September 15, 1944, is the Quebec agreement on Germany's future. It opens by calling the disposition of the Ruhr and the Saar an essential feature of preventing renewed German rearmament. Germany's metallurgical, chemical, and electric industries, it notes, convert from peace to war with an ease already impressed on the allies by bitter experience.

Those industries in the Ruhr and Saar would therefore be put out of action and closed down. Injured countries, Russia above all, could remove the machinery they needed to repair their losses. A body under the world organization would supervise the dismantling and prevent any restart by subterfuge. The program, the text concludes, looked forward to converting Germany into a country primarily agricultural and pastoral.
frus-1944-quebec-d83: Number 83 is one of the editorial notes written by the volume's historians. The Quebec 1944 volume uses them where the wartime file has gaps. Notes summarize missing background or direct readers toward related papers. The setting is the run-up to the second Quebec Conference. In September 1944, Roosevelt and Churchill planned the endgame against Germany and Japan. The note keeps that crowded preparation readable for later readers.
frus-1945-50-intel-d183:
The title "Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 18" heads a text dated 23 January 1947. It is document 183 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

A numbered directive joined a growing shelf of rules that told the new agencies how to run themselves. Staff could be held to each line, which is why the words were fought over before issue. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d283:
On 3 June 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 12th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. Readers meet it as document 283 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

Staff trusted these notes because they were made at once, and files across Washington cite them as the record of a talk. For a reader, the gain is scene and voice, rare goods in a file of stiff forms. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d383:
A memorandum dated 27 April 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was Secretary of Defense Johnson. The reader was the Secretaries of the Army (Royall), the Navy (Sullivan) and the Air Force (Symington). It stands as document 383 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The debate now was about reform: the Dulles survey had judged the CIA, and the replies and counter-replies were piling up.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d83:
McCormack wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 31 December 1945, closing the year for the State intelligence office. He had run the office since it rose from the OSS research branch in September. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A New Year's Eve memorandum from an office chief to his secretary reads like a report and a plea in one. McCormack knew the central settlement coming in January would fix his office's place, and not at the center. Readers can set his December paper beside his hopeful October letters from Byrnes. The arc between them, favor to foreboding in one season, is the State intelligence office's whole story in brief.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d183:
Lord Halifax sent Stettinius London's true feelings about Count Sforza on 5 December 1944. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, encloses a personal telegram from the Prime Minister dated the day before. It answers American anger over Britain's step in Rome.

There is no question, Churchill writes, of a British veto on Sforza as premier or foreign minister. What is certain is that Sforza will not command the slightest trust or confidence from His Majesty's Government. Halifax adds his own gloss. The State Department's soreness, he has told London, rests chiefly on being given no word before Britain spoke. London's defense is that the matter blew up suddenly, and its man in Rome had to speak at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d283:
The British chiefs accepted the American subject list on 20 January 1945, with one addition about France. Their representatives' memorandum, C. C. S. 765/4, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the United States paper of three days before.

The British Chiefs of Staff agree with the subjects proposed for the next American-British-Soviet staff conference. Their single point concerns the occupation zones item. The French now sit on the European Advisory Commission, and they have already stated their views on taking part in the control of Germany and Austria. Any conclusions the conference reaches on the military side of the zones must therefore take French aspirations into account. Failing that, they must be open to discussion with the French after the conference ends.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d383:
Matthews scribbled the ministers' February 8, 1945 agenda in shorthand: an Austria-Yugoslav boundary for administration, control commissions, reparations the next day, and Iran. On Iran, his notes hold a surprise. There was no dispute, he wrote, over the Soviets getting oil from northern Persia. No obstacle stood against a Russian concession, once Persia was ready to negotiate.

The Western side was ready to say all three powers would press no further until Allied troops withdrew. A statement offered earlier withdrawal, step by step, as the supply route closed. Molotov split the matter in two: oil was one question, troops another and new. The notes catch a bargain half-made.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d483:
French developments lead these excerpts from Grew's cable of February 7, 1945, marked for Hopkins's eyes. Ambassador Caffery reported that Foreign Minister Bidault had shown him the French Dumbarton Oaks committee's first reports. They matched American ideas closely. Our ideas are so similar, Bidault stressed, that it would be wicked to let anything come between us.

Bidault remained troubled, though, by the doings of the captured German general von Paulus under Soviet auspices. He feared they might bear on the Big Three conference. He also made clear his alarm at the idea of a Soviet-dominated government on France's frontier. Grew's digest shows France courting Washington while watching Moscow.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d83:
Progress on Security Council voting was slow, and the President was displeased. Secretary of State Stettinius recorded that mood in a short note to his special assistant, Leo Pasvolsky, on 22 December 1944. The note is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Stettinius says he has reported the latest developments to the President in person. The Department is pressing the Russians and the British for an early decision. If both answer yes, he hopes invitations can go out for a March meeting to found the United Nations. The President thought that entirely appropriate, but showed displeasure that things were moving so slowly in this field.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d183:
Justice Robert Jackson warned against summit debate on war crimes trials in a telegram from London on July 4, 1945. The extracts form document 183 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Jackson was negotiating the four-power agreement for trying the principal Nazi war criminals.

The talks go slowly, Jackson reports, because the Russians have trouble grasping the Anglo-American system of law, and the other side has the same trouble in reverse. He is rather appalled at the thought of the Big Three debating so technical a subject, where small phrases hide important differences. The British suggestion, he is told, aims only to calm Russian suspicion that prosecution is being dodged. If the leaders do take it up, he wants to brief the President and Byrnes in detail first.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d283:
An editor's note records the signing of the Austrian zones agreement, printed as document 283 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The note itself is the whole entry: no letter or telegram follows it.

The agreement on zones of occupation in Austria and the administration of Vienna was signed, subject to ratification, at a European Advisory Commission meeting in London on July 9, 1945. The four governments approved on different days: the United Kingdom on July 12, France on July 16, the Soviet Union on July 21, and the United States on July 24. The note points readers to the official treaty series for the text and its annexed maps. It marks the legal settlement of how Austria would be divided and jointly governed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d383:
Washington answered London's caution on German assets abroad in a cable to Winant dated July 6, 1945. The Department said it hoped the British views cabled on June 28 concerned procedure only. It trusted London was not turning against the policy of rooting out spearheads of German economic penetration in the neutral countries of Europe and in Turkey.

The American proposal for joint notes to neutrals, the cable explains, was a holding device until the Control Council could act. Reports from the Iberian Peninsula warned that delay encouraged the assets to slip away. Presenting the notes, Washington added, need not at once raise hard legal questions in the neutral states.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d483:
Poland's new start is outlined in a briefing book extract dated June 29, 1945, summarizing suggested American policy. Policy toward Poland, as defined at Yalta, aims first at a truly democratic government of the Polish people's own choice. It also seeks Poland's rapid return to international life as a United Nation, and her early reconstruction, with mutually beneficial relations restored between the United States and Poland.

The Moscow Polish Commission ended its work on June 22, with agreement among the three Polish groups on a Provisional Government of National Unity. Questions left for immediate consideration, the summary says, include establishing American representation in Poland, and holding free and unfettered elections there.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d583:
One short follow-up cable from Foreign Minister Togo to Ambassador Sato forms document 583 in the Potsdam volume. Dated in the small hours of July 12, 1945, it adds a single point to Togo's main cable of that day. That cable carried the Emperor's wish to send Prince Konoye to Moscow as a peace envoy.

Togo's whole point here is secrecy. When Sato puts the matter to the Soviet side, he must make clear that the subject is to be treated as absolutely secret. Togo says he knows he is presuming in stating this. He mentions it merely to be sure. The two-line cable shows how much weight Tokyo placed on keeping the peace feeler hidden, above all from its own foes in the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d683:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded British word of Soviet demands on Turkey in a memo dated June 18, 1945. It is document 683 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. John Balfour of the British Embassy had called that afternoon.

Balfour left a British report from Istanbul and an aide-memoire on a talk in Moscow. Foreign minister Molotov had told the Turkish ambassador that old questions must be settled before any new Soviet-Turkish treaty. Three items were named. Land ceded by Russia to Turkey in the 1921 treaty was claimed to have been yielded under duress and to need revision. Turkey should cede bases to Russia in the Straits. The Montreux Convention should be revised by agreement between the two states. The Turkish ambassador had answered that his government would not reopen the 1921 treaty, which it held was freely negotiated.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d83:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent the State Department a draft protest for Moscow on June 20, 1945. Their memorandum, signed by Admiral Leahy, is document 83 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It asks that the enclosed message go to Ambassador Harriman without delay, for delivery to the Soviet Foreign Office.

The draft says Washington is informed that Soviet authorities are holding back permission for the American advance party to enter Berlin. The needed work on communications and housing should already have begun, it argues, and permission should be granted at once. If it cannot be, the meeting date may have to slip, and the only explanation would be the missing Soviet permission. The blunt threat shows American patience wearing thin over summit logistics.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1083:
Britain's delegation proposed this closing statement on southeast Europe at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. The three heads of government would voice regret at charges of aggression traded between governments in that region. Fears of violent, one-sided moves to settle questions ahead of the peace treaty are also noted.

The draft declares the three powers strongly opposed to any such attempts. They offend the principles the war was fought for, and the Charter of the United Nations. Governments that suffered together under fascist occupation, the text urges, should settle their differences in peace. Their peoples deserve a time of growth and democratic advance. Bevin apparently withdrew the paper the next day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1183:
Truman wrote to Churchill on 25 July 1945, the day before the British count pushed Churchill out of the summit. The message reached the prime minister on his last full day at Potsdam. By the next evening, Clement Attlee would lead the British team.

The two men's partnership had steered the Western alliance through years of war. This note catches that bond at the moment it changed hands. Leader-to-leader letters did work no staff paper could: they held trust between governments. Whatever its errand, this one passed between a president and a prime minister at a turning point for both their countries.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1283:
On 17 July 1945, the day the conference opened, the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Notes of this kind put the staff's analysis on paper so leaders could decide. The chiefs' office began its Potsdam file as the talks began.

An opening-day memorandum holds the services' first framing of the questions. Later papers in the run react to deals and drafts; this one stands before them. Its value lies in that clean starting point. It shows what the American military staff thought the summit had to settle, before the bargaining taught anyone otherwise.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1383:
The Protocol of the Proceedings of the Berlin Conference, dated 1 August 1945, is the Potsdam summit's own signed record of its choices. Truman, Attlee, and Stalin set their names to the results it lists. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Inside, readers find the core bargain of 1945: how Germany would be run, where Poland's borders would lie, and how reparations would be drawn. The protocol is dry, dense, and of the first rank among the century's papers. Every cable and proposal earlier in the volume leads toward it or flows from it. Anyone who reads one Potsdam text in full should start with this statement of what the three powers agreed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-83:
Charles Bohlen, assistant to the Secretary of State and the delegation's best-known Russian expert, sent this message to President Truman on July 24, 1945. Bohlen served as interpreter and adviser at the Potsdam Conference. His note reached the President while the Big Three talks were in full swing near Berlin.

Short notes from Bohlen carried weight because he heard the Soviet side at first hand. He could flag tone, intent, and shifts in wording across the table. The message forms part of the day-by-day staff record in the second Potsdam volume. It shows how much of the conference ran through a small group of trusted aides.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d783:
Philip Mosely set down this memorandum on July 27, 1945, as document 783. Mosely advised the American representative on the European Advisory Commission in London. The Commission had drafted much of the Germany settlement in advance. His memo joined the second Potsdam volume of the conference papers.

A second Mosely paper in this run shows his steady role. He linked the London planning staff to the Potsdam team. Readers see preparatory work being defended and adapted at the summit. The document shows how long the settlement's roots were: ideas drafted in 1944 faced their test in 1945, carried by the men who wrote them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d883:
Secretary of State James Byrnes and Secretary of War Henry Stimson signed this memorandum for the President on German interim financing. The editors date it between July 25 and July 29, 1945. It follows a July 5 paper that set out agreed views across four agencies.

The two secretaries ask Truman to direct the War Department to buy and first finance essential imports for Germany. They note the department can fund food imports through October loadings. They also stress a limit set by Congress. Funds given for this year may be used only to prevent disease and starvation. A draft letter of instructions for the President is attached.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d983:
Covey Oliver, acting chief of the Division of Economic Security Controls, cabled Emilio Collado on July 17, 1945. He reports the chief development on German external assets: Britain has agreed to join in warnings to neutral governments. In Spain, Franco's state industry body wants to acquire German subsidiary firms, and Madrid has sent its ambassador to raise the matter in Washington.

Oliver adds that France is being pressed to concur in the joint proposal. Washington will likely urge that German assets in Rumania, Hungary, and Bulgaria fall under a four-power trusteeship. It will also object to a Soviet attempt to acquire the German legation buildings in Stockholm. Talks with the Swiss touch on a blocked firm, Scintilla.
frus-1952-54Guat-d283: A 1952-1954 FRUS telegram from the CIA on Guatemala. Headquarters directed the Central American operation. This entry holds that cable. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
frus-1961-63v05-d83: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum of conversation from Vienna on the Soviet Union. Kennedy and Khrushchev met. This document preserves that conversation. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
galton-inquiries-into-human-faculty-1883:
Francis Galton, Darwin's cousin and a restless investigator, published Inquiries into Human Faculty in 1883. He gathered his experiments on how minds differ from person to person. Twins, prayer, and mental imagery all come under his measuring eye.

Galton reports word-association tests and studies of people picturing scenes. He also argues that ability runs in families and can be bred. That program became eugenics, now read with well-earned caution. The book founded behavioral genetics while showing how measurement can serve a harmful cause. His laboratory at South Kensington later measured thousands of willing visitors in similar ways.
gao-gaoreports-b-296483: Rand & Jones Enterprises took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-296783: ITT Federal Services doubled its October 2005 protest — two case numbers, one services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298583: SunEdison doubled its October 2006 protest — two case numbers, one solar fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict. The solar fight got its hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298883: Management Solutions, doing business as EssTech Engineering, doubled its December 2006 protest — two case numbers, one engineering fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer.
