gao-gaoreports-b-299083: Fantastic Data took its February 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Great names get the same grounded hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299383: Able Business Technologies took its April 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest. Small tech firms get the same full hearing as the giants.
gao-gaoreports-b-299883: Paraclete Contracts took its 2007 award dispute to GAO, and this ruling ends it. The firm said the agency's pick violated bid law; the call measures the claims and decides. One more published verdict in the long public record of how federal contracts must be contested — and won.
gao-gaoreports-b-311383: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by SKE International, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-183: Navy ship cost overruns needed taming in 2005, and GAO's report says better shop habits could shrink the bills. The review writes the prescription. The sailors' ships deserved the budget discipline. The discipline had to come. The bills had to shrink.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-283: The Klamath water bank got a GAO check in 2005, and the report says Reclamation met its obligations, though stakeholder information fell short. The review balances the credit with the gaps. The farmers' water deserved the honesty. The information had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-383: Federal Wi-Fi defenses lagged in 2005, and GAO's report says the shops had to toughen the shields. The findings demand the fixes firmly. The report warns that the airwaves deserved protection. The airwaves deserved protection. The shields had to hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-383: Critical infrastructure info sharing needed promoting in 2006, and GAO's report says DHS should encourage wider use of its sharing program. The findings demand the outreach. The report warns that the vital systems' secrets should be shared wisely. The use had to be widespread.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-483: Treasury's financial-crime duties got a GAO review in 2006, and the report examines roles under the Patriot Act provisions. The findings parse the responsibilities. The report warns that the money-laundering fight needed clear roles. The duties had to be defined.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-883: The Pentagon's lab-to-field pipeline needed fixing in 2006, and GAO's report says stronger practices were required to improve technology transition. The findings prescribe the discipline. The report warns that the brilliant prototypes had to reach the troops. The tech had to transition.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-283: Peak oil loomed over 2007, and GAO's report says the uncertainty about future supply made a strategy for the crunch essential. The findings demand the plan. The report warns that the end of cheap crude needed a playbook, not wishful thinking.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-383: Ambulance bills were a lottery in 2007 — GAO's report finds costs and Medicare margins swung wildly among providers. The findings map the uneven economics of the emergency ride. The report asks what a fair price for saving lives really is, and who should set it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-483: The double-decker jumbo was coming in 2007 — GAO's report eyes the safety and capacity questions around the giant A380. The findings size up the super-jumbo's fit. The report asks whether the skies and gates were ready for the whale.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-83: The Justice Department's secrets needed better staffing in 2007, and GAO's report says a fuller strategy was required for managing classified information. The findings demand the plan. The report warns that the nation's secrets deserved dedicated keepers. The staffing had to match the stakes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-283: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on health-Care-Associated Infections in Hospitals: Leadership Needed from HHS to Prioritize Prevention Practices and Improve Data on These Infections. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-383: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at media Ownership: Economic Factors Influence the Number of Media Outlets in Local Markets, While Ownership by Minorities and Women Appears Limited and Is Difficu. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gateway-process-assessment-1983:
An Army intelligence officer took a school of consciousness with full gravity in 1983. Wayne McDonnell's Analysis and Assessment of Gateway Process, dated June 9, weighs the Monroe Institute's Gateway training for Army use. The paper went to the Army Intelligence and Security Command.

Gateway uses sound, trance, and trained focus to shift the mind out of its common bounds. McDonnell treats the claims with care, maps them to physics and brain science, and finds them worth a soldier's study. The text is calm where its theme is wild. It is the military's most famed sober look at altered states.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_aa83_Nat:
In February 2019 the National Security Archive sued the Defense Intelligence Agency. The suit sought records on Able Archer 83. That NATO exercise came in the most dangerous autumn of the late Cold War.

The Archive uses Freedom of Information lawsuits as one of its main tools. This briefing book explains the fight in plain terms. It states what document was asked for, why the DIA withheld it, and why historians want it. Able Archer papers matter because Soviet leaders may have feared the exercise was real. The briefing lets readers follow an open-records battle over a moment when the world came quietly close to war.
green-conquest-of-england-1883:
John Richard Green tells of England's conquest and remaking in The Conquest of England, from 1883. Danish kings rule first, then Cnut and the Godwin family hold the land. The tale ends in 1071, amid the Norman aftermath of Hastings.

Green wrote history from the people's side, not the palace's alone. Towns, laws, and daily life matter as much as battles in his pages. He traced how a nation absorbs its conquerors and stays itself. The book stands as a classic of history from below for the medieval age, learned yet warm, and full of sympathy for ordinary English folk.
green-prolegomena-ethics-1883:
T. H. Green published Prolegomena to Ethics in 1883, the year after his death. Green was the leading British idealist of his generation at Oxford. He argues that the good lies in the full realization of human capacities. Against hedonism, he holds that pleasure alone cannot be the end of life.

The common good is his central idea: a good shared by all and diminished for none. Moral progress, for Green, grows as people widen their sense of that shared good. The book shaped welfare liberalism and the thought of later reformers. It is demanding but rewarding. Green gave British philosophy a moral seriousness that lasted decades.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol7-1883:
Seven volumes in by 1883, the Guiding Symptoms had become a fixture of homeopathic libraries. Volume VII holds more of Constantine Hering's lifetime harvest: symptoms proved on the healthy, then checked in the sick room. The entries keep their strict order, region by region through the body.

Reading a remedy here means reading a crowd of small, exact reports. One sign may note the hour a pain strikes, another the side it favors. Hering's marks sort the gold from the sand, lifting the guiding symptoms clear. The series rolls on from his notes, still two years past his death.
hermes-curiosus-sive-inventa-et-experime: Hermes curiosus, sive inventa et experimenta physico-chymica nova, 1683. The curious Hermes. This book preserves that alchemy. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
John Lothrop Motley ends his History of the United Netherlands with chapters fifty-two and fifty-three, the treaty and the conclusion. The States-General vote on the groundwork of the treaty after long debate. Forty-three years had passed, Motley reckons, since the nobles laid their Request before Margaret, the Regent, at Brussels. Those high-born beggars kindled a war little knowing what they were doing.

Philip's successor has now recognised the provinces as a sovereign republic, independent and protestant. In the ratification the most Catholic king makes his own request, asking favours of the States-General. Motley's ring closes with that reversal. The conclusion chapter is short and magisterial, the peroration of a life's work. Readers who finish here have watched a suppliant petition become a sovereign state, in one historian's grand design.
im-thurn-among-the-indians-of-guiana-188:
Everard Ferdinand im Thurn traveled in British Guiana as a young magistrate and explorer, living among the Carib and Arawak peoples of the forests and rivers. His 1883 book became the classic early account of the colony's native inhabitants.

Much of the book concerns belief: the peaiman, or shaman, who heals and fights spirits, and the unseen world pressing on daily life. Im Thurn describes hunts, feasts, burials, and myths alongside plants, animals, and journeys into the interior. He wrote with respect for people others dismissed. His observations still anchor the study of Guiana's forest tribes.
jevons-methods-social-reform-1883:
Methods of Social Reform and Other Papers came out in 1883, the year after Jevons's death. It collects the essays in which the great theorist of marginal utility turned to practical questions. Jevons had strong views on how the state should, and should not, try to improve working-class life.

The papers treat labor unions, education, public libraries, and the proper limits of state action. Jevons favors experiment and local trial over grand schemes, testing each proposal against evidence. His famous caution about the dangers of state socialism runs beside a real sympathy for workers' aims. The volume shows economics with its sleeves rolled up: the abstract thinker of value theory judging concrete evils and concrete cures. It remains a sharp statement of Victorian liberal reform at its most thoughtful.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manuscripts-103:
Manuscripts, the materials and forms of Jewish books, are surveyed in a long Jewish Encyclopedia article of 1906. Four scholars share the writing. The entry begins with stone, wood, and metal, engraved with a stylus. Animal skins soon became the standard writing surface. The Bible's word sefer itself points to skin.

The article sets out the rules of sacred copying. Bible copies were made from whole skins of clean animals, prepared by the scribe himself. Three grades of skin are named, from plain leather to fine parchment. The skin was ruled, with fixed margins and line counts. Only black, erasable ink was allowed for biblical works. Metallic ink was known but forbidden, though legend gave Ptolemy a copy in gold. Books kept the scroll form for a thousand years after the Bible. Synagogue Torah scrolls keep that form still.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattathias-b-si:
Mattathias ben Simon was a son of the Hasmonean prince Simon. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling remember him in a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. His whole recorded story is the journey he made with his father at the end of Simon's life. Simon's son-in-law Ptolemy invited the old prince to a banquet in the fortress of Docus, near Jericho. Mattathias went with him, together with his brother Judah and their mother.

The banquet was a trap. Simon was murdered at it, and his sons were first put in fetters and then killed. The one scholarly point of the entry is a disagreement between its sources. The First Book of Maccabees and Josephus differ on whether Mattathias died with his father or afterward. The article judges Josephus, who drew on further sources, to be probably the more correct.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-b-samuel-o:
Meir ben Samuel of Sczebrszyn, a Hebrew author of the seventeenth century, is remembered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, in an entry by Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein, as a witness of catastrophe. An honored member of his community in Russian Poland, he fled when the Cossacks invaded during the massacres of 1648 and 1649 and reached Cracow. There in 1650 he published "Zok ha-Ittim," Strain of the Times, an account in Hebrew verse of what the Jews had suffered in the uprising.

The entry adds a literary theft. Meir's book was afterward published by Joshua ben David of Lemberg under Joshua's own name, and it was Steinschneider, the bibliographer, who first exposed the plagiarism. One earlier work is also recorded: "Mizmor Shir," a Sabbath hymn in Aramaic and Judaeo-German, printed at Venice in 1639.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menken-10683:
Menken is an American family founded by a Westphalian immigrant. Cyrus Adler and Elvira N. Solis present it in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia as linked biographies. Solomon Menken was born in 1787. Sent to New York in 1821 as supercargo on his uncle's ship, he settled at Cincinnati. His sons Jacob Stanwood and Nathan Davis Menken were merchants. Both became Union captains in the Civil War. Nathan fought in thirty-seven battles and skirmishes. He died at Memphis in the yellow fever epidemic of 1878. He had stayed to help the Howard Association, after funding the escape of his coreligionists.

The line runs on to Percival S. Menken, president of the Young Men's Hebrew Association. He was a director of the Jewish Theological Seminary too. S. Stanwood Menken founded the Hall of Records Association. It is a family record of commerce, war service, and civic institution-building.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-jesofov:
Michael Jesofovich, born at Brest-Litovsk about the middle of the fifteenth century, became the first senior of the Jews of Lithuania under King Sigismund I of Poland. Herman Rosenthal wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. With his brothers Abraham and Isaac, he ranked among Lithuania's leading Jewish tax-collectors and lease-holders.

Expelled with all Lithuanian Jews in 1495, Michael stayed true to his faith in Poland while his brother Abraham converted, and he came home only when return was allowed in 1503. A royal decree of February 27, 1514, made him senior over Lithuania's Jews, mediating with the king and judging and punishing within the community. His attempt to force the Karaites under rabbinical law met their chartered refusal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mitau-10883:
Mitau, capital of the Russian government of Courland, twenty miles from Riga, is given a community history by Herman Rosenthal in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The castle was founded by the German Knights in 1263, and under their rule Jews could not live in the town at all. Even as Polish territory, Jewish merchants traded there without the right to settle or organize.

After the Cossack uprising of 1648 the townspeople drove the Jews out entirely. The turning point the article records is personal: Bär ben Benjamin, whose father was killed in the uprising, became court jeweler to Duke Ferdinand in 1730 and showered gifts on the community. That same year the duke granted a cemetery and a burial society was founded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-probab:
Mordecai is the hero of the Book of Esther. Isidore Singer, M. Seligsohn, and Wilhelm Bacher trace him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They start with his name, probably belonging to Marduk, a Babylonian god. He was a Benjamite of the exile and cousin and adoptive father to Esther. He sat at the king's gate in Shushan. There he overheard two eunuchs plotting the king's murder.

The article follows Esther's plot beat by beat. The conspiracy is exposed and entered in the royal chronicles. Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman. Haman answers with a purchased decree for the destruction of every Jew in the Persian kingdom. Mordecai replies in sackcloth and ashes. He sends word to Esther through the chamberlain Hathach. It is biblical biography retold in the encyclopedia's critical register.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-harif-ii-:
Phinehas Moses ben Israel, called Moses Harif the Second, was chief rabbi of Lemberg, where he died on September 17, 1702. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn. He was a grandson of Moses Harif the First, and apparently born at Lemberg.

He was the first man to serve as chief rabbi of both Lemberg communities, the urban and the suburban. In the Council of Four Lands he was an active member and sometimes presided. His signature stands first on the approbations given at the Yaroslav fair in 1697. He also added notes and a supplement to his grandfather's Seder Gittin, a work on divorce documents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahmani-samson-:
Samson Hayyim Nahmani was an Italian Talmudist of the later eighteenth century, noticed briefly in the Jewish Encyclopedia by its editorial committee and J. S. Raisin. He studied under Ephraim Cohen of Ostrog, rabbi of Modena, and under Basilla, rabbi of Mantua. For Cabala his teacher was Benjamin Alexander ha-Kohen of Reggio.

Two of his books reached print. Toledot Shimshon, a commentary on the Mishnah tractate Abot, appeared at Leghorn in 1766. Zera Shimshon, on the Pentateuch and the Five Scrolls, came out at Mantua in 1778. The notice preserves the line of his teachers and the record of his works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-natronai-ii-b-h:
Natronai II, son of Hilai, headed the academy at Sura. Wilhelm Bacher and S. Mendelsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served early in the later ninth century, after Sar Shalom. His father had held the post some thirty years before. Natronai was old, and his term lasted under a decade.

Yet about three hundred of his responsa survive. Questions reached him from all over the Diaspora. He answered in the tongue each writer knew best. He used Aramaic, newer Hebrew, and even Arabic. He is called the first gaon to write Arabic for scholarship. He fought the Karaites hard and pushed one rite for all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neutitschein-11:
Neutitschein is a city in Moravia, in Austria. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mandl wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish congregation lived there in the Middle Ages. It was expelled on Aug. 30, 1563. The town took the cemetery under a promise.

The Jews deeded their cemetery to the city then. The deed required that it be preserved forever. It has, in fact, entirely disappeared since. No new settlement began until after 1848. Law then let Jews settle across the empire. A congregation formed in 1893 for four districts. It numbers about six hundred persons in all. Charitable societies serve it, but no synagogue yet. Dr. Mandl became its first rabbi in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nones-11583:
Nones is an American family of early Jewish stock. Cyrus Adler and A. S. W. Rosenbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It traces descent from Benjamin Nones of Philadelphia. He lived at the close of the 1700s. Bordeaux was his native city in France.

He crossed to Philadelphia about the year 1777. At once he took arms for the colonies. He served through the whole Revolutionary war with honor. Under Pulaski he fought at the siege of Savannah. A certificate praised his gallant conduct in battle. Peace brought him into brokerage with Haym Solomon. Citizenship came to him in October of 1784. In 1791 his congregation made him its president. He held the parnas post for many years. His printed defense of Judaism appeared in 1800.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oser-baruch-117:
Baruch Oser was a German chief judge of the Jews' court. Isidore Singer and Alfred Feilchenfeld wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Prague about the year 1743. He died at Hamburg in the year 1822. From 1783 to 1814 he was a dayyan at Hamburg.

A dayyan is a judge in a Jewish court of law. In 1814 Baruch became head of the Hamburg rabbinate. French troops held the town and sacked it just then. In 1818 a new Temple rose with reforms in prayer. Baruch spoke out hard against those reforms in print. He warned he would cast out all who backed them. He asked famed strict rabbis for their views on the case. He put their words out in a book in 1819.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedro-iv-11983:
Pedro the Fourth ruled Aragon from 1336 to 1387. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He showed more grace to Jews than any king before him. His own doctor was a rabbi, Menahem. His long reign gave them rare steady ground.

Pedro studied astrology under Menahem and prized his counsel. When a Jew-baiter urged forced conversion on him, he refused. He said force had never brought good results. After taking the Balearic Isles he confirmed the Jews' old rights. He guarded Jewish lenders and curbed torture by his officials.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pforzheim-12083:
Pforzheim is a city in the grand duchy of Baden. Gotthard Deutsch and Moses Löb Bamberger wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish story opens with the first Baden persecution. Reuchlin, the great scholar, was born there later.

In 1267 a blood slander inflamed the town's mob. An old woman claimed Jews had killed a Christian child. Three rabbis took their own lives to escape torture. Their bodies were then broken on the wheel. The date is still kept as the Fast of Pforzheim. By 1904 the town held twelve hundred Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porcupine-12283:
Porcupine is a word some readers use for the Hebrew word kippod. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the short article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The writers say the English Bible is right to read bittern instead. Still, the true porcupine is common in Palestine. Local people treat it as a big kind of hedgehog.

The Arabic word for hedgehog is often used for the porcupine too. The Talmud seems to name the beast in a few places. One tale tells of Herod and Baba ben Zuta. Herod had the man's eyes put out with porcupine skin. The skin was bound tight around them. The article sorts out these old names and tales for the reader.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-matna-: Rabbah bar Matna was a Babylonian teacher of the fourth set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a friend and fellow of Zera the Second. Rabbah was slow and careful in his way of work. His end views were most often held to be right. Men took them as the rule in hard cases. Two more Talmud passages name him in brief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roads-12783:
Roads in ancient Palestine first served communication with markets. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Later they served armies moving troops and supplies. Three great trading lands surrounded the region.

The article says Palestine linked Egypt and Assyria by land. The Arabian desert forced caravans onto one main route. That Pilgrim Road still runs from Damascus toward Arabia. Damascus, not Jerusalem, became the central market city. All roads lead to Damascus, the writers quip. Four chief roads ran through the Holy Land to it. The coast route passed Gaza, Ashdod, and Tyre. Another route went from Beersheba through Jerusalem. The entry maps trade before it maps theology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosewald-julie-:
Julie Eichberg Rosewald was an American prima donna born in Stuttgart on March 7, 1847. Cyrus Adler and Henrietta Szold wrote her entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. She was a daughter of Moritz Eichberg, cantor in Stuttgart.

After training at Stuttgart's conservatory, Rosewald joined family in Baltimore in 1864. She studied voice further in Europe and debuted with the Kellogg Opera Company in 1875. From 1880 the Abbott Company engaged her as its leading soprano. Settled in San Francisco, she became a famed singing teacher, nicknamed the Marchesi of the West. For ten years she sang the cantor's parts at Temple Emanu-El there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sackheim-tobiah:
Tobiah b. Aryeh Löb Sackheim was a Russian Talmudist and communal worker of Rosinoi. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He died there, at an advanced age, in 1822.

Sackheim descended from Israel b. Shalom, martyred at Rosinoi in 1659. In youth he was a wealthy merchant in the town. In middle life he left business for study and charitable work. For many years he served as dayyan, a judge of the community there. The entry stresses his piety and the respect it won him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-13083:
Samuel was tax-gatherer and treasurer to King Ferdinand IV of Castile. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Andalusia, he served the young king from 1295 to 1312.

The queen mother, Maria de Molina, hated Samuel bitterly, the entry says. Spanish historians friendly to her blame him for court intrigues there. They charge he fed the king's prodigality and led his thoughtless acts. At Badajoz in 1305 an assassin attacked and dangerously wounded him. The king procured such care that Samuel's life was saved in time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-santangel-sanct:
Cyrus Adler and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Luis de Santangel. The name was borne by several men of one Marano family of Spain. The first was a learned jurist of Calatayud. He became a magistrate of the Aragonese capital. Others farmed royal taxes and salt pits for King John of Aragon. One joined a plot against the inquisitor Pedro Arbues and was burned in 1487.

The most famous Santangel served Ferdinand of Aragon as chancellor of the royal house. He played a key part in the discovery of America. When talks with Columbus broke down, Santangel won over Queen Isabella. He lent the needed money himself, some 17,000 ducats, without interest. Columbus sent his first full report of the voyage to Santangel. Ferdinand rewarded the family richly. He shielded Santangel's children and grandchildren from charges of apostasy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlettstadt-sa:
Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Samuel ben Aaron Schlettstadt. He was a German rabbi, born at Schlettstadt. He lived at Strasburg in the second half of the fourteenth century. There he headed an important yeshibah. Jews and pupils alike held him in high respect. Then one hard case nearly cost him his life.

About 1370 two informers plagued the Strasburg community. Their tips brought raids by the knights of Andlau. The community asked its rabbi for help. Schlettstadt formed a secret court, which condemned both men to death. One was executed, but the other escaped and turned Christian. The knights stormed in demanding vengeance. Schlettstadt hid for six years in the castle of Hohelandsberg. He sailed to Babylonia to plead his case. A ban from the exilarch finally armed his return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seer-13383:
Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the seer. English versions render a Hebrew word as seer. First Samuel says it was the old popular name for the later prophet. The seer was a man of God. For a fee he would inquire of God for those who came. He then gave directions from God's answer.

Samuel is the seer above all in the Bible. Saul met him while hunting his father's lost asses. Hanani also bears the title in Chronicles. Gad is called David's seer, and Heman the king's seer. Their written visions carry a matching name. The article's critical view calls the early seer a clairvoyant. Unlike the priest with his lots, the seer used no tools. He learned God's will in a trance. Arab sheiks offered similar counsel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shinnuy-ha-shem:
Shinnuy ha-Shem is the custom of changing a person's name for a reason. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the custom. A new name can honor a person's achievements. It can also signal hope for a better condition.

Above all, a new name was thought to aid recovery from illness. The Bible offers many famous cases of renaming. Abram became Abraham, father of many nations. Sarai became Sarah, and Jacob became Israel. Pharaoh renamed Joseph with an Egyptian title of honor. Moses turned Hoshea into Joshua before the spying mission. Kings renamed vassal rulers in Jerusalem as well. The entry gathers these cases into one custom with deep roots.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-absalo: Simeon ben Absalom was an amora whose period of activity is not known. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Only two of his homiletic sentences have been preserved. One explains why Deborah sat under a palm tree instead of at home. She wished to escape any possible suspicion, he said. The other asks why David, fleeing Absalom, wrote a psalm and not a lament. That comment appears on the third psalm in Berakot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sippai-13783: Sippai was a Philistine giant, one of the sons of Rapha. Emil G Hirsch and M Seligsohn wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was slain at Gezer by Sibbechai the Hushathite. Sibbechai was one of David's warriors. The parallel passage in Second Samuel calls him Saph. It also places his death at Gob instead of Gezer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-mos:
Solomon ben Moses of Melgueil was a French philosophical writer and translator. Isidore Singer and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived in the thirteenth century in southern France. His name may mark him as a native of Melgueil. Scholars still debate that point and his true identity.

Some link him to a Solomon of Béziers in Latin records. Those records in 1284 call him a Jew of the king. Others link him to the translator of Aristotle into Hebrew. He certainly wrote Bet Elohim, a philosophic commentary. It deals with the building of Solomon's Temple in Kings. The entry weighs each doubtful identification in turn with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stadthagen-jose:
Joseph Stadthagen was a German rabbi, apologist, and author of note. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Stadthagen on September 5, 1715. He took his name from that place of residence. For decades he served as Landesrabbiner for Schaumburg-Lippe district.

He knew apologetic literature and the New Testament very well. That knowledge fit him to lead in religious controversies of the day. At Hanover in 1704 he debated a convert before the elector. The disputation, held before Electress Sophie, went very successfully for him. In 1705 he published Dibre Zikkaron at Amsterdam in two parts. It held ethical reflections on the rules for ritual slaughter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ta-anit-fasts-1:
Ta'anit is a Mishnah treatise devoted to fast days. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. It appears in the Mishnah, Tosefta, and both Talmuds. Most editions rank it ninth in the order Mo'ed. Four chapters hold thirty-four paragraphs in all.

Chapter one sets when prayers must mention rain. It grades fasts for drought in rising strictness. Three-day fasts can grow to a final seven days. Chapter two gives the rites of a public fast. Trumpet blasts and special prayers mark the day. Priests take part in the fasts as well. Some days bar public fasting by an ancient scroll. Chapter three covers fasts for other dangers and troubles. The entry maps how a community mourns for rain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-traube-ludwig-1:
Ludwig Traube was a German physician who led in experimental pathology. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Ratibor in 1818 and died at Berlin in 1876. He took his medical degree in 1841. He set up practice in Berlin the next year.

His animal experiments studied lungs after cut vagus nerves. The essays of 1846 and 1847 made his name. Berlin's Charité Hospital made him chief physician in 1857. The university made him full professor in 1872. Students prized him as one of its best teachers. His monographs treated digitalis, fever, and medical thermometry. Heart and kidney disease links won special fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-unger-manasse-1:
Manasse Unger was a German art critic who restored old paintings with rare skill. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Coswig in 1802, he died at Berlin in 1868. He trained as an architect and passed Berlin's state examination. He chose an artist's career instead of building.

A government scholarship took him through Italy in the 1840s. In Holland in 1852 he found Rubens' Sacrifice of Abraham. Few of his own paintings survive beyond some portraits. His fame rests on technique and connoisseurship instead. Das Wesen der Malerei set out his view of painting in 1851. Critical studies of old and new painting followed. In 1848 he captained the artists guarding Berlin's museums.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-warsaw-14783:
Warsaw is the capital of Russian Poland, on the Vistula River. Herman Rosenthal, J. G. Lipman, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Polish writers date Jewish settlement there to the twelve hundreds. Hebrew documents survive in the city archives. Jews first lived on a Jewish street near Dunai.

Growth bred conflict with Christian merchants. Rivals pushed the strict Magdeburg Law against them. In 1525 Prince Janush banned Jews from the city. A second decree in 1527 barred even the suburbs. Neither ban held for long. Jews settled just past the walls and waited. The entry follows their return and growth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weyl-meir-b-sim:
Meir ben Simhah Weyl was a German rabbi. Isidore Singer and Louis Lewin wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Lissa in 1744. He died at Berlin in 1826. He studied under Hirsch Janow. In 1771 he became associate rabbi at Lissa. In 1784 Berlin called him as associate rabbi.

In 1800 Weyl became Berlin's chief rabbi. He published no separate books of his own. His legal opinions fill other rabbis' collections. Akiba Eger and Jacob Lissa both printed his rulings. His calendar rulings carried the Berlin Academy's sanction. Though opposed to ritual change, he backed seminaries. He helped found schools for rabbis and teachers in Prussia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zoroastrianism-:
Zoroastrianism is the old religion of Persia, founded by the prophet Zoroaster. Kaufmann Kohler and A. V. W. Jackson wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry calls it one of the world's great faiths, closest in spirit to Judaism and Christianity. Tradition dates Zoroaster to the seventh century before Christ, though many scholars put him far earlier.

His teachings survive in the Avesta, the faith's sacred book. At their heart stands a war between good and evil. Ahuramazda, the Wise Lord, leads angels for the good. Angra-Mainyu heads demons for the evil side. Zoroaster, once a Magian priest, reformed the older nature worship of Persia. His faith was in force across Iran before the Jewish captivity began.
kardec-genesis-colville-1883:
Kardec closed his Spiritist canon with Genesis, the fifth and final book of the set. The first English translation appeared in Boston in 1883, from Colby and Rich. Its title page credits the spirit guides of W. J. Colville as translators. The book reconciles the Genesis narrative with science through Spiritism.

Miracles and predictions receive natural readings inside Kardec's system. Creation, the fall, and prophecy are retold as stages of spirit growth. The English edition carried his canon to American readers of the occult. It completes the five book structure he planned. Spiritists treat the set as one connected teaching. The Boston printing is a period piece in itself.
las-casas-spanish-colonie-1583:
English readers first met Las Casas in The Spanish Colonie, printed in 1583. An unnamed translator Englished the Brevísima relación for an Elizabethan audience. The short book brought Spain's crimes in the Indies home to London readers.

Its grim tales of cruelty fed what later ages call the Black Legend. English readers used the tract as proof of Spanish cruelty abroad. At the same time, its moral charge went far past mere propaganda. The pamphlet warned England what empire could do to its soul. Few short books have shaped two nations' views of each other so long.
lee-sea-fables-explained-1883:
Lee turned from serpents to the whole stock of sea fable in a mate volume of 1883. Sea Fables Explained takes up mermaids, the kraken, and the other wonders of sailor lore. Henry Lee writes as a working naturalist who has heard the tales in port and at sea.

Tale by tale, he traces each fable to the real thing that bred it: a dugong, a squid, a trick of fog and light. His aim is not to mock the old sailors, but to show how wonder grows. The book is the great Victorian clearing of mermaid lore. It pairs with his serpent volume as one work of cool reason.
lee-sea-monsters-unmasked-1883:
Henry Lee brought the sea serpent down to earth in 1883 with a smile and a scalpel. Sea Monsters Unmasked explains the famed sightings by known beasts, chief among them the giant squid. Lee was a naturalist at the Brighton Aquarium and knew the sea's true stock well.

A squid's arms, a line of porpoises, a mass of weed: each famed serpent falls to a plain cause in his hands. His wit is dry and his proof is fair, drawn from the reports themselves. The book is the great Victorian debunking of the serpent. Believers and skeptics still fight on the ground Lee chose.
maine-early-law-custom-1883:
Henry Maine published his Dissertations on Early Law and Custom in 1883, gathering his later essays. Maine was by then the elder statesman of historical jurisprudence. The essays state his mature thought on how law grows from custom.

He writes on sovereignty, the king in early law, and the theories of primitive society then in fashion. Maine is skeptical of grand schemes that ignore the records. His comparative eye moves from Rome to India to Ireland. The book closes his career's argument: to know law, study its childhood. Modern legal history still starts its debates where Maine left them.
melitsat-kai-hermeneia-das-ist-onomastic:
Leonhard Thurneisser zum Thurn wrote his Onomasticum, dated 1583 in the record. Thurneisser served as court physician to the Elector of Brandenburg. His long German title calls the book a full account of strange words.

It explains names, words, proverbs, and signs found in Paracelsus. Other authors' works hold the same hard terms, he notes. The words stand in alpha order for readers to look up. The record adds that one part, a plant word book, was never printed at all. A woodcut portrait of the author stands on the title page's back. Red and black print marks the book's grand, learned air.
memoir-correspondence-and-miscellanies-f:
Volume three of Jefferson's papers opens in Paris in 1789. Thomas Jefferson Randolph edited the set, as with the other volumes. Letter one goes to John Jay on July 19, 1789.

Jefferson fears some channel for his mail has proved untrue. He lists months of letters sent with no reply since November 1788. News fills the rest: Algerine pirates took three French merchant ships. France, he says, has armed frigates at Toulon to punish them for the act. Spain, he adds, gets worse treatment from the pirates than France. Such news shows Jefferson's Paris post at a tense hour.
menger-untersuchungen-1883:
Carl Menger published his Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences in German in 1883. Menger, the Viennese founder of the Austrian school, had already recast value theory in his Principles of 1871. The new book defends the method behind that theory against the German historical school, opening the famous battle of methods, the Methodenstreit.

Menger argues that economics can state exact laws, much as the natural sciences do, and that history alone cannot supply them. He sorts the social sciences into kinds and gives each its proper task. The historical school answered hotly, and the quarrel split German-speaking economics for a generation. Menger's side of the argument, stated with the founder's authority, shaped the Austrian tradition down to Mises and Hayek. The book remains its methodological charter.
mirabeau-erotica-biblion-1783:
The Comte de Mirabeau published Erotica Biblion in 1783, a treatise mixing erotic subjects with learned philosophy. The copy hosted here is a German edition from the Hyperion press. Its opening section, headed Anagogie, begins with the ancient manuscripts of Herculaneum. Mirabeau describes the slow, frustrating work of unrolling papyrus rolls charred by Vesuvius.

That scholarly frame introduces a book about love, marriage customs, and the body. A footnote admits that the Greek title will puzzle many readers. Mirabeau wraps scandalous matter in classical learning and wit. The treatise made his name as a bold writer even before his revolutionary fame.
mortillet-le-prehistorique-1883:
Gabriel de Mortillet, a French sage of deep time, set out his scheme of the stone age in this French book of 1883. The title means the prehistoric, the time of man before writ records. Mortillet had built his scheme from years of work on French finds.

He sorts the stone age into named spans: Chellean, Mousterian, Solutrean, and Magdalenian. Each span bears the name of a site and is known by its own tools and art. That scheme, with small changes, is the one the field still uses for those old times.
moses-spirit-teachings-1883:
William Stainton Moses took dictation from the dead in Spirit Teachings, out in 1883. Moses was a priest and school man of good rank. His hand, he said, wrote words not of his own mind as he sat in a daze. The voice named its self Imperator, a guide of high rank, and laid out a creed of love, growth, and life past death.

The words came through years of such sittings. Moses at first fought the claims, then gave his life to them. The book is a chief text of the faith in England. Its calm tone sets it past wild tracts.
openalex-w1566641083:
Paulina Bravo, Marion McAllister, and co-authors wrote this study. It came out in a health services journal in 2015. Health plans aim to give patients more say and strength. Yet no clear shared meaning of that aim existed. The team set out to map what the term should mean.

They read past work and talked with key people in care. The search found scores of texts with mixed meanings. Nineteen talks added views of patients and health chiefs. Five parts anchor their map of the idea. Patient strength forms a scale from low to high. The map links it to skills and shared choices.
openalex-w2010328983:
Dionicia Gamboa, Mei-Fong Ho, Jorge Bendezu and colleagues found a flaw in malaria testing in Peru. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2010. Fast test kits detect a parasite protein called HRP2. Peru planned to use these kits widely. The team asked if local parasites all carry the needed genes.

Tests on samples from Iquitos gave weak or negative results. Lab checks showed many parasites lacked the key genes. A wider study checked samples across the Peruvian Amazon. Many samples lacked one or both of the genes. Without them, fast tests can miss real infections. The finding matters for test choice in the region. Control programmes must allow for these missing-gene parasites.
openalex-w2129852583:
Annette Peters, Bellina Veronesi, Lilian Calderón-Garcidueñas, and colleagues published this review in Particle and Fibre Toxicology in 2006. They sum up evidence on how fine and ultrafine particles in polluted air move through the body. Air pollution is already tied to lung and heart disease, and the authors focus on possible effects on the brain.

The review explains how tiny particles cross from the lung surface into tissue and blood. From there they can reach the liver, spleen, kidneys, heart, and brain. Studies of dogs and people exposed to heavy pollution show signs of brain degeneration. The authors point to oxidative stress as a likely damage pathway.
openalex-w2266202083:
B. Abbott and colleagues in the LIGO and Virgo collaborations published this study in the Astrophysical Journal Letters in 2016. It draws out the astrophysical meaning of GW150914, the first gravitational-wave source ever detected. The signal proved that binary black hole systems exist which spiral together and merge within the universe's lifetime.

The measured masses show that heavy black holes, at least twenty-five times the Sun's mass, form in nature. Making such heavyweights requires weak winds from massive stars, which points to a low-metal birth environment. The merger rate inferred from this single event sits at the high end of predictions. Both rival formation stories, lone binaries and crowded star clusters, remain in play.
openalex-w2835525083:
Martín Thiel, Guillermo Luna-Jorquera, and Rocío Álvarez-Varas lead this 2018 review of plastic pollution in Frontiers in Marine Science. It covers the southeast Pacific, from continental coasts out to the subtropical gyre where floating debris collects. Plastic arrives from land, beach visitors, aquaculture, and fisheries. Rivers carry large loads of both macro- and microplastics.

Most land-based litter stays trapped near its coastal source, the evidence suggests. Strong offshore currents in the Humboldt system sweep the rest toward the open ocean gyre. Microplastic ingestion is now documented across many marine invertebrates. Some species raft on large floating items into habitats they never reached before. Vertebrate interactions, from fish to seabirds, are the best documented impacts. The review assembles a regional picture of a global problem. Its coastline-to-gyre framing shows pollution as a connected journey, not scattered accidents.
openalex-w2912968083:
Herbert Reitsamer, Chelvin Sng, Vanessa Vera, and colleagues report two-year results in Graefe's Archive for Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology in 2019. Their study tested a small gelatin implant, placed from inside the eye, for people whose open-angle glaucoma did not respond to drug treatment.

The trial was prospective, open-label, and run at many centers over two years. Patients began with eye pressure in a set range while using one to four topical drugs. Some received the implant alone, and others received it with cataract surgery. The team tracked changes in eye pressure and drug use at one and two years, plus safety problems during and after surgery.
openalex-w2978107983:
Óscar Serrano, Catherine Lovelock, Trisha Atwood, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2019. It gives the first national account of blue carbon stored in Australia's coastal ecosystems. Tidal marshes, mangroves, and seagrasses lock away carbon that would otherwise warm the planet.

The team measured carbon in living growth and in the top meter of soils across the continent. Mangroves held the great bulk of the above-ground carbon, while seagrasses held most of the soil carbon and did most of the yearly storing. For marshes and seagrasses, nearly all carbon sits in the soil. The totals mark Australia as a global hotspot, strengthening the case for protecting these coasts.
openalex-w2980759483:
Hossein Alishah Aratboni, Nahid Rafiei, Raúl García-Granados, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Microbial Cell Factories. It covers ways to boost biomass and oil output in microalgae grown for biofuel. Fossil fuels drive warming and pollution, so replacements are in demand.

Microalgae grow fast, need no farmland, and hold far more oil than land oil crops. Their weakness is cost, since wild strains often store too little oil to pay off. The review gathers induction strategies that push the algae to build more biomass and pack in more lipids. It also notes other uses for the enriched biomass. The goal is algae fuel that can compete in price with fossil fuel.
openalex-w3011485783:
Jhan Espinoza, René Garreaud, Germán Poveda, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Earth Science in 2020. It is the first part of a survey of the hydroclimate of the Andes, the weather and water patterns of South America's great mountain chain. The Andes form the longest mountain range on Earth.

The chain runs from Patagonia to Venezuela and holds the highest peaks in the inner tropics. Steep, complex terrain and a thin, short weather station record have long hindered study of its air flows and rainfall. The authors gather what is known about the main circulation patterns and how they shape rain and snow across the range. The survey supports planning as climate change threatens the region.
openalex-w3155461783:
Rafael Sarkis-Onofre, Ferrán Catalá-López, Edoardo Aromataris, and Craig Lockwood wrote this editorial for the journal Systematic Reviews in 2021. It explains how authors should, and should not, use the PRISMA Statement. PRISMA is a well-known checklist for reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses in health research.

Many writers misuse PRISMA as a guide for designing studies or as a tool for judging study quality. The authors stress that it is neither. It is a minimum set of reporting rules meant to make reviews open and complete. Used well, it helps readers see what was done and what was found.
openalex-w7204165083:
Tiago Cicotti Furtado wrote a Portuguese-language legal paper, published in Brazil in 2026, on the hidden risk criteria behind pretrial detention in drug trafficking cases in São Paulo. Judges justify preventive prison with formulas such as public order, abstract gravity, and dangerousness. Furtado tests the hypothesis that these formulas carry an unspoken actuarial logic, sorting defendants by predicted risk rather than proven facts.

The study joins review, case law analysis, and a case study. Its argument is that such reasoning drifts away from constitutional rights and reproduces historical patterns of social exclusion, stigma, and penal selectivity. Vulnerable groups end up incapacitated selectively, he contends, under language that presents itself as neutral protection of public peace.
openalex-w7204270383:
Gilvana Nogueira da Silva led a Portuguese-language observational study, published in Brazil in 2026, on how menopause affects quality of life for women seen at two primary health units in Gurupi, Tocantins. The cross-sectional study covered 173 women aged forty to fifty-five, profiling their symptoms, how they perceived them, the impact on personal relationships and quality of life. Their use of hormone therapy or natural alternatives.

Menopausal symptoms were highly prevalent, led by hot flashes, sweating, joint discomfort, anxiety, sleep changes, and vaginal dryness. Hormone therapy use was low, though most users reported satisfaction with it. The effects reach beyond physiology into emotional, social, and functional life, the authors conclude, reinforcing the case for stronger comprehensive women's care in primary health services.
openalex-w7204450783:
Rafaela Oliveira Nessrala dos Santos led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on using artificial intelligence to spot osteoporosis in routine CT scans taken for other reasons. Osteoporosis weakens bone and raises fracture risk, yet it stays widely underdiagnosed until the first fracture. The team searched three sources for original studies from 2021 to mid-2026 and kept eighteen.

The models showed promise at estimating bone density automatically, classifying osteoporosis and osteopenia, detecting vertebral fractures, and predicting future risk, the review reports. But most studies were retrospective, methods varied, and external validation was limited. AI has high potential as support for this opportunistic screening, the authors conclude, though wide adoption needs common standards, multicenter validation, and proof of medical impact.
openalex-w7204569683:
Hamilton Santana Brito led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on mouth problems in people with chronic kidney disease and how dentists should manage them. Reviewing papers from 2015 to 2025 across four sources, the team found that roughly ninety percent of kidney patients show some oral alteration. Dry mouth, gum disease, oral candidiasis, pale mucosa, metallic taste, uremic odor. Heavier tartar buildup, driven by low saliva, metabolic and immune changes, and long medication use.

Gum disease and kidney disease also feed each other through systemic inflammation, the work indicates. The authors conclude that the dentist belongs inside the multiprofessional team, diagnosing, stopping, and managing oral changes to protect these patients' quality of life and overall care.
openalex-w7213110183:
Two views of schooling meet in a survey of Brazil's own journals and meets on science class. One view is Paulo Freire's: school as a path to free the poor through talk and themes from their lives. The next is Lev Vygotsky's: the mind grows in talk with peers, and words build its big thoughts. The survey swept top journals and two big state meets. It read them for the ways the two frames join.

The joins, it finds, fall in five strands. Three strands lead: the role of one's world in growth, the self as a child of its time, and the word as the seed of thought. Two more round it out: the school's part, and class plans built on the frames. The field grows each year, though most works stay at the desk. The two frames, the survey holds, fit as mates.
openalex-w7213391683:
Bianca da Silva Cardoso Porto leads a review on drug interactions in kidney transplant patients. Such patients must take immune-suppressing drugs for life, and those drugs have a narrow safe range. Their 2026 review focuses on risks that may first appear in primary care, away from the transplant centre.

Twenty-two studies from 2016 to 2026 were grouped by drug class. Risky combinations involved antibiotics, antivirals, heart drugs, stomach drugs, and herbal products. Risk rose both when a drug was started and when it was stopped or swapped. Electronic checking tools often disagreed on which risks mattered most. The authors stress careful review at every care visit.
openalex-w7213458583:
Rejane Do Couto Furtado and co-authors propose podcasts as a tool for school inclusion. Their 2026 qualitative article rests on library research. It links technology in teaching with multiliteracies work in fifth-year Portuguese classes in Brazilian elementary schools.

A classroom proposal sits at the centre of the piece. Pupils would use a podcast to make digital material raising awareness of inclusion at school. The authors first trace how technology entered teaching and how teachers responded. They then apply multiliteracies ideas to the Portuguese lesson plan. The hope is to spread teaching practice that is properly set in context and that affirms the presence of pupils with special needs.
openalex-w7213884383:
Marcus Vinícius Barbosa Chagas leads a study of gender and sexuality in nursing curricula in Maranhão, Brazil. Their 2026 documentary research examines eleven public degree courses at two state universities. Lexical searches in Python, checked by hand, covered full course projects and curriculum grids.

Fifty course components touched the theme. Most treated it crosswise, tied to culture, vulnerability, and rights, while a large share stayed biomedical. Specific components on gender and sexuality were rare and all optional. No affirmative mention of gender identity or LGBTQIAPN+ people appeared in the biomedical group. Supervised placements carried no explicit descriptors on the theme. Inclusion in training remains thin, the authors conclude.
openalex-w7214032183:
Jessica Scherrer Silva Rodrigues and co-authors review Kawasaki disease in children. That acute inflammation of small and medium blood vessels mainly strikes children under five. It is a leading cause of acquired heart disease in childhood in developed countries, they note.

No specific laboratory test exists, and symptoms mimic other febrile rash illnesses of childhood. Delay raises the risk of coronary artery aneurysms. Their systematic review covers five databases and primary studies from the last five years, in three languages. Early recognition, laboratory tests, and imaging, above all echocardiography, are essential, they find. Early intravenous immunoglobulin with aspirin remains the standard therapy discussed.
openalex-w7214105083:
Diogo Parizzotto and Rennê Leonardo Sant Anna Gomiero review nutritional supplements for athletic horses, with a critical eye. Their 2026 review covers creatine, proteins, electrolytes, vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, probiotics, fatty acids, and mixed blends. Shops sell plenty of these products, often ahead of solid science, they note.

Electrolyte replacement holds the firmest support, for long exercise with heavy sweat loss. Vitamins and minerals help when intake is low. Antioxidants, probiotics, and fatty acids showed partial effects, mostly on lab markers, without steady sporting gain. Creatine brought no steady gain in performance either. Any such product should fit each horse, they conclude, starting from the base diet and the horse's state.
openalex-w7214126683:
Helayne Cristina Carvalho do Nascimento and Alice Alexandre Pagan study nature, inclusion, and science teaching in João Pessoa, Paraíba. Their 2026 qualitative case study works in a municipal public school. Document consultation, participant observation, and interviews with nine classroom teachers and one specialist teacher supply the evidence.

Teachers link nature to life, sensory experience, memory, care, and environmental responsibility, they find. Lack of green areas limits that work. Images, sounds, objects, talk, drawing, and extended time opened access for special education pupils when tied to learning goals. Nature experience can favour curriculum accessibility, they conclude, when organized around how each student perceives, communicates, and acts.
openalex-w7214704783:
Andrei Boldrini, Rennê Leonardo Sant'Ana Gomiero, and Caroline Hoscheid Werle reported an April 2026 outbreak of bovine trypanosomiasis in a high-producing Holstein dairy herd in western Paraná, Brazil. The disease, caused by the blood parasite Trypanosoma vivax, struck a confined herd in São Pedro do Iguaçu. Of twenty-six animals checked, seventeen showed fever, apathy, loss of appetite, dehydration, weight loss, pale membranes, and a steep drop in milk yield.

Rapid testing and further lab confirmation identified the parasite, and blood measures showed severe anemia; two animals died. The likely route was cattle brought in from eastern Paraná without health screening. Treatment combined a specific anti-parasite therapy, antimicrobials, fluids, supplementation, and blood transfusion for the worst cases, with losses estimated in the tens of thousands of reais. The case underlines early diagnosis and biosecurity when animals move between herds.
openalex-w7214738083:
Kaline Oliveira de Sousa led a ten-author 2026 review of conjunctivitis, or pink eye, in eye emergency services. Following standard review steps, the team searched four databases in three languages and kept fourteen studies from 2020 to 2026. They set out to describe who arrives with conjunctivitis, what doctors find, and how cases are treated in that setting.

Conjunctivitis ranks among the most frequent findings in eye emergencies, with infectious forms, above all viral, leading. Finding the cause stays mostly clinical, based on the patient's account and an external eye exam, with extra tests kept for chosen cases. Most cases resolve on their own and receive gentle care, while antibiotic drops are limited to cases pointing to a bacterial cause. Weather and social conditions shape demand. Knowing this profile, the authors argue, sharpens decisions, cuts needless drug use, and cuts complications and referrals that are not needed.
openalex-w7218515883:
Ivânia Barros Meneses and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva wrote a 2026 library review on welcoming teaching practices in youth and adult education in Brazil, focused on women who return to study. These women's school trajectories are marked by interruptions tied to motherhood, work, the double working day, and gender inequality. The review reads books, articles, dissertations, theses, and documents on adult education, women's paths, school retention, and welcome in school.

Teaching grounded in dialogue, valuing what students already know, meaningful learning, participation, and building a sense of belonging can strengthen women's bond with school, the literature shows. Welcoming, inclusive practices sensitive to women's own situations favor both learning and permanence, the authors conclude, and thereby support success across the whole school path. In a sector built for second chances, how a student who comes back is met is itself a policy for keeping students.
openalex-w7220949583:
Elizabeth Regina Streisky de Farias and Francielly Pereira Campos Clemente studied school management for inclusive education in the first years of primary school, in a 2026 article. Their question is practical. What do school leaders actually decide and do? The test case is pupils with special needs joining ordinary classes.

From a guided search of Portuguese-language studies, five works formed their core material. The themes were space and resources, teacher training, family taking part, and shared school leadership. School leadership, they find, carries inclusion. Yet schools still lack money, trained staff, and expert help. The authors close plainly. Inclusion takes planning, joined-up work, and steady funding, not goodwill alone.
openalex-w7221047483:
Filipe Magno Arouche de Oliveira and three co-authors reviewed research from 2015 to 2025 on eating habits and type 2 diabetes in obese adolescents aged twelve to fifteen. Their 2026 review joins scientific studies with official Brazilian health documents to explain how daily food choices raise the risk of a disease once seen mainly in adults.

Heavy use of ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks, skipped main meals, and few fresh foods emerged as the determining pattern. Such habits feed insulin resistance and obesity, and obese teenagers face up to four times the diabetes risk. The authors stress prevention aimed at adolescents and give nutritionists a central role in changing these habits early.
petrie-pyramids-temples-gizeh-1883:
Young surveyor William Flinders Petrie measured Gizeh with unmatched care for his 1883 book. Petrie later became a founder of modern Egyptology. This early work shows the method that made his name.

He records base lines, angles, and casing stones to fine fractions. His numbers let him judge how the builders planned their work. He faults loose claims made by pyramid writers before him. The prose is dry, exact, and full of tables. Scholars called the survey a gold standard for decades. It remains the measure-first reply to pyramid guesswork.
plos-pbio-0000083:
Keiichi Kondo, William Y. Kim, Mirna Lechpammer, and their team reported a cancer finding in PLOS Biology in 2003. Some kidney tumors grow after the VHL gene is lost. That loss lets a protein called HIF2α build up and push tumor growth forward.

The authors asked a sharp question: is HIF2α the main driver, or just one of many? Their tests show that blocking HIF2α alone is enough to stop these tumors from growing. That narrows a complex pathway to one key target. For drug research, the message is direct. A treatment that lowers HIF2α action might help patients whose tumors lack working VHL.
plos-pbio-0020383:
Stuart H. M. Butchart, Alison J. Stattersfield, and a huge team built a trend index for birds in PLOS Biology in 2004. The Red List ranks species by extinction risk. The team tracked how bird species move between ranks over time. From that, they made an index of whether bird life is gaining or losing.

The index fell, showing birds slipping toward extinction faster than they recovered. A single number that sums thousands of species accounts is a strong tool for policy. Governments had pledged to slow biodiversity loss, and this index lets the world check their progress. Birds were the test case, with like indices for other groups soon to follow.
plos-pone-0000083:
Domenico Girelli, Nicola Martinelli, Oliviero Olivieri, and a large team studied heart surgery outcomes in PLOS ONE in 2006. High blood levels of homocysteine, an amino acid by-product, mark a state called hyperhomocysteinemia. The team checked whether patients with high levels fared worse after coronary artery bypass grafting.

In their group, high homocysteine went with higher death rates after surgery. A blood marker that flags risk before an operation is useful: it can guide watchfulness and care after the graft. The result also adds to the long debate on homocysteine and heart disease. Whether lowering it with vitamins helps remains a separate question the data invite.
plos-pone-0000183:
Philip C. Hill, David J. Jeffries, Roger H. Brookes, and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Contacts of TB patients are checked with skin tests, but a positive result can be a false alarm. The authors use ELISPOT, a blood test that spots immune cells reacting to TB, to expose such false positive conversions.

A skin test that flips positive wrongly can trigger months of needless preventive treatment. Comparing the two tests in the same contacts shows where the skin test misleads. The work supports using blood-based tests to confirm conversions, sharpening TB control programs that track transmission through households.
plos-pone-0000283:
Mathieu Paoletti, Sven J. Saupe, and Corinne Clavé published this fungal genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fungi can tell self from non-self, rejecting tissue from genetically different individuals of the same species. The authors study the genesis, the evolutionary origin, of the repertoire of genes behind that non-self recognition.

A recognition repertoire must be diverse enough to tell many strains apart. Tracing how that diversity arose shows how fungi built an immune-like system without antibodies. The work bears on fungal biology and on the general question of how self-recognition systems evolve.
plos-pone-0000383:
Feng Chen and colleagues compared computer methods for spotting orthologs, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Orthologs are genes in different species that descend from one gene in a shared ancestor. Finding them correctly is a basic step in comparing genomes and tracing how genes evolved.

Several detection strategies exist, and they do not always agree. The team assessed how well the strategies perform when applied to eukaryotic genomes, the DNA of organisms with cell nuclei, from yeast to humans. Benchmarks like this help researchers choose tools they can trust, and they show where methods still mistake look-alike genes for true counterparts.
plos-pone-0000483:
Cesare Massone and colleagues proposed an everyday device as a skin cancer screening tool, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their subject was melanoma screening with cellular phones: using phone cameras and messaging to capture images of suspicious moles and send them for expert review.

Melanoma is curable when caught early and dangerous when late, yet dermatologists are scarce in many regions. A phone-based screen could extend expert eyes to distant patients cheaply. In 2007, phone cameras were still crude, so the idea was forward-looking. The study tested whether the images were good enough to base triage decisions on.
plos-pone-0000583:
Dinesh Adhikary and colleagues prepared immune cells aimed at a lifelong virus, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Epstein-Barr virus infects most people and hides in their cells for life. The team studied Epstein-Barr virus-specific CD4+ T cell preparations made for therapy. They asked which lytic cycle antigens dominate. In other words, which viral proteins do the therapeutic T cells mainly recognize?

Cell therapy grows a patient's own T cells against the virus and returns them, a strategy used when drugs fail. Knowing which antigens dominate the response tells makers whether their product aims at the right targets. Lytic antigens come from the virus's active phase, relevant when it reactivates in immune-suppressed patients.
plos-pone-0000683:
Marcella Funicello, Michela Novelli, Maurizio Ragni and co-authors studied mice lacking a fat-related enzyme for PLOS ONE in 2007. Proteases, proteins that cut other proteins, are implicated in fat formation and the onset of obesity. The team had reported that one cysteine protease, cathepsin K, is overexpressed in the white fat tissue of obese individuals.

Here they characterized the fat tissue of mice with the cathepsin K gene knocked out. The title states the result: during the rapid buildup of fat stores, these mice showed reduced adiposity. Linking one protease to fat gain suggests a drug target, and it reshapes how fat tissue growth is understood.
plos-pone-0000783:
Alberto Viera, Rocío Gómez, María T. Parra and colleagues watched a chromosome-shaping complex at work in mouse meiosis, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Chromosomes must be shaped and individualized so genomes segregate correctly in mitotic and meiotic divisions. In vertebrates, three multiprotein complexes drive that shaping: cohesin and condensins I and II. Meiosis, the division making sperm and eggs, has its own special chromosome choreography.

Their title promises new insights from condensin I on mouse meiotic chromosome structure and dynamics. Errors in meiosis cause infertility and conditions such as Down syndrome. Knowing which complex does what, and when, fills a basic gap in reproductive biology.
plos-pone-0000883:
Michael Lombardo, Jennifer Barnes, Sally Wheelwright and co-authors tested self-focused thought and empathy in autism, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. People on the autism spectrum often find social life hard. Whether they also differ when thinking about themselves, rather than about others, was much less clear.

The team used several well tested measures to compare self-referential cognition, thinking tied to oneself, with empathy for others. Keeping those two domains apart matters: a person can struggle with one and not the other. The study helps refine what autism affects, and what it may leave intact. That sharper picture can guide fairer tests and better support.
plos-pone-0000983:
Aparna Nittala, Soumitra Ghosh and Xujing Wang modeled how the layout of insulin cells shapes their rhythm, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Insulin leaves the pancreas in pulses, and that pulsing is basic to healthy blood sugar control. The pulses come from beta cells in each islet firing together, coupled to their neighbors.

The team built a new beta cell cluster model to ask what islet cytoarchitecture, the physical arrangement of the cells, does to the oscillation. Arrangement is easy to overlook beside chemistry. Yet if layout tunes the rhythm, then damage to islet structure in diabetes matters in its own right, not just cell loss.
plos-pone-0001083:
Dan Valente, Ilan Golani and Partha Mitra analyzed how fruit flies move in a circular arena, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Describing the full behavior of a freely moving animal is hard. Yet studies of the brain and behavior need exactly such records.

Existing metrics for movement are partial at best. They capture speed or turning, but not the whole pattern. The team present an analysis of the fly's trajectory as a complete record. Drosophila is the workhorse of genetics, so a rigorous behavior language for it serves many labs. Their approach treats the path itself as the phenotype to be explained.
plos-pone-0001183:
Diabetes often comes with reduced thyroid function and poor muscle repair after injury. Bernhard Baumgartner and colleagues went looking for a missing piece of thyroid hormone action in muscle, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They identified a gene, named DOR, that is abundant in insulin-sensitive tissues and is repressed in diabetic rat muscle.

The authors describe DOR as a novel modulator of thyroid hormone receptor-mediated action. A modulator is a protein that tunes how strongly a hormone's receptor works. Finding one that diabetes turns down connects two features of the disease, low thyroid action and weak muscle regeneration, in a single mechanism.
plos-pone-0001283:
Chuuk State, in the Federated States of Micronesia, saw its first two locally acquired HIV infections, and health officials moved to assess the risk. Toya Russell and colleagues surveyed sexual risk behaviors there, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The purpose was to assess the need for HIV education and prevention services and to develop recommendations for those services.

Remote, at-risk populations are often reached only after an epidemic is established. This study gathered first evidence before that happened in Chuuk. Its case is for early prevention fitted to a small island population.
plos-pone-0001383:
Vladimir Hampl and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a tiny single celled creature called Trimastix. Most complex cells hold small power plants called mitochondria. A few gut parasites were once thought to lack them and to have split off before such plants arose. Trimastix was one of those cases.

The team found gene proof that Trimastix did once have such power plants. Its stock of genes fits a past with them, not a past without them. That shifts where this creature sits on the tree of life. It also adds weight to the view that all complex cells share one root that held these power plants.
plos-pone-0001483:
Héctor Pálmer and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on skin growth signals. Two signals, one from the Wnt path and one from vitamin D, jointly steer how skin cells mature. Many skin genes switched on by the Wnt path carry vitamin D response marks. The team traced how the two signals share control of hair growth.

They show the vitamin D receptor acts as a Wnt effector in skin. It helps set how hair base cells mature and which tumor type forms in adult skin. That dual role was not in the standard account. It may guide new care for hair loss and skin tumors alike.
plos-pone-0001583:
Lisa Lindqvist and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the first drug aimed at one RNA helicase. Helicases unwind RNA and serve in making proteins, splicing, and RNA decay. They have little aim by nature, so blocking just one was a hard task. The team sought a drug that hits a single helicase tied to protein making.

They report a compound that does pick out that one helicase. A first in class drug proves the family can be drugged with aim. Such drugs could serve as probes, and in time as cures for ills where this helicase runs high. The work opens a new shelf in drug design.
plos-pone-0001683:
Michael J. Stringer, Marta Sales-Pardo, and Luís A. Nunes Amaral tested how well journal rankings help scientists find information, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Electronic publishing, preprint archives, blogs, and wikis had raised doubts about the place of journals and peer review. If readers can find anything online, do ranked journal lists still guide them to what matters?

The authors measured the effectiveness of ranking schemes as search tools. The full text gives their model of how scientists search, the rankings tested, and how often each scheme led readers to relevant work. The results feed a live debate about how science sorts its own flood of papers, and whether prestige rankings serve readers or mainly reward journals.
plos-pone-0001783:
Chee Gee Liew, Nadia N. Shah, Sarah J. Briston, and their co-authors pushed stem cells toward becoming insulin-making cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Human embryonic stem cells, grown as floating aggregates called embryoid bodies, differentiate into a haphazard mix of cell types from all three germ layers. Steering them to one fate is the challenge.

The team reports that PAX4, a transcription factor, enhances the differentiation of these stem cells into pancreatic beta cells. Those are the cells that make insulin and are lost in diabetes. The full text gives the culture method and the beta-cell markers. Reliable beta-cell production in the lab is a long-sought step toward cell replacement therapy for diabetes.
plos-pone-0001883:
Camille Boutin and co-authors shared a new lab method in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Their method slips genes into the brain of young mice. Testing what a gene does inside a live animal is still a core task in medical research. The front part of the brain, the forebrain, is a key site for thought and acts.

The method injects DNA into the fluid space of the brain in newborn mice, then uses a mild electric pulse to push it into cells. The team shows the trick works well in pups soon after birth. A cheap, fast way to add genes lets more labs test brain gene roles without slow breeding of mutant lines.
plos-pone-0001983:
James Curtin and co-authors sounded a caution on removing a class of immune cells in cancer therapy, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Regulatory T cells, or Tregs, damp down immune attack. They infiltrate glioblastoma, a deadly brain tumor, and track with tumor grade. In mice, wiping Tregs out briefly had shrunk such tumors.

The team tested Treg depletion alongside cancer immunotherapy, which tries to turn the immune system on the tumor. As the title states, depletion inhibited the therapy's efficacy instead of aiding it. That surprise matters for trial design: a step that helps alone may hurt when paired with immune therapy.
plos-pone-0002083:
Lesley Brennan and co-authors studied a bacterium that lives inside mosquito cells and shifts the host's stress defenses, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Wolbachia pipientis is an obligate inside-cell bacterium that commonly infects arthropods. Passed from mother to young, it can alter host development, sex, and reproduction in striking ways.

The team used a cell line from the mosquito Aedes albopictus that carries Wolbachia. As the title states, the endosymbiont induces the expression of host antioxidant proteins, which guard against chemical damage. A guest that raises host defenses may change how mosquitoes carry viruses, a trait vector control hopes to use.
plos-pone-0002183:
Fang Tang, Wei Liu, Fang Zhang, and co-authors looked for gene variants that change the risk of SARS, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. SARS, severe acute respiratory syndrome, swept through China and beyond in 2003. Cytokines, the immune system's signal proteins, play key roles in fighting viruses, so genes that tune them may shape who gets badly ill.

The team ran a case-control study in Chinese SARS patients, focusing on variants in the gene for the IL-12 receptor, IL-12RB1.
