They report that some variants add to a person's chance of catching SARS or faring worse. Such findings help explain why the same virus strikes some people far harder than others.
plos-pone-0002283:
Yasuhide Iwata, Katsuaki Suzuki, Tomoyasu Wakuda, and co-authors tested whether radiation in adult rats can model schizophrenia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Population studies had suggested that radiation exposure may be a risk factor for schizophrenia in adult humans. No animal model had directly tested that link with adult exposure.

The team gave adult rats a total dose of 15 gray of irradiation in six fractions and checked their behavior. They looked for abnormalities relevant to schizophrenia, such as changes in activity and response to startling sounds. A radiation-based model, if it holds, would give researchers a new handle on how this illness can arise in adult life.
plos-pone-0002383:
McGrath led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are John McGrath, Takeshi Iwazaki, Darryl Eyles, among others. Its subject is protein Expression in the Nucleus Accumbens of Rats Exposed to Developmental Vitamin D Deficiency. Developmental vitamin D (DVD) deficiency is a candidate risk factor for schizophrenia.

Animal models have confirmed that DVD deficiency is linked to a range of altered genomic, proteomic, structural and behavioural outcomes in the rat. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002483:
Gennaro and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Luigi De Gennaro, Fabiana Fratello, Cristina Marzano, among others. Its subject is cortical Plasticity Induced by Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation during Wakefulness Affects Electroencephalogram Activity during Sleep. Sleep electroencephalogram (EEG) brain oscillations in the low-frequency range show local signs of homeostatic regulation after learning.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002583:
El-Bchiri joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Jamila El-Bchiri, Agathe Guilloux, Peggy Dartigues, among others. Its subject is nonsense-Mediated mRNA Decay Impacts MSI-Driven Carcinogenesis and Anti-Tumor Immunity in Colorectal Cancers. Nonsense-mediated mRNA Decay (NMD) degrades mutant mRNAs containing premature termination codon (PTC-mRNAs).

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002683:
Mogens Kilian and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on evolution of streptococcus pneumoniae and its close commensal relatives. The catalog record names Mogens Kilian first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a member of the Mitis group of streptococci which, according to 16S rRNA-sequence based phylogenetic reconstruction, includes 12 species. It goes on to note a further point. While other species of this group are considered prototypes of commensal bacteria, S. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002783:
Jean-Jacques Parienti and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was not all missed doses are the same: sustained NNRTI treatment interruptions predict HIV rebound at Low-to-Moderate adherence levels. Authorship is credited in the record to Jean-Jacques Parienti and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. While the relationship between average adherence to HIV potent antiretroviral therapy is well defined. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002883:
Giovanna Vinci, Xuhua Xia and Reiner A. Veitia asked in PLOS ONE in 2008 why some animals keep genes they no longer seem to need. Enzymes that build sterols are much alike across species that make sterols from scratch. Yet two animals that cannot make cholesterol still kept copies of the matching genes.

Those animals are called cholesterol auxotrophs, meaning they must get cholesterol from food. The paper weighs facts and possible reasons for the genes staying in place. It may be that the genes now serve other jobs. The puzzle helps readers think about how genomes shed, or keep, old tools.
plos-pone-0002983:
Haichun Gao, Donna Pattison, Tingfen Yan and co-authors built a clone collection for the bacterium Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 in 2008. They constructed the set with a recombinase cloning system that lets genes be moved between plasmids with ease. In total, 3,584 individual genes, about 85 percent, were cloned successfully.

To validate the set, three groups of genes were tested in protein expression and phage display. Published in PLOS ONE, the resource serves work on a bacterium prized for breathing metals and cleaning polluted sites. Shared clone sets save every lab from rebuilding the same tools. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003083:
Giuseppe Pagnoni, Milos Cekic and Ying Guo scanned the brains of Zen meditators in 2008. Brain imaging had identified a default network active during wakeful rest that deactivates during demanding tasks. That network was linked to the stream of thoughts running through the mind at rest.

Their study, titled around thinking about not-thinking, examines conceptual processing during Zen meditation. Published in PLOS ONE, meditators offer a trained case of quieting that stream. The work tests how a practiced mind handles the default network differently. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003183:
Thomas L. Turner, Eric J. von Wettberg and Sergey V. Nuzhdin search for local adaptation genes in a rockcress in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Serpentine soil is naturally high in heavy metals and has a low calcium to magnesium ratio, making a difficult home for most plants. Yet many species live only on serpentine, and many wider taxa have been shown to adapt to it.

The team analyse genomic differences between soil types in Arabidopsis lyrata to reveal candidate genes for local adaptation. Readers see adaptation traced to specific genome regions. The work helps explain how plants colonize harsh soils that would poison most species.
plos-pone-0003283:
Digna R. Velez, Stephen J. Fortunato, Poul Thorsen and colleagues link gene variants to preterm birth in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Spontaneous preterm birth, before thirty-seven weeks, occurs in about twelve percent of pregnancies in the United States and is the largest contributor to neonatal morbidity and mortality. Preterm birth is a complex disease potentially induced by several causes from multiple pathways.

The title reports that preterm birth in Caucasians is associated with coagulation and inflammation pathway gene variants. Readers see two biological routes, clotting and inflammation, tied genetically to early birth. Such variants may help identify pregnancies needing closer care.
plos-pone-0003383:
Frank Ludewig and colleagues studied a chemical bypass in plants in this 2008 paper. The bypass, called the GABA shunt, skips two steps of the cell energy cycle. It runs in microbes and green plants alike. The team worked with Arabidopsis plants missing one enzyme of the shunt.

Plants without that enzyme, named ssadh, grew very poorly. Adding a fault in a second enzyme, GABA transaminase or POP2, eased the damage. That rescue shows the two enzymes balance each other in the pathway. The result helps explain how plants keep this bypass under control.
plos-pone-0003483:
Richard M. Cubbon and co-authors weighed diabetes risk after heart events in this 2008 study. Diabetes is linked to worse outcomes after acute coronary syndrome. That added risk may vary with each patient's total risk load. The team split cases into first events and repeat events.

They asked if diabetes raised death rates in both settings alike. Comparing the groups gave a more nuanced risk picture. First and recurrent events do not carry the same meaning. Such detail helps doctors set follow-up care for diabetic heart patients. Heart events remain the top cause of death for people with diabetes.
plos-pone-0003583:
Brendan J. Keating and co-authors built a heart-focused gene chip in this 2008 paper. Gene-centric arrays target variants inside and near known genes. Their array packed fifty thousand SNPs for cardiovascular study. SNP markers are single-letter DNA differences between people.

The paper covers the concept, design, and implementation of the array. Large-scale association studies were its intended use. A shared platform lets many teams hunt cardiac risk genes comparably. Purpose-built tools can beat generic genome scans for one disease area. Heart gene hunts need very large samples, which shared chips make cheaper.
plos-pone-0003683:
Arun T. Kamath, Anne-Françoise Rochat, Mario P. Valenti, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Newborns usually answer subunit vaccines more weakly than adults do. Their responses lean away from the Th1 style that fights microbes inside cells. That gap has slowed work on infant vaccines.

The team tested a vaccine with the antigens Ag85B and ESAT-6 in the adjuvant IC31. Given to newborns, it drew T cell and dendritic cell responses much like those of adults. Such adult-like responses at birth are a step toward tuberculosis vaccines that protect from the start of life.
plos-pone-0003783:
Liraz Kantor, Dalia Pinchasi, Michelle Mintz, and colleagues published this brain disease study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Faults in a protein called eIF2B cause a childhood disease where brain white matter vanishes under stress. The protein helps start the making of new proteins in cells. Oligodendrocytes are the cells that build myelin.

The team studied a point mutation in eIF2B in cells derived from oligodendroglia. The single change left the cells in a continuous hyper stress state. That constant alarm helps explain why myelin is lost when the body is stressed in this disease.
plos-pone-0003883:
Sandra Spronk, Johanna L. Bosch, Constance Ryjewski, and co-authors weighed heart rehab costs in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article looks at patients with coronary artery disease. Many such patients also have blocked leg arteries, called peripheral arterial disease. That leg problem often gets in the way of rehab exercise programs.

The authors compared new rehab plans that also find and treat the leg disease. They asked whether the added care pays for itself in health gained. Cost studies of this kind help clinics choose programs they can afford. The work speaks to hospitals planning rehab for patients with both heart and vessel disease.
plos-pone-0003983:
Yuji Ikegaya, Wataru Matsumoto, Huei-Yu Chiou, and co-authors tested precision in neuron firing patterns in 2008. Synaptic transmission is probabilistic, so exact repeats seem unlikely. Some brain theories still predict millisecond-accurate patterns can emerge. Networks might use such precision as a code.

Their PLOS ONE article weighs the statistical significance of repeated patterns. Recordings came from synapses inside cells in their experiments. Precise repeats beyond chance would support timing-based coding. The study gives other labs a method to judge pattern claims. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004083:
Yasuyuki Hashiguchi, Yoshimi Furuta, and Mutsumi Nishida surveyed smell receptor families in fish in 2008. Teleost fish lack the separate vomeronasal organ found in land animals. Their vomeronasal-type receptors sit in the main smell tissue instead. Odorant and trace amine receptors share that same tissue.

Their PLOS ONE article traces evolutionary patterns across receptor gene families. It also weighs the selective pressures shaping each family. Fish smell systems reorganized as vertebrates moved between water and land. Comparing families clarifies what pheromone sensing does in fish. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004183:
Weiping Qin and colleagues published this Alzheimer's study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia in older people. There is no cure, and there were no early diagnostic tests when this study appeared. So the hunt for a biomarker, a measurable sign of disease, was urgent.

The team studied S100A7, a protein they put forward as a novel biomarker. They report that it acts by selectively boosting ADAM-10, an enzyme that cuts the amyloid precursor protein in the safer, non-amyloid route. One protein thus offers both a possible early sign of disease and a clue to slowing it.
plos-pone-0004283:
Robert De Lisle and colleagues published this cystic fibrosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cystic fibrosis affects the gastrointestinal tract in many ways, and poor nutrition is a common problem. In the CF mouse, an innate immune response floods the small intestine's muscle wall with mast cells. The same mice show disordered movement of the gut.

The team examined how those mast cells relate to the gastrointestinal dysmotility, the faulty movement of food through the gut. Separating cause from bystander matters, because mast cells can be targeted by existing drugs.
plos-pone-0004383:
Malaria still kills many children across Africa each year. Tools that cut contact with mosquitoes save lives now. Azra Ghani, Colin Sutherland, Eleanor Riley, and co-authors asked a longer question in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper weighs what happens to group immunity when exposure falls. It also asks how that change can distort readings of disease trends.

People in high-malaria areas build partial immunity through repeated infection. Cut exposure, and that shield can fade over time. Later case counts may then shift for reasons beyond control efforts alone. The authors argue trends must be read with immunity loss in mind. Their warning supports steady, lasting control rather than short campaigns.
plos-pone-0004483:
Two lab methods that are hard to run at once are combined by Daniela Moralli and Zoia Monaco in PLOS ONE in 2009. One method, called FISH, uses glowing probes to find and locate specific DNA stretches in cells. The other labels newly copied DNA with a chemical called BrdU, which shows where and when DNA replication happened.

Running both together on fixed, cultured cells lets scientists watch replication and know exactly which DNA is being copied. Earlier, the treatments for one method tended to wreck the other. The authors set out a way to detect both signals in the same cells. That pairing gives cell biology a sharper tool for studying how genomes copy themselves, a process that goes wrong in cancer.
plos-pone-0004583:
Losing one copy of several genes at once may drive a group of bone marrow disorders, argue Timothy Graubert, Michelle Payton, Jin Shao, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disorders are myelodysplastic syndromes, in which the marrow makes faulty blood cells. Deletions spanning a region of chromosome 5, called 5q31.2, are among the most common recurring abnormalities in these syndromes.

Earlier studies suggested haploinsufficiency: half dosage of multiple genes in the region, together, contributes to the disease. The team used integrated genomic analysis to test that idea in patients whose disease arose anew. Their evidence implicates the combined loss, as the title states. That shapes therapy thinking: no single missing gene means no single fix.
plos-pone-0004683:
Marine Grandgeorge and colleagues asked how home and social life shape speech growth in autistic children, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Normal growth is known to mix genes and life events. For mental health traits, past work has stressed genes and body causes far more than daily surroundings.

The team shifted focus to the world around the child. They looked at factors in family and social life that may help or hold back speech growth. That view can guide support that goes past drugs or clinic drills. It points to changes at home and school that may help a child learn to speak.
plos-pone-0004783:
Xuejun Xu and colleagues found chemical probes that selectively block Stat3 activation, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Stat3 is a signaling protein that is switched on in many cancers and helps drive tumor growth. Finding compounds that hit Stat3 without harming related proteins is a key goal for drug discovery in this pathway.

The team screened a vast library of drug like compounds on a computer. Top hits were then tested for selective, competitive blocking of Stat3. Selective probes help scientists dissect Stat3 roles in cells. They are also starting points for cancer drugs. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory.
plos-pone-0004883:
Hiroki Sugiura and Michael Dickinson measured generation of forces and moments during visual evoked steering in flying Drosophila, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sideslip, long term force, rolling moment, and pitching moment generated by tethered fruit flies were measured during optomotor reactions within an electronic flight simulator. Forces and torques were acquired by optically measuring angular deflections of a sensitive sensor as flies attempted steering maneuvers.

Precise force records decode fly flight control. Insects adjust forces within milliseconds of visual change. Robotics borrows such agile strategies. Tethered assays reveal natural aerodynamics. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004983:
Animals flash ornaments to advertise their quality. Why should rivals or mates believe the ad? Gary Bortolotti and colleagues tested one answer in PLOS ONE in 2009. The classic idea involves testosterone and immunity. They focused instead on physiological stress. Stress is measured through the hormone corticosterone.

Their results show stress mediates the honesty of social signals. Only birds in good condition can afford the full display. The stress hormone links body condition to ornament quality. That keeps the signal truthful. The study supports a physiological basis for honest advertising. It refines a long-standing debate in behavioral ecology.
plos-pone-0005083:
People judge health from faces. Skin color carries much of that judgment. Ian Stephen and colleagues tested the cues in PLOS ONE in 2009. They let participants manipulate calibrated face images. The controls changed skin blood perfusion and oxygenation color. Other participants then rated the faces for health.

Faces with richer blood color and oxygenation looked healthier. Skin blood state depends on cardiovascular and hormonal health. Our eyes read circulation as a health signal. Other primates use similar signals for dominance and status. The finding shows a deep perceptual habit. It may explain why illness so visibly pales the face. It also matters for designing health displays and avatars.
plos-pone-0005183:
The hearing cortex of the brain is laid out in fields that respond to sound, much like keys on a piano. Less was known about how other features of sound, or focused attention, change those maps. Woods and colleagues used brain scans to study the question in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Volunteers heard sounds while the team recorded activity with functional magnetic resonance imaging. The maps showed that sound features and attention both reshape how the cortex responds. Hearing, in other words, is not passive intake. The brain edits incoming sound, and this work shows where that editing takes place.
plos-pone-0005283:
Glucocorticoids are stress hormones that rise in wasting illnesses, and muscle melts away in those states. Part of the loss may come from eating less rather than from the hormones directly. You and colleagues separated those two factors in rodents in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team gave high glucocorticoid doses, restricted food, or both, then measured muscle energy use and protein metabolism. Separating the factors shows how much damage each one does on its own. That split matters for feeding and drug plans in patients losing muscle. When a sick man or woman eats less, the muscle loss that follows can slow their cure. So care teams need to know which share of the loss food can and cannot fix.
plos-pone-0005383:
Persistent bacterial infections, such as tuberculosis, are far harder to cure than acute ones. Where the bacteria hide in the body during those long infections is poorly known. Eswarappa analyzed that location problem with game theory in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Game theory treats host and pathogen as opposing players choosing strategies. Applied to hiding places, it predicts where pathogens gain most by locating. A strategic lens cannot replace experiments, but it can tell researchers which locations are worth searching first. Where germs hide sets the dose and the length of care, since drugs reach some parts of the body well and others barely at all. So a good guess at the map saves real lives in the end.
plos-pone-0005483:
Kedar Mate and co-authors studied health data systems in South Africa in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. South Africa runs a large program to stop mothers from passing HIV to their babies. New rules had raised hopes that passing rates could fall to a very low level.

The authors looked at how routine health data are gathered and managed in that program. Weak data make it hard to know which clinics need help or whether care reaches mothers at all. Their findings point to fixes in forms, training, and checking that could make the program's own numbers trustworthy.
plos-pone-0005583:
Mandi Murph and co-authors studied a fat-like signal in ovarian cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A signal called LPA is rich in the fluid that builds up in the bellies of ovarian cancer patients. Cancer cells there carry unusual levels of receptors for it.

The team profiled which genes LPA switches on in ovarian cancer cells. That pattern matched the aggressive form of the disease and worse patient outcomes. A gene pattern tied to LPA could help doctors judge a patient's outlook and choose treatment. Ovarian cancer is often found late, so any sign tied to outlook is weighed with great care.
plos-pone-0005683:
Athe Tsibris and co-authors used deep sequencing in 2009 to watch HIV change inside patients on a new kind of drug. The drug blocks CCR5, a doorway HIV uses to enter cells. When the doorway is blocked, virus types that use a second doorway can take over.

Reading thousands of viral gene copies at once let the team spot rare types early. They followed four people with long-term HIV through treatment. The data show big shifts in the virus mix as the drug pressed on it. Such close tracking helps doctors see escape coming and adjust therapy before it fails.
plos-pone-0005783:
Christopher Brooks and co-authors asked in 2009 what drives forest clearing near a Madagascar national park. The highland forests around Ranomafana hold species found nowhere else, and some of the world's poorest people live beside them. Fast population growth adds pressure to farm more land.

The team weighed demography against markets as causes of deforestation rates. If markets pull the clearing, price and access fixes may help; if sheer numbers push it, other plans are needed. Knowing the true driver keeps conservation money from being spent on the wrong lever. The study grounds that choice in local data.
plos-pone-0005883:
Konika Banerjee and co-authors tested in 2009 whether general intelligence exists in a small New World monkey. In humans, scores across many mental tasks rise and fall together, defining the trait called g. Almost nothing was known about whether other primates show the same pattern.

Cotton-top tamarins took a battery of cognitive tasks, and individuals' scores correlated across domains. That is evidence for g beyond humans. A shared factor in a distant primate suggests deep evolutionary roots for general intelligence. The study opens comparative work on how such a factor arises and what it costs.
plos-pone-0005983:
Common spelling changes in DNA each shift cancer risk by a little. Lydia Quaye, Jonathan Tyrer, Susan Ramus and colleagues hunted such changes for ovarian cancer in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study tests variants across ninety-four candidate genes or regions in women with the invasive epithelial form of the disease and in women without it.

Known strong risk genes explain only part of family risk, so the search turns to these weaker, common variants. Testing so many candidates at once sets a fair bar for which links are real. The work feeds the slow build of a risk map for ovarian cancer, one that may one day guide screening for women at higher risk.
plos-pone-0006083:
Knowing how hard malaria strikes a place guides where control money goes. Laveta Stewart, Roly Gosling, Jamie Griffin and colleagues offered a faster gauge in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tests age-specific sero-conversion rates, blood markers that show past infection, as a rapid way to assess malaria transmission in a community.

Bugs and blood smears, the older gauges, are slow and costly to gather well. Antibody patterns by age can be read from a single survey round. A rapid local estimate lets health teams focus bed nets, spraying and drugs where transmission truly runs hot, a gain for countries where malaria money must stretch far.
plos-pone-0006183:
Staring at a pattern for a long time changes how the next pattern looks. Kai-Markus Mueller and colleagues studied this effect, called visual adaptation, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Brain cells that sense tilted and curved lines are thought to be basic building blocks for seeing shapes and objects.

Long exposure to such lines produces two after-effects that feel linked at first glance. The team shows the two effects can come apart, so they rest on partly separate processes. That split tells vision scientists that one simple fatigue story cannot explain adaptation. It refines how labs should test early shape vision in the brain.
plos-pone-0006283:
Peer review decides which science gets published, and reviewers bring their own records with them. Lonnie Aarssen and colleagues asked whether publishing in top journals changes reviewer behaviour, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on ecologists. The team compared reviewers' own publication records with the rejection rates they recommended.

Reviewers who publish often in high-impact journals recommended rejection more often. Reviewer age showed no such link. The pattern suggests success in prestige publishing may harden the gate for others. The finding feeds wider debate about fairness in how science judges itself.
plos-pone-0006383:
During a fast eye movement, the brain squeezes the seen world toward the movement's target. Atsushi Noritake and colleagues tested that saccadic compression with rectangles and Kanizsa figures in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Earlier studies suggested compression vanishes when dots are perceived as one unified object, like a rectangle.

The team investigated whether illusory-contour figures behave like real rectangles. Their title jokes about the effect: now you see it, now you don't. How compression treats grouped shapes reveals the brain's object rules. Vision corrects for eye jumps so seamlessly that only experiments expose the trickery.
plos-pone-0006483:
Nicolas Penel and co-authors built a bedside score for a hard cancer situation in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some patients have cancer of unknown primary, where spread is found but the starting site is not. The team investigated predictors of death within ninety days in a large cohort of such patients. They identified predictors with statistical tests on patient data.

From those predictors they developed and validated a simple bedside score. A score that flags early death risk helps doctors choose between aggressive treatment and comfort-focused care. It also helps families plan. Validation in separate data is what makes such a score safe to use.
plos-pone-0006583:
Christopher Phillips, Lourdes Prieto, Manuel Fondevila, and colleagues applied ancestry analysis to a bombing investigation in PLOS ONE in 2009. The 11-M Madrid commuter train bombings of 2004 were the second biggest terrorist attack in Europe after Lockerbie. The subsequent investigation became a major forensic effort. DNA evidence from the scenes needed interpretation.

Ancestry analysis uses DNA markers to infer a person's geographic origins. Applied forensically, it can guide investigators when other leads are thin. The study shows how population genetics served a real investigation. It also raises questions about the proper use of such inference.
plos-pone-0006683:
Rachel M. Brown, Edwin M. Robertson, and Daniel Z. Press studied learning and aging in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some mental abilities clearly decline as people grow older. Memory for facts and events is known to weaken with age. Less clear is how aging affects learning a new skill. The authors focused on sequence skill acquisition in healthy older adults.

Participants practiced a sequence task, and the team tracked off-line learning. Off-line learning means gains that appear after practice ends, often after rest. Comparing younger and older learners showed where aging changes the process. The findings help separate normal aging from disease in skill learning. They also inform how training might be timed for older adults.
plos-pone-0006783:
Traude H. Beilharz and her team pinned down how small RNAs mute gene messages in mammal cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The small RNAs are microRNAs. They latch onto gene messages and cut how much protein gets made. They also trim the tail at the end of the message. A short tail is a step toward the message being destroyed.

The team asked how much that tail trim, called deadenylation, does the muting. Their tests show the trim is a true part of the act in mammal cells. With its tail cut, the message breaks down fast. Less protein gets made as a result. Knowing the steps helps those who build RNA drugs.
plos-pone-0006883:
Andreas Kurth and colleagues reported a cowpox outbreak in zoo animals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cowpox virus infections are described as an extremely rare zoonosis. Cases in Germany are nevertheless increasing. The virus is rodent-borne with a broad host range. It carries the largest genome of all poxviruses.

Banded mongooses and jaguarundis fell ill in the outbreak. Human infection followed after a time delay. The delay shows how animal outbreaks can precede human cases. Zoo settings bring exotic species and keepers into close contact. Tracking such outbreaks protects both collections and staff.
plos-pone-0006983:
Maria Antonietta Costa, Carney Matheson, Lucia Iachetta, and colleagues found an ancient disease in Chile in PLOS ONE in 2009. Leishmaniasis is a parasitic infection still common in parts of South America. The team studied skulls from Coyo Oriente, an old cemetery in the Atacama desert near San Pedro. The site sits in a highland desert of northern Chile.

Four female skulls carried signs of the infection. The evidence was both in bone shape and in molecules. Finding the disease in ancient remains pushes its known history back in the region. It also shows desert peoples long lived with this parasite.
plos-pone-0007083:
M. Melissa Gilbert, Carolyn Beam, Brian Robinson, and colleagues crossed fly tumor genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The human gene TSG101 helps route membrane proteins to disposal. It is suspected as a target in cancer, though its loss effects in vertebrates are unclear. In fly tissues, by contrast, losing its counterpart ept clearly changes growth.

The team tested genetic interactions between ept and stat92E, a transcription factor gene. Pairing mutations reveals which signals cooperate in growth control. Such interaction maps show how disposal defects and signaling defects combine. They help explain why some mutation pairs drive tumors while singles do not.
plos-pone-0007183:
Yvonne Vercoulen, Ellen J. Wehrens, Nienke H. van Teijlingen, and colleagues studied human regulatory T cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. These cells, often shortened to Tregs, keep the immune system in balance. Without them, the body risks autoimmune disease, where immunity attacks its own tissues.

One open question was how Tregs calm activated effector T cells in humans. Mouse work had suggested they might force those cells to die. The authors test that idea directly and report that suppression works independently of such cell death. Their result narrows the search for the real mechanism.
plos-pone-0007283:
Frank W. King, Sylvia Fong, Chandi Griffin, and colleagues studied a plant compound that kills tumor cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. An extract of the plant Anemarrhena asphodeloides kills various cancer cells. It is much less toxic to normal, non-transformed cells, a selectivity drug hunters prize in early leads.

Fractionation linked the killing power to timosaponins, a family of steroidal compounds. The authors focus on timosaponin AIII. They report it is preferentially cytotoxic to tumor cells through blocking mTOR signaling and inducing stress in the endoplasmic reticulum. That dual action makes it a lead for cancer drug research.
plos-pone-0007383:
Ombretta Caspani, Sandra Zurborg, Dominika Labuz, and colleagues studied cold pain sensors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Cold allodynia is enhanced sensitivity to cold, a common feature of neuropathic pain. Its underlying mechanisms were not known, leaving patients with few targeted treatments for this disabling symptom after nerve injury.

Two channels, TRPM8 and TRPA1, had been proposed as molecular cold sensors. The authors test the contribution of both channels to cold allodynia and neuropathic pain. Their experiments separate the roles of the two sensors. Knowing which channel drives cold pain could focus drug development.
plos-pone-0007483:
Mailyn Gonzalez and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on naming the trees of the Amazon rainforest. Conservation planning depends on large inventories of plant diversity. Classic taxonomy, naming species by eye, is slow and expert-hungry. That bottleneck is worst in megadiverse tropical forests. The team tested DNA barcodes, short genetic tags, as a faster way to identify trees from a detailed forest census.

Working from a census of the study forest's trees, they checked how reliably barcodes could name them. Genetic tags matched many trees to their correct species. The approach will not replace taxonomists, but it can scale surveys far beyond hand identification. Faster inventories mean conservation choices can rest on fuller counts of what is actually there. The study is a field test of barcoding where diversity is highest.
plos-pone-0007583:
Shibing Yu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how parathyroid hormone builds bone. The hormone is a potent treatment for osteoporosis because it stimulates new bone rather than only slowing loss. Its mechanism inside bone-forming cells was not well understood. The team tested mice lacking a protein called activating transcription factor 4, or ATF4. They gave the hormone to growing and adult animals and measured the response.

Without ATF4, the hormone's bone-building action was severely impaired. That makes ATF4 a critical link in the chain from hormone signal to new bone. Knowing the link refines how the therapy is understood. It may also suggest ways to strengthen the treatment or mimic it. For a disease that thins the skeletons of millions, each part of the building machinery matters.
plos-pone-0007683:
Nicholas Levinson, Patrick Visperas and John Kuriyan published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on an enzyme called Csk. Csk belongs to a set of enzymes that switch other proteins on or off by adding a phosphate group. Its own activity is tuned by two key sites on related enzymes.

The authors show that Csk joins with a second Csk molecule to form a pair. The pairing happens through a part of the protein called the SH3 domain. How enzymes pair up can change how strongly they work. This detail helps explain how Csk is controlled inside the cell.
plos-pone-0007783:
Herman Pontzer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uses the physics of running to test whether two-legged dinosaurs were warm-blooded. Whether dinosaurs were endothermic, ectothermic or in between is a classic unsettled question. The answer also bears on when warm-bloodedness arose on the line to birds.

Running costs energy, and warm-blooded animals can sustain far higher energy output. The authors calculated the metabolic demands of running for bipedal dinosaurs. Their biomechanics point toward endothermy in these animals. Physics thus joins fossils and growth rings as evidence on dinosaur physiology.
plos-pone-0007883:
Alejandra Delprat and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how a jumping gene can flip a chunk of chromosome in fruit flies. Jumping genes, or transposons, are known sources of chromosomal inversions. Flies carry many inversions, both within species and between them.

Direct evidence for how inversions arise in flies was thin. The team traced inversions to the transposon they named Galileo. Copies of Galileo at two sites can recombine in the wrong pairing, flipping the segment between them. The mechanism explains a common kind of genome change. It helps connect mobile DNA to evolution.
plos-pone-0007983:
Siming Liu and colleagues linked insulin signals to cell power plants in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their stage was the pancreatic beta cell, the cell that makes insulin. Inside it they found a complex that ties mitochondria, the power plants, close to the sugar-sensing machinery.

With that tie in place, insulin signals could tune how the power plants work. A beta cell must sense sugar, make energy, and release insulin in step; the tie helps join those jobs. The find adds a layer to how these cells keep blood sugar in range, and where that control may fail in diabetes.
plos-pone-0008083:
Lucia Marucci and colleagues gave recipes for turning a gene circuit into a clock or a switch in PLOS ONE in 2009. Synthetic biologists build small circuits from gene parts and want them to behave as planned. Two prized behaviors are steady ticking and clean flipping between two states.

Using math models, the team showed how tweaks to one basic circuit yield each behavior, and how to tune the tick or the flip. Recipes like these bring built biology closer to the trust we place in built electronics, where parts do what the diagram promises.
plos-pone-0008183:
Jonathan C. Schisler and co-authors explored ancestry and metabolism in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. People of African descent in the United States face higher rates of obesity and diabetes. They also face more hypertension and heart disease linked to those conditions. The team asked whether gene activity tied to carbohydrate use differs by geographic ancestry.

Using a combined approach, the authors looked for stable patterns of gene expression. Stable patterns are ones that hold up across samples and conditions. If ancestry shapes how the body handles sugars, that could help explain unequal disease rates. It could also guide more precise study of metabolic disease.
plos-pone-0008283:
Ruchika Srinivasan and colleagues studied blood vessel growth in mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2009. Angiogenesis builds new vessels through a complex, stepwise process. Endothelial cells first break through the vessel wall, then migrate and multiply. The Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK pathway is required for endothelial cell function. Within it, Erk1 and Erk2 are close partner proteins.

The team asked how each partner regulates cell proliferation and migration. Separating their roles matters for understanding vessel development. It also matters for diseases where vessel growth goes wrong. The study maps part of the signaling chain behind embryonic angiogenesis.
plos-pone-0008383:
Julie Tenenbaum and colleagues studied mutant hormone receptors in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Some patients have the nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, or NSIAD. They carry mutations in the V2 receptor, at positions named R137C or R137L. The mutant receptors are constitutively active, switched on without their hormone. Clinical features were known, but molecular mechanisms remained elusive.

The team found these mutants respond only weakly to agonist and antagonist regulation. Drugs that normally raise or block the receptor lose much of their grip. That explains features of the syndrome. It also shapes treatment expectations for patients.
plos-pone-0008483:
Duarte Viana and co-authors test cooperation in rats in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. They use a social game based on the Prisoner's Dilemma. In that game, working together pays both players, but each is tempted to defect. Game theory has long used the dilemma to study reciprocity. The team ask what rats need, in mind and motive, for cooperation to emerge in play.

Rats face the game with a partner over repeated rounds. The authors vary what rats can learn and expect from partners. Cooperation grows only when those conditions are met. The study helps explain when simple animals can sustain shared, costly help.
plos-pone-0008583:
Teal Hallstrand and co-authors profile genes in asthma in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. One common form is triggered by exercise. It occurs in many people with asthma. During attacks, the airways release lipid signals that drive swelling. The team measure gene activity across the genome in distinct asthma types. They seek genes that are more active in the exercise form.

They find an enzyme called TG2 is a new regulator of those lipid signals. TG2 had not been linked to this path before. It is a fresh target for drugs to curb exercise attacks. Sorting asthma by type reveals drivers that pooled studies miss.
plos-pone-0008683:
Michael Russello, Nikos Poulakakis, James Gibbs, and colleagues reported a happy surprise from the Galápagos. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study concerns a tortoise kind long thought extinct. The species once lived only on one island and vanished from the wild. Old DNA, drawn from museum bones, gave the team a reference.

Captive tortoises held far from home carried genes matching that lost species. In other words, descendants of the extinct kind still live in zoos and collections. Breeders could use those animals to rebuild a wild population. The case shows how old DNA can steer modern rescue work.
plos-pone-0008783:
Hai-Guo Zhang, Yao-Fong Chen, Ming Ding, and colleagues completed a fingerprint survey of all Chinese ethnic groups. Their huge project appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dermatoglyphics is the study of finger and palm ridge patterns. Such patterns form before birth and never change. A full survey of a diverse country was once thought nearly impossible. Teams across China gathered the data over many years.

Ridge measures varied in clear geographic patterns across groups. Northern and southern populations showed their own signatures. The completed map serves anthropology, genetics, and medical studies. It stands as a reference atlas of human variation in China.
plos-pone-0008883:
Mirjam Metzner, Wolfgang Schuh, Edith Roth, and colleagues sorted an antibody-editing enzyme into two forms. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, AID, mutates antibody genes in B cells on purpose. Those mutations let antibodies sharpen their grip on germs. Hunting for AID's partner proteins is a standard research route. Oddly, the enzyme behaved inconsistently in a common lab material, agarose.

Two forms of AID differed in how they bound that material. Separating the forms clears up confusing partner hunts. Form differences may also reflect real regulation inside B cells. Antibody science gains a cleaner picture of its key mutator.
plos-pone-0008983:
Caia Duncan and Kevin Weeks mapped how a helper protein grips a self-cutting RNA in yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some RNA molecules, called ribozymes, can cut and rejoin themselves. The bI3 intron in yeast mitochondria is one of them, but it works poorly alone. It needs two proteins, and one of them is the splicing factor Mrs1.

The team found Mrs1 holds the intron at two separate grip points. Each grip is a tetraloop-receptor motif, a small folded shape in the RNA. Holding both points likely folds the intron into its working shape. Mrs1 began as a DNA-cutting enzyme family member, later retrained for RNA work.
plos-pone-0009083:
Matthew Henn and co-authors compared ways of reading and labelling the genomes of phages, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Phages are viruses that infect bacteria and steer whole ecosystems. They kill hosts and shuttle genes between them. Despite that importance, phage genomes were poorly charted when the study ran.

High-throughput sequencing had just made reading many phage genomes cheap. The team tested strategies for sequencing and for annotating what the genes do. Different pipelines gave different completeness and accuracy. Their comparison offers a practical guide for labs entering phage genomics.
plos-pone-0009183:
Kathryn Chu and co-authors published this clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It follows HIV patients in a primary care treatment program in South Africa. At the time, most African programs used a fixed-dose drug mix containing nevirapine. Doctors worried that nevirapine could damage the liver early in treatment.

The team measured how often early liver harm occurred in the program. They also looked for patient traits that raised the risk, and counted deaths linked to the damage. Such numbers matter because programs had to weigh nevirapine's benefits against its dangers. The findings helped clinicians decide who needed closer liver checks when starting treatment.
plos-pone-0009283:
Linda Ferencko and Boris Rotman published this spore engineering study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bacillus spores are among the toughest objects in biology. Each spore wears a coat built from about sixty different proteins. That coat was long seen as static armor, giving the spore its rigidity and protection.

The authors decorated coat proteins with water-repelling chemical groups. The treatment made the spores glow under the right light, creating fluorogenic spores. Glowing spores can be tracked as they move through soil, water, or instruments. The trick turns a passive survival capsule into a useful tracer for science and industry.
plos-pone-0009383:
Natalia de Groot and Salvador Ventura published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proteins that fold wrongly can clump into toxic aggregates. Such clumping harms the cell by removing useful proteins and by poisoning it. How likely a protein is to clump is written into its amino acid sequence.

The authors profiled aggregation across the proteins of the bacterial cytosol, the cell's inner soup. They asked which proteins live near the edge of clumping and why. A whole-cell profile shows how bacteria keep hundreds of proteins soluble at once. Those rules also inform diseases of human protein aggregation, from Alzheimer's to cataracts.
plos-pone-0009483:
Chin Hur and colleagues built a computer model of a throat cancer in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancer of the esophagus, the tube from throat to stomach, has risen fast in the United States. White men face the highest rates. The team set out to make a model of how this cancer starts and grows in that group.

They tuned the model to match known data and then checked it against other data. A sound model lets researchers test ideas that would take decades to test in people. It can show which factors drive the rise. It can also weigh which screening or treatment plans might help most.
plos-pone-0009583:
Shaun Morris and colleagues studied how doctors judge causes of child death in India in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most child deaths worldwide occur where no doctor was present. A method called verbal autopsy asks families about the illness, and physicians assign a cause. The team used records of more than twenty seven thousand deaths. They asked what affects whether physicians agree on a cause.

Agreement varied with the cause suspected and with the details families gave. Knowing where judgments split helps improve the method's training and forms. Verbal autopsy is a key tool for counting deaths that would otherwise go unrecorded. Better counts point health spending where it saves the most young lives.
plos-pone-0009683:
Pulmonary fibrosis scars the lungs until breathing grows hard. Lynne Murray and colleagues tested a possible treatment in mice and reported the results in PLOS ONE in 2010. They gave the animals serum amyloid P, a protein found in blood, after using bleomycin to trigger lung scarring.

Treated mice developed much less scarring than untreated ones. The protein seemed to work through macrophages, immune cells that help drive the scarring process. The study also laid out how the treatment changed the cells' behavior. Because no cure exists for this lung disease, a blood protein that slows it down drew wide interest.
plos-pone-0009783:
W. John Sheward and co-authors published a physiology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks how the brain's daily clock, set in the suprachiasmatic nuclei, steers heart rate and blood pressure. The team tracked mutant mice whose clock gene Vipr2 was missing, using implanted radio senders.

The mutant mice showed flatter daily swings in rest, activity, and sleep than normal mice. Most of the gap in heart rate and blood pressure came from the shifted timing of activity and rest, the team found. A modest daily rhythm in resting heart rate and pressure stood apart from movement. The authors back mice as a model for this question in people.
plos-pone-0009883:
Madagascar's mouse lemurs are tiny primates, and telling their species apart is tricky. David Weisrock and colleagues faced that problem where the usual genetic test fails. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mouse lemurs are among the smallest primates on Earth.

Delimiting species means drawing the lines between one species and the next. The usual test needs nuclear monophyly, a clean family-tree split in nuclear DNA. Without that signal, the team needed other evidence to draw the lines. Clear species limits matter for counting and protecting Madagascar's wildlife.
plos-pone-0009983:
Manasa Ramakrishna and colleagues hunt for growth-driving genes in ovarian cancer in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Ovarian tumors carry many scrambled stretches of DNA, but which extra-copy genes truly push growth is mostly unknown. Finding them could guide new tests and treatments.

The team matched gene copy counts with gene activity in sixty-eight tumors. Extra copies clustered on four chromosomes, covering many genes. For hundreds of them, more copies meant more activity. A smaller set in strong gain zones matched especially well. Known cancer gene ERBB2 checked out, and new leads such as MYNN, PUF60, and TPX2 emerged for follow-up work.
plos-pone-0010083:
Ludovic Sauguet and colleagues solve a protein structure in a 2010 PLOS ONE study of how DNA copying starts. Copying needs short RNA starter pieces made by an enzyme called primase, which has a large and a small part. An iron-sulfur tip on the large part is vital, but its role was murky.

The team crystallized that tip from yeast and mapped its atoms in fine detail. Surprisingly, one half matches the active site of DNA photolyase, a light-using repair protein family. Shared spots include residues known to matter for starter making. The match hints at how primase grabs its building blocks to begin a primer.
plos-pone-0010183:
The authors were Adam Anas, Joppe Hovius, Cornelis van 't Veer, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mice to test a sensor in lung inflammation. Lipopolysaccharide, or LPS, is a molecule on Gram-negative bacteria that the body must sense to defend itself. Lab work suggested a protein called CD14 was needed to pass that signal onward.

The team induced acute lung inflammation with different LPS chemotypes, forms that vary in structure. They then checked how much CD14 mattered for each form in living mice. The answer shapes understanding of lung injury during severe bacterial infection.
plos-pone-0010283:
The authors were Kelly Tremblay, Kayo Inoue, Katrina McClannahan, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked how repeated listening reshapes hearing in the brain. Auditory training programs are being built to help people with communication disorders. Training improves perception, and biological changes in the brain come with that improvement, raising interest in markers of progress.

The team exposed listeners repeatedly to sounds and tracked how brain encoding changed. If a brain signal marks training gains, clinics could measure progress objectively. Their results add to the science behind hearing rehabilitation and listening therapy design.
plos-pone-0010383:
Veronika Sander and co-workers studied two competing signals in fruit fly wings for PLOS ONE in 2010. In backboned animals, two signal families often push in opposite directions during development. One family builds bone and related tissues; the other guides different fates. The balance between them shapes structures like the gastrula organizer. Flies offer a simpler place to test that rivalry.

In the fly wing, the protein Smad2 worked against the rival pathway's signal, Mad. That opposition helped pattern the veins of the wing. A fine wing pattern thus becomes a readout of signal balance. The fly work may clarify how the same balance fails in birth defects. Small wings, here, carry a general lesson about development.
plos-pone-0010483:
Makoto Wada and co-workers hunted for brain areas that judge the order of events in mice, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Knowing which of two sensations came first is a basic mental skill. Its brain basis was still unclear despite long study. The team had built a behavior task where mice judge time order. They then measured a marker gene, c-Fos, that lights up in recently active neurons.

The lit-up areas point to circuits used during order judgments. Mapping those circuits is a step toward explaining timing disorders. Mice that can report order give researchers a rare animal handle on time perception. The marker approach freezes a moment of brain activity for inspection. This study links a trained behavior to specific active regions.
plos-pone-0010583:
Weimin Zhong and colleagues asked how well immune memory holds up against changing flu viruses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Killer T cells can recognize flu strains a person has never met. Much of that recognition targets a virus protein called the nucleoprotein.

The team compared nucleoprotein versions from different influenza A strains. Even small sequence changes weakened the protection that memory T cells provided. Some variants escaped notice almost entirely. The results set a clear limit on how broad T-cell protection can be. Vaccine designers need to allow for that drift when they aim for wider flu coverage.
plos-pone-0010683:
Muthu Bhaskaran and Bret Smith studied cannabis-like compounds in a mouse model of epilepsy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Temporal lobe epilepsy reshapes circuits in a brain area called the dentate gyrus. Extra excitatory loops form there, and those loops can help trigger seizures.

Compounds that mimic the body's own cannabis-like signals calmed those loops. They cut the repeated firing that spreads through the dentate circuit. The site of action was precise, not a blanket dulling of the brain. Knowing exactly where the calming acts helps explain past seizure results and guides safer drug design.
plos-pone-0010783:
Vishnu Chaturvedi and colleagues characterized the fungus behind white-nose syndrome in bats, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Since 2006, little brown bats had been dying in huge numbers around Albany, New York. A white fungal growth coated the muzzles of hibernating bats. The fungus loved the cold of winter caves, matching the disease's season.

Lab work described the fungus, named Geomyces destructans, in shape and by DNA. Its traits fit a cold-loving invader new to North American caves. Naming the killer and its habits is the first step toward any defense. Options range from cave closures to antifungal trials for a fast-spreading wildlife disaster.
plos-pone-0010883:
Walter Gall, Kirk Beebe, Kay Lawton and co-authors published this biomarker study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insulin resistance raises the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease, but standard blood sugar tests spot it late. The team searched the blood chemistry of nearly four hundred nondiabetic adults for an earlier warning sign.

Volunteers spanned a wide range of insulin sensitivity, measured with a gold-standard clamp test and glucose tolerance testing. Untargeted chemical profiling combined with machine learning ranked one small molecule, alpha-hydroxybutyrate, as the strongest separator between resistant and sensitive people. Gall and colleagues propose it as an early marker that rises before blood sugar goes wrong. An early flag could let doctors intervene with lifestyle or drug treatment while prevention still works.
plos-pone-0010983:
Rolf Spirig, Siamak Djafarzadeh, Tomas Regueira and co-authors published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dendritic cells link the body's first alarms to its targeted defenses, maturing when they sense danger through toll-like receptors. HIF-1alpha is a factor usually switched on by low oxygen, and the team asked whether danger signals switch it on too, and whether it drives maturation.

In human dendritic cells grown from blood cells, stimuli for two toll-like receptors raised HIF-1alpha even with normal oxygen. Yet blocking the factor three different ways did not consistently change maturation or cytokine release, and forcing it on did not mature the cells either. Spirig and colleagues separate correlation from cause: HIF-1alpha rises with danger, but it is not the lever that matures these cells.
plos-pone-0011083:
Rouge, Butel, Piloquet and colleagues reported newborn research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They measured a protein called calprotectin in the stool of preterm infants. The protein rises when the gut is inflamed, so levels in the first weeks of life could signal gut health.

The team tracked how much of the marker babies passed during the newborn period. Their data set a baseline for what is normal in these fragile infants. A clear baseline could help doctors spot dangerous gut disease sooner. Early warning matters greatly for babies born too early, whose guts are still weak.
plos-pone-0011183:
Khademi, Etemadi, Kamangar and colleagues tested death reporting in Iran for PLOS ONE in 2010. Where death certificates are weak, health workers interview family about the final illness, a method called verbal autopsy. The team checked how reliable and valid that method was in a large cohort study in Golestan.

Their estimates show how well interviews can pin down causes of death. Solid cause data guide health policy, since leaders must know what kills people to act. A validated method strengthens mortality statistics for a whole region. It also lets past deaths in the cohort be used with more confidence in research.
plos-pone-0011283:
Alais and Cass trained timing perception in PLOS ONE in 2010. Judging which of two events came first is a basic skill of the senses. Practice with sound and vision together was tested for whether the gain carries over when only one sense is used afterward.

Learning did transfer to vision alone, but not to hearing alone. That one sided transfer reveals an asymmetry in how the senses share training. Brain training works best when it targets the right sense for the goal. The finding also shows senses do not simply pool all learning; each keeps its own accounts.
plos-pone-0011383:
Pramod Dash and colleagues tested in 2010 whether a long-used epilepsy drug could protect the brain after a severe injury. A blow to the head kills brain cells not only at impact but over the hours that follow, and few drugs can slow that second wave. The team gave valproate to rats after a traumatic brain injury and compared them with untreated rats.

Treated animals lost fewer brain cells and did better on tests of thinking and memory. An approved drug with a known safety record showing this benefit is valuable, since it could reach patients faster than a brand-new compound. The study supports trials of valproate as an early treatment after head injury. It also suggests that calming certain cell pathways soon after trauma can save tissue that would otherwise be lost.
plos-pone-0011483:
Antonia Kalushkova and co-authors reported in 2010 that a set of development genes is switched off in multiple myeloma. Myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow, and its gene control is badly scrambled. The Polycomb system is a master silencer that keeps embryo genes off in adult cells, and its normal targets should be handled with care in blood cells.

In myeloma, genes targeted by Polycomb were found silenced, a pattern pointing to hijacked developmental controls helping drive the cancer. Silencing the wrong set can lock cells in an immature, ever-dividing state. The finding matters because drugs that undo abnormal silencing already exist for other cancers. If myeloma's silencing pattern is a driver rather than a bystander, those epigenetic drugs deserve testing against it, guided by the pattern itself.
plos-pone-0011583:
Krishna Kumar Veeravalli and co-authors studied human glioma cells, a form of aggressive brain tumour, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Three helpers called MMP-9, uPAR and cathepsin B are known to aid tumour spread. They help cancer cells stick, move, invade nearby tissue and grow new tumours elsewhere.

Using short RNA tools, the team switched off all three helpers in tumour cells grown in dishes and in mice. Levels of integrins, the proteins cells use to grip their surroundings, then fell sharply. Weakening several helpers at once may therefore slow glioma spread, and the work points to combined targets for future treatment.
plos-pone-0011783:
Mareike Fett and co-authors tested a guard protein in a zebrafish model of Parkinson's disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Faults in the gene for parkin cause most cases of the inherited, early form of the disease. Mice that lack parkin, though, show little brain harm, which left researchers with no good living model of its guard role.

In engineered zebrafish, parkin held off protein-poison stress, the harm done by misfolded proteins that pile up in cells. The fish test backs the guard's protective role in a living animal. Small zebrafish may also give a faster test bed for Parkinson's drugs than mice.
plos-pone-0011883:
Yimo Liu and Diane Bassham showed in 2010 that a growth regulator also restrains recycling inside plant cells. The regulator is TOR, a protein that senses nutrient conditions. The recycling process is autophagy, in which cells break down and reuse their own contents during stress or aging.

Working in Arabidopsis thaliana, the small plant used in labs worldwide, the team found TOR acting as a negative regulator, holding autophagy down. The same broad control had been seen in animals, so the plant result suggests an ancient, shared switch. Understanding that switch matters for how plants survive hunger and how their aging leaves are dismantled.
plos-pone-0011983:
Rajwahrdhan Yadav and co-workers described in 2010 an odd effect of whooping cough toxin on immune replies to the body's own tissues. The toxin is most known for making self-attack diseases worse in lab animals, boosting models of eye and brain disease in which the immune system turns on the self. How it does that boosting is still argued about.

Yet in this study the toxin held back a slow, cell-led immune reply to self proteins in mice, the flip side of its usual name. A tool long used to stir up self-attack acting as a brake in a new setup warns against one-line tales about immune drugs. Dose, timing, and place all matter, and the work pushes labs to state those terms before they call a drug a booster or a brake.
plos-pone-0012083:
Luis Fernandes and co-workers used in 2010 a branch of math born of phone lines and codes. With it they audited the maps that chart how proteins touch each other in the cell. Those maps are built from tests of many kinds, and each kind has its own blind spots and quirks. The team brought in scales from that math to sum up each map's shape in a few firm traits.

Read with those scales, the maps showed two things at once. One was warps left by the tests that made them. The other was traits that stay the same from one kind of life to the next. Telling warp from truth is a must before such maps are mined for drug aims. The scales also give the field a way to check its own work, map by map.
plos-pone-0012183:
Ming Li, Dankyu Yoon, Jong-Young Lee, and co-authors tested smoking-linked gene variants in a Korean population for PLOS ONE in 2010. A cluster of nicotine receptor genes on chromosome fifteen had been tied to nicotine dependence in many large studies, but nearly all those studies drew on people of European descent. Whether the same variants matter in Asian populations was an open question.

The team checked the cluster's variants against smoking behaviors in Korean subjects. Confirming or refuting the link in a new population decides whether the finding is a general human trait or a local one. Such cross-population checks keep genetics honest and can sharpen the search for what makes quitting so hard.
plos-pone-0012283:
Robert Jenkins, Rasha Bennagi, John Martin, and co-authors found a folded switch controlling a growth factor's production, in PLOS ONE in 2010. TGF-beta 1 steers cell growth, movement, and survival across the body, yet its message is notoriously reluctant to be translated into protein. That reluctance is itself a control point, lifted under certain stimuli.

The team pinned the control to a conserved stem-loop shape in the message's opening region. A shape-based switch explains how cells can keep the message ready yet silent until needed. Since too much of this factor drives scarring and helps cancers, its translation switch is a plausible drug target that DNA-level studies would never have shown.
plos-pone-0012383:
Osbaldo Resendis-Antonio, Alberto Checa and Sergio Encarnación charted the core metabolism of cancer cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Cancer cells burn sugar in a wasteful way even when oxygen is plentiful, a quirk called the Warburg effect, and they pour building blocks into new amino acids, fats, and DNA parts. The authors mapped the network of reactions that sustains this growth mode.

By surveying the layout of the network, they highlight the hubs and backup routes that let tumor cells keep growing. A map like this shows where a drug might starve a tumor and where the cell could reroute around a block. It gives drug hunters a systems view rather than one enzyme at a time.
plos-pone-0012483:
León Martínez-Castilla and Rogelio Rodríguez-Sotres proposed a quality score for computer-built protein models, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Predicting a protein's three-dimensional fold from its sequence remains a central problem, because shape decides function. Modelers need a trustworthy way to grade a predicted shape before trusting it.

Their score asks how well a model can retrieve its own sequence when the sequence is threaded back onto the shape. A good fold should welcome its true sequence more than others. Such self-consistency checks give modelers a cheap internal grade, useful when no experimental structure exists to compare against, which is most of the time.
plos-pone-0012583:
Wiebke Mohr, Tobias Großkopf, Douglas Wallace and colleagues checked whether standard methods undercount ocean nitrogen fixation, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Fixing nitrogen gas into usable forms feeds ocean life and the global nitrogen budget. Two methods dominate measurement: a tracer addition test and the acetylene reduction assay, and their results often disagree.

The team found methodological reasons the tracer method can underestimate true fixation rates. Undercounted fixation means ocean productivity and carbon uptake models rest on low numbers. Correcting the method ripples through climate science, since the ocean's nitrogen supply limits how much carbon marine life can draw down.
plos-pone-0012683:
Sughra, Birbach, de Martin and co-authors traced contacts between three proteins in the inflammation pathway. The pathway centres on NF-kappa B, a switch for genes of inflammation and cell survival. One key enzyme in it is IKK2, and helper proteins called TRAFs shape its action.

Their 2010 study showed TRAF1 binding both IKK2 and TRAF2, hinting it regulates the pathway. A regulator sitting between two known players gives drug hunters another handle on inflammation. Unchecked NF-kappa B drives many diseases, so each control point counts. Fine wiring of this kind is what drug design builds on.
plos-pone-0323983:
Hannock Tweya and colleagues traced how people starting HIV treatment in Lilongwe, Malawi, stayed connected to care over their first two years. Staying on antiretroviral therapy keeps people healthy and lowers spread of the virus. Clinics there support new patients either with a peer helper called a Buddy or with a two-way texting service for those with phones. Their 2026 study covered more than six thousand clients at two public clinics.

Texting clients stayed most consistently engaged through the first eighteen months, and about seven in ten were still in care at two years. Buddy clients without phones fared worst, with only about a quarter retained. Many who stayed had gaps, arriving late or returning after long absences. The authors argue support should adapt to each person's pattern of attendance over time.
plos-pone-0332983:
Zahra Jahanbakhti and Zahra Momeni present this 2026 PLOS One dental study from Karaj, Iran. It covers orphaned children aged six to twelve in four state-run centers. The team asked the children about oral health knowledge, attitudes, and habits. Then they examined teeth, gums, and cleanliness with standard clinical tools.

Knowledge scores were low. Fewer than a third of baby molars were fully sound. More than half of the first permanent molars already showed early decay. Hygiene overall was fair, and gum inflammation was mild. Frequent brushing predicted better oral status. So did more positive attitudes. Knowledge alone did not. The authors recommend teaching aimed at caregivers. They also recommend routine dental checks for this vulnerable group.
plos-pone-0337883:
Nadine Schrode and co-workers catalog the immune cells living in human breast milk, one cell at a time. Milk carries a mother's white blood cells that help guard and shape a baby's defenses. Their 2026 study reads gene activity in more than twenty-three thousand milk cells from nine healthy donors, hunting for cell types earlier work had missed.

Eighteen distinct groups appeared, most of them scavenger and messenger cells of the immune system. Two odd groups mixed skin-like and immune traits. Many cells showed signs of adapting to milk's fatty setting, handling fats and presenting germ clues to other cells. Each mother also had her own mix, with some groups found in only one or two donors.
plos-pone-0343183:
Clement Torrent, Melania Capasso, and co-authors fed aging mice low-dose rapamycin, a transplant drug that extends lifespan in many species, to see exactly which immune changes it causes in old age. Worry persists that a proven immune suppressant is a risky anti-aging bet. Their 2026 study profiled immune cells across tissues after long treatment, then challenged the animals with a bacterial trigger of inflammation.

Most immune populations, including the brain's resident microglia, barely changed. What did shrink was the age-related buildup of a specific T cell type that produces an inflammatory signal, especially around the abdomen. After the challenge, that signal ran lower in treated animals and their brain immune cells stayed calmer. The authors describe a narrow, targeted effect rather than broad suppression.
plos-pone-0344883:
Nguyen Huy Hoang Vu and Bao Long Nguyen ran a large statistical sweep on seventy eight thousand proteins to find which sequence traits separate proteins that dissolve well from those that clump. Dissolving matters for making proteins in labs and factories. Thirty six chemical traits were compared with strict error control, effect sizes, and accuracy curves.

Nearly all traits differed significantly, yet most effects were tiny with heavy overlap. Size traits led, and a share of negative charge helped modestly. Size measures duplicated each other almost perfectly. A lean score joining length and negative charge did best, but accuracy stayed modest. Dissolving is governed by many weak pushes, not one master trait.
plos-pone-0345383:
Ivan P. Gorlov, Olga Y. Gorlova, and Aaron P. Thrift asked whether differences in liver gene activity help explain why fatty liver disease strikes Black and White Americans at different rates. They analysed gene expression from liver biopsies of more than three hundred people who had weight-loss surgery, comparing samples across stages from healthy liver to advanced inflamed disease.

Over two hundred genes behaved differently between the groups, and genes driving disease progression were over-represented among them. Each group carried its own candidate drivers, and the expression gap widened as disease advanced. The authors argue that biology inside the liver, not only lifestyle and income, shapes the racial disparity, with implications for targeted prevention.
plos-pone-0346583:
Max Wiedemann, Christopher Mai, Luca Eisentraut, and Ricardo Buettner built an image-reading system that estimates how much cotton a fabric contains. Knowing fibre content is essential for recycling old textiles, but checking by hand is slow and laboratory spectroscopy is costly. Their 2026 system instead learns from ordinary camera photographs, merging two neural network designs, one good at fine detail and one at overall pattern.

Tested with repeated cross-checks on a reviewed dataset, the model estimated cotton content with an average error of about fourteen percent, the best result yet for a camera-based approach. The authors argue such cheap visual sorting could make textile recycling pay, cutting manual work at sorting plants.
plos-pone-0347783:
Touria Essayagh and colleagues surveyed more than eighteen hundred Moroccan schoolgirls aged eleven to fourteen about the vaccine against human papillomavirus, which prevents most cervical cancer. Face-to-face interviews across the country in spring 2025 measured what the girls knew and how hesitant they and their families felt. Hesitancy turned out to be overwhelming.

Nearly nine in ten girls were classified as hesitant. The strongest driver was having unvaccinated peers, followed by a father who could not read, weak recommendation from health workers, and the belief that the vaccine encourages sexual activity. Each factor is a lever: strong advice from trusted health staff and better parent information directly address the largest risks the study found.
plos-pone-0348083:
Shuang Deng and Zhongqiang Guo hunt for tipping points in blood fats and frailty. Their study of older adults appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The data came from a large Chinese aging survey. It held close to three thousand people. Several hundred had severe limits on airflow, a late stage of lung disease.

Two measures stood out from the rest. One fat-based index tied to lower odds of severe limits overall. Leftover cholesterol in the blood showed a sharp threshold. Below that line, its tie was very strong. Above it, the tie faded but stayed real. Age, sex, and schooling shifted some links. Such cut points could help doctors set precise goals.
plos-pone-0348283:
Dawit Errega and colleagues gathered everything published on heart and blood vessel disease among Ethiopians living with HIV. People with HIV face extra cardiovascular risk from the virus itself and from some of its medicines, yet Ethiopian evidence had never been pulled together. Their 2026 scoping review, searching six databases, found twenty-six studies.

Nearly two-thirds of the research concerned high blood pressure alone, which affected between eleven and forty-one percent of patients depending on the study. Smoking, alcohol, older age, weight, and long treatment histories recurred as risk factors. Other conditions, from stroke to heart muscle disease, were barely studied. The authors call for broader, stronger, community-based research.
plos-pone-0348383:
Sickle cell disease strains the heart over time, yet heart ultrasound data from Latin America are scarce. Martin E Arrieta-Mendoza and colleagues profiled adults with the disease at a major hospital in Cali, Colombia, in this 2026 PLOS One record review covering 2022 to 2024.

Fifty-seven patients qualified from hundreds screened. Most were in their twenties, and about two thirds took hydroxyurea, a standard protective drug. The team recorded heart size, pumping and filling function, and pressure measures, alongside blood values. Their aim was to spot which ultrasound signs travel with higher cardiovascular risk in this population, guiding closer follow-up for those who need it.
plos-pone-0348583:
Jemil Yasin Shifa and Abrham Seyoum Tsehay asked if climate-wise farm work lifts poor homes in more ways than cash. They spoke with four hundred sixteen small farms in the Siltie Zone of Ethiopia. Their gauge of want spanned health, school, and home needs. They also used care in the sums, to guard against rich farms just taking up more new ways.

Take-up of climate-wise work cut want in a clear way. More take-up brought more gain. The team reads this as proof that such work does two jobs at once. It shields farms from harsh skies and eases daily want. They urge aid aimed at the poorest homes.
plos-pone-0348683:
Johan Azañero-Haro and Alonso Soto raced four scoring systems that predict death in hospitalised COVID-19 pneumonia against each other using Peruvian patients from the first pandemic wave. All the patients were unvaccinated, and just over a thousand had complete data for every score. The scores blend bedside observations and lab values into a single risk number meant to guide scarce care.

The quickest score, built from breathing rate, oxygen level, and consciousness, separated survivors from those who died better than the three rivals, including the large international benchmark. The weakest score lagged well behind. Checking how the groups compared also showed the analysed patients fairly represented the whole cohort. The authors recommend the winning score for busy hospitals, while noting calibration quirks that local teams should watch.
plos-pone-0348783:
