Patients at a major Chinese hospital were assessed before surgery and at one, three, and six months after; 209 completed the follow-up. Group modelling found three distinct frailty trajectories, including a low-fluctuation path. The team then built an interpretable machine learning model. It is explained with a method that shows each factor's contribution. They turned it into a web-based calculator for individual risk prediction in the early recovery period.
pmc-13271983:
Davide Mulfari and coauthors present in 2026 a case where a speech recognition system was trained on one woman's severely disordered speech. A stroke fifteen years earlier left her with global aphasia and severe dysarthria, so only familiar partners could follow her. Standard recognition software performs poorly on such atypical speech.

The woman recorded over a thousand samples of thirteen target words, which trained a compact neural network inside a communication app. On fresh recordings the tailored system reached notably higher word accuracy than twelve rehabilitation professionals who knew her speech. Personal training may give profoundly disordered speakers a workable voice tool.
pmc-13272083:

These boards weigh gene profiling results to match patients with targeted drugs. Sarcoma lacks the standard analysis tools available for more common cancers, so practice may vary widely.

Six of ten contacted centers answered a thirty-question survey prepared in 2021. All six reported having a board, though membership differed, with a dedicated oncologist present in most centers. Most centers met national alliance criteria for board structure. The authors use the findings to judge whether Italian sarcoma care is on the right track.
pmc-13272383:
Jacob D Fairholm and coauthors review in 2026 why Staphylococcus aureus bacteria persist in cystic fibrosis airways despite fierce immune attack. Host factors matter too, since the faulty channel protein behind cystic fibrosis weakens killing inside neutrophils. Neighboring Pseudomonas bacteria add further protection. The review weighs each factor's evidence.
pmc-13272583:

Residents took three flipped-classroom sessions, where study came first and class time was for practice, plus one game-based review, from July to December 2024. Bedside scores for leadership rose after the course, with the newest residents gaining most. Confidence in leading resuscitations also rose at all levels, and residents praised the active, game-like parts of the course.
pmc-13272783:

Expert pathologists are the standard for such checks, but they form a bottleneck for large screening. The team fine-tuned a vision model on pixel-marked slides and used a distance measure to catch out-of-pattern samples, such as cell death and staining artifacts. Only 0.16 percent of harmed tissue was classed as healthy, and 0.35 percent of healthy tissue as harmed. The authors call this a feasibility step for faster preclinical work.
pmc-13272883:
Andargachew Almaw leads a 2026 study of intestinal parasites in psychiatric patients at a hospital in Debre Tabor, northwest Ethiopia. Such infections are a health concern in care settings for people with mental illness, yet prevention there gets little attention. The team tested stool from 402 patients between August and October 2024.

Overall, 26.6 percent had an intestinal parasite, and the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides was most common at 9 percent. Risks were higher for rural residents, people from large families, and those drinking surface water. Eating raw vegetables or fruit, walking barefoot, untrimmed nails, and lack of latrine access also raised risk. The authors highlight hygiene and sanitation steps for this patient group.
pmc-13273283:

The improved ribozyme turned over about thirteen GTP molecules. Paired with a second ribozyme that builds RNA, it supplied five guanosine units into a growing chain. The authors call this a step toward rebuilding an RNA based stage of early life in the lab.
pmc-13273483:
Wenhao Xiong and co-authors studied how copper and growing conditions affect a pesticide in pea seedlings in a 2026 environmental study. Copper changed transport in mixed ways, sometimes helping and sometimes hindering uptake. The chemical broke down fast, with half gone in under four days. Calculated exposure risk stayed negligible under their measures. The findings guide residue checks for peas grown under different systems.
pmc-13273583:

Markers such as receptor levels, specific mutations, and spread to organs inform that judgment. Open questions on sequencing and marker precision remain for ongoing studies.
pmc-13273883:

Cell death appeared early, in the proliferative zone. That disrupted the plate's layered structure. Proliferation did not keep pace with the losses. The authors link this imbalance to bone loss. The findings concern prolactin-raising drugs used around pregnancy.
pmc-13274883:

Even lesser legal contacts acted as stressors, the authors conclude.
pmc-13275283:

The authors support adding the drug in this combined condition.
pmc-13276583:

pmc-13276783:

The authors link a bone-related protein pair to the kidney inflammation.
pmc-13278683:
Yuting Liu and colleagues combine gene sequencing with machine learning to find candidate genes for pulmonary stenosis, in a 2026 study. The condition narrows the heart's pulmonary valve and can threaten life when severe. Its genetic roots involve many genes and remain only partly mapped.

Random forest agreed most closely with the burden results. Seventeen candidate genes survived the combined screen, including several known in heart development. Lab checks confirmed the candidates are active in human pulmonary artery cells.
pmc-13278983:

pmc-13279183:

pmc-13279283:

pmc-13279383:

pmc-13279483:

The authors back joint team care that shares work with family doctors and uses current clinics.
pmc-13279683:
Hua Gao and colleagues report a 2026 study of a surgery checklist for three bone ankle breaks. Trimalleolar fractures break three ankle bones at once, and joint fit quality drives results. Usual checks, X ray scopes or joint cameras, each have blind spots alone. The new SGSC checklist joins both views in a traffic light score for step, gap, joint space and match.

Stage two split patients in All Green and Non All Green groups by their scores. Foot and ankle scores and early joint wear on scans were compared at follow up. pmc-13280083:
Xiaojia Wang and colleagues present a 2026 feasibility study on brain connectivity in major depressive disorder via EEG. Major depressive disorder, a severe low mood illness, links to frontal lobe dysfunction. Brain network order matters for the illness, so the team read effective connectivity, meaning directed influence between brain zones. Resting EEG, a scalp record of brain waves, came from three frontal sites.

Spectral dynamic causal modelling then inferred links between them and their change across trials. Depression groups showed a clear drop in the mean strength of excitatory links between pyramidal cells across the lobes. Link fluctuation across trials also fell in mild and moderate groups. pmc-13280583:
Renato Lorenzon Maisano offers a 2026 reflective essay, Learning to remain, on silence, suffering and the hidden curriculum of care in medical training. pmc-13280883:

pmc-13281383:

pmc-13281583:
Hanna Morian and colleagues studied remote teamwork in rural Swedish emergency care in a 2026 paper. Small rural hospitals are often the first stop in a crisis. Control of the scene felt thin and rested on others' reports. The title quote, we feel abandoned out here, sums up the strain. pmc-13281883:

pmc-13282083:

pmc-13282283:

pmc-13282383:

pmc-13282483:

pmc-13282683:

Autotransplantation moves a patient's own tooth into a gap, a biological option that preserves jaw bone as they grow. pmc-13282783:

pmc-13282983:

pmc-13283183:

pmc-13283383:

pmc-13283883:

pmc-13284083:

pmc-13284483:

pmc-13285583:

pmc-13285683:
The full power-plant genome of an invader catfish from Vietnam is laid out in a 2026 data paper by Thu Thao Thi Huynh and co-authors. The leopard pleco, sold for home tanks, has escaped and spread across many Vietnamese waters. High-throughput reads built its whole mitochondrial genome.

pmc-13285983:

pmc-13286783:

pmc-13287983:

pmc-13288683:

pmc-13288883:

pmc-13289083:

pmc-13289183:

pmc-13289783:

pmc-13290683:

pmc-13290783:

pmc-13291283:

pmc-13291383:

pmc-13291483:

pmc-13291783:

pmc-13291983:

pmc-13292683:

pmc-13292783:

pmc-13292983:

pmc-13293383:

pmc-13293783:

pmc-13293983:

pmc-13294383:

pmc-13294483:

pmc-13294683:

pmc-13295083:

Tests ruled out a blood protein disorder and inherited forms, confirming wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis, a condition where a normal liver protein misfolds with age and stiffens the heart. Her device was upgraded to a resynchronization defibrillator because pacing demand was high, and she started tafamidis, a drug that stabilizes the protein. The authors use the case to argue for early imaging when heart failure behaves atypically, since amyloid-specific treatment works best when started soon.
pmc-13295283:
Christian Caglevic and a large team review antibody treatments for gallbladder cancer in a 2026 article. The tumour is usually found late, varies widely in its genes, and answers standard chemotherapy poorly. Mapping its immune surroundings has opened paths for targeted biological drugs.

Single-target antibodies, dual-target antibodies, and antibody-drug pairs that carry poison cargo are all surveyed. Early work on self-made antibodies as blood markers and on how tumours dodge immunity is also covered. The authors warn against stretching results from wider bile tract trials onto gallbladder cases, and discuss early tests of immune therapy around surgery.
pmc-13295483:
Afsaneh Naderi and colleagues measure tiny retinal vessels in short-sighted Iranian adults in a 2026 study. Vessel thinning may start early in myopia, before sight suffers, but scan artefacts can distort readings. Careful artefact removal and magnification correction were built into every measurement here.

The study covered 218 eyes from adults aged 20 to 52, grouped as normal, mildly, or moderately short-sighted. Deep layer vessel density fell step by step across the three groups, while surface density dropped only at the moderate stage. The central vessel-free zone also widened only in moderate cases, marking deep density as the earliest warning sign.
pmc-13295783:
Nuradh Joseph, Sanjeewa Kularatna, and Sameera Senanayake weigh new lung cancer drugs for value in Sri Lanka in a 2026 study. Targeted and immune drugs given around surgery improve survival in stage two and three disease but strain public budgets. A lifetime cost model judged each option against local willingness to pay.

At the main threshold, surgery-time osimertinib in two settings, surgery-time alectinib, and pre-surgery nivolumab counted as good value for both sexes. At a stricter threshold only the osimertinib plans held firm, while other drugs would need steep price cuts. Full rollout of the good-value set would cost roughly 11.8 million dollars over five years.
pmc-13295983:
Nauman H Malik and colleagues review, in 2026, efforts to soften treatment for throat cancer linked to human papillomavirus. These cancers respond well, so patients may endure harsh therapy they do not all need, yet early attempts to cut back failed to change practice.

The review covers robot surgery, lower radiation doses, altered drug plans and new guides such as virus DNA in blood, immune profiling and imaging. Off-trial cutbacks have fared worse, so caution rules. The authors say safe lightening will need marker-guided selection, team decisions and patient choice, not stage alone.
pmc-13296383:
Mingda Zhao and co-authors review microelectrode array technology for brain-on-a-chip systems in a 2026 article. Such chips grow living neural networks on engineered devices so researchers can model brain activity in the laboratory. Electrode arrays form the two-way link between the neurons and the electronics, recording signals and delivering stimulation.

Planar arrays suit flat cell cultures, while newer three-dimensional flexible arrays wrap or integrate with brain organoids. High-density active arrays built on chip technology are replacing simple passive electrodes. The review also covers pairing arrays with fluid channels, light-based tools, and chemical sensors for richer monitoring. Remaining problems include scaling up, long-term stability, and using artificial intelligence to handle the data.
pmc-13296983:
Solomon Habtemariam proposes, in 2026, a four-layer scale for how deeply gut microbes are woven into drug action. At the shallow end sit whole-microbe treatments such as stool transfer; next, common drugs whose handling the microbes sway, including metformin and levodopa.

Deeper still are plant compounds that only work after microbes transform them, from polyphenols to ginseng extracts. The deepest layer engineers microbes themselves as programmable delivery systems. Habtemariam argues drug discovery should treat the microbiome along this scale, from passive bystander to active partner and designable programmable treatment platform.
pmc-13297583:
Could old plastic be made into new shoe insoles? Elena Arce and her team weigh that idea in a 2026 review of 3D-printed foot supports made from recycled PLA. Printed supports let clinics shape how load spreads through the foot for each patient, a real help in care for sore and diabetic feet.

Recycled feedstock costs less and saves new plastic. The catch is wear from re-melting: heat and grinding can change how the plastic flows, sets, and holds layers, so strength can vary from batch to batch. Most print studies still use new plastic, so proof in real patients is thin. The team calls the idea worth testing, with strict checks on feedstock and print settings first.
pmc-13298083:
Antonio Facciorusso and a large team compare biopsy needles used during endoscopic ultrasound guided liver sampling, in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Five randomised trials covering 251 patients compared aspiration needles with several biopsy needle designs in two gauges. Outcomes centred on total specimen length and counts of complete portal tracts, which help pathologists judge samples.

Two larger-gauge biopsy needles, the Franseen and Fork-tip types, ranked highest on both outcomes. No severe adverse events were reported in the trials. Evidence quality was generally low because of bias risk and small numbers, so the authors call for more randomised trials before firm guidance follows.
pmc-13298183:
Cancer immunotherapy sometimes inflames the liver in a pattern resembling autoimmune hepatitis, and Sarita Chonat with Jonathan Soldera reviewed the published cases in 2026. They searched for reports of this injury after immune checkpoint inhibitors and gathered diagnosis, treatment, and outcome details.

Twenty-two studies covered 195 patients. Steroids were the main first treatment, with recovery in 102 of 105 patients treated with steroids alone, and mycophenolate rescued most steroid-resistant cases. The cancer drug was stopped in 141 patients, and 55 were later rechallenged without the liver problem returning in the records reviewed. Nineteen patients recovered with no drug treatment at all.
pmc-13298383:
Delivering nerve growth factor in a gel directly into the epileptic hippocampus calmed later seizures in mice, report Yuanyuan Bai and colleagues in a 2026 study. They used a kainic acid model of temporal lobe epilepsy, treating animals starting three days after the initial seizure episode and repeating doses every fifteen days.

Treated mice kept more of their dentate gyrus stem cells, and newborn neurons settled and matured more normally. Inflammation and scarring eased, inhibitory neuron markers partly recovered, and circuit measures improved. Chronic seizure counts fell while recognition and spatial memory strengthened. The authors suggest biomaterial-delivered growth support as a way to rebuild balance in epileptic circuits.
pmc-13298483:
Yanfang Zhang and others map how sunflower roots and leaves respond to salt stress at the gene level, in a 2026 transcriptomic study. A tolerant cultivar and a sensitive cultivar both got salt treatment, and their active genes were set side by side. Sunflower is a major oil crop, yet salt still limits yield and quality.

Tens of thousands of genes changed activity, clustering in antioxidant defence and carbohydrate pathways, especially starch and sucrose handling. Dozens of gene-switch families helped steer the response, and spot checks confirmed most sequencing results. The tolerant cultivar joined antioxidant activation, sugar redistribution for osmotic protection, and broad regulatory control, the authors say.
pmc-13299383:
Aurora Scrivo, Liliana Bernardino, and Antonella Consiglio review the double-edged role of vesicles released by brain support cells in brain decline, in a 2026 survey. These tiny parcels carry proteins, RNAs, and organelles between cells. Depending on origin and cargo, glial vesicles can spread harmful signals or deliver helpful ones.

Human stem cell models of glia, above all when joined with brain organoids, recreate disease features of Alzheimer, Parkinson, and motor neuron conditions inside three-dimensional tissue. The review covers survival pathways, barrier crossing, and biomarker hopes. Engineered or patient-specific vesicles may enable targeted therapy, yet clinical use still needs thorough checking.
pmc-13299483:
Three genes stand out in childhood leukemia when two large datasets are read together, report Pasquale Primo and colleagues in a 2026 integrative analysis. They examined PXDN, TCF4, and TSPAN7 expression across a microarray cohort and a pediatric RNA sequencing collection in acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

TCF4 and PXDN were consistently switched up in B-cell disease, while TSPAN7 ran higher in T-cell disease and varied in B-cell cases; initial lab checks in patient samples agreed. Network modeling linked the first two genes to developmental pathways and the third to nerve-lineage programs. The authors present the trio as candidates for sorting patients and for future drug targeting, pending experimental proof.
pmc-13299883:
Sophia Victoria Weiß leads a team staining common skin tumours for a pH-sensitive calcium channel, in a 2026 pathology study. Tumours flip the usual acidity gradient, which makes this channel interesting as a signalling molecule. Samples covered basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, and benign melanocytic moles, a first survey of this channel across these cancers.

Fewer than half of basal cell tumours stained positive, and their expression ran significantly lower than every other group. The other cancers and moles stained strongly in most cases. The authors suggest the channel could help separate squamous from basal tumours under the microscope, with functional studies still needed.
pmc-13300083: Christopher K. Haddock and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their paper on a pain coalition and opioid marketing to veterans. The notice is a correction only: the first statement declaring no conflicts of interest was wrong, because one author's disclosure arrived after printing. The corrected statement records jobs, expert witness fees in opioid litigation, and a charity presidency for the named authors. Scientific conclusions are unaffected, and the first publication has been updated.
pmc-13300183:
Hiba Abuelhija and co-authors report a 2026 study of cell-free DNA, fragments released from injured cells, as an early warning marker after heart surgery in children. The retrospective cohort covered fifty patients under eighteen who had open-heart surgery with a heart-lung bypass machine at an Israeli congenital heart center during 2017 and 2018. Blood levels measured six hours after surgery were compared with kidney injury grades and liver enzyme results.

Cell-free DNA rose sharply within six hours of bypass, and higher values tracked with more severe kidney injury. The six-hour level also correlated with creatinine, urea, and two liver enzymes, and it stayed linked to injury after adjustment for bypass time and other factors. Because the study was small and exploratory, the authors call for larger prospective work before clinical use.
pmc-13300383:
Rui Nascimento and co-authors test a forensic DNA panel in Portugal in a 2026 study. The panel uses microhaplotypes, small clusters of linked variants. These markers promise low mutation rates and rich detail, yet Portugal lacked reference data for them. The team genotyped 237 unrelated people with a seventy-four marker panel on a high-throughput sequencing platform. They then measured allele frequencies and variety, and tested kinship calls through simulations.

The panel showed high genetic variety. The odds of a random match were tiny, near ten to the minus fifty-five. Portuguese samples grouped with other European populations in the structure analysis. In test runs with sibling, half-sibling, and cousin pairs, the markers gave stronger likelihood ratios and fewer false negatives than standard short tandem repeat markers, most of all for close relatives. The authors back the panel as a useful add-on to current forensic tools.
pmc-13300683:
Words shape how surgeons read their own numbers, Mohamed Badie Ahmed and colleagues argue in a 2026 commentary on statistical reporting in plastic surgery. The piece targets two habits: calling results significant at the 0.05 line, and calling interval estimates confidence intervals, which hints at certainty the math cannot give.

The authors propose statistical divergence in place of significance, and uncertainty intervals in place of confidence intervals. P values, they urge, should be read as a sliding scale of divergence rather than a pass-fail gate. Journal guidelines that enforce plainer language could curb binary thinking and P-hacking, especially in the small samples common to surgery.
pmc-13300783:
Two antifungals that attack a deadly fungus in different ways do not necessarily help each other, Le Hoang Ngoc Lan and colleagues find in a 2026 laboratory study. They paired olorofim, a new drug that blocks pyrimidine building, with the membrane-targeting amphotericin B against Talaromyces marneffei. Checkerboard tests covered fifty-five clinical isolates from talaromycosis cases.

Every pairing scored as indifferent, with interaction indices between just above 0.5 and 1.03, so no synergy appeared. Time-kill tests matched: amphotericin B killed in a dose-dependent way, while olorofim only held growth back. The authors doubt olorofim will strengthen opening therapy, but see a possible place for it in later consolidation treatment.
pmc-13300883:
Plant polyphenols hit many targets at once, a profile Caterina Carollo and colleagues explore for polycystic kidney disease in a 2026 narrative review. Autosomal dominant PKD resists single-target drugs, so the authors scan two decades of work on resveratrol, curcumin, naringenin, quercetin, and EGCG. Cell and animal findings take center stage.

In preclinical models these compounds slowed cyst growth by damping inflammation, cell division, and scarring, and by correcting the skewed energy use of cyst cells. Naringenin even binds polycystin-2 directly. Human proof lags, though: a curcumin trial missed its mark largely because little drug reached the kidneys. Better formulations and realistic animal tests come next, the authors urge.
pmc-13301183:
Nearly six decades of Turkish mucormycosis cases come together in a 2026 analysis by Melike Yaşar Duman and colleagues. They mined 155 publications from 1966 to 2024, assembling 199 patients with this invasive fungal infection. Sites, background illness, treatments, and survival were tallied across the reports.

Diabetes underlay 65.8 percent of cases, and the rhino-cerebral form dominated, filling the great majority of reports. Tissue proof carried the diagnosis in nine of ten cases, while cultures confirmed fewer than half. Overall, 43.7 percent of patients died. Surgery reached about seven in ten patients and came with lower crude death rates, backing combined drug and surgical care.
pmc-13301583:
Curt Fritts-Davis, Andrew T. E. Hartwick, and Marjean T. Kulp link two eye problems after mild brain injury in a 2026 study. Seventeen people with a history of mild traumatic brain injury had their pupil light responses measured by an automated pupillometer, and their focus was tested clinically. The group was split by whether focus was impaired. The analyses adjusted for age and time since the injury.

The impaired group showed larger pupil constriction amplitudes and faster average constriction speeds when light hit the eye. Drilling down, the pupil differences tracked with reduced accommodative facility, the speed of refocusing, rather than with reduced focus amplitude. Across everyone, worse facility in each eye correlated moderately to strongly with bigger, faster constrictions. The authors suggest the two systems share autonomic or eye movement circuitry that injury disturbs together. A pupil test, they add, could be a useful window on focus complaints.
pmc-13302183:
L Cocchiara and colleagues check, in a 2026 study, how reliably an implanted loop recorder measures the QT interval, a timing stretch on the heart trace linked to rhythm danger. Continuous monitoring could catch recovery problems early, but only if the implanted reading matches a surface ECG. Signal strength was the authors' main suspect for errors.

Paired measurements came from 141 recordings, with implanted values averaging slightly longer than surface values. Agreement was only moderate overall, and the spread of differences was wide. Taller R waves strongly predicted smaller errors, while wide QRS complexes and younger age predicted larger ones. A simple R-wave rule separated accurate from inaccurate readings almost as well as the full model, guiding when recorder trends can be trusted.
pmc-13302383:
Yihong Pan and co-authors test, in a 2026 laboratory study, drug and alternative-remedy combinations against Candida biofilms behind recurrent vaginal yeast infections. Biofilms, dense fungal communities stuck to tissue, shrug off most standard antifungals. The team screened three conventional drugs and three remedies used in clinics, including boric acid and garlic extract.

All agents killed free-floating Candida cells, although acidic conditions like those in the vagina blunted several of them. Against mature biofilms, almost everything failed except one drug, caspofungin. Pairing fluconazole at blood-achievable levels with povidone-iodine at skin-achievable levels killed biofilms as well as caspofungin did, even in acid. Microscopy and cell counts confirmed the pairing, which the authors propose for managing recurrent infection.
pmc-13302483:
L Donisi and colleagues use the French HONEST registry, in a 2026 study, to compare general anaesthesia against lighter sedation for implants of a defibrillator worn under the skin. Avoiding full anaesthesia could simplify the implant, but outcome differences were unclear. The registry captured every implant in France from 2012 to 2019.

Nearly five thousand patients across 150 centres were included, with about four fifths given general anaesthesia. Use of lighter approaches climbed steeply over the study years. After adjustment and about four years of follow-up, complications, repeat operations, shocks, and deaths showed no real differences between strategies. Results also matched between the two lighter sedation styles, supporting wider use of non-general approaches.
pmc-13303683:
Filippos Filippatos, Konstantinos Kakleas, and Athanasios Michos review reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption in children in a 2026 narrative review. In this syndrome, severe mouth and surface sores follow a recent infection, while skin involvement stays limited.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the classic trigger, but flu, COVID-19, and other airway viruses can produce the same picture. The review traces how airway sensing, inflammasome activity, cytokine surges, white cell influx, and T cell shifts injure moist body surfaces. New protein data, possible inherited risk, look-alike conditions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and care notes are covered for doctors.
pmc-13303983:
Guiyu Liu and colleagues simulate tiny indentations in zirconium carbide in a 2026 computer study. Heat, carbon shortages, and crystal direction may all change how this hard ceramic dents and cracks at the smallest scale.

Molecular dynamics runs varied temperature, carbon-to-zirconium ratio, and the face being pressed. Hotter runs needed less force, dented deeper, and spawned more sliding defects inside the crystal. Missing carbon weakened the bonds and lowered hardness and stiffness in straight lines with dose. Stiffness also fell as the pressed face changed, owing to differing slip routes and surface energies.
pmc-13305383:
Kinlabel Okwen Tetamiyaka Tezok and colleagues set out a 2026 framework for turning fast evidence reviews into living systems that stay current. Quick reviews help policy during crises but freeze in place while new studies and local knowledge keep coming.

Drawing on work by eBASE Africa, the plan weaves continuous watching of journals, gray reports, social media, and Indigenous knowledge into standard rapid review steps. Computer tools help under human watch. Aimed at lower-income countries, the pathway promises less repeated effort and evidence that stays useful for live policy choices.
pmc-13305883:
Anthony Maher and colleagues surveyed Irish parents in 2026 about how they would choose primary care for a child's chest infection. A total of 469 parents completed twelve choice tasks that varied waiting time, provider, antibiotic plans, advice, and cost. Many childhood respiratory infections settle without antibiotics, so parental expectations shape prescribing.

Parents valued short waits, care led by a general practitioner, and low out-of-pocket cost most strongly. Immediate and delayed antibiotic plans both raised a service's appeal, as did self-care advice with clear warning signs. Pharmacist-led care scored lowest among provider options. The authors read antibiotic demand partly as a search for reassurance under uncertainty. Services that reduce that uncertainty, they argue, could support stewardship without losing parental trust.
pmc-13306583:
Duo Gao and co-authors compare compact mathematical models in 2026 for how polymer-based energetic materials creep and relax over time. Such materials fill solid propellants and polymer-bonded explosives, and slow deformation affects storage safety. Fourteen candidate models built from springs and spring-pot elements were fitted to published data.

Two six-parameter fractional models described both creep and stress relaxation with very high fit quality. Fitted on only the first tenth of a test's time span, they predicted behaviour about ten times further ahead with small errors. Classical series and power-law approaches needed more terms for similar reach. The authors offer the winning forms as compact tools for judging long-term structural response. Careful model choice, they note, supports service-life estimates for stored energetic components.
pmc-13307183:
Yao Wu compared gut recovery after two treatments for chronic stone-blocked appendicitis in a 2026 hospital study. A total of 101 patients split between endoscopic retrograde therapy, 40 people, and laparoscopic appendix removal, 61 people, in reported counts.

Every endoscopic case finished with full tube entry and stone removal, and no severe events followed in either group. Endoscopic care ran shorter in operating time and hospital stay with clear statistical gaps. Symptom rating scores tracked gut function before and after, testing whether keeping the appendix speeds digestive recovery. The scores also hint that gut ease may set how fast men and women leave care.
pmc-13307283:
Qingtian Zhang mapped DNA methylation change across grape berry growth in the Cabernet Franc variety in a 2026 study. Berries were sampled at 7 days and 78 days after flowering, the early and late stages with the sharpest shape contrast.

Overall methylation rose from 12.57% to 14.16% between stages in reported figures, driven by CHH marking climbing from 5.88% to 7.92% in the given values. Most changed regions gained marks late, mainly in that same context. Joint gene activity analysis tied extra marking to lower activity of a berry size brake gene. The maps give growers a base for timing pick dates and wine style by berry growth stage.
pmc-13307383:
Orlane Pivert and co-authors report a 2026 study of how family doctors in the Poitou-Charentes area of France spot violence between people during routine visits. Visits with three doctors were recorded from June to September 2019, and only visits where violence came out were studied in depth.

Among 326 patients, 25 shared an account of violence. Vague body complaints and blurred hints about injury gave early clues, while direct questions worked best to open the topic. Warmth, trust, and a willingness to return to the topic over time also helped. Training in patient centred talk could lift detection rates in daily practice.
pmc-13307583:
Christopher Rhyne and co-authors use United States claims data in 2026 to see whether onabotulinumtoxinA care for cervical dystonia cuts fills for pain and spasm drugs. Among 564 patients with past use of such drugs, they tracked opioid, benzodiazepine, and muscle relaxant fills for 12 months after care began.

Among those with more than one opioid fill at the start, 30.4 percent had no opioid fills in the year that followed care. Mean opioid fills per patient fell by 17.0 percent over that year, and daily dose strength fell as well. Like drops appeared for the other two drug groups, which hints at less reliance on habit forming care.
pmc-13307683:
Haochen Li and co-authors map in 2026 RNA transcripts that appear only in cancers, using long read sequencing data across many human tumour types. They charted 44,405 such transcripts and studied those found in more than 10 cancer types for links to survival, pathways, and immune traits.

The set proved highly varied in form and rich in pathways tied to malignancy and spread. Gene splicing, copy changes, and chemical marks on DNA all helped shape which transcripts arose in each tumour. A risk score built from 131 hallmark linked transcripts tracked survival and stage. Lab tests that silenced two transcripts slowed tumour cell growth, which hints at future drug targets.
pmc-13307783:
Guo-Qiang Zhu and colleagues review in 2026 the state of cystic echinococcosis across Africa, a tapeworm larval disease passed between dogs, livestock, and people. Pastoral communities bear the heaviest burden because close contact with dogs and herds is routine. The review covers prevalence, spread, risk factors, diagnosis, treatment, and control.

Hydatid cysts grow in organs of people and animals who swallow eggs shed by infected dogs. Human and animal rates vary widely by region and surveillance strength. Molecular data are scarce, and Central Africa is especially poorly monitored, leaving the true map incomplete. Control depends on dog management, slaughter hygiene, and community education working together. The authors aim the review at guiding research and prevention planning. Better species and strain data, they argue, would sharpen every control decision.
pmc-13307883:
Weronika Marta Balas and co-authors check in 2026 whether children with hen's egg allergy tolerate the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine at their clinic. Thirty-nine hospitalised patients, averaging nineteen months old, were reviewed, including fifteen who had previously suffered anaphylaxis after eating egg. Histories, skin tests, and antibody measures against milk and egg were collected.

No child had a whole-body reaction to vaccination. One developed a widespread spotty rash that settled after a single antihistamine dose. Worries had nevertheless delayed vaccination in nearly two-thirds of the group, with the longest delay passing nine years. The vaccine virus grows in chick embryo cells but carries no meaningful egg protein, the authors note. They argue that severe reactions are rare and far outweighed by measles risk. Clearer communication of safety data is their main prescription for closing the delay gap.
pmc-13308483:
C Spering and co-authors compare in 2026 same day versus next few day surgery to fix severe chest wall injuries, using a German trauma registry from 2015 to 2023. They matched 500 pairs of badly hurt patients who had chest wall repair on day zero or on days one to three.

Same day patients died far more often in hospital, at 10.6 percent versus 3.6 percent for the later group in matched pairs. The same day group also started with worse wounds and higher risk scores that matching could not fully erase. The authors read the gap as a sign of who gets rushed to theatre, not proof that fast surgery harms. Care within three days, timed to each patient, stays the safer broad rule.
pmc-13309283:
Darui Jin and co-authors build in 2026 Hetairos, an AI tool that reads stained tissue slides to guess methylation based brain and spine tumour subtypes. That call now needs slow, costly gene tests. The model trained and checked on 9606 patients and over 11,000 slides from 11 centres across four continents.

Hetairos gave a sure call on 50 to 70 percent of cases, with 0.87 accuracy on its top rated guesses across 102 subtypes. In a head to head on slides alone, it beat five board passed brain path doctors, 0.68 against 0.30 in the same test. In live clinic use, calls came in 12 minutes, not 12 days. Poor sites could triage cases far faster.
pmc-13311083:
Ying Guo and co-authors hunt yield trait loci in Chinese wheat landraces through genome scans in a 2026 study. Wheat yield rests on spike shape, grain count, and grain weight, all under complex gene control. Old local types from Gansu Province may hold fresh useful variants for breeding.

A panel of 372 landraces was scored for four yield traits over four years at two sites and genotyped on a marker chip. Five scan models found 19 loci in total across the traits, each with distinct type groups. Sixteen candidate genes were flagged, spanning growth and splicing roles. New loci give breeders fresh targets for higher yield.
pmc-13311183:
Jun Chen and colleagues contrast lake sediment metals across a decade on the Qinghai Xizang Plateau in a 2026 study. Alpine lakes face climate shifts and human pressure, yet plateau wide risk maps with source splits were scarce. Sediments from 110 lakes in 2014 and 2024 were compared with a hybrid source model.

Arsenic topped baseline marks in both decades, while mean chromium fell. Overall risk stayed low, driven by cadmium, with hot spots at three named lakes. Mixed human and rock sources grew as a share of variance over the decade, while the solo arsenic source held steady. Road growth zones need targeted guards.
pmc-13311283:
Johannes Burtscher and colleagues give their 2026 review of biomarkers and possible subtypes of acute mountain sickness. The illness brings headache, gut upset, dizziness, and tiredness at high altitude and can turn dangerous.

The review pulls together what is known about the body's response to thin air and which blood or body measures have been proposed as markers. No firm test for the illness exists yet. The authors argue the sickness may come in kinds, driven by too weak or too strong a response to low oxygen. Sorting these kinds could lead to tests that rest on body measures, not symptoms alone.
pmc-13311683:
Abu Sayeed and colleagues, in 2026, analyze a multi-country survey study on emergency obstetric care readiness in eight low-income and lower-middle-income countries. Skilled emergency care at birth is a proven guard against maternal death.

Facility surveys from 2014 to 2022 covered 4382 sites offering normal delivery care, from Afghanistan to Tanzania. Availability was judged by seven basic and two added emergency functions. Readiness scores summed staff training, gear, and medicines into a mark out of 100. The study shows how far facilities fall short of full readiness and where the gaps cluster, giving ministries a shared yardstick.
pmc-13311783:
Mahdieh Daneshvar, Arsalan Parvareh, and Neda Azimi report a 2026 study on using high-frequency ultrasound to boost a tiny three-phase photocatalytic reactor that cleans dye from water. Sound waves stir the mix and speed the chemistry.

The custom reactor holds four diamond-shaped chambers with sound plates running at 1.7 megahertz. A magnetic iron-titanium catalyst plus oxygen did the cleaning work on methylene blue dye. Sound plus light removed 44.3 percent of the dye, beating light alone by about 13 percent in this setup. Calorimetry showed just over half the sound power reached the liquid. The design points to compact water treatment units.
pmc-13311983:
Kai Chen and colleagues present a 2026 single-cell multiomics study of fibroblasts that secrete complement proteins inside pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic tumors host fibroblast types that can either feed or restrain growth. Sorting them out could guide therapies that reprogram the harmful ones. Combining gene, chromatin, and spatial data, the team characterized a complement-secreting subtype and compared it with inflammatory fibroblasts.

The two subtypes overlap heavily in gene activity. The complement-secreting cells, though, look like an earlier state from which inflammatory ones may develop. Their share shrinks as cancer progresses. Tumor regions rich in them held fewer suppressive macrophages and lower levels of a key growth signal. They also exchanged signals with T cells through a defined molecular pairing. Patients whose tumors carried more of these fibroblasts lived longer and stayed recurrence-free longer. The authors propose coaxing inflammatory fibroblasts back into this state as treatment.
pmc-13312083:
Tanveer Teranikar and colleagues introduce, in a 2026 methods study, a platform that tracks single heart muscle cells in three dimensions to measure how the heart wall deforms in living zebrafish embryos. Standard imaging usually flattens this motion into two dimensions, which limits accuracy and repeatability.

Their setup pairs a fast benchtop light-sheet microscope with a deep learning pipeline built on a 3D nnU-Net. The microscope captures cell-level detail across a millimeter-wide view at millisecond speed, letting the team rebuild the paths of individual cell nuclei over time. Extra image processing steps split nuclei that touch or overlap, a common failure in layered heart tissue. The authors present the workflow as a scalable base for modeling how disease changes heart mechanics.
pmc-13312583:
Maria Triantafyllou and Nikolaos Michalopoulos present a 2026 systematic review of how breast reconstruction affects sexual function and body image after mastectomy. As survival improves, quality of survivorship matters more. The reviewers searched PubMed for studies from January 2016 to January 2026. They graded them with established quality tools across several study designs.

Twenty-seven studies covering more than 25,000 survivors qualified. Women who had reconstruction generally reported better sexual function and body image than women with mastectomy alone. Using the patient's own tissue beat implants on long-term satisfaction and sexual well-being. Breast-conserving therapy preserved nipple sensation better than total mastectomy. Age, body mass index, and relationship satisfaction also shaped outcomes. Counselling about sexual health before surgery was often thin. The authors call reconstruction a core part of holistic recovery and urge teams to build sexual health into routine care.
pmc-13312783: The Frontiers Editorial Office issued this 2026 retraction notice withdrawing a 2022 article from Frontiers in Psychiatry. That article had tested a virtual reality simulation of psychosis in medical students against illness stigma, empathy, and knowledge. After readers raised concerns, an investigation under the publisher's policies found the complaints valid and judged that the article fell short of editorial and scientific standards. The chief editors approved the retraction, the original authors did not answer correspondence about it, and they are invited to submit a corrected manuscript.
pmc-13313183:
Susana Delgado Ocaña heads a 2026 mouse study on how gut microbes shape cocaine use and relapse. Earlier work by the group showed that cocaine raises gut Proteobacteria, which drain the amino acid glycine and change gene activity in a brain reward area, the nucleus accumbens.

Here the team asked whether that glycine loss also drives cocaine self-administration, the lab task that best mirrors human drug taking. The study links the microbe shift to brain plasticity, drive, and return to drug seeking after a break. Its value lies in pointing to the gut as a possible treatment target for addiction, a field where approved drugs remain few and weak. By tying a gut change to relapse-like acts, the work gives that search a clear test case.
pmc-13313383: A retraction notice issued in the journal Plants in 2026 withdraws an article by Yaqin Wang and co-workers on drought stress in Scaevola taccada seedlings. pmc-13315983:

pmc-13316183:

pmc-13316283:

pmc-13316583:

pmc-13316683:

pmc-13316783:

pmc-13318383:

pmc-13318783:

pmc-13318883:

pmc-13319083:

pmc-13319483:

pmc-13319683:

pmc-13319883:

pmc-13320283:

pmc-13320383:

pmc-13320583:

pmc-13321883:

pmc-13323083:

pmc-13323183:

pmc-13323583:

pmc-13325283:

pmc-13328083:

pmc-13331183:

pmc-13332483:

pmc-13332783:

pmc-13333283:

pmc-13333683:

pmc-13334083:

pmc-13334983:

pmc-13335783:

pmc-13336083:

pmc-13336383:

pmc-13337083:

pmc-13337383:
