A favorable cluster held 246 patients, or 56.2% of the trial group, while 192 patients formed a less favorable cluster in the analysis. The second group was older, with longer disease and more prior TNF blocker use. Most outcomes already diverged by week 2 and stayed apart through week 24. Models using baseline plus week-2 data could flag each path early, helping doctors adjust sooner.
pmc-13337783:
Xue-Qiao Wang and co-authors review Wilson disease through the gut, liver, and brain link in a 2026 article. Faults in the ATP7B gene cause copper to build up in liver, brain, and cornea. That direct buildup stays the main cause of harm, the authors stress.

Copper imbalance also reshapes gut microbes, and disturbed microbes then alter copper uptake and removal, forming a harmful cycle. Barrier damage lets bacterial products enter the blood and fuel inflammation. Microbe-made compounds such as short-chain fatty acids and bile acids carry signals between organs. Chelator drugs, zinc, diet, and microbe-based care are weighed for how they interact.
pmc-13338583:
Mário Luiz Santana and co-authors derive genetic indicators of performance resilience in Brazilian barrel racing Quarter Horses, asking whether consistency itself can be bred for. Their 2026 study uses race records from 2010 to 2024 covering 10,665 horses, extracting each horse's short-term deviations from its expected performance once horse and rider effects are removed.

Three consistency measures were tested: typical deviation size, the spread of deviations, and the share of better-than-expected runs. Heritability was low, between 0.06 and 0.09, but nonzero, meaning some exploitable genetic variation exists. Two measures were genetically almost identical, while the third captured partly separate information. All three favoured horses that ran faster and earned more over their careers. The authors conclude longitudinal race records can supply scalable resilience indicators that complement traditional speed traits in genetic evaluation of sport horses.
pmc-13339183:
Faxue Li and colleagues review Bayes syndrome and heart scarring in a 2026 article. The syndrome means advanced block of signals between the atria, tied to atrial fibrillation and stroke. Scar tissue in the heart muscle may both cause and follow that block.

Scarring delays atrial conduction, while blocked conduction strains the atria and may deepen scarring. Studies cited show the syndrome predicts fibrillation, stroke, and death on its own. Heart scans with magnetic resonance and ultrasound can gauge scar burden without biopsy. Pairing tracing markers with scan patterns may sharpen risk sorting, though proof from forward-looking trials is still thin.
pmc-13341183:
Diabetes drug guidelines from four bodies are compared in a 2026 review led by Suk Kyeong Kim. The American, British, Japanese, and Korean frameworks all rest on outcome trials from the past decade, yet they organize treatment in noticeably different ways.

The ADA takes a person-centered, risk-based line favoring SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 drugs when heart or kidney disease is present. NICE works within cost-effectiveness rules and moves early to combined therapy. Japan's society tailors choices to East Asian physiology, while the Korean framework keeps glucose control central but adds comorbidity checks and flexible early combinations. Shared evidence, the authors conclude, still yields diverging strategies.
pmc-13341283:
Predicting stroke after a torn neck artery is the goal of a 2026 study by Xuanxiao Zhang and colleagues. The team reviewed 129 patients with cervical artery dissection covering 148 torn vessels, combining clinical data with high-resolution vessel wall MRI features.

At vessel level, white blood cell count, clot inside the channel, severe narrowing or blockage, and alcohol use each tied independently to ischemic events. The patient-level model added male sex, and a nomogram built from these factors discriminated well, with a corrected area under the curve of 0.837. Such a tool could flag dissection patients who need the closest early monitoring.
pmc-13341483:
Heat-linked heart deaths in the United States are tracked over 25 years by Hassaan Abid and colleagues in a 2026 CDC WONDER analysis. The team pulled deaths from 1999 to 2024 where heat exposure contributed and circulatory disease was the underlying cause, among adults aged 25 and older.

In all, 10,731 deaths qualified. Rates fell early in the period, then rose sharply from 2015 to 2024 with an annual percent change of 17.58%. Men showed a significant overall increase, Hispanic populations the steepest recent climb, and the West and South carried the heaviest burden. The reversal underlines heat as a growing cardiovascular threat.
pmc-13343483:
Julia R Greer comments in 2026 on a framework by Li and colleagues for the mechanics of twisted two-dimensional materials. Twisted bilayer graphene sparked a rush after its odd superconductivity appeared, but math linking tiny deformations to twist angle lagged, leaving quantum behavior hard to predict or control.

Li's team used dislocation theory to write exact expressions for rotation, strain, and stress inside the moiré patterns that form between rotated layers. Their model captures triangles of favored stacking at small angles, a switch near two degrees, and hexagonal domains at larger twists. Predictions matched both big atomistic simulations and microscope measurements, giving designers a validated tool for layered materials.
pmc-13347683:
Mpho S. Ramano, Tania Buys, and Carla Kotzé explore how occupational therapists judge their own role in arranging workplace adjustments for staff with major depression, in a qualitative study from 2026. Seven therapists were interviewed one by one, and themes were built from their accounts of helping workers who return after sick leave with lingering limits.

Two themes stood out, covering adjustment as a moving, negotiated process and the skills therapists need to lead that process well. Staying current, handling cases in an organised way, and knowing the law were stressed as core strengths. A step-by-step picture of the process is offered as a guide other therapists can follow in practice.
pmc-13349783:
Hao Chen and fellow editors introduced a research collection in a 2026 editorial on mindfulness in media and communication studies. The collection gathers 21 articles on how mindful attention shapes life in an always-on media setting.

Topics span social media, news habits, learning online, the uptake of AI tools, digital self-control, kind responses to media content, and immersive tools such as virtual reality. The editors frame mindfulness not just as a private practice but as a resource that shapes how people notice, judge, and answer mediated messages. Constant feeds, social comparison, and AI contact can overload thinking and strain attention, and the collection asks how mindfulness might ease those pressures.
pmc-13349883:
Cailu Shen and colleagues wrote a narrative review in 2026 on integrative oncology for colorectal cancer, covering prevention through long-term survivorship. The disease brought roughly 1.9 million new cases in 2022, and more than 900,000 deaths, yet proven supportive strategies are used unevenly in routine care.

High-fibre and Mediterranean diets, calcium, regular activity, and healthy weight each lowered risk in large studies. A phase 3 trial showed structured exercise after chemotherapy cut recurrence and death. Aspirin prevention needs case-by-case judgement, and gut bacteria such as Fusobacterium nucleatum are shown to push cancer growth through several routes. The review gathers these options into one care-spanning account.
pmc-13349983:
Yuhan Zhang and co-authors explored ultra-high-field MRI for examining fetuses after death in a 2026 single-centre study. Traditional autopsy rates are falling for cultural and personal reasons, yet families and doctors still need to know why a baby died.

Twenty fetuses delivered by induced labour at a mean age of 26.4 weeks were scanned at 7.0 Tesla, which gives near-microscopic detail; 19 also had a standard autopsy for comparison. The team tuned scan settings and built a team workflow covering specimen handling and reading. Matching scan findings against autopsy results tests whether this gentle method can answer families' questions.
pmc-13350883:
D. Deepa and K. R. Jothi set out in 2026 an adaptive, mobility-aware hierarchical task offloading scheme for delay-sensitive uses in fog computing, where Internet of Things devices need instant replies but fog nodes have thin resources. Offloading remains hard since users move and fog nodes vary in processing power.

Their design adds a multi-level fog layer and treats capable IoT devices themselves as fog nodes, based on computing power and mobility. A random mobility forecast model predicts future sites of users and devices, and a location-aware module optimises offloading before engaging a device. Simulations in MobFogSim showed effective convergence, lower latency, and better user experience. The scheme suits uses such as linked vehicles and health tracking where delay matters.
pmc-13353183:
Suyeon Kim and co-authors test a marker protein for a hard-to-diagnose liver tumour in a 2026 case study. Hepatic angiomyolipoma belongs to the PEComa family and varies so much in scans and tissue that diagnosis often stalls. A 39-year-old man with past Hodgkin lymphoma had belly pain and a growing mass in his left liver lobe.

Core biopsy showed fat, epithelioid cells, and thick-walled vessels without clear atypia. Staining was patchy for HMB45 and Melan-A but diffuse for GPNMB and smooth muscle actin, supporting the diagnosis. He then had the left lateral liver segment removed. The authors present GPNMB as a helpful extra stain when classic signs are faint.
pmc-13353883:
Lin Zhang and Alexander Kuhn surveyed how patchy bits are made at phase edges, in 2026. Unlike uniform colloids, patchy bits carry distinct surface regions, which lets them assemble in planned ways and serve as drivers or medical carriers. Making those regions well is the central challenge.

The review groups making ways by the edge used to create asymmetry. Solid-gas settings use shade for aimed coating. Liquid-gas settings exploit surface tension for tunable masks. Solid-liquid settings anchor bits for picked care. Readers gain a clear map of which edge suits which particle design, and where the field still needs simpler, scalable routes.
pmc-13354383:
Bassel Hallak and others told of an augmented reality navigation system for treating isolated Onodi sinusitis, ran the case report in 2026. The Onodi cell is a posterior ethmoid air cell sitting beside the sphenoid sinus, close to the optic nerve and a major artery. Swelling confined to this cell is rare, but surgery near it carries a high risk of vision injury.

The case involved an eighty-six-year-old woman whose isolated Onodi sinusitis was found incidentally on a routine CT scan during workup for general decline. Augmented reality guidance overlaid anatomical detail during care, helping the team navigate the tight, high-risk space. The report shows how navigation technology can make a rare and dangerous sinus problem safer to treat.
pmc-13356783:
So Izumi and co-authors studied in 2026 how downtime, the span from collapse to restored circulation, affects survival after surgery for a torn aorta with cardiac arrest. A type A aortic dissection is a tear in the main artery that is often deadly, and arrest makes it far worse. Records covered 711 patients from 2003 to 2024, of whom 222 had arrest and only 30 had repair surgery.

All arrest patients without surgery died early, while 40 percent of those with surgery died early, and six went home. Five-year survival after surgery was about 30 percent. Longer downtime and poor heart blood flow raised later death risk, and downtime under about eighteen minutes best predicted going home.
pmc-13358483:
Song Bai and co-authors report a 2026 study on a distinct type of thyroid cancer. These papillary tumors have a ring of calcium around the edge, and they may spread in their own way. Doctors lack a tool to judge, before surgery, if the cancer has reached the central neck lymph nodes. The team set out to build one from ultrasound scans.

They studied 210 patients whose tumors fit this type and who had the central nodes removed at surgery. Lab results after surgery showed which scans had truly spread. The model built from these cases aims to help doctors plan the right scope of surgery for each patient, no more and no less.
pmc-13358583:
Jing Wang and co-authors pool past studies on heart fat and heart attack outcomes in a 2026 review. A pad of fat sits directly on the heart, and it can release signals that stir inflammation. The team asked whether the size of this fat pad, measured on scans or ultrasound, predicts how patients fare after a heart attack.

They searched four databases for studies that measured the fat and tracked major heart events over time. Pooling the risk figures can show whether the fat pad adds news beyond standard risk factors. If it does, a measure already visible on heart scans could help doctors spot patients who need tighter follow-up.
pmc-13359683:
Sereen Hej-Ali and co-authors give a practical guide to the side effects of new myeloma therapies in a 2026 review. Multiple myeloma, a blood cancer of plasma cells, is now treated with CAR-T cells, bispecific antibodies, and antibody-drug conjugates. These powerful tools can cause fever, low blood pressure, and confusion within days, and infections, movement problems, and low blood counts over months.

Such treatments once stayed in specialist hospitals but now reach community clinics. The review tells clinicians what to expect, when each danger tends to strike, and how to prevent or treat it. Clear guidance helps wider teams deliver these therapies safely.
pmc-13359783:
Uma Bapat and co-authors review how the heart fuels itself across life in a 2026 paper. A healthy adult heart switches flexibly between fuels, but aging and disease narrow that flexibility and remodel its energy use. The review maps these shifts from fetal life to old age, in health and in sickness.

It also explains how heart muscle cells trade signals with their neighbor cells to govern fuel use. The lessons feed a practical goal: lab-grown heart cells from stem cells stay immature in part because their metabolism is immature. Fixing that could make them far better models for testing drugs and studying disease.
pmc-13359983:
Małgorzata Pudełek and co-authors measure fitness in blood cancer patients in a 2026 study. Patients with chronic lymphoid cancers who receive antibody-based therapy form a growing group of survivors. Staying able-bodied during treatment protects independence and quality of life. The team compared these patients' physical performance with that of healthy controls.

Patients showed weaker lower-body strength and poorer balance and agility, and some had lower exercise capacity. Older age tied to worse performance across the board. The authors argue that fitness checks should be a routine part of care for this group, so limits are caught early and tailored rehabilitation can start in time.
pmc-13360083:
Kai-Ti Tseng led a 2026 study of young children who were born very early and very small. The team followed 96 children, 57 born preterm and 39 born at term, and checked them at age five to six. They used DXA scans to measure body fat and lean mass, and blood tests to check insulin resistance.

Fat and lean mass looked much the same in both groups at preschool age. But the preterm group had higher insulin levels and higher insulin resistance scores. Among preterm children, those who were overweight had more trunk fat and worse scores. Fast weight gain between ages two and five also tracked with more fat and higher insulin. The authors urge early checks for these children.
pmc-13360783:
Andrea Severo and co-authors present a 2026 nationwide study of heart failure in Spain, split by sex. Heart failure is a major public health burden, and men and women often differ in how it starts and shows. Yet Spain lacked national data that lay out those gaps. The team used a health records database covering about 1.8 million people in seven regions.

They picked out adults first diagnosed with heart failure between 2013 and 2019. Cases were sorted by how strongly the heart pumps, from weak to preserved. The study counts new cases, total cases, and patient traits across age groups for each sex. This first national picture can guide fairer care planning and show where men's and women's needs diverge.
pmc-13361183:
Otman Sandali and co-authors ran a 2026 trial on light exposure during cataract surgery in patients with macular degeneration. Bright microscope light during surgery might stress the macula, the center of sharp vision. The team assigned 42 eyes to standard surgery or to a 3D digital viewing system that needs far less light. Macular function was tested with electric eye signals before and after surgery.

Light exposure in the 3D group was far lower than with the standard microscope. One hour after surgery, the drop in the main light-response signal was about the same in both groups. But a timing measure worsened in the standard group while staying stable in the 3D group. Follow-up ran to one month. The trial tests whether gentler light protects fragile maculas.
pmc-13361383:
Olga N Alekseeva and co-authors combined two engineered viruses to attack breast tumors in mice in a 2026 study. Oncolytic viruses infect and burst cancer cells, but single viruses often kill too little and stir too little immunity. The team armed two vaccinia virus versions: one carrying a herpes enzyme that turns a drug toxic inside tumor cells, the other carrying an immune receptor part. A mouse breast cancer model served for tests.

In dishes, the herpes-armed virus killed cancer cells in step with dose, and the partner drug boosted the kill. Immune killer cells added to infected tumor cells raised the effect further. In living mice, the combined treatment shrank tumors and extended survival compared with single-virus care. Pairing viruses with different weapons may beat solid tumors harder.
pmc-13361683:
Ziye Xu and co-authors review high-tech ways to judge egg freshness without breaking the shell in a 2026 paper. Eggs are a main source of quality protein, and freshness fades as water shifts and proteins break down during storage. Standard lab tests destroy the egg, so they cannot screen the flood of eggs in industry. Light-based scans can read the inside through the shell, but each method alone has limits.

The review gathers recent work pairing several scan types with artificial intelligence. The methods include visible and near-infrared light, Raman scattering, fluorescence, and hyperspectral imaging, which captures many wavelengths at once. Combined sensors plus smart models read freshness signs more reliably than single tools. The authors map what works and what still blocks factory use of these systems.
pmc-13362483:
Ikhlas Laasri and Vaibhav Shrivastava present a 2026 review on turning farm and food factory waste into crop boosters called biostimulants. Their survey covers green extraction methods, tiny nano-scale carriers, and artificial intelligence tools that predict how well a product will work. The aim is a circular model where waste streams become inputs instead of pollution.

The review cites waste-based products that raised crop growth sharply in trials, and AI models that forecast results with fair accuracy. Gentle enzyme methods kept active compounds intact while cutting carbon output versus synthetic fertilizer. The authors also weigh rules and carbon credit income across countries, arguing these decide how fast such products reach farms at scale.
pmc-13363583:
Anna Gościniak and colleagues present a 2026 study on chokeberry extract as a diabetes aid, and on keeping its fragile pigments alive. The berry's anthocyanins fight cell stress and slow starch breakdown, but they fade fast. The team tuned extraction with a structured design, tested the extract on the starch enzyme amylase, modeled which compounds do the work, and then blended the extract into yeast beta-glucan carriers.

The tuned extract blocked amylase more strongly than the standard drug acarbose in the same test, and modeling credited the cyanidin pigment family. Blending into glucan slowed pigment breakdown in a dose pattern, with the best mix, one part extract to two parts glucan, cutting the fade rate nearly five-fold. The work links extraction, action, and shelf life in one chain.
pmc-13363983:
Wenhua Xu and colleagues present a 2026 study on converting fiber-optic seismic signals into the kind of data standard geophone tools expect. Distributed acoustic sensing reads strain along a cable, not ground velocity, and the math that converts the two amplifies noise, above all in faint field records. Their inversion pairs two pattern rules: one keeps the signal compact and calm, the other guards weak but steady events from being wiped away.

Solved with a standard splitting algorithm, the method restored wave shape and strength under low signal-to-noise conditions in both synthetic and field tests. Weak coherent events survived while stray artifacts fell. The authors offer the converter as a robust bridge between new fiber sensing and the mature seismic software built for geophones.
pmc-13364183:
Peng Liu and colleagues present a 2026 study on scheduling joint maintenance for a four-part fatigue testing machine, where parts wear by different rules and some states are hard to observe. Their deep reinforcement learning method gives the network a shared encoder and an attention step that weighs how parts affect each other. Each part gets its own head for its repair choices. Impossible actions are masked out, and a data-quality penalty tied to sensor wear shapes the rewards.

Against calendar-based upkeep, the method cut average yearly cost by about three fifths. Against threshold-based care it cut cost by over two fifths. Failures fell from about ten a year to under two, and data efficiency climbed. Tests that removed each design element confirmed all three carried weight.
pmc-13364383:
Junrui Zhang and co-workers sum up a 2026 review of fiber sheets glued to the out side of concrete to add pull strength. The review drew on 174 past studies with near four thousand tests. It split the works by whether steel or fiber anchors held the sheet ends down.

Plain sheets fail most by peel off, ruled by sheet stiffness, glue, and surface prep. Anchored sheets held more load and peeled late. Yet tests with many anchors were rare, and most strength math held only in its home test range. The gaps mark where new tests should aim.
pmc-13364683:
Yipeng Xie and co-workers show in 2026 how loose DNA rings in cancer cells hitch to chromosomes to pass to child cells. These rings carry growth genes and spread at random, which feeds tumor spread and drug dodge. The team finds the rings latch to a bright histone mark on packed DNA.

Reader proteins grip that mark and hold the rings in place, each in its own cell set. A quiet form of the copy enzyme also helps the latch. Cuts to ring control zones broke the pass on, and stray rings left the cell core. That loss cut growth gene use and drug dodge.
pmc-13370683:
Eloise K. Tarry and colleagues ask why some fit young men burn fat at higher rates during exercise in a 2026 study. Thirty-four lean, active men were tested for aerobic capacity, peak fat burning, body make-up, and blood markers, and a small muscle sample was taken from each. Protein levels in muscle were measured with mass spectrometry.

Absolute peak fat burning tracked aerobic capacity, but few single proteins matched it. When fat burning was scaled to body size, and when the exercise intensity at peak burning was used, many mitochondrial proteins lined up clearly. Overall mitochondrial protein abundance rose with both measures. The work points to the cell powerhouses, rather than any one protein, as the key driver of fat-burning capacity.
pmc-13370783:
Alexander J. Heiler and colleagues develop a precise way to load two different payloads onto one nanoparticle in a 2026 paper. Combination drugs often work better together, but fixing two drugs to the same carrier at exact ratios and with distinct release timing has been hard. The team pairs thiol-disulfide exchange with strain-promoted click chemistry on a polymer nanoparticle platform.

The method gives defined control over how much of each payload is attached and how each is released. Tested as a subunit vaccine carrier, the particles tuned how dendritic cells in lymph nodes matured and presented antigen. The platform could sharpen combination therapy and vaccine design, letting researchers test exact ratios rather than settling for rough mixtures.
pmc-13374083:
Akihiro Odagaki and co-authors tell of a hip break that hid from top scans in a 2026 case report. A woman aged 64 with a blood cell ill fell and had lasting pain high in her left leg. Plain films, two types of scans, and a magnet scan all showed no break.

Pain stayed for a month, so scans were run again. They now showed a hip neck break with no shift of the bone. Screws and a plate fixed it, and she healed with no hitch. Her blood ill had changed the bone's core, which likely hid the break's marks. Lasting pain after a fall still counts, the team says.
pmc-13374183:
Laura Julià and others compare methods for grouping long-term symptom courses in mental-health research in a 2026 study. Grouping courses helps capture medical variety, yet distance-based and model-based methods may behave in other ways with few follow-ups, variable tests, and mixed patient replies. The team checked 237 first-episode that illness patients and ran 500 computer tests per scenario.

Computer tests varied group numbers, group sizes, and spacing levels. Finding of true group counts, sorting how right, and medical clarity were compared, with soundness indices used to judge each method. The contrast gives psychiatric teams evidence on which grouping approach to trust for a given data shape, rather than falling back to the most well-known tool.
pmc-13374283:
Ziteng Zhang and colleagues compare tumour microbes in triple-negative breast cancer patients who did or did not respond fully to chemotherapy before surgery in a 2026 study. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy helps only a minority reach pathological complete response, and a predictive marker is needed. Tumour tissue from 44 patients, 25 with complete response and 19 without, was sequenced with 2bRAD-M.

Nearly 1,900 microbial species were found. Microbial diversity was higher in non-responders, while overall composition was broadly similar. Gram-negative bacteria such as Klebsiella and Escherichia were more prominent in non-responders. The work suggests that tumour microbes, already present before treatment, may help predict chemotherapy response and could one day guide treatment choice.
pmc-13379983:
Carneiro and colleagues report lepromatous leprosy in a Brazilian man living in Portugal, in a 2026 case report. Hansen's disease, caused by Mycobacterium leprae, is rare in Europe, with Portugal reporting 4 cases in 2023 and 4 in 2024, mostly imported. The patient had recurrent leg ulcers with violet halos for a year, and non-tender growths on his ears, eyelids, and nose. He also had inflammatory pains in small and medium joints that mimicked autoimmune disease in early checks.

Blood tests deepened the confusion, showing positive antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor, raised inflammatory markers, and excess antibodies, pointing clinicians toward sarcoidosis as the alternative. Skin biopsy settled it: foamy cells packed with acid-fast bacilli, the leprosy bacteria, on special staining. Therapy with rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone brought resolution of the ulcers and the joint pains. Carneiro urges European clinicians to keep leprosy in mind for ulcers with joint pain in migrants.
pmc-13380983:
Adam E Brown and colleagues present a 2026 study on predicting, at emergency department triage, which patients will need a hospital bed. Crowded emergency departments must sort patients fast and fairly. Computer models can help, but clinicians need to see why a model makes each call before they will trust it.

The team built models from structured triage data for visits to three large emergency departments between 2020 and 2024. They then used a method called SHAP to show which features drove each prediction, both for single patients and across the whole group. Age, vital signs, arrival mode, and existing conditions were among the inputs. The work aims to make such tools transparent and fair.
pmc-13382583:
Jesús Muñoz-Estrada and colleagues present a 2026 study improving lab-grown neurons made from stem cells for protein analysis. Turning on a gene called NGN2 quickly converts stem cells into neurons, which can model brain disease. Two problems plagued the cultures: a marker signal often faded, and leftover dividing precursor cells spoiled the neuron samples.

The team traced the fading marker to chemical silencing of its switch, and showed the silencing did not change the neurons themselves. The real confounder was incomplete conversion, which left clumps of mixed cells. Raising the dose of the conversion signal increased the share of true neurons. Cleaner cultures give more reliable protein data for disease studies.
pmc-13383483:
Peiyang Zheng's team linked combined heart-kidney-metabolic burden to return of disease after first ablation for ongoing atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 study. Return after first radiofrequency ablation remains common, and multisystem burden may remodel the atria unfavorably. The team enrolled 730 patients and scored cardiac, kidney, and metabolic domains into a weighted burden score.

During follow-up, 228 patients, or 31.2 percent, had a return of fibrillation. Mid- and high-burden groups faced significantly higher return risk than the low-burden group, with hazard ratios of 1.49 and 1.60 in the primary model. Adjusting for atrial substrate markers weakened the links, suggesting burden acts partly through atrial remodeling itself.
pmc-13385783:
Fei Dong's team traced how clary sage evolved to make the antifungal compound sclareol, in a 2026 genome study. Plant special metabolites diversify through unclear mechanisms. A complete end-to-end genome of Salvia sclarea, compared with related mint genomes that lack sclareol, revealed a recent tandem copy of the diterpene synthase gene SsLPPS.

The copied enzyme gained a new catalytic job, making labda-13-en-8-ol diphosphate, the direct precursor of sclareol. Structure models and mutagenesis pinpointed the amino acid changes behind this new function. SsLPPS and partner genes sit in a trichome-specific co-regulated cluster, showing how enzyme innovation plus control rewiring births a new pathway.
pmc-13386683:
In a 2026 capture-recapture study, Jingpei Xu's team estimated monkeypox prevalence in a major Southwest China city among men who have sex with men. Since June 2023, indigenous mpox transmission has persisted in China, concentrated in this population. The team ran two captures in Chengdu, tagging 1501 people first and recruiting 1538 second, with 31 and 18 mpox cases respectively.

Capture-recapture put mpox cases at 303 in this population, while population size estimates ran near 105,070 or 115,577 depending on method. Prevalence came to about 3 per 1000 by one estimate. The figures guide targeted prevention and control work where transmission concentrates.
pmc-13386883:
Lijuan Guo's team reviews glycolytic reprogramming in endometriosis and its non-hormonal treatment promise, in a 2026 survey. The disease, marked by ectopic tissue growth and heavy illness burden, often recurs despite hormone and surgery treatment or brings severe side effects. Growing evidence points to aerobic glycolysis, the Warburg effect, as a core driver of lesion growth.

The review covers ramped-up key enzymes, including HK2, PFKFB3, and PKM2, driven by signal axes such as ALKBH5-HK2, PAK5-PKM2, and S1PR4/mTOR. Higher sugar-burning flux and lactate buildup promote cell growth, spread, and cell-type switching while building an immune-evasive niche via M2 macrophage shifts and lactate tagging. Blocking glycolysis may open non-hormonal treatments for a disease with few good options.
pmc-13387483:
Ron Gabriel A. Peji, Diane D. Lipat, and Alyssia M. De Rojas pool trials of EMDR therapy for posttraumatic stress in a 2026 meta-analysis. Searches of four databases covered randomized trials published from 2000 through 2024, with the final search in August 2025. Eleven studies entered the combined analysis under a random-effects model.

EMDR cut symptom severity significantly against control conditions overall in their results. Effects ran larger against passive controls like waitlists and smaller, though comparable, against active rival therapies. Most studies carried some bias concerns on standard checks, which tempers certainty while still supporting EMDR as an effective option.
pmc-13387683:
Xiaohan Zhou and Xumin Wang measure worry about sleep among clinical nurses in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Nurses at one large urban Chinese hospital were surveyed between June and November 2024 with a validated sleep worry scale. A total of 285 nurses took part in the analysis.

Sleep worry affected 64 percent of the nurses surveyed, a rate the authors call high enough to demand action. Age, department, job title, years of experience, and monthly night shifts each linked significantly to worry levels. Those same factors survived combined modeling, which gives hospital planners concrete levers for targeted support programs.
pmc-13391983:
Yea-Ji Kim and colleagues review, in 2026, machine learning for predicting and controlling meat quality in industrial production. Meat quality drives consumer acceptance, value, and safety, yet traditional checks are laborious, destructive, and too slow for real-time factory use.

The review surveys learning systems fed by spectroscopy, imaging, electronic sensors, and biochemical analysis to estimate quality traits without destroying the product. Food industry readers gain a map of current applications for intelligent quality management, from carcass grading to spoilage prediction, and the data hurdles that still separate pilot models from line-speed deployment.
pmc-13392983:
Zukerman and colleagues compared three groups in 2026 to test how exercise links to well-being after mass trauma. One group survived the October 7, 2023 Nova festival attack directly, a second group of students lived through the same period at a distance. A third was surveyed in 2022 before the event. The study split exercise into two parts: how much people value fitness, and how much hard activity they do each week.

Survivors reported lower happiness and more body complaints, such as aches and fatigue, than the other groups. Weekly hard activity went with fewer body complaints in all groups and with milder trauma symptoms among survivors. Valuing fitness went with higher happiness and fewer complaints only among survivors, and checks showed that link held only in that group. The findings suggest low-cost activity programs after trauma should build both habit and personal meaning.
pmc-13393283:
Jianhui Yang and twelve colleagues wrapped therapeutic bacteria in a programmable polymer shell so the microbes stay quiet in healthy tissue and wake only inside tumours. Engineered bacteria promise living cancer drugs but raise safety fears and delivery problems. Their strain of Escherichia coli Nissle was built to convert tumour ammonia into arginine, a nutrient immune cells crave, and to secrete a blocker of the PD-1 immune brake.

The cross-linked coat lowers immune visibility and freezes growth while the bacteria travel. At the tumour, an enzyme abundant there, matrix metalloproteinase-2, digests the shell, freeing the bacteria to multiply locally, feed the immune response with arginine, and sustain brake blockade. pmc-13393483:
Sylvain Gourier and colleagues analyze whether sex affects recovery after aneurysmal bleeding under the brain's surface in a 2026 French cohort study. Bleeding of this kind, called subarachnoid hemorrhage, carries high illness and death rates, and earlier evidence on sex differences in outcomes has been mixed.

The main outcome was favorable brain function at day 90, with age, hemorrhage grade, and pupil signs taken into account. The paper helps intensive care teams judge prognosis without leaning on untested assumptions about sex.
pmc-13393683:

The third separated recipient and caregiver priorities. The fourth fixed recruitment barriers and messaging. pmc-13393883:
Rüştü Ersoy Sakarya, Kaan Yerliyurt, and Osayd Alawawda tested surface treatments for gluing veneering resin onto PAEK plastics. Dentists mill these high-performance polymers into crowns and bridges. pmc-13394483:

Shining light changes drag, so spin and height can be tuned without wires. Several flyers were steered at once, and swirling air drew them together mid-flight. Flow models showed uneven pressure behind the spin. The authors see a path to feather-light craft for sensing and display.
pmc-13394683:
Roberto De Ponti and colleagues write, in 2026, a commentary that asks whether extra ablation helps in atrial fibrillation. Their letter discusses a sub-study of the SUPPRESS-AF trial in lasting cases of the rhythm disorder. Standard care seals the lung veins, and the sub-study added burning of low-voltage patches. Results showed no gain in rhythm control or in ranked health outcomes.

The writers warn that win ratio scores bend with preset choices, such as outcome order. They note the trial could only judge its main aim well. Extra burns also lengthen the procedure and may add risk. For now, they say, wide use of patch ablation stays in doubt.
pmc-13395983:
Valentina Gasco and co-authors tackle a testing shortcut in hormone care in their 2026 study: when can doctors safely skip the stimulation test used to prove growth hormone deficiency in adults? Such tests are standard, yet they are costly, slow, and known to mislead.

The group focused on adults with disease of the hypothalamus or pituitary who had no other hormone losses. For this group they built a probability model based on IGF-I levels, a blood marker tied to growth hormone action, drawing the inputs from published data. The aim was a rule that flags patients whose chance of deficiency is so low that dynamic testing adds nothing.
pmc-13396083:
Ajay S. Gupta and co-authors compared cladribine tablets with three other oral drugs for multiple sclerosis using United States insurance claims, in a 2026 study. With many disease-modifying therapies on offer, doctors and payers need long-term, real-world comparisons of switching, care use, and cost.

Records from a large claims database covered April 2018 to March 2024. Adults were followed for four years from their first claim for cladribine, fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, or teriflunomide, and had to stay enrolled the whole period. The analysis counts how often each group switched therapy, used health services, and what their care cost, filling a gap left by shorter trials.
pmc-13396383:
Petrov and co-authors propose, in 2026, a crossed laser phase plate for transmission electron microscopy, aiming to sharpen images of weakly scattering specimens like biomolecules. A phase plate boosts contrast by shifting the phase of the unscattered electron beam. The existing laser design uses one standing light wave; the crossed version intersects two laser standing waves in the diffraction plane, splitting the optical load between two cavities.

Running both cavities at a numerical aperture of 0.08 needs only 31 percent of the power per cavity that a single-beam plate requires at 0.05 in their calculations. pmc-13396983:

Fifty-three professionals described their views. Nearly half affirmed an unconditional duty grounded in professional ethics. Many others made duty depend on having protective equipment and institutional backing, and 8 percent were unsure. Uneven gear distribution, patchy training, and rumor-based information shaped how risky the work felt, the authors found, and with it how far the duty was felt to reach.
pmc-13397383:

Their 2026 review notes that current drugs slow decline but rarely fix the faulty molecular switches behind a weakening heart.

Base editing rewrites single DNA letters without cutting both strands of the double helix, which makes it cleaner and efficient in living tissue. Beyond repairing inherited mutations, editors could dial key signaling proteins up or down inside heart cells. The authors weigh which pathways are ripe for such tuning and what stands between mouse results and patients.
pmc-13397683:
Chao Wang and colleagues review how a warming climate may spread chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus, into new regions. Places with no past exposure and no immunity, including parts of the temperate world, face growing risk as conditions shift.

After screening, 104 studies fed shared datasets on spread factors, forecasts and responses. Research since 2014 leans toward Europe and South America, with warmth studied in 38 papers and rainfall in 32 studies. Spread peaked within a warm band around 23 to 30 degrees, and the authors map where evidence is thin and what adaptation steps stand out.
pmc-13398183:
Jeni Baykoca and colleagues gather what reviews say about why adults with long-term illness keep using, or drop, health apps. Their 2026 overview of systematic reviews starts from a plain fact: an app only works if people engage with it. Outside trials, no clinician nudges the user, so inner motivation must carry the habit.

The overview asks how engagement gets defined and measured, whether it tracks with better health, and which inner and outer motives drive it. Past reviews mostly counted taps and logins rather than explaining the machinery underneath. From the combined findings the authors shape practical advice for building self-guided apps that people with lasting conditions actually stay with.
pmc-13398483:
Qian Liu and co-authors design a collector coating that stops potassium metal from dying inside anode-free batteries. Their 2026 study attacks dead potassium: metal that plates out, loses electrical contact and can never cycle again. Anode-free designs promise lean, energy-dense cells, but potassium's messy stripping behaviour had drawn little study.

Single iron atoms, held in an FeN4O2 grip on hollow carbon bowls, tune how potassium lands and lifts off while steering the surface film that forms. The springy bowls soak up swelling during cycling, keeping the interface whole. Cryo-microscopy, surface chemistry depth profiles and theory together back the design, which kept potassium cycling far more reversibly in their cells.
pmc-13398583:
Carlos E Buss and colleagues release MagmaFlow, a desktop app that turns gene-change charts into connected evidence maps. Their 2026 paper notes that plain volcano plots flag the loudest changes in omics data but leave readers to chase papers and pathways by hand. MagmaFlow works across computer platforms and needs no coding from the user.

Three tools anchor the app. A literature module pulls gene links from PubMed with direct reference links attached. Pathway maps are drawn as layered circles. Other views update together when a gene is picked. Smart labels, drag-and-drop notes and style controls aim at publication-ready figures. The pitch is speed with context: every highlighted gene arrives with its evidence already attached.
pmc-13399283:
Larissa Krokovsky and colleagues studied what happens when mosquito-borne viruses meet inside the same cells, in a 2026 laboratory paper. Zika virus now circulates where West Nile virus and Mayaro virus also circulate. One host can therefore pick up two viruses at once or in sequence. Using Vero cells, the team compared single infections with simultaneous coinfections and staggered superinfections.

Six days after infection, the researchers measured each virus's RNA and watched for cell damage. When Zika entered alongside either partner virus, its RNA levels dropped, a pattern called viral interference. When Zika infected first, the later virus still grew, an accommodation pattern. When Zika arrived second, it was shut out entirely, a pattern called superinfection exclusion. West Nile and Mayaro RNA stayed unaffected in every arrangement. The authors frame these results as a first step toward predicting co-circulating viruses in real outbreaks.
pmc-13400083:
Busra Sisik and Cengiz Sarikurkcu give the first full profile of Stachys milasensis, a recently described mint-family plant found only in Türkiye, in this 2026 study. The team extracted its aerial parts with water and with methanol. They measured total phenolics and flavonoids, identified individual compounds by liquid chromatography, and ran antioxidant and enzyme tests.

Methanol proved the richer solvent, pulling 77.69 milligrams of gallic acid equivalents and 71.53 milligrams of rutin equivalents per gram of extract, against lower figures for the water extract. pmc-13400183:

PET imaging two weeks later showed 5-HT2A binding restored toward normal. Microglial cell counts in the prefrontal cortex fell, suggesting the drug calmed the lingering inflammatory cell population. The authors argue the results justify deeper investigation of psychedelic treatments for post-TBI symptoms.
pmc-13400483:
Patrícia Arriaga and Erin M Buchanan present, in 2026, a dataset pairing 556 street artworks with the feelings they stirred in viewers. Artworks were chosen for themes tied to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The project links art research with questions about how public images move people on social and environmental themes.

More than 1,200 participants in Portugal and Brazil each rated ten randomly shown works. They scored pleasantness, arousal and specific feelings such as awe, hope, sadness and being moved. People keen on street art or on sustainability felt more positive responses, while age and gender mattered little. Feeling moved and emotionally connected sat at the center of the emotion network, bridging warm and negative clusters.
pmc-13400583:
Laura Kanzler, Carmela Moschella and Christian Schmeiser develop, in 2026, a math correction for models that assume collisions happen instantly. Real collisions take a short time, during which moving agents, from gas particles to bacteria, keep changing. Ignoring that span can bias models of alignment and flocking.

Working where collision time is short, the authors derive a first-order improved model. It is a system of two equations. They prove it is well behaved. They also show it tends to the classic instant model as the span shrinks. A simpler single-equation version with the same accuracy is also suggested. The work extends earlier studies of drawn-out collisions beyond the quantum setting.
pmc-13400683:
Andrew J Aschenbrenner and colleagues build, in 2026, a test battery for measuring thinking skills in everyday life. Cognition rises and falls within the same person across a day, and phone-based studies now sample it many times. Such studies use only a few brief tests, leaving the quality of most candidate tasks unknown.

Their Cognitive Variability Battery holds nine tests across attention control, processing speed and episodic memory. Participants took tests three times daily for three weeks, with each test repeated up to sixty times. The authors report how much scores varied, how reliable they were and how stress, mood and social contact shifted them, plus power calculations to help others design studies.
pmc-13400983:
Zijiang Yang, Chenggen Guo, Ziao Deng and Xinxuan Xue review, in 2026, urolithin A, a compound gut bacteria make from pomegranate-type plant chemicals, and its promise for aging and disease. Interest centers on its ability to trigger mitophagy, the recycling of worn-out cell power stations, a core quality control process.

Human evidence, by contrast, is still preliminary, covering mainly muscle function, exercise outcomes, some metabolic markers and short-term safety. Response also depends on each persons gut microbe makeup. The authors call for longer, high-quality randomized trials.
pmc-13401283:

The virus is extremely common and is linked to several cancers and autoimmune disorders, including multiple sclerosis.

They collected paired serum and spot samples from 417 members aged 18 to 25 years. The protocol aims at semi-quantitative results, which would let large population studies screen for past EBV infection far more cheaply.
pmc-13401483:
Fatiha Bousnina and colleagues present a 2026 analysis of myelodysplastic neoplasia, a blood cancer where the marrow makes blood cells badly, based on twenty clinical cases plus a literature review. The disease shows up as low blood counts across the three myeloid lineages and carries a risk of turning into acute myeloid leukemia.

Anaemia appeared in about 83 percent of cases, with mean haemoglobin under 8 grams per decilitre, while low platelets affected about 56 percent and low neutrophils about 44 percent. Cases were classed under the World Health Organization 2022 system. The authors note that diagnosis can be slow and difficult, often needing repeated examinations before the profile becomes clear.
pmc-13401583:

Blood clots in the lungs remain deadly and hard to manage, and guideline use lags in many settings for economic and other reasons.

Breathlessness was the leading symptom at 64 percent, and bed rest over three days the leading risk factor at 32 percent. pmc-13401683:

Outside hospital, mildly low haemoglobin is linked to reduced cognition, but transfusion policies inside hospital tolerate much lower levels, and older patients may be especially sensitive.

Any adult whose haemoglobin fell below 10 grams per decilitre between March 2017 and February 2020 was eligible. Cognition was scored with the Short Portable Mental Status Questionnaire, where higher scores mean worse thinking. Statistical models related each patient's lowest haemoglobin and age to cognition while accounting for race, sex, and a comorbidity index. The question matters for how low clinicians should let blood counts drift.
pmc-13401783:

They measured the outcome as coronary artery calcification, calcium build-up in the heart's arteries readable on a scan.

Exercise habits were captured by interview as both time spent exercising and total weekly energy use in metabolic units. People who did no exercise carried roughly a third more calcification than active people in early results. Models adjusted for age, sex, and schooling then tested the interplay: whether being active changes how strongly the genetic score shows itself in the arteries.
pmc-13401883:

By contrasting the genomic landscape of IL-6-secreting cancers with the rest, the authors aim to surface candidate markers that later studies can validate and, eventually, drugs might aim at.
pmc-13402583:

The framework gives explorers a physics-based map for hunting continental resources.
pmc-13402883:

Cases were chosen one by one, only where spread was mainly peritoneal and ovaries were the sole other site, after careful consent and joint surgeon-gynecologist review. The authors argue the sequence, drug control then laparoscopic removal by skilled gynecologists, deserves wider testing in this grim corner of stomach cancer.
pmc-13402983:

Stigma and low mental health literacy delay formal care further.

pmc-13403383:

pmc-13404583:

pmc-13406483:

Forty adults with the diagnosis and forty healthy peers completed standard questionnaires. Measures covered ADHD symptoms, difficulty regulating emotions and reflective functioning, meaning the ability to read mental states.

Adults with ADHD showed weaker reflective functioning and stronger emotion dysregulation than controls in the reported comparisons. Uncertainty about mental states may form a bridge between symptom severity and poor emotion control, the mediation analysis suggests. pmc-13407683:

pmc-13407883:

pmc-13408083:

pmc-13408283:

When radiation was given during first-line treatment, both overall and within-liver control lasted longer. Side effects stayed mild, with severe liver enzyme problems almost absent. The authors present the approach as a reasonable addition for selected patients, while the retrospective design limits certainty.
pmc-13408483:

pmc-13408883:

pmc-13408983:

pmc-13409083:

The protocol paper fixes the design in public before results exist, so readers can later judge whether the team kept its promises.
pmc-13409283:

Both regions stayed engaged to hold an observer viewpoint during recall itself. Activity in specific subregions predicted how vivid and stable the perspective felt. pmc-13410283:

Pooled results gave modest sensitivity of about 61 percent and stronger specificity near 83 percent for rejection overall. pmc-13410383:

pmc-13410883:
