The usual label points to face and arm attacks, yet their 62-year-old patient suffered short, painless leg attacks dozens of times a day, often set off by starting to move.

Seizure drugs did not help, steroids helped little, and plasma exchange cleared the attacks, while blood tests confirmed LGI1 antibodies. The case widens the picture of this immune brain disorder, warning doctors not to rule it out when attacks favor the leg rather than the face and arm.
pmc-13411283:
Kaya and colleagues check whether questionnaires about mattering, the feeling of being significant to others, measure the same thing in Turkish teenagers and university students, on and offline. Feeling valued protects mental health, while its dark twin, anti-mattering, tracks with loneliness and depression. Their 2026 study gives the general, anti, online, and online anti mattering scales to 888 participants: 434 high schoolers and 454 college students. It tests the scales' structure and fairness with factor analysis and Rasch modeling, a yardstick for survey items.

All scales held their shape in groups, with reliability above thresholds. The Rasch analysis found measurement invariance. Items behaved alike for high school and college students, and for men and women. Score gaps thus reflect feelings rather than biased questions. The set, the authors argue, gives Turkish researchers a toolkit for studying significance and neglect across social worlds half face to face and half on screens.
pmc-13411783:
Chia-Chen Wu and colleagues expose in 2026 aged male zebrafish to lead and read the chemical marks it leaves on brain DNA. Lead is a proven nerve poison in the young, yet its added risk in old brains was murkier. Two-year-old fish swam for five days in water spanning a wide range of lead levels.

Higher doses raised overall DNA methylation in the aged brain. Changed genes clustered in ion transport and signal relay pathways, with marks landing mostly inside gene bodies rather than at their switches. Few changed genes altered their activity, yet several tied to movement, including one altered at the top dose. The pattern suggests epigenetic scarring worth probing for links to behavior.
pmc-13411983:
Cillian Cheng and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the overlooked microbes of gut cancers, beyond bacteria. Fungi, viruses, and archaea in the gut have been called the dark matter of the microbiome, long ignored while bacteria took the spotlight in tumor research.

Across bowel, liver, stomach, pancreas, and mouth-throat cancers, the review maps how these microbes shift in disease, sway host cells and immunity, and interact with bacteria. Readers get leads for new tests and treatments from these hidden communities, plus a call for studies that track all microbial kingdoms together.
pmc-13412283:
Zeyi Lu and colleagues uncover in 2026 a route by which kidney cancer cells escape the drug pazopanib. The drug is a first-line treatment for advanced renal cell carcinoma, yet tumours commonly grow resistant with time. Gene profiling of resistant cells flagged ALYREF, a reader of the m5C mark on RNA, as sharply increased in the cells that no longer responded.

ALYREF steadies the message for CCNA1, raising cyclin A1 levels in the cell. The cyclin then partners with CDK2 to tag the brake protein p21 and push it out of the nucleus, freeing the cell to divide despite looking senescent. The authors name this ALYREF, cyclin A1, and p21 chain as a target for restoring drug sensitivity.
pmc-13412883:
Emilia Biedroń and colleagues review in 2026 what is known about lateral epicondylitis, the overuse injury better known as tennis elbow. The condition causes pain where forearm extensor tendons anchor to the outer elbow, and debate persists over best care. Their non-systematic review searched major databases for prior reviews on definition, diagnosis, risk factors, and treatment options.

Diagnosis rests mainly on clinical examination rather than imaging. Structured physiotherapy and easing the load on the tendon form the backbone of treatment in the literature surveyed. Injections of platelet-rich plasma or the patient's own blood may help longer term, while steroid shots relieve pain briefly. Acupuncture and shock wave therapy showed weak or inconsistent support. Surgery stays a last resort for stubborn cases.
pmc-13415483:
Letícia Condolo and colleagues test whether violet or blue light improves office tooth bleaching with a mild peroxide gel, in 2026. Sixty extracted sound premolars were split into three groups of twenty: gel alone, gel with violet light, or gel with blue light. Color, peroxide reaching the inner pulp chamber, gel strength, and heat were all measured.

Light groups let less peroxide into the pulp chamber than gel alone. Violet light gave the highest whitening values of the three. Gel alone kept more of its starting peroxide concentration. Lit gels warmed more and lost more acidity balance, a safety point the authors flag for care.
pmc-13415883: Beny Trabelcy and co-authors issued this author correction in 2026 for their 2023 Nature Communications article on gut bacteria detoxifying plant defenses for fruit eating birds. The correction is narrow: colors in each column of Figure 1c were interchanged, and the corrected version shows blue on the left and yellow on the right. One species name in the discussion was also wrong, replaced so the sentence credits P. agglomerans with easing the effects of a plant chemical. The figure and text now stand amended in both article formats.
pmc-13415983:
Chuhan Guo and co-authors pool the evidence on intraoperative radiotherapy for colorectal cancer, radiation delivered during surgery directly to the tumour bed. Their 2026 meta-analysis examines device types, doses, long-term survival, and complications across the published literature through November 2023.

Twenty-five studies covering 2,664 patients met the criteria, covering electron, low-energy X-ray, and brachytherapy techniques, most at doses around ten to twenty gray. Patients receiving intraoperative radiotherapy tended to show better five-year survival than those without it, with the clearest gain for the electron technique. Local control also favoured radiotherapy. Importantly, complication rates, including leaks at the bowel join, pelvic collections, wound problems, and bowel obstruction, were not higher with the added radiation. The authors say device and dose choices deserve closer study.
pmc-13416883:
Ibtihal S Alduhaymi and colleagues review minicircle DNA vaccines in a 2026 article. DNA vaccines are stable and quick to design, yet they work weakly in people because cells take them up poorly and switch them off. Minicircles are tiny DNA rings stripped of bacterial parts such as resistance genes.

Without that extra material, the rings trigger less unwanted immune reaction and stay active longer in both dividing and resting cells. The review covers how minicircles are built, where they are being tried for infection and cancer vaccines, and which delivery tricks raise uptake. Limits that block clinical use are also set out plainly.
pmc-13417983:
Wenli Cai and co-authors uncover a switch protein that pushes a seafood borne bacterium toward surface living, in a 2026 study. Vibrio parahaemolyticus causes food poisoning from raw seafood, and films it forms on surfaces resist cleaning. The regulator protein LtrB was tested by deleting its gene and tracking behaviour and gene activity.

Without LtrB, bacteria swam and swarmed more but built poor films and less surface matrix. The protein directly switches matrix genes on and movement genes off at their control regions. Adhesion to mussel, shrimp, glass, and steel surfaces also fell. Blocking such switches could help keep processing plants cleaner.
pmc-13418483:
Kadeejathul Kubra and Munawar A Shaik review how models and smart software can improve antibody drug making, in a 2026 article. Antibody drugs cost a lot to make. Cell growth is hard to predict, the cleaning steps are dear, and plant wide jams add time and cost. The review covers growth, cleaning, and whole plant work.

Models now guide food for cells, dense cultures, and non stop reactors. Smart tools can guess quality traits and tune the cleaning steps. Yet data are messy and rules for such tools are strict. The authors say gains in cost and trust will come once firm case proof builds up.
pmc-13418783:
Isaac Sanchez-Gonzalez and colleagues pooled evidence in 2026 on work-related illness among hotel housekeepers, a workforce facing heavy loads, repetition, time pressure, and little recognition. The review searched five databases through early 2026 for observational studies of health conditions in this job.

Eight studies qualified, all reporting high rates of muscle and joint disorders, and five fed a pooled analysis of prevalence. The paper gives hotel employers and labor health teams a consolidated case for redesigning rooms, loads, and schedules to protect housekeepers and for inspectors checking hotel working conditions.
pmc-13419183:
Niu and colleagues charted in 2026 the burden of heart failure across Asia using Global Burden of Disease data. Heart failure, where the heart cannot pump enough blood, is a growing public health problem in the region. Their study covered 48 Asian countries from 1990 to 2021.

Asia had 29.5 million heart failure cases in 2021, a rise of about one and a half times since 1990. Years lived with disability also rose by the same share, reaching 2.86 million. China alone accounted for about 44 in 100 of Asia's cases and the highest disability burden. Treated heart failure was the most common severity level, but severe cases drove most disability. The middle-high development group of countries had the highest age-standardised rate, and most regions trended upward except Japan and Cyprus.
pmc-13419283:
Ting Kang and colleagues grade five large language models on advice around surgery for hypospadias, a common birth condition in boys that needs an operation. Parents often face hard choices before and after the procedure, and chatbots now field many of their questions. Eight reviewers, most of them senior specialists, scored the answers for safety and quality from both doctor and caregiver views.

Scores differed sharply across the five models in both scoring rounds. One tool's citations checked out fully, while two rivals invented sources at rates of 33 percent and 24 percent in the counts reported. One further model invented nothing yet leaned on vague guideline mentions instead of exact sources. The audit gives hospitals a concrete warning about which chatbot habits can mislead worried parents.
pmc-13420283:
Talita Priscilla da Silva Guerra and colleagues study the mental toll of needlestick and sharps injuries on primary care workers in a mid-sized town in São Paulo state, Brazil. Such injuries pair infection risk with psychological aftershocks that managers often underrate. The mixed study joined surveys with an event-impact scale for the injured and open written accounts.

Injury odds looked higher for dentists and for workers who felt vulnerable to catching disease, though both links stayed short of firm statistical proof with wide ranges. The survey also covered safety knowledge, vaccination status, and what workers did right after exposure. Support after injury, including mental health backup, proved a recurring theme in the accounts. Safer sharps systems protect bodies, yet this study insists the mind needs a protocol too.
pmc-13420483:
Km Megha and colleagues build and validate Nadamay, a sound-based meditation protocol meant to support psychosocial well-being. Stress, anxiety, and poor emotional control touch every age group, and structured meditation is one low-cost response. Their protocol runs seven stages in order, from prayer and breath work through sound focus on AUM to silence and a closing peace chant.

Twenty-one experts from varied fields scored each stage for content validity with two standard index methods. Every stage passed, with top-range scores from 0.52 to 1.0 on one index and 0.76 to 1.0 on the other in the reported results. The design drew on scripture, the expert panel, and a literature scan spanning 2000 to 2023. A validated script now exists for trials that can test whether the promised calm is real.
pmc-13421383:
Diógenes Honorato Piva leads a twelve-author team engineering, in a 2026 paper, a zeolite that captures acetone from indoor air even when humidity competes. Zeolites are porous minerals; the MFI type suits acetone, yet in pure silica form both acetone and water crowd onto the same silanol groups, and water wins too often.

Computer simulations showed that adding molybdenum removes many of those water-loving groups, so acetone instead binds at metal sites through its oxygen atom. Infrared measurements confirmed the change, and flow-through tests showed the molybdenum zeolite captured more acetone than the plain version in moist air. The authors present silanol suppression as a general design rule for selective indoor-air sorbents.
pmc-13421483:
Anne-Kathrin Grimm and six colleagues describe, in a 2026 methods paper, a gentle way to load genetic material into cells that stay attached to their growing surface. Getting DNA, mRNA or silencing RNA across the cell membrane without detaching the cells is a standing technical hurdle in cell engineering.

Their in situ electroporation applies a brief electric field through thin-film electrodes under the culture well, opening temporary pores exactly where cells sit. Fluorescence confirmed delivery of all four cargo types into several mammalian cell lines. Electrical impedance readings tracked how invasive the pulse was and how fast cells recovered, revealing cell death within twenty hours when survival genes were silenced. The authors propose the setup for screening experiments.
pmc-13421583:
Juliana B. Yazigi and six colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their study reporting cancer-causing HPV types in ancient human genomes. The genomes came from the Ice Age hunter Ust'-Ishim and the Alpine mummy Ötzi. The original article, in Scientific Reports, had printed an earlier version of Figure 5 by mistake.

The notice republishes the intended figure with its full legend. The figure maps single-letter DNA changes in the viral E6 and E7 genes from both ancient individuals. It sets them against their sublineage references. It also marks the amino acid substitutions each change produces, plus the protein domains involved, including zinc-finger regions. Readers can now see which variants the authors actually identified in each genome.
pmc-13422883:
Callaghan examines in 2026 a pandemic paradox. Nations rich in scientific capacity often suffered the worst early COVID-19 outcomes. Culturally tight countries, where social norms are strong and deviance is punished, often fared better before vaccines arrived.

Using cross-national data, Callaghan tested whether scientific capacity protected countries once cultural tightness and structural factors were counted. It did not: scientific capacity showed no robust direct link to lower cases or deaths in the pre-vaccine phase. Cultural tightness, measured on an established scale, was consistently tied to fewer cases and deaths. The author argues that knowledge alone does not become population protection by itself. Norm strength and coordinated behavior, the capacity to turn knowledge into action, appear to be the conditions that made science count.
pmc-13423083:
Aji and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for GROW-MY, a ten-year study in east coast Malaysia on how a mother's weight gain in pregnancy shapes her child's later nutrition and health. Child overweight is rising in Malaysia, and early-life factors may set long-term patterns. The study returns to 499 mother and child pairs first recruited during pregnancy in 2014 from clinics in Kelantan and Terengganu.

At the ten-year follow-up in 2026, the team will measure body size and composition and record diet for both mothers and children, who are now around ten years old. Pregnancy weight gain will be classed against Institute of Medicine guidelines and linked to child outcomes such as body mass. The results should guide advice on healthy weight gain in pregnancy in a region where child obesity is climbing.
pmc-13423483:
Chunjie Wang and eight colleagues trace how a secreted protein, CRLF1, drives kidney scarring as acute injury turns into chronic disease. The protein is barely present in healthy kidneys but rises in damaged ones, and patient data linked higher levels with more scarring and worse kidney function.

Blocking CRLF1 in mouse models of kidney injury protected function and slowed scarring. In cultured tubule cells the protein stirred inflammation and scar-type changes. Mechanistic work showed a scarring switch, SMAD3, turning the CRLF1 gene on, while CRLF1 itself grabbed a partner protein, integrin beta 1, and fired a growth pathway. The chain makes CRLF1 a candidate drug target for halting the slide into chronic kidney disease.
pmc-13423583:
Hunt and Georgiades review why young people stop antipsychotic medication after a first episode of psychosis, a turning point where staying on treatment cuts relapse risk. Adherence in this group is poor: only about four in ten take medication consistently, by the figures they cite. Their 2026 systematic review follows standard PRISMA rules and gathers seventy six studies on reasons, attitudes, and beliefs, plus trials of programs meant to help.

Nineteen stated reasons folded into ten themes, from weak insight and a wish for control to side effects, stigma, family influence, substance use, and simple practical barriers. What helped ran in mirror image: insight, fear of relapse, trust in the clinician, family support, and digital reminders. Talk based programs worked, including cognitive behavioral therapy, motivational interviewing, and adherence therapy, best of all in combination. Stopping, the authors show, is rarely mere defiance; it is a knot services can help untie.
pmc-13424083:
Amar Jaffar and colleagues built AgriChain-FL in 2026, a federated blockchain system for smart farming that trains models across farms without pooling raw data. Farm sensors raise privacy, trust, and scale problems, so the framework pairs federated learning with a hybrid Byzantine fault-tolerant and proof-of-authority chain for auditable, incentivized collaboration.

On a smart-farm sensor dataset the system reached 92.4 percent accuracy with 2350 transactions per second and one-second block latency, cutting privacy leakage by 73 percent and energy cost by 45 percent against rivals. Farm networks gain a privacy-conscious template for shared agricultural intelligence.
pmc-13424783:
Blackman and co-authors pool the long-term evidence in this 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. The question comes from athletes who tear an anterior cruciate ligament. Does reconstructive surgery protect the knee from arthritis? The team found comparative studies of surgical versus nonoperative care. They tracked radiographic osteoarthritis, further meniscus surgery, and later total knee replacement.

Eighteen studies with 33,540 patients fed the analysis. Follow-up ran 12.3 years across the included reports. Arthritis rates were identical between groups. The risk ratio was 1.01 for reconstruction against conservative care in the pooled estimate. Meniscus reoperation rates also matched. One outcome diverged sharply, though. Reconstruction cut the risk of total knee arthroplasty to a risk ratio of 0.17 against nonoperative care. The authors conclude surgery stabilizes the knee without preventing degeneration. They call that a nuance patients deserve in counseling.
pmc-13425883:
Yilin Zhang and coauthors tracked gum disease and complete tooth loss in older women across China and Southeast Asian nations in a 2026 burden study. Using Global Burden of Disease 2023 data for women aged sixty and over, they analyzed disability rates from 1990 onward and projected trends to 2033 with ARIMA models. In 2023, gum disease burden was highest in Thailand and Indonesia at about 184 per 100,000 in each.

Tooth loss burden peaked in the Philippines and Malaysia, while tooth loss declined across most countries from 1990 to 2023 even as gum disease rose in Indonesia and Thailand. Planners gain country-level forecasts for dental services for aging women.
pmc-13425983:
Alina Flintere-Flinte and coauthors evaluated two blood markers for peripheral nerve involvement in multiple sclerosis in a 2026 retrospective study of 149 patients. Neurofilament light chain signals nerve fiber damage and glial fibrillary acidic protein signals astrocyte injury, yet both vary in accuracy, especially when other nerve conditions coexist. Serum levels were tested for diagnostic and prognostic value in this cohort.

Multiple sclerosis mainly attacks the central nervous system, so proving peripheral involvement needs objective support beyond symptoms. Marker performance here helps neurologists judge whether blood testing can clarify mixed presentations and forecast course. A blood test is cheap and fast to run, so even a rough guide from these marks could help staff sort who needs more tests soon.
pmc-13426083:
Christian M. Räz and colleagues report a 2026 case of recurrent strokes from herpes simplex virus 2 brain inflammation in a 76-year-old woman with antisynthetase syndrome. Her rare autoimmune condition involves lung disease, muscle inflammation, and arthritis and requires immune-suppressing treatment, which can invite severe infection. She developed aphasia, confusion, seizures, gait trouble, headache, and fainting as cerebral vasculitis caused repeated ischemic strokes.

Brain imaging, angiography, and lumbar puncture supported HSV-2 encephalitis with vessel inflammation as the final diagnosis. The case warns that new strokes in immunosuppressed autoimmune patients may signal infection-driven vasculitis needing antiviral thinking alongside stroke care. Stroke care here must pair brain scans with a hunt for germs. The sick woman had care from brain, lung, and joint staff, since her ills crossed all three fields at once in this hard case for the team.
pmc-13426383:
Vanessa Joy A. Timoteo-Garcia and coauthors linked water, sanitation, and hygiene factors with iodine status in Filipino women in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Iodine deficiency persists in pockets of the Philippines despite national progress, and women aged 15 to 49 matter doubly because deficiency harms both their health and their children's development. Urinary iodine concentration served as the marker of recent intake.

Models weighed hygiene-related variables alongside nutrition status and social and demographic factors to see which track with iodine levels. Findings could steer combined programs, where safe water work and nutrition work reinforce each other in deficient communities.
pmc-13426483:
Jarawee Supanta and colleagues ran a clinical trial on dogs in Thailand that show aggression toward their own owners, including dogs that have bitten. They tested a calming drug, a feeding toy, both together, and guidance alone across 80 dogs.

All dogs also got behaviour guidance, and aggression was scored before and after four weeks of treatment. Every group improved, but dogs on fluoxetine, an anti-anxiety drug, improved more than toy-only or guidance-only groups. Adding the toy to the drug gave no extra gain, though it seemed to soften early side effects like drowsiness. How owners handled and managed their dogs linked to aggression more than the dogs' own traits did.
pmc-13426983:
Lerona and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on a pill facing a rising parasite threat in Asia. Leishmaniasis spreads by sandfly bites and can scar skin or kill. Miltefosine is the only approved pill for it, a big practical plus. New parasite species in Thailand and neighbors respond unevenly to standard care.

One Thai case improved on the pill paired with a drip drug after other care failed. Alone, though, the pill could not hold gains in a patient with weak immunity. Lab work maps several routes by which parasites may resist the pill. Shared drug pressure may also dull response to the main drip drug. The authors urge testing and tracking before wider pill rollout.
pmc-13428483:
Patrycja Zaborska, Jurek Olszewski, and Piotr Henryk Skarżyński chart, in a 2026 study, two decades of head and neck cancer in Poland. No single long-term picture existed for the whole group, which spans the mouth, throat, voice box, and thyroid. National cancer registry data ran from the year 2000 through 2022. The authors compared new cases and deaths at the start and end of that span, site by site.

Thyroid cancer more than tripled and became the commonest site by 2022, a rise the authors link partly to overdiagnosis. Throat cancer cases also jumped, while voice box cancer fell by about a third. Deaths from mouth cancers rose sharply. The authors call on ear, nose, and throat specialists to teach patients about HPV infection, a preventable driver of several of these cancers.
pmc-13429283:
Yu and colleagues survey school nurses across Taiwan about their role in student mental health care. Nurses are often first to spot a struggling student, yet their training for that role varies. Their 2026 survey drew 305 replies from 658 nurses sampled in proportion to school size. A 33 item questionnaire scored how responsible nurses felt for six skill domains, how capable they felt, and how much training they wanted.

Three quarters had never worked in psychiatric or psychology settings. Nurses felt most responsible and capable in referral, mapping outside help, and crisis response, and least in managing psychiatric medicines. Training hunger ran high for crisis response and for spotting and assessing problems early. Felt responsibility, not confidence, was the sole clear driver of training demand, accounting for nearly a third of its variation. Clearer role rules plus standard crisis protocols, the authors argue, should anchor new training.
pmc-13429683:
Armands Sebris and colleagues test water-soluble triazolylpurine compounds as rust blockers for mild steel in strong hydrochloric acid. Six single-triazole derivatives and one double-triazole derivative were screened, a practical need for acid cleaning and pickling.

The double-triazole compound blocked up to 93 percent by impedance tests and 98 percent by weight-loss tests at the top dose. A methylamino single-triazole compound hit 95 percent by polarisation tests at the same dose. Blocking generally rose with dose, and quantum calculations found little difference among compounds, so performance, not orbital theory, sorts the winners.
pmc-13430183:
Ruohua Lyu and colleagues present, in a 2026 methods paper, a gentler way to tag the neighbors of a protein inside living cells. Proximity labeling marks nearby proteins with a chemical tag so they can be fished out and identified. Standard methods fuse a bulky enzyme to the protein of interest, which can distort its behavior. Their method, ASAP-ID, instead attaches only a tiny peptide tag to the target. A matching antibody piece carries the tagging enzyme to that spot.

The system worked with two different tag-and-antibody pairs on a human nuclear protein. It can run inside living cells or be applied later to fixed cells. The fixed-cell version found more than 448 possible partners for a nuclear scaffold protein. Applied to ALS-linked mutant proteins, it revealed partner shifts matching where each mutant clumped. Cell biologists gain a less invasive probe.
pmc-13430783:
Vsevolod Shurkhay and colleagues review surgery for open degloving injuries of the limbs, where skin and soft tissue are torn away, risking loss of blood supply, infection, and poor function. Varied presentations have left standard protocols thin.

Twenty-eight consecutive patients at a Level II trauma centre from 2020 to 2024 were reviewed. Median age was 49 years, 57.1 percent were men, and road crashes caused 40.7 percent of injuries, with 56.7 percent hitting upper limbs. All but one patient had surgery, with first debridement in 51.9 percent, repeat debridement in 33.3 percent, and negative-pressure dressings in 63.0 percent. Trauma teams get a realistic operative picture for a brutal injury.
pmc-13432283:
Vince Elter and colleagues offer CEEN, a free Python tool that runs three lab tools as one for flow-battery and synthesis work. Live tests once meant three screens: one for current, one for EPR, and one for NMR, which made live tracking hard.

CEEN links a small NMR tool, a small EPR tool, and a current tool, so all three read in step, with live plots of each stream. The team shows it on water-based flow batteries, both organic and inorganic, and on synthesis by current. The same rig fits any flow test read by magnetic resonance, giving labs one clean workflow in place of three split ones.
pmc-13432683:
Traeger Max and co-authors surveyed men's health patients in Germany in 2026 on where they hunt for facts before visits, then graded those sources and chat models side by side. Shame around such faults pushes many men to search in private first. Four centers gave forms to 283 patients across a near-year span.

Two thirds had searched before their visit, most by web, with the young leaning hardest on web sources. Official doctor group sites and a famed free wiki led picks, while a third also hit sales-driven sites. Graders found most top sites and chat models fair on facts yet hard to read and grasp. The authors urge official bodies to post clear, plain pages, and they stress that chat tools cannot swap for a real talk with a doctor.
pmc-13432883:
Jingchen Hao and co-authors pulled a fresh virus in 2026 from a drug-proof lung germ that carries its own virus defense, then traced what germs give up to shrug the virus off. Virus care ranks as a strong swap for failing antibiotics. The new virus grips the germ's outer coat to latch on and stays stable in mild heat.

Germs that beat the virus had lost that coat through a break in one sugar-handling gene, a call the team proved by cutting the gene on purpose. Coat loss cut the germ's killing power in a wax moth test and left it open to blood clearing, yet it grew thicker slime mats. Gene voice maps showed mat genes lit across the board. Two antibiotics paired with the virus wiped mats and blocked fresh proofing in dishes.
pmc-13432983:
M F Tinajero and co-authors asked in 2026 whether a sound-wave read of the eye artery can stand in for a blood ratio that flags placenta strain late in pregnancy. The ratio weighs a brake factor against a growth factor, and high marks warn of a grave pressure disease. Their cross-check sat inside a larger trial of first-time mothers near term.

Two hundred three women gave both reads, and the scan reader stayed blind to blood marks. As the blood ratio climbed across thirds, the eye artery's peak speed ratio climbed with it, while its pulse index fell. Blood pressure rose in step. A set cut on the eye read split high blood ratios with fair skill. The authors pitch the eye scan as a handy stand-in where blood tests run scarce.
pmc-13434583:
Madura Katta's team ran a 2026 online experiment in Australia on how wording shapes backing for food aid in far-flung Indigenous communities. The policy at issue was a community-backed electricity subsidy meant to ease food insecurity in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander places. More than 1,500 adults across the country were sorted at random into groups that saw a rights frame, a fairness frame, a community frame, or no frame.

Wording moved support only a little overall, with the rights frame drawing the most backing and the fairness frame the least, though the gaps were small. Support ran higher among Greens voters, degree holders, and frequent news watchers no matter which frame they saw. The paper is a sober check on advocacy, arguing that one slogan alone will not shift views on help for disadvantaged places.
pmc-13434683:
Manel Essid's team made nine vanillin-based sulfonate compounds in 2026 and tested them as blockers of alpha-glucosidase, an enzyme that frees sugar from carbs. Strong blockers can blunt blood sugar spikes after meals, a key goal in diabetes care. The compounds were built from vanillin by sulfonation and further tweaks, then checked with lab enzyme tests, animal feeding tests, and computer docking and motion studies.

Three compounds beat the reference drug acarbose in the enzyme test, and chosen leads cut post-meal blood sugar in animals without clear acute harm. Computer models showed steady binding in the enzyme pocket, backing the lab results. The paper offers early drug leads for diabetes, with safety and human trials still far ahead.
pmc-13434783:
Péter Pikó and colleagues measure how smoking reshapes good cholesterol in 314 Hungarian adults in 2026. Blood fat was split into ten small HDL fractions, since size shapes how well HDL protects the heart. Five gauges of smoking were tested, from daily count to years smoked.

Every gauge linked to lower cholesterol in HDL fractions, most in the middle sizes. Total HDL and its main carrier protein also fell with smoking. Harmful fat ratios rose in step with dose. Heavier and longer smoking tracked worse profiles in a clear dose pattern. Heart risk from smoking may run partly through these small fractions.
pmc-13435583:
Zihao Zhang and a large team probe how blood fats and genes jointly shape sleep length in 410,493 British adults in 2026. Triglycerides, total cholesterol, and LDL were checked against nightly sleep hours. Gene risk scores for each fat added a second lens on cause.

Measured triglycerides linked to longer sleep, while measured total cholesterol linked to shorter sleep. Gene scores for all three fats linked to shorter sleep instead. Fat level and gene score for triglycerides pushed against each other. Blood protein patterns tied to both fats and sleep also surfaced. Sleep advice may need to split by fat type.
pmc-13436083:
Tannemann and colleagues validated in 2026 a checklist for scoring medical students' emergency medicine skills during simulation training in Germany. The checklist follows the national competency catalogue and grades three domains drawn from a standard handover framework: evaluation, background, and action. It was applied to 265 students across semesters and scenarios.

Statistical analysis supported the three-part structure, with items loading cleanly on their domains and a good overall model fit. The full checklist showed acceptable internal consistency, though the background and action subscales were weaker on their own. Differences between raters and stations accounted for about fourteen percent of score variance. The authors conclude the instrument is valid and reliable for overall assessment, while single domain subscores should be read with care.
pmc-13436683:
Gamze Babur Guler, Arda Guler, and Ibrahim Halil Tanboga clarify the design of their AI ECG study in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in 2026. Their cohort held only confirmed cases of the disease, the letter stresses. No healthy comparison group was enrolled at all.

Terms like performance thus meant spread of AI outputs within the sick group, not detection accuracy. Agreement with hand read ECG classes and links to scan and clinical marks form the real outcomes. Formal accuracy scores were not reported and should not be inferred. Case only designs suit behavior checks of a tool, the authors argue. Open science norms frame the reply.
pmc-13437383:
Xiaowen Zhang and co-authors linked eating habits with kidney stones in China. Diet can push stone-forming chemicals into urine, yet most past work came from Western countries. Their 2026 study used a food frequency questionnaire with 830 people, 299 with kidney stones and 531 without. The team compared intake of pork, other meats, processed meat, and fish, adjusting for factors that sway stone risk.

Pork stood out: the heaviest pork eaters had more than triple the odds of stones compared with the lightest group, though the pattern across middle groups was uneven. Sea fish ran the other way: the highest intake group showed about a third of the odds of the lowest. The authors frame both findings as associations from a one-time survey, unable to prove a food caused or prevented a stone. Even so, the contrast gives diet advice for Chinese patients a local evidence base.
pmc-13437683:
Ray Campbell and George Ochoa introduce FAIR Health Atlas, a free tool mapping chronic disease among Americans with commercial health insurance. Policy debate on chronic illness, the country's top killer, has leaned on Medicare and Medicaid data, yet most working-age adults hold private coverage. Their 2026 piece presents claims drawn from the nation's largest set of recent commercial records, charted across all fifty states and the District of Columbia.

Early looks show wide contrasts. In 2025, West Virginia held the highest diabetes share among the commercially insured, roughly twice Colorado's lowest rate. Such flips warn against treating any state as simply sick or healthy. Users can flip between state and county maps, pick a disease and a year, and download the figures. The authors, writing for the nonprofit that built the tool, argue filling the commercial data gap gives lawmakers a fuller picture of where chronic disease presses hardest.
pmc-13439083:
Ziyi Zhao's team denoised long-haul fiber vibration signals in 2026 for overhead power lines, where distance degrades signal quality and clean labels are scarce. Distributed sensing along a 220-kilovolt line in Anshan, China, gave a sixty-kilometer field data set, but attenuation and environmental noise blurred fault features. Two fibers in one cable provided paired noisy views of the same spots, enabling Noise2Noise training without clean targets.

An attention-gated U-Net learned to denoise space-time blocks end to end, beating bandpass, Wiener, and a rival deep model on maps, spectra, waveforms, and time-frequency patterns. Grid operators get a field-tested denoiser for line monitoring over long distances. Wider lines and weather extremes will test robustness further.
pmc-13440683:
Taís de Azevedo Picinini and colleagues gather what is known about ringing ears in people with jaw joint disorders, publishing a 2026 systematic review. Temporomandibular disorders affect the jaw joint and chewing muscles, and tinnitus often travels with them. How that tinnitus sounds, its pitch, loudness, and pattern, had not been pooled. Searches across six databases under standard review rules found 271 records, of which five studies qualified for synthesis.

Across those studies, tinnitus linked to jaw disorders was mostly one-sided, continuous, high-pitched, and moderate in loudness. Some patients could shift the sound by moving the jaw or neck, hinting at body-sense input to hearing circuits. Quality of life impact ranged from mild to moderate, even among people with normal hearing tests. The authors call the profile fairly consistent while demanding larger, stronger primary studies to confirm it.
pmc-13441183:
Omar Hajjaji and colleagues recalibrate a workhorse similarity measure used to sort DNA fragments by genome of origin, reporting in 2026. Metagenomic binning rebuilds genomes from shredded community DNA. Fragments are compared by tetranucleotide frequency, the rate of each four-letter DNA word, and distances between profiles become probabilities that two fragments share a genome. Those distances are never negative and pile up with a long right tail, which standard models fit poorly.

Their likelihood-based framework fits flexible right-skewed distributions to distances within and between genomes. Fitted curves then convert raw distances into calibrated probability scores inside a MaxBin-style binning scheme. The authors say the approach puts threshold choices on a transparent statistical footing instead of rule-of-thumb cutoffs. Code is public, and the stated goal is sturdier, more interpretable bins for genome reconstruction.
pmc-13441283:
Jiawei Li and Jonathan Hunter Huggins propose a fairer way to grade Bayesian statistical models, introducing split predictive checks in a 2026 methods paper. Analysts need model checks whose verdicts mean what they claim. The classic posterior predictive check reuses the same data for fitting and grading, which breaks its calibration. Their split checks divide data into training and test parts, fit on one part, and grade predictions on the other, keeping the familiar workflow.

Theory developed for two variants shows both yield properly calibrated p-values in the large-data limit, unlike the classic check. Single splits catch gross model failure well. Divided splits, which repeat the split across partitions, detect even subtle departures from assumptions. Simulations and real-data runs showed the checks surfacing prediction problems that rival methods missed. The authors present the approach as general-purpose, efficient, and ready for everyday model criticism.
pmc-13441883:
Jun Pyo Kim and colleagues tie blood lipid profiles to Alzheimer's disease biomarkers tracked over time, reporting a 2026 cohort analysis. The ATN scheme sorts Alzheimer's biology into amyloid, tau, and neurodegeneration markers. Whether circulating fats move with those markers was largely uncharted at scale. Plasma from 1,395 participants in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative was profiled for 749 lipid species at baseline, then set against marker levels and their change.

Dozens of lipid species, several whole classes, and network modules of kindred lipids tracked with markers at single time points and across follow-up. One choline lipid family aligned with amyloid and neurodegeneration readings at every level of analysis. Ether-linked lipids and a ganglioside called GM3 also recurred across marker types. A fifth of the species tied to milder disease patterns carried DHA, the omega-3 fat. The authors offer the lipid map as leads for mechanism and monitoring work.
pmc-13442883:
Xueming Liu and colleagues find the nodes whose loss breaks directed networks fastest in a 2026 paper. Most past work tackled plain webs, yet real webs such as trade and the World Wide Web carry one-way links. In such webs, the strongly linked core keeps loops alive and holds the system together.

Their score, named network incoherence centrality, ranks nodes by how much they warp the web's flow order. Nodes fall in score order under their trophic method, which peels the core apart in steps. Tests on fake webs and 14 real directed webs beat rival methods each time. Their picks also sparked the largest knock-on splits. The authors frame the tool for stopping epidemics and rumors, and for building webs that bend without breaking.
pmc-13443783:
Alisha Saifi and coauthors report a 2026 randomized trial testing whether a pearl millet diet improves strength, endurance, and immune markers in young male athletes under heavy training stress. Sixty athletes aged 18 to 25 were split into a millet group of 28 and a control group of 30. The millet group swapped one third of regular cereals for pearl millet over 60 days.

The millet group gained muscular strength and aerobic capacity and lowered resting heart rate. It covered more ground in endurance tests, while controls kept their usual diet. Blood markers of inflammation, including Hs-CRP, TNF-alpha, and IL-6, did not shift significantly. The diet looks useful for performance, though its immune claims remain unproven and recovery effects need sharper measures.
pmc-13444183:
Yong Beom Kim and colleagues test a 2026 ex vivo rat model of how breathing-related acid-base shifts change muscle blockade by rocuronium and its reversal by sugammadex, a balance anesthetists manage daily. Diaphragm specimens from 30 rats were split into control, alkalosis, and acidosis gas mixtures and stimulated in a train-of-four pattern.

Only acidosis shifted the dose-response curves for twitch strength and train-of-four ratio against alkalosis, and recovery paths differed across groups. Total drug doses also differed between control and acidosis groups and between acidosis and alkalosis groups. The authors caution that carbon dioxide shifts may matter clinically, though group differences were not uniformly decisive.
pmc-13445483:
Eric L. Colomb and colleagues study why a small set of replacement knees came loose without infection, focusing on how well metal sleeves and stems fill the shin bone, in a 2026 records review. Loosening of this kind is rare, and the usual way of judging stem fill on X-rays has blind spots. The team devised a new area-based measure to fill the gap.

Eighteen patients had revision surgery for loose shin parts with sleeves at one center between 2011 and 2024. More than half showed poor support under the inner edge of the base plate. Both the old and the new measures found stems sized too small for the canal. The authors link loose parts to weak support and small stems, and offer their measure for fuller checks.
pmc-13446183:
Rashid Al Sheheimi describes a patient whose severe urine infection left tiny bleeds scattered through the brain, a pattern tied to critical illness itself, published in 2026. The bleeds favor the band joining the brain's halves, outer white matter, the brainstem, and the cerebellum, while often sparing deep gray cores. Blocked urine flow and septic shock set the stage in this case.

The patient's clouded mind lingered past the worst of the illness, and a special MRI view revealed the bleed pattern. Likely drivers span vessel wall failure, a leaky brain barrier, and low oxygen injury to small vessels. The author warns that the condition is missed often, since scans are rare in such patients, and that it clouds forecasts and blood thinner choices.
pmc-13446483:
Christian Näther reports the making and crystal structure of a cadmium bromide polymer threaded with a two-methyl pyrazine linker, in a 2026 study. Metal halide networks with such linkers vary widely in form, and heating can strip linkers step by step to yield leaner compounds. Cadmium usually favors six-fold wrapping, which made its iodide cousins' four-fold form a surprise worth chasing with bromide.

In the new crystal, pairs of bridging bromide ions tie cadmium ions into chains. The pyrazine linkers then join those chains into flat layers. Heat tests trace how the compound sheds its linker on warming, in line with the group's wider map of stepwise loss. The structure adds a bromide case to the cadmium halide family record.
pmc-13446883:
Elena Pavicic and colleagues set out the design of the Frauenherzen study, in a 2026 paper. The study tests whether wearable data can stand in for missing blood values in a heart risk score for women. The SCORE2 calculator needs blood pressure and blood fats, often absent in healthy women aged forty to sixty-nine. A wrist device worn for a week might fill the gap.

The single-center study in Bern pairs two clinic visits with seven days of watch data on heart rate, steps, and sleep. Blood tests, body measures, and deep surveys on food, mood, stress, and life quality round out the record. The team will test math routes that guess the missing score inputs from age, body mass, and watch features, and grade how far the guesses cut doubt.
pmc-13447183:
Moon-Seung Soh discusses exercise training for a stiff-heart form of heart failure in a 2026 commentary. People with this condition often cannot exert themselves, and improving daily function matters alongside drug treatment. Much of the exercise evidence comes from Western patients, so a pooled analysis focused on East Asian patients fills a gap.

Across four small studies with about two hundred people, training raised peak oxygen use by a meaningful amount versus usual medical care. Usual resting ultrasound measures of heart filling did not change, though each rested on only two studies. Soh argues that benefit may come from blood vessels, muscle and other body systems rather than the resting heart alone. Larger and firmer trials are still needed to pin down the size of the gain.
pmc-13447283:
Yuan and colleagues studied in 2026 how DNA methylation helps the timber tree Populus deltoides cope with heat paired with short days. Methylation adds chemical tags to DNA that can quiet genes without changing their code. Heat waves are growing longer in the tree's temperate home, and how this tag system steers survival was poorly known.

The team read methylation and gene activity in five tree lines. Lines far from their home climate showed unstable tags at key genes, linked to weaker survival. One tag type rose on gene switches under stress, turning on calcium entry and heat shock protection while easing growth hormones. A spray that strips methylation partly undid one gene's stress response, lifting a growth hormone and easing damage, which offers breeding targets for heat-hardy poplar.
pmc-13447483:
Suheir Sabbah and co-authors survey feeding, pica-related behaviour and sleep in children with autism in the West Bank, Palestine, in a 2026 parent-report study. Eating non-food items and sensory feeding struggles carry real health risks, and sleep problems often travel with them. Arab and Palestinian data on the combined picture were scarce before this survey.

One hundred five parents recruited through care centres in August 2025 completed two study scales. Feeding and pica-related scores sat at a moderate level overall, as did sleep disturbance, with sleep anxiety the highest sleep feature. No demographic factor split feeding scores, while younger children and girls showed worse sleep scores, with caution urged for a tiny oldest group. Higher pica-related scores tracked with worse sleep in a moderate link, joining the two problems for clinicians.
pmc-13448083:
Wenlang Yu and colleagues run a 2026 pilot study of acute moderate exercise effects on uric acid handling in young men with underexcretion hyperuricemia, where exertion might spike blood urate dangerously. Eighteen patients completed a single moderate continuous training bout, with blood and urine sampled before, right after, and 30 minutes later.

Blood and urine uric acid did not change significantly, while excretion indices, including fractional excretion and the Simkin index, rose markedly by 30 minutes. Lactate and creatinine rose transiently. Moderate exercise caused no large acute urate surge in this small cohort, though larger controlled trials must confirm safety.
pmc-13448483:
Birgül Erdoğan and Tuba Arpaci explore school re-entry after childhood cancer from the viewpoint of school staff in Türkiye in a 2026 qualitative study. Returning to class involves catching up academically, rebuilding friendships and managing health limits, yet evidence from teachers and school nurses was scarce. Twelve staff across roles, from teachers to a school nurse, gave online interviews between spring 2025 and early 2026.

Eight themes grouped into adjustment, reintegration and support needs domains. Absence left academic gaps, weakened belonging and peer vulnerability in staff accounts, calling for individual pacing. Help often depended on single motivated adults, with little usable health information, fuzzy role boundaries and weak coordination between school and hospital. Gradual, planned returns with clear communication channels are urged, and oncology nurses are flagged as possible coordinators.
pmc-13448683:
Kflay Gebrehiwot and Magdalena Szymura pull together a 2026 area analysis of invading plants across the Horn of Africa, spanning height, road nearness, and land use. Using thorough evidence roundup standards across major data sets, the team listed 250 invading species in 63 groups, led by Fabaceae, Asteraceae, and Poaceae.

Herbs led growth forms, most species came from New World or African native ranges, and Kenya and Ethiopia held the most records while Djibouti and Eritrea held the fewest. Invaders fell with height and distance from roads, gathering in farmed, shrubland, and urban areas. The authors call for expert-led area check tools and joint care.
pmc-13448783:
Bei Zhan, Ran Xia, and Liming Tao test in 2026 whether ginkgolide B, a compound from the ginkgo tree, can shield human retinal pigment cells from oxidative damage. They exposed cultured cells to hydrogen peroxide, a standard way to mimic the stress tied to age-related macular degeneration. Groups also received the compound, a blocker of the AMPK energy-sensing pathway, or both.

Ginkgolide B kept more cells alive, lowered cell death, and raised the activity of protective antioxidant enzymes while cutting a marker of fat oxidation damage. Under the microscope, it also limited swelling and structural damage inside the cells' mitochondria. Every benefit faded when the AMPK blocker was added. That points to the AMPK and Nrf2 pathway as the likely route of protection, though the authors say more work is needed to confirm it.
pmc-13449283:
Weiping Zhu and Panjanat Vorawattanachai study in 2026 whether a term of AI-enhanced learning tasks lifts the digital literacy of future preschool teachers. Their 212 students were in early childhood education at a university in Jiangxi Province, China. After the semester, a set questionnaire gauged digital literacy alongside engagement with the AI tasks, and the data were read with correlations and structural equation models.

Students landed at a moderate overall level, strongest in finding and sorting information and weakest in self-checking and problem solving. Engagement with the AI tasks tracked positively and significantly with every literacy dimension. The models further showed the tasks making a marked positive contribution to overall digital literacy. The authors suggest weaving such activities into teacher training so new teachers can bring AI into early childhood classrooms with purpose rather than novelty.
pmc-13449483:
Li Li Shao and co-authors review in 2026 how lung cancer stem cells conspire with their surrounding immune environment to dodge treatment. These stem-like cells renew themselves, spawn varied tumor cells, and shrug off chemotherapy, radiation, targeted drugs, and immunotherapy alike. Around them sits a microenvironment of macrophages, suppressor cells, regulatory T cells, fibroblasts, and oxygen-starved zones that keeps the stem cells supplied and hidden.

The review traces traffic in both directions. Environmental partners sustain stemness through signals, metabolic rewiring, and direct contact. The stem cells in turn release suppressive cytokines and vesicles, recruit more suppressor cells, blunt killer T and natural killer cells, and hide their identifying antigens. The authors catalog biomarkers that expose this partnership and strategies to break it, arguing that pairing stem-cell targeting with immune reactivation offers the best route to durable immunotherapy responses.
pmc-13449583:
Yang Xie and colleagues apply in 2026 protein-wide profiling to dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, a rare skin sarcoma that often returns after surgery and can transform into a more dangerous form. Comparing tumor tissue with matched normal skin, they mapped which proteins and pathways run hot. The splicing machinery stood out, alongside pathways for matrix interaction, pointing at how these tumors assemble their messenger RNA differently.

Two players were confirmed raised in tumors: components of the SF3B splicing complex and SerpinB9, a shield protein that blocks the immune system's granzyme weapon. SerpinB9 ran especially high in the transformed, worse-prognosis subtype. A splicing blocker drug, pladienolide-B, cut tumor cell viability, and silencing SF3B parts lowered SerpinB9 without touching its raw message, proving splicing control. Immune mapping also found natural killer cell and macrophage signatures inside the tumors, marking the SF3B-SerpinB9 axis as a candidate drug target.
pmc-13450583:
Bennett and colleagues built protein-based ageing clocks in 2026 for a large East Asian population study. The team used the China Kadoorie Biobank, measuring proteins from two platforms in about four thousand people. From proteins enriched in single organs, they trained models for eighteen organ-specific ages plus an overall age.

People whose protein age ran ahead of their real age faced more age-related traits and more new diseases, even after accounting for real age. Kidney ageing stood out: each extra year of kidney age gap raised risks of stroke, chronic liver disease, and chronic kidney disease. A gene study tied overall protein ageing to two genes, AFF3 and IL1RAPL1. The authors say organ clocks could aid risk checks and serve as trial endpoints, once validated further. The work extends ageing-clock evidence beyond European populations.
pmc-13451883:
Bangyue Wang and co-authors show in 2026 that brain immune cells run out of fuel after a stroke, and that a drug packed in tiny cell bubbles can save them. Stroke starves brain zones, and the cleanup cells, microglia, over-prune their own power plants until they cannot eat dead cells. Single-cell data from mouse stroke brains flagged that over-pruning.

In dishes, the pruning surge drained cell fuel and cut cleanup power. A blocker eased swelling but did not fix the power plants. The drug NBP steadied them and restored fuel and cleanup. Bubbles shed by microglia-like cells ferried the drug to stroke zones and lifted recovery in mice.
pmc-13453583:
Sergio Rius-Pérez and ten co-authors tease apart the roles of two sibling enzymes in acute pancreatitis, a sudden and painful swelling of the pancreas. The enzymes, NOX1 and NOX2, both make reactive oxygen species, the harsh molecules that drive swelling. Their 2026 study uses mice missing one enzyme or the other to watch each one's part in the disease.

NOX1 sat in the pancreas's own tissue and fired first, producing the early burst of reactive oxygen. Mice without NOX1 drew far fewer immune cells into the organ. Mice without NOX2 swung the other way: swelling signals soared and a brake protein, PP2A, fell. In obese mice with the disease, NOX2 dropped in the organ's cleanup cells, which then ate debris poorly. The pair thus pull in opposite directions, one fanning the fire and one damping it.
pmc-13453683:
Alise Emma Raika, Maria Elena de las Heras Alonso, Diana Sproge, and Elga Bataraga review melanoma that runs in families, covering its genes, skin signs, and follow up care. This inherited form makes up about 5 to 10 percent of all melanoma cases and tends to strike earlier in life. Their 2026 review notes that up to a fifth of such patients grow more than one primary melanoma.

Two genes, CDKN2A and CDK4, act through sun damage and cell cycle faults, while other gene changes work apart from sun exposure. The same inherited changes raise the risk of cancers of the pancreas, kidney, and other sites, so whole families need watching and gene advice. Under the skin scope, carrier tumors show odd pigment nets and dots, though some gene pairings mute those signs. The authors back photo based tracking every three to six months plus strict sun care.
pmc-13453783:
Gioia Di Stefano and seven co-authors report a skin lymphoma that changed character over three years and spread into the blood. The cancer, mycosis fungoides, began in its usual form in their patient. Their 2026 case report traces biopsies over time with a wide panel of cell markers, including an extended set for a helper T cell type.

After three years the disease had shifted: large cells, growth into hair roots, and markers of the T follicular helper type covered the tumor. A protein called GATA3, tied to worse outlook in such lymphomas, stained widely as well. Looking back at the first biopsy, the team found that a small share, about 10 percent, already carried the new markers. The case backs early wider marker testing to spot patients headed for a harsher course.
pmc-13454083:
Lin and colleagues mined public cancer data for ferroptosis-related genes that separate breast tumors. Ferroptosis is the iron-driven cell death program. They zeroed in on EPAS1 and its influence over tumor macrophages. Machine learning over pooled GEO and TCGA data picked EPAS1 and ACO1 as the key genes for deeper analysis.

High EPAS1 expression was significantly associated with better overall survival, while ACO1 carried no prognostic weight in the survival analyses performed. EPAS1 alone predicted survival with moderate accuracy, an area under the curve of 0.837 in the receiver operating analysis. Patients in the high-risk score group had both poorer survival and lower EPAS1 levels than low-risk patients in the dataset. Immune profiling showed EPAS1 tracking with tumor-fighting M1 macrophages positively and with the tumor-supporting M2 type negatively, supporting a role in steering macrophage polarization.
pmc-13454283:
Mateja Virovec and eight colleagues describe a 2026 feasibility study of museum-based dance classes for stroke survivors and their caregivers. The team first shaped the classes with a small focus group, then ran a single-group pilot with sessions held in a museum. Sixteen people joined, and the final analysis covered four patients and four caregivers.

Classes ran for one hour each week over 20 weeks, and attendance and satisfaction stayed high. No harmful events were reported. Early measures hinted at gains in thinking skills for both patients and caregivers, plus a possible drop in unsteady walking among patients. Caregiver burden scores did not change. The authors present the classes as a workable community option that deserves a larger trial.
pmc-13454383:
Zhang and colleagues review new blood based tests for ovarian cancer, a disease often found late because early symptoms are vague. Their 2026 review covers liquid biopsy, which means testing tumor material shed into blood or other fluids instead of cutting tissue. The authors survey tumor DNA in blood, whole tumor cells, platelets changed by tumors, small RNA rings, and tiny cell parcels called exosomes.

Tumor DNA in blood can aid diagnosis, guide drugs aimed at BRCA gene faults, and spot tiny amounts of disease left after treatment. Clusters of tumor cells give clues about spread and drug response. Newer signals, such as tumor educated platelets and exosomes, also show promise for diagnosis and outlook. The review is frank about limits: tests vary in method, miss some cases, and need shared standards before clinics can rely on them.
pmc-13454583:
Sercan Gucenmez and Adil Emrah Sonbahar read sex function in men with familial Mediterranean fever in 2026, a passed-down swelling disease. Sex woes are more and more seen in swelling diseases, yet FMF data were thin. Fifty grown men who met Tel-Hashomer rules were checked in calm spells.

Sex function was scored with the IIEF form, mood with the HADS form, and life quality with an FMF form. Erection failure, set by an erection score of twenty-six or less, hit fifty-six percent of the men. Low-mood scores ran higher in the failure group, and age tracked with better scores on several sex domains. Doctors gain rates and links to steer checks in FMF care.
pmc-13455383:
Fang and a large team found how Salmonella Typhimurium, hiding inside a shielding vacuole within host cells, steals glucose to fuel its growth despite being walled off from cell nutrients. Glucose is the bacterium's key carbon source, yet how cytosolic sugar could reach the walled-off compartment was unknown before this work.

The bacteria pull a three-pronged trick built on the host glucose transporter Glut1 and the cell's own signaling machinery. Infection first activates the MAPK cascade to raise Glut1 levels, increasing glucose uptake and glycolytic flow in the host cell. Salmonella then docks Glut1 onto its vacuole membrane, creating an import conduit for cytosolic glucose into its compartment. A previously unrecognized K29-linked ubiquitin tagging on the vacuole boosts the transporter's activity further. Blocking Glut1 strengthened innate immune responses and weakened bacterial virulence in cells and animals.
pmc-13455483:
Pei-Zhu Zhang and colleagues trace how emotion worsens tremor in Wilson disease in a 2026 study. Copper build-up in Wilson disease shakes the brain's movement circuits, and patients report that feelings change tremor strength, yet the brain basis was unclear. Forty-five tremor-dominant patients and 20 healthy controls took emotion, face recognition and tremor tests, with brain-wave microstates tracked during emotion induction and scans mapping atrophy.

Patients avoided social contact more, recognised faces more slowly and chose more negative faces, while negative emotion raised tremor size from 3.16 to 3.79 pixels in the tracking measure. A brain-wave pattern called microstate C grew more frequent and longer during negative emotion and tracked tremor severity, while lentiform, cerebellar and frontal damage predicted arousal. The work nominates microstate C as a marker for therapies aimed at emotion-linked tremor.
pmc-13456983:
Mei, Emery, and Eddie sought in 2026 a body mark of drink craving that a wrist or chest strap could catch on its own. Craving strikes fast in the first year of quit, and foretells slip and drop out. Folk in that span read their own states poorly, so self warns come late. The team strapped heart read gear on forty folk in early quit. Phone pings through the day logged each urge as it rose.

Four hundred urge logs fed the math. One heart sway mark rose in step with urge at the same span. A twin mark fell as urge rose, a small but firm link. Both marks live in how the heart's beat gaps flex. The team says passive reads could fire aid at the right span. Just in time phone help is the aim.
pmc-13457383:
Xinyue Wang and Jintang Guo review PBAT, a biodegradable polyester that pairs flexible fatty chains with stiff aromatic units to mimic the toughness of ordinary plastic while still breaking down. Their 2026 review covers the polymer's structure and physical behavior, how it degrades in soil, compost, and water, and the tweaks researchers use to fix its weaknesses.

Blending PBAT with other biodegradable polymers or natural macromolecules improves strength, processing, and barrier properties without giving up full biodegradability. Mineral fillers and nanomaterials add heat resistance and extra functions. Current uses run from farm mulch films and packaging to biomedical scaffolds and textile fibers. Costs stay high, breakdown demands the right conditions, and degrading fragments may form microplastics along the way. The authors point future work toward cheaper catalytic synthesis, smarter blends, and enzyme-assisted or chemical recycling that closes the loop on the material.
pmc-13457483:
Jheng-Yan Wu and colleagues compare two hormone-blocking drug families in diabetic kidney disease patients with sepsis-related heart weakness. Mineralocorticoid receptor activation may worsen the cardiac slump of sepsis, and the non-steroidal blocker finerenone was untested against older steroidal rivals for this complication. Their 2026 study used the TriNetX health record network to build matched groups of 1,378 patients each. One group started finerenone and the other a steroidal agent, during sepsis episodes from 2021 to 2025.

Heart failure-type complications struck 3.3 percent of the finerenone group against 5.2 percent of the steroidal group, a hazard ratio of 0.59. All-cause death was less frequent too, at a hazard ratio of 0.45, and markers of heart muscle injury favored finerenone. The pattern held across subgroups, weakening only among patients not on SGLT2 inhibitors. The authors urge caution: record-based comparisons can hide bias, so these results are hypothesis-generating and need prospective trials.
pmc-13458083:
Yongbo Wang and colleagues find what caps yeast growth when oxygen is off the table. Industrial fermentation runs Saccharomyces cerevisiae without oxygen, yet the rules limiting its speed under single-nutrient scarcity were murky. Their 2026 study combines steady-state chemostat cultures, multi-omic profiling, and engineering under anaerobic conditions, starving the yeast of carbon, nitrogen, or phosphorus.

Glucose uptake topped out near 14 millimoles per gram per hour under every limitation, a ceiling. What differed was the bottleneck behind it. Too little ATP choked growth under carbon and phosphorus scarcity, while a shortage of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, the enzymes loading transfer RNAs, choked it under nitrogen scarcity. The yeast shifted the protein budget toward building functions, rewiring phosphorylation to cope. A push-pull fix, boosting the energy gene VMA3 and the translation gene WRS1, lifted growth by 27.2, 47.5, and 52.5 percent under the three limitations, framing energy-translation coupling as the master constraint.
pmc-13458483:
Laura Miro-Mezquita and nine colleagues published this 2026 study developing RutiSafeNet, a monitoring tool for open-door acute mental health inpatient units. Open doors reduce coercive measures such as locked seclusion, but staff worry about safety risks and workload. The team set out to build a structured observation tool covering behavioural risks, from self-harm and aggression to leaving without permission, alongside the nursing workload those risks create.

The work was qualitative: three in-depth interviews and two focus groups with 19 staff members of one hospital unit. From these, the team identified 34 items and sorted them into low, moderate and high risk levels. Staff judged the categories suitable for daily monitoring. The authors are explicit that RutiSafeNet is a preliminary prototype meant to support structured observation, not to predict events. It still needs formal testing of reliability and validity before any clinical rollout as a scale.
pmc-13458583:
Shenao Zhang and colleagues fuse handcrafted and deep MRI features to predict chemotherapy benefit in glioma in a 2026 study. Gliomas vary widely in biology and treatment response, and single imaging models miss much of that complexity. From preoperative multimodal MRI in the TCGA low-grade glioma cohort, the team extracted 726 radiomics features and two deep embedding sets, defining benefit as survival of at least 24 months versus less.

Radiomics captured tumour volume, shape and coarse texture, while deep features captured local heterogeneity and infiltrative margins, and their fusion performed best. The fusion model reached an area under the curve of 0.75 on real-world data and 0.99 on an augmented, feature-rich dataset, with attention maps landing on tumour cores and infiltrative edges. The gap between datasets warns that data quality drives performance, so prospective validation must precede treatment decisions.
pmc-13459283:
Yunfei Liu and colleagues identify motor units in real time from surface muscle signals with only seconds of training data in a 2026 study. Deep learning for high-density surface muscle-signal splitting needs large data sets, limiting handy neural links. A spatio-temporal network was pretrained on fake signals and spike trains, then fine-tuned with clear lab-made samples generated by a sample rebuild plan.

Lab signals from thumb muscles of ten subjects, recorded with an 8 by 8 sensor array, yielded about 93 percent matching in online motor unit spotting. Only 6 seconds of lab fine-tuning data were needed. It beat rival methods. Rehab and robotics experts gain a data-efficient route to real-time motor unit tracking, pending tests across muscles, movements and patient groups.
pmc-13459683:
Lehlohonolo, Mphasha, and Skaal published a 2026 survey of health workers in Limpopo Province, South Africa. Their topic is how work settings shape eating habits and body weight. Clinic staff are expected to model healthy lives, yet their own risk runs high. The study covered 174 workers in one local district.

Three in four workers were overweight or obese by body mass index measures. Half ate fast food each week, and many clinics sat near fast-food sellers. Diets leaned on full-cream milk, fried food, and chicken served with skin on. Fewer than one in four ate local leafy greens each day. pmc-13460183:

pmc-13473583:

pmc-13473983:
Gunvanti Rathod and Pragnesh Parmar argue in 2026 that smart image tools can widen access to molecular typing for womb cancer. pmc-13474083:
Andreas Stephanou and a wide team study a benign but invasive dog mouth tumor in 2026 at single-cell scale. pmc-13474383:

pmc-13474783:
Zhou and colleagues studied lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, in 2026 to find why some tumors resist anti-PD-1 drugs, which release the brakes on immune cells. pmc-13474883:
Mesut Ergan and co-authors run a three-way trial in 2026 on virtual world teaching for physiotherapy students. pmc-13474983:
Lan and colleagues pooled studies in 2026 on whether TP53 mutations found in tumor DNA floating in the blood predict how cancer patients fare. pmc-13476583:

pmc-13476783:
Mojgan Alishahi and co-authors test melatonin in 2026 as an add-on to aspirin for preventing preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy blood pressure disorder. pmc-13476883:

pmc-13477083:

pmc-13477383:

pmc-13479383:

pmc-13480183:
Mowafag Salih and fourteen colleagues surveyed in 2026 dialysis patients in Al-Qadarif State during the Sudan conflict. War disrupts clinics and supply chains, forcing missed sessions, drug shortages, and heavier mental strain.

Added illness raised the odds of complications, while low-frequency dialysis was the norm and distress tied to older age and trouble getting medicines. Anxiety scores sat mostly in the minimal to mild range, and the authors warn that cross-sectional data cannot prove cause.
pmc-13481283:

pmc-13482283:

pmc-13482583:

pmc-13483583:

pmc-13484183:

pmc-13484483:

pmc-13486083:
Neslihan Gokcen writes a 2026 perspective on what systemic sclerosis does to identity and body experience beyond organ damage scores. pmc-13487183:

pmc-13488183:

pmc-13491683:

pmc-13491783:

pmc-13493683:

pmc-13493783:

pmc-13493883:

pmc-13495183:

pmc-13495283:

pmc-13495483:

pmc-13499583:

pmc-13499683:

pmc-13499883:

pmc-13499983:

pmc-13500083:

pmc-13500383:

pmc-13500683:

pmc-13501583:

pmc-13501683:

pmc-13501783:

pmc-13502783:

pmc-13503283:
Sireesh Kumar Teertam leads an eleven-author team reporting a 2026 study of why early melanoma depends on a cyclic AMP sensor, and how that dependency is wired into the cell's redox balance. The sensors EPAC1 and EPAC2, which activate the small protein RAP1, switch on during malignant transformation of pigment cells. Blocking them chemically, or deleting them genetically, prevented melanoma formation in Braf/Pten mice. Patients whose primary tumours expressed little EPAC message and little active RAP1 enjoyed better recurrence-free survival.

Sequencing matched primary and metastatic cells treated with an EPAC blocker identified TXNIP, a governor of redox homeostasis, as a downstream effector. The chain runs through mTORC1, which stabilizes the transcription factor HIF-1 alpha, which in turn switches on TXNIP and glycolytic enzymes. Through this circuit EPAC signalling holds mitochondrial reactive oxygen species in check. The authors suggest attacking the machinery melanomas use to outgrow this dependency.
pmc-13503683:
Rahul Yadav and three co-authors describe the design of a tall electric farm vehicle in a 2026 paper. The vehicle carries a robot that picks cotton, so it must pass over dense rows without harm. A Python model was used to fix the main size and motion values.

The model placed the center of weight about 1,083 mm above the ground. Tests of tilt showed the vehicle could climb slopes up to about 28 degrees and come down steeper ones safely. Top safe turn speeds were near 25 km/h. In field runs the top speed reached 12.19 km/h. The design fits row gaps of 900 mm and 675 mm, which suits standard cotton fields.
pmc-13503883:
Yiran Han and three colleagues test whether belly massage helps rats with obesity-linked type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 study. The hands-on method is a staple of Chinese medicine and is gaining clinical use for weight and blood sugar. The gut wall often leaks in this illness, which feeds body-wide swelling.

Thirty male rats were split into healthy, sick, and treated groups; the sick groups ate a fat-rich diet and got a drug that harms sugar control. Four weeks of daily massage lowered blood sugar and improved tolerance to sugar and fats. Swelling in blood and gut fell, and the gut wall sealed better. Tests point to a known alarm pathway in gut cells being dialed down. The team calls for longer, deeper studies to confirm the path.
pmc-13504783:
Shanshen Yu, Jia Sun, and Xufeng Mei report a rare myeloma case where two cell clones attacked the kidneys in two ways at once, in a 2026 case report. Myeloma is a cancer of antibody-making cells in the bone marrow. Its loose antibody chains can clog kidney filters and also build up inside kidney tube cells.

Their patient, a 54-year-old woman, came in with heavy protein in her urine yet a normal kidney waste marker. Blood and urine tests split oddly: one clone's full antibody showed in blood, while the other clone's free chains showed in both. A kidney biopsy confirmed both injury forms at once. Chemo improved her protein and chain levels, then her red cell production crashed; a treatment change restored it. The case widens the picture of two-clone disease.
pmc-13505083:
David Chinaecherem Innocent leads a team reviewing image-based machine learning for neglected tropical diseases in poorer countries, in a 2026 systematic review. These diseases burden poor regions where labs are thin. Teaching computers to read microscope and skin images could widen diagnosis, but real clinic value was unclear.

Eight studies met the review rules. Microscope-based models scored high, often above ninety percent on sensitivity and specificity, above all for malaria and worm infections. Models reading skin photos varied much more. Few studies tested their models on outside data or in live clinics, which limits trust in wider use. The authors call for data sets that mirror real patients and for trials built around deployment, not just accuracy.
pmc-13507083:
Guangqiang Ye and colleagues identify, in 2026 work, a little-known immune protein, IFI208, as a helper in the fight against viruses. The protein lacks the DNA-sensing part found in its family, yet its output rises after virus exposure through interferon signals. Mice and cells lacking it handled DNA and RNA viruses poorly.

After infection, IFI208 leaves the nucleus with help from a transport protein and meets MDA5, a sensor for double-stranded RNA. That meeting helps MDA5 spot viral RNA, clump together, and form liquid-like droplets that boost interferon output. Viral copying then falls. The pathway adds a fresh target for antiviral design.
pmc-13507383:
Xinyuan Zhang leads a 2026 team that scans the genomes of 266 five-year-old Dongfeng sika deer stags for markers tied to body weight. Sika deer farming in China prizes meat yield, and mature weight captures growth potential with little environmental noise. Whole-genome resequencing supplied the markers, and a mixed model hunted associations while correcting for family structure.

Twelve significant marker sites landed near seven candidate genes, including ERC2, FHIT, and NRXN3. Enrichment pointed to brain signaling through GABA, a calming messenger, plus DNA repair and cell cycle control pathways. Weight in deer may hinge partly on appetite and growth regulation in the nervous system. Breeders gain candidate markers for selection programs.
pmc-13508283:
