Mirriam Ogunja, Zhao Shurong, and Luo Ailing study how authentic leadership, where managers act openly and by clear values, affects worker wellbeing and quitting plans, in 2026 work. Modern workplaces face churn, remote work strain, and demand for psychological safety. The team ran two studies in Kenya. One followed 312 employee-leader pairs over three survey waves. The other tested a six-week leadership course in a factory, with 60 leaders and 280 staff, using a wait-list comparison group.

Each leadership trait worked through a different channel. Openness built trust and safety, fairness in decisions cut exhaustion, and strong values made work feel meaningful. Wellbeing gains fully explained the drop in quitting plans. After the course, quitting intention scores fell by nearly one third at three months. The study gives firms a practical route: train specific honest-leader behaviors, and staff health and loyalty follow.
pmc-13509283:
Nielza Moreira de Souza and eight co-authors examine how body function, lung function, and social conditions intertwine in people left with lung damage after tuberculosis, in 2026 work. Poverty and tuberculosis feed each other, yet social factors in the aftermath are little studied. The study covered sixty-nine patients with post-tuberculosis lung disease. Social data came from a standard assessment form, even though most patients had adequate housing. Lung tests measured airflow and lung volumes, and strength tests covered breathing muscles and thighs.

Patients showed low exercise capacity and impaired lung function overall. Links among physical function, lung measures, and social conditions were real but weak to moderate in strength. The authors say follow-up care should track social and environmental strain beside lung numbers. They propose trials that add social protection during and after tuberculosis treatment to test whether support lifts physical performance.
pmc-13510183:
Manuel Casal-Guisande, María Torres-Durán, and Alberto Fernández-Villar argue in a 2026 editorial that engineers should sit inside clinical lung departments as steady members of the team. Hospital innovation often stalls when tools built away from wards fail to fit daily routines. Lung medicine leans ever more on long-term monitoring, digital health, and computer aids, so fit with workflow decides whether a tool earns use.

Placed inside a department, engineers can spot needs that never become formal requests, such as slow diagnosis paths, uneven patient sorting, or routine data going unused. The authors stress that embedded engineers add to clinicians and hospital engineers rather than replacing either. They also note the model is not required for every project, since many strong studies grow from outside partnerships. The claim is narrower: earlier, closer contact between wards and builders raises the odds a tool is adopted.
pmc-13511083:
Hebah Altaweel, Jamal Abu-Ashour, Borhan Aldeen Albiss, and Bassim Abbassi build a fuel-cell sensor that reports how much oxygen demand a wastewater sample carries, in 2026 work. That measure guides plant operation, yet the standard lab test takes days and much labor. Their two-chamber cell uses graphite felt electrodes and microbes grown from oxygen-free sludge to turn waste breakdown into voltage.

After a month of film growth, the cell produced a steady voltage. Output rose in a straight line as the oxygen demand of lab-made wastewater climbed across six levels. Five real household wastewater samples, read through that line, landed within a few percent of standard lab results for most, with the widest gap near a tenth. The authors say the sensor could give plants near-live readings at low cost.
pmc-13511683:
Rafael Gómez-García, María de los Ángeles Cardero-Durán, Luis Espejo-Antúnez, and Carlos Fernández-Morales run a pilot trial of blood flow restriction exercise on thigh muscle electrical activity, in 2026 work. Twenty people trained one leg with a pressure cuff and the other without, at one fifth of maximum strength, in one session with order shuffled. The cuff pressure was set from each person's own artery closing pressure.

Muscle signal strength ran clearly higher in the cuffed leg across the full set scheme of 75 repetitions. Whole-session averages and peaks also ran higher with the cuff, while the drift of the signal within the session matched between legs. After exercise, the drop in a strength-linked signal measure was smaller in the cuffed leg. No side effects appeared. The authors say light cuff training can raise muscle drive without heavy loads.
pmc-13511783:
Zhiguo Hu, Yuyuan Wu, Jiahui Liu, Xusheng Guo, and Baohua Duan measure genetic variety in the oriental river prawn across the Huaihe River system, in 2026 work. The prawn is an important farmed species in China, and knowing its wild genetic health guides breeding and conservation. The team sampled twelve populations, one farmed stock and one outgroup from the Yangtze River, typing 342 prawns at ten microsatellite markers.

The panel proved rich, with 213 allele versions found in total and high diversity scores across populations. Genetic differences between populations stayed small, gene flow ran high, and nearly all variation sat inside single populations rather than between them. A grouping analysis hinted at two loose clusters, though a single-group reading could not be ruled out. The authors conclude the Huaihe prawns hold high diversity with weak structure, a base worth protecting from farm escape mixing.
pmc-13513483:
Philip Ogah Abutu, Marcia Y. Shade, Susan Barnason, Chad Abresch, Nada Fadul, Regina Idoate, and Keyonna M. King review HIV and tuberculosis co-infection care for immigrants and refugees living in the United States, in 2026 work. Tuberculosis is the leading killer of people living with HIV worldwide, and newcomers account for most United States tuberculosis cases. The review joins evidence from many study types on what shapes care in this population.

Stigma, social exclusion, fear of deportation, language gaps, and past trauma all delay diagnosis and weaken treatment follow-through. Barriers proved social and structural as much as medical, which pushes solutions beyond clinics alone. The authors recommend screening, education, and treatment programs shaped with communities and delivered in patients' own languages. Multi-field teams that pair medical care with social support, they argue, are needed to close the disparity.
pmc-13515883:
Hongmei Chen leads a ten-author team engineering a bacteria-killing enzyme against a duck pathogen in a 2026 study. Riemerella anatipestifer infects ducks, chickens, and geese, and growing drug resistance plus many strain types blunt antibiotics. Virus-made enzymes called endolysins chew through bacterial walls, yet the tough outer membrane of this Gram-negative germ blocks them. The team's natural enzyme indeed showed no killing power on its own.

They built three fusions, grafting the enzyme to parts meant to cross that membrane: a binding protein, a cell-penetrating peptide, or a charged tail. All three killed in a dose-dependent way, and the peptide fusion, ALC005, performed best, clearing about seventy-two percent of tested strains. Microscopy showed it bursting the cell envelope. Chen's team names peptide fusion a dependable route to working endolysins against this pathogen.
pmc-13518783:
Bardia Nabavi leads a ten-author team reporting in 2026 a new route to strong optical nonreciprocity, where light behaves differently depending on its direction of travel. Many photonics tools need that one-way effect in the infrared, yet few materials deliver it strongly. Magnetic Weyl semimetals helped, though choices stayed narrow.

Nabavi and colleagues instead doped cadmium arsenide, a Dirac semimetal, with manganese. The magnetic atoms ordered together, split the material's cone-shaped energy bands, and produced magnetic Weyl cones with a strong one-way response. Changing the doping level or applying a magnetic field tuned the effect. The result offers materials designers a fresh platform for infrared devices.
pmc-13518983:
Tianqi Song and colleagues surveyed how artificial intelligence interacts with health-related stigma, a field split across many disciplines. Published in 2026, the scoping review sifted 11,769 records from 2016 through 2025 and kept 70 studies. The goal was to map the whole two-way street, from AI measuring or easing stigma to stigma shaping how people use AI.

Most studies used AI to measure stigma, while fewer looked at stigma steering AI use, AI deepening stigma, or AI reducing it. Mental health dominated the coverage, leaving other conditions thinly studied. Definitions of stigma varied, cross-cultural views were scarce, and few studies tested AI tools in real-world care. The authors argue that closing these gaps is essential if AI is to lessen, rather than harden, the exclusion that keeps people from seeking care.
pmc-13520183:
Xingfang Zhang leads an eleven-author review in 2026 on laminins, scaffold proteins of the basement membrane, as controllers and possible drug targets in nervous system disorders. Laminins do far more than hold tissue together: they guide growing axons, build synapses, support myelin insulation, and maintain the blood-brain barrier.

Through receptor partners including integrins and dystroglycan, laminins pair physical support with cell signaling across brain growth, upkeep, and repair. The review maps where family members appear and when, then traces their roles in stroke, degeneration, demyelination, mental illness, and trauma. Whether laminin-based therapies can work in practice closes the survey, with barrier repair and synapse layout as prime arenas.
pmc-13520383:
Carla R Lamb leads a 2026 randomised trial of an enzyme treatment placed inside the chest to help drain infected fluid around the lung when standard drainage fails. Earlier small testing suggested the single-chain urokinase drug LTI-01 was safe enough for a larger check.

Forty patients received one of three drug doses or a dummy treatment once daily for up to three days. Need for alternative chest therapy within a week did not differ between drug and dummy groups overall. Two planned sensitivity checks hinted at benefit, while scan measures of fluid clearing were also tracked. Enrolment stopped short due to the pandemic, limiting firm conclusions.
pmc-13520483:
Marc-Antoine Rey and colleagues map in 2026 how sugar metabolism across eleven major organs hangs together in advanced pulmonary arterial hypertension, a disease of high pressure in lung arteries. Whole-body metabolic links might reveal strain beyond the lungs and right heart.

PET scans from 29 patients and 46 controls were segmented with automated tools, then compared with heavy statistical resampling. Standard uptake values differed little except for higher uptake in the right heart in patients. Network-style comparisons still found clear between-group divergence in organ coupling. Detailed organ-pair results follow, offering a systems view of metabolic rewiring in advanced disease.
pmc-13522483:
Surawy-Stepney and colleagues studied in 2026 the Pine Island Glacier in Antarctica and its floating ice shelf, which at times regrounds, meaning its underside keels bump back onto the seabed. Such contact was thought to add drag, slow the glacier, and perhaps halt its retreat. Using satellite radar tracking, the team built a history of shelf regrounding events going back to 2009 and paired it with ice sheet modelling.

Surawy-Stepney found the regrounding added little extra drag to the shelf base, so it did not brake the glacier as hoped. Instead, the contact plausibly helped trigger iceberg calving between 2015 and 2020. That calving is held largely responsible for the glacier's faster flow over the last decade. The work warns that a process long seen as a stabiliser may, for this glacier, have fed the very retreat it was meant to slow.
pmc-13522583:
Jonathan Munro and colleagues develop a nasal vaccine platform against SARS-CoV-2 in a 2026 study using a disabled flu virus as the carrier. The flu virus was rebuilt so it cannot replicate, and it displays a key piece of the coronavirus spike, either anchored on its surface or released. Two versions were grown successfully by standard virus engineering methods.

Given through the nose in mice, the surface-anchored version produced stronger blood antibody binding and virus neutralization than the released version. Mixing versions from two related coronaviruses in a prime-boost schedule widened antibody binding, although cross-neutralization did not clearly improve. The results support further work on intranasal vaccines that aim for both body-wide and airway immunity.
pmc-13522883:
Takahide Maeda and colleagues test whether image analysis can separate mature from immature ovarian teratomas in a 2026 imaging study. Teratomas are germ cell tumors whose treatment depends on maturity and grade. Scans from sixty-four patients aged thirty or younger with confirmed tumors were reviewed, comparing expert visual findings with radiomics, meaning hundreds of computed measures taken from CT and MRI images.

Visual findings and image measures both separated mature from immature tumors well. Grading immature tumors by eye proved difficult, with only the size of fatty nodules differing between low and high grade. Several MRI measures, especially from one fat-suppressed sequence, did differ by grade, as did selected CT measures. The authors see radiomics as a promising noninvasive grading aid that still needs more testing.
pmc-13523283:
Ksenia Kotiusheva and co-authors study what motivates or deters older adults from joining brain imaging research in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Two focus groups with eleven healthy adults aged fifty-five to seventy-three were combined with a questionnaire answered by more than three hundred adults across a wide age range. Imaging methods covered included magnetic resonance, electrical recording, brain stimulation, and eye tracking.

Older adults prized clear information about aims, procedures, and safety, wanted medical and non-medical research distinguished, and valued contributing to the collective good. Altruism grew with age while pay mattered less, and trust in researchers was higher among older respondents. Eye tracking drew the fewest negative feelings and brain stimulation the most. The authors offer age-tailored recruitment advice to widen participation in neuroscience.
pmc-13523583:
Henry D Huang and colleagues tested whether half-normal saline still enlarges ablation lesions when power is capped by temperature. Published in 2026, the ex vivo study burned 104 lesions into pig left-ventricle tissue with an open-irrigated catheter, comparing half-normal against normal saline under power-controlled and temperature-controlled modes. Weaker saline boosts current delivery, which can deepen lesions in power-controlled ablation.

With power control, weaker saline indeed made deeper and wider lesions at set power and time. With temperature control, lesion size did not differ between salines at either power level, since temperature cutoffs trimmed actual power and raised irrigation flow. Fewer steam pops appeared with temperature control. The authors conclude that temperature limits erase the saline edge while possibly improving safety.
pmc-13524083:
Pelech and co-authors review how plant pores respond to red and blue light. Their 2026 update covers stomata, the adjustable pores that balance carbon dioxide intake for photosynthesis against water loss. Two light pathways are known: a red light response tied to photosynthesis in leaf tissue, and a blue light response in the guard cells that saturates at low light levels.

Textbooks treat the pathways as independent, but the authors argue recent evidence shows they interact closely, with the blue light component depending on red light. The guard-cell blue response also varies between species rather than being universal, for reasons still unknown. Both guard cell and leaf tissue photosynthesis appear needed to activate the pump protein that opens stomata. The authors propose research directions aimed at crops that use water more efficiently without losing yield.
pmc-13524583:
Revathi Thirumushi Sairaj and others compare, in a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis, herbal products for metabolic problems in fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction. This liver condition travels with abnormal lipids, insulin resistance, and poor glucose control. Herbal remedies are widely used, yet their relative effects and evidence certainty were unclear.

Following standard review guidance, the team searched four databases through September 2025 and included 123 randomized trials with 8,595 adults. Network methods ranked products separately for triglycerides, fasting glucose, and insulin resistance. Korean red ginseng and naringenin led for triglycerides, green tea and a hesperidin-flaxseed pairing led for glucose, and sumac led for insulin resistance. Several other products, including artichoke leaf and curcumin, also beat placebo on selected results, with certainty formally graded.
pmc-13525183:
Varsha Srinivasan, Rajkumar Kannan, and Sampath Vadivelu estimate, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how common thyroid problems are among patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria, a long-lasting hives condition without a clear trigger. Earlier work focused on autoimmune thyroid disease, while routine function testing alone had been less studied.

The study enrolled 123 adults attending a specialist urticaria clinic at Rajiv Gandhi Government General Hospital. It used a validated questionnaire, clinical examination, and blood tests for free T3, free T4, and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Thyroid abnormalities appeared in 29 patients, 23.5 percent of the cohort. Nearly all were hypothyroidism, with a single hyperthyroid case. Rates were higher in women and in patients under forty-five, although neither difference reached significance. The authors suggest considering thyroid testing where suspicion exists.
pmc-13525783:
Leybengrub and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on sun protection for skin of color. Darker skin carries more melanin, which blocks some sun damage naturally. That partial shield breeds a false belief that no protection is needed. Yet skin cancers in darker skin are found later and kill more often.

Visible light and deep UVA rays drive much pigmentation harm in darker skin. Dark patches after inflammation and melasma rank among the top complaints listed. Sun-driven aging and light-triggered rashes also burden these populations in the review. Standard sunscreens built around UVB miss those deeper rays entirely. The authors call for tailored products, teaching, and fairer care access. Education gaps inside clinics worsen the outcome gap, they argue.
pmc-13526883:
Fan and colleagues reported in 2026 a new way to copy one light signal onto many color channels on a single chip. Optical broadcasting matters for fast communication and computing, but one cavity could not both make the multi-color pump light and do the copying well. A basic trade-off in how waves behave blocked that single-device design.

The team built a paired-cavity system with matched exceptional points, which are special settings where two light modes merge. Their design joined comb generation and broadcasting in one process. It gave more than 100 usable channels across a wide color range, with throughput near a terabit each second. That rate beat the old cavity limit by about a thousandfold. The group also built an optical device that speeds up image-style computing tasks.
pmc-13527683:
David Rojas-Rueda argues in this 2026 essay that air pollution should sit at the center of One Health, the movement linking human, animal, and ecosystem wellbeing. He opens with the 2023 Canadian wildfire smoke that filled emergency rooms, cut milk output, and stunted wild bird chicks across North America.

Rojas-Rueda notes that the joint One Health plan for 2022 to 2026 mentions air pollution only in passing, with no tasks or measures attached. Yet pollution was tied to millions of deaths in 2023, raised death rates in dairy cattle, and increased vet visits for pets. Tools to measure its burden exist only for humans. He urges the next plan to build shared monitoring and action across all three domains.
pmc-13528083:
Gertjan J. L. Kaspers leads a multinational consortium describing the CHIP-AML22 trial for children with acute myeloid leukemia in a 2026 paper. Survival in rich countries now reaches about eighty percent. Relapse and treatment harm remain major problems. The trial covers patients up to age eighteen with new disease. It is sponsored by the Princess Máxima Center.

One linked study adds the targeted drug quizartinib for a gene-defined subgroup. Another randomly tests two doses of an antibody-drug conjugate during first treatment. Risk groups use finer gene and residue measures than before. A further question asks whether two consolidation rounds match three for standard-risk children. A heart-protecting drug is advised for all. The design leaves room to slot in future drugs. Safety checks are built in throughout.
pmc-13528383:
Sandrine Boulet and fourteen colleagues argue that drug-style testing fits AI medical devices poorly in a 2026 review. Such devices differ from pills in deep ways. Algorithms keep learning and shifting after approval. Measures of success can be digital and slippery. Effects ripple through hospital organization too. The team walks through the choices that shape a fair trial.

Defining users and intended use comes first. Dataset picks for lab and clinic checks matter next. Outcomes, comparators, and real-world studies all need fresh thought. A device judged like a drug may pass the wrong test. Or it may fail despite real value. The authors map questions rather than give one recipe. Their goal is evaluation that matches how these tools actually live and change in care.
pmc-13529883:
Taylan Sahin and colleagues report a 2026 study of anesthesia care during combined body contouring surgery. They compare patients who had a Brazilian butt lift with liposuction and a tummy tuck against patients who had only the first two procedures. Records covered operations performed between 2020 and 2025.

The combined group numbered 550 people, while the smaller-procedure group numbered 570. Longer operations, more fluid, and larger fat volumes appeared in the combined group, yet only nine patients developed complications overall. Longer surgery and earlier operations were linked to problems without reaching firm proof. The authors judge combined surgery safe when a skilled team watches patients closely.
pmc-13530083:
Na Shen, Rui Zong, Jie Li and Xuemei Liu published this 2026 study on making colorectal cancer more sensitive to radiation by blocking ATR. ATR is a kinase that helps cells survive DNA damage. The drug, VE-822 or berzosertib, was tested on three models: one with normal p53, one with mutant p53, and one with p53 silenced. The question was whether broken p53 predicts response.

Silenced-p53 cells were most sensitive to the drug, needing the least drug to halve growth. A low dose barely touched normal-p53 cells but cut survival of p53-silenced cells, especially with radiation. The drug suppressed the ATR pathway's signal and left DNA damage marks. After radiation, normal cells paused in the cell-cycle phase with death, while p53-deficient cells piled into the later phase and died more, with signs of entry into division. The authors nominate p53 as a response biomarker.
pmc-13532183:
Rubén Díaz-Rúa and co-authors benchmark in 2026 how lab preparation choices and read lengths shape microbe recovery from a tough environmental mix of mangrove sediment and palm soil. Six short-read preparation routes at two lengths ran beside long-read sequencing, each in triplicate, on the same blended material.

Longer short reads with the best kit recovered over seven times more distinct proteins than the same kit at shorter length, and nearly matched long-read genome recovery at under half the cost. Novel gene clusters for natural products also surfaced. Careful method choice can unlock hidden diversity cheaply.
pmc-13536583:
Signe Salanson Jensen-Smidt and colleagues set out in 2026 the plan for Nature Impact, a feasibility study of group nature-based care for adults with mild to moderate anxiety, depression, or stress. Such group programmes in nature are gaining interest, yet how to deliver them well is unclear. Sessions will run weekly for ten weeks at three sites in Denmark.

The plan checks how delivery works in practice, what drives change, and which local factors help or hinder. Data will come from observation, group talks, forms, and questionnaires on health and ties to nature. Findings will guide a later full trial.
pmc-13536783:
Munnal Gulzar and co-authors compare two pulling tools for closing tooth gaps in braces care in a 2026 split-mouth trial. After first premolar removal, canine teeth must slide back to close spaces. Each of 46 patients received a metal coil spring on one side and an elastic chain on the other side of both jaws. Movement speed, root shortening, plaque buildup, and gum health were tracked at four time points.

Coil springs closed spaces faster overall and in two of the measured intervals. Root shortening did not differ clearly between sides, though older age tracked with more shortening. Springs held more plaque at several checks, while gum scores differed only at single time points in opposite directions. The authors conclude that springs move teeth faster at the cost of more plaque.
pmc-13541583:
Udbhav Kharad and colleagues puzzled over a shifting heart tracing in a paced patient after heart surgery. Published in 2026, the case covers a 66-year-old man with a junctional rhythm plus a pre-existing right bundle branch block in acute care. Short-term pacing wires sat on his right atrium and right ventricle, pacing in DDD mode at 89 beats per minute.

Monitor strips showed abrupt, brief flips from a fairly narrow QRS to a wide-complex rhythm and back. The authors trace the narrow beats to fusion: the paced right-side impulse beat native right activation while matching left-side firing through the left bundle. That fusion beat ran slimmer than both the native block beat and a fully paced beat. Readers get a worked example of how pacing and native conduction can blend on the monitor.
pmc-13543383:
Riaz Hussain, Lianxi Xing, and Yuan Hua published a 2026 comparison of white and sulphur butterflies, the Pierinae and Coliadinae subfamilies, across Taiwan Island and mainland China. Island and mainland landscapes impose different climates and human pressures, so the team modelled distributions for both regions and projected them across past periods and a warming future.

On Taiwan, ranges hug the lowlands because temperature falls steeply with height, and elevation alone explained about four-fifths of one subfamily's pattern. On the mainland, cold and dry conditions at altitude both constrained the butterflies, which also avoided human disturbance at high elevations, the opposite of their island behaviour. Highly suitable ground first expanded then shrank for one subfamily over past periods, with the reverse for the other. Warming is projected to reduce prime habitat for both without much upward movement, leaving island populations especially exposed.
pmc-13543583:
Peipei Xu's team tested in 2026 whether two cheap blood-derived indices predict left ventricular hypertrophy in people with type 2 diabetes. That is a thickening of the heart's main pumping chamber. The triglyceride-glucose index gauges insulin resistance, and the systemic immune-inflammation index reflects inflammatory cell balance. Six hundred diabetic patients were divided by whether ultrasound criteria for the thickening were met. The indices were tested one by one and as a pair.

Both indices ran far higher in patients with hypertrophy and rose with heart-wall mass. After allowances, each on its own pointed to the condition, the metabolic index most strongly. Paired, they split patients with an area under the curve of 0.857, catching about eighty-four percent of cases. Two numbers already sitting in routine blood work, the authors argue, could flag diabetic patients who need a heart scan.
pmc-13547283:
Agata Czerwińska and colleagues followed Polish bariatric surgery patients for at least ten years in 2026, focusing on the highest-risk group whose body mass index reached 50 or more. Eighty-nine such patients, operated on between 2007 and 2014, were compared with patients who started below that threshold. Weight loss, remission of linked diseases, complications, and repeat operations were all tracked.

The heaviest group actually reached a twenty percent total weight loss more often than the comparison group, and disease remission rates were similar, including about three in five diabetes cases. Final weight still sat higher, as expected. The clear cost was repeat surgery: about 44 percent needed revision, mostly for weight regain, against 20 percent of the lighter group.
pmc-13547383:
Tianjiao Zhou and colleagues charted cancer burden among older Asians from 1990 to 2023. Published in 2026, the planned analysis drew on Global Burden of Disease 2023 counts for 34 Asian countries. Older adults carry a rising share of Asia's cancer load, yet trends, place gaps, and unfair gaps were thinly mapped.

In 2023, older Asians faced 4.59 million new cases, 3.27 million deaths, and 57.49 million lost healthy years. East Asia bore the worst load, while South Asia started lowest but rose fastest in new cases and deaths. Lung cancer led, gut cancers topped system burden, and growth plus aging drove the climb, with better trends only in East and Southeast Asia. The authors urge fairer, age-wise stopping of new cases and care across Asia.
pmc-13547983:
Verena A. Katzke led an EPIC cohort study in 2026 testing 92 immune proteins in blood samples taken before diagnosis, hunting for early warning signs of pancreatic cancer. Within the long-running European nutrition and cancer cohort, 406 people who later developed the disease were matched with 406 who did not. Eight proteins first looked linked to risk.

After full adjustment, only MMP12, an enzyme that chews through tissue scaffolding, kept a clear association, with double the level tied to about fifty-six percent higher odds. Correcting for the many tests erased formal significance, yet the MMP12 link was strongest for cancers found within four years of the blood draw. The authors call for confirmation in other cohorts before any screening use.
pmc-13548583:
Arezoo Shahsavari, Sima Hejazi, and Fatemeh Estebsari follow thirty-one dialysis patients through eight weeks of nurse-led telephone support, in a 2026 single-group study at an Iranian hospital. People on hemodialysis need steady monitoring between sessions, and phone follow-up plus text messages offer a cheap bridge. The team measured quality of life with a standard questionnaire and tracked weight gain between sessions and blood chemistry before, during, and after the program.

Most measures shifted significantly across the study period. Gains showed in quality of life scores, weight control, and several biochemical values. A couple of blood markers changed only between the start and end points. With no comparison group and a small sample, the authors urge caution. They still present tele-nursing as a promising companion to in-person dialysis care, pending controlled trials.
pmc-13550083:
Siripa Bumrungtien and colleagues report two decades of focused radiation results for rare nerve sheath tumors inside the skull, in a 2026 retrospective study from a Bangkok hospital. Schwannomas on nerves other than the hearing nerve are uncommon, and surgery, the standard, can injure delicate structures. The team reviewed fifty-seven patients treated between 2000 and 2020 with stereotactic radiotherapy, most in a few large fractions and a few spread over twenty-five days.

With a median follow-up near ten years, tumors were controlled in all but two patients, who then had surgery. Control rates stayed at one hundred, ninety-seven, and ninety-two percent at five, ten, and fifteen years. Nearly half the tumors shrank. Side effects were minimal, with one case of worsened facial numbness. The authors say the long record supports focused radiation as a safe, effective alternative to the knife.
pmc-13551283:
Chinnawut Suriyonplengsaeng and Jariya Waisayarat published a 2026 study of muscle biopsy tests where frozen tissue is not on hand. Many hospitals cannot snap-freeze muscle samples. The team built a staining method for tissue fixed in formalin and set in wax. They used twenty cases across several muscle diseases. They stained for five markers and compared the results with frozen samples.

Three markers stained as well in fixed tissue as in frozen tissue. Their match rates reached 80 to 90 percent. Two markers failed in fixed tissue and could not be used. A few cases differed on one marker only, which may reflect patchy disease. The team offers the three working markers as a practical choice for low-resource labs.
pmc-13551683:
Hongtao Zhu, leading a large team of co-authors, published a 2026 study of how a complement protein helps glioblastoma, the most aggressive adult brain tumor, protect itself. Glioma stem cells and tumor-associated macrophages support each other, and screening pointed to complement 5a, secreted mainly by the stem cells, as a key messenger. Its receptor, C5aR1, acts on both cell types.

In stem cells the signal boosted growth, self-renewal, and resistance to killer T cells through a chain involving STAT3 and PD-L1. In macrophages it drew cells in and pushed them toward an immune-suppressing state. Silencing or blocking the pathway disrupted both partners and slowed tumor growth, and human tumors with an active axis fared worse, marking a treatment target.
pmc-13551783:
Jingfeng Zou, leading seven colleagues, published a 2026 overview of systematic reviews on screening tools for sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle strength and mass. No single diagnostic standard exists, so the team appraised reviews of the questionnaire SARC-F and its modified versions using established quality and evidence grading tools. Four reviews covered the original tool and two covered modifications, with heavy overlap among their source studies.

The original questionnaire's pooled sensitivity ranged widely and its evidence quality ran from very low to moderate in the reported appraisals. Modified versions performed better on the same measures, with higher specificity ranges. Despite the overlap, review methods were largely rigorous, and the authors supply a comparison table to help clinicians choose a screening version.
pmc-13551883:
Malika Karunaratne, with thirteen colleagues, published a 2026 report on Sri Lanka's new antibiotic stewardship program. Stewardship means using antibiotics wisely to slow resistance. The health ministry and the national microbiology college launched the program in 2024. It spread four low-cost tools to hospitals. One was a local version of the World Health Organization's antibiotic classes. A training-of-trainers model carried the rollout to all nine provinces.

After one year, uptake passed half on every key measure. The antibiotic class tool reached the highest uptake, at about three quarters. Working teams and prevalence surveys lagged near the halfway mark. The team argues that central control plus cheap tools can root such programs in poor settings. They offer the design as a model for peer countries.
pmc-13552583:
James X Sotiropoulos leads a thirteen-author team setting out a 2026 plan to pool trial data on lung care for preterm babies. Their focus is bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a lung disease that harms many babies born very early. Some trials suggest adding budesonide, a steroid, to the lung fluid called surfactant may help. Other trials disagree, so the group will gather raw data from each child in each trial.

The plan searches databases and trial lists for babies born before thirty-two weeks. Two main outcomes matter: death before leaving hospital, and lung disease at thirty-six weeks. Bias checks, subgroup work, and a grading of proof strength are built in. If the mix works, it could offer a cheap gain in survival.
pmc-13557483:
Shawn Stapleton, Renu Sara Nargund, and Caroline Chung argued in 2026 that cancer care needs high-reliability habits as artificial intelligence spreads through its workflows. AI tools now draft clinical notes, outline tumours for radiation, and assist diagnosis, yet their errors can look convincing. A model that performs well in general patients may quietly do worse in cancer patients, and nobody may notice.

Oncology makes the stakes plain: decisions carry narrow safety margins, care crosses many settings, and records shape choices for years. The authors describe how note-writing AI can insert omissions or invented details into a permanent record, and how busy teams placed as human checkers may overtrust or dismiss the tools. They propose a framework that joins high-reliability organisation principles with a layered defence model, treating reliability as a continuous team function rather than a one-off technical check.
pmc-13558383:
Mehmet Asıl and colleagues tracked short-term shifts in blood antioxidant balance after ERCP, publishing the prospective controlled study in 2026. The bile-duct procedure is invasive and may stir oxidative stress, yet most earlier work looked only at pancreatitis cases or single markers. The team measured thiol and disulfide levels, a sensitive gauge of redox balance, in patients undergoing ERCP and in controls.

Patients showed lower protective thiol pools and higher oxidised disulfide levels than controls, even after age adjustment. Levels partly recovered after the procedure but stayed below control values at 24 hours, regardless of pancreatitis or enzyme rises. The authors link the lingering imbalance to both the underlying bile disease and procedure stress, while noting its clinical meaning still needs pinning down.
pmc-13559083:
Tingyi Lv and colleagues published a 2026 retrospective cohort study of high blood lactate arising during surgery in newborns who needed gastrointestinal operations. Lactate above 2.0 mmol/L, called intraoperative hyperlactatemia here, can signal that tissues are not getting enough blood. The team reviewed 570 neonates treated between May 2020 and October 2022.

About a third of the babies, 34.6 percent in the cohort count, developed the condition during their operation. Those babies died within 30 days far more often and needed breathing support for longer. They also suffered more complications after surgery, including lung problems. Regression analysis tied the condition to younger age, acid imbalance before surgery, emergency operations, and blood transfusion during the procedure. The authors suggest that spotting high-risk newborns early could sharpen monitoring and risk planning around these operations.
pmc-13559683:
Zhao and colleagues name a protein called CST2, also known as cystatin SA, as a driver of melanoma, the most dangerous skin cancer, in 2026 oncology research. CST2 levels were much raised in melanoma tissue compared with healthy skin, and higher levels tracked with poorer patient survival in cancer database records. The team then tested what the protein does inside melanoma cells grown in the laboratory, changing its levels and watching cell behavior and signaling.

Raising CST2 boosted melanoma cell growth, colony formation, and migration, the traits that make tumors grow and spread. The protein binds interleukin-6, an inflammatory signal, and switches on its downstream STAT3 and NF-kappaB pathway. Silencing CST2 reduced levels of all three signals, while adding back interleukin-6 reversed that suppression. Zhao suggests CST2 as a prognostic biomarker and possible drug target, while noting animal and clinical validation is still missing.
pmc-13561883:
Nathaniel F. Henneman and colleagues reveal an unexpected second job for class 3 PI3K, the lipid kinase best known for launching autophagy, the cell's self-digestion program. Their 2026 study finds the enzyme inside the nucleus acting as a co-activator of the transcription machinery during fasting. Nutrient sensing and gene switching turn out to be physically linked on chromatin.

The nuclear enzyme overlaps with actively transcribing RNA polymerase and with the Setd1a complex that lays down an activating histone mark. It binds both partners and helps anchor them to genes. Removing it stripped the activation marks from selected genes, while extra enzyme boosted them and recruited further activators. In starved liver, the kinase switched on autophagy genes and pushed metabolism toward ketone production and fat burning. The authors frame chromatin-bound PI3K as the relay between empty fuel gauges and adaptive gene programs.
pmc-13562383:
Hela Saidi and five colleagues describe a keen volleyball player, a 55-year-old man, who turned out to have a false aneurysm of a small artery near the shoulder. Only 52 cases of true aneurysm in that vessel appear in print, mostly in athletes whose sports demand repeated overhead arm motion. The man felt armpit pain and noticed a lump after playing. Two years earlier he had felt a sudden pop during a game, and his symptoms grew until any overhead activity set them off.

Surgeons opened the area, removed the damaged segment, and repaired the main arm artery directly. The report warns that such injuries are often mistaken for muscle or joint problems, which delays care. A clot breaking loose from the weakened vessel can starve the arm of blood. The authors urge clinicians to think of this rare cause when overhead athletes report pain, tingling, and a growing mass.
pmc-13562583:
Alice Luddi and seventeen colleagues trace a set of ring-shaped RNA molecules that help switch human sperm toward self-destruction. Male fertility is falling, and obesity is one driver, since sperm from obese men die off readily and fertility treatment fares worse. The 2026 team profiled circular RNAs in top-quality sperm from normal-weight and obese men. Sperm from obese men carried a distinct set of these rings, tied to death-promoting networks.

The rings arrive two ways: sperm make them through a splicing route steered by the protein FUS, and vesicles deliver more. A fat-signalling balance involving sphingosine 1-phosphate and ceramide was skewed toward death in obese samples. When the team triggered sperm death, a subset of rings responded and fed a growing loop that armed the executioner protein caspase-3. The authors propose these rings as early warning markers that could sharpen sperm quality checks.
pmc-13563483:
Kathrine Agergård Kaspersen and colleagues examined whether frequent plasma donation tracks infection risk in Denmark, publishing the multicentre observational study in 2026. Demand for plasma-derived medicines is rising, but long-term donor health evidence is thin, and European guidance recently trimmed the maximum donation frequency on expert opinion alone. The team followed 45,615 first-time voluntary, unpaid donors from 2016 to 2024, recalculating donation rates every 90 days.

Higher donation rates came with lower recorded infection risk, with the most frequent donors showing roughly half the hazard of single donors. The authors warn against reading this as protection: healthier people keep donating, a bias that observational data cannot remove. The study therefore shows the limits of non-randomised safety evidence rather than clearing frequent donation.
pmc-13563783:
Rui Yuan and seven colleagues hunt for blood-cell cut-offs that warn of opportunistic infections in people living with HIV, beyond the CD4 count. Those infections remain a leading danger, and CD4 alone misses patients whose immune patterns are abnormal at seemingly safe counts. Their 2026 study drew blood between August 2021 and April 2023 and sorted lymphocyte subsets by flow methods. Subsets were checked against CD4 counts, then tested for how well thresholds separated patients who developed infections from those who did not.

One subset, CD4 cells carrying the CD28 marker, tracked CD4 counts perfectly and predicted infections with an accuracy score of 0.819 at a cut-off of 129 cells per microlitre. Five subsets scored above 0.800, each catching over ninety percent of the cases. Abnormal activation patterns mattered even when headline counts looked fine. The authors offer the cut-offs as a sieve for spotting patients who need closer watching.
pmc-13563883:
Allison J. Smith and three colleagues compare telemedicine with in-person care for keeping people on buprenorphine, the opioid-use-disorder medicine patients quit within months. Their 2026 retrospective study drew records from a large academic centre in the southeastern United States covering 2018 to 2021. Two eras sat side by side: 247 patients treated face to face before the pandemic and 204 treated by telemedicine. Retention meant holding a buprenorphine-linked visit at six months.

Only 35.3 percent of the 411 patients with complete data stayed in treatment that long. Telemedicine patients were more likely to be among them, with adjusted odds 1.87 times the in-person group's. Non-White patients also retained better, at 2.05 times the odds of White patients, a pattern the authors flag for confirmation. With telehealth prescribing rules under debate, the team argues remote care removes travel and scheduling friction that ends treatment, especially for groups the system has served worst.
pmc-13563983:
Weiwei Wang and colleagues feed, in a 2026 mouse study, a fermented soybean meal enriched with Artemisia argyi to animals challenged with a diarrhea-causing E. coli strain known as ETEC K88. Groups compared no treatment, an antibiotic, and the fermented feed, with checks on growth, diarrhea, immune markers, gut lining genes, and gut microbes and chemicals.

Treated mice recovered weight faster, had less diarrhea, and showed calmer immune signals plus stronger gut barrier genes. Their gut communities shifted toward lactic acid bacteria, and chemical profiles pointed to purine metabolism as the biggest change. Feed researchers get a candidate diet ingredient for protecting young farm animals from this infection.
pmc-13564083:
Masaki Ryuzaki and colleagues present, in a 2026 study, evidence that growth hormone made locally inside the prostate, rather than by the pituitary gland, helps drive benign prostate enlargement with age. Human prostate tissue, cultured prostate cells, and mice carrying hormone-producing grafts were examined for DNA damage and for a cell-change program linked to tissue growth.

Tissue samples expressing local growth hormone rose more than tenfold after age sixty, alongside more DNA damage markers. Hormone-treated cells showed more damage, more growth signals, and greater movement, while mouse prostates near hormone grafts developed changes resembling enlargement. The authors propose blocking the hormone receptor in the prostate as a treatment idea.
pmc-13566483:
Uruski and colleagues tested in 2026 whether blood pressure drugs undo the ageing that hypertension causes in blood vessel cells. Serum from untreated hypertensive patients damages endothelial cells, the lining of vessels, driving them into senescence, a worn-out state. The study involved 71 newly diagnosed patients randomised to amlodipine, nebivolol, or perindopril. Serum taken before and after six weeks of treatment was applied to vessel cells in the lab.

Serum from nebivolol-treated patients helped the cells most consistently. It reduced cell proliferation and levels of growth signals such as VEGF, and lowered several inflammatory signals. It also carried less TGF-β1, a protein linked to hypertension-driven cell ageing. Oxidative stress, measured by damaged DNA products, also fell under nebivolol serum. The authors conclude nebivolol best reverses the senescence-driving effects of hypertension on vessel lining cells.
pmc-13569383:
Maturawan Tunhikorn and colleagues tested a dog itch drug in horses with allergic skin disease, publishing the pilot study in 2026. Allergic dermatitis in horses causes intense itching, wounds, and secondary infection, yet evidence for treatments is thin. Oclacitinib, a Janus kinase blocker approved for dogs, targets itch-signalling pathways also found in horses. Sixteen horses aged at least 18 months received the drug daily for 21 days.

Itch scores fell from a median of 5 to 2.5, lesion scores roughly halved, and 15 of 16 horses improved on itch. Blood tests, however, showed rises in liver and kidney markers and falls in white cells, so caution is advised for horses with organ disease. The drug looks effective for equine allergic itch, pending larger safety studies.
pmc-13572383:
G. E. Jackson, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 model study of a hormone receptor in the stick insect Carausius morosus. The hormone at issue, called Carmo-HrTH-II, is a chain of ten amino acids that helps the insect mobilise fuel. The work maps the shape of the hormone and how it docks into its receptor.

The team mixed NMR measures, computer motion runs, and docking tests. The hormone proved flexible, with a bend near its middle that showed in both the lab data and the runs. In the docked pose, two ring-shaped units sat deep in the receptor pocket. Swapping single units showed which spots drive the fit most. A screen of insecticide-like compounds then flagged some that might block the receptor at the same site.
pmc-13572483:
Jiping Wang, with five colleagues, led a 2026 study of scent compounds that could grade jasmine flowers by chemistry rather than by eye. Jasmine scents tea and yields oils, and flower grade sets the price. Current grading rests on look and sieve size, with no firm chemical markers.

The team sampled buds of grades A and B plus open flowers of grades I and II, then trapped and read their volatile scents. Twenty-five compounds split the bud grades, and 134 split the open flower grades. Six compounds appeared in both splits. Three stood out as markers: (E)-3-hexen-1-ol, caryophyllene, and a third ketone. A combined S-score with a cut near 9.5 split the grades in this data set. The authors stress that fresh samples across seasons and regions must confirm the cut first.
pmc-13573083:
Nutthakarn Ratanasereeprasert, with seven colleagues, reports a study of skull and tooth growth in Thai children with craniosynostosis. In this condition, skull seams fuse too early and warp head growth. The syndromic form comes with broader body syndromes, while the plain form stands alone.

The study covered 19 patients, 13 syndromic and six not, with a mean age near nine years. Seventeen skull and tooth measures were set against Thai norms for age. Syndromic children showed a pulled-back upper jaw, a steep growth tilt, and a short front skull base, with lower front teeth tipped to compensate. The plain group differed mainly in the short skull base alone. Dental age matched real age in both groups. The authors say treatment timing should rest on each child's own skull pattern, not tooth age.
pmc-13573383:
Man Hung, with nine colleagues, presents a 2026 scoping review of what happens when towns stop adding fluoride to drinking water. Fluoride in water prevents tooth decay at a population scale, yet more places debate ending it. The team mapped health, service, cost, and fairness outcomes after stops around the world.

Searches of 17 databases and grey sources to October 2025 kept 19 studies from 1970 to 2025, across Europe, North America, Australia, and Israel. Places with no backup fluoride plan more often saw decay rise, in one case by up to 75 percent on a standard decay score. Treatment use and costs rose too, above all for young and worse-off children. Places with other fluoride routes often held steady or kept improving. The authors call for tougher head-to-head studies.
pmc-13573483:
Satoshi Kamata, with four colleagues, carried out a 2026 study of air leaks after lung cancer surgery. A leak from the cut lung is the most common snag after such surgery, and one that lasts five days or more can seed infection and long stays. The team asked which patients with a day-one leak will go on to a long one.

Records covered 329 patients who had a lobe or segment removed at one Japanese hospital from 2015 to 2019. Male sex, low body mass, smoking load, lung capacity, and long operations all tied to leaks in the first place. Among day-one leakers, low body mass, current smoking, total smoking load, and blood loss marked the long leaks. A four-point score split risk cleanly, from no long leaks at zero points to over four in five at four points.
pmc-13575183:
R Sachin and five colleagues introduce Thermo-CR, a 2026 system that removes cloud shadows and cloud cover from satellite images using physics rather than image guessing. Clouds hide about two-thirds of Earth's surface at any time, breaking up data feeds for farming and disaster work. Recent AI tools can invent ground detail under thick cloud, a risky flaw.

Thermo-CR pulls live humidity and temperature data, works out how much light the air blocks, and reverses that effect with a transfer model. Clear-sky history and location anchors steady the result. On test images from rainforest, London, and Seattle scenes, it scored high similarity to true images and ran in under 13 milliseconds per frame. Performance degraded in a predictable way under 90 percent cover.
pmc-13578283:
Jong-Hyun Kim and Jung Lee build a 2026 graphics method that wets virtual cloth in a way that looks and behaves like the real thing. Cloth drinking in water mixes four actions at once: flow through pores, soaking up, leaking out, and spreading. Particle based scenes often turn unstable or slow when all four run together.

Their system runs all four in one pipeline on the graphics chip. A virtual pressure rule guides flow near cloth edges, a wetness score governs soaking and leaking, and spreading runs as its own pass. A fast sorting trick speeds the search for nearby particles. Tests on wet cloth scenes kept the soaking steady, held total water close to the starting amount, and cut sorting time.
pmc-13578683:
Yong Song and colleagues use moving CT scans to spot lung spots stretched too far by a ventilator, in a 2026 mouse study. Ventilators save lives, yet the same air pressure can injure lungs, and a whole lung average can hide local strain. Four breathing settings varied peak pressure and the small pressure kept between breaths.

Local pressure and volume loops, read slice by slice, told a different story from the global loop. One gentle looking setting, low breath size with no kept pressure, showed marked local overstretch that the global view missed. Collapse measures looked alike by both views. The authors argue care teams should judge settings by local strain, not by the lung wide average alone.
pmc-13582883:
Chih-Hung Wang and colleagues built ANTIBIOTIC, a deep-learning system that identifies bacteria and predicts drug resistance straight from MALDI-TOF mass spectra. Standard microbiology takes hours to days to report resistance, delaying the right antibiotic. Their 2026 study trained 26 species models and 248 resistance models on a public dataset plus 89,026 local hospital records.

Species identification was excellent, with median accuracy scores of 0.99 internally and 0.96 on later external data. Resistance prediction scored 0.94 internally but fell to 0.55 on later data, recovering to 0.61 after retraining on recent records. Linked to a language model, the system also drafted antibiotic advice. The authors warn that resistance models need regular updating to stay useful.
pmc-13584583:
Shiuan-Hui Wang and colleagues use a classic jaw triangle to measure facial asymmetry in jaw surgery patients in Taiwan. The Bonwill triangle joins the front lower teeth point with the two jaw joint centers, and a balanced face should give near-equal sides. Their 2026 study read 3D scans from 109 adults, 54 who had jaw-correcting surgery and 55 who had not.

The surgery group showed clearly wider gaps between the left and right side lengths than the comparison group, which fits, since uneven jaws are a main reason for such surgery. The gap ran largest in men, and only in men in the surgery group did it shrink with age. The jaw width across both joints did not differ between groups. The authors propose the triangle as a handy planning aid before surgery.
pmc-13585783:
Erika Esposito and colleagues compare ways of preparing blood samples for chemical fingerprinting in parkinsonian disorders. Parkinson's disease and two look-alike conditions, called MSA-P and PSP-P, are hard to tell apart early, and no simple blood test can yet do it. Their 2026 study built a careful plasma testing platform and tried three preparation routes on samples from 102 patients.

One route, which strips out fatty phospholipids, gave the cleanest readings and the most signals that could be named, even though it found slightly fewer raw signals overall. Disease-linked patterns stood out most clearly between Parkinson's disease and PSP-P, while comparisons with MSA-P stayed weak. The authors stress that no chemical ID reached the highest certainty level, so every pattern here is a lead for targeted follow-up.
pmc-13588683:
Michaela Bergmann and two colleagues compare a new blood-clotting concentrate against two products already on pharmacy shelves. The products supply fibrinogen, the protein that forms clots, to patients born without enough or who lose it through bleeding, surgery, or childbirth. Their 2026 lab study tested three batches each of the new BT524 concentrate and two rivals, measuring purity, stray particles, and how firm a clot each could build.

BT524 carried no active forms of three other clotting factors found in some products, and its breakdown markers, clumps, and fine particles ran markedly lower, a sign of cleaner manufacture. Its clots matched one rival and beat the other on firmness, and added factor XIII strengthened them further. The authors conclude that look-alike concentrates differ enough in makeup to matter for clot quality.
pmc-13590483:
O. Petrucci and colleagues released FFEM-DB 2.0, an updated bank of flood deaths in the Euro-Med region from 1980 to 2024. Knowing who dies in floods, where, and doing what needs one-by-one records, yet prior reach was patchy. Their 2026 data paper lists 3,737 deaths across 16 areas, 12 of them whole countries, stretching the earlier bank through December 2024 with four new areas.

A new event ID code enables event-based analysis and match-ups with global crisis banks. Records carry nameless victim records, event places, and death details, coded with matched methods for cross-region match-ups, though gaps vary by area. The authors present the open, scalable bank as a basis for tracking flood-death trends and aiming at stopping deaths under changing climate risk.
pmc-13591183:
Taychapat Makkong and David Brienza review, in 2026, tools that gauge the risk of falls on stairs for older adults. Stair falls cause harsh harm, from broken bones to head injury, yet most fall checks test flat ground balance and miss stair skills. The pair searched four databases through October 2025. From hundreds of records, 10 studies with 1,778 people met their bar.

Most tools were timed stair tests done in person, plus one scored watch based tool and some self rating scales. Trustworthiness and link to real stair skill held up best, while power to predict future falls stayed thin. Makkong and Brienza advise using stair tools as one part of a wider fall check, not as a stand alone verdict.
pmc-13592083:
Sabin Aryal, Yiteng Tang, and Liangfeng Sun report a strikingly strong Raman signal from flat lead sulfide sheets at room temperature. Raman scattering reads lattice vibrations, and in tiny quantum dots the signal usually stays faint unless surfaces oxidize. Their two dimensional sheets, grown in solution, outshone dot samples by orders of magnitude without any such help.

Two effects team up in the sheets, the authors argue. Vibrations stay in step across the wide flat lattice, and a step like spread of energy states boosts coupling between light born charges and those vibrations. As porous dot networks merge into smooth sheets, the peak sharpens and swells. Aryal and the team frame the effect as a clean probe of lattice motion in flat quantum materials.
pmc-13592483:
Francesco Misirocchi and six colleagues study, in 2026, hidden seizures in emergency care: status epilepticus without convulsions, which is easy to mistake for stroke or confusion. Their single center study held 74 adults diagnosed by brain wave testing in the emergency department. Half failed to return to their prior state by discharge, and about one in five died in hospital. Treatment times were clocked from arrival.

Median waits ran past three hours for both calming drugs and seizure medicines. Each extra hour to seizure medicine raised the odds of a poor recovery, and underdosed medicine tripled those odds. Calming drug dose showed no such tie, and nothing predicted death. Misirocchi and the team urge fast brain wave pathways and full first doses.
pmc-13592583:
Yu Wen and six colleagues study how moisture, cold, and rain shift the stability of waste rock dumps inside a cold region coal mine in Heilongjiang, China. Dump slopes are loose, man made piles whose strength swings with weather. Lab crushing and shearing tests ran at four moisture levels and three temperatures, feeding a three dimensional slope model. Field drainage data checked the model's calls.

Wetter material weakened sharply at room temperature, and the safety margin sagged. Frozen samples instead grew stiffer and stronger as pore ice glued grains, and rain barely dented their safety scores. Drainage pipes lifted safety margins notably in the unfrozen case. Wen and the team offer the combined lab, model, and field frame for cold mine dump control.
pmc-13592783:
Manuela Beatriz Velho leads a team linking birth care practices to exclusive breastfeeding when mothers leave hospital. Their cross sectional study covered 756 postpartum women at a Baby Friendly Hospital in Brazil, scored against a woman friendly care standard. Practices ranged from privacy and a calm room to skin to skin contact and hands on help with positioning the baby. Breastfeeding status at discharge was checked against each practice.

Eighty five percent of mothers left nursing exclusively. Privacy with a welcoming room, skin to skin contact, and positioning help each tracked with higher rates of the outcome. Cesarean birth, by contrast, tracked with lower rates. Velho and the team argue that respectful, low intervention birth care does double duty, protecting both the birth experience and early feeding.
pmc-13594683:
Calobrace and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how one fine breast implant face, etched at a four micron scale, steers the body's guard cells. Implant faces are classed as smooth or rough, but fine grain may rule the long game. A bad guard turn can scar the shell round an implant hard and tight. The review pools beast tests, shell reads, and clinic counts on this one face. Its grain sits far below the rough class and far past smooth.

The face drew fewer flare guard cells than smooth and rough kin. It drew more calm guard cells, the kind that call peace. Scar calls ran low, and shells grew thin yet springy, not thick and stiff. Clinic counts tied the face to low rates of hard scar squeeze. The authors say the guard turn can be tuned by face craft, to aid breast spare cuts.
pmc-13594783:
Go and co-authors issued a correction to their study of a Japanese medulloblastoma cohort. That is a group of patients with a childhood brain tumor. Subgroups were used to forecast outcomes with affordable diagnostic methods. The original article appeared in Brain Pathology in 2026, and the correction repairs a series of numbers in its figures and text.

One legend value was aligned with the main text, and the frequency of TP53 mutations was corrected to eight of sixty cases in one subgroup. A case count for classic tumors and a p-value for chromosome 11 loss were also set right. The most substantial fix repeated a survival analysis after removing fifteen cases. Their MYCN amplification status was actually unknown. With only the forty-five evaluable cases, the link between MYCN amplification and poorer outlook stayed significant. Every conclusion of the study remains unchanged, the authors state.
pmc-13594983:
David Etoori and a team of co-authors estimated how many deaths from liver cancer and decompensated cirrhosis in England are attributable to viral hepatitis. That figure is needed to prove progress toward elimination targets. Six hospital trusts reviewed the records of 563 people flagged in routine data as dying with these conditions up to the end of 2023.

Review confirmed most of the liver cancer cases but only about a third of the flagged cirrhosis cases. Applying the resulting fractions, hepatitis C accounted for roughly eighteen percent of the liver cancer burden. Hepatitis B accounted for about six percent. Both viruses explained only a small slice of cirrhosis deaths. Converted to population rates, the figures sat comfortably below the World Health Organization's impact ceiling, matching what linked surveillance data show and supporting England's claim to be meeting the target.
pmc-13595383:
Samuel F. Lopez and co-authors dissected mercury chemistry in two duck species hunted at Utah's Great Salt Lake, where waterfowl carry high mercury loads. Their 2026 study measured mercury forms and isotope signatures in brain, breast muscle, liver, and kidney from northern shovelers and cinnamon teal, using advanced X-ray spectroscopy.

Both species were breaking the toxic form, methylmercury, down inside their bodies, storing the residue bound to sulfur and selenium compounds. The share remaining as methylmercury fell from brain to muscle to kidney to liver. Shovelers held far more mercury in the liver yet had detoxified a larger share of it than teal, showing species differ in handling the metal. Because total mercury no longer mirrors the toxic form, the authors say consumption advisories built on totals alone can mislead hunters.
pmc-13596783:
Sarah Alexandra Marshall and co-authors interviewed thirty-one stakeholders about a proposed intervention. The intervention uses universal basic income to open up healthcare access in a southern American state. Stakeholders included Black men with low incomes and chronic illness. Their study sorted pre-implementation concerns through a socioecological lens, from the individual to the institution.

Five themes emerged. The men typically delay care until problems are severe. Incarceration and poverty strain the relationships they would lean on. Correctional and healthcare systems are not built to help them. Community-level barriers stack up, from transport to cost. Racism and poverty intertwine as entrenched obstacles. The authors conclude that an income-based intervention must act on all these levels at once to be equitable. They also concede a limit. Structural racism and generational poverty may exceed what any single program can fix.
pmc-13597583:
A. Taheri Amin leads a thirty-two-author expert panel. The panel used a Delphi process, three rounds of structured voting, to set recommendations. The recommendations cover genicular artery embolization. That knee pain procedure blocks small arteries feeding an arthritic joint. Twenty-nine interventional radiologists scored seventy-five statements, with consensus defined in advance in their 2026 report.

The panel agreed the procedure suits patients whose knee pain from arthritis, tendon problems, or past surgery has resisted conservative care for at least three months. It also suits those with repeated bleeding into the joint. Assessment should pair standardized scores and examination with plain X-rays, and MRI is optional. Technique guidance covers access route and embolizing every artery showing abnormal blush, with no proven winner between temporary and permanent particles. Structured long-term follow-up and definitions of success anchored in what patients can feel also won consensus.
pmc-13599183:
Ching-I Huang and colleagues modelled Uganda's path to eliminating gambiense sleeping sickness transmission. Uganda cut reported cases from 948 in 2000 to zero local cases since 2020, yet confirming elimination and sustaining gains needs numbers. Their 2026 study fitted several mechanistic transmission models to seven districts reporting cases from 2000 to 2022, then weighed the models to price future strategies.

Models put the last transmission event in or before 2021 with over 95 percent certainty. The 2019 local case may have been the last, with only about a 1 percent chance of cases after 2025. Since transmission stays low under every plan, the cheapest sound path is Stop 2026: passive screening only, with reactive screening and vector control if cases appear, costing about 193,000 dollars to 2040. Huang and colleagues recommend Stop 2026 in all seven districts.
pmc-13601483:
Lindsay M Reynolds and three colleagues report a 2026 pilot study on whether aging clocks fit into diet trials. Geroscience aims to slow aging biology itself. DNA-based measures can estimate biological age and pace of aging, yet few diet studies have tested whether such measures are practical to collect. The team ran a four-week trial in 34 adults aged 48 to 81 who had metabolic syndrome.

Participants ate an ounce of tree nuts and two tablespoons of olive oil daily. Adherence topped 95 percent, and most would join a longer one. At the start, every participant aged faster than average on the DunedinPACE measure, supporting metabolic syndrome as a target group. Participants wanted to learn their biological age, and said proof of slower aging would motivate lasting change. Four weeks brought no measurable shift in the aging markers. The approach is feasible and engaging, the authors conclude, with design lessons for longer trials.
pmc-13612883:
Van Weelderen and colleagues published a 2026 review on stopping unneeded medicines near life's end. People with palliative needs often keep taking drugs that no longer help. Primary care teams struggle to cut those medicines in daily practice. The team gathered 23 studies on what helps or blocks such cuts.

Four themes shaped whether deprescribing, the planned cutting of drugs, happened. Views and skills formed the starting stance of patients and staff. Talks then weighed each drug for the person, with shared decisions. Clinic routines and teamwork decided whether talks happened at all. Wider care culture framed everything, favoring prescribing over cutting by default. The authors ask for a cultural shift toward cutting as routine.
pmc-13614283:
Lim and colleagues reported in 2026 on a diffraction grating, a surface that splits light by its slit spacing, whose spacing can be switched with electric fields. The device holds carbon black nanoparticles, tiny dark particles, in a fluid between a flat top electrode and a patterned bottom one. Vertical fields move the particles up or down, which changes whether the open slits act wide or narrow and so steers the diffracted light.

Lim found the device kept both slit states with no field applied once the fluid mix was thickened, a trait called bistability. It worked across a wide heat range, from well below freezing to at least the boiling point of water. Its action also did not depend on the light's polarisation, the direction of its wave swing. The authors see strong promise for advanced light-control devices such as tunable optics and displays.
pmc-13614983:
Isaiah Luc, Drew Carter, and Tracy Merlin analyse in 2026 a new Australian deal for cancer immunotherapy drugs that treat many kinds of cancer under one listing. Normally each use of such a drug is judged and priced on its own, which slows access and stacks up reviews. In 2025 the national advisory committee placed three drugs, nivolumab, ipilimumab, and pembrolizumab, under a single broad listing for advanced cancers, with one weighted-average price and rebate caps tied to use.

The authors weigh what this means for fairness, budgets, and clinic practice. A broad listing can speed patient access, cut review workload, and block price gaming between uses. Risks remain around paying fairly for uses of very different value. Other countries wrestling with multi-use medicines can learn from how Australia struck the balance.
pmc-13615083:
Martin Kaňa and colleagues review in 2026 the hard task of repeat surgery for vestibular schwannoma, a benign tumour on the balance nerve, after earlier surgery or focused radiation has failed. At one high-volume centre, 19 patients had such revision surgery between 1998 and 2025, a small 2.6 percent of all 741 tumour cases treated there. Most tumours were large, at the most advanced grade in 74 percent of cases.

Surgeons removed the whole tumour in 79 percent of the revision cases. Right after surgery, 58 percent had complete facial nerve weakness, the study's main worry, though function improved with time. The authors weigh radical removal against the risk to the facial nerve and hearing. Their long record helps other centres counsel patients facing a second operation with no easy options.
pmc-13616283:
Daniele Callegari and colleagues build a self-healing separator for lithium batteries, the thin sheet that keeps a battery's two sides apart while letting ions pass. Standard separators tear easily and tolerate damage poorly, which can end in failure or fire. Their sheet starts from a polyethylene blend carrying special units that pair up through four hydrogen bonds, forming a network that can rejoin after damage.

Three versions with different densities of the healing units were blended with a second polymer that loves battery fluid, boosting ion flow. Sheets 35 to 40 micrometres thick were made by hot pressing, with no solvents. The looser, more mobile chains healed defects on their own and moved ions well. A separator that repairs itself could stretch battery life and cut a known safety risk at its root.
pmc-13616583:
Qui Minh Nguyen and colleagues present a 2026 case report of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy affecting both sides of the heart. Their patient was a 56-year-old man. He came in with odd, sharp chest pain shooting to his left arm, plus dangerous heart rhythms. This inherited disease replaces heart muscle with scar and fat, usually strikes the right ventricle first, and can kill young people without warning. His family history held artery disease and heart failure, but no known muscle disease or sudden deaths.

Standard ultrasound showed no abnormality in the right ventricle, which could have ended the search. Magnetic resonance imaging of the heart told the fuller story and secured the diagnosis. The case argues for advanced imaging when rhythms misbehave and the first scan looks clean, since this disease hides well and its first symptom can be fatal.
pmc-13618383:
Sherif Elmahgoub and two colleagues describe emergency abdominal surgery in a patient with advanced motor neurone disease, the progressive condition that weakens breathing and swallowing muscles and upsets body control. The patient needed an emergency laparotomy for small bowel obstruction, leaving no time for the fine-tuning that planned surgery allows. Anesthesia used a total intravenous technique with cautious use of muscle relaxants, to which such patients can be very sensitive.

The patient came off the ventilator afterward and the early course looked smooth. Progressive respiratory failure then developed against a background of ongoing abdominal disease. After team discussion and shared decision-making, care shifted to a comfort-focused approach. The authors draw the lesson plainly: emergency anesthesia in advanced motor neurone disease can be technically successful yet fail to change the overall prognosis. Realistic planning toward the patient's goals should start early.
pmc-13619683:
Michal Dory, Sebastian Forster, Yasamin Nazari, and Tijn de Vos work on a hard problem in graph algorithms: keeping shortest-path estimates current while edges are deleted one by one. Exact answers for every pair of points are too slow for huge networks, so researchers accept near answers that run faster. The question is how much accuracy must be traded for speed.

The team presents four new algorithms, two for weighted graphs and two for unweighted ones, each with its own balance of stretch and total update time. Their bounds improve on earlier tradeoffs in the ranges they target. Readers get formulas stating how the running time grows with the number of nodes and edges, together with proofs that the stated accuracy holds. The work is theoretical, aimed at algorithm designers who maintain routes on changing networks.
pmc-13620283:
Yanping Yang and thirteen colleagues traced an immune chain reaction that strips synapses from newborn brains after oxygen loss at birth. In a rat model of this injury, mast cells in the hippocampus grew more numerous and released more tryptase, an enzyme that can switch on a receptor called PAR-2. That receptor sits on microglia, the brain's cleanup cells.

Once switched on, the microglia tagged and swallowed synaptic material at a harmful rate, and signaling through two stress pathways rose. Silencing the receptor gene in microglia calmed the pathway and cut the swallowing. Two blocking drugs did the same job, and one of them preserved the tiny spines where synapses sit and rescued the animals' later memory in maze tests. Parallel cell experiments confirmed tryptase alone could drive the effect. The authors name mast cell tryptase as an upstream trigger worth targeting.
pmc-13621883:
Aishwarya Pantula and four co-authors survey how brain organoids, small balls of brain-like tissue grown from stem cells, might grow from simple models into working research platforms. Organoids mimic early brain growth and let scientists study development and disease, yet they stall at an early stage. Poor blood supply, dead centres, and weak wiring hold them back.

The authors bring together several fixes now in progress. Tiny fluid channels and printed scaffolds can feed tissue and shape it, while better imaging and electrical recording let teams watch activity inside. Artificial intelligence tools help read the large data sets these systems produce, and shared standards could make results easier to repeat. Ethics rules also need to keep pace, since more brain-like tissue raises new questions. The piece maps what must improve before organoids can serve drug testing and disease research well.
pmc-13623383:
Rui An and a large team investigate a fat-handling protein called FABP5 in hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer. The protein was suspected of helping tumours hide from the immune system, which would make it a drug target. The study mixes public cancer data, single-cell analysis, cell experiments, and computer drug screening.

FABP5 levels ran high in liver tumours and marked worse survival, and the protein sat in support cells and immune cells called macrophages inside tumours. Silencing it in cancer cells slowed growth and movement.
