Tumours rich in the protein showed more immune entry yet more immune brakes, including higher PD-L1, a shield molecule tumours use against attack. Follow-up tests confirmed the protein raises that shield through an inflammatory pathway. A screened compound, CZS-241, bound the protein stably in simulations, and the authors propose it as a lead for drug development.
pmc-13624383:
Kyaw Linn and colleagues present a case series of four children in Yangon, Myanmar, whose speech delays turned out to hide hearing loss. Myanmar has no routine newborn hearing screening, so losses surface late, and their signs, inattention, poor speech, and odd behaviour, easily mimic autism or attention disorders. All four children, aged five to seven, had been referred for those concerns.

Hearing tests alongside developmental assessment found a different picture per child. One had moderate loss in both ears; another, first suspected of attention-deficit disorder, had severe-to-profound loss; a third, a child with autism, had a one-sided loss. In some children the hearing loss explained the referral; in others it rode alongside a developmental condition and worsened difficulties. None had been screened as infants. The authors urge that every child with speech delay receive hearing assessment as a routine step.
pmc-13625283:
Ben Sindayigaya and colleagues measured undernutrition among women living with HIV of child-bearing age in Rwanda's Mahama refugee camp. Despite food rations and free care, poor nutrition still threatens women in crises. Their snapshot study surveyed 170 women chosen at random, judging undernutrition by body-mass index and arm girth.

One-quarter were undernourished, including about 4 percent very thin. Most earned below the poverty line, and many relied on loan-shark credit. Only schooling counted in stats: women with no formal or only primary schooling faced about triple the odds of poor nutrition. The authors urge schooling-linked feeding support in camps.
pmc-13627183:
Melih M Bakacak and four colleagues ask whether antibiotics after closing a hole between mouth and sinus actually prevent trouble. Pulling an upper back tooth can open such a passage, and unclosed holes invite sinus infection, yet practice on antibiotics varies. Reviewing Amsterdam records from 2000 to 2025, the team studied 505 closures and compared patients who did or did not receive antibiotics afterward.

About half got the drugs. Complications struck roughly one patient in nine overall, and the antibiotic group fared significantly better on total and infectious complications and on holes that stayed open. Roughly seven patients needed treatment for one to benefit. Autoimmune disease and a clotting aid placed in the socket raised risk instead, which helps surgeons aim antibiotics at the patients likeliest to gain.
pmc-13630583:
Leila Regina de Castro and five colleagues compared ageing in Brazilian adults with mild or moderate intellectual disabilities, asking whether those with Down syndrome decline faster. Published in 2026, the cross-sectional study assessed fifty-two adults in São Paulo, twenty-four with Down syndrome and twenty-eight with other causes, across function, physical performance, nutrition, and cognition.

The Down syndrome group scored significantly worse on learning and remote memory, with near-significant trends toward weaker grip and more falls. Sex and degree of disability shaped several outcomes, while age itself showed no clear effect in this sample. The authors read the profile as greater vulnerability to age-related decline, while cautioning that the small, one-moment design needs confirmation in larger, longer studies.
pmc-13638983:
Mingcheng Zhu and six colleagues report a 2026 artificial intelligence system designed to diagnose skin cancer more fairly across genders. Earlier fairness work focused on skin tone, while gender bias in skin image models had received little attention.

Their algorithm, LesionAttn, steers the model's attention toward the lesion itself, much as a clinician would focus on the spot rather than surrounding features. Tested on two large image collections, it cut gender bias while keeping accuracy high, beating other bias-reduction methods. The authors present attention guidance as a practical route toward diagnostic tools that serve patients more evenly.
pmc-13639683:
Hironori Tsujimoto and eleven colleagues describe a 2026 surgical technique for closing the entry hole in robotic esophagojejunostomy, the connection made between esophagus and small bowel after stomach removal for cancer. Leaks or narrowing at that joint can delay recovery and further treatment.

In ten consecutive patients, the surgeons closed the hole from its midpoint outward in both directions with a bidirectional barbed suture that needs no final knot. Closure took about sixteen minutes on average, and no patient suffered a leak, narrowing, or related complication. The team presents the method as feasible and safe in this first experience.
pmc-13641883:
Jon P. Evans and four colleagues present a 2026 study on scoring patient questionnaires in shoulder surgery trials. Scores such as the Oxford Shoulder Score are usually summed in the traditional way, which treats every question as equal and measurement error as uniform.

The team rescored patient-level data from two large United Kingdom trials, UK FROST with 503 patients and PROFHER with 250. Modern item response scores and simulated adaptive testing gave nearly identical treatment effects and conclusions. Adaptive testing cut the median questionnaire to four or five items at early follow-up. The authors see lower burden for patients without loss of meaning.
pmc-13642483:
Joong Hyun Pyo and three colleagues present a 2026 photonics paper on designing guided-mode resonance devices without trial and error. Such devices shape light spectra for filters, sensors, and lasers, yet their key traits, center frequency, band width, and line sharpness, usually shift together when geometry changes.

The team proposes a compound unit cell with two ridges and derives a compact map linking geometry to those traits directly. The map allowed fully independent control of several resonance measures at once. It also shows how exotic spectral features, including Fermi arcs and exceptional points, arise in these structures, giving designers a deterministic route to target performance.
pmc-13645783:
Lucia A Leone and four colleagues run a randomized study comparing three free food prescription programs for older adults who struggle to get fresh produce. Sixty-seven patients aged sixty-five and older from hospital clinics were assigned for twelve weeks to a delivered produce box, a delivered meal kit, or a mobile market voucher, the control option. Weekly phone or text surveys tracked whether people used their prescriptions.

Enrollment rates were similar across the three programs. Delivered programs far outperformed the voucher on use: people in both delivery groups redeemed about nine tenths of their offer, against under a third for the mobile market group. Meal kits did not raise produce use beyond the plain box. The authors conclude that home delivery itself, more than recipe extras, drives whether food prescriptions reach older adults' tables.
pmc-13645883:
Kazuya Miyaguchi and four colleagues report, in 2026, the case of a nineteen-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis who developed a liver abscess while on a standard immune drug. She first had lasting fever, worsening diarrhea, and bleeding, then pain under her right ribs. Scans showed active bowel inflammation together with the abscess, a rare and dangerous complication. The bowel drug was stopped, and strong antibiotics were started.

Once tests confirmed the infection was controlled and the abscess was shrinking, doctors began a newer bowel drug called mirikizumab, which targets a narrower immune signal. Her symptoms eased quickly, and she reached lasting remission of both bowel symptoms and scope findings, with no return of the abscess over long follow-up. The authors suggest this drug can be a workable restart option after deep infection, while calling for larger studies to confirm the safest choice.
pmc-13646283:
Weiwei Zheng and eleven colleagues assemble the first complete genome of the stone flounder, a flatfish of growing commercial value in East Asia. No genome for this fish existed before, which held back genetics and breeding work. The team combined four sequencing technologies to read the genome end to end without gaps. The finished assembly spans about five hundred eighty-eight million letters and sorts onto twenty-four chromosomes.

Nearly all of the sequence landed on chromosomes, and end caps called telomeres were found on most chromosome tips. The team catalogued more than twenty-two thousand protein-coding genes and annotated nearly all of them with likely functions. Quality checks rated the assembly highly complete. Because the fish tolerates cold and wide salt ranges and sells well, the authors expect the genome to speed selective breeding and evolutionary comparisons with other flatfish.
pmc-13648483:
Kaiyuan Hao and eleven colleagues uncover a circuit that keeps self-reactive killer T cells active in autoimmune hepatitis, a disease where the immune system attacks the liver. Persistent T cells usually exhaust, yet in this mouse model they stayed functional despite constant exposure to self material.

Mice lacking two protective genes developed progressive liver inflammation driven by self-DNA sensing. Inside the liver, stem-like progenitor T cells continually replenished exhausted-looking but effective descendants, and nearby inflammatory macrophages supplied a signal called IL-27 that sustained them. Blocking that signal shrank the T cell pool and weakened its function. The findings identify a local maintenance loop that could become a treatment target.
pmc-13649283:
Alexander Muacevic and six colleagues report a rare blood infection by Robinsoniella germs in a woman aged 49. She had past colon and anal cancer, treated with radiation and chemo. The germs are hardy gut dwellers that form spores and shun air. Labs miss them with ease, so true counts are likely low.

She came in with fever, hard breathing, and worse loose stools. Blood tests grew Robinsoniella plus two more gut germs, a hint the source was her radiation-hurt bowel. Drug care was swapped in steps and settled on ertapenem. No set cure exists for this germ. The authors warn it can strike hard in people with weak immune shields and gut disease.
pmc-13649583:
Semiha Zeynep Özsaydı and five colleagues tested whether the world body mass cut-off for obesity fits Turkish adults, in a study published in 2026. The team measured height, weight, and body fat in adults aged 18 to 65 across four districts of Kayseri.

Body mass tracked body fat closely in both sexes, more so in women. The best cut-off for spotting true obesity by fat share sat below the global line of 30, at just under 29 for women and men alike. Using that line raised the obesity share in their sample from about 28 percent to about 34 percent. The authors back national, sex-aware thresholds for fairer counts and care.
pmc-13649783:
Haoyue Huangfu and eight colleagues hunted for the rodent species that host the most viruses on Hainan Island, China, in a study published in 2026. Rodents make up over two fifths of mammal species and seed many human diseases. The team trapped 2,550 animals across 18 counties in 2023 and 2024 and pooled gut samples from a chosen subset.

The scan found more than five hundred viral RNA types and near-complete genomes for a third of them. Two rat species alone held over four fifths of all virus types, most new finds, and most viruses shared across species. Of 13 viruses known to harm humans, 12 turned up in those two rats. The authors name them hub hosts worth close watch.
pmc-3441783:
Teixeira, Carraca, Markland, and co-authors review exercise research in a planned way through the lens of self-determination theory. Motivation is a critical factor in keeping exercise going over time. Sustained activity, in turn, is linked to important health outcomes.

Research using this theory of motivation had grown sharply in recent years. The review gathers that work to ask which forms of motivation best predict lasting activity. Its answer favours enjoyment and personal value over pressure and guilt. Programme designers use those findings to build exercise schemes people stick with.  Enjoyment-based programmes retained participants longer than those built on external rewards alone.
pmc-3701683:
Xia, Wang, and He present BrainNet Viewer, a network visualisation tool for human brain connectomics. The brain is a complex system, and its organisation can be represented as a network of connected regions. Studies had shown that such connectomes can be built from various brain imaging technologies.

Sophisticated analytic methods can then characterise those networks, but researchers still need clear pictures to grasp them. BrainNet Viewer renders brain networks in three dimensions, showing nodes and connections together. Visual tools like it help neuroscientists share and compare findings about brain wiring.
pmc-3789683:
Chaimani, Higgins, Mavridis, and co-authors present graphical tools for network meta-analysis in the STATA statistics package. Network meta-analysis synthesises direct and indirect evidence across trials that compare multiple treatments. It has the potential to rank competing treatments for a given outcome.

Despite its usefulness, the approach is often criticised, partly because results are hard to display and check. Their graphs show the network of comparisons and where evidence is strong or thin. Clearer pictures help readers judge whether treatment rankings rest on solid ground.  Forest-style plots in the paper show how indirect evidence shifts treatment rankings.
pmc-5210583:
Forbes, Beare, Boutselakis, and their co-authors updated COSMIC in 2016. COSMIC catalogues the somatic mutations found in human cancer at fine detail, letting users explore targets and trends in cancer genetics. It was already the widest store of cancer mutations anywhere.

Expert curators build its content from published studies and large cancer genome projects. Users can trace which mutations recur in each cancer type and how often. Recurrent mutations point to genes that drive cancer growth. Oncologists and researchers use that knowledge to classify tumors, choose targeted drugs, and design new studies of cancer genetics.
pmc-5605883:
The GBD 2016 Causes of Death Collaborators reported in 2017 on mortality by cause worldwide. Tracking who dies early, and whether those rates rise or fall, is key to cutting premature death. The study behind the report, GBD 2016, assesses deaths by cause in full for this purpose.

The analysis covers cause-specific mortality for hundreds of causes in nearly two hundred locations, by age and sex, from 1980 to 2016. It reveals which causes retreat, such as many infections, and which advance, such as dementias. Governments and funders use these trends to judge whether health programs work. The dataset is the reference scoreboard for global mortality.
pmc-6252083:
The GBD 2017 DALYs and HALE Collaborators published this disability analysis in 2018. It measures not just how long people live, but how much of that life is spent in poor health. Those patterns shape policy, planning, and care services.

The study reports disability-adjusted life years for a long list of diseases and injuries across most countries. Back pain, headache, and depression rank among the top causes of years lived unwell. As deaths fall, nonfatal burdens take a larger share. The findings argue for health systems built for chronic care, not only for saving lives.
pmc-6425583:
Alexander Wolf, Fiona Hamey, Mireya Plass, and coauthors introduced PAGA for single-cell data in 2019. Single-cell RNA data hold both distinct cell types and smooth transitions between them. Older methods forced a choice between grouping cells and ordering them along paths.

PAGA builds a graph that shows how cell groups connect, keeping the overall shape of the data. That map can then guide detailed trajectory fitting within each branch. The result reads like a subway map of cell development. Analysts use it to reconcile cluster labels with the continuous nature of real differentiation.
pmc-7689983:
Hyuk Sung Kwon and Seong-Ho Koh reviewed in 2020 how inflammation inside the brain drives diseases that slowly destroy nerve cells. Such neuroinflammation accompanies conditions including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Two kinds of support cells, microglia and astrocytes, act as the main controllers of inflammation in the central nervous system.

The authors explain how these cells normally protect neurons, and how their activation can turn harmful and feed the disease process. They survey the signals that pass between the two cell types and the rest of the brain. Understanding this switch from defense to damage is central to the search for treatments that slow these diseases rather than merely easing their symptoms.
pmc-7778883:
Ivica Letunic, Supriya Khedkar, and Peer Bork reported in 2020 the latest state of SMART, a web tool for studying the building blocks of proteins. Proteins are assembled from domains, reusable parts that each carry a function. SMART lets researchers identify those domains in a protein and map how they are arranged along it.

The update describes new additions and the status of the resource, whose ninth version holds carefully curated models for well over a thousand protein domains. The authors explain how the models are built and checked by hand. Resources like SMART turn a raw protein sequence into a readable plan, which is often the first step in guessing what an unknown protein does.
pmc-8689983:
Marc Gillespie and colleagues described the 2022 state of the Reactome pathway knowledgebase, a free resource that maps the chemical reactions of human biology. Reactome records, in expert checked detail, how molecules interact across a wide range of normal and disease processes. It covers inherited conditions as well as illnesses acquired through life.

The article reports the growth of the database and the tools for exploring it, from pathway diagrams to analysis of a user's own data. Every pathway is curated by hand from the published literature, which keeps the detail trustworthy. Biologists consult Reactome when they need to know not just which genes changed, but which chain of reactions those changes belong to.
pmc-8728283:
Fiona Cunningham and colleagues presented Ensembl 2022, the annual report of a genome resource now serving all eukaryotic life, not only vertebrates. Ensembl annotates genomes, marking genes, regulatory regions, and variation, and it is built to deliver that annotation at very large scale. For key species such as humans and farm animals, the annotation runs especially deep.

The article describes recent growth in species coverage, data types, and access routes, including rapid release tracks for new genomes. It also explains the infrastructure that keeps the service flexible for very different kinds of users. Ensembl's yearly reports double as a census of how far genome annotation has spread across the tree of life.
pmc-9034083:
Kai Hou and co-authors reviewed in 2022 the roles of the microbiota, the communities of microbes living on and in the body, in health and disease. Since microbes were first linked to wellbeing, study after study has widened their importance. The authors sort these communities by where they live: gut, mouth, airways, and skin.

Each community lives in a working partnership with its host, and each can fall out of balance in characteristic ways. The review describes what each community does when healthy and the diseases tied to its disruption. It gives readers one map of a body-wide system that medicine increasingly treats as an organ in its own right.
proctor-great-pyramid-1883:
Richard Proctor pushed back at stone mystics in The Great Pyramid: Observatory, Tomb, and Temple, out in 1883. Proctor was a famed voice on the stars for the crowd. He grants the heap is a tomb and a gauge of the stars. He denies it holds codes of fate or a god given inch.

Clear sums and star lore fill his case. He treats Smyth's claims with wit and some scorn. The book is the chief cool reply of its age. All who write on the heap since must pass through its claims.
questioni-filosofiche-sociali-mediche-e-: Questioni filosofiche is an Italian work of philosophical, social, medical, and medico-legal questions whose first pages are garbled beyond reading in the scan. The legible matter is a bookplate of the Historical Library of the Harvey Cushing and John Hay Whitney Medical Library at Yale University, recording a gift of George Mora, M.D. No author, argument, or printing detail can be recovered from pages this broken.
ramusio-navigationi-et-viaggi-vol-1-1583:
Giovanni Battista Ramusio, a Venetian official, assembled Delle Navigationi et Viaggi between 1550 and 1559. Volume one here follows the Venetian Giunti printing of 1583, in Italian. Ramusio gathered reports of voyages from travelers and envoys, many printed in full for the first time in his pages.

His collection became the first great voyage book of the modern age, the model Hakluyt and Purchas later followed in England. Its first volume gave Marco Polo's travels their first complete printed home. African and Asian voyages stand beside that famous text. For readers of exploration, Ramusio is where the printed record of the wider world truly begins.
ramusio-navigationi-et-viaggi-vol-2-1583:
Volume two of Giovanni Battista Ramusio's Delle Navigationi et Viaggi follows the Venetian Giunti printing of 1583. The Italian collection first appeared from 1550 to 1559, built by a Venetian secretary with access to reports from every trading sea. Ramusio printed whole travel accounts that had lived only in manuscript.

The set as a whole earned its rank as the first great voyage collection, ahead of Hakluyt and Purchas. Its pages carried Marco Polo's complete text into print and spread the voyages to Africa and Asia. Volume two keeps that breadth, in the Italian of the Giunti house. Together the three volumes mapped the world as the 1500s came to know it.
sbe-23-zend-avesta-2-1883:
Book Twenty-Three of the Sacred Books of the East is the same ground as Part Two of the Zend-Avesta. James Darmesteter made the English dress, and it came out in 1883. The Zend-Avesta holds the old texts of the faith of Persia. This part holds hymns and prayers, not law or rite rules.

The Sirozah texts name the divine guards of each day of the month. The Yashts are hymns to beings such as Mithra and Anahita. The Nyayish are short prayers to the sun, moon, and fire. The book is the hymn book of the old faith in English dress.
schiller-fiesco-1783:
Fiesco, Schiller's second play, appeared in 1783 and reached English in the Bohn Standard Library translation. The scene is Genoa in 1547, where Count Fiesco plots to overthrow the ruling Doria family. Schiller frames the plot as a republican tragedy about ambition and freedom.

Fiesco hides his design behind pleasure and charm while allies gather in secret. His wife Leonore loves a man she cannot fully know or trust. Plots cross plots until the night of the rising arrives. Schiller, still in his early twenties, was learning to build history into drama. The play shows his lasting theme: how power tempts even those who claim to serve liberty.
scientific-american-supplement-no-384-ma: A locomotive for the St. Gothard Railway leads Supplement No. 384, dated New York, May 12, 1883, in Volume XV. The Mersey Railway Tunnel and a dam across the Ottawa River with a new canal at Carillon, Quebec, shown with figures and map, follow. An architecture section gives William Hennan's hints on building dwelling houses. They cover damp courses, dry walls and roofs, heating, lighting, refuse, cesspools, and drainage. A house at Heaton and a mansard roof dwelling follow.
scientific-american-supplement-no-385-ma: Fishes of Cuban waters open the natural history contents of Supplement No. 385, dated New York, May 19, 1883, in Volume XV. A Panax Victoriae, a note on sap by Professor Attfield, the crow, the praying mantis and its allies, and may flies follow, several with illustrations. A technology section lists a quick way to ascertain the focus of a lens and A. J. Hipkins on the history of the pianoforte.
scientific-american-supplement-no-388-ju: Farcot's improved Woolf compound engine, in four figures, leads Supplement No. 388, dated New York, June 9, 1883, in Volume XV. The Swallow, a new vehicle, boring an oil well, a cement reservoir in two figures, and a piece headed Flying complete the engineering list shown. A technology section opens with Barnard Samuelson on iron and steel.
scientific-american-supplement-no-392-ju: Volume XVI, Number 392, dated New York, July 7, 1883, opens with an improved dynamo machine in eight figures. An improved manganese battery by George Leuchs and Professor D. E. Hughes on the cause of evident magnetism in iron, steel, and other magnetic metals follow, with heads on neutrality, superposed magnetism, and the elastic nature of the ether. Engineering then gives the Westinghouse brake in two figures and B. F.
scientific-american-supplement-no-401-se: Chemistry leads Supplement No. 401, dated New York, September 8, 1883, in Volume XVI, with the different modifications of silver bromide and silver chloride. Analysis of New Zealand coal, determination of manganese in steel, cast iron, and ferro-manganese, manganese and its uses, and ozokerite or earth-wax follow. William L. Lay's paper on ozokerite, read before the New York Academy of Sciences, shows the nature, sources, and applications of that product. A piece on the constitution of the natural fats closes the section.
scientific-american-supplement-no-415-de: Carbon in steel opens the chemistry contents of Supplement No. 415, dated New York, December 15, 1883, in Volume XVI. Heat made in forging follows. So do new studies on what alkaloids are made of, from a talk by Samuel P. Sadtler at a Philadelphia pharmacy college. Engineering lists a tool for taking starch from potatoes. It also lists E. J. Hallock's simple tool for drawing ellipses, and a new propeller engine by Professor Maccord, with many engravings.
scientific-american-supplement-no-417-de: A machine for making electric light carbons, in two figures, leads Supplement No. 417, dated New York, December 29, 1883, in Volume XVI. The earliest gas engine and the moving of large masses follow. One piece shows a belfry removed at Cresentino in 1776. Another shows winged bulls moved from Nineveh to Mosul in 1854. Walter R.
seeley-expansion-england-1883:
John Robert Seeley taught history at Cambridge and gave the lectures printed in 1883 as The Expansion of England. He told his students that British settlement overseas was the main story of English history. The book helped invent the idea later called Greater Britain.

Seeley argued that colonies in America, India, and Australia were not side shows but the heart of the national past. He urged readers to see those lands as one wider England across the seas. His lectures shaped how a generation of Britons thought about empire and duty. Its short, sharp argument reached far beyond the lecture hall and into public debate.
smith-use-and-abuse-freemasonry-1783:
Captain George Smith, an artillery officer and provincial grand master, published The Use and Abuse of Free-Masonry in London in 1783. Smith writes as an insider with a warning. His treatise distinguishes true Masonry from its false forms, criticizing lodges that had drifted into feasting, faction, or worse.

The critique is pivotal because it comes from within the Craft's own leadership. Smith calls for reform in the working of late eighteenth-century English lodges. His standards are discipline, charity, and knowledge of the ritual's meaning. Reform talk across the lodges took shape under his influence. The Use and Abuse remains the sharpest insider's diagnosis of what ailed Georgian Masonry, written by a man who wanted it healed.
sophocles-plays-whitelaw-1883:
Robert Whitelaw translated all seven surviving plays of Sophocles into English verse in 1883. Sophocles, the most honored tragedian of ancient Athens, wrote more than a hundred plays, of which these seven alone survive whole. Whitelaw's version was the standard Victorian verse rendering of them.

Oedipus the King hunts a murderer and finds himself, while Antigone buries her brother against a king's decree. Ajax, Electra, and the Trachiniae turn on honor, revenge, and a poisoned robe. Oedipus at Colonus gives the outcast a holy death, and Philoctetes strands a wounded hero on an island. Campbell's prose Sophocles also sits in the library; Whitelaw supplies the verse counterpart.
spinoza-chief-works-elwes-vol-1-1883:
R H M Elwes published Volume 1 of The Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza in 1883, in the Bohn translation series. Spinoza, the Dutch lens grinder and philosopher, had been banned by his own synagogue for his views. Elwes's volume made his political and biblical writings standard reading in English.

The Tractatus Theologico-Politicus argues that scripture must be read historically and that the state should allow free thought. Spinoza there founded modern biblical criticism and made an early case for liberal politics. The unfinished Tractatus Politicus follows, on the forms of the state. Elwes added an introduction on Spinoza's life. The volume is the classic Victorian English Spinoza, still quoted today.
spr-proceedings-vol1-1882-1883:
Volume 1 of the Proceedings of the Society for Psychical Research appeared in 1883, covering work from 1882 and 1883. The society had just formed in London to study claims such as thought reading, ghosts, and trance states with care. Its members included scholars, scientists, and clergy.

Reports inside cover sittings, tests, and case reports, along with debate over how such claims should be checked. The writers tried to separate fraud and error from facts they could not yet explain. The volume marks the start of a long effort to study strange mental claims with records, witnesses, and repeat tests rather than rumor.
stepniak-underground-russia-1883:
Underground Russia was printed in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1883. This second edition gathers profiles and sketches from life by Stepniak. He was once editor of the paper Zemlia i Volia, or Land and Liberty. A preface by Peter Lavroff opens the volume, and the text reaches English readers in a version made from the Italian.

Lavroff's preface notes how the socialist and revolt-minded movement in Russia drew the notice of western Europe, and how books on it split between plain fact-telling and digging for causes. The sketches that follow give close, lived portraits of people inside that hidden movement, so readers abroad could meet the men and women behind the news.
stevenson-treasure-island-1883:
Robert Louis Stevenson published Treasure Island in 1883, a novel of pirates and buried gold. Young Jim Hawkins finds a treasure map in a dead sailor's chest. He sails on the Hispaniola with Dr. Livesey, Squire Trelawney, and a crew led in secret by Long John Silver. Silver, the ship's cook, plans a mutiny.

On the island, Jim must choose sides and act with courage beyond his years. Silver is charming, ruthless, and hard to pin down. Battles, escapes, and the hunt for the cache keep the pace fast. Stevenson set the pattern for almost every pirate tale since. The book still thrills new readers.
symonds-greek-ethics-1883:
John Addington Symonds wrote A Problem in Greek Ethics in 1883, printed privately for a small circle. Symonds was an English man of letters who studied Greek culture deeply. The essay asks how ancient Greece viewed love between men. He traces the custom from Homer and the gymnasium to Plato's dialogues.

Symonds argues that Greek love, at its best, joined physical desire to honor and education. He wrote against the harsh laws and silence of his own England. The essay was the first English apologia for Greek love of its kind. It circulated quietly and influenced later defenders of reform. Symonds printed only a handful of copies in his lifetime.
the-dominion-in-1983:
The Dominion in 1983, a thirty-page booklet first printed in 1883 under the pen name Ralph Centennius, looks back from a bright future. Its notes say the author's true name is unknown and that this copy was checked word by word against the first printing. Writing in the year of grace 1983, the narrator surveys a century of Canadian change.

From that perch, past struggles explain a rich, advanced Dominion. The tale counts as an early work of future-guessing in Canada. Odd spellings and rocket cars mark its age, and its pride in growth still reads clear.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
No. 557 of The Mirror, dated July 14, 1832, shows the birthplace of Bewick the engraver. The cottage stands at Cherryburn, near Ovingham on the Tyne's banks, roughly twelve miles west of Newcastle. Thomas Bewick, born there on August 12, 1753, revived the art of engraving on wood.

Bewick drew animals from childhood, covering village walls and doors with chalk sketches. Mr. Beilby, a Newcastle copper-plate engraver passing through Cherryburn, spotted the drawings and took the boy as his apprentice in 1767. A year later Bewick cut his first wood block, the diagrams for Dr. Button's Treatise on Navigation. The memoir stresses the industry that carried him from that cottage to fame in his craft.
the-trampling-of-the-lilies-pg2783: A second record of Rafael Sabatini's Trampling of the Lilies repeats the same contents list found in its sibling. The parts are called The Old Rule, The New Rule, and The Everlasting Rule. The chapters run the same from Monsieur the Secretary onward. Where the other listing runs into part three, this one breaks off at chapter fifteen, La Boulaye baits his hook. The shared matter is plain: identical titles and headings, no story text in either record. This is the shorter table of the same novel.
tob-10483:
Israel Abrahams wrote Judaism as a clear, compact introduction to the Jewish faith for the general reader. First published in the early 1900s, it explains rather than argues. Abrahams brought warmth and authority to a subject often described by outsiders with hostility or confusion in his time.

Chapters cover what Jews believe about God, how the Sabbath and festivals are kept, and how law shapes daily life at home and in synagogue. Prayer, charity, family life, and hope for the future all appear in plain terms. Readers new to Judaism get a doorway in, guided by a scholar describing his own tradition from inside.
tob-13583:
Sixty-six books, from Genesis to Revelation, make up the King James Bible, the English translation first published in 1611. King James ordered it, and teams of scholars worked from Hebrew and Greek texts. Their version held first place in English worship and letters for three hundred years.

Inside stand law, history, poetry, prophecy, the Gospels, and the letters of the early church. Its phrases passed into daily speech, from salt of the earth to a thorn in the flesh. Even readers who never open it for worship meet its language in law, song, and story. Few books have shaped a language so deeply.
tob-13783:
H. P. Blavatsky tried fiction in Nightmare Tales, a gathering of occult stories rather than doctrine. Haunted houses, possessed jewels, and karma working through lifetimes supply her plots. She wrote the tales to show Theosophical teachings in story form, letting reincarnation and hidden forces drive events instead of lectures.

The results are lurid, earnest, and, by V1 evidence, great fun. Blavatsky the storyteller is looser and stranger than Blavatsky the system builder, and the tales preserve the ghost-story atmosphere of the Victorian occult revival. Readers curious about the Theosophical movement's founder will find her imagination on display here, nightmares included, each with a moral worked into the machinery.
tob-14183:
R. H. Charles edited The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament for Oxford's Clarendon Press in 1913. Volume one holds the Apocrypha, books found in old Bibles but left out of the Hebrew canon. Named scholars wrote the introductions and notes.

Readers get Tobit, Judith, the Wisdom of Solomon, Ecclesiasticus, and the books of Maccabees, among others, in fresh English with full apparatus. For a century this volume stood as the standard English edition for study. It remains a base reference for anyone reading the books that stand at the edge of the Bible.
tob-14483:
Wilhelm Reich, then a young psychoanalyst in Freud's Vienna circle, wrote The Impulsive Character as one of his first books. It studies patients who act on sudden drives they cannot govern. The work predates the orgone theories that later made Reich notorious.

Reich describes the impulsive personality's urges, its weak defenses against them, and the guilt and chaos that follow each outbreak. He asks how analysis can treat such patients, whose trouble lies in character, not single symptoms. The study belongs to his character-analysis period, the phase of his work that later therapists most respected.
tob-4083:
W. B. Yeats's Poems gathers his early work, before the tower, the winding stair, and the great public poems of his later career. The Lake Isle of Innisfree, his most beloved lyric, imagines peace in a small cabin by a lakeshore, bean rows and a hive for the honeybee included. Faery courts, wandering Aengus, and Celtic twilight fill the surrounding pages.

Written in the dreamy, musical manner of the 1890s, the poems also carry the first stirrings of Yeats's occult symbolism and Irish nationalism. Readers meeting Yeats here see the foundation of modern English poetry's greatest career: a young Irishman inventing a mythology out of folklore, longing, and craft.
tob-4283:
Volume one of the Medici Society's Book of the Dead presents the Papyrus of Ani, the finest copy of Egypt's afterlife guide ever found. Ani was a royal scribe of Thebes. His papyrus, published in facsimile in 1913, joins hieroglyphic text, painted vignettes, and E. A. Wallis Budge's translation.

Ani and his wife pass the weighing of the heart, greet the gods of the underworld, and claim the fields of the blessed. The pictures carry half the meaning: jackal gods, feathered judges, green fields of grain. Verified public-domain text supports the entry. No other manuscript shows the Egyptian hope of eternity so completely.
tob-9283:
John B. Peterson surveyed the Apostolic Fathers for the Catholic Encyclopedia, in a compact reference article rather than a book. The Fathers are the church's first writers after the apostles: Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp, and the authors of the Didache and the Shepherd of Hermas.

Peterson sets out their dates, works, and doctrine in brief, so readers can place the early texts in order. The article serves as a map before the territory: who wrote, when, and why it matters. For students meeting the second-century church for the first time, the summary gives names and bearings in a few pages.
treaty-of-paris-1783:
Signed in Paris in 1783, the treaty ended the American Revolutionary War between the United States and Great Britain. Britain formally accepted that the thirteen colonies were now an independent nation. The new country's borders ran from the Atlantic coast to the Mississippi River, and from Canada down to Florida.

Inside, the terms cover fishing rights, debts owed on both sides, and the fair treatment of Americans who had stayed loyal to Britain. The text also promised that Britain would withdraw its troops without delay. It stands as the founding diplomatic act of the American republic, the moment independence became real on paper after eight years of war.
trevisanvs-de-chymico-miracvlo-qvod-lapi: Trevisanus on the chemical miracle called the philosopher's stone survives here through repeated ProQuest frames from the Wellcome Trust copy. The Latin title page names the work De Chymico Miraculo, quod Lapidem Philosophiae appellant. A companion piece by Dionysius Zacharias of France appears with it on the same page. The frames credit Early European Books and the Wellcome Trust, London. Only the copyright frames and the start of the title page are present here, so the alchemical text itself does not appear.
un-ga-res-1883:
Alarm over Southern Rhodesia runs through Resolution 1883, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 14 October 1963. The Assembly had studied the British colony, where a white minority regime held power under a constitution most of the people had no fair part in choosing. It recalls the 1960 call to end colonial rule and two past votes on the same land.

The text calls racial bias a breach of the Charter's core pledges, fit to be condemned wherever it occurs. It notes that the UN's decolonization team had flagged the worsening, explosive state of the territory to the Security Council. The record shows the Assembly pressing Britain, the ruling power, to hand power to the majority.
un-ga-res-a-69-83: Joint work with the Council of Europe fills Resolution A/69/83, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The two bodies first struck a deal in 1951, and the Council has sat as an observer at the Assembly since 1989. The text praises the Council's work for human rights, free rule, and the rule of law across Europe, through its norms, checks, and watch bodies. Its part in the growth of world law is noted as well.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1883 (XVIII), adopted on 14 October 1963, warned against handing power to the sitting government of Southern Rhodesia. The Assembly noted that that government rested on an unfair constitution most people opposed. It noted that giving it control of armed forces would make a tense situation worse.

Britain was invited not to pass any powers or marks of sovereignty to the colony as then governed. It was invited to wait for a government speaking for all the people. The text also asked Britain not to send armed forces and aircraft to the colony. It asked Britain to carry out the earlier Assembly resolutions on the question.

Resolution 69/83, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, covers cooperation between the United Nations and the Council of Europe. It calls for reinforced joint work on human rights, democracy and the rule of law. It recognizes the European Court of Human Rights as the key guarantor for the Council's 47 member states. It lists shared fields, from torture prevention, trafficking and children's rights to data protection, cybercrime and anti-corruption work.
un-sc-res-1383: This library holds Resolution 1383 as an official Council record, dated 2001 in its catalog. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1483:
Resolution 1483 is the Security Council's main Iraq decision from the weeks after Saddam Hussein's government fell in 2003. Adopted that May, it lifted the trade sanctions placed on Iraq during the 1990s. It also set the legal frame for the country under occupation.

Inside, the Council recognizes the United States and Britain as occupying powers with duties toward Iraqi civilians. It ends the old oil-for-food limits, calls for Iraqi oil money to fund rebuilding, and backs a UN role in forming a new government. Readers get the exact terms on which postwar Iraq was first organized.
un-sc-res-1583:
Lebanon's United Nations force was renewed by the Security Council on 28 January 2005. Tension and violence persisted along the Blue Line, the withdrawal line confirmed after Israel's pullout in 2000. Lebanon's government had asked on 11 January for six more months of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, UNIFIL. The Secretary-General's report of 20 January noted the risk of escalation.

The Council endorsed that report and extended UNIFIL's mandate to 31 July 2005. It restated its strong support for Lebanon's sovereignty and territorial integrity. The Lebanese government was called to extend its sole authority through the south, including by deploying its armed forces there. All parties had to give UNIFIL full freedom of movement and respect the Blue Line in its entirety. The Council condemned all acts of violence, including recent fire across the line that had killed and wounded United Nations staff.
un-sc-res-1683:
Liberia's own security forces gained narrow arms exemptions on 13 June 2006. The Council welcomed the leadership of the newly elected president, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, and her work to restore peace and harmony. Newly vetted Liberian forces needed to take over more security work. The arms embargo of resolution 1521 (2003) blocked their supply.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ruled that the embargo would not cover weapons already given to the Special Security Service for training with the sanctions committee's advance approval. Those arms could stay with the service for full operational use. Small supplies for vetted, trained police and security staff could also pass, case by case, with the committee's prior consent. Each grant needed a joint request from Liberia and the exporting state. Liberia then had to mark and register the weapons.
un-sc-res-1783: Security Council Resolution 1783 survives in official-record form in this collection, transcribed by English Wikisource. Resolutions are filed by number and cited by number, and 1783 is this act's permanent place. Within it, the members state their grounds and then their decision, in the sequence the Charter's practice has made standard.
un-sc-res-183:
Resolution 183 returns to the question of the territories under Portuguese rule, after the Secretary-General tried to open talks between Portugal and African states. The text was adopted on 11 December 1963, though the catalog record gives 1964. The contact failed to produce agreement on what self-determination means.

The Council regrets that failure and deprecates Portugal's refusal to comply with Resolution 180. It restates the meaning of self-determination from Assembly Resolution 1514: all peoples have the right to choose their political status freely and to pursue their own economic, social, and cultural growth. It also notes the territories' listing as Non-Self-Governing Territories.
un-sc-res-1883:
For another year, Resolution 1883 renewed the UN mission in Iraq in 2009. UNAMI's advisers were helping Iraqis run elections, settle disputes over internal borders, and bring refugees home. The Council judged that the work was unfinished and extended the mandate.

The text repeats the mission's tasks and asks for regular reports from the Secretary-General on security and progress. It also stresses that Iraq's government must protect UN staff so they can move around the country. Readers can trace, in these yearly renewals, how the UN's Iraq role shrank as the war wound down.
un-sc-res-283:
Namibia's isolation from South Africa was spelled out on 29 July 1970. The mandate had been ended by the General Assembly, and resolutions 264 (1969) and 276 (1970) declared South Africa's presence illegal. Pretoria still refused to withdraw its administration. Its courts and laws ran on in the territory against the territory's international status.

The Council asked all states to cut every tie with South Africa that implied recognition of its authority over Namibia. States with missions in South Africa had to declare formally that they did not recognize that authority. Consular posts covering Namibia were to be closed. State-owned companies had to halt all dealings and new investment in the territory. Governments were told to withhold loans and credits from firms working there and to discourage their nationals from investing in Namibia. The package aimed to starve the occupation of money and legitimacy at once.
un-sc-res-383:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was kept on during a hard winter on 13 December 1975. The Secretary-General's report of 8 December held that the force was still needed to hold the cease-fire. Talks between the two communities offered the best path, he said, but only if the negotiators came ready to bargain on every core issue. Both parties had agreed to six more months.

The Council restated resolution 186 (1964) and its texts 365 (1974) and 367 (1975). It called for their urgent and effective application. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint and to speed their cooperative work toward a settlement. The stationing of the force in Cyprus was extended for six months, to 15 June 1976. All parties were asked again to give the force their full cooperation. The Secretary-General would continue his good offices mission and report on the talks.
un-sc-res-83:
North Korea had ignored the order to pull back to the 38th parallel. Fighting in Korea raged on at the end of June 1950. On 27 June 1950 the Security Council found that urgent military measures were needed. North Korea had neither stopped fighting nor withdrawn. United Nations reports from Korea confirmed the defiance. The Council now moved from words to collective action.

It recommends that member states give South Korea the help needed to repel the attack. The goal was to restore peace and security in the area. The vote was seven to one, with Yugoslavia against. Two members did not take part, and the Soviet Union was absent. The text supplied the legal base for the United Nations Command in Korea.
un-sc-res-983:
The Macedonia mission gained a new name and shape in March 1995. On 31 March 1995 the Security Council turned UNPROFOR's force there into UNPREDEP. The letters stand for United Nations Preventive Deployment Force. The Secretary-General's report of 22 March supplied the plan. The Council approved the arrangements he set out. The mission's job was to watch borders and deter trouble before it started.

The Council restated its support for Macedonia's independence and borders. It worried about events that could shake the young state's stability. The force would keep working with the European security mission in the country. Member states were asked to help it do its work. It was the United Nations' first preventive deployment.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Afghan groups had signed the Bonn Agreement the day before, and on 6 December 2001 the Council endorsed it. The deal set up temporary arrangements after the fall of the Taliban, to hold until permanent institutions could be rebuilt. An Interim Authority was due to take office on 22 December.

All Afghan groups are called on to carry out the agreement in full and work with the Interim Authority. The United Nations role in supporting the process is backed. Groups are also pressed to let aid reach people in need, protect aid workers, and respect human rights, while donors are asked to fund relief and rebuilding.

Iraq after the fall of its government in war is the subject of this framework text of 22 May 2003. Iraqis, the Council stresses, must govern themselves soon and control their own resources. The United Nations is cast in a vital role in relief, rebuilding, and restoring representative institutions.

Acting after the invasion, the Council lifted the trade and financial sanctions imposed since 1990, except for the arms embargo. It recognized the occupying powers' joint administration, called the Authority, and urged it to restore security and conditions for self-rule. A Development Fund for Iraq would hold oil revenues under world oversight, and a Special Representative would lead the United Nations work in the country.

Resolution 1583, adopted unanimously on 28 January 2005, extends the UN force in southern Lebanon for six more months. UNIFIL had patrolled since 1978, but its job had changed: the Secretary-General had confirmed that Israel completed its withdrawal from Lebanon in June 2000, as an earlier landmark resolution required. What remained was restoring calm along the Blue Line, where tension and violence persisted.

Answering Lebanon's request, the Council renewed the force's mandate for a further six-month period. It repeated that UNIFIL was an interim arrangement, not a permanent fixture. The text also echoed earlier calls on peacekeeper safety and on training personnel to prevent the spread of HIV/AIDS and other diseases in UN operations.

Resolution 1683, passed on 13 June 2006, opens two small gaps in Liberia's arms ban. The ban dated from 2003, when guns fed the war. By 2006 a new elected chief, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, led the state. Her guards and her new police and troops needed arms to train with. Yet the ban blocked even those. The Council said vetted state forces must take on more of the guard work at home.

The ban would not touch guns and rounds sent in the past for the guard unit's training. Those could stay in its hands for real use. Small lots for other new, vetted units could pass too. Each lot needed the bans team's prior nod, case by case.

Two rounds of talks between Morocco and the POLISARIO Front had been held since June 2007. They were the first face-to-face meetings in years. On 31 October 2007 MINURSO is renewed in Western Sahara, with backing for the new negotiations. Both sides' April proposals remained on the table.

The parties are called on to keep showing political will and to continue negotiating in good faith toward a mutually acceptable solution providing for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara. The mission's mandate is renewed alongside the talks. The Secretary-General is to report on the negotiations by 31 January 2008 and on the wider situation before the mandate period ends, and states are asked to fund family-visit measures.

Portugal's African territories return to the agenda on 11 December 1963, after talks failed. The Secretary-General had opened contact between Portugal and African states, but no agreement was reached on what self-determination means. That failure is regretted, as is Lisbon's refusal to follow the July resolution on the territories.

The meaning of self-determination from the General Assembly's 1960 declaration is restated: all peoples may freely choose their political status and pursue their own development. Portugal's non-compliance is deprecated, and all states are called on to honour the arms measures of the earlier text, which barred help for repression. The Secretary-General is to keep working on the question and report by 1 June 1964.

Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended for twelve months on 7 August 2009. Iraq's government was praised for work on democracy, the rule of law, and public order against terrorism and sectarian violence. Security gains were real but fragile, and they had to be locked in by political progress and national reconciliation.

The mandate set in 2007 and 2008 is kept. The mission's head is to advise Iraq on dialogue, elections, constitutional review, internal boundaries, and regional engagement, and to support aid, refugee returns, and human rights. The Secretary-General is to report every three months. Member states are again called on to give the mission the staff, funding, and security support its wider role requires.

Resolution 283, adopted on 29 July 1970 by thirteen votes to none with France and Britain abstaining, tightens the legal isolation of South Africa's rule in Namibia. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966 and the Council had since declared Pretoria's continued presence illegal. South Africa nonetheless kept enforcing its laws and courts in the territory as if nothing had changed.

The Council reaffirmed that everything South Africa did for or about Namibia after the mandate ended was illegal and invalid. It pointed to the arms embargo on South Africa agreed the week before as part of the pressure. And it pressed states to deal with Namibia only through the United Nations, denying Pretoria the recognition it craved.

Resolution 383, passed on 13 December 1975, keeps the UN force in Cyprus for six more months. A UN report of 8 December judged the force still key, to hold the truce and to aid the hunt for a peace pact. The best path, the report held, was talks between the two groups' men. Such talks could bear fruit if the men came primed and cleared to strike real deals on all the hard points of the Cyprus row.

Both sides backed the plan the report urged, and Cyprus agreed the force should stay past 15 December. Its term thus ran to June 1976. The text cites a November Assembly call as well. That call pressed for swift work on past pledges: troops out, and the displaced back home.

North Korea's tanks rolled south on 25 June 1950. The Council had ruled the attack a breach of the peace. It told the North to halt and pull back to the 38th parallel. The North did not obey. Word came that its troops fought on. Resolution 83 passed on 27 June 1950 by seven votes to one. Yugoslavia said no. The Soviet team was away, in boycott.

The Council urged all member states to help South Korea. Aid could flow in what shape the fight required. The aim was to beat back the attack. Peace and safety in the area had to be restored. Seoul's plea for swift help was cited in the text. Two states, Egypt and India, sat the vote out. The plea built the legal base for the US-led war under the UN flag.

Macedonia, newly independent from Yugoslavia, feared the wars around it might spill across its borders. The UN force already watching its frontier was given a new name and identity by Resolution 983, adopted unanimously on 31 March 1995, following the Secretary-General's report of 22 March.

The troops serving with the protection force in Macedonia became UNPREDEP, the UN Preventive Deployment Force, a mission notable for deploying before a conflict starts rather than after. Its mandate was set to run until 30 November 1995. The Council urged cooperation with European security observers and asked member states to support the force's needs.
vairo-de-fascino-latin-1583:
Leonardo Vairo, an Italian churchman, published De fascino, on fascination, in Latin in 1583. Three books study the evil eye, the belief that a mere look can sicken children, spoil milk, or wither love. Vairo treats its species and causes with scholastic care and many examples.

He asks how a gaze could harm at a distance, and what spirits or humors might carry the harm. Learned medicine and demonology meet in his pages. The treatise became the classic early-modern study of bewitchment by sight. Few superstitions have so long a history or so wide a map. Vairo gives the evil eye its fullest Renaissance hearing, argued like a case at law.
van-dale-de-oraculis-ethnicorum-latin-16:
Anton van Dale, a Dutch physician and scholar, published his two dissertations on the heathen oracles in Latin in 1683. He asks how long the oracles of Greece and Rome truly lasted, and who really spoke through them. His answers demolished the reigning theory that demons had talked from the shrines.

Van Dale shows priestcraft at work. The oracles, he argues, were human frauds kept up for gain, and they ended with politics, not with Christ's birth. Fontenelle later popularized the argument in French, and the Enlightenment ran with it. Van Dale's Latin remains the source. Few scholarly books have so quietly rearranged what educated Europe believed.
ward-dynamic-sociology-vol-1-1883:
Lester F Ward published Volume 1 of Dynamic Sociology in 1883. Ward, a government scientist in Washington, set out the first systematic sociology written in America. He wrote against the laissez-faire teaching that society should be left alone to sort itself out.

Volume 1 lays out his system: the forces that move society, drawn from nature, mind, and feeling. Ward sorted human striving into the wish for food, shelter, and wider life, and traced how those wants built civilization. He insisted that mind can steer social change once its laws are known. The volume is dense and ambitious, the work of a man building a science almost from the ground up.
ward-dynamic-sociology-vol-2-1883:
Volume 2 of Ward's Dynamic Sociology appeared in 1883, completing Lester F Ward's two-volume system. The first volume had set out social forces and their laws. The second turned theory into a program: applied social science aimed at reform.

Ward argued that education, spread to all, was the great lever for lifting society, and that government could act on knowledge rather than drift. He attacked the claim that meddling with markets and schools must do harm. His word for guided progress was sociocracy, rule informed by social science. The volume completes the first great American system of sociology and its bold claim that society can plan its own improvement.
warhafter-bericht-vom-philosophischen-at: A German title page heads this 1783 printing of Heinrich Khunrath's True Report of the Philosophical Athanor. The book treats the athanor's use and benefit. Khunrath is styled a doctor of medicine and a true lover of divine wisdom. The title page explains why the text appears again. The work is very rare, so it is reprinted from the third edition, printed at Magdeburg in 1615 at the author's own cost. A historical foreword on all his writings goes with it. Pages present here are that title page only.
zend-avesta-yashts-sbe23-1883:
James Darmesteter turned the hymns of the old faith of Persia into English in 1883. His book forms Part II of the Zend-Avesta in the Sacred Books of the East set. It holds the Sirozahs, the Yashts, and the Nyayish. These are prayers and hymns of Zoroastrian worship.

The Yashts praise beings called yazatas, among them Mithra and Anahita. Each hymn tells myths, lists gifts the god can grant, and names the lands where faith held firm. The Sirozahs name the divine beings who guard each day of the month. English readers met these hymns here first.
zola-ladies-paradise-1883:
Hutchinson issued The Ladies' Paradise at London in 1895, in Vizetelly's free English rendering. His opening essay warns readers not to fear the book's sound moral. He traces a drift toward joint ventures and near monopolies in modern trade.

A giant Paris shop, glittering and ruthless, swallows small traders street by street. Young Denise comes from the provinces to work inside that bright machine. She survives its harsh rivalries through goodness and grit. Owner Mouret, a genius of selling, remakes shopping itself around her. Love story and business epic in one, the novel stands as the first great tale of consumer capitalism.
